en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory."
Victorious is Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara and the delighter of Satyavatī’s heart,
from whose lotus-like mouth the world drinks the nectar of speech.
I take refuge in the divine Lord Īśāna, eternal, constant, and imperishable;
in Mahādeva, the Great-Souled One, the Lord of the entire world. ||1||
To Brahmā, the creator of the world, the omniscient, the unconquered, the lord of the past, the future, and the present, the true master. ||2||
He who possesses incomparable knowledge and detachment, as well as sovereignty and righteousness— these four perfections together belong to the Lord of the World.
He who perceives these entities as being eternally composed of both the existent and the non-existent— indeed,
they enter that Lord once again for the sake of the manifestation of activity.
The creator of the world, who knows the true nature of the world and understands reality, having resorted to yoga,
brought forth all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
Desirous of knowing the ancient narratives, I go for refuge to that unborn Lord, the architect of the universe, the lord of thought, and the witness of the world.
Having paid homage with a concentrated mind to Brahmā, Vāyu, and Mahendra, and to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the most excellent among the sages; ||7||
To his grandson, the highly illustrious Ṛṣi Jātūkarṇa, to the pure Vasiṣṭha, and to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana. ||8||
I shall fully proclaim this Purāṇa, spoken by Brahmā and equal to the Vedas,
beautifully adorned with traditional teachings endowed with dharma, artha, and nyāya.
While that best of kings, a kṣatriya of boundless power and incomparable splendor, was ruling this earth according to dharma. (1.1.10)
The sages were of refined soul, devoted to the vow of truth;
they were upright, free from passion, tranquil, self-controlled, and masters of their senses.
In Kurukṣetra,

the field of dharma, those who dwell in the Naimiṣa forest performed a long sacrificial session on the bank of the holy Dṛṣadvatī river with its pure shores, having been initiated according to the scriptures.
In order to see them, that highly intelligent Sūta, the best of those who know the Purāṇas,
caused the hair on the ears of his listeners to stand on end with his eloquent sayings;
because of that deed, he became famous in this world as Lomaharṣaṇa.
There was a wise disciple of the intelligent Veda-vyāsa—the treasure-house of austerity, sacred learning, and right conduct—who was renowned throughout the three worlds. ||14||
For in it the entire Veda is perfectly established, as well as the vast Bharata, which increases the Mahābhārata. ||15||
In this work are established discourses concerning dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; they are well-spoken and contain excellent expositions, like medicinal herbs upon the earth. (16)
Having approached those wise and eminent sages, who were experts in logic and well-versed in reason,
he drew near, paid his respects with palms joined,
and that intelligent man gratified those ṛṣis by prostrating himself before them.
And those powerful performers, together with the members of the assembly, being delighted,
offered him both musical accompaniment and worship in the prescribed manner.
Then, having seen that learned Lomaharṣaṇa was extremely confident, a desire to hear the Purāṇa arose within them. ||19||
At that sacrifice, the householder, who was proficient in all the sciences,
perceived their inner disposition through their gestures and urged the charioteer Sūta.

O Sūta, you have properly served the highly intelligent and venerable Vyāsa, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman; indeed, you have milked from his intellect the narrative based upon the Purāṇas.
O one of great intelligence, these foremost of sages, who are wise, have a desire to hear the Purāṇa; therefore, you ought to cause it to be heard by them.
For all these great-souled ones, gathered here from various lineages,
shall hear of their own respective ancestral traditions from the ancient teachers who discourse on Brahman.
Then, you should cause the sages, together with their sons, to hear [this] at this long sacrificial session;
for by us, as we were about to undergo initiation, he was previously remembered in our distress.
Thus was Sūta formerly exhorted by those very sages,
who were experts in the Purāṇas and devoted to the vow of truth, for the sake of the Purāṇa.
This is the inherent duty of a charioteer, as observed by the virtuous of old, toward the deities, the seers, and kings of immeasurable splendor. (26)
One must maintain the lineages and the sacred traditions of the great-souled ones,
which have been declared in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas by the exponents of Brahman.

Indeed, no qualification for the Vedas is seen for a Sūta. For it was at the sacrifice of the high-souled Pṛthu, son of Vena, while the Soma-pressing was underway, that the Sūta first came into being through a mixture of castes. ||28||

There, the oblation of Bṛhaspati was mixed with the oblation of Indra; he offered it to the god Indra, and from that, a Sūta was born. He was born there through negligence, and an expiation was required for the ritual acts.
When the preceptor’s oblation was mixed with and overwhelmed by the oblation of the disciple, a transformation of the colors arose through the upward and downward movement of the breaths. ||1.1.30||
And that which arose from the Kṣatriya as a lower birth for the Brāhmaṇa is therefore proclaimed to have equal duties, due to its similarity with the former [the Brāhmaṇa]. ||31||
For this is the middling duty of a Sūta: subsisting by the profession of a Kṣatriya;
the management of chariots, elephants, and horses is the lowest, as is the practice of medicine. (32)
Being thus questioned by you, who are exponents of the Veda, why should I not correctly declare that ancient dharma which is honored by the seers? (33)
The mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs became Vāsavī;
having been cursed by the Pitṛs, she was born in the womb of a fish.
From her was born the great yogi Vyāsa, the best among those who know the Vedas, whose birth had her as its cause, just as the fire-drill is the cause for the production of fire.
Having offered salutation to that Blessed One, Vyāsa, the creator.
To the ancient Puruṣa, the one who set in motion the words of Bhṛgu, to Viṣṇu, the all-powerful one who assumes the guise of a human form. ||36||
As soon as he was born, the Veda with its compendia approached him;
honoring dharma alone, he received it from Jātūkarṇya.
Having churned the churning-stick of his intellect, he brought forth from the ocean of sacred revelation that moon of the Mahābhārata which has been made manifest in the world. (38)
And having reached him, the tree of the Vedas became possessed of branches, just as a tree attains many branches upon reaching the qualities of soil, time, and moisture. (39)
Therefore, having heard this Purāṇa from that knower of Brahman, who is omniscient, honored in all the Vedas, and possessed of radiant splendor; || 1.1.40 ||
I shall fully proclaim this Purāṇa, which was formerly spoken by Mātariśvan when he was questioned by the high-souled sages of Naimiṣa.
Maheśvara is the supreme unmanifest, four-armed and four-faced;
he is inconceivable, immeasurable, self-existent, the cause, and the Lord.
It is certain that the unmanifest cause, which is eternal and consists of both being and non-being, creates everything from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa). ||43||
From that, there arose an incomparable golden egg;
and the egg was enveloped by water, and the water by fire.
Its sky is enveloped by wind;
that [wind] is enveloped by the *bhūtādi*; and the *mahat* is likewise enveloped by the unmanifest (*avyakta*). ||45||
Therefore, the manifestation of the Viśvedevas and the sages is described here; likewise, the appearance of the rivers and the mountains is praised in this work. (46)
There is a detailed description of all the Manvantaras and Kalpas;
the lineage of the Brahmins and Kshatriyas is proclaimed, and the birth of Brahmā is glorified. 47.
Therefore, the creative power in Brahman, the description of the creation of progeny, and the various states of Brahman, who is born from the unmanifest, are here proclaimed. 48.
The years of the kalpas, as well as the establishment of the world, the reclining of Hari, and likewise the lifting up of the earth; 49.
The layout of cities and other settlements according to the divisions of caste and stage of life; the arrangement of trees and houses; and the non-destruction of the perfected ones (siddhas). 1.1.50.
The extensive wandering along paths measuring many yojanas,
and the distribution of abodes in heaven for mortals who roam upon the earth.
The enumeration of trees, medicinal herbs, and creepers is proclaimed; likewise, the state of being a tree, a hell-being, or an insect for mortals is fully described. 52.
Two paths are proclaimed for the deities and the ṛṣis:
the creation and the non-creation of bodies such as those consisting of food and the rest. ||53||
First, the Purāṇa was remembered by Brahmā as the source of all scriptures;
immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths.
The limbs, the treatises on Dharma, as well as the vows and observances, and the origin of both animals and humans have been fully described. ||55||
Likewise, the etymological derivation and the acceptance of the Kalpa were proclaimed;
furthermore, the nine creations of Brahmā, preceded by his conscious intent, were declared. (56)
The other three, however, were preceded by intelligence; from them he fashioned the worlds, and from the limbs of Brahmā arose dharma and the rest.
Those twelve who are born again and again as progeny throughout the kalpa—
the interval between two kalpas and the junction (pratisandhi) that occurs between them have been declared.
And because Brahman was veiled by the quality of darkness (tamas), unrighteousness (adharma) came into being;
likewise, after that, Śatarūpā came into existence.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, as well as Prasūti, Ākūti,
and those others, are celebrated as being cleansed of all sin, upon whom the worlds are established.
After Ruci and Prajāpati, a pair was born from Ākūti;
likewise, from Prasūti, there arose the birth of Dakṣa’s daughters.
Furthermore, among the daughters of Dakṣa, beginning with Śraddhā, the creation of the high-souled Dharma is proclaimed; it is characterized by goodness (sāttvika) and results in happiness.
Likewise, the creation of unrighteousness (adharma) and violence is proclaimed as the tamasic and inauspicious aspect;
and the creation of progeny is proclaimed as the aspect of Maheśvara associated with truth.
Furthermore, the treasure-house of Yoga spoke of such a Nirāmaya Brahma to the twice-born who long for liberation.
The incarnation of Rudra, as well as his great majesty, the narrative concerning the three Vedas, and a most sublime dialogue [are told]. (65)
And where the hymn was proclaimed by Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa;
praised by those two, the Lord of Gods, the Blessed Śiva, was pleased. ||66||
Now, the manifestation of Rudra from the body of the high-souled Brahmā is proclaimed,
along with the reason why that great-minded one wept.
Just as the Self-born One obtained the eight names beginning with Rudra,
and how by them this triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, was pervaded.
Therein is the description of the creation of progeny by the sages beginning with Bhṛgu, and the proclamation of the lineages of the Brahman-sage Vasiṣṭha. (69)
The origin of Agni and of progeny was proclaimed in Svāhā;
immediately thereafter, that of the two classes of Pitṛs was proclaimed in Svadhā.
In connection with the lineage of his ancestors, the curse of Dakṣa upon Maheśvara, as well as that of the wise Bhṛgu and others, is narrated for the sake of truth. (71)
In this [chapter], the curse of Rudra upon Dakṣa of wondrous deeds, as well as the prevention of their enmity, is recounted in detail. (72)
Their respective appointments over the islands and regions were detailed, followed by a further recitation of the creation of Svāyambhuva.
The emission from the navel of the Great-Souled One has been described, as well as the enumeration of the islands together with their oceans and mountains. ||74||
[He knows] the years, the rivers, and all their various divisions, as well as the thousands of different islands and their internal subdivisions within the seven [continents]. 75.
The extent of the continent of Jambūdvīpa and the ocean, along with the mountains, is proclaimed in detail according to their measurement in yojanas.
Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, Meru, Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavat are celebrated as the mountain ranges that demarcate the regions. ||77||
The intermediate diameters, heights, lengths, and breadths of these [mountains], as well as those who dwell there, are described in yojanas. (78)
The regions, such as Bhārata and others, are situated along with rivers, mountains,
and living beings— both those that are mobile and those that are stationary.
The continents, beginning with Jambūdvīpa, are surrounded by seven oceans;
beyond that lies the watery region, which is celebrated as Lokāloka.
Within this egg are these worlds, the earth with its seven continents,
and the realms beginning with Bhūḥ, along with the primordial material elements.
And all that pertains to the measurement of the primary [element], as well as its measurement with its extensions, is proclaimed here in brief. (82)

The dimensions of the sun and the moon, as well as of the earth in its entirety, have been stated in yojanas by those who possess current knowledge. The meritorious assemblies of Mahendra and the other gods are situated upon the summit of the Mānasottara mountain. (83)
Beyond this, the movement toward heaven is described as being like a whirling firebrand;
now, the characteristics of the Nāgavīthī and Ajavīthī are proclaimed.
By means of the two sticks, the two lines, and the application of the mandalas, as well as the twilight of the Lokāloka mountain, the day, and the equinox; ||85||
The world-protectors (Lokapālas) who are celebrated as being situated in the four directions stand above;
the paths of the ancestors and the gods lie to the south and the north respectively. 86.
In the discourse concerning householders and renunciants, it is declared that by relying upon the qualities of passion (rajas) and purity (sattva),
the station of Viṣṇu is attained, wherein Dharma and the other [guṇas] are established.

The movement of the sun and the moon, as well as that of the planets and the luminaries, is proclaimed to be due to the power of Dhruva; likewise, the auspicious and inauspicious fortune of living beings [depends upon it]. 88.
The solar chariot was fashioned by Brahmā himself for a specific purpose;
it is by means of this that the Blessed One himself moves across the sky. 89.
That chariot was occupied by the gods, the Ādityas, as well as the ṛṣis,
Gandharvas, Apsarases, Grāmaṇīs, Sarpas, and Rākṣasas.
Likewise, the chariot of the moon, which consists of the essence of the waters, is described;
and the waxing and waning of the lunar orb are said to be caused by the sun.
The movement of the sun and other celestial bodies is proclaimed to originate from Dhruva alone;
and the Śiśumāra (the Aquarius constellation) is also mentioned, in whose tail Dhruva is situated.
All the stars in the form of constellations, together with the planets, are proclaimed there as the dwellings of the merit-performing gods. 93.
And within the thousand sunbeams, there is the emission of rain, cold, and heat;
furthermore, there is the differentiation of the rays according to their names, their functions, and their purposes. (94)
The dimensions and movements of the planets have been described in relation to their dependence on the sun;
and how Śambhu’s throat attained its blueness from consuming poison so rapidly. (95)
The dejection of the wielder of the trident (Śiva) was quickly dispelled by the grace of Brahmā;
being praised by the gods, Viṣṇu then offered praise to the god Maheśvara. 96.
The sacred narrative of the emergence of the Liṅga destroys all sins;
this is the wonderful transformation of Pradhāna from its universal form. 97.
The proclamation of the greatness of Purūravas, the son of Āyu, and the offering of libations to the two classes of ancestors with nectar. 98.
Thereafter, the lunar festivals (parvan) and the junctions of the festivals are proclaimed, as well as the attainment of the heavenly world by some and the descent to the lower realms by others;
and the great favor bestowed upon the two classes of ancestors through the śrāddha rite. ||99||
The measure of the number of ages is proclaimed for the Kṛta Yuga,
and in the Tretā Yuga, due to the decline [of dharma], the practice of agriculture and trade is set in motion.
The enumeration and the initiation of the social classes and the stages of life, as well as the establishment of the social classes and the stages of life according to dharma. ||101||
It also contains the commencement of the sacrifice and the dialogue that is celebrated there between the sages and Vasu, as well as the subsequent descent of Vasu to the lower regions. ||102||

The difficulty of answering questions is described, as is the praise of austerity, except for Manu Svāyambhuva; the conditions of the various ages (yugas) are also told in their entirety, with a brief account here of the Dvāpara and Kali ages. 103.
The dimensions of gods, animals, and humans in each successive age are proclaimed according to the power of that age, as are their girth, height, and lifespan. (104)
The instruction of the cultured and others is proclaimed, as well as their manifestation; and there is the glorification of the Veda and the mantras born from it. 105.
The measurement of the branches [of the Veda], the designation of the Vedavyāsa and others, the dissolution of the Manvantaras, and the re-manifestation at the end of the dissolution; ||106||
It is not possible to describe in detail [the lineage] of the gods, the sages, Manu, and the host of ancestors; thus it has been stated in brief. ||107||
The number of a Manvantara has been proclaimed according to human reckoning;
this indeed is the characteristic of all the Manvantaras. ||108||
The past and future are described by means of the present;
likewise, it is the same for the characteristic of the connection between the Manvantaras. ||109||
And regarding the past and future, it is declared in the Svāyambhuva period that the three Manvantaras and the knowledge of time are proclaimed.
The glorification of the gods and the lords of progeny during the Manvantaras,
and also the grandsons of Dakṣa, who were the sons of his beloved daughter.
They were begotten by Brahmā and others, as well as by the wise Dakṣa himself.
The Manus beginning with Sāvarṇi, who reside on Mount Meru, are celebrated; as well as the description of the creation of progeny by Dhruva and Uttānapāda. 112.
Pṛthu, the son of Vena, also initiated the milking of the earth;
he distinguished the vessels, the milks, and the lineages.
Furthermore, this Earth had already been milked by Brahmā and others in the past.
From the ten Pracetas, the sons of the Prajāpati Dakṣa,
the birth of the wise Soma was proclaimed through Māriṣā as a portion of himself.
His lordship over the past, the future, and the present is proclaimed, as well as his status among the great Indras;
he will become the Manu and others, surrounded by many traditional narratives.
The detailed account of the creation under Vaivasvata Manu is proclaimed; likewise,
the birth of Bhrigu and the other sages from the seed of Brahmā, while the Great God was bearing a body of Varuṇa at a sacrifice, is recounted.
When the creation of beings by Cākṣuṣa Manu had ceased during the auspicious interval of Vaivasvata,
the creation of Dakṣa is now being proclaimed through meditation.
Nārada, who speaks pleasing words, [addressed] the mighty sons of Dakṣa.
The son of Brahmā brought about his own destruction by means of a curse.
Then Dakṣa begot daughters, renowned as the Vīriṇīs;
and the creation of Dharma and of the wise Kaśyapa is now proclaimed.
Henceforth, the oneness, the distinctness, and the specific differentiation of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Bhava are proclaimed.
And because of his lordship, just as the gods were cursed by Svayambhū,
Marutprasāda was born from the Maruts and Diti, having originated from portions of the gods.
Now, the seven groups of seven Maruts are proclaimed;
their divinity arose by the word of the Pitṛs, and their abode is the wind-sphere (vāyuskandha).
The origins of the Daityas, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas,
as well as all Bhūtas, Piśācas, animals, birds, and plants, and the origins of the Apsarases, are recounted in great detail. 123.
The birth of the elephant Airāvata brought about by his union with the ocean, as well as the origin of Vainateya and his consecration. 124.
The detailed account of the Bhṛgus has been told, as well as that of the Aṅgirases,
and likewise of Kaśyapa, Pulastya, and the high-souled Atri.
Then follows the detailed account of the progeny of the sage Parāśara, as well as the subsequent origin of the gods and the ṛṣis. 126.
Three daughters are celebrated, in whom the worlds are established;
therein is described the lineage of the fathers and grandsons, as well as the birth of the gods.
The detailed account of the five great-souled sons of the Blessed One has been told;
thereafter, the detailed account of Ilā and of Āditya was spoken.
The deeds of Vikukṣi and the destruction of Dhundhu have been told; the lineage beginning with Ikṣvāku, ending with Bṛhadbala, has been briefly proclaimed.
The detailed account of the kings beginning with Nimi and ending with the lineage of Jahnu,
as well as that of King Yayāti, is proclaimed.
The summary of the Yadu lineage and the detailed account of Haihaya have been told, as well as the subsequent expansion of the lineage following Kroṣṭu. ||131||
The greatness of Jyāmagha and the creation of progeny are glorified, as well as those of Devāvṛdha, Arka, and the high-souled Vṛṣṭi. ||132||
The lineage of Atrimitra, the divine accusation against Viṣṇu, and then the acquisition by Vivasvat of the wise jewel-gem. 133.
The creation of progeny won through battle is celebrated for that high-souled one;
and the illustrious lineage of the royal sage Devamīḍhuṣa is also recounted.
Furthermore, the birth and the life of the Great-souled One were told, as well as the absolute wickedness of Kaṃsa and his origin. ||135||
The birth of Viṣṇu, the Lord of Creatures, as Vāsudeva from Devakī;
and following that, a detailed description of the creation of beings by Viṣṇu. ||136||
Long ago, when the war between the gods and the asuras had broken out and Viṣṇu had slain a woman,
he incurred a curse from Bhṛgu for protecting Śakra from death;
Bhṛgu then raised up the divine mother of Śukra.
Twelve tens of thousands of battles between the gods and the asuras, beginning with the Man-lion incarnation (Nārasiṃha), which resulted in the destruction of lives, are celebrated. ||138||
The propitiation of Sthāṇu by Śukra was performed with steadfast austerity;
there, Śarva was praised by him who was enticed by the granting of a boon.
Immediately thereafter, the activities of the gods and asuras were described. 139.
While the high-souled Śukra was engaged with Jayantī, the wise Bṛhaspati, who possessed great splendor, deluded the Asuras by assuming the form of Śukra; then Śukra cursed them. ||1.1.140||

And it has been told that the majesty of Viṣṇu and the proclamation of Viṣṇu’s births and so forth [are contained herein]. Turvasu, the grandson of Śukra through Devayānī, was born of Yadu; Anu, Druhyu, and Pūru were likewise the sons of Yayāti, O King. (141)
In this regard, those high-souled descendants of the lineage, the best among kings, are celebrated for their long-lasting fame and their abundant wealth and splendor. (142)
And [the account] of the brahmin-sage Kuśika’s complete recourse to dharma,
wherein Surabhi here removed the curse of Bṛhaspati.
The glorification of the lineage of Jahnu, the proclamation of Śantanu’s heroic deeds, and likewise the proclamation of the destruction of future kings. (144)
There is a description of the seven future Manus, and a description of the dissolution at the end of the Kali Yuga of Bhauma, when it has been exhausted. (145)
The characteristics of the two parārdhas are proclaimed, as well as the determination of the measurement of Brahmā’s world in terms of yojanas. (146)
The dissolution of all beings is declared to be threefold: it is remembered as occasional (naimittika), natural (prākṛtika), and absolute (ātyantika). ||147||
Drought, the terrible fire of universal destruction from the sun,
the clouds, the single vast ocean, and likewise night, belong to the Great Soul.
The definition of number has been indicated, followed by that of the Brāhma [kalpa] in particular;
then there is a detailed description of the seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, and here the hells of evildoers, such as Raurava and others, are proclaimed. 149.
Above the world of Brahmā, however, is the supreme abode of Śiva,
where all beings go to their dissolution at the time of universal destruction.
The determination of the transformation of all beings, and the description of the total dissolution during the re-absorption of Brahmā. 151.
Therefore, the eightfold nature of the vital breath (prāṇa) has been declared, as well as its eightfold group;
and its movement upwards and downwards is said to be due to its reliance upon merit and demerit.
In every eon, there is the destruction even of the great beings;
having reckoned these sufferings, one realizes the impermanence even of Brahmā.
The wickedness of enjoyments, the determination of their transformation, the rarity of liberation, and the perception of defects through detachment. ||154||
Having abandoned both the manifest and the unmanifest, the pure being (sattva) is established in Brahman; through the vision of non-duality, it then returns from that state.
Then, transcending the threefold affliction, formless, beyond description, and stainless, bliss is declared to be Brahman; such a one fears nothing whatsoever. (156)
Furthermore, the creation of another Brahmā is recounted as before, and the lineage of the sages, which destroys all sins, is also proclaimed. (157)
Thus has the summary of duties been described for the Purāṇa;
for herein are recounted all the transformations of dissolution in the world, as well as the activities of beings and the fruits of their renunciations. (158)
The manifestation of Vasiṣṭha, likewise the birth of Śakti, and his subjugation by Viśvāmitra at the hands of Saudāsa. 159.
The birth of Parāśara and how the Lord became invisible, as well as how the sage Vyāsa was born from the daughter of the Pitṛs—[all this has been told]. (1.1.160)
Likewise, the birth of Śuka along with his wise son, and how Viśvāmitra harbored hatred toward Parāśara. 161.

O Brahmin, the fire maintained by Vasiṣṭha was employed by the powerful and wise Skanda, who desired the welfare of Viśvāmitra, according to divine ordinance for the sake of ensuring his progeny while intending to destroy Viśvāmitra. (162)
Just as the Lord Vyasa divided the single Veda, which consists of four quarters, into four parts by means of his own intellect,
so too were further divisions of the branches (śākhā) made by his disciples and grand-disciples. ||163||
When questioned by the Self-Existent One regarding practices and the sixfold qualities,
those sages, seekers of dharma, were in turn questioned by him.
Desiring a meritorious region, they were [instructed] by the Lord who seeks their welfare.
This wheel, which has a beautiful hub, is called of divine form, possesses true limbs, and has auspicious movement;
it is incomparable. Following it as it revolves without weariness, go with self-restraint, and then you shall attain that which is beneficial. 165.
"Wherever the rim of the turning wheel of Dharma breaks,
that place should be considered meritorious," the Lord said at that time.
Having spoken thus to the sages, Brahmā indeed vanished once more.

The sages then performed the Gaṅgāgarbhasamāhāra and the Naimiṣeya rites; they also sacrificed with a long sacrificial session (sattra) at Naimiṣa. Furthermore, when Śaradvat had died, his restoration to life was likewise accomplished.
The sages of Naimiṣa, with supreme faith,
having made this entire earth boundless,
brought forth the king and honored him with hospitable rites according to the prescribed rules and the scriptures. ||168||
Then, while the king was thus gratified and had been duly honored with hospitality,
the cruel Asura Svarbhānu, having become invisible, carried him away.
And they pursued the slain king, just as they had done before with Aida;
for they saw him accompanied by a Gandharva, a resident of the village of Kalapa.
Furthermore, his assembly was like that of the great seers at a sacrifice,
having seen all the golden sacrificial implements belonging to those high-souled ones.
At that time, during the twelve-year sacrificial session of the Naimiṣeya sages,
Aiḍa was indeed restrained by them while he was disputing.
Having begotten a son for his lineage at the edge of the forest according to the span of his life,
and having completed that sacrificial session, he attends upon the remainder of his lifespan.
O best of the twice-born, all this has been explained exactly as it occurred;
herein lies the supreme and unsurpassed system of the world for the sages. 174.
That which was formerly proclaimed by Brahmā—the ancient and supreme knowledge—and the incarnation of Rudra for the sake of bestowing grace upon the twice-born. ||175||
Likewise, the Pāśupata yogas, the glorification of the sacred sites, and the reason for the god's blue-throatedness (nīlakaṇṭhatva) arising from the emergence of the Liṅga. ||176||
Wherein it is narrated by Vāyu, the expounder of Brahman, for the sake of the brāhmaṇas—[a narrative] that is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, meritorious, and a destroyer of sins;
[and which brings merit through] its recitation, hearing, and especially its retention. (177)
For it is by this sequence that this Purāṇa is proclaimed;
thus, even a great subject is easily understood in brief.
Therefore, having first indicated a certain point, I shall later explain it in detail. (178)
Whoever, having conquered their senses, correctly studies this first quarter-verse, has thereby studied that entire Purāṇa; of this there is no doubt. (179)
If a twice-born man should know the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and the Upaniṣads, yet he does not know the Purāṇa, he would not truly be a learned man. ||1.1.180||
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will deceive me. (181)
By practicing this chapter, which was spoken directly by the Self-Existent One, one shall be liberated upon encountering calamity and attain one's desired goal. 182.
Since this existed before and was not created [by anyone], it is therefore remembered as "Purāṇa.
He who knows its etymology is liberated from all sins. ||183||
Nārāyaṇa exists pervading and setting in motion this entire universe;
yet even he, the creator of the world, has Maheśvara as his creator. ||184||
Therefore, listen to this summary: Maheśvara is the entirety of this Purāṇa;
at the time of creation he brings forth all creations, and at the time of dissolution he withdraws them once again. (185)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Table of Contents," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu. 1.1.
Śuka said:
Those ṛṣis, whose wealth was their asceticism, replied again to the charioteer:
"Where did the sacrificial session of those performers of wonderful deeds take place? (1)
And for how long did that time last, and how did it proceed? And how did the Destroyer (Vāyu) relate that ancient account to them? ||2||
"Tell us this in detail, for our curiosity is great.
Thus urged, the Sūta replied with these auspicious words: ||3||
Listen to where those wise ones performed that supreme sacrificial session (sattra), for how long a time it lasted, and how it proceeded. ||4||
For there, in ancient times, the creators of the universe, desiring to emit the entire world,
performed a holy sacrificial session for a thousand years.

In that sacrificial session of the high-souled ones, where austerity was the householder and Brahmā himself became the Brahman priest; where the wise and highly effulgent Mṛtyu performed the office of the Śamitṛ, and where Ilā served as the wife.
The wise gods performed sacrifices there for a thousand years,
at the spot where the rim of the revolving Wheel of Dharma was shattered;
because of that deed, the place became renowned as Naimiṣa, honored by the sages.
Where that meritorious Gomatī flows, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, there Rohiṇī gave birth; from her, Saumya was born as a son. ||8||
Śakti was born as the eldest son of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha;
there, Arundhatī gave birth to one hundred sons of supreme splendor.
There King Kalmāṣapāda was cursed by Śakti,
and there the enmity between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha arose.
It was at Adṛśyantī that the sage Parāśara was born, and it was upon his birth that the humiliation of Vasiṣṭha occurred. ||11||
There, in Naimiṣa, those exponents of the Veda performed a sacrificial session;
because they performed the sacrifice in Naimiṣa, they are known as the Naimiṣeyas.
That sacrifice of those wise ones lasted for twelve years while the valiant Purūravas was ruling the earth.
Purūravas, consuming the eighteen islands of the ocean, was not at all satisfied; for we have heard that it was due to his greed for jewels. 14.
And he whom Urvaśī, impelled by Devahūti, desired—he performed that sacrificial session, having been united with celestial nymphs. (15)
While that lord of men was presiding over the sacrifice, the sages of Naimiṣa performed the rite;
for the placenta of that child of blazing splendor whom Gaṅgā had borne from Agni,
having been cast upon a mountain, turned into gold.
Then the divine Viśvakarman himself, bringing joy to the creator of the worlds, constructed a golden sacrificial enclosure for those great-souled ones. ||17||
Then, while Bṛhaspati was there among those of immeasurable splendor,
Purūravas, the son of Ilā, arrived at that place while wandering on a hunt.
Seeing that great wonder, the golden sacrificial enclosure,
his discernment destroyed by greed, he proceeded to seize it.
Then the sages of Naimiṣa became exceedingly enraged at that king;
filled with wrath, those wise men struck him with kusha-grass darts as if they were thunderbolts.
Then, at the end of the night, the sages, impelled by destiny, approached the king.
Crushed by the Kuśa-vajras, that king abandoned his body;
thereafter, they made his son, the offspring of Urvaśī, the king upon the earth.
That high-souled king whom they call the father of Nahuṣa, that lord of the earth who is devoted to righteousness, dwells among them;
in him, that best of men, resides an exceedingly intense lifespan and health. (22)
And having consoled the king, those best among the knowers of Brahman then began to perform the sacrificial session (satra) according to rule for the sake of the prosperity of Dharma.
That sacrificial session of those high-souled ones was full of many wonders,
like that of the creators of the universe in ancient times when they desired to bring forth the world.
It was frequented by the Vaikhānasas, his dear friends the Vālakhilyas, the Marīcikas,
and other sages who possessed the splendor of the sun and fire.
It was graced by the ancestors, gods, apsarases, siddhas, gandharvas, serpents,
and cāraṇas with auspicious offerings, just like the assembly hall of Indra.

They honored the gods with hymns, sacrificial offerings, and oblations; the ancestors with ancestral rites; and the Gandharvas and others according to their respective classes and in accordance with the prescribed rules.
Then, desiring to propitiate him, the Gandharvas sang Sāman hymns during the intervals between the ritual acts, and the hosts of Apsarases danced. ||28||
The sages, who were knowers of the true nature of mantras and other sacred sciences, spoke auspicious words consisting of variegated syllables and phrases, and they conversed with one another.
And some, using cavilous speech, struck down their opponents—learned sages there who were experts in the principles of Sāṅkhya and in logic. (1.2.30)
There, neither the brahmarākṣasas wrought any evil,
nor did the daityas who destroy sacrifices, nor the asuras who steal sacrifices, cause any harm.
Neither expiation nor any ill-performed rite occurred there;
the ritual was perfectly executed through the application of power, wisdom, and action. ||32||
Thus the wise sages, Bhṛgu and the others, performed the sacrificial session for twelve years; those steadfast seers individually performed all the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices,
proceeding through the Pṛṣṭha rites, with sacrificial fees of ten thousand.
When their sacrifice was completed, they all questioned Vāyu, the great lord of immeasurable soul, saying, "O twice-born ones, that which I have been urged by you regarding the sake of our lineage"—
and that powerful lord spoke to them.
The disciple of the Self-Existent Lord is a deity who perceives everything directly and has mastery over all things; he is endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers, beginning with *aṇiman*.
He who supports all the worlds through the qualities of animal births and so forth,
and who eternally floats upon the seven constituent elements (skandhas) and the rest, is superior even to a yojana.
He in whom the seven groups of elements are established and fixed within their respective domains,
who, being of great strength, arranges the arrays of the three elements,
and who bestows upon this embodied being the supreme bliss of splendor.
The five functions, beginning with prāṇa, along with the functions of the organs, being impelled, effect the maintenance of the bodies. (38)
For the quality of sound has space as its source and is endowed with touch;
yet this entity is also described by the wise as having fire as its primary nature.
Therein was the Lord Abhimānin and Vāyu, whose nature is supreme action;
he is celebrated as Vātāraṇi, a master of the science of sound.
Like one gladdening all the sages with gentle speech,
he who was learned in the Purāṇas addressed those well-disposed men with words grounded in the Purāṇas.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Twelve-Year Sacrificial Session," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vyāsa. 1.2.
Sūta said:

Salutations to Maheśvara, whose actions possess supreme heroism; to the bull among gods, of immeasurable wisdom and splendor; to him who possesses the radiance of a thousand suns and fires; salutations to the one who effects the creation and destruction of the three worlds. 1.
[He saw] the Prajāpatis honored by the worlds, as well as the great lords such as Svayambhū and Rudra;
Bhṛgu, Marīci, Parameṣṭhin, Manu, Rajas, Tamas, Dharma, and also Kaśyapa.
Having bowed his head with devotion to Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Atri, Pulastya, Kardama, Ruci, Vivasvat, Kratu, as well as the sage Aṅgiras, Prajāpati, and Pulaha; ||3||
In that very same way, Cukrodhana ruled over twenty-one generations who were dedicated to the task of increasing their subjects;
likewise, he governed those of ancient times, others of the future, and other eternal ones, along with their respective hosts, all established in their positions.
In the same way, having bowed to other sages who are adorned with fortitude, led by Bṛhaspati and Uśanas,
as well as to the ṛṣis whose conduct is purified by austerity and who are endowed with compassion, I shall proclaim [this work] which destroys the sins of the Kali age.
O Lord of the Gods, this unsurpassed creation of Prajāpati is adorned by hosts of divine sages;
it is auspicious, incomparable, faultless, dear to the ṛṣis, and even more radiant than the blazing splendors of the lords of progeny.
[He saw] that supreme [splendor] of those who maintain austerity, which belongs to the time of the day of Brahmā and so forth, which has manifested abundant glory through manly prowess,
which is spread throughout the Śruti and Smṛti, which is proclaimed as the highest of the high, and which is celebrated by the Wind-god (Anila).

In which [work] the first activity is composed with fixed compound constructions according to the facts, expressed in a manner that delights the mind, and is both fundamental and brought about by the Lord. (8)
That which is known as the immeasurable cause, Brahman, Pradhāna, Prakṛti, and Prasūti;
the Self, the cave, the womb, and also the eye, the field, and likewise the immortal and the imperishable. (9)
That Śukra is austerity, the essence, and exceedingly luminous; it is the eternal second Puruṣa, joined with that immeasurable Puruṣa, the self-existent Grandfather of the worlds.

Due to its generative nature, the predominance of the quality of passion (rajas), its conjunction with Time, and its adherence to the injunctions of the Vedas, Primordial Matter (prakṛti) gave birth, by the mere will of the Great Lord, to eight fixed transformations associated with the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), which serve as the causes for the continuity and expansion of the world. ||11||
Of the gods, asuras, mountains, trees, and oceans; of men, lords of creatures, sages, ancestors, and the twice-born;
of piśācas, yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas; and of stars, planets, the sun, constellations, and night-stalkers. ||12||
Of the months, seasons, years, nights, and days; of the conjunctions of direction and time, the yugas, and the solstices;
and also of the forest trees, medicinal herbs, creepers, aquatic creatures, apsarases, and animals—(he knows the origin). ||13||
Whether it be the lightning, the clouds, or the birds; that which moves subtly on earth, that which dwells in the sky;
whatever is stationary, or wherever anything exists—of all that, there is both a course and a division. (14)
The Vedas—the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman hymns—as well as the Soma sacrifice, their means of subsistence, and whatever else is desired, all belong to that very god Prajāpati. (15)

The origin and progeny of these meritorious ones, who are honored by the three worlds, have been described prior to this Vaivasvata Manu; by the offspring of these lords of the gods, celestial sages, and leaders of men, the three worlds have been filled and adorned from above. (16)

Furthermore, there is the rebirth of Dakṣa due to the curse of Rudra; his dwelling on earth in the world of men, as well as the residence of Bhava on earth by way of a vow, and here, Dakṣa’s receipt of a counter-curse. ||17||

The revolutions of the Manvantaras, the manifestation and differentiation within the Yugas, the state of being a Rishi, the increase of the Vedic seers, and how these occur at the beginnings of the Yugas—all that is here. (18)
O ignorant one, those Vyāsas who propagate the Vedas during the Dvāpara ages have been described by me in succession;
here also [are given] the calculation of the Kalpa, the calculation of the universe, and the calculation of a day of Brahmā. (19)

By means of reasoning, one may also establish the existence of those living beings who are born from eggs, from sprouts, from sweat, or from a womb, as well as those of virtuous nature dwelling in heaven, or those who have gone to the places of torment. (1.3.20)
The absolute, the natural, and that which is occasional—these are the causes of dissolution;
therein bondage and liberation are specifically explained, as well as the supreme course of worldly existence.

Regarding these causes in their states of primordial nature, both that which is their stability and that which is their further evolution— listen as it is being told exactly as it is, having been fully disclosed by me through the application of scripture and reasoning, my own intellectual effort, and my wisdom and fortitude, to you, the brahmins and sages. ||22||
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Section on Creation," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Then, having heard that, all the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest spoke in reply to Sūta with eyes agitated by emotion.
"You are indeed well-versed in the genealogies and have direct perception through Vyāsa;
therefore, describe the entire world-system of that realm."
We desire to know each and every one of those who belong to their respective lineages,
as well as that diverse creation of Prajāpati by the ancient seers.
Being questioned by them repeatedly, that great-souled and most excellent Lomaharṣaṇa recounted [the matter] in detail and in proper sequence.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
And this divine story, gentle, destructive of sin, wonderful, full of many meanings, and consistent with the Vedas, was asked and was being narrated by me. ||5||
Whoever should constantly uphold this, or listen to it repeatedly, or indeed cause it to be heard by Brahmins and especially by ascetics; ||6||
Pure and self-disciplined on the sacred festival days (parvan), whether at holy fords or shrines, one attains a long life through the recitation of the Purāṇas;
having ensured the continuity of his own lineage, he is glorified in the heavenly world. ||7||
Listen as I proclaim the detailed accounts of them all, according to the words and according to what has been heard, which increase the fame of everyone. ||8||
The recitation of the names of all those of steadfast fame who have performed meritorious deeds brings wealth, renown, the destruction of enemies, and leads to heaven while increasing one's lifespan.
Cosmic creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manus, and the history of the dynasties—thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics. (1.4.10)
Indeed, that Purāṇa which is more ancient than the Kalpas, pure and eternally fixed among the pure, I shall proclaim; it is the Māruta, equal to the Veda. 11.
Awakening, dissolution, maintenance, and indeed origination—this first chapter, concerning the process [of manifestation], comprises the selection of the subject matter to be described. (12)
The introduction, the connection, and the conclusion—this [work] is righteous, conducive to fame and long life, and the destroyer of all sins. (13)
Thus, these four feet have been briefly proclaimed by me;
I shall, however, explain them again in detail according to their sequence. (14)

Having paid homage to that self-existent Brahmā, the golden-germed (Hiraṇyagarbha), the Puruṣa, the Lord, the final, the primordial, the distinguished, the soul of all creatures, and the sustainer of the worlds; ||15||
Beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa), characterized by diversity and possessing their own defining marks,
consisting of five means of knowledge and six objects of perception, and presided over by the Puruṣa—
without doubt, I shall proclaim this unsurpassed creation of the elements. 16.
That which is the unmanifest cause, eternal, and consisting of both being and non-being—what the seekers of truth call Pradhāna and Prakṛti. ||17||
Devoid of smell, color, and taste, and free from sound and touch;
unborn, stable, imperishable, eternal, and established in its own self. ||18||
The primordial source of the world, the great being, the supreme and eternal Brahman, indeed became the unmanifest body of all beings. 19.
Without beginning or end, unborn, subtle, composed of the three qualities, the source and imperishable, inconceivable and unknowable, Brahman existed in the beginning. 1.4.20.
By his own self, all this was pervaded as consisting of darkness;
for at that time, while the equilibrium of the qualities prevailed, it existed in the state of the quality of darkness.
At the time of the primary evolution, when presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
the Great One (mahat) indeed manifested, being designated as such due to its state as a subordinate quality.
Then, enveloped by that which is subtle, great, and unmanifest, the Great Principle (Mahat) arises first, characterized by the predominance of Sattva; it is the illuminator of pure Sattva alone.
The Mind (Manas) is to be understood as being the Great Principle, and the Great Principle is traditionally held to be the cause of the Mind. ||23||

Arising from the mere *liṅga* (subtle body) and presided over by the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), Mahat— impelled by the desire to create— brings about the manifestation of the forms of dharma and the other qualities, which are the causes for the true nature of the world. ||24||

The wise declare that the mind (manas), the great one (mahat), the intellect (mati), Brahmā, the city (pūr), the awakened consciousness (buddhi), renown (khyāti), the Lord (īśvara), wisdom (prajñā), thought (citi), memory (smṛti), pure awareness (saṃvit), and the triple fortress (vipura) are all one. ||25||
Because the all-pervading Lord perceives the activity and the fruit of all beings,
even as they increase in subtlety, it is for that reason called "manas" (the mind).
Because he is the first-born among the principles (tattvas) and is "great" (mahān) in terms of magnitude compared to all other qualities, he is therefore remembered as Mahat.
The person (puruṣa) maintains pride, conceives of division, and even considers [himself as an agent]; because of his connection with experience, he is therefore known as "thought" (mati). ||28||
Because he causes all entities to grow and because he is the support for them like water, Brahmā is so designated by virtue of his causing entities to expand. (29)
And because, having filled all bodies with its favors, it makes the states of the principles constant, it is therefore called "Pūrī" (the Filler). 1.4.30.
In this context, the person perceives all things as beneficial or harmful;
and because it causes one to perceive, it is therefore defined as "intellect" (buddhi). ||31||
Since manifestation and individual experience proceed from it, and since experience is grounded in knowledge, it is therefore remembered as "manifestation" (khyāti). ||32||
Or it is manifested through its qualities, such as names and so forth, in manifold ways;
therefore, the designation for that Great One (mahat) is called "manifestation" (khyāti). ||33||
The Great-Souled One directly perceives everything, and for that reason he is the Lord;
from him the planets were born, and by virtue of that wisdom, he is called Prajāpati.
Because it accumulates forms such as knowledge and the like, as well as the fruits of sacrificial acts, for the sake of experience, it is therefore called *cit* (the accumulator). ||35||
It remembers all actions—those of the present, those of the past, and likewise those of the future; therefore, it is called *smṛti* (memory). ||36||
And one attains complete knowledge; therefore it is called "māhātmya" (greatness). Because of that knowing and the act of knowing, it is designated as "saṃvit" (consciousness). ||37||
He exists in everything, and everything exists in Him;
therefore, He is called "Consciousness" (saṃvit) by those who are truly wise. ||38||
The Blessed One, the repository of knowledge, has declared that from knowledge comes knowledge;
and because of the dissolution of dualities, it is called "Vipura" by the wise. (39)
Because he is the lord of all worlds, he is necessarily the Īśvara;
because of his vastness, he is remembered as Brahmā, and because he has come into being, he is called Bhava.
Because of his knowledge of the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and because of their oneness, who is he remembered as being?
Because he dwells within the city (puri), he is called the Person (puruṣa).
Because he is unproduced and because he is primordial, he is called the Self-existent (svayambhū). ||41||
Thus has the primordial, unsurpassed reality been explained by those who know the nature of reality and contemplate true existence, using synonymous terms. 42.
Impelled by the desire to create, the Great One undergoes transformation into the creation;
his two functions are traditionally known as volition (saṅkalpa) and determination (adhyavasāya). ||43||
And forms such as dharma and the rest are the causes for understanding the true nature of the world;
that [nature] should be known as consisting of the three qualities: sattva, rajas, and tamas.
From the triple-guṇa principle, when rajas predominates, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) arose;
enveloped by the Great Principle (mahat), that creation is indeed a transformation of the "origin of the elements" (bhūtādi).

And from that *ahaṅkāra* in which *tamas* predominates, there arose the creation of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the gross elements (*bhūta*); it is this *ahaṅkāra*, known as *bhūtādi*, that is characterized by *tamas*. (46)
Space is hollow; therefore, it is characterized by sound in its predominant state.
Furthermore, the source of the elements (bhūtādi) then envelops space, which consists of sound alone.
That [Ahaṃkāra] indeed created space as the subtle element of sound alone;
but the Bhūtādi (the ego-sense of the elements), undergoing transformation, created the subtle element of sound alone.
The powerful wind is born; it is indeed considered to have touch as its quality.
Space, which consists of sound alone, then enveloped the subtle element of touch.
Those waters, consisting of the subtle element of taste, enveloped the subtle element of form;
then the waters, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of smell.
From that, the aggregate (saṅghāta) is born; therefore, fragrance is known as its quality.
That water, consisting of the subtle element of taste, then enveloped the subtle element of fragrance.
Because each [element] consists only of that [specific quality], it is known as a "tanmātra" (merely-that).

Because they denote the non-specific, they are therefore known as "aviśeṣas" (non-specific). Furthermore, because they are neither tranquil, nor terrible, nor deluded, they are again called "aviśeṣas. (52)
This creation of the gross elements and the subtle elements (tanmātras) should be understood as arising from one another;
however, from the *vaikārika* ego, which is characterized by the predominance of *sattva*, that *vaikārika* creation proceeds simultaneously. (53)
There are exactly five sense organs and five organs of action;
these ten organs are the effectors, the deities born of *vaikārika* [sattva].
The eleventh among them is the mind (*manas*), which is also traditionally held to be a deity born of *vaikārika*.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth— these,
joined with the intellect, will be described as being for the purpose of perceiving sound and the other objects.
The feet, the anus, the generative organ, the hands, and speech shall be the tenth; their functions are locomotion, excretion, pleasure, manual skill, and speaking. (56)
Space enters into sound alone and touch alone;
then wind, consisting of two qualities, came into being as sound and touch. (57)
In the same way, sound and both qualities of touch and form enter it;
thereafter, fire arises, possessing the three qualities and endowed with sound, touch, and form.
And that which possesses sound, touch, and form entered into taste alone;
therefore, water should be known as having four qualities and being essentially composed of taste. ||59||
Among those [elements] possessing sound, touch, and form, smell entered them.
United with mere smell, they gather this earth;
therefore, earth is seen among the gross elements as possessing five qualities. ||1.4.60||
They are known as the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded because of their specific distinctions;
through mutual interpenetration, they support one another.
Everything within the earth is intensely hot and enveloped by the Lokāloka mountain;
the specific qualities are those perceivable by the senses, and they are so designated because of their fixed nature.
Each subsequent one acquires the qualities of each preceding one;
whatever the extent and nature of those [qualities], it is recorded as possessing that many and those very qualities.

Having perceived a pure fragrance, some, due to a lack of skill, might think it belongs to the earth alone; yet they should know it to belong to both the earth and the wind, because of their mutual dependence.
These seven of great prowess, though distinct and separate,
were unable to create progeny without coming together as a whole; yet,
having come together, those high-souled ones, by resorting to one another's wombs, [accomplished their task].
And because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of the Unmanifest,
those principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the Egg.
Arising simultaneously like a bubble upon water,
that vast egg and the water within it were produced from the specific elements; at that time, the body and the organs of Brahmā were fully perfected therein.
When the primordial egg has awakened, he who is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is designated as Brahman;
he is indeed the first embodied being, and he is called the Puruṣa.
And Brahmā, the first creator of beings, existed at the beginning;
that four-faced Hiraṇyagarbha appeared as the foremost in this world. In creation and in every subsequent re-creation, he is the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), designated as Brahman.
Together with the instruments of action they are created, and in the state of withdrawal they are abandoned; again, they assume bodies during the junctions of non-concentration. (1.4.70)
The golden Mount Meru is the amnion of that Great Soul;
the oceans are the fetal fluid, and the mountains are his bones, beginning with old age.
Within that egg, indeed, these seven worlds were contained,
as was this earth with its seven continents and seven oceans.
Within him are these worlds with their vast mountains and thousands of rivers; within him is this entire universe.
The moon and the sun, together with the stars and the planets, along with the wind, and whatever exists in that egg— including the Lokāloka mountain— are all contained therein.
The egg is surrounded on the outside by water ten times its size;
indeed, that water is itself surrounded on the outside by fire ten times its size.
Fire itself, possessing ten times its own quality, is surrounded on the outside by wind;
and wind, possessing ten times its own quality, is surrounded on the outside by space. ||76||

The wind is enveloped by space, and space is enveloped by the source of the elements (bhūtādi); the source of the elements is also enveloped by the Great Principle (mahat), and the Great Principle is enveloped by the Unmanifest (avyakta). By these seven primordial coverings, the cosmic egg (aṇḍa) is enveloped.
Enveloping one another within these, the eight primary natures remain;
having existed during the time of manifestation, they devour one another.
In this way, having arisen from one another, they support each other through the relationship of the container and the contained, as the modification [is supported] by the modified entities. //79//
The Unmanifest is designated as the field (kṣetra), and Brahmā is called the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). Thus is this primordial creation; yet it is presided over by the knower of the field.
It existed previously without conscious intent, manifesting like a flash of lightning.
He who knows in truth this birth of Hiraṇyagarbha becomes long-lived, famous, fortunate, and possessed of progeny. ||81||
Even a man desiring liberation, if he is pure in soul, attains the supreme goal;
by constantly listening to the Purāṇas, he shall obtain happiness and security.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Section on Creation," in the Great Purāṇa spoken by Vāyu. 1.4.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O twice-born ones, that period of time which has been calculated by me as the duration of creation—this very interval of time should be known as a single day of the Supreme Lord. 1.5.1.
The entire night of the Supreme Lord should be known to be of this same duration; his day is the creation, while his night is said to be the dissolution. 1.5.2.
"The day exists for him, but not the night"—this is the established tenet;
such a figurative expression is employed out of a desire for the welfare of the world. (1.5.3)
The subjects, the lords of creatures, the seers together with the sages, and the seers known as Sanatkumāra along with those who have attained union with Brahman; ||1.5.4||
The sense organs and the objects of the senses, the five gross elements, the subtle elements, the group of organs, the intellect, and the mind. (1.5.5)
All these remain during the day of the wise Supreme Lord; at the end of the day they are dissolved, and at the end of the night the source of the universe [reappears]. 1.5.6.
When the being has become established in its own self and modification has been withdrawn, both Pradhāna and Puruṣa abide in a state of similarity. (1.5.7)
These two qualities, tamas and sattva, exist in a state of equilibrium;
when they are intensified or produced, they likewise act upon one another.
When there is equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), it should be known as dissolution (laya); when there is disequilibrium, it is called creation (sṛṣṭi). ||1.5.8||
Just as oil exists in sesame seeds or as clarified butter resides in milk,
so too does rajas reside within darkness and goodness, supported by the unmanifest.
Having spent the entire night in the supreme worship of Maheśvara, when the break of day had arrived,
he who was born of Prakṛti appeared before him.
The Supreme Lord, the Great Ruler, having entered both Pradhāna and Puruṣa within the cosmic egg, agitated them by means of his supreme yoga.
From the Pradhāna, as it was being agitated, Rajas indeed came into being;
Rajas is the activator there, just as water is for seeds.
Having reached an imbalance of the qualities (guṇas), [the elements] are produced under their governance.
From the qualities being agitated, the three gods were born; they are the supreme refuge, most secret, the self of all, and the embodied ones. 1.5.13.
Rajas is indeed Brahmā, tamas is Agni, and sattva was born as Viṣṇu;
Brahmā, the illuminator of rajas, is established in his role as the Creator.
Agni, who illuminates darkness, is established as Time;
Viṣṇu, who illuminates the quality of goodness (sattva), is established in neutrality.
These indeed are the three gods; these indeed are the three fires.
For they are mutually dependent and devoted to one another. 1.5.16
They exist by means of one another and support one another;
for they are mutual pairs and depend upon one another for their livelihood.
Indeed, there is not even a moment's separation among them, nor do they ever abandon one another.

For Īśvara is the supreme deity, but Viṣṇu is beyond the Mahat; Brahmā, however, being predominant in the quality of rajas, proceeds here for the sake of creation. The Puruṣa is to be known as the highest, and Prakṛti is remembered as the supreme. ||1.5.18||
For he, being presided over by Maheśvara, proceeds when impelled from all sides;
indeed, only the great ones, having long remained established, follow along out of affection for their own domain.

At the time of creation, the Pradhāna proceeds from the previous state due to the inequality of its qualities (guṇas), being presided over by Īśvara; from that [Pradhāna], which consists of both the existent and the non-existent, Brahmā and Buddhi arose simultaneously as a pair. ||1.5.20||
Therefore, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), consisting of the unmanifest darkness (tamas) and designated as Brahman,
having become fully perfected through the effects and instruments [of creation], came forth as Brahmā in the beginning.
By his splendor, the wise and unmanifest one shines forth as the first;
he is indeed the first embodied being, established in the state of the cause.
He was endowed with unimpeded knowledge and sovereignty, and he was possessed of unimpeded righteousness and dispassion. (1.5.23)
The unimpeded knowledge of that Lord, characterized by dispassion,
and the intellect pertaining to Brahmā, which effects mastery over the qualities (dharmas), were born from Him who possesses self-consciousness.

And from the unmanifest, he is born; and whatever he desires through his mind [is accomplished] because of his mastery, because of the absence of the three qualities, because of his lordship over the gods, and by his very nature. ||1.5.25||
As Brahmā he was four-faced, and as Time he became the Destroyer;
the thousand-headed Puruṣa—these are the three states of the Self-born One.
Sattva and rajas exist in the state of Brahmā, while rajas and tamas exist in the state of Time;
and sattva exists in the state of Puruṣa—such is the functioning of the qualities (guṇas) of the Self-born One.
In the state of Brahmā he creates the worlds; in the state of Kāla he withdraws them;
and in the state of Puruṣa he remains indifferent—these are the three conditions of Prajāpati.
Brahmā has the luster of the interior of a lotus; Kāla has the brilliance of natural collyrium; and Puruṣa has the form of a white lotus—such is the form of the Supreme Self.
The Lord of Yoga creates and transforms bodies by His own play, assuming various forms, actions, appearances, names, and functions. 1.5.30
Because he exists in the world in three ways, he is called "possessing the three qualities" (triguṇa);
because he is divided fourfold, he is celebrated as the "fourfold manifestation" (caturvyūha). ||1.5.31||
Because it attains, because it takes up, and because it exists in relation to its objects, and because that is its constant state of being, it is therefore called the *ātman*. 1.5.32.
And because He is all-pervading, the Seer is Himself the Lord of the body and so forth;
Viṣṇu possesses all lordship over this [body] because of His entry into everything. (1.5.33)

He is called Bhagavān because of the presence of the *bhaga*s; he is *Rāga* because he teaches passion (*rāga*); he is *Para* because he is the supreme subject under discussion; and he is remembered as *Ava* because he protects (*avana*). (1.5.34)

Because he is all-knowing through his universal consciousness, and because everything arises from him as the All, and because he is the refuge (ayana) of men (nara), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa. ||1.5.35||
Dividing himself threefold, he sets the three worlds in motion;
for by means of these three, he creates, devours, and beholds.
First, he manifested as Hiraṇyagarbha, the four-faced one.
Because he is the beginning, he is the Āditya; because he is unborn, he is remembered as the Unborn (Aja); and because he protects all creatures, he is therefore remembered as Prajāpati. ||1.5.37||
Among the gods he is the great god; therefore he is remembered as Mahādeva.
Because he is the lord of all worlds and because he is not subject to any other's control, he is likewise called Īśvara.
He is remembered as Brahmā because of his vastness; he is called Bhūta because he has come into being.
He is the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) due to his knowledge of the field, and he is the All-pervading One (Vibhu) because he is omnipresent. (1.5.39)
Because he dwells within the city (the body), he is called Puruṣa;
because he is unproduced and is the primordial one, he is remembered as Svayambhū. ||1.5.40||

He is called Yajña because he is worthy of worship; Kavi because his vision is far-reaching; Kramaṇa because he is capable of traversing all things; and Varṇaka because he protects the castes. 1.5.41.
Known as Āditya, Kapila is remembered as the first-born fire (Agnir agraja).
Hiraṇya was his embryo, and he was born from the embryo of Hiraṇya;
therefore, in this Purāṇa, he is designated as Hiraṇyagarbha.
The time that has elapsed since the Self-Existent One withdrew from activity— that which is prior to the beginning of the current aeon—
is impossible to calculate even in hundreds of years.
The period following the cessation of the reckoning of kalpas is known as the "Beyond" (para) of Brahmā; the remainder of his time is of that same duration, at the end of which he creates again.
Indeed, those thousands of millions upon millions of eons that have already passed, as well as those remaining in the future—[all these are contained within it]. (1.5.45)
Now, learn of this current aeon (kalpa) known as Vārāha;
O twice-born ones, of all those [aeons], this first one is currently unfolding.
In that [kalpa], there were fourteen Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva—those who have passed, those who are present, and those who will indeed be in the future. (1.5.47)

By those lords of men, this entire earth with its seven continents was to be protected on all sides for a full thousand yugas; listen now to the details of how they were sustained by their subjects and through their ascetic power.
By means of a single Manvantara, all the intermediate periods (Antaras) that are yet to come are indeed encompassed;
and by means of one Kalpa, all the Kalpas that are yet to come are likewise encompassed.
One should consider the past eons along with their waters and their successions, and likewise, a wise person should apply such reasoning to those yet to come. (1.5.50)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Section on Creation," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
For when the fire was extinguished upon the surface of the earth, the waters came into being;
when this world had dissolved into the intermediate state, both the stationary and the moving had perished.
Then, while that world was a single ocean, nothing at all could be discerned;
at that time, the blessed Lord Brahmā appeared, possessing a thousand eyes and a thousand feet.
The Puruṣa with a thousand heads, golden-hued and beyond the senses,
known as Brahmā Nārāyaṇa, then slept upon the waters.
But when he had awakened through the predominance of the quality of goodness (sattva) and beheld the world as empty, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa in this regard: ||4||
"We have heard that 'nārāḥ' is indeed a name for the waters, meaning 'expansions';
and because he rests within the waters, for that reason he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. (5)
Having passed a period of night equal to a thousand yugas, at the end of that night,
he assumes the state of Brahmā for the purpose of creation.
But Brahmā, having become the wind, moved about within that water here and there,
like a firefly at night during the rainy season.
Then, having discerned through inference that the earth was situated within those waters,
he remained undeluded regarding the means of raising it up.
He assumed another body, just as he had done in former ages at the beginnings of the kalpas;
then that great-souled one conceived a divine form in his mind.
Seeing the earth submerged on all sides by the waters, he thought:
"Assuming what great form shall I lift up the earth?"
During his water-sports, he meditated upon the beautiful form of the Boar, which is invincible to all beings, composed of speech, and known as Dharma. ||11||
Ten yojanas in width and a hundred yojanas in height,
it resembled a dark blue cloud and possessed a sound like the thundering of clouds.
He was as tall as a great mountain, white in hue, with sharp and fierce tusks; his eyes flashed like lightning-fire, and his splendor was equal to that of the sun.
He possessed thick, rounded, and long shoulders, walked with the stride of a lion,
had a full and elevated waist, and was exceedingly smooth with auspicious marks.
Assuming the vast and immeasurable form of a boar, Hari entered the netherworld for the purpose of uplifting the earth. 15.
He has the Veda for his voice, the officiating priests for his eyes, the sacrifice for his chest, and the sacrificial layers for his face;
he has fire for his tongue, darbha grass for his hair, and the Brahman for his head—possessing great ascetic power.
He has day and night for his eyes, the Vedāṅgas for his ear-ornaments,
the clarified butter for his nose, the sacrificial ladle for his snout, and the sound of the Sāmaveda for his great voice.
Consisting of truth and dharma, glorious, established in the valor of dharma,
devoted to expiatory rites, formidable, born of animals, and of great form.

With his body rising upward, he has the sacrificial fire as his emblem; he is the seed of the sacred site, the great medicinal herb; he is the inner self within the altar, with the mantra as his buttocks and the clarified butter as his touch; he has the Soma as his blood. ||19||
The Vedas were his shoulders, the fragrance of oblations was his scent, and he possessed great speed in carrying offerings to the gods and ancestors;
the eastern hall was his body, and he was radiant, endowed with various initiatory rites.
The yogi has the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as his heart; he is the all-pervading lord consisting of the great sacrifice (mahāsatra);
he is beautiful with the Upākarma and Iṣṭi rites, and adorned with the Pravargya ritual as his wealth.
Having various paths of movement through diverse meters, seated upon the secret Upanishads,
accompanied by his consort Chāyā, the Lord indeed entered the waters after becoming the Sacrificial Boar, lofty like a mountain peak of jewels.
While consuming that earth covered by waters, Prajāpati approached it and quickly drew them out; he then deposited those waters in their various places.

The Lord, for the sake of the welfare of the world, lifted up with his tusk the Earth— which was submerged in the depths of the netherworld and had gone down into the subterranean realm— along with those parts of her belonging to the oceans and those belonging to the rivers.
Then the upholder of the earth, the maker of the earth, having first sustained her in his mind, brought her back to her own place and released her.
Standing above that flood of water like a great ship,
and because of the power of the god's conduct, the earth does not undergo destruction.
Then, having extracted the earth with the desire to establish the world,
the lotus-eyed Lord set his mind upon the division of the earth;
and having leveled the earth, he constructed mountains upon it.
Previously, all those mountains had been scorched by the Saṃvartaka fire;
by that fire, they were shattered in every way across the earth.
In that single ocean, the waters were condensed by the wind due to coldness;
wherever they were poured down, there a mountain came into being. (29)
They are called *acalas* (immovable) because they do not move; they are known as *parvatās* (mountains) because of their joints (*parvan*);
they are *girayaḥ* (hills/mountains) because they have swallowed [the earth] within, and they are *śiloccayāḥ* (rock-heaps) because of their accumulation of stones.
Then, when those mountains of the world-ocean have been shattered,
Viśvakarman distributes them again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas.
He then fashioned this earth together with its oceans, its seven continents, and its mountains;
he further established the four worlds beginning with Bhūḥ.
Having arranged the worlds, he indeed set forth the creation of living beings.
The Lord Brahmā, the self-existent, desiring to create various progeny,
brought forth a creation of that same nature as in former ages at the beginning of the Kalpas.
As he was then meditating upon creation with conscious intent,
that which consists of darkness (tamas) appeared simultaneously with Pradhāna.
Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and that which is called andhatāmisra—this fivefold ignorance has manifested from the Great Soul. ||35||
And this fivefold creation belongs to the one who possesses self-consciousness (abhimānin) while in a state of meditation;
it is entirely enveloped by darkness like a lamp covered by a jar, being luminous both within and without, yet pure and devoid of perception. ||36||
Because their intellect and their primary organs are restrained by these [virtues], therefore those trees are proclaimed as "restrained-souled" (saṃvṛtātman) and "primary" (mukhya). ||37||
Having seen that the primary creation was thus ineffective and unaccomplished, Brahmā,
with a dejected mind, then resolved upon the Nyāsa [creation].
As he was meditating there, a stream turned sideways;
because it turned sideways, it is therefore known as Tiryañcsrotas. ||39||
Because of their abundance of darkness (tamas), they are all considered to be full of ignorance;
they follow wrong paths and, through meditation, merely imagine themselves to be meditators.
But having seen the second world-stream as one flowing crosswise,
the Lord [created] those characterized by egoism and self-conceit, consisting of twenty-eight types.
The elevenfold arrangement of the senses, as well as the ninefold manifestation of the vital breaths (udaya),
and the eight [energies] beginning with Tārakā— these are recorded as the various modalities of their power.
Therefore, all of them are luminous, yet they are again veiled externally;
because their movement proceeds obliquely, he is called Tiryaksrotas (the one whose stream flows crosswise). ||43||
And having seen the second universe with its beings flowing horizontally, the Lord,
perceiving that agitated intention and seeing everything as being of that same nature, there arose from him,
as he meditated constantly, a being of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
The third, however, is the Ūrdhvasrotas, who is established in the upward direction;
because he turned toward the upper realm, he is therefore known as Ūrdhvasrotas. ||45||
Abounding in happiness and joy, restrained both internally and externally, and luminous within and without, they are known as those born in the upward stream (ūrdhvasrotas). ||46||
By that [means], those such as Tādi, whose natures were created, remained established;
indeed, the third was the upward-streaming (ūrdhvasrotas), and by that it is remembered as the creation (sarga). ||47||
When the gods belonging to the upward-streaming class had been created,
the Lord Brahmā then became joyful; thereafter, he directed his mind toward another [creation],
and that powerful Lord brought forth another creation intended for accomplishment.
Then, as he was meditating with truthful intent, there emerged from the Unmanifest a downward-streaming [being] well-suited for accomplishment;
because it turned toward the downward direction, it is therefore called "downward-streaming" (arvāksrotas). ||49||
And they abound in light, yet their darkness, passion, and goodness are predominant;
therefore, they experience much suffering and are repeatedly active in their deeds.
They are luminous both externally and internally; they are human beings and practitioners, established in eight ways by means of characteristics such as the Tāraka and others. ||51||
Those humans who have perfected their souls share the same nature as the Gandharvas;
thus has this creation of radiant beings, known as the arvāksrotas (downward-flowing), been described. ||52||
The fifth is the creation of grace (anugraha-sarga), which is established as fourfold:
through error (viparyaya), power (śakti), contentment (tuṣṭi), and perfection (siddhi).
They know the past and the present objects in their true nature. ||53||
