That is called the sixth creation, consisting of the beings beginning with the Bhūtas; it is established through the reversal [of the previous order] and by means of incapacity. ||54||

The first creation is to be known as that of the Mahat; it is indeed the Mahat. The second, however, is the creation of the subtle elements (tanmātras); that is called the elemental creation (bhūtasarga). ||55||
The third creation is known as the Vaikārika, which pertains to the senses;
thus is the Prākṛta creation, which arose preceded by intelligence. ||56||
The fourth is the primary creation (mukhya-sarga), for the immobile beings are indeed known as primary;
and that creation which consists of those with horizontal currents is the fifth, the animal womb (tiryañ-yoni).

Likewise, the sixth creation of the gods is known as that of the "upward-streamers" (ūrdhvasrotas); and the seventh creation is that of the "downward-streamers" (arvāksrotas), which is the human creation.
The eighth is the Anugraha creation, which is both Sāttvika and Tāmasa.
These five are known as the Vaikṛta creations, while three are remembered as the Prākṛta creations. ||59||
The Prākṛta, the Vaikṛta, and the Kaumāra is recorded as the ninth;
the first three creations were indeed fashioned with deliberate intelligence. (1.6.60)
Those six creations of Brahmā proceed from his conscious will;
now learn of the creation known as the "creation by expansion" (vistarānugraha) as it is being described.
Then he is established in four ways among all beings in their entirety:
by way of error, by power, by contentment, and likewise by perfection.
In stationary beings there is perversion; among animals there is limited power;
human beings are perfected souls; and among the gods, contentment exists in its entirety.
Thus, these nine creations are recorded as both primary (prākṛta) and secondary (vaikṛta);
furthermore, many varieties of these are recorded as being mutually related.
In the beginning, Brahmā indeed created from his own mind beings equal to himself:
Sanandana, Sanaka, the wise Sanatana, and Sanatkumāra.
Those of great power have returned by means of consciousness through the process of reversal;
though they are all fully awakened, these three are likewise cast aside due to their diversity.
Without having brought about the creation of beings, they have again entered into the state of re-absorption.
When they had passed away,
Brahmā then created other mental sons as practitioners, who were once again invested with pride for their respective stations;
learn their names according to the state that lasts until the dissolution of all beings.
Water, fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, and the directions;
heaven, the celestial realm, the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, and the lords of the forest (trees). ||68||
Likewise, they are the selves of the medicinal herbs, the selves of the trees and creepers;
they are the lava, the kāṣṭhā, the kalā, the muhūrta, the junctions, the nights, and the days.
The half-months, months, solstices, years, and yugas—
all these are known as the "abiders in places" (sthānābhimāninaḥ) and are designated by the name of their respective stations.
From his mouth the Brāhmaṇas were produced; from his chest the Kṣatriyas from the front parts;
from his thighs the Vaiśyas, and from his feet the Śūdras—all castes were produced from his limbs. (71)
Nārāyaṇa is beyond the unmanifest; from the unmanifest arose the cosmic egg.
From that egg was born Brahmā, by whom the worlds were himself created. (72)
This first quarter has been told to you in brief, but not in detail;
by this first quarter, the Purāṇa has been fully proclaimed. (73)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Section on Creation," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Thus has this first quarter, concerning the exposition of the system, been proclaimed.
Having heard this, Sanātana, the son of Kaśyapa, was delighted in his heart. (1.7.1)
Having addressed the charioteer with these words, he then asked for the subsequent narrative:
"O knower of the Kalpas, from this point forward, describe to us the reconnection [of the world]."
We wish to know this: the interval between the two eons—the one that has passed and the one that is present—and their point of reconnection; for you are exceedingly skillful in this.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
In this regard, I shall explain to you the reconnection between those two—
the past eon and the present one— of both of them.
O you of virtuous vows, those *manvantaras* which occurred within the various *kalpas*, and this auspicious *kalpa* currently proceeding, known as Vārāha—[all these have been described]. (5)
Learn now of the intermediate state between this kalpa and that eternal kalpa which preceded it and has passed away.
When the previous aeon has been withdrawn and there is indeed a reconnection therein,
another aeon proceeds again and again from the world of living beings.
From the interruption of one kalpa until the next kalpa, all activities are entirely cut off at the end of that kalpa;
therefore, the transition from one kalpa to the next is called *pratisaṃdhi*. ||8||
Even the transitions between the periods known as Manvantaras and Yugas, though severed,
proceed one after another together with the Manvantaras and Yugas.
Those previous kalpas which have been described in brief for the sake of the exposition—
of those parārdha-kalpas, that which was prior to this [present] one has indeed passed away; it is the one beyond [this] parārdha.
O twice-born ones, there will be other future kalpas that are double the number of the past half-cycle; of these, this present kalpa is the first, O brahmins.

In which [cycle] the first is called the prior half (pūrvārddha) and the second the latter half (para), such is the duration of the period of stability (sthitikāla); from that, the withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is traditionally taught.
But that eternal kalpa which preceded this one passed away at the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, long ago, along with its manvantaras. (13)
When that eon had come to an end and the time of its conflagration had arrived,
those gods who were then inhabitants of celestial mansions in that eon—
The constellations, planets, and stars, as well as those which are the sun and moon—these twenty-eight crores belong to those of virtuous soul. (15)
In one such Manvantara, and likewise across all fourteen,
it is recorded from of old that there were three hundred and ninety-eight million, seven thousand, and eight hundred [incarnations]. (16)
Regarding the gods of the celestial mansions who existed when a kalpa had passed:
indeed, in each individual kalpa, those who were gods of the celestial mansions are thus remembered. ||17||
Now, throughout the fourteen Manvantaras in heaven,
there were indeed gods, ancestors, sages, and Manus.
Their followers, as well as the sons of Manu,
those gods who were worthy of praise by those in the [four] castes and stages of life at that time,
and those inhabitants of heaven who existed in the various Manvantaras in the world of the gods— [all these were present]. ||19||
When the dissolution has arrived along with those agents of conjunction,
they all reach an equal end when the absorption of all beings occurs.
Then, having realized that their own turn had arrived due to the inevitability of what was to happen, the gods dwelling in the three worlds [prepared] when that calamity had indeed come upon them.
Having abandoned their abodes out of a sense of spiritual longing, free from both worldly desire and despondency,
they then set their minds upon the Maharloka with great agitation for the sake of liberation.
They are born endowed with magnificent bodies;
all are abundant in purity and established in mental perfection. ||23||
Together with those who dwell in the Kalpa,
including Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and other people devoted to him, he has attained greatness.
But having considered Maharloka, those fourteen hosts of gods then set their minds upon Janaloka with haste.
All were abundant in purity and established in mental perfection;
together with those dwellers of the Kalpa who had attained greatness, they [remained].
By returning ten times as it were, they go from there to Svastapas;
having remained there for ten kalpas, they indeed go again to Satya.
By this sequential process, those who dwell in the kalpas proceed.
In this way, thousands of divine ages have passed one after another to the world of Brahmā, which is indeed a state from which there is no returning.
Indeed, even without sovereign power, they become equal to him in lordship;
they are equal to Brahmā in form and in their objects of experience.
There they indeed abide, filled with joy through constant absorption;
having attained the bliss of Brahman, they are liberated along with Brahman.
Then, by the very nature of things, those beings existing at that time were themselves connected to diversity through an inevitable and natural process. (31)
Just as [an action] occurs intentionally according to its own nature for one who is awake, so too does their knowledge proceed at that very time. (32)
But in the process of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), those subtle elements which possess distinct characteristics are dissolved together with their respective effects and instruments.
Due to their perception of diversity, those inhabitants of the world of Brahmā—whose authority was lost even as they remained established in their own dharma—[fell]. ||34||
Established as having identical characteristics, they are pure-souled and stainless; having transcended the cause that is primordial nature (prakṛti), they abide solely in their own self. ||35||
For once it has made itself known in all respects within those [elements] as their primordial nature (prakṛti),
it does not proceed further, being perceived as distinct from the Puruṣa.
Furthermore, when creation proceeds again, the cause for them is their conjunction with primordial nature (prakṛti),
even though they are disciplined seers of reality.
In this regard, for those who have attained liberation and do not return to the path of rebirth, there is no further arising, just as with extinguished flames. (38)
Then, when those great-souled ones had departed upward from the three worlds,
the people who had been brought from the Maharloka along with them remained here; they stay until the end of the Kalpa, awaiting their bodies.
From the Gandharvas down to the Piśācas, humans such as Brāhmaṇas and others, as well as beasts, birds, and stationary beings including reptiles. (1.7.40)
While those inhabitants of the earth's surface remained at that time,
the thousand rays of the sun that shine here became seven rays each, and thus each one arose as a sun.
Rising up in succession, they burn the three worlds—
both the moving and the stationary beings, as well as all the rivers and mountains—
which had previously been withered by drought and scorched by those suns.
Then they all entered [the fire], scorched by the rays of the sun— indeed,
all things, both moving and stationary, consisting of both merit and demerit.
Then, at the end of that sinful age, their bodies were indeed consumed by fire;
yet they remained unreleased from that womb, which was bound by the consequences of both merit and demerit.
Then those people, being of similar form, are reborn among humans;
all are abundant in purity and established in mental accomplishment.
Having dwelt there for a night, they become the mind-born offspring of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest, at the time of his subsequent creation.
Then, when those inhabitants of the three worlds had set out,
and when the worlds had been consumed by the seven suns,
the earth was flooded by rain and all dwellings were shattered.
The oceans, the clouds,
and all the waters upon the earth indeed become a single ocean, for they are then designated as "water" based on their dependence upon it.
When that great water, coming from wherever it came,
had covered this entire earth and remained there, it was then called the ocean (arṇava).
Because it shines, while other lights do not shine—since "ābhā" signifies both pervasion and radiance—it is perceived as the water that has completely inundated them from all sides. (1.7.50)
Because that water extends throughout the entire earth on all sides, and since the verbal root *tan* signifies expansion (*vistāra*), it is therefore known as *ambhas-tanu*. (51)
The particle *aram* is considered by poets to signify "quickly";
because the waters in the single ocean were not so swift, those men [were not called *āraṇya*]. 52.
When that day of Brahmā had come to an end after a thousand yugas, while the night was still prevailing,
he remained in the form of water.
Then, when that fire had vanished into the waters upon the surface of the earth,
the wind subsided and there was darkness on all sides, devoid of light.
For he by whom this was indeed presided over— that Brahmā, the Lord—
is desirous of once again effecting the division of this world.
Then, when that single ocean has arisen and all things mobile and immobile have perished,
he becomes Brahmā, possessing a thousand eyes and a thousand feet.
The thousand-headed Puruṣa, golden-hued and beyond the senses,
known as Brahmā Nārāyaṇa, then slept upon the waters.
But when awakened by the predominance of *sattva*, having beheld the world as empty, they cite this verse here concerning Nārāyaṇa: ||58||
We have heard that the name "Nara" refers to the subtle waters;
because he dwells there, filling the navel, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa. (59)

He who is described as the Puruṣa on the path of the Triple Veda—the thousand-headed, benevolent one, with a thousand feet, a thousand eyes, a thousand faces, a thousand-fold enjoyer, and a thousand arms—is the first Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati). (1.7.60)
He who has the luster of the sun, the protector of the world, the one, the unprecedented, the first, the subduer of the powerful;
he is indeed recited as the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha), the Great-Souled Puruṣa, existing beyond darkness. 61.
At the beginning of the kalpa, becoming Brahmā with an excess of rajas, he created all beings;
at the end of the kalpa, becoming Time (Kāla) with an excess of tamas, he swallowed them again.
He who is indeed known as Nārāyaṇa, overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva), while sleeping upon the ocean,
divided himself threefold and manifested throughout the three worlds.
He creates and indeed devours them, and He observes them with three [eyes];
when the world has become a single ocean and all things mobile and immobile have perished.
At the end of a thousand cycles of the four yugas, when everything was enveloped in water,
Brahmā, known as Nārāyaṇa, was sleeping within the unmanifest ocean.
Having swallowed the four kinds of beings during the night of Brahmā in the great ocean,
the great seers behold that Time sleeping in the Maharloka.
Just as Bhrigu and the other seven great seers [appeared] in this kalpa,
so too was the supreme Great One encompassed by them as they evolved.
The derivation of the name "ṛṣi" originates from the root meaning "to go" (ṛ);
therefore, because they are devoted to the Ṛṣis, they are great, and thus they are called Mahārṣis.
Then Kāla was seen by those residing in the Maharloka, who were asleep;
for they were the seven great sages, headed by Satya, who had existed in the kalpa that had passed.
Thus, after thousands of such Brahma-nights had passed,
other great seers likewise beheld Time asleep.
Brahmā indeed fashioned it; therefore, it is called Kāla (Time). ||71||
He is the creator of all beings again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas;
Mahādeva is both manifest and unmanifest, and this entire world belongs to him.
Thus has this reconnection between you two been described for the interval between the present and the past Kalpas, as well as that which was the prior state.
It has been proclaimed in brief, in each and every Kalpa, according to its nature;
now I shall declare this Kalpa to you—understand it!
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Proclamation of Rebirth," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Having passed a period of night equal to a thousand yugas,
he assumes the state of Brahmā at the end of the night for the purpose of creation.
Then Brahmā, having become the wind,
moved about within that water while all things mobile and immobile had perished in that darkness.
When the surface of the earth was completely pervaded by water on all sides,
and when all beings were situated everywhere in an undifferentiated state.
Then, like a firefly in the night during the rainy season,
he moved here and there through the sky, being watched by the Self-born One.
For while searching for the site of the foundation,
the Lord then realized that the earth was submerged within those waters.
But through inference, regarding the lifting up of the earth,
it is remembered that the Fully Awakened One assumed another body during the beginning of previous kalpas.
Having assumed the form of a boar, the Lord,
the Prajāpati, entered the waters after beholding the earth submerged by the waters.
Having lifted the earth from the waters, he deposited those waters in their respective places:
the oceanic waters in the oceans and the river waters in the rivers;
having thus established the earthly elements upon the earth, he then fashioned the mountains.
But when the world was being consumed by the fire of destruction at the time of the previous dissolution,
those mountains were entirely dissolved upon the earth by that fire.
In that single ocean, the waters were withdrawn by the wind due to coldness;
wherever they settled, there a mountain came into being.

They are called *acalas* because they do not move; they are known as *parvatas* because of their joints (*parvan*); they are *girayaḥ* because they swallow with water; and they are *śiloccayāḥ* because of the heaping together of stones. ||11||
Then the Lord, having lifted that earth from within the waters and established it in its own place, again divided it.
Having leveled the uneven terrain across her seven islands, he constructed mountains there for each of the seven regions over the course of seven years.
In those continents, there are likewise forty regions (varṣas),
and as many mountains situated at the borders of these regions;
they were established at the beginning of creation by their very nature, and not otherwise.
The seven continents and the oceans, by their very nature, are situated in proximity to one another's circles, each encompassing the next.
In the beginning, Brahmā indeed fashioned the four worlds known as Bhūḥ, along with the moon, the sun, and the planets, as well as all these various abodes in their entirety.
And at the beginning of this kalpa, Brahmā indeed created the inhabitants:
water, fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, and likewise heaven. (17)
He is heaven, the quarters, the oceans, all the rivers, and the mountains;
likewise, he is the self of the herbs and the self of the trees and creepers.
The lava-s, kāṣṭhā-s, and kalā-s, as well as the muhūrta, the junctions, night, and day;
the half-months and months, and the solstices, years, and yugas. ||19||
Having created those who pride themselves on their positions as well as the various positions themselves,
he, whose self is the position, indeed fashioned the conditions of the Yugas.
At the beginning of the Kalpa, during the first age, the Kṛta Yuga, he created the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and likewise the Kali ages, as well as all living beings.
Those progeny which I previously described to you in former times were then consumed by fire during that dissolving kalpa.
Those who have not reached the world of heat (Tapoloka) but have taken refuge in the world of men (Janaloka),
indeed become the seeds for creation once again when the cycle begins.
They abide there in the sense of being seeds for the sake of further creation;
then, as they are being created, they indeed exist for the purpose of procreation.
In this world, they are remembered as the means for accomplishing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
likewise, the gods, the ancestors, the sages, and the Manus.
Then, endowed with ascetic power, they indeed fill the various abodes;
for those sons of Brahmā’s mind become perfected souls.
Those beings who, through action joined with hatred, have gone to heaven,
return here again and are born in age after age.
Through the remnants of the fruits of their own karma, beings arise from the world of people, characterized by such natures and bound by the doubts regarding their actions. (28)
In that regard, intention (āśaya) should be understood as the cause of actions;
indeed, by those auspicious and inauspicious actions, people are born into various worlds.
They take up bodies of various forms within the various wombs; they are born one after another, from the gods down to the level of stationary beings.
Whatever actions they performed prior to creation, those very same actions they assume again and again as they are created.

Violence and non-violence, gentleness and cruelty, righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood—they are permeated by that [inner disposition] and thus attain it; therefore, each person finds pleasure in that very thing.
Whatever forms and names existed in the kalpas that have passed away, those very same ones have for the most part been adopted again in the future time.
Therefore, those very names and forms were attained;
again and again, in successive kalpas, they are born from name and form.
Then, when the creation had been obstructed, as Brahmā was desirous of creating and was meditating upon progeny,
those beings appeared to him who was intent on true contemplation.
Then he indeed created a thousand pairs from his mouth;
those people were born with the quality of goodness (sattva) predominant and possessed of noble minds.
From his chest, he indeed created another thousand pairs;
they were all overflowing with passion (rajas), both vigorous and non-vigorous. ||37||
Having again created another thousand pairs from his thighs,
those who were intensified by rajas and tamas are remembered as being of a striving nature.
From his two feet, he created another thousand pairs;
all of them were overwhelmed by darkness, devoid of splendor, and possessed little luster. ||39||
Then, indeed, those living beings, filled with joy and born of pairs,
being afflicted by mutual desires of the heart, proceeded to engage in sexual union.
From that time forward in this kalpa, the birth of couples is described;
whatever seasonal [fluid] occurs month after month, that is brought about by the power of the woman’s command.
Therefore, at that time, they did not procreate even through the practice of sexual intercourse;
rather, at the end of their lifespan, they gave birth to twins only once.
From that time forth, in this kalpa, there arose those who were destined for death— the Kuṭakas and the Kuvikas— along with the birth of human pairs.
When these are meditated upon by the mind, there arises for those beings a pure object—sound and so forth—which occurs simultaneously and possesses five characteristics each. ||44||
Thus, those who were first produced by Prajāpati through his mind prior to creation were born into his lineage,
and by them this world was filled.
In that age, people indeed frequent rivers, lakes, oceans, and even mountains; the water they use is neither excessively cold nor hot.
They indeed consumed food produced from the essence of the earth;
those creatures moved according to their will, having attained mental perfection. ||47||
In those [ages], dharma and adharma did not exist; those subjects were without distinction.
In that Kṛta Yuga, their lifespan, happiness, and form were equal.
In that Kṛta Yuga, dharma and adharma did not exist;
however, in the Kṛta Yuga, they were born according to their respective offices.
They say that the first age, Kṛtayuga, consists of four thousand divine years, with four hundred years for each of its twilights (sandhyās).
Then, although those progeny were multiplied by the thousands,
there was no obstruction among them, nor any pairs, nor even any succession.
Dwelling among mountains and oceans, they were indeed without fixed dwellings;
free from sorrow, abounding in goodness, and their subjects lived in absolute happiness. 52.
Indeed, those beasts and birds were able to move about at will and were always joyful in mind; at that time, there were no reptiles.
There are no plants that sprout from the earth, nor hell-beings, for they are born of unrighteousness; there are no roots, fruits, or flowers, nor seasonal changes, for there are no seasons.
The time was one of every sensual pleasure, for the heat and cold were not excessive;
their desires were all fulfilled according to their hearts' wish at all times and in all places. (55)
Indeed, those [beings] who were meditated upon by them arise upon the earth, produced from the essence;
their accomplishment brings about strength and complexion, and it is the destroyer of disease.
Those creatures possessed bodies that were beyond the need for refinement and remained in perpetual youth;
from their pure intention, offspring were born as pairs.
Their birth and form were equal, and they died at the same time;
then truth, freedom from greed, forgiveness, contentment, happiness, and self-restraint [prevailed]. (58)
All were made indistinguishable by their form, lifespan, conduct, and activities; the behavior of the subjects arose spontaneously, without prior conscious intent. (59)
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was no engagement in either auspicious or sinful actions;
there were no regulations for castes and stages of life, nor was there any intermixture at that time.
Free from desire and aversion, they dwell together with one another;
all are equal in form and lifespan, devoid of the distinctions of low or high. ||61||
For in the Kṛta Yuga, beings are born for the most part happy and free from sorrow;
they have minds that are eternally joyful, and they are great-souled and possessed of great strength.
Gain and loss, friend and foe, the pleasant and the unpleasant—
these objects of the senses do not affect them in their minds, for they remain free from desire.
Indeed, they do not covet one another, nor do they seek to favor one another.
Meditation is supreme in the Kṛta age; wisdom is said to be the best in the Tretā;
ritual sacrifice is prevalent in the Dvāpara; and charity is the most excellent in the Kali age.
Sattva is established in the Kṛta age, Rajas in the Tretā, while Rajas and Tamas characterize the Dvāpara;
however, in the Kali age, Tamas alone is to be known, according to the influence of the progression of the ages.
Such is the duration of time in the Kṛta Yuga; learn its specific measure:
the Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years.
The two twilight periods of his [day] numbered eight hundred divine years;
at that time, their lifespan was such, and there were neither afflictions nor calamities.
Then, when that Kṛta Yuga has indeed passed away during its twilight period,
the dharma of the Yuga remains in its entirety as only one quarter.
Even when the twilight of the age had passed, at the time of its end,
the dharma of that age’s twilight remained as a quarter;
and when that was thus completely performed, Siddhi then vanished from sight.
And when that mental perfection had fallen away,
another perfection was then established in that age during the interval of the Tretā Yuga.
Those eight mental [perfections] which were indeed proclaimed by me at the beginning of creation—
those eight perfections come to an end through the process of gradual progression.
At the beginning of the kalpa, this perfection indeed occurs through the mind during the Kṛta age;
in all the Manvantaras, according to the divisions of the four yugas,
the arising of success in action is recorded as being produced by the conduct of the castes and stages of life.

By means of the quarter of the Sandhyā and the quarter of the Sandhyāṃśa, these [ages] have each performed a portion of the Sandhyā; thus, through the qualities of the Yugas, they diminish one another in respect to austerity, sacred learning, strength, and lifespan. (73)
Then,
O best of sages, when one quarter of the Kṛta age had been exhausted, there followed immediately thereafter another age, the Tretā.

When that [period] had been exhausted and its purpose fulfilled, while the remaining subjects here were still present, at the very beginning of the Tretā age as it commenced at the start of the Kalpa; ||75||
Then, through the conjunction of time, that accomplishment perishes and not otherwise;
when that accomplishment has perished, another accomplishment comes into being. ||76||
When the subtlety of the waters had then returned, those two, in the form of clouds,
initiated the release of rain from the thundering clouds.
As soon as the surface of the earth was joined with that rain,
trees appeared there, serving as dwellings for them.
But all their enjoyment arises from those [fires];
for at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, beings maintain themselves by means of them.
Then, after a long time, due to a reversal in their very nature, a state consisting of passion and greed suddenly arose among them. (1.8.80)
That which occurs for women at the end of life is their menses;
indeed, by the power of the [current] age, that does not occur again. (81)
Furthermore, their menses occurred month after month;
then, by that very same union, they lived as a couple.
Because they were subject to that state at that time, they approached one another month after month.
For indeed, there was the occurrence of menstruation at the wrong time, and the birth of a fetus came about [at the wrong time]. ||83||
But by that future reversal of these [conditions],
all those trees situated as houses will then perish.
Then, when those [obstacles] had vanished, they, bewildered and with agitated senses,
meditated upon that perfection, being intent on truth at that time.
And for them, those trees appeared situated within their homes;
they produced garments as well as fruits and ornaments.
In those very [leaves], there arises within each and every leaf a honey, free from bees, possessing great potency, and endowed with excellent fragrance, color, and flavor. (87)
By means of that, they subsisted during the mouth of the Tretā Yuga;
indeed, through that accomplishment, the subjects were joyful, contented, and free from all affliction.
Again, after some time, those women, once more shrouded by greed, forcibly seized those trees for the sake of honey or beeswax. (89)
Due to that misconduct committed by them against the Creator of the World,
the Kalpa-trees perished along with the honey in various places.
When that [night] had almost passed away due to the power of the twilight hour,
their rivalries then began to arise once more.
Then, due to intense cold, wind, and heat, they became exceedingly distressed.
Being tormented by these pairs of opposites, they indeed created coverings.
Having provided remedies for their hardships, they indeed caused them to enjoy dwellings;
for previously, those who were intent on seeking [shelter] had been utterly without recourse to a home.
They dwelt again in their dwellings according to what was appropriate and pleasing—
among the desert wastes, in lowlands, on mountains, and by rivers— and they took refuge in fortresses and in arid tracts that possessed perennial water.
According to their requirements and as they desired, on both level and uneven ground,
they indeed began to construct dwellings to ward off cold and heat.
Then he established market-towns,
cities, and villages according to their respective portions, as well as inner palaces.
Then, according to their wisdom, they established the lengths, widths, and internal layouts of those cities; however, that region was designated by them as "Saṃjñita."
The span between the thumb and the forefinger is called a *prādeśa*; that measured by the middle finger is known as a *tāla*, and that by the ring finger is a *gokarṇa*. (98)
A span measured by the little finger is said to be twelve finger-breadths;
a ratni is twenty-one finger-joints in number. (99)
Twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) constitute one cubit (hasta);
a span (kiṣku) is traditionally held to be two cubits, or forty-two finger-breadths.
A bow-staff of four cubits and two nālikās [make one dhanus];
by those [measures], two thousand dhanus are understood as a gavyūti.
Eight thousand bows are said to constitute one yojana;
by this very measure of the yojana, the layout was then established.
Of the four types of fortresses, three indeed arise from nature itself;
the fourth is an artificial fortress, and I shall now describe its method of construction. (103)
With its high palaces, ramparts, and walls, and surrounded on all sides by cātaka birds,
that single Svastika gate was indeed the very precinct of the princesses' quarters.
That opening for the conduits should be dug again to a depth of eight, ten, or nine cubits;
these are considered the best, while others are regarded as eight [cubits]. ||105||
Of all the market-towns, cities, and villages, as well as the three kinds of fortresses—those on mountains, those by water, and those enclosed by embankments. ||106||
And regarding the three types of fortresses, their width and length shall be such that the length is half of one-eighth of a yojana [of the width]. ||107||
The city should have a length of half of half the ultimate measure (one-eighth), extending toward the north;
it should have its corners cut off, be square, possess distinct features, and be well-proportioned. ||108||
A city that is irregular, deficient, or elongated is not praised; rather, a supreme city is one that is square, straight, and situated according to the cardinal directions. 109.
The first [type] is twenty-four cubits, and the highest is eight hundred cubits;
in this regard, they praise the middle [size], which is free from being too short or too long.
Now, they say that eight hundred *kiṣkus* constitute the primary settlement;
beyond that, a *kheṭa* (market town) or a *grāma* (village) has a width equal to half that of the city. (111)
A *kheṭa* is one *yojana* from a city; a village is half a *yojana* from a town.
The maximum boundary is two *krośas*, while the boundary of a field is four *dhanus*. ||112||
A path for the cardinal directions was made by them twenty *dhanus* wide;
a village road was twenty *dhanus*, while a boundary road was ten *dhanus*.
The illustrious royal highway is recorded as being ten *dhanus* in width;
it is free from congestion for men, horses, chariots, and elephants, and is easy to traverse.

Four *dhanus* were made by them as the main streets (*śākhārathyā*), while the house-alleys (*gṛharathyā*), side-alleys (*uparathyā*), and sub-alleys (*uparathyakā*) were each two *dhanus* wide. ||115||
The main road is four paces wide, the interior of the house three paces;
the paths for the dwellings are half a pace, while the front hall (prāgvaṃśa) is prescribed to be one pace. ||116||
Having constructed drains and outflows and cleared a space of one pace all around,
they indeed rebuilt their houses in those very places.
Having reflected again and again, they set about doing exactly as those trees had previously been situated within the house. 118.
The branches of the trees had gone forth, yet they did not go beyond;
from there they went upwards, and likewise previously they had gone crosswise.
Having understood and investigated the principle of how the branches of the tree had spread, they fashioned branches accordingly; therefore, those dwellings are known as *śālās*.
In this way, from the branches (śākhā) both the halls (śālā) and the houses (gṛha) became well-known;
therefore, those halls are called "śālās," and the quality of being a hall (śālātva) resides in them.
The mind finds delight in them, and they cause the mind to become serene;
therefore, they are designated as "houses" (gṛha), "halls" (śālā), and "palaces" (prāsāda). ||122||
Having suffered those mutual afflictions and failing to consider means of livelihood,
when the wish-fulfilling trees had perished along with the honey,
those creatures were then overwhelmed by despair, characterized by thirst and hunger.
Then, in the Tretā Yuga, their perfection (siddhi) manifested once again;
indeed, another mode of livelihood for them, which accomplishes the goals of worldly affairs, arose according to their desire.
The waters of rain that flow here through low-lying places,
having become streams by virtue of that rain, are known as rivers because they have been channeled into hollows.
Thus, when the second discharge of rain had begun,
those drops of water which fell upon the surface of the earth from beyond [the clouds] became rivers.
From the conjunction of water and earth, medicinal herbs came into being;
those herbs were born possessing flowers, roots, and fruits. ||127||
Fourteen kinds of plants—both cultivated and wild—grew forth without being ploughed or sown; likewise, trees and shrubs appeared, bearing flowers and fruit according to the seasons.
And in the Tretā age, the manifestation of medicinal herbs occurred for the sake of livelihood;
at that time, during the Tretā Yuga, the people subsisted by means of those herbs.
Then, however, passion and greed arose among them in every respect,
due to the inevitable course of events and the influence of the Tretā Yuga.
Then they seized the rivers, fields, and mountains, as well as the trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs, by force according to their strength. ||131||
Those perfected souls who were previously described by me in the *Prākṛta* [Purāṇa] as human beings indeed arose here from Brahmā at the beginning of the Yuga.
Then, being peaceful yet passionate, and performing ritual acts while experiencing suffering,
they were born again as they proceeded during the Tretā age.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and likewise people of hostile intent—these were all conditioned in their previous births by their own auspicious and inauspicious actions. (134)
But those who were strong in truth, virtuous, non-violent, free from greed, and self-controlled, indeed dwelt among them. (135)
Some accept them and act upon them, while others of lesser luster do not;
thus they fall into disagreement with one another as they encounter each other.
Due to that fault, while they were looking on, those medicinal herbs then vanished as they were being carried away,
like sand held in a closed fist.
By the power of the foremost and true pair, fourteen [plants], both cultivated and wild, bear fruit;
furthermore, some bear fruit through flowers and others through leaves. (138)
Then, when those [plants] had perished,
those creatures, bewildered and overcome by hunger, approached the Lord Svayambhū, the Prajāpati.
At the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, desiring to obtain means of subsistence,
the blessed self-born Brahmā, having understood their intention, [acted accordingly].
Having reflected upon the fact that the medicinal herbs had been swallowed by the earth, as confirmed by direct perception and investigation, he milked them back out once again.
Having made Sumeru the calf, he milked this earth;
by him, these seeds were then milked from the cow onto the surface of the earth.
Those seeds were born again as both cultivated and wild plants;
these medicinal herbs, which end with the ripening of their fruit, are seventeen times seven in number.
Rice, barley, wheat, millet, sesame, fine priyaṅgu, udāra, kāraṣa, and satīnaka grains. ||144||
Māṣa, mudga, masūra, niṣpāva, along with kulattha, āḍhakī, and caṇaka—these are traditionally known as the seven kinds of pulses (saptasaptadaśāḥ). ||145||
Thus, these are recorded as the species of cultivated plants;
including those plants fit for sacrifice, there are fourteen types, both cultivated and wild. 146.
Rice, barley, beans, wheat, millet, sesame, and priyaṅgu as the seventh—these are the grains; the eighth is the horse-gram (kulattha). ||147||
Now, there were śyāmāka grains, wild nīvāra rice, jartila seeds along with gavedhuka,
kuruvinda, bamboo-seeds, as well as those that are markaṭaka.
These fourteen medicinal herbs are indeed recorded as being both cultivated and wild;
they first appeared at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga.
Herbs not ploughed by the furrow, both cultivated and wild;
trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and species of grasses. 1.8.150.
By taking [them] with roots, fruits, and flowers, one becomes a Rohiṇī;
indeed, the earth was milked by the Self-born One for those seeds which were [formerly] [extracted]. (151)
Indeed, those herbs here were born with flowers and fruits according to the seasons;
but when the herbs were released [by him], they did not sprout again.
Then the Lord Brahmā, the Self-born, having seen that success arises from action, devised a means of livelihood for them.
From that time forward, medicinal herbs grew on plowed land;
and once their livelihood was fully established, the Self-born One (Brahmā) then fixed their mutual boundaries according to how they had been initiated.
Those who were indeed chosen as husbands for them were of the three orders;
for the others, he established Kṣatriyas who had provided protection.
Those who attend upon them, as many as there are, likewise become fearless;
and those Brahmins who speak of Brahman as truth, exactly as it has come to be, they too are such.
And those others who were weak and established in the duties of Vaiśyas, being diligent, destroyed the ploughs upon the earth;
they are called Vaiśyas indeed, those Kīnāśas who provide their livelihood. ||157||
To those who were grieving and running about, devoted to menial services, lacking luster and possessing little vigor—he called them Śūdras. (158)
The Lord Brahmā ordained their respective duties and qualities for the sake of the fourfold varṇas in their entirety, once the primordial creation was established.
Furthermore, those subjects, through delusion, failed to observe those duties;
not living according to the duties of their respective castes, they obstructed one another.
Having understood that matter exactly as it is, the powerful Lord Brahmā ordained the strength of the Kṣatriyas, punishment, and warfare as their means of livelihood.
Sacrificing for others, teaching, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts—He, the Lord, assigned these as the specific duties of the Brāhmaṇas. (162)
The Lord assigned cattle-rearing, trade, and agriculture to the Vaiśyas;
he ordained the livelihood of crafts and service for the Śūdras. (163)
Furthermore, the common duties of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—namely, sacrifice, study, and giving—are indeed shared among them all. (164)
Then, having assigned their means of livelihood to one another, the Lord granted them stations in other worlds through his supernatural power. ||165||
The realm of Prajāpati is ordained for Brāhmaṇas who perform their duties;
the realm of Indra is for Kṣatriyas who do not flee from battle. (166)
The station of the Maruts belongs to the Vaiśyas who live by their own dharma;
that of the Gandharvas belongs to those of the Śūdra caste who remain in service. ||167||
He himself established these stations for the social orders whose conduct had become perverted;
then, once the social orders were stabilized, he established the stages of life (āśramas).
The Lord formerly established these four stages of life: the householder, the student, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant. ||169||
Those who do not perform the duties of their respective castes here on earth—how can those residing in the various stages of life (āśramas) say that such people have fulfilled their duty? 1.8.170
Brahmā established them as hermitages according to their respective names;
then, for the sake of instructing them, Brahmā proclaimed the duties,
the stages of life, and the restraints and observances.

In former times, the stage of the householder was ordained as consisting of the four castes; it is indeed the foundation and the source of the other three stages of life. I shall describe to you, in due order, its restraints and observances.
Wife, sacred fires, hospitality toward guests, sacrificial offerings, funeral rites for ancestors, and progeny—this, indeed, is the summary of the duties of a householder. ||173||

Carrying a staff, wearing a girdle, sleeping on the ground, and likewise having matted hair—these, along with service to the teacher and subsisting on alms, one should know to be the duties of the student (brahmacārī). 174.

For those dwelling in the forest, there should be garments of bark, leaves, and skins; grain, roots, fruits, and medicinal herbs; and they must perform ablutions at both twilights and offer oblations. 175.
Begging for alms when the pestle has been set aside, non-stealing, purity, vigilance, celibacy, compassion toward all beings, and forbearance—[these are the duties]. (176)
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, and truthfulness is recorded as the tenth;
for this tenfold dharma was proclaimed by the Self-Existent One. ||177||
In this [religion], there are five primary vows for a monk and likewise five secondary vows (upavrata):
purity of conduct, restraint, cleanliness, ritual purification, and right vision—these indeed are the five secondary vows as well. 178.
Meditation, concentration, and the restraint of the senses; having approached for alms from those who dwell by the ocean;
silence; and liberation through the accumulation of purities—these they call the dharma of the wandering mendicant. (179)
All these stages of life were proclaimed by Brahmā himself for the sake of the highest good;
they consist of truth, uprightness, austerity, patience, yoga, sacrifice, and self-restraint as their foremost quality.
The Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, the sacrifices, the vows, and the observances—
all these do not bear fruit for one who is corrupt when a defect of disposition has arisen.
All external actions may perhaps succeed at some time, even for one who exerts great effort, provided his internal disposition is not corrupted. 182.
Even if one were to give away all one's possessions with a defiled inner self, one would not partake of the merit thereby; for in this matter, the internal disposition alone is the cause.
In this manner, the gods, along with the ancestors, the sages, and likewise the Manus—their station among those established in that [heaven] is proclaimed. (184)
It is recorded that there are eighty-eight thousand sages of perpetual celibacy;
that very place is known as the abode of those who dwell with their preceptor.
That which is known as the station of the Seven Sages belongs indeed to the dwellers of heaven;
it is the domain of Prajāpati for householders, and the abode of Brahmā for renunciants. For yogis, there is the immortal station, but for those of various [worldly] thoughts, it does not exist. 186.
These are the stations of the forest-dwellers who are established in their own duty;
these four paths leading to the gods have been fashioned. 187.
In the first Manvantara on earth, by Brahmā, the sustainer of the world, those paths for the journey of the gods were established, and the Sun is remembered as their gateway. (188)
In the same way, the moon is said to be the gateway for those who travel the path of the ancestors.
Thus, when the divisions of the castes and stages of life had been established,
the subjects consisting of those castes and stages did not deviate from them.
Then, during the Tretā age, he created other mental offspring from his own body; they were indeed equal to himself in nature.
When that first Tretā Yuga had gradually reached its middle,
he then proceeded to create other mental offspring there.

Then that Lord created beings in whom the qualities of sattva and rajas were predominant, who are the means for accomplishing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as the worldly livelihood (vārttā). ||192||
The gods, the ancestors, the seers, and likewise the Manus,
who, in accordance with the dharma and according to the nature of the ages, have sustained these created beings.
When that duty toward progeny had thus presented itself to Svayambhu,
he meditated upon all manner of mental offspring of diverse forms.
Those whom I have previously described to you as having resorted to the world of Jana were,
indeed, the gods and other beings here when that kalpa had passed.
As he was meditating, all those [energies] appeared for the sake of manifestation;
they are considered here to exist in the order of the Manvantaras, beginning with the youngest as the first. (196)
In this world, all beings are permeated by those various manifestations and their continuations,
as well as by all objects consisting mostly of wholesome and unwholesome deeds;
supported by the remnants of the fruits of those actions, they are born.
Through various states of being—as gods, asuras, and ancestors;
as beasts, birds, and reptiles; and as trees, hell-beings, and insects—he indeed fashioned himself into the objects of the mental afflictions and into the progeny.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Division of the Four Stages of Life," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Then, as he was meditating, mental offspring were born;
from his body, along with those effects and causes produced from it,
the conscious beings (kṣetrajñas) emerged from the limbs of that wise one.
Then, desiring to create the fourfold group consisting of gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans, he joined them together with his own self.
Then, as that self-disciplined Prajāpati, the Self-born One, meditated upon creation, an effort arose from his own essence.
Then, from his hindquarters, the Asuras were first born as sons;
O Brahmins, "asu" is known to mean vital breath (prāṇa), and since they were born from that, they are called Asuras.
With that body by which the gods were created, he cast it aside;
that discarded body immediately became night. ||5||
Because that [night] abounds in darkness, it consists of three watches;
therefore, during the night, the creatures of the Self-born One are enveloped by darkness.
Having seen the gods, the Lord of Devas assumed another body—
unmanifest and abounding in the quality of goodness (sattva); then he applied his mind to it,
and as he was thus engaged, it truly became dear to the Lord.
Then, as he was gambling, the deities were born from his mouth;
because they were born while he was gambling (dīvyataḥ), he is therefore celebrated as Deva. ||8||
The element which was proclaimed as "dvi" is understood to signify play;
from within that divine [element], the deities were born by means of it. ||9||
Having created the gods, the Lord of Gods then assumed another body; thereafter, the God assumed yet another body, consisting solely of the quality of goodness (sattva).
Regarding them as his fathers, the Lord meditated upon those sons;
for he created the Pitṛs from his two armpits during the interval between night and day.
Therefore, they are the divine Pitṛs, and that quality of being a father exists in them by virtue of their being his sons.
He cast off that body by which the Pitṛs had been created;
that discarded body immediately became the twilight (saṃdhyā).
Therefore, that which is day for the gods is known as night for the Asuras;
between those two, however, the form belonging to the ancestors (the Pitṛs) is indeed the most significant.
Therefore, all the gods, asuras, sages, and likewise the Manus,
being disciplined, worship that middle body of Brahmā.
Then that Lord Brahmā again assumed another body;
by his mind, he created one consisting of the quality of rajas. ||15||
Then, from that state characterized by a predominance of *rajas*, he created the Mānasas as his sons;
from that mind of his, the Mānasa progeny were born.
Having seen his subjects once more, he cast off his own body;
that discarded body immediately became moonlight.
Therefore, when the moonlight arises, living beings become clearly visible;
these are the bodies that were cast away by that Great-Souled One. 18.

Immediately, night and day, as well as twilight and moonlight, were born. Day, moonlight, and twilight are composed of the quality of goodness (sattva) itself; night is composed of the quality of darkness (tamas). Therefore, it indeed consists of three parts.
Therefore, because they were seen and created from the divine principle by means of his mouth,
and because their birth occurred during the day, those powerful ones are [called] Divas (the Gods) for that reason.
When the Lord, having slain the Asuras with his body during the night, released them.
For those born at night are unbearable to living beings during the night; therefore, they [are so]. (21)
These very same [omens] indeed become the signs for all future gods, asuras, and ancestors, as well as for men, throughout all past and future manvantaras. ||22||

Moonlight, night, day, and twilight—these four are indeed illuminated. Since they shine because of you, you are therefore called "Bhā" by the wise; this word "bhā" is declared by them to mean both pervasion and radiance. Furthermore, Prajāpati said: 23. Moonlight, night, day, and twilight—these four are indeed illuminated. Since they shine because of you, you are therefore called "Bhā" by the wise; this word "bhā" is declared by them to mean both pervasion and radiance. Furthermore, Prajāpati said: 23. Since they shine because of you, you are therefore called "Bhā" by the wise; this word "bhā" is declared by them to mean both pervasion and radiance. Furthermore, Prajāpati said: 23. Moonlight, night, day, and twilight—these four are indeed illuminated. Moonlight, night, day, and twilight—these four are indeed illuminated. Since they shine
Having seen these waters, he then created gods, Dānavas, and humans,
as well as other Pitṛs and divine beings from himself once again.
Having cut that entire body apart, the Lord then created another form,
which was predominantly characterized by rajas and tamas, and joined it once again.
Then, overcome by hunger in the darkness, he created another;
those beings created by him, being of the nature of hunger, were intent on seizing the waters. (26)
"We shall protect these waters," they said, and among them were those known in the world as Rākṣasas—night-stalkers whose very nature was wrath. ||27||
Those who said, "We shall exhaust the waters," were seen by one another;
because of that deed, those Yakṣas and Guhyakas became performers of cruel acts.
This verbal root is understood to mean both protecting and guarding;
whereas this element *kṣi* is specifically said to mean perishing. (29)
Upon seeing them, the hair of that wise one fell out due to his displeasure;
then, rising up from the cold and heat, it grew back upon that lord.

Because serpents were inferior to the heads of fish and were driven away from them, serpents are known as *vyāla* (the inferior), and because they are inferior to the *vyāla*, they are known as *ahi* (the snake). ||31||
Because they have fallen away from wisdom, they are called pannagas and sarpsas, as well as apasarpiṇas;
their dwellings on earth are below the sun and the moon.
That most terrible fire born of his anger, which had a womb of flame,
entered the serpents who were born together with him and whose very nature was poison.
Then, seeing the serpents, he who was of wrathful nature created from his anger fierce beings that devour flesh, brownish in color.
Because they had come into being (bhūta), they were called Bhūtas; because they ate flesh (piśita), they were called Piśācas.
Then, from his sighing (vayata) for the cows, the Gandharvas were born at that time.
The verbal root *dhyai* is indeed taught in the sense of "to go";
from it were born cows that drink [milk], and for that reason they are remembered as *gandharvas*. 36.
When these eight divine species had been created, that Lord then,
by his own will, created other birds from those [very] birds.
Those meters covered even the birds and the young of birds;
seeing them empty, the Lord indeed created flocks of winged creatures as well.
Then Brahmā created goats from his mouth, and he brought forth birds from his chest; he produced cows from his belly and fashioned them from his two sides.
On foot, they pursued horses, elephants, śarabhas, gavayas, deer, camels, asses, and various other species of animals.
Herbs, fruits, and roots were produced from his body hair;
having thus created the animals and the plants, the Lord employed them in the sacrifice. 41.
Therefore, at the beginning of the Kalpa, at the onset of the Tretā Yuga, the cow, goat, man, sheep, horse, mule, and donkey—these they call domestic animals; now learn of those that are wild. 42.
Beasts of prey, cloven-hoofed animals, elephants, monkeys, and birds as the fifth; aquatic creatures were created as the sixth class of animals, and reptiles as the seventh. (43)
From his first mouth, he fashioned the Gāyatra, Varuṇa, the Trivṛt, the Saumya, the Rathantara, and the Agniṣṭoma among sacrifices.
From his southern mouth, he created the Triṣṭubh meters, the rite, the fifteen-fold Stoma, the Bṛhat Sāman, and the Uktha.
From his western mouth, he created the Sāman chants, the Jagatī meter, the Pañcadaśa stoma, the Vairūpa, and the Atirātra sacrifice. ||46||
Then, from his northern mouth, he created the Ekaviṃśa, the Atharvāṇa, the Āptoryāmāṇa, the Anuṣṭubh, and the Svarāja.
At the beginning of the kalpa, the blessed Lord created lightning, thunderbolts, clouds, red-hued portents, rainbows, and birds.
High and low beings were born from his limbs as Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, was creating the progeny. ||49||
Having first created the fourfold progeny— the gods, asuras, ancestors, and [human] beings—
he then creates all other creatures, both stationary and moving.
Yakṣas, piśācas, gandharvas, as well as throngs of apsarases,
nāgas, kinnaras, rakṣasas, birds, domestic animals, wild beasts, and serpents.
Both the imperishable and the perishable— whatever exists here, whether stationary or moving—
they, being created again and again, obtain those very same actions which they performed in a previous creation. (52)

Violent and non-violent, mild and cruel, righteous and unrighteous, true and false—impregnated by those very qualities, they resort to them; therefore, each finds pleasure in that which accords with it.
The Creator himself ordained the diversity among the great elements, the objects of the senses, and physical forms, as well as the specific functions of the beings.
Some men say it is human effort and action;
others, O Brahmins, say it is destiny; and those who contemplate destiny say it is inherent nature.

They do not know human effort and destiny to be either identical with, separate from, superior to, or both identical and separate from the nature of the fruit's manifestation; nor do they know them as neither one nor both,
nor even as both.
Established in the quality of goodness (sattva) and possessing equal vision, they shall declare the fields of action and the objects of the senses;
and that Great Lord, in the beginning, fashioned from the very words of the Veda the names and forms of all beings and the expansion of created things. ||57||
He bestows upon him those very names of the sages and those same visions which exist among the gods for those born at the end of the night.
Just as the various characteristic signs of the seasons appear in their recurring cycle,
so too do those very same states of being reappear at the beginnings of the Yugas.
When such beings had been created by Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest,
they were seen at the end of the night, having resorted to mental perfection (siddhi).
Thus were created all beings, both moving and stationary;
yet when those creatures had been created by that wise one, they did not multiply.
Then he created other mind-born sons who were like himself:
Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and likewise Aṅgiras.

Marīci, Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha, who was born of his mind—these are determined in the Purāṇas to be the nine Brahmas. Of all these who were of the nature of Brahmā and were exponents of the Veda, [they were the foremost]. (63)
Then Brahmā, the progenitor of even the ancients, again created Rudra from his own wrath, as well as Saṃkalpa and Dharma.
In the beginning, Brahmā indeed created from his own mind four beings equal to himself:
Sanandana, Sanaka, the wise Sanātana, and [Sanatkumāra]. (65)
And Sanatkumāra, the all-pervading one, as well as Sanaka and Sanandana—
those eternal ones, being free from desire, do not create within the worlds.
For they had all attained knowledge, were free from passion, and devoid of envy;
yet, though they were thus indifferent, [he acted] out of conformity with worldly custom.
The blessed Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, the Supreme Being, indeed reflected;
from his wrath there arose a person with the brilliance of the sun,
possessing a body that was half-female and half-male, blazing like fire with its splendor.
"Everything has become composed of splendor, possessing a brilliance equal to that of the sun.
Having said, "Divide yourself," he vanished right there.
Having spoken thus, he divided himself into two, becoming separately a woman and a man;
and that Lord manifested himself elevenfold, dividing his own self in half.
Then all those great-souled ones were addressed by that Great-Souled One, who, desiring their welfare, spoke concerning the expansion of the world.
Therefore, for the sake of the world's affairs, strive with vigilance for the establishment and the welfare of the entire universe and all its people. (72)
Thus addressed, they wept and fled in every direction;
because of their weeping and fleeing, they became renowned by the name "Rudras."
For by them this entire triple world, with all its moving and non-moving beings, is pervaded;
they are the attendants in the world, the ultimate refuge for all worlds.
There were lords of the Gaṇas, possessing the strength of many elephants, valiant and fierce;
among them was that illustrious lady who forms half the body of Śaṅkara.
I have previously told you that the woman who emerged from the mouth of the Self-Existent One had the right half of her body white and the left half black. (76)
"Divide yourself," the Self-born Lord said to that goddess;
and being thus addressed, O twice-born ones, she became twofold—white and black.
I shall declare her names; listen with full concentration. (77)
Svāhā, Svadhā, Mahāvidyā, Medhā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Aparṇā, Ekaparṇā, and likewise Pāṭalā. (78)
Umā, Haimavatī, Ṣaṣṭhī, and Kalyāṇī by name—these illustrious ones are known in the world as Gaurī, who is Wisdom and Fame. (79)
Now hear, in brief and according to the proper sequence, how the Noble One manifested her universal form through the differentiation of separate bodies. 1.9.80.
She is Prakṛti, the fixed one, Raudrī, Durgā, Bhadrā, Pramāthinī, Kālarātri, Mahāmāyā, Revatī, and the leader of spirits (Bhūtanāyikā). ||81||
Listen to my recitation of the names of the Goddess during the transformations at the end of the Dvāpara age:
Gautamī, Kauśikī, Āryā, Caṇḍī, Kātyāyanī, and Satī. (82)
The maiden, the goddess of the Yādavas, the bestower of boons, dark-brown as a black bee, having a peacock-feather banner, bearing a trident, and a supreme practitioner of celibacy. ||83||
Māhendrī, Indrabhaginī, Vṛṣakanyā, Ekavāsasī, Aparājitā, Bahubhujā, Pragalbhā, and Siṃhavāhinī. ||84||
Ekānasā, Daityahanī, Māyā, Mahiṣamardinī, Amoghā, Vindhyanilayā, Vikrāntā, and Gaṇanāyikā. ||85||
These names of the Goddess, which are free from modification, have been declared in their proper order as the true names of the Goddess Bhadrakālī. 86.
For those men who recite this, there is no defeat, whether they be in a forest, a wilderness, a city, or even in their own home. (87)
One should employ this protection whether in water or on land,
especially against tigers, crocodiles, and thieves, and particularly in haunted places;
one should also recite the names of the Goddess in all instances of mental anguish.
One should employ this protection for children who are constantly afflicted by infant-seizing spirits, elemental beings, and the Pūtanā mothers. (89)
Within the Mahādevī family, two are proclaimed as Prajñā and Śrī;
by these two, thousands of goddesses are manifested, by whom the entire world is pervaded.
She brought forth resolve (vyavasāya) and dharma, which brings happiness to all beings;
and at the beginning of the kalpa, volition (saṅkalpa) was likewise born from that source which is unmanifest (avyakta-yoni). ||91||
And the son of Brahmā known as Ruci was born of his mind;
from his breath he created Dakṣa, and from his two eyes Marīci.
Bhṛgu was born from the heart of the water-born one;
likewise, Aṅgiras was born from his head, and Atri from his ear.
Furthermore, Pulastya was born from his udāna breath, and Pulaha from his vyāna breath.
From Samāna he created Vasiṣṭha, and from Apāna he fashioned Kratu.
He created the auspicious Nīlalohita, whose nature is pride.
Thus, these are remembered as the twelve sons of Brahmā, born from his vital breath (prāṇa). ||95||
Thus these sons of the mind are to be known as the progeny of Brahmā;
however, those such as Bhṛgu who were created [later] are not expounders of the Veda.
Those ancient householders were the ones by whom dharma was first set in motion;
these twelve, together with Rudra, O descendant of Vipa, continue to prevail.
R̥bhu and Sanatkumāra—these two are of perpetual celibacy (ūrdhvaretas);
they were born earlier than those [others], being the ancestors of them all. (98)
When the first ancient kalpa had passed, those two, the achievers of the world, remained in the Vairāja world, having withdrawn their splendor within themselves.
Having established themselves within their own selves through the practice of yoga, those two,
possessing great luster, continued to carry out the duties toward their subjects as well as the pursuit of desire.
Just as he was born, so too is he called "Kumāra" (the Youth) here;
therefore, this name "Sanatkumāra" has been proclaimed for him.
Their twelve lineages were divine, endowed with celestial qualities,
devoted to sacred rites, possessed of progeny, and adorned by great seers.

Thus, this transformation of Prakṛti itself—arising from the instruments and beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣas)—is for the sake of creating the worlds by the Self-born One. 103.
It is illuminated by the light of the moon and sun, adorned with planets and constellations, and encompassed by rivers, oceans, and mountains. ||104||
And with various kinds of cities and likewise contented provinces,
Brahmā passes the night in that unmanifest Brahma-forest.
Originating from the seed of the Unmanifest and arising through its very grace, it consists of the trunk of the intellect and has the sense-faculties as the hollows of its sprouts. (106)

It has the great elements as its branches, is possessed of leaves by way of specific qualities, has dharma and adharma as its beautiful flowers, and results in the arising of the fruits of pleasure and pain. ||107||
This eternal tree is the livelihood of all beings;
it is indeed the power of Brahman and the very tree of Brahman.
That which is the unmanifest cause is eternal, consisting of both being and non-being;
this is the "favorable creation" (anugraha-sarga), which is the primordial (prākṛta) creation of Brahmā.

The six creations beginning with the primary one (mukhya), which are modified and preceded by intelligence, came into being throughout the three periods of time from Brahmā; they are characterized by self-conceit (abhimāna).
Furthermore, those emanations are remembered by the wise as being mutual causes of one another;
they are like two divine, well-feathered birds, joined together, with branches, and possessing wings of gold and coral.
But only one knows the tree; no other does, because [he is] the Self of all. ||111||

He whose head the sages praise as heaven, whose navel is the sky, whose two eyes are the moon and the sun, whose ears are the quarters, and whose feet are the earth—he is the inconceivable Self, the source of all beings. 112.
From his mouth the Brāhmaṇas were born; from the front part of his chest the Kṣatriyas;
from his thighs the Vaiśyas; and from his feet the Śūdras—all the social orders were produced from his limbs. (113)
Maheśvara is beyond the unmanifest; from the unmanifest arose the cosmic egg, and from the egg was born Brahmā, by whom these worlds were created. (114)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation of the Gods and Others," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
When the worlds had become thus, and for some reason those creatures did not multiply, Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, [acted].
Enveloped by the quality of darkness (tamas), Brahmā was then filled with sorrow;
thereupon, he applied his intellect toward the determination of the matter.
Then, having overcome the quality of passion (rajas) that was prevailing according to dharma, he beheld within himself the pure quality of darkness (tamas) as the regulator.
The Lord of the World was tormented by that sorrow and created the wheel of grief;
He dispelled that darkness and enveloped it with passion and ignorance.
That darkness was indeed dispelled, and he begot a pair;
from the practice of unrighteousness, violence was born, and from grief, sorrow was born.
Then, when that couple consisting of the two feet had arisen,
the Blessed One was pleased and took up his residence there in this manner.
Then Brahmā cast off that non-luminous body of his;
he divided that body into two parts, and by one half he became a male (Puruṣa).
From the other half, that lord produced Śatarūpā as his wife;
she was the primordial sustainer of beings, whom the all-pervading Lord created according to his will.
Pervading both heaven and earth with her majesty, she stands established;
she is the primordial body of Brahmā, remaining after having encompassed the heavens.
But she who was born as a woman from half [of his body], Śatarūpā, that goddess, having performed most difficult austerities for a period of a thousand years, [became his wife]. (1.10.10)
She obtained as her husband a man of blazing fame;
he was indeed the first Manu, the son of Svayambhū, who is called Puruṣa. ||1.10.11||
A period of seventy such yugas is here called a manvantara.
Puruṣa, having obtained Śatarūpā as his wife, who was not born from a womb, [proceeded].
He delights with her; therefore, she is called Rati.
That was the first union, which occurred at the beginning of the Kalpa.
Brahmā created Virāj; he became the Puruṣa Virāj. From that mental form, O King, the sovereign Manu is remembered as having arisen.
That Vairāja was the creator of progeny; he was Manu, the Puruṣa at the beginning of creation.
From that heroic Puruṣa Vairāja, Śatarūpā was born.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were two sons, the best among those who possess sons;
and there were two highly fortunate daughters, from whom these creatures were born. (16)
O auspicious one, those two were named Devī, Ākūti, and Prasūti;
the Lord Svāyambhuva bestowed Prasūti upon Dakṣa.
Prāṇa is to be known as Dakṣa, and Saṅkalpa is called Manu;
he then brought forth Ākūti from Ruci and Prajāpati.
From the mental radiance (Ruci) of Manu, a beautiful pair was produced through Ākūti in the sacrifice;
Yajña and Dakṣiṇā were born as twins.
Twelve sons were born from Yajña and Dakṣiṇā;
they are known as the gods called the Yāmas in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
They were the sons of Yama and of Sacrifice; therefore they are remembered as the Yāmas.
Furthermore, two hosts, the Ajitas and the Śūkas, are recorded as belonging to Brahmā.
The Yāmas, from whom the celestial beings (divaukasas) derive their name, were previously born;
they are the mothers of the world, born of Prasūti, the daughter of Svāyambhuva.
Upon her, the lord Dakṣa begot twenty-four daughters;
they were all highly fortunate and all had lotus-like eyes.
And all those wives of the Yogas were all mothers of Yoga:
Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Medhā, Kriyā, as well as Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapu, Śānti, Siddhi, and Kīrti as the thirteenth. (24)
The Lord Dharma accepted the daughters of Dakṣa as his wives;
these were ordained by the Self-born One as the very gateways to him.
From them were born eleven younger daughters with beautiful eyes:
Khyāti, Satī, Saṃbhūti, Smṛti, Prīti, and Kṣamā. (26)
Sannati, Śacī, Anasūyā, Ūrjā, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā—these were then obtained once more by other great ṛṣis. ||27||
Rudra, Bhṛgu, Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Pulastya, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, the Pitṛs, and likewise Agni. ||28||
He gave Satī to Bhava, Khyāti to Bhṛgu, Sambhūti to Marīci, and Smṛti he gave to Aṅgiras. (29)
He gave Prīti to Pulastya, Kṣamā to Pulaha, Sannati by name to Kratu, and likewise Anasūyā to Atri.
He gave Ūrjā to Vasiṣṭha, and indeed Svāhā to Agni;
and Svadhā to the Pitṛs. Their offspring shall now be described.
All these highly fortunate ones, established in their own duties, remain wise throughout all the Manvantaras until the dissolution of all beings.
Śraddhā indeed gave birth to Kāma; Darpas is remembered as the son of Lakṣmī.
Niyama was the son of Dhṛti, and Santosa is said to be the son of Tuṣṭi. ||33||
From Puṣṭi comes gain and also a son, Medhāputra, as well as Śruta;
from Kriyā, however, Naya is said to arise, along with Daṇḍa and Samaya.
Buddhi’s son was Vaudha, and Apramāda was the other;
Vinaya was the son of Lajjā, and Vyavasāya was the son of Vapuḥ.
Kṣema was born from Śānti, and Sukha was born from Siddhi; Yaśas was also the son of Kīrti—these are the sons of Dharma.
Harṣa was indeed the son of Kāma, born of the goddess Rati;
thus has this creation of Dharma, which results in happiness, been described. ||37||
From Adharma were born both Hiṃsā (Violence) and Nikṛti (Deceit), as well as Anṛta (Falsehood).
From Nikṛti and Anṛta were born Bhaya (Fear) and Naraka (Hell).
Māyā and Vedanā were a pair;
from fear of these two, Māyā then gave birth to Mṛtyu, the destroyer of beings. (39)
From that feeling, moreover, suffering was born from Raurava;
then death, disease, fever, sorrows, anger, and envy were produced.
These are all known as the intervals of suffering, and they all possess the characteristics of unrighteousness (adharma).
Their wives or sons—all these are considered to have met their end.
Thus was this tāmasa creation born, which regulates dharma.
Commanded by Brahmā to "create progeny," Nīlalohita meditated upon his wife Satī and brought her forth from his own self.
He created from his mind thousands upon thousands of beings who were neither superior nor inferior to himself,
all equal to him in appearance, splendor, strength, and sacred learning, and clad in garments of silk.

[He saw] those with tawny complexions, those carrying quivers, those with matted hair, those who were deep red, those who were naked, those with golden hair, those whose very sight was blinding, and those who carried skulls.
They were of many forms, deformed, and of universal forms;
they were embodied beings—chariot-warriors, clad in armor, righteous, and protected by defensive shields.
They had hundreds of thousands of arms, reaching into the heavens, the earth, and the intermediate space;
they possessed massive heads, eight tusks, two tongues, and three eyes.
There were those who eat food, those who eat flesh, as well as those who drink clarified butter, those who drink soma,
those who drink fat, and the Śitikaṇṭhas, all of whom possess fierce wrath.
Indeed, there were archers equipped with quivers, arm-guards, and finger-protectors,
some seated, some running, some yawning, and others standing firm.
Then [he saw them] reciting, muttering prayers, engaging in yoga, and likewise meditating;
blazing, raining, shining, and emitting smoke.
He saw Buddhas and those most perfect in Buddhahood, those most devoted to Brahman, those of auspicious appearance,
those with blue necks, the thousand-eyed ones, and all the night-wandering spirits.
He created by the thousands those supreme gods in the form of Rudras, endowed with great yoga and great power, who were invisible to all beings and who were thus engaged in weeping and running about.
Brahmā, having seen them, said to them: "Do not create such offspring;
you must not create progeny equal to yourself, nor indeed superior. Create others—may prosperity be yours! Remain steady and create your subjects. (52)
"These thousands upon thousands of Virūpas and Nīlalehitas who have indeed been tasted by me are certain to be equal to myself. (53)
These gods shall become known as the Rudras, possessed of great strength;
they shall be celebrated by the name of Rudra on earth and in the intermediate space.
Those recited in the Śatarudriya will become worthy of sacrifice here;
they shall all partake in the sacrifice together with the hosts of gods.
Those gods born of the Vedic meters who will exist here during the future Manvantaras—
being worshipped together with them, they shall remain here until the end of the Yuga.
Thus addressed by the wise Mahādeva, the Lord of Creatures, Brahmā,
being greatly delighted, then replied to Bhīma.
"So be it; may it be well with you, O Lord!
Whatever has been spoken by you shall indeed always come to pass, for you have been authorized by Brahmā."
From that time forward, the Lord of Gods indeed produced no more offspring;
remaining with his vital energy drawn upward (ūrddhvaretas), he stood as Sthāṇu until the dissolution of all beings.
And because he said, "I stand" (sthito'smi), he is therefore remembered as Sthāṇu. ||59||
Knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, austerity, truth, forgiveness, fortitude,
the power of creation, self-awareness, and the power of presiding—
these ten qualities abide eternally in Śaṅkara.
Because the god transcends all the gods and sages assembled together with the asuras by his splendor, he is therefore remembered as Mahādeva.
He surpasses the gods by his sovereignty, the great asuras by his power,
all sages by his knowledge, and all beings everywhere by his yoga.
The sages said:
O great sage, explain to us the means for attaining the knowledge of Maheśvara, as well as yoga, austerity, truth, and dharma.
O Lord, I wish to hear all that regarding the Maheśvara Yoga, by which means the twice-born shall indeed attain their respective destinations.
Vāyu said:
In the Purāṇa, however, five dharmas were proclaimed by Rudra,
just as the state of Maheśvara was described by the Rudras of unblemished deeds.
Together with the Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, and both Aśvins in every way,
as well as the Maruts, the Bhṛgus, and all other inhabitants of the abode of the gods.
Preceded by Yama and Śukra, as well as by Pitṛ, Kāla, and Antaka,
these and many other such beings attended upon those Dharmas.
Having indeed exhausted their karma and being as pure as the autumnal sky,
those hosts of sages worship, having unified the self within the Self.
Devoted to the pleasure and welfare of their gurus and desiring to do what is pleasing to their teachers,
they cast off human birth and sport like gods.
Learn now, as they are being declared in their proper sequence, all those five eternal duties which were proclaimed by Maheśvara.
In this yoga, five practices are proclaimed: breath control (prāṇāyāma), meditation (dhyāna), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), and mindfulness (smaraṇa). ||71||
I shall explain their characteristics and causes according to their specific sequence, as well as the reality exactly as it was spoken by Rudra.
