The practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) is also described as the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa);
and that too is said to be threefold: namely, mild, moderate, and intense.
The restraint of the vital breaths is designated as *prāṇāyāma*;
the measure of *prāṇāyāma* is traditionally said to be twelve *mātrās*. (74)
The slow [breath] consists of twelve mātrās, while the exhalations (udvātas) are recorded as twelve;
the medium [breath], having two exhalations, consists of twenty-four mātrās. ||75||
In that regard, the highest [intensity] of the three-fold exhalation is said to consist of thirty-six measures;
indeed, it is traditionally held to be the highest, as it generates perspiration, trembling, and despondency.
Thus, this threefold characteristic of breath control (prāṇāyāma) has been declared; understand now its measure and its definition in brief. ||77||
Whether it be a lion, an elephant, or any other wild beast in the forest,
once captured and treated with care, it becomes gentle.
In the same way, the vital breath (prāṇa) is difficult to master for all those who have not disciplined themselves;
yet, when cultivated through yoga, it proceeds by means of practice. ||79||
For just as even a lion or an elephant, though once powerful, may become weak through the passage of time and be overcome by forceful pressure, so too is he.
Having clothed the mind, one attains mastery over it;
having clothed the god that is the mind, the vital breath likewise lives. (81)
For just as one established in yoga attains mastery over the wind, so too he leads the vital breath wherever he desires by his own will. ||82||
Just as a lion or even an elephant, remaining under control, proceeds toward wild animals for the sake of providing safety to human beings. ||83||
Just as this wind, which indeed faces all directions, when well-practiced and restrained within the body through meditation, burns away all impurity. 84.
For the Brahmin who is disciplined in breath control and whose mind is restrained, all defects perish and he becomes established in purity. 85.
Whatever austerities are performed, whatever vows and observances there are, and even the fruit of all sacrifices—prāṇāyāma is equal to them all. (86)
He who drinks a drop of water with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month for a full hundred years, and he who practices breath control (prāṇāyāma)— these two are equal.
One should burn away defects by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), and sins by means of concentration (dhāraṇā);
one should withdraw the sense-objects by means of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), and the unstable qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna). ||88||
Therefore, a disciplined yogi should always be devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma);
with his self purified of all sins, he attains the supreme Brahman. ||89||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manvantaras and Other Epochs," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Vāyu said:
For one great day, or even for a full day and night, or likewise for half a month, a month, a season, a year, or a yuga. ||1||
For thousands of great yugas, the high-souled sages, established in austerity, worship Prāṇa with their divine vision. ||2||
Henceforth, I shall declare the purpose of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and its specific fruits, exactly as the Lord, the Master, has spoken.
Know that there are four purposes for breath control (prāṇāyāma):
tranquility, perfect tranquility, illumination, and clarity—this is the quartet. (4)

The arising of the fruits of actions—whether performed by oneself through time in this world or the next—is for embodied beings even when those actions take a terrible form, such as that of jackals. (5)
Indeed, the exhaustion of the impurities (kaṣāyas) resulting from the corruption of one's father, mother, kinsmen, and relatives is called peace (śānti). ||6||
Indeed, the restraint even of those evils consisting of greed and pride for the sake of welfare in this world and the next, and which results in tranquility, is called austerity (tapas). //7//
The range of perception would be equal for the sun, moon, planets, and stars, as well as for the renowned rishis who possess the wealth of knowledge and realization. (8)
The vision of the past, the future, and the present—when these attain equality for the Buddha, that radiance is called austerity (tapas). //9//
Because it clarifies the senses, the objects of the senses, the mind, and the five vital breaths, it is designated as "prasāda" (serenity). 1.11.10.
Thus, this first dharma, consisting of the fourfold prāṇāyāma, should be known as yielding immediate results, arising from grace at that very moment. ||11||
Henceforth, I shall declare the characteristics of prāṇāyāma,
as well as the posture (āsana) according to its true nature, for one who is indeed practicing yoga.
Having first uttered the syllable Oṃ and having paid homage to the Moon and the Sun,
one should assume the Svastika posture, or likewise the Padmāsana or the Ardha-āsana.
Having made his two feet even, with knees together or one knee raised, and remaining well-established in an even and firm posture, he should withdraw both his feet.
With his mouth covered, his eyes closed, and his chest pressed forward,
he should likewise shield his testicles and genitals with his two heels.
With his head slightly raised, and likewise his neck, he should gaze at the tip of his own nose without looking toward the directions. ||16||
Having veiled *tamas* with *rajas*, one should veil *rajas* with *sattva*;
then, established in *sattva*, one should practice yoga with a concentrated mind. (17)
Having restrained the senses, the objects of the senses, the mind, and the five vital breaths, as if in a formal assembly, one should undertake the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra). 18.
But he who withdraws the desires from all sides, as a tortoise draws in its limbs,
being self-reliant and delighting in the Self alone, beholds the Self within the self.
Having filled his body, both internal and external, with purity,
he should begin the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) by fixing [the breath] from the navel up to the throat.
A mere fraction [of time] should be understood as the closing and opening of the eyes;
likewise, a breath control (prāṇāyāma) is prescribed to consist of twelve such measures.
Twelve breath-retentions constitute one *dhāraṇā*, and indeed yoga consists of two such *dhāraṇās*.
Thus, one who is truly engaged in yoga attains sovereign power and beholds the Supreme Self, blazing with its own splendor. ||22||
For the Brahmin who is disciplined in breath control and self-restrained, all defects perish and he becomes established in the quality of purity (sattva). ||23||
Thus, with his food strictly regulated and devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), the sage should always ascend the stages of the earth, conquering them one by one. 24.
For an unconquered great element would produce many faults;
it increases delusion. Therefore, one should not cultivate what is unconquered. (25)
Just as one endowed with strength might drink water through a tube by means of a mechanical device with effort,
so too should one who has conquered fatigue draw in the breath with diligence.
At the navel and the heart, at the throat, the chest, and the face;
likewise at the tip of the nose, the eyes, the middle of the eyebrows, and then at the crown of the head. ||27||
When [the mind] is held slightly above and in the supreme [space], it is known as the highest concentration (dhāraṇā).
Through the complete restraint of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, that is called prāṇāyāma. ||28||
The fixing of the mind is indeed proclaimed as *dhāraṇā* (concentration);
the withdrawal from sense objects, however, is designated as *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal). ||29||
When all these come together, there arises the perfection characterized by yoga.
For the yoga thus produced, meditation is indeed the characteristic of perfection.
One who is constantly engaged in meditation shall behold the Self like the sun and the moon.
But when a sentient being is not established, seeing does not exist;
for one who is not joined with place and time, seeing does not exist. (31)
Near a fire, or in a forest, or likewise upon a heap of dry leaves;
in a cremation ground infested with creatures, or in a ruined cow-pen, or at a crossroads. ||32||
One should never discharge [urine or excrement] in a place where there is noise or fear, nor upon a shrine, an anthill, a water well, or a river. (33)
A yogi devoted to meditation should always practice supreme meditation when he is free from hunger, satisfied, and not agitated in mind.
Having determined these defects, if one indeed engages in them through negligence, his own defects become provoked within the body and act as obstacles. ||35||
He incurs dullness, deafness, and muteness;
as well as blindness, loss of memory, old age, and likewise disease. (36)
The defects of one who practices yoga out of ignorance indeed become provoked;
therefore, a yogi, being composed, should practice with pure knowledge. ||37||
One who is always vigilant shall never incur defects;
I shall describe the treatment for those defects in their proper order, and how those defects arising from breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma) are eliminated. 38.
Having eaten very warm, unctuous gruel, one should apply [therapeutic measures] therein;
by this sequential method, the vāta-gulma is pacified. ||39||
One should perform this medical treatment as a remedy for *gudāvarta*;
after consuming curd or barley gruel (*yavāgū*), the wind (*vāyu*) will then move upward.
Then, having pierced the wind-knot, one should apply [the breath] to the region of the wind;
yet if even then no distinction [of sensation] occurs, one should maintain the concentration (dhāraṇā) upon the head. ||41||
For that embodied being who is engaged in yoga and established in sattva, this treatment should be administered when there is an obstruction in the rectum or its surrounding area. ||42||
For the yogin who has begun [practice] with a trembling of all his limbs, one should perform this medical treatment; by means of it, he becomes happy. (43)
Whatever vow one has undertaken mentally, having steadied it, one should maintain it;
in the case of a heaving of the chest, one should fix the mind on the region of the chest and the throat.
Upon an affliction of the skin, one should contemplate that [affliction] in speech; likewise, in deafness, in the two ears;
in the location of the tongue, one afflicted by thirst should contemplate the essences of moisture with threads at the tip;
the yogi should indeed contemplate the fruit, and thereupon he becomes happy. (45)
In cases of consumption, leprosy, and chronic cough, one should employ the Sarvasātvikī [mudrā];
in whatever region of the body the *rajas* (passion/impurity) is located, there one should apply it accordingly.
This is the medical treatment to be performed for a Brahmin who has attained yoga:
one should strike the head of him who is holding it steady with a bamboo peg;
having fixed a peg in the head, one should strike the wood with a piece of wood. (47)
If he is terrified, his consciousness will return from that state;
or else, she shall support him there with her two hands while his consciousness is lost.
Having then regained consciousness, one should maintain concentration upon the crown of the head;
one should eat food that is oily and small in quantity, and thereby one becomes happy. (49)
When the knower of yoga awakens by means of a superhuman being,
he should sustain both heaven and earth, as well as wind and fire.
By means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), all that being consumed by fire shall be brought under control;
even if it should enter the body, one should then repel it. ||51||
Then, having steadied it through yoga and holding it at the crown of the head, all that [impurity], burnt by the fire of breath-control (prāṇāyāma), shall go to dissolution. ||52||
One should bear the offense of a black serpent within the core of one's heart;
having placed the worlds of Mahar, Janas, Tapas, and Satya within the heart, one should indeed maintain them there.
Having drunk the fruit of poison, one should then hold the Viśalyā [mantra];
having encompassed the entire earth together with its mountains, one should hold it in the mind. (54)
Having placed within his heart the oceans as well as all the deities,
the knower of yoga, joined with a thousand jars, should perform the ritual bath.
When standing in water up to the neck, one should maintain the concentration on the head;
when overcome by a poison that flows against the current, one should maintain the concentration on all the limbs.
One who has suffered from hemorrhaging should drink anthill earth using cups made of *arka* leaves;
for this is the renowned method of treatment devised through yoga.
But the definition of a Brahmin has been explained in brief by means of the reasoning seen through Yoga; know that one who speaks [thus] may occasionally declare it. 58.
Moreover, if one should say out of delusion that "that consciousness dissolves," then the engagement of yoga must not be described in any way whatsoever. ||59||

Vigor, health, freedom from greed, a radiant complexion, a melodious voice, gentleness, a pleasant fragrance, scanty urine and excrement, and the onset of yoga—these are the first signs [of success] in the body. (1.11.60)
If he sees himself and the earth itself as blazing,
and having done so, enters another [body], he should know that perfection has arrived.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Pāśupata," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu. ||1.11||
Sūta said:
Hereafter, I shall explain exactly how those afflictions arise, which are the defects that appear for an embodied being who has perceived the reality. (1)
One who knows yoga, when approached by women, may desire various human pleasures and the fruit of bestowing knowledge during their fertile season. ||2||
The Agnihotra, the Havis sacrifice, and likewise this ritual foundation—these are but the work of illusion, wealth, and heaven; yet one who is afflicted still longs for them.
One who is engaged in ritual actions has fallen under the power of ignorance;
one should recognize that he is afflicted and should release him through wisdom.
One who is constantly devoted to Brahman and disciplined is liberated from such afflictions.
For the embodied being who has conquered the secondary afflictions and mastered his breath, the primary afflictions—
consisting of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas— continue to arise.
The appearance of flashes of inspiration, the hearing [of sounds], and the vision of deities—these, including the whirling and revolving, are designated as the signs of accomplishment (siddhi). ||6||
Knowledge, poetry, and likewise the arts—all these are indeed encompassed by speech;
and the objects of knowledge present themselves [to one who possesses it], which is itself the characteristic of power.
He hears sounds that ought to be heard even from a distance of a hundred yojanas;
he is omniscient, a knower of the ordinances, and a yogi who acts like one intoxicated. ||8||
The great yogi beholds the yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and divine humans;
he knows them and perceives the signs of the obstacles.
If he gazes everywhere at the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, as well as the ṛṣis and the ancestors, one should designate him as insane.
The yogi wanders through delusion, impelled by his inner self;
for one whose intellect is bewildered by delusion, all knowledge perishes. (11)
Worldly affairs destroy the mind even when one is being urged by the inner self;
for one whose intellect is overwhelmed by worldly involvement, all knowledge perishes.
Having covered [the area] with his mind using a white cloth or likewise a woolen blanket, he should then quickly contemplate the Supreme Brahman. 13.
Therefore, a wise person who desires his own success should completely abandon the faults of the self and the calamities that have arisen. 14.
Sages, gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and great Asuras, when beset by calamities, revolve again and again. ||15||
Therefore, the disciplined yogi, moderate in diet and having conquered his senses, should always remain thus;
even while sleeping, he should maintain concentration upon the most subtle [elements] at the crown of his head.
Then, for the yogin who is disciplined in yoga and has conquered sleep, further obstacles known as "vital breaths" (prāṇas) arise at the end. ||17||
He should sustain the entire earth, and immediately thereafter the waters;
then indeed fire, as well as space and the mind of all beings. (18)
Thereafter, the ascetic should diligently maintain a higher state of awareness; having repeatedly observed the signs of those with deficient intellect, he should abandon them. (19)
As he sustains the earth, the earth becomes subtle;
as he sustains the waters, the waters indeed become subtle. Cool essences flow forth, for they are subtle and resemble nectar. ||1.12.20||
For one who maintains the fiery energy (tejas), a subtle energy comes forth;
he considers himself to be that energy and perceives its very nature. ||21||
O Lord, he considers himself to be the wind, like the wind-circle;
for one who sustains space, the subtle ether comes forth.
He perceives a subtle mandala, and his voice proceeds;
he constantly conceives of a self, and the subtle wind proceeds. (23)
Likewise, for one who holds the mind steady, the subtle mind proceeds;
indeed, through the mind he enters the minds of all beings. When he joins the intellect with the intellect, then, having discerned it, he understands. (24)
Having known these seven subtle elements, the wise one who understands yoga renounces them; through his intellect, he shall go to the Supreme. ||25||
Whichever characteristic of sovereignty a being is joined with, he develops attachment to that very thing and is destroyed by it. (26)
Therefore, having understood these subtle things that are mutually entangled, the twice-born who renounces them through his intellect shall attain the Supreme. ||27||

For great-souled seers with divine vision are indeed seen to be attached to subtle states; those [attachments] are designated as faults in them. Therefore, one should never form a definitive judgment regarding subtle matters in this world.
From sovereignty arises passion; dispassion is called Brahman. ||29||
Having understood the seven subtle principles and Maheśvara with his six limbs, one who knows how to apply the *pradhāna* attains the supreme Brahman. ||1.12.30||

Omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, eternal unimpaired power, and infinite power—those who know the sacred injunctions declare these to be the six limbs of the all-pervading Maheśvara. (31)
The one who is constantly devoted to the wealth of Brahman is liberated from calamities.
For the yogi who has conquered the breath and its disturbances and has conquered passion, a single concentration (dhāraṇā) directed outside this body fulfills all desires. 32.
When the disciplined twice-born enters [this state], wherever he may direct his mind,
he can enter even other beings or cause even the three worlds to tremble.
By means of this, one should enter the body, having abandoned the body once again here;
for one should designate the mind as the gateway of yogas and the sun as well.
The Sun is said to be the agent of actions such as taking up [the rays] and so forth.
By this method, the yogi, free from passion and devoid of the subtle body, transcends primordial nature (prakṛti) and is glorified in the world of Rudra. ||35||
But that Lord, having attained the quality of sovereignty and become one with Brahman, turns away from all the stations of the gods in every respect. ||36||
He [conquered] the Piśācas with the Paiśāca weapon, the Rākṣasas with the Rākṣasa,
the Gandharvas with the Gāndharva, and the sons of Kubera with the Kaubera.
One should propitiate Indra with the station of Indra, Soma with the station of Soma, and likewise Prajāpati with the station of Prajāpati. ||38||
In this way, Brahmā also addresses the Lord with a prayer;
yet, being attached there, he becomes intoxicated, and from that, everything proceeds.
Constantly devoted to Brahman and disciplined, he should indeed abandon these stations;
remaining unattached to these stations, the twice-born becomes all-pervading.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of Obstacles to Yoga," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vāyu said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim in detail the qualities of sovereignty, by which specific yoga one may transcend all worlds. ||1||
In that regard, the eightfold sovereignty of the yogis has been proclaimed;
understand all of it as it is being explained in its proper sequence. (2)
Aṇimā, laghimā, and indeed mahimā, as well as prāpti; prākāmya everywhere, and indeed īśitva in all respects. ||3||
Furthermore, mastery everywhere, wherein there is the power to resolve at will—that sovereignty which fulfills all desires is also to be known as being of various kinds. (4)
Both the faulty and the faultless proceed in a subtle manner;
that which is called "faulty" is traditionally held to consist of the nature of the five elements.
Likewise, that which is called the irreproachable is known to consist of the five elements;
the sense organs, the mind, and indeed the ego-sense are also known [to be included therein].
Therein, moreover, that which functions subtly consists of the five elements,
as well as the sense organs, the mind, and what is designated as the intellect and the ego.
Likewise, that which consists of everything and the manifestation residing within the Self—thus, the threefold conjunction operates precisely within the subtle elements. ||8||
Furthermore, even that which possesses eight qualities proceeds within those very same [elements];
I shall describe its nature just as the Lord, the Master, has spoken.
In the three worlds, among all beings, the life-force is known to be impermanent;
yet the subtle power (aṇimā) and the unmanifest (avyakta), upon which everything is established, are eternal.
That which is declared to be difficult for all beings in the three worlds to attain becomes attainable even by yogins through their initial power. (11)
In yoga, its form should always be characterized by sinking and leaping;
moving swiftly through all beings, that is remembered as the second stage.
The attainment of all beings in the three worlds, as well as the power of irresistible will (prākāmya), and also greatness (mahiman) wherever it may be—this is called the third yoga. 13.
In the three worlds, among all beings, he is known as one who has traversed the three worlds;
he enjoys objects of the senses at will and is never obstructed anywhere.
He ordains the pleasure and pain of all beings within the three worlds. ||14||
The knower of yoga becomes the lord everywhere through his discernment;
all beings in the three worlds, including the mobile and the immobile, become subject to him in all undertakings according to his will, yet they may also cease to be so. ||15||
In which [state] there is the power to bring desires to their fulfillment throughout the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile;
and by mere will, the senses may come to be or cease to be.
Sound, touch, taste, smell, form, and likewise the mind, proceed from his will; they do not exist otherwise than by his will.
It is not born, it does not die; it is neither divided nor cut asunder;
it is not burned, it is not deluded, it does not diminish, and it is not stained. ||18||
It is never exhausted, it does not perish, and it never suffers weariness;
it acts everywhere, yet it is never subject to transformation.
But it is devoid of smell, taste, and form, and is free from touch and sound;
for it is indeed colorless and inferior, and never possesses any color whatsoever.
He enjoys the objects of the senses, yet he is not bound by those objects;
for having known the supreme subtle [Self], he attains liberation through that subtlety. ||21||
He is all-pervading because of liberation, and because of his pervasiveness, he is known as Puruṣa;
yet, due to his subtle nature, Puruṣa stands beyond sovereignty. ||22||
But another quality within sovereignty is said to be subtler than all else:
having attained unsurpassed yoga, one reaches unimpeded sovereignty and from that proceeds to liberation, the most subtle and supreme state. ||23||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Sovereign Powers of Yoga," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Vāyu said:
One who has come from such knowledge should not perform action out of passion;
for having experienced either a rajasic or tamasic state therein, one becomes bound to that very same state. ||1||
Likewise, one who has performed good deeds enjoys the fruit in heaven;
then, fallen from that place, he is reborn as a human being. ||2||
Therefore, Brahman is said to be the supreme, the subtle, and the eternal;
one should indeed serve Brahman alone, for Brahman alone is the highest bliss. ||3||
The labor involved in sacrifices is undertaken for a great purpose, yet one falls again under the power of death; therefore, liberation is the supreme happiness.
Moreover, one who is united with meditation and devoted to the sacrifice to Brahman cannot be overcome even in hundreds of Manvantaras.

But having seen that divine Person, named Viśva, whose form is the universe— the Lord of the universe who has the universe for his feet, head, and neck, the creator of the universe, possessing universal fragrance and universal garlands, the Lord who wears the universe as his garment— ||6||

With the rays of light, she unites with the great-souled one who possesses wings, the supreme intellect, the most excellent, the ancient seer, the ruler, subtler than the subtle and greater than the great;
they behold him through yoga, not with the eye—that senseless Puruṣa, golden-hued. (7)

Through reasoning, they indeed perceive the Puruṣa as being without marks (aliṅgin), golden-hued, possessing marks (saliṅgin), devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), conscious, eternal, always omnipresent, pure, immovable, and luminous. ||8||
Purified by that [state] and blazing with splendor, he is without hands, feet, belly, sides, or tongue;
beyond the senses, exceedingly subtle, and one, he sees without eyes and hears without ears. (9)
There is nothing unknown to him, nor does he possess [ordinary] cognition; he knows all, yet he is not an object of knowledge.
They call him the foremost, the great Puruṣa, the conscious one, all-pervading, and most subtle. 1.14.10
All sages, disciplined in mind, perceive with their intellect that she is the source of procreation for all beings, whom they call Prakṛti in this world. ||11||
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, and with ears everywhere, He exists pervading all within this world. 12.
One who is disciplined through yoga perceives the Lord, the eternal one, the Puruṣa who is present everywhere within all beings; therefore, such a meditator is not deluded. ||13||
Having meditated upon that which is the self of all beings, the great self, the supreme self, the imperishable, the self of all, and the highest Brahman, one is indeed not deluded. ||14||

Just as the wind, moving through all forms, is perceivable, so too does he dwell within the city [of the body] and in the cloud; therefore, he is called Puruṣa. Furthermore, he is so named because his attributes are obscured by specific actions. ||15||
Then, indeed, in the womb of Brahmā, joined with semen and blood through the union of male and female, one is born again and again. ||16||
Then, at the time of gestation, that which is called the *kalala* arises; and with the passage of time, the *kalala* further develops into a *budbuda*. ||17||
Just as a lump of clay, pressed upon the wheel by the force of the rotation and shaped by the hands, attains the state of a vessel. ||18||
Thus, joined with a skeleton and impelled by the wind, a human being is born therein; as is the form, so is the mind. (19)
From them, wind arises; from wind, water is produced;
from water, vital breath (prāṇa) comes into being; and from vital breath, semen increases. ||1.14.20||
There are thirty-three parts of blood and fourteen parts of semen;
having made half a *pala* from these portions, one then consumes it during the period of conception.
Then, joined with the embryo and enveloped by the five vital airs,
its form as individual limbs arises from the body of the father.
Then, from his mother’s food—whether drunk, licked, or swallowed—it enters through the channel of the umbilical cord, for this is indeed the support of life for embodied beings. (23)
Afflicted for nine months, with his neck coiled and all his limbs entwined, he has arrived by a sequence that was not of his own choosing;
having dwelt for nine months, he emerges from the opening of the womb facing downward.
Then, due to those sinful actions, he falls into hell,
specifically into the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana) and the Shalmali tree, where there is cutting and tearing.
In that place, there is indeed reviling as well as the consumption of blood;
these are the terrible torments, as unbearable as the Kumbhīpāka hell. (26)
For just as waters that have been separated indeed return to their own nature, so too those who are cut asunder and divided, having reached the place of torment, [return]. ||27||
Thus, the living being, tormented by those evils committed by himself,
shall experience suffering through his actions, or else he shall go to the remaining state.
One must travel alone to the abode of all death, and one must experience [the results] alone; therefore, one should practice virtuous deeds. ||29||
For no one follows him as he sets out and goes;
rather, it is the karma performed by him that follows him. (1.14.30)
In the realm of Yama, their bodies constantly torn asunder, they cry out perpetually due to their union with the undesirable;
their bodies overwhelmed by agony, they wither away through many exceedingly severe torments of unrighteousness. (31)
Whatever is pursued through action, mind, or speech that is desired, may [the deity], being pleased, take away that evil; therefore, one should perform virtuous deeds. ||32||
Whatever kind of sinful past actions have been committed by an embodied being, he encounters a corresponding sixfold world of darkness (tamas). ||33||
From the human state one goes to the state of a beast, from the state of a beast one becomes a deer;
from the state of a deer one enters the state of a bird, and from that, indeed, one becomes a reptile. ||34||
Go from the state of a reptile to the state of a stationary being; of this there is no doubt. Having attained the state of a stationary being once more...
As long as a person remains with eyes open, they are said to whirl right there like a potter's wheel. ||35||
Thus, indeed, from human beings down to the stationary beings at the end of the cycle of existence, that which is known as the tamasic [nature] is to be understood; therein it revolves. ||36||
The worldly existence of embodied beings, beginning with Brahmā and ending with the Piśācas, situated within the realms of heaven, is also proclaimed to be of the nature of sattva. (37)
In the realm of Brahmā there is pure goodness (sattva), while in stationary beings there is pure darkness (tamas);
between the fourteen worlds, passion (rajas) acts as a support.
As the vital points are being severed, for the embodied soul afflicted by pain— ||38||

Then, how will the Brahmin remember the supreme Brahman? Impelled toward contemplation by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of his former dharma, he constantly resorts to human existence; therefore, one should always apply oneself [to meditation]. (39)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Pāśupata," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Vāyu said:
Having understood this mandala of saṃsāra to be of fourteen kinds, one who is oppressed by the fear of saṃsāra should accordingly undertake spiritual action. ||1.15.1||
Then, being whirled about by the wheel of saṃsāra, he remembers;
therefore, one who is constantly disciplined, intent on meditation, and a practitioner of yoga should apply himself to yoga in such a way that he perceives the Self. ||2||
This is the primordial supreme light; this is the unsurpassed bridge.
For this is the expansion of all beings, and it is the eternal non-distinction.
Therefore, one who knows the ritual injunctions should worship this very Self as the bridge, as the fire whose face is turned in every direction, and as that which dwells in the hearts of all beings.
Having properly offered eight oblations with a pure mind focused on Him, and having duly worshipped Vaiśvānara residing in the heart in the prescribed sequence,
one should first sip water once and remain silent while performing the worship.
The first oblation for him is prescribed as being for Prāṇa;
the second is for Apāna, and another for Samāna.
The fourth [offering] is for *udāna*, and the fifth is for *vyāna*.
Having offered the remainder with the utterances of *svāhā*, he should eat it according to his desire.
Then, having sipped water once more, and having performed the threefold *ācamana* (sipping of water), he should touch his heart. ||7||
Oṃ! You are the knot of the vital breaths; Rudra is indeed the self, the destroyer of all beings.
May that Rudra, who is the self, himself nourish these very vital breaths. 8.
You are the eldest even among the gods, you are the fierce one, you are the fourfold bull;
you are the slayer of death for us—may this oblation be auspiciously offered.
Having thus touched his heart, he should place his right hand on his right big toe;
having made it resound, he should touch his navel with that hand.
Then, having sipped water again, he should touch himself all over.
The eyes, the nose, the ears, the heart, and the head—these two, prāṇa and apāna, are declared to be the two selves. ||11||
Of these two, prāṇa is its inner self and apāna is said to be the outer;
thus, prāṇa is food and apāna is both death and life. (12)
Food is to be known as Brahman, as well as the source of the birth of creatures;
from food beings are born, by food their stability is maintained, and by it they grow; therefore it is called "anna" (food). ||13||
For the gods and the Dānavas eat that very food offered into the fire;
indeed, the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas also eat that same food.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Pāśupata," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu. ||1.15||
Vāyu said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the characteristics of pure conduct, by the performance of which a person of purified soul attains heaven after death. ||1||
But for those sages who seek purity, the supreme state is that of water;
the sage who remains vigilant regarding them does not come to grief. (2)
These two—honor and dishonor—are said to be poison and nectar;
therein, dishonor is poison and honor is called nectar. (3)
But he who is vigilant toward these [duties] does not perish; that sage, devoted to the pleasure and welfare of his teacher, should dwell with him for a year. (4)

One should always be vigilant regarding the observances (niyamas) and likewise regarding the restraints (yamas). Having obtained permission and the supreme attainment of knowledge, one may then wander this earth without contradicting the Dharma.
One should walk along a path purified by the eyes, drink water purified by a cloth, and speak words purified by truth; such is the instruction on dharma.
A knower of yoga should never go to a householder's reception at funeral rites or sacrifices;
for such is the reflection that a yogi may thus become non-violent. (7)
When the fire is smokeless and the embers extinguished, when all people have finished their meals, the wise yogi should wander; however, he should not remain constantly among them.
Just as they thus despise him and just as they treat him with contempt,
so should he conduct his life by begging for alms, without violating the dharma of the virtuous.
He should beg for alms from householders and from those families where proper conduct prevails; indeed, this is taught as his most excellent and supreme mode of livelihood.
From this point forward, the twice-born man should practice among householders who are modest, full of faith, self-controlled, learned in the Vedas, and high-souled. ||11||
Furthermore, beyond this, begging for alms from those who are neither corrupt nor fallen, but are of lowly appearance, is declared to be the lowest mode of livelihood.
Alms, rice-gruel, buttermilk, milk, or barley-meal; or cooked fruits and roots, or oil-cake, even according to one's capacity. ||13||
Thus, these indeed have been declared by me as the enhancers of the success of yogins;
among those means of sustenance, when perfected, alms-gathering is remembered as the best.
He who, by begging in accordance with justice, eats a drop of water [the size of] a grain on the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month, is superior to the one previously mentioned.
For all yogins alike, the Cāndrāyaṇa is recorded as the most excellent;
one should perform it once, twice, thrice, or four times, according to one's capacity.
Non-stealing, celibacy, non-attachment, renunciation, and indeed the vows—non-violence is the supreme goal for mendicants. ||17||
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in diet, and constant study of the Vedas—these are proclaimed as the observances (niyamas). ||18||
Born from a womb, possessing a body composed of the qualities (guṇas), and bound by very many karmas, he is treated like an elephant in the forest by human beings. ||19||
Or rather, he is attained very soon, as if restrained by a goad;
for one whose seeds are thus burnt by pure knowledge and who is stainless, being freed from bonds and tranquil, he is designated as "liberated. (1.16.20)

All sacrificial rites are praised by the Vedas; yet they say that for the wise, the chanting of prayers (japa) during sacrifice is supreme. Indeed, meditation free from attachment and the desire for rewards arises from knowledge; when that is attained, there is the realization of the Eternal. ||21||

Self-restraint, tranquility, truthfulness, freedom from blemish, silence, and straightforwardness toward all beings—those whose inner nature is purified by knowledge declare this to be the knowledge of that which transcends the senses, as well as such straightforwardness. (22)

Concentrated in mind, devoted to Brahman, vigilant, pure, delighting in the Self, and having conquered the senses—great sages of vast intellect, blameless and stainless, likewise attain this yoga. (23)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Purity and Conduct," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Vāyu said:
Having abandoned the three stages of life and attained the supreme stage, he reached unsurpassed knowledge at the end of that year. ||1||
Having obtained permission from his guru, he may wander this earth;
he should cultivate that essential knowledge which is effective for realizing what is to be known. ||2||
He who wanders about thinking, "This is knowledge" and "This is the object of knowledge," would not attain the object of knowledge even if his lifespan were a thousand eons. //3//

Having abandoned attachment, conquered anger, eating light food, and having mastered the senses, one should close the doors [of the senses] with the intellect and thus fix the mind upon meditation alone. ||4||
One should always remain constantly disciplined in empty spaces, in caves, in groves, and likewise on the sandy banks of rivers.
The staff of speech, the staff of action, and the staff of mind—these three staves are restrained by him;
he is established as a true bearer of the triple-staff (tridaṇḍin).
Established in the delight of meditation, having conquered the senses and abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious actions,
one who has cast off this body according to the scriptures is never again born nor does one ever die.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Attainment of the Supreme Stage of Life," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vāyu said:
Henceforth, I shall declare here the definitive rules for ascetics regarding those expiations which are performed unintentionally, according to their true nature;
moreover, people who know the subtle dharma have also spoken concerning those committed intentionally. ||1||
And evil is said to be threefold, arising from speech, mind, and body;
for by this, day and night, this world is constantly bound. (2)
"Neither actions nor even this [self] remain," so says the supreme scripture;
for one must employ [the self] for only a moment, since its lifespan is being sustained. ||3||
One should be steadfast and vigilant, for yoga is indeed the supreme strength.
Indeed, nothing superior to yoga is seen here among men;
therefore, the wise who are devoted to dharma praise yoga. ||4||
Having crossed over ignorance by means of knowledge and attained unsurpassed sovereignty, the wise, having seen that which is both higher and lower, go to that supreme state. ||5||
Whatever vows belong to the monks, as well as their secondary vows—
for each one of these that is transgressed, an expiation is prescribed.
Having approached a woman out of lust, one should prescribe an expiation;
likewise, one should perform the Sāntapana penance accompanied by breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Then, at the conclusion of his arduous penance, being composed in mind, he follows the instruction;
having returned again to the hermitage, the mendicant should practice without sloth.
For the wise declare that one does not strike another with words that pierce the vital organs.
Nevertheless, one must not engage in this practice, for it is a terrible consequence;
there is no unrighteousness greater than the transgression of a day and night—so says the sacred revelation.
For this [taking of wealth] is considered the greatest violence by the gods and likewise by the sages;
for that which is called "wealth" consists of the very life-breaths moving outside the body.
He who takes away another's wealth takes away his life-breaths.
Having acted thus, that evil-minded one, whose conduct has become corrupted and who has fallen from his vow,
should again fall into despondency and perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

According to the scripture, he should do so for a year according to the prescribed rule; then, at the end of that year, having further diminished his impurities and having attained renewed detachment, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow. 12.
Non-violence toward all beings through action, thought, and speech is the rule;
yet if a mendicant should harm animals or wild beasts even unintentionally,
he should perform the Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, or the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If an ascetic, upon seeing a woman, should experience a weakening of his senses,
he must certainly perform sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) to sustain himself.
For a Brahmin who has emitted semen during the day, an expiation is prescribed:
a fast for three nights as well as one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). ||15||
If one has emitted semen at night, he becomes pure by bathing and performing twelve dhāraṇās;
thus, with his soul purified through prāṇāyāma, the twice-born man becomes free from passion. ||16||
Food prepared for only one person, honey, meat, as well as a funeral feast (śrāddha) consisting of raw food, and salt that is visible [in the dish]—these are not to be eaten by ascetics (yatins). 17.
For the transgression of each one of these, an expiation is prescribed:
by means of the Prājāpatya penance, one is then liberated from that sin. ||18||
Furthermore, regarding whatever transgressions may arise from speech, mind, or body, one should deliberate with the virtuous and act according to what they say. 19.
With purified intellect, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, and moving with equanimity among all beings, he is absorbed in meditation;
having gone to that eternal, constant, and imperishable supreme state of the virtuous, he is indeed not born again. (1.18.20)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Rule for the Atonement of Ascetics," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vāyu said:
Henceforth I shall proclaim the signs of impending death;
learn them, by which specific knowledge one perceives one's own mortality. ||1||
That man who cannot see Arundhatī, Dhruva, the shadow of the moon (Soma-chāyā), and the Great Path (Mahāpatha) shall not live beyond one year.
He who sees the sun as devoid of rays and the purifier (fire) as possessed of rays shall not live beyond eleven months.
If one vomits urine or cow-dung, or likewise gold or silver—
whether witnessed directly or in a dream— one lives for ten months.
If one's footprint appears broken either in front or behind,
whether on dusty ground or in mud, he shall live for seven months.
If a crow, a pigeon, a vulture, or any other carnivorous bird should alight upon one's head,
six months shall not pass before that person dies.
If one is bound by two rows of ants, or again by a shower of dust,
or if one sees a distorted shadow, he shall live for four or five days.
If one should see lightning in a cloudless sky situated in the southern direction, or even a rainbow in the north, he lives for three or two [days]. (8)
He who does not see his own reflection in water or in a mirror,
or likewise sees himself without a head, shall not live beyond a month.
If his body should smell like a corpse or even like fat, death has indeed approached him;
he shall live for only half a month.
If one's wind is disordered such that it cuts through the vital points (*marmasthāna*), and if he does not feel refreshed when touched by water, death has arrived for him. (11)
If one dreams that he is traveling toward the southern direction in a chariot yoked with bears and monkeys while singing, one should know that death has arrived. ||12||
If, in a dream, a woman who is dark-complexioned, wears black garments, and is singing should lead one toward the southern direction, he does not survive.
If a man sees in his dream a garment that is torn, black, or has holes, or if he sees his ear broken, he should know that death is at hand. (14)
But he who sinks into a sea of mud up to the surface of his head,
having seen such a dream, does not live even for a moment.
He who for ten nights sees ashes, charcoal, hair, a dried-up river, or serpents— such a person shall not live.
He who, in a dream, is struck with stones by hideous men of dark complexion with upraised weapons, does not live long.
If at sunrise, at the break of dawn, a female jackal approaches visibly and directly toward a man while howling, that man shall have reached the end of his life.
If, immediately upon being bathed, one's heart is greatly distressed and a tingling sensation arises in the teeth, one should declare that person's life has come to an end. ||19||
He who breathes more and more frequently, whether by night or by day,
and does not perceive the scent of a lamp, should know that death has arrived.
If one should see a rainbow at night or a circle of stars during the day,
or if one does not see oneself in the eyes of others, that person does not live.
He whose one eye weeps, whose ears have fallen from their places, and whose nose has become crooked, should be known as one whose life has departed. ||22||
He whose tongue is black and rough, whose face indeed has the luster of mud, and whose cheeks are flattened and red—for him, death has arrived. ||23||
That man who goes toward the southern direction with disheveled hair, laughing, singing, and dancing, his life comes to an end there.
He whose sweat repeatedly arises resembling white mustard seeds has death standing near him. (25)
If camels or even donkeys are yoked to one's enemy's chariot, that is inauspicious;
he for whom this occurs shall not live if he goes facing the south.
And here, there are two supreme omens of death; this form becomes the ultimate sign:
one does not hear any sound in the ear, nor does one see light with the eyes. (27)
If one falls into a pit in a dream and there is no door for him, and he does not emerge from that pit of dogs, his life has reached its end. ||28||

The gaze is upward and unsteady; the tongue is red and curling back; there is heat in the mouth and a hollow in the navel; the urine is extremely hot, and the patient remains in a precarious state. (29)
Whether by day or by night, he who is struck down visibly shall see his slayer; thus struck, he does not survive.
That man who enters the fire at the end of a dream,
and no longer retains his memory, his life has reached its end.
But that man who sees his own white garment as red or even black in a dream—for him, death has arrived. ||32||
When that body, which indicates the approaching end, has reached its time, the wise man should abandon fear and despondency and rise up. ||33||
Having gone out either toward the eastern or the northern direction, being pure,
he should remain in a level, very firm place that is secluded and devoid of people.
Facing either north or east, composed and having sipped water according to the rules,
seated in the svastika posture and having paid homage to Maheśvara,
one should hold the body, head, and neck straight and must not look about. (35)
Just as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker—that is the simile remembered—therefore, the knower of yoga should apply himself in a place sloping toward the northeast. 36.

One should always take delight in the vital breath (prāṇa), as well as in the eyes, the sense of touch, the ears, the mind, and the intellect; likewise, one should fix [the mind] upon the chest. Through the yoga of such concentration, the vital air (vāyu) flows everywhere for him. ||37||

Having understood time, the nature of things, and the entire aggregate in every respect—as well as the twelvefold internal [elements]—this is called the practice of yoga-concentration (yogadhāraṇa). ||38||
One should maintain the concentration (dhāraṇā) upon the crown of the head for either one hundred or eight hundred [breaths];
through that yoga of concentration, the vital air (vāyu) flows everywhere. ||39||
Then, being composed, one should fill the body with the syllable Oṃ;
thus, the yogi who consists of Oṃ shall not perish, but become imperishable.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Ariṣṭas," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu. ||1.19||
Vāyu said:
Henceforth, I shall explain the characteristics of attaining the syllable Oṃ;
this should be understood as having three morae (mātrās), and its consonant here is accompanied by its vowel.

The first measure is known as the luminous (vaidyutī), the second is remembered as the dark (tāmasī), and one should know the third measure to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇī) and leading to the Imperishable (akṣaragāminī). ||2||
It should be known as the Gandharvī, arising from the Gāndhāra note;
its touch is like that of an ant, and when applied, it is perceived at the crown of the head. ||3||
When the syllable Oṃ is thus applied, it dissolves into the crown of the head;
likewise, the yogi who consists of Oṃ indeed becomes imperishable within the Imperishable. 4.
The syllable Om is the bow, the self is indeed the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its target.
With undistracted mind, one must strike it; like the arrow, one shall become absorbed in That.
"Om"—this is the single-syllabled Brahman, the station deposited in the secret cave.
"Om"—this is the three Vedas, the three worlds, the three fires;
it is these three strides of Viṣṇu, as well as the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus verses. (6)
In this regard, four measures (mātrās) should be understood according to the ultimate truth;
the yogi who is disciplined therein shall attain residence in the same world as that [deity]. ||7||
The letter *a* should be known as unchanging (*akṣara*); the letter *u* is remembered as the circumflex (*svarita*);
and the letter *m* should be known as protracted (*pluta*), designated as having three morae (*trimātra*). ||8||
The letter *a* is the world of the earth (*bhūrloka*), while *u* is said to be the world of the atmosphere (*bhuvar*).
And the letter *m*, together with its consonant, is prescribed as the heavenly world (*svarloka*).
The syllable Oṃ is the three worlds; its head is the triple heaven (triviṣṭapa). That which extends to the end of the universe is called the state of Brahman (brāhma padam). || 1.20.10 ||
The state with measure is indeed the world of Rudra, while the measureless is the state of Śiva;
thus, through this specific form of meditation, they worship that state. (11)
Therefore, one who desires the eternal state should always take delight in meditation upon that imperishable syllable, which is indeed measureless; for it must be worshipped with diligent effort. 12.
The first measure is short, and immediately after that, the long;
thereafter, the third is taught as being protracted.
These measures should be understood correctly and in their proper sequence;
indeed, they should be maintained only as long as they can be sustained.
He who always meditates upon the senses, the mind, and the intellect within the Self—
even if he should hear [this] for only eight measures here, he shall obtain the fruit.
Even if one were to perform the horse sacrifice every month for a hundred years, one would not attain that merit which one obtains by even a fraction [of this practice]. (16)
If a man were to drink a drop [of water] from the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month for a full hundred years, he would obtain that same measure [of merit]. (17)
One shall obtain that fruit which results from sacrifices performed for one's own desire or for public benefit, from truthful speech, and from the non-eating of meat—even in small measure. (18)
Whatever fruit is seen to belong to heroes who fight for the sake of their master and do not retreat, one shall obtain a portion of that. ||19||
One would not obtain that fruit through such fierce austerity nor through sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees as one would properly obtain it by means of this measured practice.
In that regard, that which is taught as having a half-mora and that which is called "protracted" (pluta)—this very [measure] should be employed by householders who are practitioners of yoga. ||21||
And this very [practice] is especially characterized by sovereignty;
for it is specifically within the eightfold sovereignty of yogins—beginning with *aṇimā* and the rest—that it is to be known. Therefore, O twice-born one, one should apply oneself to that. 22.
For thus the twice-born yogi who is disciplined, pure, self-controlled, and has conquered his senses, finds the Self; and he who finds the Self finds everything. (23)
Through the knowledge of yoga, a Brahmin who contemplates with meditation attains the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the Upaniṣads. (24)
Having become the dissolution of all beings, that yogi, though himself non-existent, is born;
having performed the transition, he indeed goes to the eternal state. ||25||
Moreover, having seen with his divine eye the primordial nature (prakṛti) called Viśvarūpa, which has four arms and four faces, while meditating upon it here; ||26||
This unborn one—red, white, and black—producing many offspring of her own form;
indeed, one unborn one, rejoicing in her, lies beside her, while another unborn one abandons her once she has been enjoyed.
[He is] the eight-syllabled one, with sixteen hands and feet, four faces, three peaks, and a single horn.
Having known the primordial, unborn one, who is the very nature of the creators of the universe, the wise attain immortality;
those Brahmins who realize the Praṇava do not transmigrate here again. (27)
This imperishable Brahman, known by the name of the supreme Oṃkāra—whosoever knows it correctly or likewise meditates upon it again [attains liberation]. ||28||
Having cast off the wheel of saṃsāra and being released from the bonds of bondage, one attains without doubt the auspicious, immovable state that is beyond the guṇas.
Thus indeed has this characteristic of attaining the syllable Oṃ been declared by me. 29.
Homage to Lokeśvara, who grasps the conceptualizations of thought; that which is beneficial for you approaches the Great One—homage to Brahmā!
And homage to the one who abides everywhere, who is devoid of qualities, and who is the Lord of the masters of yoga through devotion.

One should approach the pure Brahman, which is like a lotus leaf untouched by water; it is the purifier among purifiers, filled with the purifier, [contemplating] the short, long, and protracted [vowels] through that purifier. One should worship this very syllable *Oṃ*—which is soundless, touchless, formless, tasteless, and scentless—with the mantra: "To the Lord of Ignorance, the Universal Form! Salutation to Him, the Lord of Ignorance! Salutation to the Lord of Yogins! And: "By whom the fierce heaven and the firm earth were made stable, by whom the thundering sky and the intermediate space between them were established."

Viśvarūpa is the heart of the most excellent gods; there is no comparison for his out-breath and in-breath. Oṃkāra is indeed the Universal-Universal, and the sacrifice is the Universal-Universal. The Veda is indeed the sacrifice; the Veda is indeed the salutation (namaskāra). Rudra is the salutation. Homage to Rudra, the sovereign lord of the masters of yoga. Thus is the presence of accomplishment. "Homage" is [to be recited] in the evening, in the morning, and at midday.
The Great Rudra is the granter of the fruits of all desires.
Just as a ripe fruit falls from its stalk when stirred by the wind, so too is sin destroyed by the salutation of Rudra. 1.20.30.
Just as the salutation to Rudra is certain to yield the fruit of all dharmas, the salutation to another deity would not obtain that same fruit. //31//
Therefore, the yogi should worship Maheśvara three times a day;
[he should worship] the Brahman that expands the ten [directions], as well as the expansive Brahman.
At all times and in every way, the Lord ordained the syllable Oṃ;
through that very [syllable], the one of great glory established Viṣṇu-hood and the act of salutation.
Salutation likewise praises the Lord as the Praṇava;
the sacrifice praises the Praṇava, and salutation praises the sacrifice.
Rudra indeed praises salutation; therefore, the state of Rudra is auspicious.
These indeed are the secrets of the ascetics in their proper order;
he who understands this meditation shall attain the supreme state. ||35||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Attaining the Oṃkāra," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Among the sages who resembled fire and dwelt in the Naimiṣa forest,
there was a wise sage named Sāvarṇi by name, who possessed a retentive memory for what he had heard.
Standing before them, Vāyu, who was skilled in speech,
approached that one of great splendor with humility and questioned him as he was performing there with constant diligence for the sake of the patrons of the sacrificial session.
Sāvarṇi said:
O All-pervading One, through your grace, we desire to hear correctly this ancient narrative, which is firmly established and equal to the Vedas, from you who perceive all things.
How did the Lord Hiraṇyagarbha obtain from his forehead the god Nīlalohita as his own son? ||4||
And how did the Blessed One come to know Brahmā, who is born from the lotus? Furthermore, how did he [know] the state of Rudra with respect to his own son, the All-pervading One?
And how, O Viṣṇu, is there such unsurpassed affection between you and Rudra?
All the gods consist of Viṣṇu; all the Gaṇas consist of Viṣṇu.
"No other goal equal to Viṣṇu is ordained"—thus the gods constantly sing, of this there is no doubt;
Hari perpetually offers salutation at the side of Bhava. (7)
Sūta said:
When this had been said, the Blessed Vāyu spoke to Sāvarṇi:
"O virtuous one, it is well that you have asked this most excellent question. (8)
Just as he became the son of Bhava and the lotus-born source of Brahmā, so too did he become Rudra and Śaṅkara. (9)
Through both of these, there is the favor of Viṣṇu and Bhava as well;
and whatever [merit] one constantly performs by bowing down to Śaṅkara.
Listen as I speak to you in detail and in proper sequence.
O best of the twice-born, at the conclusion of the seventh Manvantara of the great-souled one, there was a Kalpa named Padya;
of those [Kalpas], the present one is Vārāha, of which I shall speak in detail.
Sāvarṇi said:
In what length of time does a kalpa come into being, and how? What is the measure of a kalpa? Tell this to us who ask you. (12)
Vāyu said:
I shall now briefly declare the sequential duration of the seven Manvantaras; listen as I speak. (13)
Two thousand crores, eight hundred crores,
sixty-two crores, and seventy million—
this is the total number declared for half a kalpa. (14)
One should declare the attained age in years by subtracting the previously mentioned [periods of] loss of qualities:
one hundred times ten million, seventy-eight times ten million, two hundred thousand, and ninety hundred-thousand (ninety lakhs). (15)
According to human measurement, as far as the interval of Vaivasvata is concerned,
this is to be known as a Kalpa, which is twice the measure of half a Kalpa.
This same measurement, applied respectively to the seven future [kalpas], should be understood as the duration of time; such is the doctrine of the Lord. (17)
In measure, there are fifty-eight niyutas, as well as eight hundred and eighty-four prayutas. ||18||
The seven ṛṣis, Manu himself, and the gods headed by Indra—this is to be understood as the measure of the end of the year of Time. 19.
Thus, a Manvantara is proclaimed to be the limit of their human lifespan.
Those gods who end with the Praṇava, the Sādhyas who are hosts of deities,
and the Viśvedevas who are eternal— these groups live for the duration of a Kalpa.
This current aeon (kalpa) that is proceeding is celebrated as the Vārāha;
it is in this that the fourteen Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, reside.
The sages said:
For what reason is this eon proclaimed by name as the Varāha-kalpa, and for what cause is the Lord celebrated as Varāha? ||22||
Who indeed was the Blessed One as a boar? Of what was he the source, and of what nature was he?
How did the boar come into being? We wish to know this. (23)
Vāyu said:
How the Boar was born, for what purpose he was conceived,
how the Vārāha Kalpa came to be, its nature as a kalpa, and the very conception of it— [all this shall be told].
I shall fully declare everything concerning the interval between the two Kalpas, as well as that which is imagined regarding this [present] one, exactly as it was seen and exactly as it was heard.
The first kalpa at the beginning of the world was formerly known as Bhava;
here, Ānanda himself is now to be understood as the Lord. (26)
This divine station of Brahmā has been attained, or it is born of the divine;
the second is called Bhuvaḥ-kalpa, and the third is called Tapaḥ. ||27||
Bhava is to be known as the fourth, and Rambha as the fifth;
likewise, the sixth is Ṛtukalpa, while the seventh is remembered as Kratu. ||28||
The eighth is Vahni, the ninth is Havyavāhana;
the tenth kalpa is Sāvitra, and the eleventh is remembered as Bhūva. ||29||
Uśika was the twelfth there, and Kuśika was the thirteenth;
the fourteenth was Gandharva, where indeed the Gandharva Svara was born, as well as Nāda, and where the Gandharvas arose.
O twice-born ones, that fifteenth Kalpa should be known as Ṛṣabha, wherein the Ṛṣis were born and the musical tone was enchanting to the world. 31.
The sixth eon was indeed Ṣaḍja, where the ṛṣis were the Ṣaḍjanas;
it consisted of the seasons of Śiśira, Vasanta, Nidāgha, and Varṣa.
Śarad and Hemanta—these were the sons of Brahmā born of his mind;
they emerged as the perfected Ṣaḍjas in the sixteenth kalpa.
Because Maheśvara was born immediately upon the birth of those six, the musical note Ṣaḍja, resembling the ocean, arose from that. ||34||
Then the seventeenth kalpa is known as Mārjālīya;
it is called Mārjālīya because he performed that purificatory rite (mārjanīya) for Brahmā.
Next, the eighteenth is called the Kalpa named Madhyama;
in which the note named Madhyama, honored by Dhaivata, was produced among all beings from the Self-existent One himself. ||36||
Then the nineteenth kalpa is known as Vairājaka,
wherein the venerable sage Vairāja was indeed the son of Brahmā.
His son was the righteous and virtuous Dadīci,
a lord of creatures of great splendor who became a ruler of the gods.
The Gāyatrī desired Prajāpati as her husband;
from him was born Svara, the smooth son of that Dadhīci. (39)

Then the twentieth kalpa was proclaimed as Niṣāda. Having seen that [creation] originating from the Self-born Prajāpati, he then desisted from creating further progeny, and Niṣāda performed austerities.
For a thousand divine years, remaining without food and with his senses subdued,
Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds and possessed of great splendor, spoke to him.
To his son, who stood with arms upraised, emaciated by asceticism, suffering, and afflicted by hunger and thirst,
the Grandfather said, "Sit down.
From that he became a Niṣāda, and his voice was that of a Niṣāda.
O twice-born ones, the twenty-first section should be known as the fifth;
it consists of Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna.
These five mind-born sons of Brahmā were equal to Brahmā himself;
by them, through eloquent and meaningful words, Maheśvara was propitiated.
Since it was sung by those five high-souled ones who were surrounded [by him],
and since the fifth note (*svara*) is smooth (*snigdha*), therefore the *kalpa* is the fifth.
The twenty-second kalpa is to be known as Meghavāhana,
wherein the mighty-armed Viṣṇu, having become a cloud, bore Maheśvara,
the wearer of the animal skin, for a thousand divine years.
As he was sighing, oppressed by the burden, there emerged from his mouth a massive-bodied Kāla, the illuminator of the worlds—
he who is recited by the Brahmins as Viṣṇu, the son of Kaśyapa.
The twenty-third kalpa should be known as Cintaka; the illustrious Prajāpati-suta and Citī were its two progenitors. 48.
Because this thought arose from Brahmā while he was meditating,
that Kalpa was indeed called Cintaka by the Self-born One.
The twenty-fourth is indeed called the Ākūti Kalpa;
and the goddess Ākūti likewise came into being as a pair [with her consort].
Because Prajāpati spoke with the intention (*ākūti*) to create progeny, that Puruṣa should be known as Ākūti, designated by the name Kalpa. ||51||
The twenty-fifth Kalpa is proclaimed as Vijñāti; from the god Vijñāti and his consort, a pair of twins is born. (52)
As he was meditating with a mind intent on obtaining a son, there arose within him a realization known as "inner consciousness" (adhyātma-saṃjñita);
having understood this in its essence, he was thereafter remembered as Vijñāta.
Then the twenty-sixth Kalpa is designated as "Mind" (Manas);
there, the goddess named Śāṅkarī gives birth to a pair.
When Prajāpati was indeed desirous of creating offspring, he was born from the Self-existent (Svayambhū) through the manifestation of progeny;
therefore, this manifestation of being is known as Prajāsambhavana. ||55||
The twenty-seventh kalpa was indeed named Bhāva;
then the goddess Paurṇamāsī became united with him as a couple.
While Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, desiring to create progeny, was meditating upon the Supreme Lord, the Paramātman, with supreme meditation; ||57||
But Agni, having become circular and enveloped in a network of rays, supports both the earth and the heavens and blazes forth with his great body. 58.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, when the circle of light was complete,
he beheld the solar orb arisen together with the Avisthā constellation.
Because the divine Lord Sūrya, with his full orb, was seen by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, even though he is invisible to all living beings. ||1.21.60||
Since all the yogas and mantras have arisen together with the mandala, and since this ritual manual (kalpa) has been seen [therein], it is therefore called "Darśa. ||61||
Because the blessed Lord Soma was formerly fully present in the mind of the supreme Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, it is therefore known as Paurṇamāsī.
Therefore, for the sake of their own welfare, yogis should indeed perform the Parva on the new moon and the Paurṇamāsa on the full moon during both fortnights.
Those twice-born who perform the New Moon and Full Moon sacrifices shall never return from the world of Brahmā.
One who has not maintained the sacred fires, or one who is pure even while traveling on a hero’s path,
should concentrate his mind intensely and slowly recite the mantra.
"O Agni, you are Rudra, the Asura of the great heaven; you are Śarva, you rule over the host of Maruts;
you are Pūṣan, the Gandharva of the noose, who provides protection with his bow.
Thus the twice-born should properly recite this mantra in his mind.
He who enters the fire goes to the world of Rudra. ||66||
"Soma is indeed Agni, and the Blessed One is Time, Rudra"—so says the Śruti.
Therefore, whoever enters the fire does not return from Rudra.
The twenty-eighth Kalpa is known as Bṛhat;
it belongs to Brahmā, who, desiring sons and wishing to create progeny,
meditated in his mind upon the Bṛhat Sāman and the Rathantara.
Because the Bṛhat [fire] arises there, facing in all directions, therefore this Kalpa of Bṛhat should be understood by those who contemplate reality. (69)
The supreme solar orb is to be known as eighty-eight thousand yojanas in measurement;
from that, the Egg (the universe) is to be known as the indivisible solar orb.
Having pierced through the sphere of the sun, the Bṛhat Sāman is further divided;
having thus pierced through, the twice-born whose souls are united in yoga and who are firm in their vows proceed.
Others, having reached the Saṅghāta [region], attain other kalpas during the Rathantara.
Thus has this wonderful vision of the supreme self been proclaimed by me;
hereafter, I shall explain in detail the auspicious Kalpas.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Kalpas," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
The sages said:
O Great Sage, all this is most wonderful; you have indeed fully explained this secret, as well as the ritual application of the mantras, at the end of the kalpas. || 1 ||
There is nothing in the three worlds that is unknown to you;
therefore, tell us in detail all the enumerations of the kalpas.
Vāyu said:
In this regard, I shall describe to you the enumeration of the kalpas, as well as the extent of the yugas and the years of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, exactly as they are.
One thousand kalpas are proclaimed to be a single year of Brahmā;
eight thousand such years are remembered as one yuga of Brahmā.
One thousand yugas constitute a single *savana* of Prajāpati;
and a thousand *savanas*, doubled and likewise tripled, [constitute his full lifespan].
All this has been proclaimed regarding the period of Brahmā’s duration;
I shall now declare its numerical measure in due order.
Regarding those twenty-eight kalpas that have been proclaimed by name,
I shall hereafter describe their designations in due order.
Now listen to the names of the Rathantara Sāman at its conclusion,
and the origin of the mantra belonging to each.
The nineteenth kalpa is to be known as Śrutilohita,
in which Brahmā likewise meditated upon that supreme dhyāna.
Wearing a white turban, white garlands, and white garments, with his topknot intact, the Kumāra of great splendor was born, resembling a fire. ||1.22.10||
His face was terrifying, most fierce, and exceedingly dreadful, white and red;
it was blazing with a radiant body, possessing a great mouth and white splendor.
Having seen him, the illustrious Puruṣa, Brahmā indeed whose face is on all sides,
beheld the youth, the sustainer of the worlds, the one of universal form, Maheśvara.
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, long worshipped the ancient Puruṣa, the God who is the soul of the universe and the Lord of the gods of gods, for the sake of the yogins.
Having placed Mahādeva, the Supreme Self, the Lord, within his heart,
Brahmā then meditated upon the Brahman as Sadyojāta.
Having realized this, the Lord of Gods, the Master of the World, was delighted and let out a laugh.
Then, from his side, there appeared great-souled white sages, endowed with the splendor of Brahman, adorned with white garlands and unguents. ||15||
Sunanda, Nandaka, Viśvananda, and then Nandana—
these were indeed his high-souled disciples by whom Brahman was subsequently chosen.
Before him was born the great sage named Śveta, who possessed a white complexion and great splendor; from him this man was born.

There, all those sages— who are twice-born, devoted to breath control, disciplined, and resolute in Brahman— behold Maheśvara as Sadyojāta, and from him, indeed, they behold the god Viśveśvara. ||18||
All of them, liberated from sin, stainless, and endowed with the splendor of Brahman, transcend the world of Brahmā and proceed to the realm of Brahmā. ||19||
Vāyu said:
Then the thirtieth eon is proclaimed by the name Rakta;
there, the one of great splendor, Rakta, assumed a red complexion.
As Brahmā Parameṣṭhin was meditating with a desire for a son,
there appeared a youth of great splendor, with a red body,
wearing red garlands and garments, possessing red eyes, and full of majesty. ||21||
Having seen that Mahādeva Kumāra clad in red garments,
he attained the highest state of meditative yoga and realized the Lord as the universe itself.
Having bowed down to him, the Blessed Brahmā, being supremely self-restrained,
then meditated upon Vāmadeva as the very essence of Brahman.
When Mahādeva had been thus meditated upon by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin with a mind full of affection, he then spoke to the Grandfather.
O best of beings, because I, your grandfather, was seen here by you while meditating with supreme devotion and through the yoga of meditation, desiring a son; (25)
"Therefore, having attained supreme meditation, you, a great ascetic, shall know me in age after age as the Great Being, the Lord and Sustainer of the worlds.
Having spoken thus, Śarva then let out a loud, boisterous laugh.
Then there were born to him four high-souled sons, who were themselves great-souled and shone with pure intellects. ||27||
Virajas and Vivāha, Viśoka and Viśvabhāvana;
they were devoted to Brahman, equal to Brahmā, heroic, and resolute. ||28||
All of them wore red garments, were adorned with red garlands and unguents;
their limbs were smeared with red ashes, and their faces and eyes were red. ||29||
Then, at the end of a thousand years,
those high-souled ones, devoted to Brahman and resolute, were chanting that Vāmadevya hymn of the Veda.

Having themselves imparted the entirety of the instruction on dharma for the sake of favoring the worlds and out of a desire for the welfare of their disciples, those brahmins re-entered the great god Rudra, the imperishable.
And those other best of the twice-born who, practicing yoga, take refuge in the auspicious Lord Mahādeva—being his devotees and devoted solely to him. ||32||
All of them, freed from sin, stainless, and endowed with the splendor of Brahman,
shall go to the world of Rudra, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Number of Kalpas," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vāyu said:
The thirty-first Kalpa is known as Pītavāsas (the Yellow-Robed),
wherein the Greatly Resplendent Brahmā assumed a yellow complexion.
As Brahmā Parameṣṭhin was meditating with a desire for a son,
a youth of great splendor appeared, clothed in yellow garments.
His limbs were anointed with yellow sandalwood paste, he wore yellow garlands, was young, possessed a yellow sacred thread, a yellow turban, and mighty arms. ||3||
Seeing that Lord, the Master of the World, absorbed in meditation, Brahmā,
the Sustainer of the Worlds, mentally paid homage to the Supreme Lord.
Then, absorbed in meditation there, he beheld the supreme cow of Maheśvara, who was multiform and had issued from the mouth of Maheśvara. ||5||
She who has four feet, four faces, four hands, and four breasts;
who has four eyes, four horns, four tusks, and four mouths;
who is endowed with the thirty-two worlds, the sovereign goddess facing in every direction.
Having seen that great goddess Maheśvarī, the immensely radiant Mahādeva,
who is saluted by all the gods, spoke to her again.
Singing again and again, "O Mati! O Smṛti! O Buddhi!", the Great Goddess rose up with palms joined in reverence, crying out, "Come, come! ||8||
Enveloping the universe with your yoga, bring the entire world under your control;
or else, you shall become Rudrāṇī together with Mahādeva,
and for the sake of the welfare of the Brahmins, you shall become the Supreme Reality.
Then, while the Supreme Lord was meditating with a desire for a son,
the Lord of the gods of gods bestowed upon him that Great Goddess who consists of four quarters.
Thereupon, through the yoga of meditation, he recognized her as the Supreme Sovereign.
Brahmā, who is worthy of worship by the worlds, having approached that Great Goddess Maheśvarī and then meditated upon the Raudrī Gāyatrī, remained perfectly self-controlled.
Having recited this Vedic knowledge, the Raudrī Gāyatrī,
which is dedicated to the Great Goddess and honored in the world of Rudra,
he took refuge in Mahādeva with a mind absorbed in meditation.
Then Mahādeva again remembered his divine yoga and once more bestowed upon him sovereignty, the perfection of knowledge, and dispassion. ||13||
Then the Lord let out a terrifying, blazing laugh;
thereupon, radiant youths appeared from him on all sides.
Wearing yellow garlands and garments, anointed with yellow perfumes and unguents, they have yellow turbans upon their heads, yellow faces, and yellow hair. ||15||
Then, after having dwelt there for a thousand years, those of stainless vigor,
whose souls were absorbed in yoga, bathed and became well-wishers of the Brahmins.
Endowed with the power of union with the Dharma, they taught the yoga of the sages who perform long sacrificial sessions and then entered into Rudra, the Lord.
In this manner, those others who have taken refuge in Maheśvara according to this rule—being self-restrained, engaged in meditation, and having conquered their senses—[attain the same goal]. ||18||
Having cast off all evil, stainless and endowed with the splendor of Brahman,
they enter Mahādeva, O Rudra, never to be born again.
Then, when that Pītavarṇa Kalpa of Svayambhū had passed away,
another commenced, known by the name of the Śitakalpa.
When the world was thus enveloped in a single ocean for a thousand divine years,
Brahmā, desiring to create living beings, became distressed and began to reflect.
As that lord, desiring a son, was thus reflecting while meditating upon the Supreme Lord, his complexion became dark.
Then the one of great splendor beheld a boy who had appeared,
dark-complexioned, possessed of great heroism, and blazing with his own radiance.
He wore excellent black garments and a black turban, had a black sacred thread, was endowed with a black crown, and was adorned with black garlands and unguents. ||24||
Having seen that high-souled, immortal, and formidable minister,
