he paid homage to the Lord of the gods of gods, the Lord of the universe, who is dark and tawny.

Devoted to breath-control (prāṇāyāma), the illustrious one, having placed Maheśvara within his heart and being joined with mental meditation, took refuge in the Lord of Ascetics; then Brahmā, contemplating Brahman itself, uttered "Aghora. (26)
While the supreme Brahmā Parameṣṭhin was meditating in this manner,
the blessed Lord Rudra let out a loud, boisterous laugh.
Then, by his side, there appeared four great-souled youths who were dark-complexioned and adorned with dark garlands and unguents.
They were dark-complexioned, with black turbans, black faces, and black garments;
from them arose a great, boisterous laughter and abundant sounds of "hūṃ," as well as a mighty salutation uttered again and again. ||29||
Then, at the end of a thousand years, having worshipped that supreme state of the Lord through yoga, those highly fortunate ones transmitted it to their disciples.
Through yoga, those perfected in yoga, having entered Śiva with their minds, have entered the stainless, attributeless abode, the Lord of the universe. ||31||
In this same manner, by means of this yoga, those other twice-born ones who know the ritual procedure and remember [this] shall go to the imperishable Rudra.
Then, when that terrifying Kṛṣṇa-kalpa had passed,
another kalpa was set in motion, known by the name Viśvarūpa.
But when the dissolution had ceased and the world of moving and non-moving beings was created again,
Sarasvatī— of universal form and accompanied by a great sound— manifested herself as the supreme lord Brahmā meditated, desiring a son.
Wearing a universal garland and universal garments, with a universal sacred thread, a universal turban, universal fragrance, and a universal abode, he possessed mighty arms. (35)
Then, having meditated upon him with his mind, the Grandfather, with a disciplined soul,
paid homage to the divine Īśāna, the Lord of all, the omnipresent Sovereign.

"O Īśāna, salutations to you; O Mahādeva, let there be salutations to you. To the Grandfather (Brahmā), who was thus absorbed in meditation and bowing there, the Blessed Lord Īśa said: "I am pleased with you; what do you desire?"
Then, having bowed down and praised Maheśvara with words,
the blessed Brahmā, being pleased, spoke with a joyful heart.
That you are the one of universal form, moving everywhere, and the Lord of all—this I desire to know; who indeed is this Supreme Lord? (39)
Who is this divine lady, four-footed and four-faced, with four horns, four mouths, four tusks, and four breasts? (1.23.40)
How is she remembered as having four hands, four eyes, and universal forms?
What is her name, what is her essence, and what is her power or her activity? (41)
Maheśvara said:
Listen to this supreme secret, the purifier of all mantras and the increaser of prosperity, exactly as it occurred at the beginning of creation. 42.
This current aeon is known as Viśvarūpa,
in which the gods beginning with Bhava and twenty-six Manus are recorded.
O Lord, since this station of Brahmā was attained by you,
this has been the thirty-third kalpa from that time until now.
O Lord of Gods, O Great Sage, hear from me those hundreds of thousands of Self-Existent Ones who have passed away prior to you. (45)
That bliss is to be known as Ānanda; you are that great abode of bliss.
By virtue of your asceticism and your lineage of Gālava, you have come here as my son.
In you reside yoga and Sāṅkhya, austerity, knowledge, ritual procedure, and action; truth, steadfastness, that which is Brahman, non-violence, continuity, and transcendence. ||47||
Meditation, the embodiment of meditation, peace, knowledge, the intellect beyond knowledge, fortitude, splendor, tranquility, memory, intelligence, modesty, purity, Sarasvatī,
contentment, nourishment, action, shame, and patience are established there. ||48||
O Brahmā, know her to be Prakṛti, the Great Goddess who gives birth to you; she possesses twenty-six qualities and is designated by thirty-two syllables. 49.
This very same blessed goddess is the progeny of the Self-born;
she is the four-faced one, the source of the universe, celebrated as Prakṛti and Gauḥ,
whom those who contemplate the principles call Pradhāna and Prakṛti.

"I am indeed the unborn, the wise one; having realized this Gāyatrī as the cow of all forms—the unborn, red, white, and black, who emits the entire universe and is beautiful in form—I am the omniform one.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva let out a loud, boisterous laugh.
With the sound of snapping and clapping, and likewise with the sounds "kahā" and "kahanada. ||52||
Then, from his side, divine youths of every form were born:
one with matted hair, one with a shaven head, one with a topknot, and one with half-shaven hair.
Then those of great splendor, having worshipped Maheśvara for a thousand divine years by means of the yoga as previously described, [attained their goal].
Having firmly established the instruction in the Dharma consisting of yoga,
those of self-restraint entered the Lord Rudra, the ruler of the disciplined.
Vāyu said:

Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, filled with wonder, sought refuge in Mahādeva with a mind endowed with devotion and spoke these words: "O All-pervading Lord, how did you become white? (56)
The Blessed One said:
Indeed, when the Śvetakalpa existed, I then became Śveta;
I was Śiva, wearing a white turban, white garlands, and white garments.
With white bones, flesh, and hair, with white skin and white-red [complexion],
he was renowned by that name, for at that time it was indeed the Śveta-kalpa.
And by my grace, O Lord of Gods, the Lord became white-bodied and white-and-red;
at that time, Gāyatrī, known as Brahman, was indeed white in color. (59)

"O Lord of Gods, because I was known by you through your own ascetic power as being established in the secret state, and because I am the eternal one born instantly, this Brahman is proclaimed as 'Sadyojāta' (the Instantly Born) and is indeed declared to be secret. (1.23.60)
Therefore, those twice-born ones who shall know that which has attained this state of secrecy will go to its proximity,
from which a return [to this world] is difficult to obtain.
Furthermore, when I was known by the name Lohita,
the Kalpa was indeed remembered as Lohita after my own color.
Then, resembling blood, flesh, bone, and milk-blood, the cow known as Gāyatrī is proclaimed to have red eyes and udders. (63)
Then, due to the reversal of his blood and complexion,
and because of the leftward nature of his yoga, he attained the state of Vāmadeva.
Nevertheless, O Great Being, because I was recognized by you, who are self-restrained and white in complexion, I am therefore remembered as the "Supreme among Complexions" (Varṇottama).
Consequently, I attained renown on the surface of the earth as Vāmadeva. ||65||
And those twice-born ones here who shall know the state of Vāmadeva,
O Lord, having recognized this Gāyatrī, the mother Rudrāṇī.
Freed from all sins, stainless, and endowed with the splendor of Brahman,
they shall go to the world of Rudra, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
But when he again becomes black in color and terrifying, and because of his color caused by me, he is called Kṛṣṇa, being like unto me.
In that regard, O Brahmin, I am like Time itself—Time who reveals the world; I have been recognized by you as the terrible one of terrible prowess. (69)
Therefore, for those on the surface of the earth who shall know me as having attained this state of fierceness,
I, the imperishable one, shall become non-terrible and peaceful for them.
Therefore, for those on earth who behold me as the All-pervading,
I shall always be both auspicious and gentle toward them.
Therefore, this ritual procedure (kalpa) is indeed proclaimed as Viśvarūpa,
and likewise this Sāvitrī is proclaimed as Viśvarūpā.
Likewise, all these forms have become my sons;
they are declared to be four, indeed regarded by the world as the feet [of Dharma]. (73)
And from that, I shall possess all castes and the state of being a progenitor; I shall be an eater of all things, yet pure, and distinguished by my color.
Liberation, dharma, as well as artha and kāma—this is the fourfold [set].
Therefore, both the knower and the object of knowledge shall indeed become fourfold. ||75||
The four classes of beings, the four stages of life,
and the four feet of Dharma— these are my four sons.
Therefore, this world, including all things mobile and immobile, shall exist in four states during the four ages and shall likewise consist of four quarters.
The world of Bhūḥ, then Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and likewise Mahaḥ; Janas, Tapas, Śānta, and beyond that, the world of Rudra.
Svarloka is indeed the third, while the fourth is known as Mahaḥ;
there, the world is the supreme station, and that is remembered as the ultimate goal for yogins.
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, devoid of desire and anger,
those who know that [reality], being disciplined and devoted to meditation, shall behold it.
Since this Sarasvatī was seen by you as having four feet,
therefore all animals shall become four-footed;
and for that reason, they shall indeed possess four teats.
O Brahmin, since this Soma, conjoined with mantras, has issued from my mouth,
it is the life-force of all living beings, just as everyone drinks ghee from their breasts.
Therefore, this shall consist of Soma and be designated as nectar;
by that means, cows will become four-footed and it [the moon] will possess whiteness.
And because this Maheśvarī, having become an action, was seen by you as having two feet— this Sāvitrī, the creator of the worlds—
therefore all men are remembered as being bipedal and possessing two breasts. ||84||

And because you have seen the Great Goddess, the Supreme Sustainer of all beings, who, though unborn, has become all the castes, therefore the state of universal form shall indeed belong to the unborn ones.
The goat, possessed of great splendor, shall indeed become the universal form;
his seed is infallible everywhere, and the consumer of oblations (Agni) resides in his mouth.
Therefore, the consumer of oblations, though present everywhere, is pure when embodied in the form of a sacrificial animal.

Those twice-born ones whose souls have been purified by austerity shall indeed behold Him who is all-pervading and eternally stable everywhere, both in His state of sovereignty and in His state of auspiciousness.
Freed from passion and darkness, having cast off this human coil,
they shall go to my presence, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
O twice-born ones, having been addressed in this manner by Rudra, the Blessed Lord Brahmā,
the Grandfather, bowed down, became composed, and spoke again.
Brahmā said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Maheśvara whose form is the universe!
O Mahādeva, these are your bodies, which are worshipped by the world.
O Viśvarūpa, O Mahāsattva, at what time, O mighty-armed one, and in which manifestation of the age will the twice-born behold you? (91)
By what yoga of reality, or by what yoga of meditation,
O Mahādeva, can your forms be seen by the twice-born?
The Blessed One said:
Neither by austerity, nor by yoga, nor by the fruit of the duty of giving, nor by the attainment of the fruits of sacred fords, nor by sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees; ||93||
I cannot be seen by mortals through the study of the Vedas, nor through the mind, nor through various forms of knowledge; indeed, there is nothing higher than meditation [for this purpose]. 94.
Sādhya and Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu the lord of the three worlds, shall here become renowned by the name Vārāha. ||95||
Then, having become the Year itself, he will take the form of the sacrifice— four-armed, four-footed, four-eyed, and four-faced;
possessing six limbs, three heads, and a triple body in three locations.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four ages (caturyuga).
Its four feet are the four Vedas, and likewise the sacrificial rites (kratavaḥ).
The arms are the four Vedas, the joints are the seasons, the faces are two, the solstices are two, and the eyes are likewise four. (98)
The three joints are the lunar mansions Phālgunī, Āṣāḍhā, and Kṛttikā;
the three locations are those which are celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial;
and origination and dissolution are proclaimed as the two stages of life (āśramas). ||99||
When he, appearing like the form of Time, is established in the state of a boar,
then the Lord Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa will become the one to be accomplished.
Then you too, O Lord of Gods, shall become four-faced;
Viṣṇu, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, shall be worthy of homage in the world of Brahmā. ||101||
When you behold the Lord of Gods, the Great Sage Hari, reclining upon his couch in the single ocean of universal dissolution, absorbed in meditation; ||102||
Then, deluded by my yoga and deprived of our senses, we two vied with one another at night, not recognizing each other. (103)
Having seen the worlds, both moving and unmoving, situated within the belly of each one,
and having attained the highest wonder, those two men understood through meditation.
Therefore, O eternal one, you shall be born from a lotus and possess a lotus-navel;
then, in that kalpa, you will attain great renown as the one marked by the lotus. 105.
Then, O Lord, in that seventh kalpa of the future,
Viṣṇu of great splendor, Time who destroys the worlds,
will again become your son, named Vaivasvata Manu.
Then, during that kalpa at the end of the age, when the four ages have reached their conclusion,
I shall become the great sage named Śveta, endowed with a topknot.
On the delightful peak of Himavat, on Chāgala, the best of mountains,
my four disciples shall then be devoted to Śiva.
Śveta, Śikha, Śvetāśva, and Śvetalohita—these four were great-souled Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas. ||109||
Then those who have become predominantly absorbed in Brahman, having beheld the supreme state of Brahman,
will go into its proximity from which a return to this world is difficult to obtain.
Furthermore, O Lord of Gods, when the Lord Vyāsa, the Prajāpati named Satya, shall appear in the second Dvāpara age, he will be mine. ||111||
Then, for the sake of the welfare of the world, I shall appear in that Kali age by the name Sutāra, for the purpose of bestowing grace upon the people.
There too, those sons of mine shall be known by the names Dundubhi,
Śatarūpa, Ṛcīka, and Kratumat.
Having attained yoga, as well as knowledge and the eternal Brahman itself,
they shall go to the world of Rudra, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
And in the third Dvāpara age, when Vyāsa is indeed Bhārgava,
then I shall become Damana at the end of that Yuga.
And there too, four sons shall be born to me:
Viśoka, Vikeśa, Viśāpa, and Śāpanāśana. (116)
Those of great splendor shall also go by that very path described in Yoga to the world of Rudra, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
And in the fourth Dvāpara age, when Vyāsa is remembered as Aṅgiras,
even then I shall exist, known by the name Suhotra.
There too, O best of the twice-born, I shall have four virtuous sons, rich in asceticism, whose souls are absorbed in yoga and who are firm in their vows. (119)
Sumukha, Durmukha, Durdama, and Duratikrama—
having attained the subtle path of yoga, stainless and with their sins burnt away,
they too shall go by that very same path; of this there is no doubt.
And when Savitṛ becomes Vyāsa in the fifth Dvāpara age,
then I too shall appear as Kaṅka, a man of great asceticism,
whose soul is absorbed in yoga and who performs manifold deeds for the sake of favoring the worlds.
But my four sons shall be highly fortunate, free from passion, of pure birth, yogic in nature, and firm in their vows.
Sana, Sanandana, the lord Sanātana,
Ṛtu, and Sanatkumāra— being free from possessiveness and egoism—
they shall go to my presence, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
Furthermore, when the sixth cycle has turned and the powerful Vyāsa passes away,
I too shall come to be known by the name Lokākṣi.
And those divine disciples of mine, whose souls are absorbed in yoga and who are firm in their vows, shall become highly fortunate and honored by the world—there will be four of them. ||125||

Sudhāmā, Virajas, Śaṅkhapāda, and Drava—all these great-souled ones, whose selves are absorbed in yoga and whose sins have been burnt away—they too shall go by that very same path; of this there is no doubt. ||126||
In the seventh chapter, however, when Vyāsa was Śatakratu, there was formerly a Śatakratu named Vibhu who possessed great splendor. ||127||
Even then, at the end of that Yuga in the Kali age, I shall exist, renowned as Jaigīṣavya, the best among all yogins. ||128||
At that time, in that age, those sons shall also be mine:
Sārasvata, Sumedhas, Vasuvāha, and Suvāhana.
They too, relying on that very same path and the practice of meditation,
will become great-souled beings whose ultimate goal is the world of Rudra.
Vasiṣṭha will be the Vyāsa in the eighth cycle;
likewise Kapila, Āsuri, the sage Pañcaśikha, and the great yogi Vāgbali—all of whom possess immense power. ||131||
Having attained the yoga of Maheśvara, those who are meditative and whose impurities have been burnt away shall go to my presence,
from which a return is difficult to obtain.
Then, in the ninth cycle, when Vyāsa shall be Sārasvata,
I too shall exist by the name of Ṛṣabha;
and there also those sons of mine shall be possessed of great luster.
Parāśara, Gārgya, Bhārgava, and likewise Aṅgiras—these high-souled Brāhmaṇas shall be masters of the Vedas. ||134||
All those ascetics, preeminent in the power of their austerities and skilled in the bestowal of curses and favors,
shall likewise proceed by that very path described in yoga,
having attained the way of meditation.
O brahmins, when Vyāsa named Tridhāman appears in the tenth Dvāpara age, then I shall appear once again.
On a delightful peak of the Himalayas, on Bhrigutunga, the best of mountains—that peak belongs to Bhrigu by name;
therefore, that peak is called Bhrgu.
Right there, those sons of mine shall be born, firm in their vows:
Balabandhu, Nirāmitra, Ketuśṛṅga, and Tapodhana. (138)
Those great-souled ones whose nature is yoga, who are endowed with the yoga of meditation,
and whose impurities have been burnt away by austerity, shall go to the world of Rudra.
In the eleventh Dvāpara age, Vyāsa will be Trivṛt;
then too, I shall be present at Gaṅgādvāra at the onset of the Kali age.
Right there, my dear sons, shall become known as the Ugras, great in roar, possessed of mighty energy, of virtuous conduct, and renowned throughout the world. ||141||
Lambodara, Lamba, Lambākṣa, and Lambakeśaka—having attained the yoga of Maheśvara, they are established for the world of Rudra;
they too shall go by that very path to the supreme goal. ||142||
In the twelfth cycle, however, the great sage Śatatejas will become the Mahāsattva Vyāsa, the most excellent among the best of poets.
After that, at the end of the Yuga, I shall become one named Atri,
having reached the Haimaka forest on earth and established myself in yoga.
In this matter as well, O Mahāyoga, let not your sons become those who smear themselves with ashes for bathing, but rather let them be intent upon the world of Rudra. 145.
Being omniscient and possessed of equanimous intellect, they shall all likewise attain the goal; devoted to the yoga of meditation, they will go to the world of Rudra.
Furthermore, when the thirteenth cycle arrives in due order,
there will be a Vyāsa named Dharma-Nārāyaṇa.
Even then, I shall become a great sage named Vālin on the Gandhamādana mountain, in the holy hermitage of the Vālakhilyas.
There too, those sons of mine shall be rich in asceticism:
Sudhāman, Kāśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Virajas. (149)
Endowed with the power of great yoga, stainless and with vital energy drawn upward, they will undoubtedly proceed by that very path of yoga. ||1.23.150||
When Vyāsa is Surakṣaṇa during the fourteenth cycle,
I shall likewise appear once again at the end of that age.
In the lineage of Aṅgiras, there will be an eminent knower of yoga named Gautama;
because of him, that forest shall become meritorious and known by the name Gautama.
Even there, in the Kali age, those sons of mine shall likewise exist:
Atri, Ugratapā, Śrāvaṇa, and Sraviṣṭhaka.
Those great-souled ones whose nature is yoga, who are devoted to the yoga of meditation, they too, by that very path, become dwellers in the world of Rudra. ||154||
Then, when the fifteenth cycle has arrived in its due course, the lord Aruṇi shall become Vyāsa during the Dvāpara age. ||155||
Even then, O twice-born ones, I shall exist there by the name Vedaśiras;
and that supreme weapon of the Lord shall be known there by the name Vedaśiras.
O one of great heroism, there shall be the mountain Vedaśīrṣa on the ridge of the Himavat,
that best of mountains situated by the Sarasvatī.
Even then, those sons of mine shall be rich in asceticism:
Kuṇi, Kuṇibāhu, Kuśarīra, and Kunetraka. (158)
Those whose nature is yoga, the great-souled ones, most devoted to Brahman, and those of sublimated vital energy—they too have gone to the world of Rudra by that very same path. ||159||
Then, when the sixteenth cycle has arrived in due order,
the lord Vyāsa will be known by the name Sañjaya.
Even then, I shall exist there by the name Gokarṇa;
therefore, that forest shall become meritorious under the name Gokarṇa.
There too, those sons of mine shall be possessed of great luster—
Kaśyapa, Uśanas, Cyavana, and Bṛhaspati;
they, too, shall go by that very path to the supreme state.
Then, when the seventeenth chapter has arrived in its proper sequence, there will arise a Vyāsa named Devakṛtañjaya. ||163||
Even then, I shall be known by the name Guhāvāsī on a very lofty peak of the Himavat, at Mahālaya;
and that Mahālaya shall become a field of perfection, greatly meritorious. ||164||
There too, those sons of mine will be devoted to Brahman, knowers of Yoga,
high-souled, omniscient, and free from egoism.
Utathya, Vāmadeva, Mahākāla, and Mahālaya—these had a hundred thousand disciples who were accomplished in the practice of meditation. ||166||
In that kalpa, they will all be practitioners of meditation;
established in yoga and placing Maheśvara within their hearts, they shall cast their feet upon Mahālaya and enter the imperishable Śiva. ||167||
And there were other great-souled ones as well at that time, near the end of the age—pure and of purified intellects, with minds absorbed in meditation. ||168||
Having gone to the great and meritorious Mahālyam and beheld the station of Maheśvara,
one swiftly delivers ten ancestors and ten descendants.
Having crossed the great ocean, they shall, by my grace, reach the world of Rudra, freed from all suffering, having delivered themselves and twenty-one others.
Then, when the eighteenth Parivarta occurs, there will be a sage Vyāsa named Ṛtañjaya;
at that time, I too shall exist, known by the name Śikhaṇḍin. ||171||
In that field of accomplishment, most meritorious and worshipped by gods and dānavas,
on the sacred peak of the Himalayas where Mount Śikhaṇḍin stands,
there is also the forest of Śikhaṇḍin, frequented by sages and perfected beings.
There too, those sons of mine shall be rich in asceticism:
Vācaḥśravas, Ṛtīka, Śāvāsa, and Dṛḍhavrata. (173)
All those great yogis, possessed of supreme power and masters of the Vedas,
having attained the yoga of Maheśvara, proceed to the world of Rudra.
Then, when the nineteenth cycle arrives in due order,
there will be a great sage named Vyāsa, known by the name Bharadvāja.
There too, I shall exist by the name Jaṭāmālī on the delightful peak of the Himalayas, where the mountain Jaṭāyu is located. ||176||
There too, those sons of mine shall be of great majesty:
Hiraṇyanāman, Kauśilya, Kākṣīvat, and likewise Kuthumi. (177)
All those lords who possess the nature of Yoga and maintain perpetual celibacy, having attained the Yoga of Maheśvara, will undoubtedly proceed to that state. ||178||
Then, in the twentieth eon and cycle, the high-minded Vācaḥśravas will successively become the Vyāsa known as Smṛta. (179)
Even then, I shall indeed exist by the name Aṭṭahāsī,
and men will likewise be fond of loud laughter at that time.
Right there on the slopes of the Himalayas, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
your sons shall be born to me— possessing great splendor,
disciplined in soul, of great being, devoted to meditation, and firm in their vows. ||181||
Sumantu, the learned Varvari, Subandhu, and Kuśikandhara—having attained the yoga of Maheśvara, they have gone to the world of Rudra. ||182||
Furthermore, when the twenty-first cycle had arrived in its proper sequence, that best of sages, Vyāsa, was known as Vācaspati. ||183||
Even then, I shall exist there by the name of Dāruka;
therefore, that great forest of Devadāru trees shall become meritorious.
There too, those sons of mine shall be of great prowess:
Plakṣa, Dākṣāyaṇi, Ketumālin, and Baka.

Those great-souled ones, whose nature is yoga, who are self-restrained and have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), having taught the supreme yoga, have likewise attained Rudra, being free from all taint. 186.
In the twenty-second cycle, when Vyāsa is Śuklāyana,
even then I shall become a great sage in Vārāṇasī.
Known by the name Lāṅgalin Bhīma, in that Kali age the gods, together with Indra, shall behold me descended as Halāyudha.
There too, those sons of mine shall be very righteous:
Tulyārcis, Madhupiṅgākṣa, and likewise Śvetaketu. (189)
Having attained the yoga of Maheśvara and being devoted to meditation,
they became free from passion, absorbed in Brahman, and established in the world of Rudra.
In the twenty-third cycle, when the sage Tṛṇabindu becomes Vyāsa,
then I shall become once again,
a son of a sage named Śveta, possessed of a great body and very righteous. (191)
There, on that best of excellent mountains, I shall meet my end;
therefore, that mountain shall be known by the name Kālañjara. ||192||
There too, those sons of mine shall be of great luster:
Uṣija, Bṛhaduktha, Devala, and Kavi;
for having attained the yoga of Maheśvara, they have indeed gone to the world of Rudra.
In the twenty-fourth cycle, Vyāsa will become Ṛkṣa;
there, O Brahmin, at the end of that Yuga, I shall be born as the great yogi named Śūlin in Naimiṣa, which is honored by yogis. (194)
There too, those ascetics shall become my sons:
Śālīhotra, Agniveśya, Yuvanāśva, and Śaradvasu.
Endowed with the power of yoga and firm in their vows, they too shall go to Rudra.
Furthermore, when the twenty-fifth cycle arrives in due order,
Vasiṣṭha will become the Vyāsa named Śakti.
Even then, I shall be the Lord Daṇḍimuṇḍīśvara, having reached the city of Koṭivarṣa, which is worshipped by the gods. (197)
There too, those sons of mine shall be born in succession;
they will all be great-souled masters of yoga, with their vital energy drawn upward.
Chagala, Kumbhakarṣāśya, Kumbha, and Prabāhuka—having attained the yoga of Maheśvara, they too shall likewise go [to that state]. (199)
In the twenty-sixth cycle, when Parāśara shall be the Vyāsa,
even then I shall exist by the name Sahiṣṇu,
having reached the meritorious Rudravana forest at the end of that Kali age.
There too, those sons of mine shall be most righteous:
Ulūka, Vaidyuta, Sarvaka, and Āśvalāyana;
having attained the yoga of Maheśvara, they shall likewise go [to that realm]. 201.
When the twenty-seventh successive cycle has arrived,
Jātūkarṇya will become the Vyāsa, O ascetic.
Even then, I shall become Somaśarman, the best of the twice-born,
renowned throughout the world, having reached the sacred site of Prabhāsa with my soul absorbed in yoga.
There too, those sons of mine shall be rich in asceticism:
Akṣapāda, Kaṇāda, Ulūka, and Vatsa.
Those great-souled ones, whose nature is yoga, who are stainless and pure in intellect, having attained the yoga of Maheśvara, have then gone to the world of Rudra. ||205||
Furthermore, when the twenty-eighth successive cycle arrived, the illustrious Viṣṇu, son of Parāśara and grandfather of the world, [appeared]. ||206||
When the lord Vyāsa, named Dvaipāyana, comes into being,
then Kṛṣṇa, the best of men, with a sixth portion,
will become Vāsudeva, the foremost of the Yadus, born from Vasudeva.
And at that time, through my yogic power, I shall become a soul of yoga, possessing the body of a celibate student for the purpose of causing wonder in the world. ||208||
Seeing the world leaderless and a corpse abandoned in the cremation ground,
he entered through his power of yoga-māyā for the sake of the welfare of the brahmins.
O Brahmā, at that time, together with you and Viṣṇu, I shall dwell in the divine and meritorious cave of Meru, known by the name Nakulī.
Thus, this place shall become known as Siddhakṣetra, "The Field of the Perfected," and it will remain renowned as long as the earth endures. ||211||
There too, those ascetics shall become my sons:
Kuśaka, Gārgya, Mitraka, and Ruṣṭaka.
The high-souled Brahmins, devoted to yoga and masters of the Vedas,
having attained the yoga of Maheśvara, being pure and possessing sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas),
shall go to the world of Rudra, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
Thus, indeed, this characteristic of the incarnations has been declared by me, from Manu up to Kṛṣṇa, according to the sequence of the twenty-eight yugas;
therein, the classification of the collections of Smṛtis constitutes the characteristic of Dharma. 214.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Māheśvara Incarnation," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Vāyu said:
The sages know that there are four ages in the land of Bhārata:
Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Tiṣya; these constitute the cycle of the four ages. ||1||
A thousand of these constitutes what is remembered as one day of Brahmā;
there are seven groups beginning with the Yāmas, and fourteen possess body hair. (2)
Accompanied by their bodies and their followers, they took refuge in Janaloka.
Thus, when the gods had passed away from Maharloka, [the inhabitants of] Tapas went to Jana.
When all the gods of great prowess had passed through the past Manvantaras,
they then ascended to the state of union (sāyujya) with those who dwell in the Kalpa.
Then, when Saṅkālaṇa had arrived, those gods met with the deities;
indeed, those fourteen Gaṇas abandoned Maharloka.
Then, when the beings beginning with the gross elements and ending with the immobile have perished,
and those worlds beginning with the earth and extending to the great realms (mahānta) are empty,
and when the gods residing for a kalpa have departed upward to the Jana-loka; ||6||
Then, through their collective power, Brahmā indeed establishes all the gods, sages, hosts of dānavas,
and others by means of fire and rain at the end of the yuga.
That seventh kalpa which I have described to you was one in which the seven oceans had become deeply united into a single great sea;
it was a terrible, undifferentiated expanse of water, consisting entirely of darkness.
Within that single ocean created by Māyā, there appeared Hari, the Lord of Śrī, bearing the conch, discus, and mace; he was cloud-colored, lotus-eyed, and wore a crown. ||9||

That eighth Puruṣottama, who emerged from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, possesses eight arms and a broad chest; he is called the source of the worlds. A knower of yoga, with his mind disciplined, he resorts to yoga and remains absorbed in that which is inconceivable.

Having spread out the immense body of the lord of great serpents, which was endowed with a thousand hoods and possessed incomparable luster, he lay upon that vast couch which shone with the brilliance of gold.
Thus, while lying there, the all-powerful Viṣṇu,
who delights in the self, created from his navel a lotus for the sake of sport.
By the powerful one, with effortless ease, [he created] a staff of thunderbolt-like hardness, a hundred yojanas in width, possessing the brilliance of the rising sun, and of immense height.
While he, the one praised by the gods, was thus sporting,
Brahmā— born from the golden cosmic egg, golden-hued, beyond the reach of the senses,
four-faced, and large-eyed— approached him by chance.
Seeing him playing with that lotus, which was endowed with splendor, fresh, radiant, and fragrant, Brahmā was indeed filled with wonder.
Then, filled with wonder, he spoke with a voice full of praise:
"Who are you that lie here, obstructed in the midst of the waters? (16)
Then Acyuta, having heard those auspicious words of Brahmā,
rose from his couch with eyes wide open in wonder.
And he replied: "Whatever is done as a response, and whatever exists—the heavens, the mid-air, and the world of beings—I am the Lord, the supreme state. (18)
Having spoken thus to him, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu then spoke again:
"Who indeed have you come to be near me? From where have you come, O Blessed One? Where must you go further, and where is your dwelling? (19)
"Who are you, O you of universal form, and what is it that must be done for you by me?
To Vaikuṇṭha who was speaking thus, the Grandfather replied.
Just as you are, so am I—the primordial creator, Prajāpati, known as Nārāyaṇa; indeed, everything rests within me. 21.
Having heard this supreme and wondrous account from Brahmā, the creator of the world,
he, the Lord Vaikuṇṭha, the source of the universe, was granted permission by the Blessed One.
Out of curiosity, the great yogi entered the mouth of Brahmā;
having entered these eighteen islands, along with their oceans and mountains,
filled with the four social orders, he of great splendor proceeded.
The seven eternal worlds, beginning with Brahmā and ending with a blade of grass. ||23||
Seeing them all within the belly of Brahmā, the highly illustrious Viṣṇu spoke again and again: "Oh, how great is the power of his ascetic penance! ||24||
Wandering through various worlds and diverse hermitages, Viṣṇu then,
at the end of a thousand years, indeed did not see its end.
Then, emerging from his mouth, the blessed Lord whose banner bears the enemy of the serpent-king— Ajātaśatru— spoke to the Grandfather.
O Blessed One, you have no beginning, middle, or end, nor do you belong to time or space;
O sinless one, I truly perceive no end to your belly.
Having spoken thus, Hari further addressed the Grandfather:
"O best of the twice-born, you too shall likewise enter my eternal belly today and behold these incomparable worlds."
Having heard his speech, which gladdened the mind, and having rejoiced in it,
the Grandfather (Brahmā) entered once again into the belly of the Lord of Śrī.
Beholding those very worlds while remaining within the womb, he of inconceivable prowess roamed about,
yet he did not see the end of the primordial god Hari.

Having understood the intention of that Grandfather and having closed all the gates, the omnipresent Viṣṇu desired to make his mind steady, thinking: "I shall sleep happily in this great flood of water. (31)
Then, perceiving that all the gates were closed, he made his own form subtle and sought an opening at his navel. ||32||

Following the path of the *Pajha-sūtra*, the Grandfather, whose face is four-faced, emerged from the lotus and assumed his own form; seated upon the lotus, he shone with a splendor like that of the interior of a lotus. ||33||
In the meantime, as each of them was engaged in full delight in the midst of that ocean, (34)
Sūta said:
Then the immeasurable Self, the Lord and Master of all beings,
Mahādeva with the trident in hand, clothed in garments of golden bark,
arrived where Hari, the infinite one, the lord of the serpent’s coils, was present.
As he strode swiftly, the broad drops of water were violently agitated by his feet and quickly scattered into the sky;
there, winds blew fiercely, both excessively hot and excessively cold.
Seeing that great marvel, Brahmā spoke to Viṣṇu:
"The drops of water are indeed thick and hot, and the lotus trembles violently.
Explain this doubt of mine; what else do you intend to do? (37)
Having heard these words of such a kind issuing from the mouth of the Grandfather, the Blessed One, the performer of incomparable deeds and the destroyer of the asuras, spoke.
"What other being indeed has made its abode here within my navel, that they speak so exceedingly pleasant words to me even when I have done them harm? (39)
Having reflected thus in his mind, he replied with this answer:
"Why indeed has the Blessed One become so agitated regarding that Puṣkara?"
"O Lord, what have I done that you speak to me with such unsurpassed affection, O best of men? Tell me the truth of why this is so. (41)
To the Lord of Gods who was speaking thus,
the lotus-eyed Lord Brahmā, the storehouse of Vedic knowledge and the knower of reality, replied for the sake of the world’s protection.
O Lord, just as all the worlds were seen by you within my belly when I previously entered your belly at your will,
in that same way, all the worlds have been seen by me in their entirety within your belly.
Then, O sinless one, when I had returned at the end of a thousand years,
surely you, desiring to bring me under your control through a spirit of malice,
quickly closed all the doors once again.
Then, O illustrious one, having reflected with my own mind, I obtained entry through the navel and emergence from the lotus fiber. (45)
"May there not be even the slightest obstacle to your mind in any way whatsoever"—this is the incidental instruction regarding the duties of Viṣṇu. 46.
Immediately after that, which I had resolved to do toward you—
desiring not to cause you distress, but rather out of sport and by chance—
I quickly closed all the doors once again. (47)
"You must not think otherwise of me; you are to be honored and worshipped by me.
O auspicious one, forgive everything that has been done wrong to you by me.
Therefore, as I entreat you, descend from the lotus, O Lord. (48)
"I am unable to endure you, O venerable one, for you are heavy and full of splendor.
He replied, "Choose a boon; I shall descend from the lotus."
Viṣṇu said:
Become my son, O slayer of enemies; you shall attain auspicious joy.
You are a great yogi whose wealth is truth, worthy of praise, and the very essence of the syllable Om.
"From this day forward, O Lord of All, adorned with the white turban, you shall be known by the name 'Lotus-born' (Pajhayoni).
O Brahman, Lord, Sovereign of all the worlds, become my son. (51)
Then that Blessed One, having accepted the boon from the Diademed One (Arjuna),
said, "So be it," with a joyful soul and free from all malice.
Then, seeing that most wonderful being with a vast mouth approaching nearby, possessing the luster of the rising sun, he spoke to Nārāyaṇa.
Immeasurable, greatly crooked, with fangs and disheveled hair,
ten-armed, marked with the trident, and facing in all directions with his eyes.
The Lord of the World himself, manifest in person, appeared transformed, wearing a girdle of muñja grass;
with his great penis erect, he roared most terrifyingly.
"O Viṣṇu, who indeed is this man, a mass of splendor and great radiance, who, pervading all the quarters and the sky, approaches from this very direction? (56)
Thus addressed by him, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu spoke to Brahmā:
"As he strides across the ocean, the impact of his feet falling upon its surface causes the reservoirs of water to tremble violently in the sky with great force. (57)
The lotus-born Brahmā is excessively sprinkled by the spray from Viṣṇu;
and the great lotus born from my navel, trembling along with you, is shaken at will by the wind arising from my nostrils.
This very Lord is indeed Īśa, beginningless, the all-pervading end-maker;
both you and I approach Him, whose banner is a bull, with this hymn of praise.
Then, filled with anger, Brahmā spoke to Keśava, who resembles the sun within a lotus:
"You do not consider yourself inferior, though you are the supreme source of the worlds."
"He knows me and Brahmā, the creator of the world, as the eternal one.
Who is this person called Śaṅkara who is distinct from the two of us? (61)
Having heard those words born of his anger, Viṣṇu spoke:
"O auspicious one, do not speak thus; do not utter calumny against the Great-Souled One."
Dharma is the master of the yoga of illusion, invincible, and the bestower of boons;
he is the ancient, imperishable Puruṣa, the cause of this world.
Indeed, this single light of all living beings shines as the individual soul;
Lord Śaṅkara himself plays with the toys of children. (64)

Pradhāna, the imperishable light, the unmanifest, Prakṛti, and Tamas—these are the names of this [reality] which is eternally characterized by productivity. It is that auspicious one (Śiva) who is sought after by ascetics afflicted by suffering, asking "Who is he? Who is he? ||65||
"You are the possessor of the seed, and I am the eternal womb.
Having been addressed thus, Brahmā, the soul of the universe, then spoke to Viṣṇu.
"Bhava is the womb and I am the seed; how then am I, Maheśvara, the possessor of the seed?
You ought to sever this subtle and unmanifest doubt of mine. (67)
Having thus understood the origin [of the world], Hari, together with Brahmā, the sustainer of the worlds,
spoke this supreme similarity as a question.
There exists no being more secret or greater than this;
it is the supreme abode of the Great, the auspicious state of those established in the self.
Having entered into himself through a twofold state,
the Great Lord Maheśvara remains established as both partless— subtle and unmanifest— and as possessed of parts.
In ancient times, the primordial seed of existence, the first of all creations, became the *liṅga* of this one who knows the methods of illusion and who is impenetrable and profound.
That seed, united with me as the womb, by the course of time,
produced within that womb a golden, boundless egg.
The cosmic egg, established upon the waters, remained for ten hundred years;
at the end of a thousand years, it was split asunder by the wind.
One skull became the sky and the other skull became the earth;
its vast elevation was that which is the mountain of gold.
Then, from that [source], the awakened self, the Lord, the best of gods,
the blessed Hiraṇyagarbha, was born as I, the four-armed one.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, having seen the world made twofold by the wind and rendered empty— devoid of stars, sun, moon, and constellations— and having reflected,
"Who is this here?", those youths then came into being.
Those ancestors of yours who have passed away, beloved to behold and of delicate form,
shall once again, at the end of a thousand years, become your sons—
resembling the fire of universal destruction and possessing eyes as broad as lotus petals.
The illustrious Sanatkumāra, Ṛbhu—
who is of perpetual celibacy— as well as Sanātana, Sanaka, and Sanandana,
were born at the same time; they possessed intellects that perceive what is beyond the senses.
At that very moment, those whose nature is aversion arose and declared:
"They will no longer undertake actions, being devoid of the threefold suffering. (79)
O gentle one, his life is full of suffering, joined with old age and sorrow,
and involves death again and again, as well as repeated rebirth.

Furthermore, having understood that all the sufferings in heaven as well as those in the hells arise from one's own actions, and having understood the entire scripture regarding the inevitability of what must come to pass; ||81||
Having seen Ṛbhu and Sanatkumāra standing under your control,
the three sons beginning with Sanaka, having abandoned the three qualities (guṇas),
those of great luster have turned away through the knowledge of returning (vaivartta). ||82||
Then, when those three, Sanaka and the others, have indeed turned away,
you shall become utterly deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Śaṅkara.
Thus, O sinless one, when the world-cycle has reached its end, all designations will cease;
only the subtle elemental remains of the cycle shall persist.
This indeed is declared to be the sovereign Māyā of the universe;
this very mountain is Meru, proclaimed as the world of the gods.
Indeed, this majesty is yours alone; for having seen it, and having known the true nature of the Lord by means of the self through the self, and having known me, the lotus-eyed one— ||86||
Having approached Mahādeva, the great yogi, the lord who grants boons to all beings,
the soul of the syllable Om, and having paid homage to that teacher of the world,
he, being enraged, would consume both you and me with his very breath.
Having thus understood this great yoga, the one of great power, rising up,
shall place you at his head and praise you, who possess the splendor of fire.
Sūta said:

Placing Brahmā at his head, he whose banner is Garuḍa then uttered this hymn of praise with names belonging to the past, the future, and likewise the present, as well as those derived from the Vedic meters.
Salutations to you, the Blessed One, of excellent vows and infinite splendor;
salutations to the Lord of the Field, the Sower, the wielder of the trident.

Salutations to the one without a penis and to the one with an erect penis; salutations to the one whose seed is Vaikuṇṭha; salutations to the eldest, to the most excellent, and to the one who is without predecessor and first.
Homage to the one worthy of oblations, to the worshipful one, and indeed homage to the one born at once;
homage to the dweller in the cave, to the lord of wealth, and to the one clad in garments of golden silk.
Salutations to you, the source of beings such as ourselves;
salutations to the source of the Vedas, of ritual acts, of sacrificial offerings, and of all material substances. (93)
Homage to the source of Yoga, homage to the source of Sāṃkhya;
homage to the Lord of the Ṛṣis, Dhruva, Niśītha, and Amṛta. ||94||
Homage to the source of lightning, thunderbolts, and clouds;
homage to the source of the oceans and the source of the islands. ||95||
Salutations to the source of mountains and the source of rain-clouds;
salutations to the source of streams and the source of rivers. ||96||
Homage to the source of medicinal herbs; homage to the source of trees.
Homage to the overseer of dharma, to dharma itself, and to the source of all stable states. ||97||
Homage to the source of tastes, homage to the source of jewels;
homage to the source of moments, homage to the source of arts. ||98||
Salutations to the source of the nimeṣa and the source of the kāṣṭhās;
salutations to the source of the days and nights, the half-months, and the months. ||99||
Homage to the source of the seasons, homage to the source of number;
homage to the source of the highest parārdha, homage to the source of that which is beyond.
Salutations to the ancient source, the source of the age;
salutations to the source of the fourfold creation, whose vision is infinite.
Homage to the source of the accounts composed at the beginning of the eon;
homage to the source of the universe, the source of Brahmā and the others. 102.
Salutations to the source of the sciences and to the lord of the sciences;
salutations to the lord of vows and to the lord of mantras. ||103||
Salutations to the Lord of the ancestors and to the Lord of animals;
salutations to you, the bull of speech, and to the ancient bull.

Salutations to the one with beautiful and lovely hair, and to the one whose eyes and head are turned upward; salutations to the Lord of Creatures, who has the bull as his emblem and the lordly bull as his banner.
Salutations to the Lord of the Prajāpatis, to the Lord of the Siddhas;
salutations to the Lord of Garuḍas, uragas, serpents, and birds. ||106||
Salutations indeed to Gokarṇa, to Goṣṭha, and to Śaṅkukarṇa;
salutations to Vārāha, the immeasurable lord of the Rākṣasas. ||107||
Homage indeed to the lord of the apsarases, to the lord of the hosts, homage to the one consisting of modesty; and likewise homage to the lord of the waters and to the lord of the splendors. ||108||
Homage be to the Lord of Lakṣmī; salutations to the illustrious one, to the modest one, to the aggregate of strength and weakness, and to the unshakeable one who shakes all things. 109.
Salutations to the bull with long horns and a single horn, the humped one; salutations to the embodiment of steadfastness, to the physical form, to splendor, and to the beautiful radiance.
Salutations indeed to the past, the future, and the present;
salutations to the one of great splendor, to the hero, to the brave, and to the transcendent one.
Homage to the giver of boons, to the most excellent, and to the all-pervading;
homage likewise to the past, to the future, and to the great Bhava.
And salutations to you, O Janārdana, and to austerity, and to the bestower of boons;
salutations to the one worthy of worship, to liberation, to humanity, and even to hell. 113.
To Bhava, to the one who bestows fortune, to the desired, to the sacrificer, to the exalted, to the radiant, to the ultimate reality, and to the one beyond qualities. ||114||
Salutations to the one who holds the noose in his hand; salutations to him who is adorned with his own ornaments;
salutations to the one for whom oblations have been offered, to the one for whom they have not been offered, and to the one who has consumed the offerings.
Salutations to the beloved one who has taken form, and to the officiating priest of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
salutations to the Eternal Law, to Truth, and to the Lord of all beings. ||116||
Salutations to the member of the assembly, to the sacrificial fee, and to the final purificatory bath;
salutations to non-violence, to the worlds, and to the animal sacrifice, the mantra, and the medicinal herb. ||117||
Salutations to the one who bestows contentment, to the three-eyed one, to the fragrant one;
salutations be to the lord of the senses, to the one who avoids [worldly ties], to the wearer of garlands. 118.
To the one who is the universe, who possesses all forms, whose eyes and faces are on every side, whose hands and feet are everywhere, to Rudra, the immeasurable. ||119||
Salutation to the one worthy of oblations to the gods and the ancestors, salutation indeed to the one worthy of both divine and ancestral offerings;
salutation to the perfected one, to the pure, to the active, and to the immutable.
To the one with excellent heroes, the most terrible, the unshakeable agitator, the one of excellent wisdom, the one with noble offspring, the radiant, and the sun-like. ||121||
Salutations to the one named Manas, to the fair-winged one, to him who resembles molten gold, to the three-eyed Virūpākṣa, to the tawny-hued one of great majesty. ||122||
Salutations indeed to the destroyer of views, and salutations to the one with gentle eyes;
salutations to the smoky-colored, the white, the black, and the red.
Salutations to you who are flesh-colored, tawny, and yellow, and who carry a quiver;
salutations to you who possess distinctions, and indeed salutations to you who are without distinction.
Homage to the one of lotus-color, and to Mṛtyu, the slayer of death;
homage to the dark one, to the fair-complexioned, to Kadrū, and to the ruddy one. ||125||
Homage to the Beloved, whose color is like the twilight clouds and who possesses many forms;
homage to him who holds a skull in his hand, who is clothed in the directions, and who has matted hair.
Salutations to the immeasurable Śarva, the invincible and the most excellent,
who bears fire before him and behind him.
To Durgā and Mahat, to Rodha and Kapila, to Arkaprabhaśarīra, and to Balin and Raṃhasa. ||128||
To the wielder of the Pināka bow, to the renowned, to the prosperous, and to the pervasive;
to the one of excellent intellect, to the one with the rosary of seeds, to the sky-clad, and to the one with the crest-lock. ||129||
Salutations to Citra, to Citravarṇa, to Vicitra, and to Dhara; salutations to Cekitāna, to Tuṣṭa, and to Anihita.
Salutations to the patient one, to the peaceful one, and to him whose body is as firm as a diamond;
to the slayer of demons, to the destroyer of sacrifices, to the blue-throated one, and to the one whose vital energy flows upwards.
Salutations to you, the enemy of Kṛtānta, who wields sharp weapons; salutations to you, the giver of equanimity and joy, who are like a barren wasteland.
Salutations to the Lord of the Praṇava, who bestows happiness upon his devotees;
to the Hunter of the Deer, the skillful one, and the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. ||133||
To the one who is all beings, the true being, and the one who surpasses all lords;
to the destroyer of the cities, the peaceful one, the fragrant one, and the supreme lord.
To the one whose form is like a flower, to the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, to Kaṇāda the most excellent, and to the burner of the body of Kama; ||135||
To the one who possesses the wheel of rays like the sun, to the subduer of the lords of serpents,
to the bringer of destruction to the Daityas, and to the one who causes divine lamentation.
Salutations to the one who eternally delights in the cremation ground, to the wearer of the three-eyed [Śiva];
salutations to you, the protector of life, and to the bearer of the garland of skulls. 137.
To him who is praised by various beings whose sorrows have been abandoned, who possesses the bodies of both men and women, and who acts for the pleasure of the Goddess; 138.
Salutations to you who wear matted hair and carry a staff, who have a serpent as your sacred thread;
salutations to you whose nature is to dance and who are fond of instrumental music and dancing. ||139||
Salutations to Manyu, who is cool-natured and sings beautiful songs; salutations to him who wears bracelets on his hands, who is formidable, and who assumes a fierce form.
Salutations indeed to Vibhīṣaṇa, to Bhīma, to the crusher of Bhaga,
to him who is praised by the throngs of Siddhas, and to the highly fortunate one.
Homage to the one with the liberated loud laughter, and to the one who roars and slaps his arms;
homage to the one who dances and to the one who is intensely joyful.
Salutations to the wonderful one, to the one who sleeps, runs, and sets out;
salutations to the one who meditates, yawns, stings, and hastens away. 143.
Salutations to the one who moves and plays, to the one whose body is Lambodara; salutations to the one who has performed his rites, to the trembling one, to the shaven-headed, and to the deformed.
Salutations to the one with the garb of a madman, salutations indeed to the one adorned with tinkling bells;
salutations to the one of deformed appearance, and to the one who is cruel, fierce, and wrathful.
Homage to the immeasurable, the radiant, and the source of radiance; homage to the one beyond attributes, to the beloved, to the speaker, and to the bearer of the jewel-seal.
Salutation to the one who is small in body yet incomparable in virtues;
salutation to the secret host, and to him who goes where he should not go. ||147||
This earth is the sustainer of the world; your feet are served by the virtuous;
and your belly is the abode of all perfected yogas. (148)
In the midst of it, the vast expanse of the sky adorned with clusters of stars;
thus does the glorious necklace upon your chest appear like the celestial path. 149.
Their ten arms indeed reached out in the ten directions, adorned with armlets and bracelets;
their broad and massive frame was like a mass of dark blue clouds.
Your glorious neck, adorned with a golden necklace, shines resplendent;
your face is incomparable, formidable with its terrifying fangs. 151.
How does the crown of his head, adorned with a garland of lotuses, shine?
His radiance is like the sun, his form like the moon; his stability is like the earth and his strength like the wind. (152)
The wise know these qualities—sharpness in fire, radiance in the moon, sound in space, and coolness in water—to be unchanging and superior to the imperishable. 153.
He is the recitation, the one to be recited, the great yogi, Mahādeva, Maheśvara, the lord of the city, the dweller in the cave, the sky-walker, and the night-stalker. 154.
The treasure of austerity, the teacher Guha, Nandana, the increaser of joy, Hayaśīrṣa, the supporter of the earth, the ordainer, and the vehicle of prosperity. 155.
He is the one to be awakened, the awakener, the leader, the bearer of the yoke, and the unshakable;
he is the great chariot-warrior, the performer of formidable deeds, the one of vast fame, and the conqueror of wealth. ||156||
He who delights in the bell, the bearer of the banner and the parasol, the lord of the flags and the standards;
he who wears armor, carries the *paṭṭiśa* spear, holds the conch, has the noose in his hand, and wields the battle-axe.
The sinless hero Agama, the crusher of the enemies of the king of the gods, was formerly propitiated by us, and thus our foes were slain in battle. (158)

You are Agni; though you drink all the oceans, you are never satiated. You are the abode of wrath yet possessed of a serene soul; the destroyer of desire and the granter of desires; the beloved. ||159||
Devoted to Brahman and a practitioner of celibacy, you are a slayer of cows yet honored by the learned;
you are the imperishable treasury of the Vedas, and by you the sacrifice has been performed.
The bearer of oblations carries the offering as prescribed by the Veda;
O Mahādeva, when you are pleased, we too become pleased. (161)
The Lord of Bhavānī, without beginning, the mass of light, you are the creator of the worlds and the first creation;
having known you as that which is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), the followers of Sāṅkhya, their meditation exhausted, do not enter into death.
But those meditators who, through yoga, are ever-disciplined, having known you, renounce enjoyments once again;
whereas other mortals who have taken refuge in you, being purified by their actions, partake of divine enjoyments.
Just as a wise one perceives the immeasurable reality according to his own capacity, so has the boundless majesty of you, the Supreme Self, been proclaimed.
Be auspicious to us everywhere; whatever you are, that you are—salutations be to you! 164.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Śarva," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Beholding those two as if drinking them in with his honey-tawny, elongated eyes, he became exceedingly joyful of countenance from the proclamation of his own glory. ||1||
The Lord of Umā, the three-eyed one, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the one with the broken axe, the one who dwells among spirits, and the three-eyed one. ||2||
Then that blessed Lord, the illustrious one, having heard the nectar of their words—
even though he already knew— spoke with prior affection.
Who are you two high-souled ones, seeking each other's welfare,
who have met here with eyes like lotus petals during this terrible flood of water?
Having looked at one another, those two high-souled ones said:
"O Blessed One, O All-pervading Lord, what indeed is the use of knowing the truth by you?
Or where, apart from acting according to your own will, could there be infinite happiness for you?"
The Blessed Lord spoke with a sweet and gentle voice:
"O Hiraṇyagarbha, O Kṛṣṇa, I speak to you both."
I am pleased by this devotion, which is eternal and imperishable;
you two are indeed worthy of honor from me, for you are both most venerable. What supreme and best of boons shall I grant you today?
When these words had been spoken by him, Viṣṇu said to Brahmā:
"Speak, speak, O highly fortunate one; what boon do you desire to declare? (8)
"O Viṣṇu, I am desirous of progeny; I wish for a son who is a bearer of burdens.
Then the blessed Brahmā, seeking a son, entered the waters.
Then Viṣṇu spoke these words to Prajāpati, who desired offspring:
"The heroic and peerless son you wish for—one who is a steadfast leader—" || 1.25.10 ||
"Accept the God of gods, Maheśvara, as your son.
Having honored those words of Keśava, the Grandfather [Brahmā]—
Having saluted the Lord Rudra, the giver of boons, with palms joined in reverence, he,
desiring a son, spoke these words together with Viṣṇu.
"If the Blessed One is pleased with me, who am constantly desirous of a son, then become my son, O Soul of the Universe—either equal to yourself or a bearer of the world's burden.
O Maheśvara, when you are pleased, I choose no other boon. (13)
Having heard that prayer of his, the Blessed One, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, spoke these words:
"So be it," a speech that was stainless and free from guile.
O you of noble vows, when anger shall overcome you at the commencement of some task or when that task remains unaccomplished,
those eleven Rudras who are ordained as the causes of the vital breaths within yourself [will manifest]. (15)
Then, indeed, I shall become the eleven-fold one, spear in hand and accompanied by my followers;
at that time, the high-souled sage Mitra shall emerge from my forehead.
Having previously bestowed such incomparable grace upon Brahmā, Viṣṇu spoke this again: "And I grant you a boon."
The illustrious Viṣṇu spoke these words to Bhava:
"O Lord, all this has been done; if you are well-pleased with me, O cloud-vehicled one, let my devotion be firmly established in you. (18)
Thus addressed, the god then spoke to Keśava:
"O Viṣṇu, eternal one, listen to how I am pleased with you, O god. (19)
Whatever is manifest and unmanifest, mobile and immobile—
all this universe, in its universal form, consists of Rudra and Nārāyaṇa.
I am Agni and you are Soma; you are night and I am day.
You are falsehood and I am truth; you are the ritual sacrifice and I am its fruit. ||21||
You are knowledge and I am the object of knowledge; by chanting which, people always enter into me when you are pleased—those people who perform good deeds.
Together with us both, there is indeed no other destination at the end of the age.
Know the Self to be Prakṛti; know me to be the auspicious Puruṣa.
You are half of my body, and I am yours, just as "I" am to you.
My left side is dark blue, marked with the Śrīvatsa;
you are my right side, while I am indeed Nīlalohita.
And you, O Viṣṇu, are my heart, and I am situated in your heart;
you are the performer of every action, and I am the presiding deity.
"Come now, may it be well with you, my child; I shall depart, O you who possess the luster of a cloud.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Viṣṇu, the Sovereign, vanished from sight.
Then, O King, when the god had vanished, Hari, being greatly delighted, entered the water once more and lay down upon his bed.
Then Brahmā, whose eyes are like lotuses and who is born from a lotus, with a heart full of joy, took his seat upon that lotus-throne which shone like the interior of a lotus.
Then, after a long time, there too appeared the two incomparable brothers,
Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who were possessed of great strength and great courage.
And they both spoke these words: "You shall indeed become our food.
Having spoken thus, they both vanished from that place.
But having perceived their grim disposition and realizing his own greatness, the one born from the lotus began to inquire further.
When he could no longer perceive the way to fashion the pericarp,
he descended into the subterranean realm (rasātala) through the lotus stalk; there,
within the waters, he beheld Hari, who was wearing a black antelope skin as an upper garment.
He awakened him, and once he had woken up, he said this:
"O God, I have fear of living beings; protect me! Arise and be my refuge! (33)
Then the Blessed Viṣṇu, the subduer of enemies, himself spoke with a smile to the sage, saying: "Do not fear, do not fear! (34)
Therefore, you previously said, "I have great fear of the bhūtas"; consequently, you shall destroy those two Daityas with words beginning with the word "bhūta. (35)
Then, uttering "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ," they entered that god who was not born from a womb;
thereafter, having performed a circumambulation, they approached him as he sat there.
When he had departed, Ananta then vomited Viṣṇu and Jiṣṇu from his mouth and spoke to Brahmā, who was intent on protection,
having learned that Madhu and Kaiṭabha were approaching once again. ||37||
Those two best of beings assumed forms resembling Viṣṇu and Jiṣṇu;
having created those similar forms, they both stood facing one another.
Then those two Daityas spoke these harsh words to Brahmā:
"Become our arbitrator while we are fighting. (39)
Then, having entered the water and solidified the waters by their own power of illusion, the two of them engaged in a tumultuous battle, each doing whatever he desired at that time.
As they were thus fighting, a hundred divine years passed;
yet neither their martial fury nor their pride in battle subsided as they continued to contend with one another.
Because they possessed form through the two types of characteristics and remained with gestures, Brahmā, his mind distracted by their resemblance, entered into meditation. 42.

Having discerned the vulnerability between those two with his divine eye, he bound upon them a subtle armor born from the filaments of a lotus; then, having equipped their bodies with waist-bands, he uttered this mantra: ||43||
As he was chanting, a maiden arose from the Viśvarūpa;
she was auspicious, with a face like the moon and the lord of the waters, holding a lotus in her hand.
Upon seeing her, the two Daityas were distressed by fear and deprived of their color.
Then Brahmā spoke to that maiden with a sweet voice:
"Who are you to be recognized here? Speak the truth, O blameless one. (45)
Then, having honored Brahmā with gentle words and with palms joined in reverence, that maiden said:
"Know me to be Māyā, the enchantress of Viṣṇu, acting upon his command. (46)
O Brahmin, being thus glorified by you, I arrived with great haste;
and Brahmā, being pleased in mind, gave her the secondary name [Gaurī].
Since you have been uttered by me and have appeared together with you,
your name shall circulate as "Mahāvyāhṛti."
Because she split her head while in the form of a woman, she is called Sāvitrī;
and because she was born from Ekānaṃśā, you shall become Anekāṃśā.
"O lady of auspicious countenance, by my grace these secondary names and others born of your actions shall belong to you. (1.25.50)
Then, being thus oppressed, the two of them requested this boon: "Let our death be open [to all], and let us become your sons. (51)
Having said "So be it," Viṣṇu then quickly led Kaiṭabha to the abode of Yama; and Jiṣṇu likewise led Madhu there as well.
Thus these two Daityas were slain by Viṣṇu, the victorious,
together with the gratified Brahmā, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Understand how the Self was indeed given as a son by the Lord; likewise,
when the conflict with Madhu and Kaiṭabha had passed, Brahmā spoke to Viṣṇu along with Jiṣṇu.
Today the full hundred years have passed and the time has arrived;
I shall go to my own abode, for the terrible dissolution is imminent.
At his word, the God then brought about the dissolution,
having rendered the earth devoid of immobile beings and having placed mobile beings in their primordial state.
If the lord of the aquatic creatures has been cast down by you, O Govinda— may it be well with you—
then tell me, O increaser of my fortune, what must be done by me for you.
"Very well, listen, O lotus-born one of golden luster, to my words:
that grace which you have obtained from the Lord through your desire for a son. (58)
Having thus rendered me free from debt by making [this] fruitful, you have become one who owes me nothing;
now, create or emit the four kinds of beings.
Having regained consciousness from Govinda, the Grandfather, whose source is the lotus,
performed great and fierce austerities, intent upon creating progeny.
As he was thus performing his austerities, nothing at all happened;
then, after a long time, anger grew within him out of his suffering.
From his two eyes, which were possessed by anger, drops of tears fell;
then, from those drops of tears, [beings] consisting of wind, bile, and phlegm emerged.
Those highly fortunate and great beings, serpents adorned with auspicious marks,
appeared with disheveled hair and possessing potent venom.
Seeing his elder brothers as serpents, Brahmā reproached himself:
"Alas, shame! If such is the fruit of my asceticism, then my progeny have been born at the very outset as the destroyers of the world."
A violent fainting spell, born of anger and resentment, came upon him;
then, due to that feverish fainting, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) gave up his life-breaths.
From the body of that one of incomparable vigor, out of compassion,
those eleven Rudras emerged from him as he was weeping;
indeed, because of their weeping (rodanāt), they are the Rudras, and thus they possess that nature of Rudra-ness.
Those who are indeed Rudras are the vital breaths (prāṇas), and those who are the vital breaths are of that nature;
the vital breaths should be known as residing within all beings among those who possess life. ||67||
To him, who possessed exceedingly fierce greatness and had performed virtuous deeds,
the trident-wielder Nīlalohita, the Lord consisting of eleven forms, restored his life-breaths once more from his forehead— the very forehead of the lotus-born Brahmā.

Then that powerful lord Rudra, his son, having restored the vital breaths to Brahmā, spoke these supreme words to the god Brahmā with a joyful countenance: "O Lord, you have granted me life; therefore, O Grandfather, grant me a boon. (70) Brahmā said: "O Rudra, choose whatever boon you desire; I shall grant it to you, for there is nothing that cannot be given by me. "Entreat me, O Brahmin; you ought to remember your own self.
You know me as Rudra, your own son; O Lord, grant me your grace."
Having heard these words of his and the abundance of his inner thoughts,
the Grandfather, with a serene soul, [looked upon him] with eyes possessing the luster of full-blown lotuses.
Then, having regained his vital breath, the Blessed Lord Brahmā, radiant as pure gold, spoke in a voice that was both affectionate and deep.
"O, O highly fortunate one, speak! You delight my mind.
Who are you, the source of all beings, who stand here as the elevenfold self? (73)
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, Brahmā of infinite splendor,
Rudra then replied after having saluted him along with his sons.
O Brahman, when I was requested by Viṣṇu for a boon, I said:
"Become my son, O God, or one equal to you who can bear the world's burden. (75)
O Lord of Gods, you ought to create the worlds by means of all those renowned throughout the worlds, who are born from the Universal Soul; do not despair. ||76||
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, Brahmā became joyful in mind;
he spoke again to Rudra, the blue-and-red one at the end of the world.
"For the sake of my work, create subjects together with me as my assistants;
you are the seed of all beings, so become one who has thus resorted to that [work].
"So be it," Śaṅkara accepted those words.
Then that blessed Lord Brahmā, adorned with a black antelope skin,
first created the mind, and thereafter the sustaining power of all beings,
as well as the tongue, Sarasvatī herself, who possesses universal forms.
The one of great splendor created seven mind-born sons: Bhrigu, Aṅgiras, Dakṣa, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and Vasiṣṭha.
He created other sons equal to himself, the progenitors of the universe;
following after them, cows were born from his mouth. (81)
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, likewise [instructed] the Vedas headed by the syllable Oṃ and the presiding deities of these [Vedas], exactly as they have been described.
The blessed Lord spoke to Dakṣa and his other mind-born sons:
"Create progeny; may prosperity be yours, together with the wise Rudra. (83)
Having then followed after that Great-Souled One, the Lords of Creatures said:
"O God, O Maheśvara, we desire to create offspring together with you;
this is the command of Brahmā and yours as well. (84)
Thus addressed by them, the Lord Rudra, the Master, spoke to those gods:
"O Suras, the sons of Brahmā have indeed seized my vital breaths."

Having made these foremost of the foremost—the Brāhmaṇas, my own sons—[and] the seven worlds from Brahmā down to a blade of grass as my very self, you ought to create them at my command; may it be well with you. (86)
Thus addressed by him, they replied to the furious Rudra, wielder of the trident:
"O God, it shall indeed be exactly as you command. (87)
Then, having obtained the permission of Mahādeva, the Lords of Creatures said to the high-souled Dakṣa: "You are the most excellent Prajāpati;
placing you at our head—may it be well with you—we shall create the subjects."
"So be it," Dakṣa replied to their speech;
desiring offspring, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) began to create along with them.
Then, while the principle of persistence remained established, Brahmā set about creating the world.
Then, when the seventh kalpa had passed, there arose two [beings],
R̥bhu and Sanatkumāra, who dwelt in the world of asceticism (tapas).
Thereafter, the Lord created other great seers from his mind.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth and Destruction of Madhu and Kaiṭabha," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Oh, how marvelous are these secrets, O Great-minded One, which you have explained according to reality for the sake of benefiting the world! (1)
In this regard, I have a great doubt concerning the incarnations of the Wielder of the Trident:
for what reason, O Mahādeva, having bypassed the previous ages, does he take an incarnation upon reaching the most terrible Kali age? ||2||
O Lord, now that this Vaivasvata Manvantara has arrived, I wish to know how you took your incarnation. (3)
There is nothing unknown to you, either in this world or in the next.
For the sake of instructing your devotees,
please speak, O one of great wisdom, if your great doctrine is fit to be heard, to me who asks with humility.
Lomaśa said:
Thus questioned, the Blessed One Vāyu, who is devoted to the welfare of the world, spoke these words;
the highly resplendent Vāyu, who is saluted by the worlds.
O son of Gādhi, listen as I explain in due order everything that you ask me, which is the most closely guarded secret in the world.
Long ago, when a single ocean had existed for a thousand divine years,
Brahmā, desiring to create living beings, reflected in deep distress.
As he was thus reflecting, a young boy appeared;
possessing a divine fragrance and seeking nectar, he uttered a divine utterance.
The Lord, uttering the Veda, discovered that [Vidyā] which is devoid of sound, touch, form, and smell, and which is free from taste. 9.
Then, joined with meditation and undertaking fierce austerity,
he reflected in his mind as to who might follow the triad.
As he was reflecting thus, that Imperishable (Akṣara) appeared to him—devoid of sound, touch, and form, and free from taste and smell. ||11||
Then he beholds his own supreme form among the worlds;
meditating upon the God at that time, he indeed sees Him once again.
There one may see that [being] as white, then red, yellow, and again black; established in its color there, it is neither female nor neuter.
Having known all that for a very long time and contemplating that imperishable syllable, as he was thus reflecting, the syllable arose from his throat. (14)
Having a single measure, a great resonance, white in color, and perfectly pure—that Oṃkāra is the Veda; he is indeed the Imperishable (Akṣara), the Great Lord (Maheśvara). ||15||
Then, as the Self-born One was meditating upon the Imperishable, there appeared a red [light]; that is remembered as the first deity.

The *Ṛgveda* is its first part; "I praise Agni, the domestic priest"—having seen this *ṛc*, the Brahmā, the creator of the world and possessed of great splendor, reflected again: "What is this syllable? (17)
While he was thus reflecting, Maheśvara then manifested as a two-measure syllable, a two-measured sound through his power of lordship.
Then again, she meditated upon a syllable of two morae;
it appeared as red, and taking it at its cutting, she [perceived] the Yajus. ||19||
"Oṃ iṣe tvorje tvā; oṃ vāyava stha; oṃ devo vaḥ savitā punar.
The Ṛgveda is said to have one mātrā, while the Yajurveda has two mātrās. (1.26.20)
Then, having seen that syllable of the Veda consisting of two measures,
the Lord again contemplated that imperishable Brahman which consists of two measures.
As he was reflecting thus, the syllable Oṃ indeed came into being;
then Brahmā meditated upon that imperishable syllable, Oṃ.
Then he saw the yellowish-red verse arisen from that very place: "O Agni, come for the feast, being praised for the giving of the oblation. (23)
Then that Lord of great splendor, seeing the Vedas standing before him,
reflected upon the three-syllabled [mantra] which exists at the three junctions of the day,
the three-colored one, the Oṃkāra known as Brahman, which is to be recited at the three libations.
And thus, from that very triple conjunction, that syllable becomes three-colored;
it is both perceptible and imperceptible, and when joined with the three heavens, it constitutes the triad.
It has three measures, three feet, and is the eternal triple-yoga;
therefore, the Lord Brahmā indeed meditated upon that Imperishable Brahman.

Therefore, he then beholds that syllable (akṣara), which is the self-existent Brahmā’s own form—the god with fourteen faces and blazing splendor. Having first uttered the syllable Om, he is to be known as the self-existent one. ||27||
From that mouth of the four-faced one, the fourteen vowels were born;
they are of various colors and divine, and that is the primordial syllable.
From that, indeed, the sixty-three letters are remembered as originating from the syllable *A*.
Then, for the common benefit of the social classes, that first vowel, which is the form of the letter 'a', was established at the beginning by the Self-born One. (29)
Then, from those vowels, fourteen great-faced divine Manus,
who are the vowels within the Manvantaras, are born.
He who has fourteen faces and whose form is the syllable *A*, designated as Brahmā,
is declared to be the Brahma-kalpa, the Lord of Creatures (*Prajāpati*) consisting of all phonemes.
From his first mouth, Svāyambhuva Manu is remembered;
he should be known as the letter 'A', white in color, belonging to Svayambhū. (32)
From his second mouth, the face known as Ākāra was produced;
he is called by the name Svārociṣa, and his complexion is said to be pale-white.
From his third mouth emerged the letter 'i', the best of the Yajus;
that Āditya consists of the Yajus, from which the Yajurveda is said to have originated.
That letter *ī* should be known as Manu, red in color and full of majesty;
from him the Kṣatra (the warrior class) originated, and therefore the Kṣatriya is red. ||35||
From his fourth mouth, the vowel *ukāra* is said to have emerged;
by its color it is remembered as copper-red, and that Manu is known as Tāmasa.
From his fifth mouth, the letter Ū is born as its name; it is yellow in color, and its mantras are mobile. ||37||
Then, from his sixth mouth, Oṃkāra was born, known as Kapila;
and from him came Variṣṭha, the sixth, who was Vijaya and a man of great asceticism.
From his seventh mouth then came Vaivasvata Manu;
there, the vowel is the letter 'ṛ', which is said to be black in color.
From his eighth mouth emerged the syllable Ṛ, which was dark blue in color;
because he was of the same color as that dark blue syllable, he is called Sāvarṇi.
From his ninth mouth, the letter *ḷ* is said to have emerged as the ninth;
