he is indeed smoke-colored (*dhūmra*) in complexion, and his mantra is called *Dhūmrasva*.
From his tenth mouth, the syllable *lṛ* emerged, which is called the Lord;
he shone as the Manu Sāvarṇika, being both equal and of the same color.
From its eleventh face, the letter E is said to be the Manu;
it is tawny in color, and thus it is called the tawny color. ||43||
From his twelfth mouth, the letter named Ai is uttered;
he is tawny (piśaṅga), with the luster of the color of ashes, and is called the tawny Manu. 44.
From his thirteenth mouth, the phoneme *o* is said to emerge;
endowed with five colors, the phoneme *o* is supreme. (45)
From his fourteen mouths, the syllable *au* is said to be his letter;
and being speckled in color, he is called the Manu Sāvarṇi.
Thus, these *mantras*, as well as vowels and consonants, should be understood according to their true nature, both by their vowels and by their consonants, in accordance with the ritual rules. ||47||
Since vowels are indeed surrounded by those of their own respective classes, their relationship is proclaimed as one of "homogeneity" (savarṇa) because of that shared quality. ||48||
Since those born at the beginning of the Kalpa were of the same color and similar in appearance, therefore, in this world, all the joints of living beings are of the same color. 49.

Just as the phonemes (varṇas) will exist according to their form, their grammatical correctness, and their meaning, so too should the euphonic combinations (sandhis) be known from practice; therefore, they are called vowels (svaras). 1.26.50.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Origin of the Vowels," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
The origin of the initial creation has been declared by me in brief;
I shall now describe its details at length, along with the names of the various bodies.
Mahādeva begot many sons upon his wives;
listen now to which kalpa that occurred when the eighth kalpa had passed.
And at the beginning of the kalpa, as the Lord was meditating upon a son equal to himself,
there appeared from his lap a youth who was blue and red;
he held a loud and terrible voice, as if burning everything with his splendor.
Seeing the youth Nīlalohita suddenly weeping, Brahmā addressed him, saying, "O youth, why do you weep? (5)
He said, "O Grandfather, give me my first name.
Being told, "O God, you are Rudra by name," he wept again.
To him who was weeping, Brahmā spoke again: "Why do you weep?
He said to the Self-born One: "Give me a second name. (7)
"O God, you shall be known by the name Bhava," it was said; then he wept again.
To Śaṅkara, who was thus weeping, Brahmā then replied, "Why do you weep? (8)
When he was told, "Give me a third name," Śiva replied to him, "O God, you shall be named Śiva. Having been told this, he wept again. (9)
To him who was weeping, Brahmā spoke again, asking, "Why do you weep?
He replied to the Self-born One, "Give me a fourth name. (1.27.10)
"You are the lord of animals, O God"—having been addressed thus, he wept again.
To him who was weeping, Brahmā spoke once more: "Why do you weep? (11)
When he was told, "Give me a fifth name," the Lord replied to him, "O God, you are Īśa by name. Having been thus addressed, he wept again.
To him who was weeping, Brahmā spoke again, "Why do you weep?
Then he said to the Lord, "Give me a sixth name. (13)
"O God, you are Bhīma by name. When he was thus addressed, he wept again.
To him as he was weeping, Brahmā spoke once more: "Why do you weep? (14)
When told, "Give me a seventh name," he replied to him, "O God, you are Ugra by name. Having been thus addressed, he wept again. (15)
Brahmā spoke again to him as he was weeping, "Why do you weep?
He replied, "O Lord, give me an eighth name. Having been told, "You are Mahādeva by name," he indeed ceased [weeping].
Having obtained these names from Brahmā, Nīlalohita spoke: "Assign beings to these names. ||17||
Then, from among these names, their subtle bodies were emitted by the Self-born:
namely, the sun, the earth, water, fire, wind, and space. (18)
The initiated one, Brahmā, and the Moon—these are the constituents of Brahman (brahmadhātavaḥ).
Rudra is to be honored and worshipped among them; indeed, he destroys those who oppose them. ||19||
Then Brahmā spoke again to that god Nīlalohita:
"That second name which was proclaimed by me for you as 'Bhava,' water shall become your second body by that name. (1.27.20)
When this was said, that which was stable within his body, consisting of the essence (rasa), entered the water; therefore, Bhava is remembered as being composed of water (āpas). ||21||
Since beings arise from them and they, in turn, nourish those beings, the origin of beings is traditionally held to result from both their arising (bhavana) and their nourishment (bhāvanā). ||22||
Therefore, one should never void urine or feces in water;
one should not bathe naked in water, nor should one ever spit therein. (23)
One should never indulge in sexual intercourse and should avoid bathing the head;
nor, while carrying [the sacred fire], should one speak with delight, even when standing still.
Water is never defiled by contact with pure or impure bodies; however, one should avoid water that is discolored, has an altered taste or smell, or is scanty. (25)
The ocean is the womb of the waters; therefore, they desire it. Having reached the sea, they become both pure and immortal. ||26||
Therefore, one should not obstruct the waters, for they long for the ocean;
the divine Bhava never harms him who thus abides within the waters.
Then Brahmā spoke again to that dark-red deity:
"Since the third name proclaimed for you is 'Śarva', let this earth be your body by that name. (28)
When this was said, that which was stable in his body, known as bone, entered the earth;
therefore, the earth is called Śarvā.
Therefore, a wise man should not discharge feces or urine; nor should he urinate in the shade, on a staircase, or even in his own shadow. 1.27.30.
Covering his head and shielding the earth with grass,
he who conducts himself thus upon the ground is indeed not harmed by Śarva.
Then Brahmā spoke again to that god Nīlalohita:
"That which was declared by me as your fourth name, 'Īśāna'—" ||32||
"The fourth [element] shall be the fourth [wife] of the fourth; your body shall be Vāyu by name.
When this was said, that which resides within the body and is designated as the fivefold vital breath (prāṇa)—||33||
Then the Lord Vāyu entered him; therefore, he is called Vāyu. One should speak of him as the pervasive Lord Vāyu.
Thus disciplined, the Lord God does not harm him.
Then Brahmā spoke again to that god Dhūmralohita:
"Since the fifth name was uttered by me here as 'Paśupati,' let your body, which is the fifth of the five, be named Agni. (35)
When this was said, the fire that resided within his body was summoned; then Agni entered him, and therefore he is Paśupati, the Lord.
The Moon is known as Soma, for his very self is the multitude of medicinal herbs.
Thus, the wise man who conducts himself in this manner at every sacred juncture (parvan) is not slain by Mahādeva; one should thus worship that Lord.
The sun protects living beings by day, while the moon does so by night;
both the sun and the moon meet together on a single night.
On the night of the new moon (amāvāsyā), one should always dwell in that [union]. ||38||
Pervading all this—along with bodies and names—he who moves alone is called both the Sun and the Moon. (39)
By the light of the sun, living beings are seen with their eyes;
yet Rudra, established as the white-souled one, drinks the water with his rays.
That body which consists of food and drink is indeed produced from the self; it is nourished within the physical bodies themselves. (41)
By means of which, with a mind that has become steadfast, he sustains all creatures—that earthly body of his, belonging to Śarva, sustains the subjects. ||42||
As long as it remains within the bodies of living beings through the functions of the vital breaths, that power of Īśāna,
consisting of the nature of wind, exists together with the life-breaths of all creatures.
That power which digests yellow and white foods within the stomachs of living beings is therefore called his digestive power, Pāśupatī.
Those cavities that exist here within the bodies for the purpose of the movement of the vital air—she is called the formidable body (tanu). ||45||
The state of those who discourse on Brahman and are consecrated for the Vaitāna sacrifice is one whose nature is fierce;
therefore, such a consecrated person is known as Ugra. ||46||
That which is his faculty of volition resides equally among all creatures here;
that is his mental body, which exists within living beings as the moon. ||47||
Being born again and again, he indeed becomes ever new;
he is led according to his desire along with the all-pervading Pitṛs.
That Mahādeva, whose essence is nectar, is remembered as the moon, which is composed of water. ||48||
His first body, which was proclaimed to be Raudrī by name, had Suvarcalā as his wife; their son was Śanaiścara.
The second body of Bhava is indeed known as water;
its wife here is remembered as Oṣā, and its son is remembered as Uśanas.
The third stage of Śarva is known as his body;
his wife is named Vikeśī, and his son is known as Aṅgāraka. ||51||
The body of the fourth Īśāna, who had departed to heaven,
was named Śivā as his wife, and his son was Manojava.
That body of Paśupati which is known by the twice-born as Agni has Svāhā as his wife, and Skanda is also known as his son.
The sixth [son], whose name is Bhīma, has as his body the ether (ākāśa);
the quarters are known as his wives, and heaven is known as his son.
The seventh body is known as Ugrā, which is remembered by initiated brāhmaṇas;
Dīkṣā is remembered as his wife, and their offspring is called the son.
The body of the eighth great [Prajāpati], known by the name Candra, is remembered as the Moon;
Rohiṇī was his wife, and his son is remembered as Budha.
Thus these bodies of his have been proclaimed by their names; indeed, each body is to be praised and saluted according to its respective name.
Through devotion to the Sun, to the waters, to the earth, to the wind, fire, and ether,
and likewise to the moon— along with their forms and names—
that man indeed attains union with the Lord and becomes possessed of progeny. (58)
Thus has this secret glory of Bhīma been recounted by me to you;
may it ever be for the welfare of our bipeds, and may it be for the welfare of our quadrupeds. 59.
Thus has been declared the origin of the Vastus along with their names; now hear of the progeny of the god Mahādeva and of Bhṛgu. 1.27.60.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Body of Mahādeva," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Then Khyāti bore to Bhṛgu two lords over pleasure and pain,
the bestowers of good and evil upon all living beings here,
the two gods Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ who move through the Manvantaras. ||1||
The elder sister of those two was the goddess Śrī, the bringer of prosperity to the world.
Having obtained the beautiful Lord Nārāyaṇa as her husband,
that virtuous woman gave birth to two sons of Nārāyaṇa, Bala and Utsāha.
Her mind-born sons, as well as others who move through the divine realms,
are those who carry the celestial chariots of the gods of meritorious deeds.
Two daughters are recorded as the wives of the Creator and the Ordainer respectively:
Āyati and Niyati. Their two sons were of firm vows.
Pāṇḍu and Mṛkaṇḍu were the two eternal repositories of the Veda;
and from Mṛkaṇḍu, through Manasvinī, was born Mārkaṇḍeya.
A son was indeed born to him from his head through Daśī;
the sons of Vedaśiras by Pīvarī are remembered as the founders of lineages, known as the Mārkaṇḍeyas—sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas. ||6||
And from Pāṇḍu and Puṇḍarīkā was born a son named Dyutimān;
both Dyutimān and Sṛñjaya were born [of her].
Their sons and grandsons intermarried with one another among the Bhārgavas.
Listen now to the progeny of Marīci after the Svāyambhuva Manvantara had passed.
Sambhūti, the wife of Marīci, gave birth to Ātmasambhava;
know that he begot Pūrṇamāsa, as well as these daughters:
Kuṣṭi, Pṛṣṭi, Tviṣā, and the auspicious Apaciti.
Pūrṇamāsa begot two sons upon Sarasvatī:
Virajas, who was most righteous, and Parvaṇas. ||9||
The learned son of Viraja was the renowned Sudhāman;
the son of Sudhāman, Vairāja, took up residence in the eastern direction.
The world-protector, virtuous-souled, the son of Gaurī, and possessed of great majesty, that highly illustrious Parvasa entered among all the Gaṇas. ||11||
Parvata begot two sons,
Yajñavāman, who was illustrious, and Kāśyapa as the second son;
those two sons were the founders of lineages and were firmly established in righteousness.
Smṛti, the wife of Aṅgiras, gave birth to two sons born from her own self and four meritorious daughters who became world-renowned. (13)
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and likewise Anumati;
and similarly both Bharata and Agni, as well as Kīrtimant. 14.
Parjanya, the lord, was born from Agni through the union of Saṃhūti;
Parjanya, whose hair is golden, begot [a son] upon Mārīcī.
He is remembered as the guardian of the world (lokapāla) who remains until the dissolution of all beings (ābhūtasaṃplava). ||15||
From Kīrtimant were also born Dhenuka and Tāvakalmaṣa;
both were the most excellent and steadfast among the best of the Aṅgirases.
Their sons and grandsons who have passed away are indeed thousands;
Anasūyā also gave birth to them for the patriarch Pulaha.
And there was a daughter named Śruti, who was the mother of Śaṅkhapada;
she was the wife of Kardama and the daughter of the progenitor Pulaha. ||18||

Satyanetra, Havya, Āpomūrti, Śanīvara, and Soma as the fifth—these were the five Ātreyas who appeared during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara; they passed away along with that Yuga which has elapsed. Thus are the five Ātreyas proclaimed. ||19||
Their sons and grandsons, indeed, were born by the high-souled Atri in hundreds and thousands during the period of the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
From Prīti, the wife of Pulastya, Dattāli was born as their son;
in a previous birth during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, he was known as Agastya.
Madhyama, Devabāhu, and Vinīta—these three were his [sons]. (21)
Their younger sister, renowned by the name Sadvatī,
was the radiant mother of Parjanya; she is remembered as the auspicious wife of Agni,
and also of the wise Rishi Paulastya, the son of Prīti.
The wife of Dattāli gave birth to many sons, beginning with Sujaṅgha;
they are known as the Paulastyas and are remembered as having flourished during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
Kṣamā, however, gave birth to sons of the patriarch Pulaha;
they were all possessed of the brilliance of fire, and their fame is firmly established.
Kardama, Ambarīṣa, and Sahiṣṇu—these were the three;
and the sage Dhanakapīvān, as well as his daughter Pīvarī.
Śruti, the daughter of Atri, was the wife of Kardama;
she gave birth to sons, namely Śaṅkhapada, as well as a daughter named Kāmyā. ||26||
That illustrious Śaṅkhapada, the guardian of the world and lord of creatures,
took his pleasure in the southern quarter after giving away the Sāmya region to Priyavrata.
Kāmyā obtained from Priyavrata ten sons equal to Svāyambhuva Manu,
as well as two sets of daughters, by whom the Kṣatriya order was established.
And a son named Sahiṣṇu, famous for his great wealth and power, was born; indeed, that slender-waisted one, the sustainer of fame, was Kāmadeva himself. 29.
From R̥tu was born a son equal to Kratu, a glorious progeny;
they had no wives nor sons, for all of them were perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas).
These sixty thousand are known as the Vālakhilyas.
Proceeding before Aruṇa and surrounding the sun, they all remain companions of the bird until the dissolution of all beings. (31)
His two younger sisters were Puṇyātmā and Sumatī;
they were indeed the daughters-in-law of Parvaṇi, the son of Pūrṇamāsa.
From Ūrjā, the seven sons of Vasiṣṭha were indeed born;
and their elder sister was Puṇḍarīkā, who possessed a beautiful waist.
She was the mother of the radiant Pāṇḍu and his beloved queen;
from her were born these seven famous younger sons, the Vāsiṣṭhas. (34)
Raja, Arddhabāhu, Savana, Adhana, Sutapas, and Śukla—these are all remembered as the seven Ṛṣis. ||35||
Moreover, the illustrious Mārkaṇḍeyī gave birth to Rajasa,
the royal Prajāpati Ketumān, in the western quarter.
The lineages by name of those high-souled Vasiṣṭhas who passed away in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara have been told; now hear of the progeny of Agni.
Thus has this lineage of the Ṛṣis been proclaimed along with its descendants;
now hear in detail and in proper sequence about the progeny of Agni.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Lineages of the Sages," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
That Agni who was indeed the presiding deity during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara,
being the mind-born son of Brahmā, from him Svāhā was born.
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and he who is remembered as Pāvamāna—
these three sons of Svāhā are to be known as Śuci, Śaura, and [Pāvamāna] respectively.
Having churned [the fire], Pavamāna is indeed pure; he who is remembered as Śaura is Pāvaka;
and those who are Vaidyuta—these are their respective stations.
The son of Pavamāna is called Kavyavāhana;
from Pāvaka comes Saharakṣas, and Havyavāha is the son of Śuci.
Agni is the bearer of oblations for the gods, Kavyavāhana for the ancestors, and Saharakṣas for the asuras; thus there are three fires for these three classes.
The sons and grandsons of these, however, are exactly forty-nine;
I shall state their names and their respective divisions one by one.
The Vaidyuta fire is the worldly fire, the first son of Brahmā;
his son was the fire known as Brahmodana, renowned by the name Bharata.
Atharvan is to be known as Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras is the son of Atharvaṇa;
therefore, he is the Laukika fire, while Dadhyañc is the son of Atharvaṇa.
Now, that Agni Pavamāna who is remembered by the sages as Nirmathya is to be known as the Gārhapatya fire; from him, two sons are said to have been born.
The Āhavanīya fire, who is remembered as the bearer of oblations, is called Śaṃsya;
the second son is said to be Śukra, the fire which is led forward. ||11||
Likewise, both the Āvasathya and the Anvāhāryapacana fires were born from the fire Śaṃsya;
and the carrier of oblations (Havyavāhana) created the sixteen rivers.
That fire which is known by the twice-born as the Āhavanīya is the presiding deity (Abhimānin). ||12||
The Kāverī, the Kṛṣṇaveṇī, the Narmadā, and likewise the Yamunā;
the Godāvarī, the Vitastā, the Candrabhāgā, and the Irāvatī. ||13||
The Vipāśā, the Kauśikī, the Śatadru, and likewise the Sarayū;
the Sītā, the Sarasvatī, the Hrādinī, and the Pāvanī as well. ||14||
Having divided himself sixteenfold among them, he then established himself individually within those sacrificial hearths (dhiṣṇyas). ||15||
The *dhiṣṇyas* are those who move through the heavens;
they were born among them, and because they were born in the *dhiṣṇīs*, they are therefore celebrated as *dhiṣṇyas*. ||16||
Thus, these sons of the rivers were indeed born within the sacrificial hearths (dhiṣṇī).
Listen now, as they are being described in brief, to those fires of theirs which are to be distributed and those which are to be attended. ||17||
Ṛtu is the Pravāhaṇa Agnīdhra; the other [Agnīdhra] is the Purastāddhiṣṇya.
They are assigned to their respective places on the Sautya day according to the sequence of the pressings (savana). ||18||
Listen to the sequence of the fires that are indescribable and inexpressible:
the Samrāṭ fire is Kṛśānu, who is the second, situated on the northern altar (uttaravedika). ||19||
Indeed, the eight fires known as Samrāj are worshipped by the twice-born;
another assembly fire, however, which is the second, is seen here below.
That which is called Nabhas has been declared to you; it is manifested as fourfold.
He who is named Vasu, the light of Brahman, is said to reside in the station of Brahman. ||21||
Unmixed with the sacrificial oblations, the sun, and other elements, he is perceived in the Śāmitra fire;
then, as the ocean of the universe, he is proclaimed in the Brahma-sthāna.
He is celebrated as Ṛtudhāman and Sujyotis in Audumbarī;
he is called Vasu, the Light of Brahman (Brahmajyotis), in the station of Brahman. ||23||
Ajaikapād is to be worshipped in the Upastha; he is indeed the Śālāmukhīyaka fire.
Though not specifically designated by a name, he is Ahibudhnya and is remembered as the Gṛhapati fire.
All the sons of Śasya alone are recorded in tradition as those who should be attended upon by the twice-born.
Thereafter, I shall describe his eight sons who were to be honored.

Kratupravāhaṇa is the Āgnīdhra; the other Dhiṣṇya hearths situated there are distributed according to their respective places on the day of the Soma-pressing (Sautya), following the sequence of the Savanas.
From him was born Agni Pautreya, who is remembered as Havyavāhana;
Śānti was his son, and Pracetas was the second, who is called Satya.
Likewise, Agni Viśvadeva is said to be in the place of Brahma;
and Avakṣuracchāvāka is perceived to be in the place of Bhuvaḥ. ||28||
The Uśīrāgni, possessing full potency, is considered the Naiṣṭhīya;
the eighth is the Vyavartti, which is proclaimed as the Mārjālīya.
Those who are to be established as hearths (dhiṣṇya) are indeed to be arranged with both Soma and another [fire];
of those two, the one named Pāvaka is said to be the embryo of the waters.
That fire is to be known as the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), for it is offered completely into the waters;
its son is the fire residing in the hearts of men, who is situated within their bellies. ||31||
Possessing fury, Agni is known as the son of the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni);
that great and all-pervading Agni is exalted among all beings through their mutual interaction. ||32||
That son of the wrathful Agni is known as the terrible Saṃvartaka;
drinking up the waters, he dwells in the ocean with the mouth of a mare.
The son of Samudravāsin is known as Saharakṣa;
the son of Saharakṣa is Kṣāma, who shall burn the houses of men.
The fire Kravyāda was born from him; he devours those men who are dead.
Thus indeed are these sons of the purifying fire Agni proclaimed.
Then, that fire which was churned by the Gandharvas and Asuras belonging to Śuci and Sūra in the forest is indeed kindled as the Agni Samidhya.
Then the Lord named Āyu was led forth as the sacrificial victim;
his son was Mahimā, and his son by name was Śāva.
That Agni, who presides over the *pākayajña* sacrifices, is known as Savana;
and the son of that Agni Savana was Adbhuta, who was of great renown.
He is remembered as the great son of Agni, though born from a wonder;
he always consumes the oblation offered in the expiation of terrible sins. (39)
From Vivicin was born Arka, and his sons were these:
Anīkavat, Vāsṛjavat, Rakṣohā, Pitṛkṛt,
Surabhi, Vasu, Ratnāda, and Rukmavat, who entered [the sun].
From Śuci Agni, fourteen Vahnis were born;
these are the Vahnis who have been described as those who are led forth in the sacrifices. 41.
Indeed, at the beginning of creation, during the previous Svāyambhuva interval, those fires, together with the Yamas and the best of gods,
were formerly possessed of self-consciousness (abhimānin).
These, indeed, are to be inhabited here among both sentient and insentient beings;
formerly, those who possessed the conceit of a fixed abode were the carriers of oblations in this world.
Established in these rites— those performed for specific desires, those for occasional occasions, and those that are constant—
in the past Manvantara that has passed, they were present together with the sons of Śukra and the high-souled,
meritorious gods during the first interval of Manu.
Thus, these abodes and their inhabitants have been described by me;
by means of these alone, however, the calculation [of time] is established even for the past and the future. (45)
In all the Manvantaras, this is the characteristic of the Jātavedases:
they are all indeed ascetics, and all likewise perform the Avabhṛtha bath;
they are all remembered as Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) and as luminous beings.
They are to be known as existing throughout all seven Manvantaras, beginning with Svārociṣa and ending with Sāvarṇi, assuming various forms for various purposes. (47)
The fires existing here abide together with the present gods;
likewise, the future fires abide together with the future gods. ||48||
Thus has this method of the fires been declared by me exactly as it is, both in detail and in its proper sequence; thereafter, that of the ancestors shall be described.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Agni," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
When Brahmā was creating his sons during the previous Svāyambhuva Manvantara, the waters were produced; from them arose humans, asuras, and gods.
For him who regarded them as his fathers, the Pitṛs were indeed born;
their creation has been described previously, and now its detailed account will be told.
Having seen [them], the god spoke to the gods, asuras, and humans:
"They have been born as if they were intended for consumption by one who regards them as his father. (3)
The six seasons, beginning with spring (madhu), are designated as the Pitṛs;
"The seasons are the Pitṛs, the gods"—this is the Vedic revelation.
Indeed, throughout all the past and future Manvantaras,
these were previously born during the auspicious Svāyambhuva interval.
Those known by the name Agniṣvāttas, as well as the Barhiṣads,
were indeed those among them who had not performed sacrifices and were householders;
they are remembered as the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs who maintained no sacred fires.
Among them, those who were performers of sacrifices and drinkers of Soma are remembered as the Barhiṣads;
they are indeed the Pitṛs who maintained the Agnihotra fire.
In this scripture, the settled opinion is that the Seasons, the Pitṛs, and the Devas are one and the same.
Madhu and Mādhava are to be known as the two juices; Śuci and Śukra are the two full of vigor;
Nabhas and Nabhasyas—these two are declared to be the two living beings (jīvas).
Iṣa and Ūrja are declared to be the two months rich in nectar;
Sahas and Sahasya are remembered as the two full of energy;
and Tapa and Tapasya are these two formidable months of the dewy season.
The six periods of time for them are established as those called months;
these are declared to be the seasons, which are indeed both conscious and unconscious.
The seasons are to be known as the sons of Brahmā, possessing self-consciousness (abhimānin).
They reside in the positions of months and half-months; the seasons and the seasonal deities occupy these stations. ||11||
Apart from these locations, one should know those who preside over them:
the days and nights, the months, the seasons, and the solstices.
The years and the stations are the presiding deities of the divisions of time;
likewise are the nimeṣas, kalās, kāṣṭhās, muhūrtas, days, and nights. ||13||
Now, those who are the inhabitants of these [worlds], established throughout the various times and states, are identical with them and possess their very nature; listen as I describe them. (14)
The lunar days (tithis) at the junctions of the fortnights are called *sandhyās*;
two halves of a month are designated as a "month" (*māsa*), and two months are said to be a "season" (*ṛtu*). ||15||
Three seasons constitute an *ayana*, and there are two *ayanās*, the southern and the northern;
a year is indeed well-established—these are the stations for those who occupy them. (16)
The seasons are to be known as having six well-formed sons, yet they are eightfold;
the sons of the seasons are remembered as five, and their offspring are characterized by the nature of the seasons. ||17||
And because it is from the seasonal essence (ārtava) that all things—both stationary and moving—are born;
therefore, the ancestors are the seasonal essences (ārtavāḥ), and the grandfathers are the seasons (ṛtavaḥ). ||18||
From Sumeka, indeed, all species of living beings are born and they die;
therefore, Sumeka is remembered as the great-grandfather of all creatures. ||19||
For these abiders in their respective places are proclaimed as being identical with those places; they are remembered as having those names because they consist of them and possess their nature.
He who is remembered as Prajāpati is considered to be the year;
for the year is remembered as Agni, and is called Ṛta by the twice-born.
From Ṛta were born the Ṛtus (the seasons), and from those Ṛtus came the months; these six seasons are to be known as the Ṛtus, and their five sons are the Ārtavas.
For bipeds, quadrupeds, birds, reptiles,
and the five classes of stationary beings, the flower is known as that which arises according to the season.
The state of being the seasons (*ṛtu*), the state of being the menstrual flow (*ārtava*), and the state of being the ancestors (*pitṛ*) have been proclaimed;
thus, these should be known as the ancestors who are both the seasons and the menstrual flows. (24)
Then all beings were born from them through the power of the seasons;
therefore, we have heard that they too are called Pitṛs, the "Seasonal" ones (Ārttavas).
In all Manvantaras, those who preside over time remain;
indeed, these who preside over the stations remain here through their self-restraint.
The ancestors are remembered as being of two kinds: the Agniṣvāttas and the Barhiṣads.
And from those ancestors were born two daughters, world-renowned. (27)
Menā and Dhāriṇī—by whom this entire universe is sustained—your father gave those two auspicious daughters of his for the sake of dharma;
both of them were exponents of the Veda and both were practitioners of yoga. (28)
Of those who are called the Agniṣvāttas, Menā was the mind-born daughter; Dhāraṇī, likewise mind-born, is remembered as the daughter of the Barhiṣads.
Meru gave birth to an auspicious daughter named Dhāraṇī for the sake of a wife;
those ancestors of yours who drink the Soma juice are known as the Barhiṣads.
The Agniṣvātta Pitṛs gave that Menā as a wife to Himavat;
they are indeed remembered as his daughters' sons—now learn of those grandsons.
Menā, the wife of Himavat, gave birth to Maināka from her womb;
and Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, was the wife whom Lavaṇa, the son of Dadhīci, took.
Maināka’s younger brother was Krauñca, from whom Krauñcadvīpa is said to have derived its name.
Meru’s wife was Dhāraṇī; she gave birth to a son, Mandara, who was endowed with divine medicinal herbs, as well as three famous daughters.
Velā, Niyati, and thirdly Ayati;
Dhātusāyati was the wife of Vidhātṛ, and Niyati is likewise recorded as his wife. (34)
In the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, the subjects at the beginning and end have indeed been described;
Velā bore to Sāgara one blameless daughter.
Savarṇā, the daughter of the ocean, was the wife of Prācīnabarhis;
she bore ten sons to Prācīnabarhis,
all of whom were named Pracetas and were masters of the science of archery.
Among them, the lord Dakṣa, the son of Svayambhū,
was born as their son during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu due to the curse of Tryambaka.
Having heard this, Śaunaka then asked Sūta:
"How was Dakṣa born from the curse of Bhava? Tell us who ask you about that which occurred previously in the lineage of Cākṣuṣa."
Thus addressed, the charioteer, having taken leave of Śaunaka, related the story concerning Dakṣa and the cause of the curse from Tryambaka.
Dakṣa had eight sons, and those daughters whom I have mentioned were brought by their father from their own homes and honored in his house;
thus, having been all duly honored, they dwelt in their father’s home.
Among them, the eldest was the wife named Satī, who belonged to Tryambaka;
Dakṣa, being hostile toward Rudra, did not indeed invite her daughter.
Maheśvara never once offered obeisance to Dakṣa;
as his son-in-law, he remained by his very nature established in his own splendor toward that father-in-law.
Then, having learned that all her sisters had arrived at their father's house,
Satī also went to her own father’s home, even though she had not been invited.
Then that goddess, provoked by anger, spoke to her father:
"O Lord, why have you, disregarding my disapproval, performed this contemptible honor for the elder sisters while excluding me, the youngest? (44)
"I am indeed the eldest and the most excellent; you ought not to do what is improper.
Thus addressed, Dakṣa, his eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke to her.
But you, my child, are always the most excellent, the most distinguished, and worthy of honor to me;
and their husbands, likewise, are always highly esteemed by me. (46)
O Satī, they were all established in Brahman, most ascetic, great yogis, and highly righteous;
they were superior in virtues and praiseworthy because of their devotion to the Three-eyed Lord.
Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Pulastya, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Bhṛgu, and Marīci—these are my excellent sons-in-law. (48)
He is the Self, and he is Śarva to you; indeed, you are always his devotee.
For that reason, I do not wish to favor you, for Bhava is adverse to me.
Thus spoke Dakṣa then, with a completely deluded mind,
regarding himself and those supreme ṛṣis who had been addressed for the purpose of cursing him.
Thus addressed, the goddess, filled with anger, spoke this to her father:
"Since you reproach me, who am faultless in word, thought, and deed, therefore, O father, I shall cast off this body, your daughter. (51)
Then, because of that insult, Satī, filled with indignation due to her grief,
spoke these words after bowing down to Maheśvara.
Wherever I may be reborn again with a radiant body, there too,
remaining undeluded and virtuous once more,
I shall go, according to dharma, to become the lawful wife of Tryambaka himself.
Then, seated right there, she composed her disciplined mind and maintained within herself the mental concentration (dhāraṇā) upon the fiery element.
Then, impelled by the wind arising from the southern quarter,
the fire issued forth from all her limbs and reduced her to ashes.
Having heard of that death,
and having understood the conversation between those two exactly as it occurred, the divine Śaṅkara,
the Lord and Master who wields the trident, became enraged at Dakṣa and the sages.
O Dakṣa, because that Satī was insulted by you on my account while all her other daughters were honored by their husbands, she has departed. (57)
Therefore, having reached the realm of Vaivasvata, those great seers shall indeed be born again— this time not from a womb— at my second sacrifice.
When the Śukta had indeed been offered by Brahmā during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu,
he addressed the Ṛṣis and returned once more to Dakṣa.
And in the lineage of Cakṣuṣa, there will be a king named Cākṣuṣa;
he will be the grandson of Prācīnabarhis and the son of Pracetas. (1.30.60)
"O sage, you shall beget a son named Dakṣa upon a maiden of the Mārīca lineage when the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara has arrived. (61)
Dakṣa said:
O evil-minded one, I shall create obstacles for you even there,
again and again, in your actions pertaining to dharma, artha, and kāma in this world.
"Since you have spoken harshly to the sages on my account,
therefore the twice-born shall certainly not worship you in the sacrifice along with the gods."
Then, having offered the oblation, the cruel one will abandon his duties;
likewise, you shall dwell right here, having left heaven at the end of the age.
Rudra said:
Of all the worlds, Bhūrloka is said to be the first;
by the command of the Supreme Lord, I shall sustain it.
All the worlds, encompassed by this earth, remain as luminous as suns;
I support them here constantly, not by your command.
"For the fourfold order belongs to the gods, and they eat together in one place;
I shall not eat with them, therefore they will give [the offerings] separately.
Consequently, he is no longer worshipped by the gods together with them, but is worshipped separately. (67)
Then Dakṣa, addressed by Rudra of immeasurable splendor,
abandoned his former state during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara and was born here among human beings.
Knowing that the householder was skillful, a lord, and a master of all sciences,
he who was named Dakṣa performed great sacrifices together with the deities.
Then, when the Vaivasvata interval had arrived, the king of mountains begot that goddess Umā, who was formerly Satī, upon Menā.
That goddess Satī, having existed previously, subsequently became Umā;
she remains with Bhava as his devoted partner, and Bhava is never released from her,
for as long as the Lord desires to remain here throughout the Manvantaras.
Just as the goddess Aditi was devoted to Kaśyapa Mārīca,
and Śrī to Nārāyaṇa Sādhyā, so too was Śacī devoted to Maghavan.
Kīrti [never] abandons Viṣṇu, Ruci the Sun, and Arundhatī Vasiṣṭha;
these goddesses never forsake these husbands.
In recurring kalpas, they are born again together with them.
Thus was Dakṣa, known as Prācetasa, born during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara;
he was the grandson of Prācīnabarhis and the son of Pracetas.
Furthermore, O King, according to the sacred tradition, it was due to the curse of Rudra that the monarch was born again from the ten Pracetasas through Mārṣā in this second creation.
All those great sages, Bhṛgu and the others,
were indeed born in the first Tretā Yuga of the Vaivasvata Manu; however,
according to the Śruti, they were born in this second [Tretā] due to the curse of Rudra during the sacrifice of the great god.
Thus, having passed into another birth, he remained possessed of residual karma (sānuśaya) toward both Prajāpati Dakṣa and the wise Tryambaka.
Therefore, one should never harbor enmity toward enemies here;
for even when one has passed into another birth, that which has been cultivated through good and evil does not leave a living being. Thus, a wise person should act with this in mind. (78)
The sages said:
O Sūta, how did the horse sacrifice of the Prajāpati Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, come to destruction during the Vaivasvata interval? (79)
Considering that death had been brought about by the Goddess, how did Dakṣa propitiate the Lord who is the soul of all and was thus enraged? How was that sacrifice completed?
We wish to know this; tell us this exactly as it happened.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, on Mount Meru there is a peak renowned throughout the three worlds,
named Jyotiṣka, belonging to Savitṛ and adorned with all kinds of jewels.
Immeasurable, invincible, and honored by all the worlds,
the Lord sat upon that best of mountains, adorned with every mineral,
shining resplendent as if seated upon a couch.
And the daughter of the king of mountains was constantly by his side,
as were the high-souled Ādityas and the Vasus of immeasurable power.
Likewise, the two high-souled Aśvins, the best of physicians, and King Vaiśravaṇa surrounded by his Guhyakas [were there]. ||84||
The glorious lord of the Yakṣas, the sovereign whose abode is Kailāsa,
and the great sage Uśanas wait upon that Great-Souled One,
as do the supreme ṛṣis headed by Sanatkumāra.
Likewise, the other celestial sages headed by Aṅgiras, as well as the Gandharva Viśvāvasu and the two, Nārada and Parvata. 86.
Multitudes of hosts of Apsarases gathered there in great numbers;
a pure, auspicious, and pleasant wind blew, carrying various fragrances. (87)
Likewise, there were trees laden with flowers, possessing blossoms of every season;
and there were Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and those whose wealth is their asceticism.
There indeed they worship Mahādeva Paśupati, as well as other beings who assume various forms. 89.
And there were most terrible Rākṣasas and Piśācas of great strength,
assuming many forms, joyful, and with various weapons raised.
The attendants of the god, resembling the sacrificial fire, stood there;
and the venerable Nandīśvara remained there with the god's permission.
O best of the twice-born, having grasped his blazing trident which was radiant with its own splendor,
Gaṅgā, the foremost of rivers born from the waters of all sacred fords,
attended upon him in her divine form.
Thus that Blessed One, Mahādeva, remained there resplendent, surrounded by celestial sages and gods of great power.
In ancient times, Dakṣa indeed commenced a sacrifice on the slopes of the Himavat,
at the auspicious site of Gaṅgādvāra, frequented by sages and perfected beings.
Then, at his sacrifice, the gods, led by Śatakratu, having assembled together, resolved upon departing. 95.
By their own celestial chariots, which were blazing with the brilliance of fire, those great-souled ones went to Gaṅgādvāra with the god’s permission; such is the sacred tradition.
It was crowded with Gandharvas and Apsarases, covered with various trees and creepers,
and surrounded by throngs of sages— Dakṣa, the best among the upholders of dharma.
Those who dwell on earth, in the intermediate space, or in the heavenly world—
all of them, with palms joined in reverence, stood before Prajāpati.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and Sādhyas, together with the hosts of Maruts,
all arrived accompanied by Jiṣṇu to receive their shares of the sacrifice.
The drinkers of heat, the drinkers of Soma, the drinkers of clarified butter, and the drinkers of smoke,
as well as the Aśvins and the Pitṛs, arrived together with Brahmā.
These and many other hosts of beings, likewise those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouts. ||101||
All the gods, summoned by means of mantras along with their wives,
shine resplendently from their celestial chariots like blazing fires.
Seeing them, Dadhīca, overcome with indignation, spoke these words:
"A man incurs great sin by honoring those who are unworthy of honor and by failing to honor those who are worthy; of this there is no doubt. (103)
Having spoken thus, the brahmin-sage addressed Dakṣa again:
"Why do you not invoke the Lord, the Master of Creatures, who is worthy of worship? (104)
Dakṣa said:
I have many Rudras, trident-bearing and with matted hair, who abide in eleven states; I know no other Maheśvara.
Dadhīca said:
All the gods have been invited by him who has invited Īśa;
just as I see no other deity superior to Śaṅkara,
so too this vast sacrifice of Dakṣa shall not come to pass.
Dakṣa said:

O hero, in this sacrifice, I offer all this oblation, purified by ritual and mantras, into the golden vessel for the sake of the incomparable Lord Viṣṇu— the eternal, all-pervading Master who is ever-present at the Āhavanīya fire.
Then, perceiving that the deities had departed, the virtuous daughter of the king of mountains spoke these words to the god Paśupati.
Umā said:
"O Blessed One, where indeed have these gods, led by Śakra, gone?
Tell me the truth, O Knower of Reality; this doubt of mine is great. (109)
Maheśvara said:
The illustrious Dakṣa, the most excellent lord of creatures, was performing a horse sacrifice; there the dwellers of heaven were going.
The Goddess said:
O highly fortunate one, for what reason have you not gone to this sacrifice?
By what prohibition is your going being forbidden? ||111||
Maheśvara said:
O highly fortunate lady, all this has been performed by Surabhi alone;
no share was assigned for me in any of her sacrifices. ||112||
O woman of excellent complexion, because of the path obtained through my previous means, the gods do not grant a share of the sacrifice to me, the wise one. (113)
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, among all the gods you are superior in power and endowed with virtues;
you are unconquerable and unassailable by virtue of your splendor, fame, and majesty.
But by this very prohibition, O illustrious one, I have fallen into extreme distress; and a trembling comes over me, O sinless one. (115)
"What kind of gift, vow, or austerity should I perform today, so that my husband may obtain a share of the sacrifice from the inconceivable Lord—whether half or even a third? (116)
To his wife, who was speaking thus and was both agitated and joyful, the inconceivable Blessed One said:
"O Queen of the Gods, O you of slender waist and limbs, do you not know what kind of speech this is that you utter? (117)
"O large-eyed one, I indeed know that the virtuous speak everything through meditation;
today, the god Mahendra has not been deluded by confusion, nor is the triple world entirely bewildered. (118)
At the sacrifice, the reciters praise me; they sing the Rathantara Sāman as it is to be sung.
The Brahmins worship me at the Brahma-sattra, and the Adhvaryu priests assign me my portion.
The Goddess said:
Even though the Blessed One is beyond the ordinary, he praises or even protects his own self in the assembly of all women; of this there is no doubt.
The Blessed One said:
"I do not praise myself, O Queen of the Gods; behold me and come near.
O lady of excellent hips, O woman of beautiful complexion, see whom I shall create for my share. (121)
Having spoken thus to his wife, who was dearer to him than life itself,
the Blessed One created from his mouth a being resembling the fire of wrath.
He beheld for a moment the thousand-headed god, with a thousand feet,
bearing a thousand mallets and holding a thousand arrows in his hands.
The god held a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, wielded a blazing bow, and carried an axe and a sword; he was exceedingly fierce and terrifying.
Blazing with a terrible form, adorned with a crescent moon,
he wore a tiger skin dripping with great quantities of blood.
With fangs formidable, wandering about, possessing a massive mouth and a huge belly,
with a tongue like lightning, protruding lips, long ears, and difficult to approach.
His hands are illuminated by a vajra, his hair is ablaze, he is encircled by garlands of flames, and adorned with strings of pearls. ||127||
Blazing with splendor like the fire at the end of an eon,
his mouth was gaped wide open as far as his ears, appearing terrifying in the four directions.
Possessing great strength, great splendor, and the sovereignty of a Great Being;
with a vast body that withdraws the universe, he is like the great circle of a banyan tree,
shining simultaneously like a hundred moons and like the fire of passion.
He has four great faces and white, sharp fangs; he is rich in great, fierce splendor, strength, and majesty.
He possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns and fires at the end of an eon, and the stainless beauty of a thousand moons.
He has the luster of all medicinal herbs set ablaze and the appearance of Mount Mandara; he is equal to Sumeru, Kailāsa, and the Himālaya mountains.
Resembling the sun at the end of an eon, possessed of great prowess, with a beautiful nose and a large face, having formidable cheeks, blazing eyes, and a mouth aglow with flames of fire. ||131||
Clad in the skin of the king of beasts and encircled by great serpents, he wears a turban and bears the moon; at times he is fierce, and at times he is peaceful.
With heads adorned with various flowers, anointed with various fragrant unguents, his limbs variegated with various jewels, and decorated with various ornaments. ||133||
Wearing a radiant garland of *karṇikāra* flowers, his eyes rolling with rage,
he dances with variegated limbs in one place and speaks in melodious tones in another.
In one place the self-disciplined one meditates; in another he sweeps the straw;
in one place the soul of the universe sings; in another he cries out again and again. ||135||
Knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, austerity, truth, forgiveness, fortitude, lordship, and self-awakening—indeed, he is endowed with these qualities that constitute his foundation. ||136||
Having touched the ground with his knees, he stood bowed with palms joined in reverence:
"Command me, O Lord of Gods; what task shall I perform for you? (137)
Maheśvara said to him, "Destroy Dakṣa’s sacrifice here.
Having heard the command of the god, the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra bowed his head at the feet of the Lord of Gods, the husband of Umā. ||138||
Then, like a lion released from its bonds,
he effortlessly destroyed Dakṣa’s sacrifice, considering it to have been an act of provocation by the Goddess.
And out of wrath, the most formidable Bhadrakālī Maheśvarī,
together with her followers, [remained] along with him for the sake of being the witness to all of his own [deeds].
This very Blessed One, enraged and having made his abode in the realm of the pretas, is known as Vīrabhadra; he is the one who wipes away the wrath of the Goddess.
From the pores of his skin, he created the lords of the Gaṇas named Raudras—followers of Rudra, possessed of great heroism, and endowed with the vigor and prowess of Rudra. ||142||
All were attendants of Rudra, all possessing splendor equal to Rudra's;
they then descended swiftly by the hundreds and thousands.
Then, a tumultuous sound of "kila-kilā," as if filling the very sky, arose;
by that great noise, all the inhabitants of heaven were terrified.
The mountains shattered and the earth trembled;
O brahmins, Mount Meru whirled about and the oceans were agitated.
The fires do not blaze at all, nor do the suns shine;
the planets do not appear, nor do the lunar mansions or the stars. 146.
Neither the sages, nor the gods, nor the dānavas spoke;
for thus, being insulted, they utterly consume that which has been turned to darkness.
Uttering lion-roars, those beings of terrible form and great strength shattered their enemies;
they were formidable and uprooted sacrificial posts.
Some crush them, while others dance about;
still others rush forward and run away with the speed of the wind and the swiftness of thought. (149)
The sacrificial vessels and the sanctuaries of the sacrifice were being pulverized;
they appeared like stars falling from the vault of the sky.
There were mountain-like heaps of divine food, drinks, and edibles;
likewise, there were rivers of milk and others with mud made of ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa);
and there were divine waters of honey-foam, with sands of sugar-candy and granulated sugar.
Others carry delightful streams of molasses containing the six flavors, as well as various meats and diverse kinds of foods, both high and low. 152.

Whatever divine foods there were— both those to be licked and those to be sucked— they ate them with various mouths and devoured them all; they played in diverse forms and threw the celestial women about.
But those who were like Rudras, dispatched by the wrath of Rudra, swiftly destroyed that sacrifice, even though it was well-protected by all the gods, as they approached from nearby. ||154||
Others likewise made sounds that struck fear into all living beings;
others, having severed the head of the sacrifice, let out terrifying roars.
Dakṣa, the lord of Dakṣas, and likewise the god who is the lord of sacrifice, began to flee through the sky in the form of a deer. ||156||
Then the great Vīrabhadra, whose nature is immeasurable, having recognized his strength,
swiftly severed the head of him as he was moving through the air.

Dakṣa Prajāpati himself, his consciousness bewildered and destroyed, was struck on the head with a foot by the enraged Vīrabhadra; overcome by old age and his spirit tormented, he fell to the surface of the earth. 158.
Those ten million deities of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, pure in nature, were swiftly bound by the noose of Agnibala and Siṃhabala. (159)
Then all the gods went to the high-souled one of great power and said:
"Be gracious, O Blessed Rudra; do not be angry with your servants, O Lord."
Then the gods, headed by Brahmā, and Dakṣa the progenitor, with palms joined in reverence, said: "Tell us, who are you? (161)
Vīrabhadra said:
He is neither a god nor the sun, nor has he come here to eat;
indeed, he is not here to see the lords of the gods, nor is he filled with curiosity. ||162||
"Know me to have arrived here for the purpose of destroying Dakṣa’s sacrifice;
I am known as Vīrabhadra, who has emerged from the wrath of Rudra. (163)
Bhadrakālī is to be known as having emerged from the wrath of the Goddess;
sent by the God of gods, she has come here to the conclusion of the sacrifice. (164)
Go for refuge, O Indra among kings, to the god who is the lord of Umā;
even the wrath of Rudra is a boon, whereas the favor of another deity is not.
Having heard the words of Vīrabhadra, Dakṣa, the best among the upholders of dharma,
gratified Maheśvara, the lord of gods, who holds the trident in his hand.
When the discourse on sacrifice had become corrupted and the twice-born had fled,
there arose a fierce and great fire, terrible and blazing, consisting of the stars and the deer.
With attendants moaning, their faces pierced by spears, and with sacrificial posts that had been driven in and uprooted scattered here and there; 168.
It was filled with vultures, greedy for flesh, flying up and swooping down,
fanned by the flapping of their wings and resounded by the howling of hundreds of jackals.
Then, having restrained the prāṇa and apāna breaths with effort through his posture,
the conqueror of enemies, possessing many insights, directed his gaze everywhere.
Suddenly, the Lord of the gods of gods emerged from the fire-pit,
possessing a splendor like that of a thousand moons and suns and resembling the fire of universal destruction.
And having laughed at him, the Blessed One spoke these words:
"O Dakṣa, your knowledge has perished; your affection for me has now vanished. (172)
Smiling, he spoke these words: "Tell me, what shall I do for you?
You have already been made to hear [the truth] by the preceptors together with the gods. (173)
Having joined his palms in reverence, Dakṣa, the lord of progeny, spoke to that god, trembling with fear and apprehension, his face and eyes filled with tears. (174)
If the Blessed One is pleased, or if I am dear to you,
or if I am worthy of your favor, or if a boon is to be granted to me— (175)
Whatever has been eaten, consumed, drunk, or swallowed, and whatever sacrificial material has been thus destroyed, pulverized, or cast away; ||176||
May that which was accumulated over a long period of time and with great effort not become false for me; this boon I choose. (177)
"So be it," said the Blessed One, Hara, whose two eyes were the sun and the moon;
Prajāpati [then addressed] the three-eyed Mahādeva, the presiding lord of dharma. (178)
Having fallen to the ground on his knees and obtained a boon from Bhava,
Dakṣa praised the bull-bannered god with eight thousand names.
Dakṣa said:
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, destroyer of the strength of the enemies of the gods;
O Indra of the gods, best among the immortals, worshipped by both gods and dānavas.
O thousand-eyed one, O many-formed one, O three-eyed one, beloved of the lord of Yakṣas!
You have hands and feet everywhere; you have eyes, heads, and mouths on all sides.
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, you abide pervading all things. 181.
O Śaṅkukarṇa, Mahākarṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, you whose abode is the ocean;
O Gajendrakarṇa, Gokarṇa, Pāṇikarṇa, homage be to you! 182.
O hundred-bellied one, O hundred-whirled one, O hundred-tongued one, O hundred-faced one!
Those who sing the Gāyatrī hymns sing of you, and likewise those who worship worship you.
You are the protector of gods and demons, you are Brahmā, and you are Śatakratu;
you are the Lord of forms, O Great Form, and the bearer of the waters of the ocean and the earth. 184.
For all the deities reside within you, like cattle in a cow-pen;
I perceive within your body Soma, Agni, and the Lord of Waters.
Then [he saw] Āditya, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā together with Bṛhaspati;
[as well as] action, the object of action, the cause, the agent, and the instrument itself. ||186||
Salutations to Bhava, to Śarva, to Rudra, and to the giver of boons—who is both unreal and real, and likewise the source and the dissolution. 187.
Salutations indeed to the Lord of Beasts, to the slayer of Andhaka, to the one with three matted locks, to the three-headed one, and to the bearer of the excellent trident. ||188||
Salutation indeed to Tryambaka, the three-eyed one, the destroyer of Tripura;
salutation to Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and Dhara.
Salutations indeed to Daṇḍin, whose ears are attached, and to Daṇḍimuṇḍa;
salutations to Arddhadaṇḍakeśa, to Niṣka, and to Vikṛta.
Homage to you who are deep red, to the smoke-colored one, and to the one with a neck like a lotus stalk;
homage to you who are incomparable, and let there be homage to you, O Śiva. ||191||
Salutations to the Sun, the Lord of the Sun, who possesses the sun as his banner and pennant;
salutations to the Lord of the Pramathas, whose shoulders are like a bull, and who wields a bow. 192.
Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha and to him whose armor is gold;
homage to him whose crest-jewel is fashioned of gold, and to the Lord of Gold! ||193||

Salutations to the destroyer of enemies, to the wielder of the staff, and to the one who holds the vessel for drinking the nectar of the castes; salutations indeed to the praised, to the praiseworthy, and to the one being praised.
Salutations to the one who consumes all that is edible and inedible, the inner self of all beings, the priest, the mantra, and the one whose banner and flag are white. 195.
Homage to the one who is being saluted, to the one worthy of salutation, and homage to Kili-kila!
Homage to you while lying down, and to you when asleep and when risen! 196.
To the one who is stationary and the one who moves, to the one with gestures and the one who is crooked;
to the one who sleeps and the one whose nature is to dance, and to the one who plays wind instruments. ||197||
Salutations to the one who is greedy for dramatic offerings, who delights in song and instrumental music,
and who is the eldest, the most excellent, and the subduer of strength.
To him who brings about reckoning, calculation, destruction, and total exhaustion;
to him whose laughter is like a terrifying drum; and to the beloved of Bhīmasena. ||199||
And salutation always to the Fierce One; salutation to you, the ten-armed one! Salutation to the one who holds a skull in his hand and who is fond of the ashes of the funeral pyre.
Salutations to Vibhīṣaṇa, to Bhīṣma, and to the observer of terrible vows; salutations to the one with a deformed chest, who has a sword for a tongue and sharp fangs at the tips.
Salutations to him who is fond of cooked and raw meat, and who delights in the lute made of a gourd;
salutations to the bull, to the one who bestows virility, to the showerer of blessings, and to the powerful one.
Salutations to Kaṭaṅkaṭa and Caṇḍa, and salutations to Sāvayava;
salutations to you, the excellent Kṛṣṇa, the supreme one, and the bestower of boons. ||203||
Homage to the one who chooses the best of fragrances, garlands, and garments; homage to the most excellent among the excellent. Homage to the rain, to the wind, to the shade, and to the heat.

Homage to him who is both attached and detached, to the beautiful one, to the one with the rosary of beads, to the one who has broken through [all bonds], to the radiant one, and to the solitary and formidable one. ||205||
Salutation to the one whose form is non-terrible, yet who is terrible and even more terrible;
salutation to Śiva, the peaceful, and salutation to him who is most peaceful. ||206||
Salutations to you who have one foot and many eyes, and who have but one head;
salutations to the ancient one, to the seeker, and to him who is fond of sharing.
Salutations to the Pāśupata, whose limbs are honored by five garlands;
salutations to Caṇḍa, to Ghaṇṭa, and to him who has devoured the apertures with his bell.
Salutation to the one with a hundred bells at once, to the one who loves garlands of bells,
to the one who wields the staff of life, to the one who bestows renunciation, and to Hili-hila!

Salutations always to the one who utters the syllables *hūṃ* and *hūṃ*, to Pāra, and to him who is dear to the one who utters *hūṃ* and *hūṃ*; salutations to Śambhu, and to him whose arts are the mountains and trees.
Homage to Garbha, Māṃsa, Śṛgāla, Tāraka, and Tara; homage to the Lord of Sacrifice, to the Swift One, and to the One Who Is Pursued.
Salutations to the one who carries the sacrifice, to the giver, to the one who is to be heated, and to the heater;
salutations to the one who is praised, to the one who is to be, and salutations to the lord of lightnings.
Salutation to the giver of food, to the lord of food, and to the source of food;
salutation to the one with a thousand heads and to the one with a thousand feet.
Salutations to him who brandishes the trident with a thousand arms and possesses a thousand eyes;
salutations to him who has the form of a child and assumes the form of a child.
Homage to the protector of children, to the one who plays with children, to the pure Buddha, to the agitator, and to the unassailable. 215.
Salutations indeed to him whose hair is marked by waves and to him whose hair is disheveled;
salutations to him who is devoted to the six duties and to him who is intent upon the three duties.

Salutations to the one who causes the distinct duties of the castes and stages of life to proceed according to rule; salutations to the resonance of the mind, to the one worthy of being proclaimed, and to the tumultuous sound.
To the one with white and tawny eyes, and with black and red pupils;
to the one who is dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; and to Kratha and Kathana. ||218||
Salutations to the follower of Sāṅkhya, the foremost of the Sāṅkhyas, the Lord of Yoga;
salutations to him who moves on the highways and byways, and who delights in the crossroads. ||219||
Salutations to you, O Hari-keśa, who have a black antelope skin as an upper garment, who wear a serpent as a sacred thread, and who possess the thunderbolt of Īśāna; salutations to you,
the sole lord of non-discrimination, the manifest and the unmanifest.
O Giver of desires, O Destroyer of desires, O Slayer of the arrogant and haughty!
O All, O Giver of all, O Omniscient One, O [Lord] of the hue of twilight, homage be to You! 221.
O mighty-armed one, O great-armed one, O being of great essence, O you of great splendor!
O you who resemble a magnificent great cloud, O Mahākāla, homage be to you! 222.
O you with matted hair from which coarse, aged limbs emerge; O wearer of bark garments and deerskins;
O you with matted locks blazing like the sun and fire; O you clothed in bark and antelope skin;
O you who resemble a thousand suns; O you ever devoted to austerity—salutations be to you! 223.

O you who whirl about a hundred times with intoxicating power, whose hair is half-submerged in the waters of the Gaṅgā, O you who possess the whirlpools of the moon, the ages, and the clouds—homage be to you! 224.
You are food, you are the maker of food, and indeed you alone are the giver of food;
you are the creator of food, its cooker, and the eater of what is cooked—to you, the cooker, obeisance! 225.
The viviparous, the oviparous, the sweat-born, and the soil-born—
the fourfold multitude of beings— you alone are, O God of gods.
You are Brahmā of the moving and the unmoving, and you alone are the Pratihartṛ priest.
You alone are the foremost among those who know Brahman, even among the knowers of Brahman.
Theologians declare you to be the supreme source of all beings, the treasury of water, wind, and light, as well as the syllable Om within the Ṛg and Sāman Vedas.

O best of gods, those who offer oblations, those who invoke, those who sacrifice, and those who utter the call with speech always offer you oblations; the chanters of the Sāman and the exponents of Brahman sing of you. 229.
Consisting of the Yajus, consisting of the Ṛks, and likewise consisting of the Sāmans and Atharvans,
you are recited by the knowers of Brahman through the collections of Kalpas and Upaniṣads.
Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras, and those of even lower castes—
all look to you alone, just as masses of clouds seek the thundering roar of the rain-cloud.
You are the year, the seasons, the months, and even the half-months;
you are the kalās, the kāṣṭhās, and the nimeṣas; you are the lunar mansions, the yugas, and the planets.
For you are the hump of bulls, the peaks of mountains,
the lion among beasts, Tārkṣya among those who fly, and Ananta among the serpents.
Of oceans, the Milky Ocean is indeed foremost; of machines, the bow;
of weapons, the thunderbolt; and of vows, truth alone. ||234||
Desire, aversion, passion, delusion, emaciation, self-restraint, tranquility, resolve, fortitude, greed, lust, anger, victory, and defeat. ||235||
You are the wielder of the mace, you are the wielder of the arrow, as well as the bearer of the skull-topped staff and the rattle-drum;
you are the cutter, the breaker, and the striker, and you are considered the leader and the Ender.
Dharma endowed with the ten characteristics is indeed the purpose and the object of desire;
Indra, the oceans, the rivers, the ponds, and the lakes [are likewise]. (237)
Climbers, creepers, grasses, herbs, domestic animals, wild beasts, and birds—the undertaking of substances, actions, and qualities, which yields flowers and fruits in due time. ||238||
The beginning, the end, and the middle are the Gāyatrī and the syllable Oṃ;
likewise, they are green, red, black, blue, yellow, and tawny.
Kadru, Kapila, Kapota, and likewise Mecaka; Suvarṇaretas is renowned, and Suvarṇa is also considered [among them]. (1.30.240)
And likewise Suvarṇanāman and Suvarṇapriya;
you are Indra, as well as Yama, Varuṇa, Dhanada, and Anala. ||241||
You are Utphulla, Citrabhānu, Svarbhānu, and Bhānu;
you are Hotra, Hotṛ, and Homa; you are the oblation, the act of offering, and the Lord of the sacrifice.
Likewise, the Suparṇa and the Brahma-yajus Śatarudriya, which is the purifier of purifiers and the most auspicious of auspicious things. ||243||
A mountain, a small stone, and likewise a tree; the individual soul (jīva), the person (pudgala), as well as goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), darkness (tamas), and procreation. ||244||
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna; as well as opening the eyes, closing the eyes, and yawning. ||245||
Red-limbed, armed with a mace, fanged, large-mouthed, and pot-bellied;
possessing fine body hair, tawny beard, upright hair, and three eyes.
He whose limbs are song, instrumental music, and dance; who is fond of singing and playing instruments;
he who is the fish, the water-dweller, the one born of water, the one moving in water, speed itself, time, the age of strife, and the beautiful.
He is the untimely hour and the auspicious time, the bad season and the destroyer of all reckoning;
he is death itself, decay, and the end, the one who brings about the destruction of the earth, the remover of all.
Saṃvarttaka, Antaka, Saṃvarttakabalāhaka, Ghaṭa, Ghaṭīka, Ghaṇṭīka, Cūḍālola, Bala, and Bala. (249)
He is the time of Brahmā, he whose mouth is fire, the bearer of the staff, the shaven-headed one, the wielder of the staff,
the four ages, the four Vedas, the four officiating priests, and the crossroads.
He is the knower of the four stages of life and the creator of the four castes;
he delights in both the perishable and the imperishable, the rogue, the uncountable, and the lord of the uncountable hosts.
Wearing garlands and garments of rudrākṣa beads, Girika and beloved of Girika, Lord of artisans, the best among craftsmen, and the originator of all arts. ||252||
Candra is the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes; Pūṣan is the destroyer of the teeth;
Gūḍhāvarta, Gūḍha, and Gūḍhapratiniṣevitā are also [names of deities]. ||253||
He is the one who crosses over and the one who causes others to cross; he is the deliverer of all beings.
He is the creator, the ordainer, and the supporter of sentient beings; he is the foundation and the sustainer.
Austerity, sacred knowledge, truth, celibacy, and uprightness;
the soul of all beings, the creator of beings, the being itself, and the source of the past, the future, and the present. ||255||
Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svar, and likewise Utpatti, Maheśvara, Īśāna, Vīkṣaṇa, Śānta, Durdānta, and Dantanāśana. ||256||
O Brahmāvarta, Surāvarta, Kāmāvarta, homage be to you!
You are the remover of the image of desire and the lover of the pollen of the Karṇikāra flower. ||257||
Mukhacandra, Bhīmamukha, Sumukha, Durmukha, Mukha, Caturmukha, Bahumukha—he was indeed always facing forward in battle. (258)
Hiraṇyagarbha, Śakuni, Mahodadhi, Para, Virāj, Adharmahā, Mahādaṇḍa, Daṇḍadhāra, and Raṇapriya. ||259||
Gotama, Gopratāra, the bull among cows, whose vehicle is a bull;
the creator of dharma, the source of dharma, dharma itself, and the supreme knower of dharma.
The protector of the three worlds, Govinda, the giver of honor, and indeed honor itself;
he who stands firm as Sthāṇu, yet is also the unshakable and the very act of shaking.
He who is difficult to ward off, difficult to approach, difficult to endure, and difficult to overcome;
he who is hard to restrain, hard to shake, hard to know, and hard to conquer—the Victorious One. ||262||
Śaśa, Śaśāṅka, Śamana, Śīta-uṣṇa, Durjara, Tṛṣ, Ādhi, Vyādhi, Vyādhi-hā, and Vyādhi-ga. (263)
He is the endurable sacrifice, the deer, the hunter, the source of diseases, and the one who has no source;
he is the crested one, the lotus-eyed, and the one whose gaze is like a white lotus.
He holds a staff and is ever accompanied by his rod; he is adorned with a shaven head and a staff;
he is a drinker of poison and a drinker of nectar; he is a drinker of wine and a drinker of milk and soma.
He who drinks honey and he who drinks clarified butter, the one of great strength who consumes all things;
he who is borne by a bull and a horse, the bull-like one, and likewise he whose eyes are like those of a bull. ||266||
The bull is indeed renowned, honored by the worlds;
the moon and the sun are your eyes, and the Grandfather (Brahmā) is your heart.
Fire and the god of water are likewise established through righteous deeds.
Neither Brahmā nor Govinda, nor even the ancient seers, are capable of knowing your majesty as it truly is, O Śiva. (268)
Those forms of yours which are extremely subtle do not come within my sight;
with those [forms], protect me constantly, as a father protects his own biological son. (269)
Protect me, for I am worthy of your protection, O sinless one; salutations be unto you!
The Blessed One is compassionate toward his devotees, and I am always a devotee unto you.
May he who, difficult to behold, stands alone at the edge of the ocean having gathered together many thousands of men, be my protector forever. (271)

Salutation to that Self of Yoga, whom those who are sleepless, who have conquered their breath, who are established in purity, and who perceive with equanimity, behold as a light while practicing yoga.
I take refuge in that one who lies within the waters at the onset of the end of the age, after having consumed all beings.
Having entered the mouth of Rāhu, he who swallows the moon at night becomes Svarbhānu and likewise Somāgni, and he also swallows the sun.
May those persons, the size of a thumb, who reside within the bodies of all embodied beings, protect me always and may they constantly nourish me. (275)
And those who have emerged from the womb, and those who are situated in the lower parts—may the *svāhās* and *svadhās* reach them and may they enjoy [them]. ||276||
Salutations eternally to those beings who, though dwelling within the body, do not weep, yet cause others to weep; who gladden others and themselves rejoice. ||277||
Those who are in the ocean, in river-fords, on mountains, in caves,
at the roots of trees, in cow-pens, or in the depths of dense forests— ||278||
Those who are at crossroads, on streets, in squares, and in assembly halls;
and those situated between the moon and the sun, or within the rays of the moon and the sun. (279)
To those who have gone to the subterranean realm (rasātala) and to those who have gone beyond that,
salutations to them, salutations to them, and salutations to them forever! To those who are subtle, gross, emaciated, or short, salutations to them always!
O Lord, you are everything, you are all-pervading, you are the master of all beings, and you are the inner self within all beings; for that reason, you were not invited.
Since you alone are worshipped with sacrifices accompanied by various sacrificial fees,
and since you alone are the creator of everything, for that reason you were not invited.
Or else, O Lord, you have been deluded by that subtle illusion of yours;
for this reason as well, you were not invited by him.
Be gracious to me, O Lord of Gods; you alone are my refuge. You are my goal and you are my foundation; there is no other resort for me.
Having thus praised Mahādeva, Prajāpati ceased;
the Blessed One, well-pleased, spoke again to Dakṣa.
I am well-pleased with this hymn of yours, O Dakṣa of noble vows;
what need is there for much speaking here? You shall come into my presence.
Then Bhava, the lord of the three worlds, who is skilled in speech, spoke these words to him—words that were well-composed and intended to provide consolation. (287)
O Dakṣa, Dakṣa, you should not harbor anger toward this obstacle;
for it was seen by you long ago that no one other than I is the destroyer of the sacrifice.
Furthermore, O observer of noble vows, accept this boon from me;
becoming cheerful of countenance, listen with a one-pointed mind. (289)
O Prajāpati, by my grace, you shall partake of the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices.

Having extracted the Vedas along with their six auxiliary limbs, as well as the Sāṅkhya and Yoga systems in their entirety, and having performed extensive austerities difficult even for gods and demons to practice; ||291||
It is composed of five topics joined together, hidden from those lacking wisdom;
it is sometimes contrary to, and sometimes in agreement with, the duties established for the castes and stages of life. ||292||

O Dakṣa, this auspicious Pāśupata vow, which effects liberation from all bonds and releases one from every sin, has been established by me for all stages of life (āśramas) as determined by the meanings of the Vedas. ||293||
O highly fortunate one, may that abundant fruit which comes from this practice performed correctly be yours; let the fever of your mind be abandoned.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva, of immeasurable prowess, together with his wife and his followers, vanished from the sight of Dakṣa.
And having then obtained that portion as prescribed by Brahmā, Bhava,
the knower of all duties, divided the fever into many parts for the sake of the peace of all beings; listen to that, O twice-born ones.

One should know that for elephants, fever of the head is the ailment; for mountains, it is the breaking of rocks; for waters, it is the reed-plant; and even for serpents, it is the sloughing of their skin.
O knower of dharma, Śauraka is the salt-waste of the Saurabheyas upon the surface of the earth; even for elephants, it is an obstruction to their vision. (298)
The emergence of sores on horses, the appearance of crests on peacocks, and eye disease in cuckoos are declared by the great-souled ones to be fever. (299)
We have heard that for all goats, the breaking of bile is called fever;
for all parrots as well, the condition known as *himikā* is called fever;
and even among tigers, O Brahmins, exhaustion is here said to be fever.
O Omniscient One, among human beings this is known as fever;
it always enters [the body] at birth, at death, and in between.
This is the splendor of Maheśvara, known as Jvara, most terrible;
he is the Lord who is to be saluted and honored by all living beings.

The man who, with a mind free from dejection and always well-composed, recites this account of the origin of fever, shall be liberated from disease and, filled with joy, obtain all his desires according to his wishes. (303)
Whoever recites or hears this hymn proclaimed by Dakṣa shall encounter no inauspiciousness whatsoever and shall attain a long life. (304)
Just as Hara, the master of yoga, is the most excellent among all the gods,
so too is this hymn composed by Brahmā the most excellent among all hymns.

Those who desire fame, sovereignty, happiness, power, wealth, long life, and riches, as well as those who seek knowledge, should diligently offer praise while establishing themselves in devotion. (306)
Whether afflicted by disease, suffering, or dejection; terrified by thieves or oppressed by fear;
or even appointed to royal service—one is liberated from great danger.
And with this very body, that lord of the Gaṇas,
having attained happiness in this world, is reborn as a Gaṇa himself.
Neither yakṣas nor piśācas, neither nāgas nor vināyakas, shall create obstacles in the home where Bhava is praised. (309)
Or if a woman, observing celibacy, should listen to this with pure devotion,
she becomes worthy of worship like a deity by both her paternal and her husband’s kin.
Whoever should hear all of this, or should recite it repeatedly, all of that person's undertakings shall reach fulfillment without obstacle. ||311||
Whatever has been conceived by the mind and whatever has been uttered by speech—all that is accomplished for one through the recitation of this hymn. ||312||
Then, having offered oblations according to one's means to the god Guha, to the goddess, and to Nandīśvara, with self-restraint and religious observance.
Then, being disciplined, that man should quickly take up the names in their proper order;
he obtains his desired objects, excessive wealth, and enjoyments,
and upon death, he attains heaven surrounded by a thousand women.
Whether engaged in all manner of actions or burdened by every sin,
one who recites this hymn composed by Dakṣa is liberated from all evils;
and upon death, being honored by gods and demons alike, he attains the same world as the Gaṇas.
Shining like a bull in a celestial chariot fashioned according to the sacred ordinances, he shall remain until the dissolution of all beings and become an attendant of Rudra. (316)
Thus spoke the Lord Vyāsa, the powerful son of Parāśara:
"No one understands this; let this not be heard by anyone. (317)
Having heard this supreme secret, even those who are evildoers—
whether Vaiśyas, women, or Śūdras— shall attain the world of Rudra.
That twice-born man who always causes [this] to be heard by Brahmins on every sacred festival day attains the world of Rudra; of this there is no doubt. ||319||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of Dakṣa’s Curse," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Thus, this sin-destroying narrative has been fully authorized—
this discourse concerning Dakṣa which has come down from Śarva.
This narrative has indeed been proclaimed in connection with the lineage of the ancestors;
following the sequence of the Pitṛs, I shall hereafter speak of the gods.
Formerly, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara,
there were gods known as the Yāmas, who were previously the sons of Sacrifice (Yajña).
The Ajitas, the sons of Brahmā, and those who were the Jitas and the Jitājitās—
these were the mind-born sons of Svāyambhuva known by the name Śukra.
These three groups of gods are indeed remembered as being satisfied;
they are the thirty-three Chandogas, all belonging to Svāyambhuva.
Yadu and Yayāti were the two gods whom Sravas contemplated with his mind;
Vibhāsa and Kratu were the progeny, and Dyuti entered into them both. ||6||
Vāyasa, Maṅgala, Yāma, Abhimanyu, Ugradṛṣṭi, Samaya, Śuciśravas, Kevala, Viśvarūpa, Supakṣa, and Madhupa— these are proclaimed as the twelve Yāmas.
