The fourth is Nirhapa; you are indeed joined with Grāvājina, Yamī, Viśvadevādya, Yaviṣṭha, and Amṛtavan.
Ajiro, Vibhu, Vibhāva, Mṛlika, Didehaka, Śruti, Śrṛṇa, and Bṛhacchukra—these are proclaimed as the twelve gods. ||9||
During the interval of Svāyambhuva Manu, these were the drinkers of Soma;
indeed, they were radiant hosts, heroic and possessed of great strength.
Their Indra was always Viśvabhuk, the first and all-pervading lord;
at that time, the Asuras were their kinsmen and heirs. ||11||
The Suparṇas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas—these eight, together with the Pitṛs and the Nāsatyas, are the divine origins. ||12||
In the past Svāyambhuva Manvantara, there were thousands of subjects, endowed with splendor, beauty, long life, and strength. (13)
They are not stated here in detail, lest there be an excessive prolixity;
the current Svāyambhuva Manu and his creation are now to be understood. (14)
He was seen by Vaivasvata in the past, along with his subjects, the deities, the sages, and the ancestors, by means of his present [vision]. ||15||
Learn now who those seven sages (saptarṣis) were who existed in former times:
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu. (16)
Atri and Vasiṣṭha, as well as Agnīdhra, Atibāhu, Medhā, Medhātithi, and Vasu, were the seven [sages] in the Svāyambhuva interval.
Jyotiṣmān, Dyutimān, Havya, Savana, and Putra as well.
These ten sons of great power were the offspring of Svāyambhuva Manu.
In the first interval, the great beings proclaimed by Vāyu were the kings;
it included the Asuras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, along with Piśācas, humans, and the hosts of Suparṇas and Apsarases. ||19||
It is not possible to describe them in their proper sequence even in hundreds of years,
because of the vast number of their names and likewise the number of those in their lineage.
Those who were indeed known as the Vrajakulas during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara have passed away over the course of much time, through the succession of solstices, years, and yugas.
The sages said:
Who is this Blessed One, Time, the snatcher away of all beings?
Whose source is he, what is his origin, what is his true nature, and whose son is he? (22)
What is its eye? What is its form? And what are its limbs said to be?
What is its name? What is its soul? Tell this to us who ask. (23)
Sūta said:
Listen to the true nature of time, and having heard it, let it be understood:
its source is the sun; beginning with the blink of an eye, it is called the eye of calculation.
Day and night are his form, and he is composed of the parts of moments;
a hundred years is his lifespan, and his name consists of the divisions of time (kalās). That Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) is the very essence of the present, the future, and the past.
Learn now the temporal divisions of these five distinct periods:
by means of half-days, fortnights, months, seasons, and likewise solstices.
The first is the *saṃvatsara*, the second is the *parivatsara*, the third is the *idvatsara*, and the fourth is the *anuvatsara*. ||27||
A year is the fifth of those, and that period is designated as a Yuga.
I shall now declare their true nature; listen as it is being told. (28)
That which is called the fire of the seasons (ṛtu-agni) is considered the Saṃvatsara;
that which is the essence within the sun is the Kālāgni, the Parivatsara. ||29||
The path is both white and black, and the bird consists of the essence of the waters;
he is the Soma of the year Iḍāvatsara, according to the settled conclusion in the Purāṇa.
And he who heats the worlds with his sevenfold bodies, the swift-acting creator of the world, is the year together with Vāyu. ||31||
From the ego (ahaṅkāra), Rudra was born weeping; thus three [beings] were truly produced from Brahmā.
That Rudra became their year, and from them Nīlalohita was born.
I shall indeed declare their true nature; listen as it is being proclaimed. (32)
Through the conjunction of limbs and minor members, he is the Grandfather, the soul of time;
he is the source of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus, the Lord and Master of the five elements.
He is Agni and Yajus and Soma; he is the elements and he is Prajāpati;
he is declared to be the year and the Sun, who is known as Agni by the wise.
For it is the Sun who has been appointed as the ordainer of the divisions of time— of months, seasons, and half-years,
as well as of the planets, constellations, cold, heat, rain, lifespan, and actions,
and likewise of the divisions of days. (35)

The Vaikārika, serene in nature, the son of Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), is the Grandfather (Pitāmaha); for him, one day is equal to one month, and one month is equal to one season. ||36||
He is Āditya, Savitṛ, Bhānu, the life-giver, honored by the Brahmanas, the source and the end of all beings; therefore he is Bhāskara.
The third year is to be known as Tārābhimānin;
since Soma is the lord of all herbs, he is the great-grandfather (prapitāmaha). ||38||
The Lord, who provides the livelihood and security for all beings, constantly sustains the world with his rays through his pervasive vision. (39)
He who is the source of the lunar days, of the junctions of the festivals, and even of the full moon and the new moon;
he who is the maker of night, the essence of nectar, and the Lord of Creatures.
Therefore, that Soma, consisting of the essence of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* Vedas, is possessed of a father through the vital breaths—
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, as well as vyāna and udāna.
In this world, he is the initiator of all activities of living beings through their karmas, and the impeller of the vital winds—prāṇa, apāna, and samāna. ||42||
As if accomplishing the functions of the five sense organs, the mind, the intellect, memory, and the vital breaths simultaneously, he appeared as their very essence.
The soul of all, the bringer of all worlds through the Pravaha and other currents, the creator of all beings, the ever-forgiving Prabhajana (the Wind). 44.
He is the source of fire, of water, of earth, and of the sun and moon;
he is the wind, the lord of creatures, the existent, the soul of the worlds, and the great-grandfather.

Because the Lord is worshipped with only three skulls by the gods headed by Prajāpati— who seek the fruits of their sacrifices perfectly— during the destruction of medicinal herbs, He is therefore called Tryambaka.
The Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Jagatī which are remembered—these, known by the name Tryambakā, are declared to be the wombs of the Soma-pressing. ||47||

Through those three types [of powers], which have become one with her own vigor, that sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is indeed remembered as having three means of accomplishment and three potsherds (kapāla). ||48||
Thus, this period of five years has indeed been declared a *yuga* by the wise;
and that which is called the year by the twice-born is likewise said to be fivefold.
He then produced the six seasons, beginning with Spring (*madhu*), as a single group of six.
The five seasonal periods, beginning with the son of Ṛtu, constitute the creation in brief;
thus indeed does this Pavamāna [wind] sustain the lives of living beings. 1.31.50.
Time runs on, withdrawing all things like the swift current of a river;
as the maker of day and night, it then became the wind once more.
These lords of progeny are the foremost among all embodied beings;
they are proclaimed as the fathers of all worlds and the very souls of the worlds. (52)
As Brahmā was meditating, Bhava emerged from his mouth;
he became the seer, the brahmin, Mahādeva, the soul of all beings, and the great-grandfather.
The Lord manifests as the Praṇava for all beings;
through his entry into the self, there arises the formation of the limbs and minor members of living beings.
Agni, the year, the sun, the moon, and indeed Vāyu— the pervasive one who is the soul of time, the presiding deity of the Yugas, the eternal bringer of dissolution,
the inspirer of madness, and the bestower of grace— he is called Idvatsara.
Possessed by the Lord through his own splendor in this world, Rudra [manifested] through bodies and names due to the union of the substratum and that which rests upon it.
Then, by his power, there arose a second auspicious union which brings grace to the worlds and serves as the sole cause for the continuity of the lineage.
Since he possesses divinity, the state of being a progenitor, and that supreme nature of time,
he is therefore honored in every way by those who are like him as one who is truly auspicious.
The Lord is the husband of husbands, the Prajāpati of the lords of creatures;
he is the abode of all beings, the Nīlalohita of them all.
Rudra restores the withered medicinal herbs again and again. (59)
Indeed, the offspring of these—sons and grandsons who are infinite in number—cannot be enumerated by measure because of their vastness. (1.31.60)
By reciting this lineage of the great lords of subjects, who were performers of meritorious deeds and possessed of enduring fame, one shall attain great perfection.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of the Gods," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vāyu said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the definitive determination of the Praṇava;
the syllable Om is the Brahman, traditionally held to consist of three letters from the beginning. (1)
Whatever color has been ordained for each deity, so too are their respective Ṛg-verses,
Yajus-formulas, Sāman-chants, as well as air, fire, and water.
From that very Imperishable One (Akṣara), moreover, there were born again others—the fourteen high-souled ones who are the deities of the gods. ||3||
Among them, he who is all-pervading, the omnipresent one, the knower of all yoga, is said to be the beginning, the middle, and the end for the sake of favoring the worlds. ||4||
The seven ṛṣis, as well as the Indras and all the gods together with the ancestors,
have all emerged from the imperishable Maheśvara, the God of gods.
They speak of the supreme state for the sake of welfare in this world and the next;
I have already told you that time which is designated as the Yuga.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara,
and the beginning of the Kali ages revolve like a wheel, rotating through those very cycles.
But then the deities, agitated and fallen under the power of Time,
were unable by themselves to restrain his pride.
Then, at the beginning of that Manvantara, those sages, gods, and Indra of great asceticism became restrained in speech. ||9||
Having fixed their minds with intense concentration for a thousand years,
they then sought refuge in Mahādeva, being terrified of Time.
For this is the time of the Lord of Gods, who possesses four forms and four faces;
O Mahādeva, O Maheśvara, who could know this unfathomable one? (11)
Then Mahādeva, seeing that four-faced Kāla, said, "Do not be afraid; what desire of yours shall be granted?"
"I shall accomplish all of that; this exertion shall not be in vain," said the Lord, the divine Time himself, who is exceedingly difficult to conquer.
That white face of his which is seen to have four tongues is indeed the mouth of that time known as the Kṛta Yuga;
that god, the best of the Suras, Brahmā Vaivasvata, is its mouth.
O twice-born ones, that which I have described to you as the third, appearing red in color, with three tongues constantly licking, is the Tretā Yuga.
In this regard, the engagement in sacrifice indeed arises from Maheśvara;
therefore, the sacrifice is performed here, consisting of three tongues and three fires.
Having offered to the fires, O Brahmins, the tongue of Time (Kālajihvā) proceeds.
"That face which is indeed terrible, double-tongued, and reddish-brown—therein I shall become two-footed; that age shall be known by the name Dvāpara. (17)
This which has the luster of black, is the fourth, with red eyes, a single tongue, and is broad and dark-blue, licking [its lips] again and again. ||18||
Then comes the terrible Kali Yuga, which causes fear to all the worlds;
this is indeed the fourth and most terrifying face of the Kalpa.
In that age, there will be neither the face [of righteousness] nor even nirvāṇa;
indeed, in that age, all living beings will be swallowed by Time.
Brahmā is to be worshipped in the Kṛta age; in the Tretā age, sacrifice is honored;
Viṣṇu is worshipped in the Dvāpara age; and I am to be worshipped in all four ages. (21)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Yajña are the three portions of Time itself;
for at all times, Maheśvara exists in four forms.
I am the person and the progenitor of you all; I am Time, the impeller of time; likewise, I am the creator of the ages, as well as the Supreme and the ultimate refuge. ||23||
Therefore, having reached the Kali age, for the sake of the welfare of the worlds and for the sake of the fearlessness of the gods in both worlds, [he appeared]. ||24||
"Then, O best of gods, I shall become worthy of honor and worship;
therefore, O you of great power, no fear should be felt upon encountering Kali."
Having been addressed thus by all the sages, all the deities bowed their heads to the God and spoke again to the Lord of the World.
The celestial sages said:
Possessing great splendor, a massive body, great heroism, and great luster—how is it that Time, the four-faced one, is terrifying to all beings? ||27||
Mahādeva said:
This Time, possessing four forms, four tusks, and four faces,
moves everywhere for the sake of protecting the world.
For him, there is nothing impossible to achieve within the entire world of the moving and the unmoving;
Time creates all beings and again withdraws them in due order.
All are subject to the power of Time; Time is not subject to anyone's power.
Therefore, Time always governs all living beings.
The seventy-one steps previously mentioned of this Vikrama correspond here to the number of Manvantaras, according to the sequence of the revolving Yugas.
When time proceeds by one step, seventy-one steps [of breath] pass;
at that time, the dissolution of a Manvantara occurs. ||32||
Having spoken thus to the celestial rishis, ancestors, and dānavas, and being saluted by them all, the Blessed One vanished right there.
Thus, in due time, that Blessed One repeatedly withdraws the gods, sages, ancestors, and dānavas, and again and again creates them anew.
Therefore, during the Manvantaras, the Blessed Lord Īśa is worshipped by the gods, sages, ancestors, and Dānavas out of fear of that very Time.
Therefore, in the Kali age, a twice-born man should perform penance with every effort;
for one who has taken refuge in Mahādeva, the fruit of his merit is great.
Consequently, the gods, having gone to heaven and descended again to the surface of the earth, [act thus]. (36)
When the most terrible Kali age arrives, the sages and the gods,
devoted to righteousness, desire to perform intense austerity;
and [the Lord], having descended, acts again and again throughout the Kali age.
In this manner, throughout the course of time, all those thousands of divine royal sages who have passed away in that Vaivasvata interval [have likewise attained their goal]. (38)
Devāpi, the Paurava king, and Manu, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage—
all endowed with the power of great yoga— wait for the change of time.
When that Kali Yuga has ended, and during the Tretā and Kṛta Yugas,
they shall again appear together with the Seven Sages in the Tretā Yuga;
these are proclaimed as the future progenitors of the lineages and the Kṣatriyas.
At the end of the Dvāpara age, the Kṣatriyas together with the sages establish themselves;
likewise, when the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages have passed away, those men who are indeed sinful are said to exist in the Kali age. ||41||
The Śruti and Smṛti exist for the sake of continuity throughout the seven Manvantaras;
likewise, the sequence of the dissolution of these entire ages is as follows.
The mutual origin of the Yugas and of the Brahmins and Kshatriyas,
as well as how their nature proceeds from them and how their decline occurs.
When the kṣatriya order had been utterly exterminated by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, all unchaste women were taken up by the kṣatriyas who became lords of the earth;
listen as I proclaim to you those who have gone to heaven. 44.
They declare that the nature of the Ikṣvāku lineage is [monarchical];
however, other Kṣatriyas on earth are kings who exist as mere guild-bound associations. 45.
Now, just as the kings of the Ikṣvāku line were born in the lineage of Aida, from them alone a full hundred dynasties were consecrated. (46)
The extent of the Bhojas, however, is recorded as double that;
the Kṣatriya territory consists of three hundred [yojanas] and is divided into four parts according to the directions. 47.
Now learn from me as I recount those kings who have passed away:
there were indeed one hundred Prativindhyas and likewise one hundred Haihayas.
There were one hundred and one Dhārtarāṣṭras, eighty Janamejayas,
one hundred Brahmadattas, and a hundred families of heroic men.
Then there were one hundred Śatantus and one hundred Kāśis, Kuśas, and others;
likewise, another thousand Śaśabindus passed away—
all of whom performed horse sacrifices with sacrificial fees of a hundred thousand.
Thus have they been described in brief; it is not possible, however, to speak in detail of all the royal sages who have passed away, together with their contemporaries.
These were the increasers of the lineage of Yayāti;
they have been glorified as radiant ones who indeed sustain the worlds.
And they obtain five boons difficult to attain, pertaining to the world of Brahmā:
long life, sons, wealth, fame, sovereignty, and even prosperity. (53)
By means of both retention and hearing, those wise ones of the five classes,
as well as those who are so described as worldly, indeed go to the world of Brahmā.
They say that the Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years;
its dawn (sandhyā) lasts for as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (sandhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
In the Kṛta age, the Prakriyāpāda is said to consist of four thousand [verses];
from that, the Sandhyā and the Sandhyāṃśa likewise each consist of four hundred.
The Tretā and the other ages consist of thousands according to the number [of years] together with the sages;
its twilight (sandhyā) is remembered as three hundred, and the twilight-part (sandhyāṃśa) is also three hundred.
The period of the Tretā age, including its subsidiary portion, is three thousand years in number;
while that of the Dvāpara age is proclaimed to be two thousand years. (58)
For that [Dvāpara] as well, there are two hundred [years] for the twilight (sandhyā) and likewise two hundred for the twilight-interval (sandhyāṃśa);
the third, the introductory section (upodghāta), is called a quarter in the Dvāpara age.
Those who know calculation say that Kali lasts for one thousand years;
its dawn (sandhyā) is one hundred years, and its twilight (sandhyāṃśa) is likewise one hundred.
The fourth quarter, known as the Saṃhārapāda, indeed belongs to the Kali Yuga;
for the four ages, together with their junctions and sub-periods, are thus enumerated.
This is remembered as a cycle of four ages (caturyuga) consisting of twelve thousand [verses].
Thus, there are five thousand and five hundred verses in each quarter.
With the Sandhyās and Sandhyāṃśakas, there are two thousand others;
thus, the wise know the Purāṇa to consist of twelve thousand verses.
Just as the Veda has four quarters, so too does an age (yuga) have four quarters.
Just as an age with its four quarters was ordained by the Creator himself,
so too were the four quarters of the gods ordained by Brahmā in ancient times.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Ages," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
In all the Manvantaras, both past and future, here in this world,
all beings are born with identical self-conceptions according to their names and forms.
The various gods and those who were the presiding lords in that Manvantara,
as well as the sages and human beings— all were possessed of equal self-conceit.
The creation of the great seers has indeed been declared; now listen as the lineage of Svāyambhuva is being proclaimed in detail and in its proper sequence.
Svāyambhuva Manu had ten grandsons equal to himself,
by whom this entire earth, endowed with its seven continents, was [ruled].
At that time, during the first Tretā Yuga of the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, [the city] was established with its oceans and rivers, and its various settlements laid out.
By those sons and grandsons of Priyavrata, who were themselves the grandsons of Svāyambhuva,
this earth was established through their acts of procreation, austerity, and yoga.
From the heroic Priyavrata, a daughter was born to those who possessed offspring;
that highly fortunate daughter [was wed] to the patriarch Kardama. (7)
The two daughters were Śatapatrā and Kukṣi;
both of them had ten heroic brothers who were equal to Prajāpati.
Agnīdhra, Vapuṣmat, Medhā, Medhātithi, Vibhu, Jyotiṣmat, Dyutimat, Havya, Savana, and indeed Sarva; ||9||
Having consecrated these seven kings over those seven continents according to dharma, Priyavrata [departed]; learn now of those continents and those kings.
He made the mighty Agnīdhra the lord of Jambūdvīpa,
and by him Medhātithi was made the lord of Plakṣadvīpa.
The Lord consecrated Vapuṣmat as king over Śālmaladvīpa, and he made Jyotiṣmat the king of Kuśadvīpa. ||12||
Priyavrata appointed Dyutimat as the king over Krauñcadvīpa,
and he also made Havya the lord of Śākadvīpa.
The lord also performed a sacrifice at Puṣkara;
at that sacrifice in Puṣkara, Mahāvīta became his son.
Dhātaki—these two were the sons of him who was the best among those possessing sons. (14)
The region known as Mahāvīta is named after that great-souled one;
and because of the name Dhātaki, it is also called Dhātakīkhaṇḍa.
The lord Havya begot sons who were the sovereigns of Śākadvīpa:
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, Maṇīcaka, Vasumoda, Sumodāka, and the seventh, Mahādruma. ||16||
The first [age] of the Cloud is said to be Jalada;
the second of the Youth is proclaimed as Kaumāra. ||17||
The third is proclaimed as Sukumāra for Sukumāra;
the fourth is called Maṇīcaka for Maṇīcaka. ||18||
The fifth region is indeed that of Vasumoda, called Vasumodaka;
and the sixth is proclaimed as the region of Modaka, called Modāka. ||19||
The seventh [region] is named Mahādruma after the great tree;
these indeed are the seven varṣas there, measured by their respective names.
The sons of Dyutimat, the lord of Krauñcadvīpa,
were indeed Kuśala, Manuṣya, Uṣṇa, Pīvara, Andhakāraka,
Muni, and Dundubhi; these were the sons of Dyutimat.
The auspicious regions situated within Krauñcadvīpa are named after them.
The region of Uṣṇa is known as Uṣṇa, and that of Pīvara is likewise Pīvara. (22)
Andhakāraka is celebrated as Andhakāra;
the region of the sage is indeed Munideśa, and that of Dundubhi is remembered as Dundubhi.
These are the seven luminous provinces in Krauñcadvīpa. (23)
In Kuśadvīpa, these seven sons of Jyotiṣmān, possessed of great majesty,
are remembered as Udbhida, Veṇumān, Svaira, Lavaṇa, Dhṛti,
the sixth Prabhākara, and the seventh Kapila.
The first region is Udbhida, the second is Veṇumaṇḍala,
the third is Svairathākāra, and the fourth is known as Lavaṇa.
The fifth is the Dhṛtimat year, the sixth year is Prabhākara, and the seventh is named Kapila; thus is the cycle of Kapila proclaimed. ||26||
In Kuśadvīpa, their respective islands bear those very same names,
and they are adorned by subjects who are devoted to the practices of the hermitages.
The seven lords of Śālmaladvīpa were the sons of Vapuṣmān;
they were Śveta, Harita, Jīmūta, Rohita, Vaidyuta, Mānasa, and Suprabha as the seventh. ||28||
The white region belongs to Śveta, the red to Rohita, the cloud-like to Jīmūta, and the green to Hārita. ||29||
Vaidyuta was the son of Vaidyuta, and Mānasa was the son of Mānasa;
Suprabha was the son of Suprabha—these seven were the protectors of the regions.
I shall now describe the seven islands, beginning immediately after Jambūdvīpa.
There were seven sons of Medhātithi who were kings ruling over Plakṣadvīpa. (31)
The eldest among them was Śāntabhaya; those were indeed his seven sons.
From that Śāntabhaya were born Śiśira, who brings the dawning of happiness, as well as Ānanda, Dhruva, Kṣemaka, and Śiva.
These seven regions, which bear their respective names,
were established by them in their portions during the previous Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
By those sons of Medhātithi, who dwell in the seven islands,
the subjects in Plakṣadvīpa were established, endowed with the conduct of the castes and stages of life.
Indeed, in the five continents beginning with Plakṣadvīpa and ending with Śākadvīpa, dharma is to be known as existing according to the divisions of caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama). ||35||
Happiness, long life, beauty, strength, and righteousness—
these five are always known to be common to all these islands.
Learn now of Jambūdvīpa, which encompasses seven islands. Priyavrata consecrated his eldest son, Āgnīdhra— the mighty one born of his daughter— as the sovereign king of Jambūdvīpa.
He indeed had sons equal in splendor to Prajāpatis;
the eldest was known as Nābhi, and his younger brother was Kiṃpuruṣa.
Harivarṣa was the third, while Ilāvṛta was the fourth;
Ramya was the fifth son, and Harimān is said to be the sixth. (39)
Kuru is the seventh among them, and Bhadrāśva is recorded as the eighth;
Ketumāla is the ninth—learn now of their regions.
The father gave the region to the south of the navel as Himādvat;
he gave the region of Hemakūṭa to Kimpuruṣa. (41)
He gave the region known as Naiṣadha to Harivarṣa,
and that which was the central region of Sumeru, he gave to Ilāvṛta.
The region remembered as Nīla was given by his father to Ramya;
and that which is to the north, Śveta, was given by his father to Harimān. (43)
He gave the region beyond Śṛṅgavat to Kuru, and he also assigned the region of Mālyavat to Bhadrāśva. ||44||
And Gandhamādana announced [his domain] in Ketumāla.
Thus, these are the nine great regions here, divided by their respective portions. ||45||
That righteous-souled one consecrated all those sons as Āgnīdhras in due order, and thereafter he remained established in asceticism.
Thus, by these seven sons of Priyavrata— the grandsons of Svāyambhuva— all the seven continents were settled.
As for the eight auspicious regions beginning with Kimpuruṣa, in them accomplishment is attained by their very nature, consisting mostly of happiness and without effort. (48)
For them there is no perversion, nor is there any fear of old age or death;
for them neither merit nor demerit exists, nor are there superior, inferior, or middling [beings].
For them there is no state of the ages (yuga), but this applies in every respect only to the fields (kṣetra).
I shall now describe the lineage from Nābhi; listen to that which took place in the land called Himavat.
The immensely radiant Nābhi begot a son named Ṛṣabha upon the queen Merudevī—the foremost of kings and the first-born of all the kṣatriyas. (1.33.50)
From Ṛṣabha was born the heroic Bharata, the eldest of a hundred sons;
having consecrated his son, Bharata then retired to the forest life.
He assigned the southern region, called Himā, to Bharata;
therefore, the wise know that region as Bhārata-varṣa after his name. ||52||
Bharata had a learned and righteous son named Sumati;
Bharata entrusted that kingdom to him, and having transferred the royal glory to his son, the king entered the forest. ||53||
The son of Tejas was also Prajāpati Amitrajit;
the learned son of Taijasa is known as Indradyumna. (54)
Then Parameṣṭhin was born, and after his death, Śobhana was born into the family of that Pratīhāra; from that lineage, a son named after him was born,
and from that wise man, the one renowned as Pratihartṛ was born.
Unnetṛ was the son of Pratihartṛ, and his son is remembered as Bhūvas.
Udgītha became his son, and Pratāvin was his son as well. (56)
Pratāvin was the son of Vibhu, and Pṛthu is considered his son;
Nakta was the son of Pṛthu, and Gaya is recorded as the son of Nakta.
Gayas had a son named Nara, and Nara’s son was Virāṭ.
Virāṭ’s son was the very powerful Dīrghabāhu, and his son was Dīma. (58)
The son of Dhīmat was Mahān, and the son of Mahān was Bhauvana;
Tvaṣṭṛ was the son of Bhauvana, and Arijan was his offspring.
Arija’s son was Rajas, and Śatajit is known as the son of Rajas.
He had a hundred sons, all of whom were kings.
By those who were the foremost among the Viśvajyotis, these subjects were increased;
by them, this land of Bhārata-varṣa was formerly divided into seven regions.
By their dynasties, this land of Bhārata has been enjoyed for seventy-one cycles of the ages known as Kṛta, Tretā, and so forth. (62)
Those kings who have passed away along with those yugas, belonging to that lineage,
existed by the hundreds and thousands in the previous Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
This is the creation of Svayambhū, by which this world is filled with sages, deities, ancestors, gandharvas, and rākṣasas.
By means of yakṣas, bhūtas, piśācas, humans, beasts, and birds—
this creation of theirs in the world revolves together with the yugas.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Genealogy of Svāyambhuva," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
The sages said:
Having thus heard the arrangement of the progeny, that bull among sages,
being skillful, questioned the Sūta regarding the length and breadth of the earth.
How many continents, oceans, and mountains are there, O Lord? How many regions (varṣas) are there, and which rivers are recorded as being within them? ||2||
The dimensions of the great elements, as well as the worlds and the non-worlds; the enumeration of synonyms and their limits, and likewise the course of the moon and the sun—
explain all of this to us in detail, exactly as it is.
Sūta said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the length and breadth of the earth,
as well as the measurements of the oceans and the extent of the islands.
The number of years and the rivers that are recorded therein,
the dimensions of the great elements, as well as the Lokāloka mountain,
the measurement of the cycles of time, and likewise the course of the moon and the sun.
Indeed, the thousands of divisions of the continents contained within these seven [oceans] cannot be described with exact measurement even in hundreds of years.
I shall now describe the seven continents together with the moon, the sun, and the planets,
regarding which men declare their dimensions by means of reasoning.
Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable should not be investigated through reasoning;
for that which is beyond primordial natures is declared to be eternal. (8)
I shall describe Jambūdvīpa exactly as it is, with its nine regions; learn of it according to its extent and its circular dimensions in yojanas. (9)
It measures one hundred thousand yojanas in extent,
filled with various provinces and diverse, auspicious cities.
It was adorned with mountains inhabited by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas,
as well as by mountains composed of all kinds of minerals and formed from masses of rock, along with rivers originating from those mountains.
Jambūdvīpa is vast and glorious, surrounded on all sides;
it is encompassed by all the worlds that sustain living beings,
and it is itself encircled on every side by the salt ocean.
Equal in extent to Jambūdvīpa on all sides,
these six mountain ranges of excellent peaks extend eastward across the continent of Jambūdvīpa.
They have plunged into both oceans, the eastern and the western.
Himavān consists mostly of snow, while Hemakūṭa abounds in gold;
Niṣadha is said to be made of gold and possesses the luster of the rising sun.
Mount Meru is said to be composed of the four classes of precious substances and made of gold; it is of the shape of a floating mass, square in form, and loftily elevated. ||15||
Possessing various colors on its sides and endowed with the qualities of Prajāpati,
it was produced from the navel-cord of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest.
In the east he is white in color and devoted to Brahman; therefore, by that [color], he is [the Brāhmaṇa]. And in the south he is yellow; by that, he is considered a Vaiśya. ||17||
That one of great strength, resembling a bumblebee in hue,
was seen by him [the sage] as being of Śūdra status due to his wings, for the sake of various purposes on Mount Meru.
His northern side is naturally red in color;
by that, his status as a Kṣatriya is established—thus the castes have been proclaimed.
He is clearly described according to his nature, his color, and his proportions. ||19||
One is blue and made of lapis lazuli; another has white peaks and is made of gold;
and one with golden peaks has the color of a peacock’s tail.
These are the kings of mountains, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas;
the distance between them is said to be nine thousand [yojanas]. ||21||
In the center, however, is Ilāvṛta, which surrounds Mahāmeru on all sides;
that mountain extends for nine thousand [yojanas]. In the middle of that Mahāmeru, it is like a smokeless fire. ||22||
The southern half of Meru is Vedyardha, and likewise the northern half is Uttara;
as for the seven regions (varṣas) here, those mountain ranges that serve as their boundaries are each two thousand yojanas in width and height.
Their length is said to be equal to the breadth of Jambūdvīpa;
the two middle mountains are each two hundred thousand yojanas.
Nīla and Niṣadha, and those others inferior to them— Śveta, Hemakūṭa, Himavān, and Śṛṅgavān.
Those which are nine thousand, twenty-eight thousand, and two thousand yojanas in extent—
among them are the inhabited regions, which indeed constitute the seven Varṣas.
Covered by those mountains with precipitous peaks and strewn with various kinds of rivers, they are inaccessible to one another;
yet within them dwell creatures of diverse species, each according to its own kind.
This region of the Himalayas is renowned by the name Bhārata;
beyond that is Hemakūṭa, which is known by the name Kiṃpuruṣa.
The Naiṣadha region is Hemakūṭa, and that is called Harivarṣa;
beyond Harivarṣa and on the other side of Meru is Ilāvṛta.
Beyond Ilāvṛta is Nīla, renowned by the name Ramyaka;
beyond Ramyaka is Śveta, which is famous as Hiraṇmaya;
and beyond Hiraṇmaya is Śṛṅgavān, known as Kuru.
And it should be understood that two regions, the southern and the northern, are shaped like a bow;
among them, four are long, while the central one, Ilāvṛta, is at the end.
To the east of Niṣadha, the southern half of the sacrificial altar (vedi) is traditionally known;
that which lies beyond Nīlava is the northern half of the altar.
On the southern half of the altar there are three regions (varṣas), and likewise three on the northern half.
Between those two, however, one should know that Ilāvṛta lies in the center of Meru;
it is to the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha.
To the north lies the great mountain named Mālyavat;
it is as vast as the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains,
measuring one thousand yojanas in breadth and thirty-four thousand yojanas in length, as it is proclaimed.
To its west, the mountain Gandhamādana is to be known;
furthermore, the one renowned as Mālyavat is equal to it in length and breadth. ||35||
In the center of the circular [continents] stands Meru, the supreme mountain;
it is four-colored, made of excellent gold, square, and lofty.
All the unmanifest elements, beginning with water, have arisen [therein]. (36)
From the unmanifest, the manifest— the great earth-lotus with Mount Meru as its pericarp and the fourfold path as its petals— arose, possessing the five qualities.
Then, O best of the twice-born, all the modes of livelihood arose through various kinds of merit acquired in many kalpas and previously earned. (38)
He who has disciplined his self, the well-trained self, the Great Self, the Supreme Person;
the Great God, the Great Yogi, the Eldest in the world, the Great Lord;
he who pervades all worlds, the Infinite, was indeed born from formlessness. 39.
His form is not composed of flesh, fat, and bone as that of ordinary beings;
rather, through yoga and his lordship, he has indeed entered into the soul of all.
On account of that, the eternal lotus of the world arose;
such is the course of time at the beginning of the remainder of a kalpa.
Within that lotus was born the God of gods, the four-faced one;
Brahmā, the Lord of the Lords of Creatures, the Ruler, and the Master of the world. ||42||
For his seed was indeed the creation of Puṣkara;
thus, the entire process of the emission of progeny is here described in detail.
From that lotus which was to be made for Viṣṇu, the earth, together with its forests and trees, emerged in the form of a lotus from his navel. 44.
Thus has the measurement of this world-lotus been revealed in detail;
listen, O twice-born ones, as it is described in its divisions and in due order. 45.
Furthermore, the four famous great continents are situated upon the petals;
from there stands the mighty one named Meru, shaped like a pericarp.
Among its various colored sides, the eastern one is said to be white;
its southern peak is yellow, and likewise, the other is black.
His northern quarter was indeed red, endowed with a beautiful color;
and Meru, white and radiant, stood established there like a king. ||48||
Shining with the color of the rising sun like a smokeless fire,
it is proclaimed to be eighty-four thousand [yojanas] in height.
Having entered sixteen units below, it is likewise extended [there].
That [element], previously situated like a shallow bowl, is thirty-two units wide at its summit.
Its circumference all around is three times its width;
by way of measurement, it is considered to be half that size when triangular.
It is proclaimed that its triangular measurement is forty-eight thousand yojanas on all sides.
Its circumference all around, measured by the same square measurement, is ordained to be sixty-four thousand yojanas.
That mountain is greatly divine, endowed with celestial herbs;
it is entirely covered by auspicious peaks made of gold.
There, all the hosts of gods, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, as well as auspicious throngs of Apsarases, were seen together with the kings of mountains. (55)
That Meru, the creator of beings, is surrounded by the worlds;
its four regions are indeed established upon its various sides.
Bhadrāśva, Bharata, and Ketumāla in the west,
as well as the Northern Kurus, are the abodes of those who have performed meritorious deeds.
The pericarp of that lotus is circular all around;
it is proclaimed to be ninety-six thousand yojanas [in circumference],
and four [thousand] and eighty [yojanas] are established at intervals within.
In measurement, it is three hundred thousand yojanas;
its masses of filaments are spread out on all sides. (59)
In the *Śatasāhasrikā*, it is said that it is eighty thousand [yojanas] in width and length;
its four petals extend for four yojanas in each of the four directions.
In that regard, listen with one-pointed attention to a brief description of that which was previously designated by me as the "pericarp" (karṇikā). 61.
Atri considered this [the earth] to have a hundred edges; the seer Bhṛgu, a thousand edges;
Sāvarṇi, eight edges; and Bhāguri, however, considered it to be four-cornered.
Vārṣāyaṇi [wore] the ocean-like [garment], Gālava a shallow earthen bowl, Gārgya his hair tied in an upward braid, and Kroṣṭaki [wore it] circular.
Whatever the Ṛṣi knows regarding this lord of mountains, that very thing he knows; he knows this Brahman in its entirety.
It was variegated with jewels and gems, endowed with light of various colors,
a mass of many hues, made of gold, and possessing a reddish glow.
Know Meru, the best of mountains, to be beloved, possessing a thousand ridges, a thousand water-caves,
and a thousand hundred-petaled lotuses.
With pillars set with precious gems and altars variegated with jewels,
its body was likewise adorned with gold and various gems, as well as with coral archways.
On every festival day, Mount Meru was illuminated on its borders by hundreds of glorious celestial chariots belonging to the inhabitants of heaven.
On this mountain of a thousand peaks, adorned with various abodes,
the hosts of all the gods are settled in great numbers.
Upon its upper surface dwelt the god of gods, the four-faced Brahmā,
the best among the knowers of Brahman and the most excellent of the inhabitants of heaven.
It was filled in all directions with many thousands of great asuras, who were accompanied by all the inhabitants of the great world-realms and who bestowed the fruits of every desire.
There is the delightful assembly hall of Brahmā, frequented by hosts of Brahmanical seers;
it is known by the name Manovatī and is renowned throughout all the worlds. (72)
There, having established a great celestial chariot for the god Īśāna, which possesses the splendor of a thousand suns, it remains forever by virtue of its majesty.
There, at that time, the hosts of sages and gods [gathered] before the four-faced one;
he was proclaimed there as the mass of splendors of all the gods.
There dwells the glorious Śrīpati, the thousand-eyed Purandara,
being worshipped by the thirty gods and the great yogic celestial sages.
There is the abode of Mahendra, the great king and lord of the world, whose splendor is equal to that of the sun, and which is saluted by all the Siddhas. (76)
That world of Indra, endowed with the supreme prosperity of the world,
shines forth, eternally frequented by the thirty gods, the foremost among the immortals.
On the second inner shore as well, in the southeastern region of Vaidiśya, there is a most delightful and exceedingly radiant place, variegated with hundreds of various minerals. (78)
Its floor was inlaid with various jewels, it was supported by many pillars,
its gardens were fashioned from Jāmbūnada gold, and it possessed beautiful altars made of diverse gems.
It was filled with many excellent palatial chambers and gabled towers;
it was a renowned great celestial mansion, radiant like the sun and like the fire-god Jātavedas.
For that great assembly hall of the Fire-god is named Tejovatī;
there, Anala himself, the best of the gods and the mouth of all the deities, is present in person.
Abounding with hundreds of thousands of crests, garlanded with flames, and radiant, he is praised and offered oblations there by the hosts of sages and the gods. 82.
That distinction, however, is declared by the wise to be caused by the presiding deities;
it consists of both differentiation and radiance, and all this is beyond doubt. (83)
Having attained another state of enjoyment, he is remembered as the all-pervading one of singular splendor;
for through reasoning, both distinctness and the mixture of cause and effect are established. (84)

That fire was saluted by high-souled, highly fortunate, and great perfected ones (mahāsiddhas) who know the worlds and their inhabitants, and who possess that same heroic vigor and devoted themselves to those same practices. ||85||
On the third inner bank as well, there is likewise the Great Assembly (Mahāsabhā), which should be known as the "Well-Restrained" (Susaṃyamā), renowned in the world as belonging to Vaivasvata. 86.
Likewise, in the direction of the fourth quarter, there is the assembly hall of the wise Virūpākṣa, the lord of the Nairṛta region, named Kṛṣṇāṅganā. (87)
On the fifth inner shore, there is likewise a great assembly hall belonging to Vaivasvata, known by the auspicious name Śubhavatī;
it belongs to the high-souled Varuṇa, the lord of the waters. ||88||
Likewise, in the northern region, on the sixth inner shore, O auspicious one, is the assembly hall named Gandhavatī, belonging to Vāyu, which possesses every excellent quality. (89)
On my inner shore as well, there is the assembly hall of the Lord of Constellations,
named Mahodayā, with its altar made of pure lapis lazuli.
Likewise, on the eighth inner shore, there is the assembly hall of the high-souled Īśāna,
named Yaśovatī, possessing the brilliant luster of refined gold.
These auspicious great celestial mansions in the eight directions indeed belong to the eight high-souled chief gods, Indra and the others.
These are always frequented by sages, gods, gandharvas, apsarases, and great serpents—highly fortunate beings who have come to attend upon them. 93.
By those learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, these synonymous terms—nākapṛṣṭha, div, and svarga—are indeed recited. ||94||
This very thing is sung in all the Vedas concerning that mountain in the world of the gods, which is the dwelling place of all the gods who have perfected their selves. ||95||
Through various observances, numerous sacrifices performed by those of self-restraint,
and other diverse merits acquired over hundreds of different births,
one attains that world of the gods, which is called heaven. (96)
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Jambūdvīpa," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
That which is indeed proclaimed as the base of the pericarp is recorded as being seventy thousand yojanas below.
Forty-eight thousand [yojanas] here is the circle surrounded by the king of mountains; it is the root of Meru, so says the sacred tradition. (2)
Among those thousands of mountains,
many very lofty boundary mountains are recorded as marking the limits in all directions.
They were beautified by groves, mountain caves, rivers, caverns, and waterfalls,
and possessed many palaces, ridges, and banks resplendent with flowers.

All the mountains were adorned with garlands of flowers upon their slopes, decorated with minerals, and graced by peaks tawny as gold and covered with many springs; they were beautified by lush trees laden with jewels.
It was also attended by incomparable groves frequented by hundreds of birds,
and by various wild animals of diverse colors and forms, including lions, tigers, śarabhas, yak-tailed bulls, and great elephants.
The seven [rivers] and the dark-bodied Hari each have ten mountains;
those which are external and internal are known to be equal in their threefold courses.
Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa are two mountains in the eastern direction;
they extend from south to north, reaching as far as Nīla and Niṣadha.
Kailāsa and Himavat are the southern and northern mountains;
these two extend from east to west and are situated reaching to the edge of the ocean.
O best of the twice-born, that lofty golden mountain Meru—listen as I describe its dimensions while I speak. (1.35.10)
Furthermore, there are four great feet of Mount Meru in the four directions;
because it is supported by them, the earth with its seven continents does not waver. (11)
Their length is taught to be ten thousand yojanas;
they are adorned with various jewels belonging to the gods, gandharvas, and yakṣas, abounding in many waterfalls and ramparts, and fashioned with delightful caves. ||12||
The variegated ridges were adorned with *puṣpaka* and *kādamba* trees on their slopes,
as well as with veins of red arsenic and surfaces of yellow orpiment.
It was surrounded on all sides by caves variegated with gold and jewels,
adorned with minerals of pure vermilion and gold.
Adorned with excellent gold and variegated coral,
beautiful and possessing a hundred joints, these dwellings of the Siddhas were filled with joy; they were illuminated on all sides by magnificent and glorious great celestial chariots.
To the east is the mountain named Mandara, to the south is Gandhamādana; Vipula is on the western side, and Supārśva is remembered to be in the north. ||16||
Upon their thousands of peaks were altars of diamond and lapis lazuli,
provided with thousands of branches, well-rooted and firmly established.
With glossy, dark, and dense leaves, they provided various shelters; they were elevated by many layers of growth and endowed with great flowers and fruits.
Served by yakṣas and gandharvas, and frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas, four great trees have arisen as the banners of the four continents. (19)
On the peak of Mount Mandara stands that great tree, the king of banners,
with its branches and summit hanging down— a tree with cavernous depths at its base.
It was adorned with flowers the size of large jars, possessing full-blown filaments,
great fragrances, and enchanting qualities, all of which were available throughout every season.
Then, fanned by a gentle breeze, he filled the directions with his fragrance for more than a thousand yojanas on every side.
O twice-born ones, he who was known as Varaketu became famous by the name Bhadrāśva,
where Hṛṣīkeśa himself is glorified by hosts of perfected beings.
At that time, Hari, the supreme among others, who was white-complexioned and a destroyer of enemies, arrived there in ancient times accompanied by him at that grove of *rudraka* trees.
And by him, O leaders of bipeds, the entire island was surveyed;
it is for this reason that it is known by the name Bhadrāśva. (25)
On the peak of the southern mountain as well, there is a Jambu tree frequented by the gods, which is always laden with flowers and fruit and is perpetually adorned with garlands. ||26||
Adorned with great roots and great trunks of glossy hue,
it is ever graced by branches bearing fresh flowers and fruits.
For upon the summit of that mountain, fruits that are of immense size, sweet, soft, and like unto nectar fall. (28)
From that mountain peak, moreover,
there flows forth again the river named Jambūnadī, carrying honeyed waters.
There, the gold named Jāmbūnada, which has the brilliance of a blazing fire, is produced; it is an incomparable ornament for the gods and a destroyer of sins. (1.35.30)
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
and pannagas drink that honey-like nectar flowing from the juice of the jambu fruit.
That banner was renowned in the worlds as Jambhū in the southern continent;
after her name, this eternal land became celebrated as Jambūdvīpa.
On the peak of the great-souled western mountain Vipula,
there grew an exceedingly vast aśvattha tree.
Adorned today with a choice garland hanging down, possessing a golden jeweled pedestal, with high and broad branches, it is an abode of the virtues of many beings. ||34||
That Ketu of the Ketumālas was served by gods and gandharvas, and possessed auspicious fruits of all seasons that were as large as jars and provided great pleasure.
O best of Brahmins, listen to the etymological explanation of how her name Ketumālā was proclaimed according to her deeds. (36)
When the churning of the Ocean of Milk had occurred and the faction of the Daityas had been defeated,
she was crushed by the agitation and upheaval caused by the friction of the great battle.
A garland fashioned by the Thousand-eyed One was offered to him,
which clung to the shoulder of that lordly Ashvattha tree.
She, indeed, is Mahāgandhā, unfading and the fulfiller of all desires;
she, of great fortune, is worshipped by various Siddhas and Cāraṇas. ||39||
A divine garland, ever-present and bestowed by the gods, shone upon that banner;
stirred by the wind, it wafted a celestial and enchanting fragrance. (1.35.40)
The island marked with their names, vast in extent in the west, is known everywhere both in heaven and here on earth as Ketumāla. (41)
And on the northern peak of his own side, there grew a great tree, a banyan with a massive trunk and a circumference of many yojanas. ||42||
Adorned with various clusters of flower garlands and fragrant incense, and hung with pendants of vegetables, it shone, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas. ||43||
With fruits that are always filled with honey and resemble coral jars,
that tree indeed shines as the banner of the Uttarakurus.
The seven highly fortunate sons of Brahmā born from his mind, who were younger than Sanatkumāra, became renowned there as the Kurus.
There, those who possessed realized knowledge, were established in the state of being, and were renowned for their merit, attained that eternal, supreme world which is imperishable and secure. 46.
The island marked with the names of those seven great-souled ones is forever renowned both in heaven and here on earth as Uttarakuru.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Jambūdvīpa," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
I shall describe, in due order, the delightful secondary ranges belonging to those four lords of mountains, which possess the seasonal flowers of every season at all times.
It was filled on all sides with sarika birds, peacocks, and cakoras intoxicated with passion, as well as with parrots, bhringarajas, and citrakas. ||2||
With the cries of the jīvañjīvaka birds, the warbling of golden-hued birds, the songs of intoxicated cuckoos, and the calls of various beautiful creatures; ||3||
They were delightful on all sides with the golden calls of the sugrīvas, the songs of the kalaviṅkas,
and the various warbling sounds from within.
In some places the forest edges were filled with the songs of bees— intoxicated, sweet-sounding, and sluggish— and in other places by the songs of kinnaras.
Where trees are seen, adorned with beautiful sprouts, releasing a rain of flowers as they are shaken by gentle breezes.
And they were endowed with clusters of blossoms, flower-buds, and copper-colored young shoots,
all swaying and oscillating under the influence of a gentle breeze.
O best of the twice-born, in some places they were adorned with hundreds of rocks of lovely forms, variegated by various minerals, and in others with scattered thorny shrubs.
They were frequented here and there by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas, as well as by hosts of siddhas and apsarases.
Now hear from me the names of those four magnificent and enchanting divine pleasure-grounds situated in the four directions. 1.36.10.
One should know that the eastern forest is named Caitraratha, the southern is Nandana,
the western is Vaibhrāja, and the northern is the forest of Savitṛ.
And in these great forests, delightful secondary groves were situated in due order, resounding with the warbling of birds. ||12||
With their sacred fords expanded by groves, these highly meritorious forests were inhabited by great elephants and frequented by high-souled beings. ||13||
The waters are as sweet as ambrosia, auspicious, and exceedingly pleasant;
their currents have been touched by perfected beings, gods, and the foremost of asuras.

Adorned with blossoming white lotuses and blue lilies of great leaves, possessing vast fragrance and captivating beauty, and equal in size to a royal umbrella, there are four great lakes; I shall describe them by name. ||15||
The lake Aruṇoda is in the east, Mānasa is known to be in the south;
Sitoda is the western lake, and likewise Mahābhadra is in the north.
Listen now from me in detail and according to the truth as I describe those mountains which are remembered as being to the east of Aruṇoda. ||17||
Śītānta, Kumuñja, Suvīra, the supreme mountain Acala, Vikaṅka, Maṇiśīla, and the supreme mountain Vṛṣabha. ||18||
Then Mahānīla, Rucaka, Sabindu, Mandara, Veṇumān, Sumedhas, Niṣadha, and Devaparvata. ||19||
Thus these excellent mountains and other hills likewise have been described as the abodes of the Siddhas situated to the east of Mount Mandara.
Learn now those great mountains by name which I have mentioned as being to the south of Lake Mānasa here. ||21||
Also Śaila, Triśikhara, and Śiśira, the best of mountains; Kaliṅga, Pataṅga, and Rucaka, the peaked one. ||22||
Tāmrābha, Viśākha, and likewise the mountain Śvetodara;
Samūla, Viṣadhāra, and the mountain Ratnadhāra. ||23||
Ekaśṛṅga, Mahāmūla, Gajaśaila, Piśācaka, Pañcaśaila, Kailāsa, and Himavat, the best of mountains. ||24||
Thus, these most excellent mountains, frequented by the gods, are said to lie in the southern direction from Meru, which possesses the splendor of the immortals. (25)
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe in due order those excellent great mountains that lie beyond the Sitoda lake.
Suvakṣas, Śikhiśaila, Kāla, Vaiḍūryaparvata, Kapila, Piṅgala, Rudra, Surasa, and Mahācala. ||27||
Kumuda, Madhumān, Añjanīmukuṭa, Kṛṣṇa, Pāṇḍara, and Sahasraśikhara. ||28||
Pāriyātra, the lord of mountains, and Triśṛṅga, the best of peaks—these are remembered as the foremost mountains in the western quarter. ||29||
To the north of the lake Mahābhadraka and also of the glorious Śrīmān,
those whom I have previously mentioned, I shall describe in their proper order.
The great mountain Śaṅkukūṭa, Vṛṣabha, Haṃsaparvata, Nāga, Kapila, and the peaked Indraśaila; ||31||
Nīla, Kanakaśṛṅga, the mountain Śataśṛṅga, Puṣpaka, Meghaśaila, Virāja the best of mountains,
and Jārudhi the lord of mountains— these are remembered as the northern [mountains]. ||32||
Learn now of the plateaus, the inner valleys, and the lakes situated in due order among these principal mountains.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Worlds," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Between the lordly mountain Śītānta and Mount Kumuñja, however,
there are valleys resounding with the cries of birds and inhabited by various creatures.
There is a lake there, three hundred yojanas in length and breadth and one hundred yojanas wide, delightful with its sweet and pure waters. ||2||
It was adorned with thousands of great lotuses, fragrant white lilies (puṇḍarīka) of immeasurable size, each possessing a hundred petals.
It was inhabited by great-bodied mahoragas who were difficult to approach,
and its auspicious waters were touched by gods, dānavas, and gandharvas.
That merit is known by the name Śrīsaras; it is radiant both in heaven and here on earth, filled with clear water, and a refuge for all embodied beings.
There, in the midst of that lotus forest, was a single great lotus with ten million petals,
possessing the brilliance of the rising sun.
It is eternally blossomed, ageless, and a vast orb due to its radiance;
it is enriched with beautiful clusters of filaments and resounds with the humming of intoxicated bees. ||7||
In that lotus, the Blessed Śrī herself is ever truly present;
there is no doubt that this lotus is the abode of Lakṣmī in her embodied form. 8.
On the eastern shore of that lake, frequented by perfected beings (siddhas),
there was a great and beautiful grove of bilva trees, always abounding in flowers and fruit.
It was a hundred yojanas wide and three hundred yojanas long,
filled with thousands of great trees whose peaks rose half a krośa high.
It was filled with great trunks covered by thousands of branches,
and with fruits that were like gold, as well as green and pale-white.
The ground was covered without any gaps by fragrant flowers, as large as drums, which were like the taste of nectar, falling and scattering about.
By name it is known as Śrīvaṇa, renowned throughout all the worlds, and frequented by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, and great Nāgas. ||13||
It is constantly crowded with Siddhas who subsist on bilva fruits,
and it is perpetually frequented by various hosts of beings.
In that forest, the blessed goddess Śrī herself is indeed eternally present;
the goddess is stationed there, saluted by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas). 15.
Between Vikaṅka, the lord of mountains, and Maṇiśaila,
it is one hundred yojanas wide and two hundred yojanas long.
The vast grove of campaka trees, frequented by perfected beings and celestial singers, shines as if eternally ablaze, enveloped in the splendor of its blossoms. 17.
That forest shines with a golden hue, filled with great trunks of leafy trees whose peaks rise half a krośa high, their branches and tips in full bloom. (18)
With a circumference of two arms and a length and width of three cubits each,
they resembled powdered realgar and were adorned with pale filaments.
Pervaded by enchanting, fully blossomed flowers rich with fragrance,
the entire forest shines forth, resounding with the humming of intoxicated bees.
That forest was frequented by Dānavas, gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas,
Kinnaras, Apsarases, and great Nāgas.

There, between two mountains of great blue hue, was the hermitage of the Blessed Kaśyapa, the Lord of Creatures; it was crowded with hosts of Siddhas and Sādhyas and adorned with various sacred scriptures.
On the bank of the great river Sukhā, frequented by perfected beings (siddhas),
there is that delightful palm grove, fifty yojanas in length and thirty yojanas in width, with its tops reaching half a krośa in height. ||23||
It was endowed with great roots, great pith, firm, dense, and auspicious;
it was surrounded by trees shaped like white water-lilies and collyrium, bearing large fruits,
possessed of pure fragrance and flavor, and frequented by perfected beings (siddhas).
The residence of the lordly elephant of Mahendra, the auspicious Airāvata, renowned throughout all the worlds, is said to be there. ||25||
To the north of Mount Veṇumān and Mount Sumedhas,
it is a thousand yojanas in length and a hundred yojanas in width.
It was filled with trees, shrubs, creepers, and clusters of all kinds of climbing plants,
and it was covered with a carpet of dūrvā grass, entirely devoid of any living beings.
Likewise, to the north of Mount Niṣadha and the Deva mountain, there is a city one thousand yojanas in length and one hundred yojanas in width. ||28||
The entire ground was a single solid rock, devoid of trees or creepers,
and it was submerged on all sides by water reaching up to the ankles.
O best of Brahmins, these various inner valleys (antaradroṇīs) situated to the east of Meru have thus been described in their proper order and according to their true nature.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Worlds," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Hereafter, I shall describe those forest valleys situated in the southern direction that are frequented by the Siddhas; hear of them in their proper order.
Between Mount Śiśira, the lord of mountains, and Mount Pataṅga,
it was endowed with the beauty of smooth ground and trees embraced by creepers.
It was adorned with trees whose lofty peaks were formed by wide-spreading branches,
a delightful grove of udumbara trees frequented by flocks of birds.
That forest shines, ablaze with fruits resembling coral, filled with honey, delightful, and like unto great jars. ||4||
Siddhas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, as well as uragas and vidyādharas, rejoice and constantly subsist upon that [merit]. ||5||
There, the rivers have clear, sweet, and abundant waters,
and there are lakes on all sides with water as delicious as ambrosia.
There was the hermitage of the blessed Prajāpati Kardama,
delightful and crowded with hosts of gods, with variegated groves on all sides;
that forest was a hundred yojanas in circumference, circular in shape.
Between Mount Tāmraparṇa and Pataṅga, however,
there was a region extending one hundred yojanas in width and two hundred yojanas in length.
It was adorned on all sides with great lotuses, blossoming thousand-petaled white lilies that resembled the rising sun.
Likewise, its waters were graced by fragrant hundred-petaled lotuses crowded with bees,
and by great red and blue lotuses in full bloom.
The lake is of great merit, frequented by gods and dānavas, inhabited by great serpents, and adorned with blue lotuses. ||11||
In its center was a country,
indeed a hundred yojanas long and thirty yojanas wide, adorned with red minerals.
Above it was a most delightful city, with high walls and arched gateways,
crowded with throngs of men and women, and flourishing with an abundance of wealth.
With gables, turrets, and balconies variegated with inlaid jewels,
their floors inlaid with wonderful gems, and their smooth surfaces covered with exquisite rugs.
There, the city of the Vidyādharas shines, radiant and auspicious, with great, lofty, and excellent rows of palaces. 15.
There dwelt the renowned lord of the Vidyādharas, Puloman, who wore variegated garments and garlands, and possessed a splendor equal to that of Mahendra. ||16||
That king of kings was surrounded by many thousands of Vidyādharas, who were radiant, dressed in variegated garments, and possessed splendor equal to the sun.
It is renowned as being situated on the eastern shore of Lake Tāmraparṇa, between Mount Viśākha and Mount Acalendra.
There was a vast and flourishing mango grove, pierced by the discharge of five arrows, possessing beautiful branches, adorned with color, and yielding fruit in all seasons. (19)
With fruits resembling gold, highly flavorful, and fragrant,
[the trees] were as large as great jars and possessed thick branches on all sides.
Gandharvas, kinnaras, yakṣas, nāgas,
and likewise vidyādharas drink there the very sweet mango juice, which is indeed like nectar.
There, in that great forest, the cries of those high-souled beings were heard— cries of those who, having drunk the juice of mangoes, were joyful, delighted, and well-nourished.
Between Sumūla, Acalendra, and Vasudhāra, there was a level region, rich and filled with fragrances, adorned by birds. ||23||
O Brahmins, there is Bilvasthalī, thirty yojanas wide and fifty yojanas long, where the trees bear pure and abundant fruit.
The ground was made wet by the falling and scattered bilva fruits, which were delicious, resembling coral in color, and as large as great shields.
Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, and numerous Nāgas constantly subsist upon that plateau, always feeding on Bilva fruits. ||26||
Between Vasudhāra and Ratnadhāra,
it was thirty yojanas wide and one hundred yojanas long.
The fragrant forest of Kiṃśuka trees, with its ever-blooming trees and enveloped in the splendor of flowers, shines as if ablaze on all sides. ||28||
By whose divine fragrance the entire circle of forests for a full hundred yojanas is perfumed on all sides. ||29||
That beautiful forest of *kiṃśuka* trees, adorned with bodies of water, was frequented by hosts of perfected beings (*siddhas*), celestial musicians (*cāraṇas*), and nymphs (*apsarases*). (1.38.30)
Therein lies the great, radiant abode of the god Āditya;
month after month, Sūrya Prajāpati enters there.
There, the hosts of Siddhas pay homage to the thousand-rayed one, the best of gods, the creator of time, who is honored by all the worlds.
Within the range of Mount Kailāsa, which has five peaks,
it is thirty-six yojanas in length and extends for a hundred yojanas in width.
Unassailable by inferior beings, white as swans on all sides, difficult for all creatures to cross, hard to reach, and hair-raising. ||34||
Thus, indeed, all these inner valleys (antaradroṇīs) on the south have been described in their proper sequence, frequented by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas). ||35||
O best of the twice-born, listen now as these regions situated within the western sea are described by me according to their true nature. 36.
In the interval between that mountain Suvakṣas and Śikhiśaila,
there is a rocky plateau extending for a hundred yojanas in every direction, level as a single surface.
It is eternally heated, most terrible, difficult to touch, and hair-raising; it is inaccessible to all beings and exceedingly dreadful even for the lords.
In the center of that rocky plateau was a most dreadful abode of fire, a circle thirty yojanas in extent, thick with thousands of flames.
There, the fire-god Vibhāvasu, though without fuel, is always garlanded with flames;
this deity, the consumer of oblations, burns there eternally and perpetually.
That portion of Agni which is ordained for the sake of the deities blazes there eternally as the fire that consumes the world at the end of an aeon. ||41||
Between those two excellent mountains, there is also a beautiful region of the gods;
there is indeed a grove of mātuluṅga trees there, ten yojanas in extent.
That great plateau was adorned on all sides with ripe fruits that possessed the luster of gold, were sweet in taste, and had the appearance of honeyed delicacies. 43.
Therein was the great and meritorious hermitage, frequented by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas),
belonging to Bṛhaspati, which was joyful and endowed with all desirable qualities.
In the same way, between the two excellent mountains Kumuda and Añjana,
there is a valley of kesara trees extending for many yojanas.
With a circumference of two cubits each and an extent of three cubits in length and breadth,
they were the color of moonbeams, fully blossomed, and resounded with the humming of intoxicated bees.
That forest shines, variegated with blossoms that bloom in all seasons—exquisite in scent and captivating to the mind—smeared with honey, clarified butter, and pollen. (47)
Therein is the great, radiant temple of Viṣṇu, the preceptor of the gods, which illuminates the three worlds and is honored by all the worlds. (48)
Between those two excellent mountains, Kṛṣṇa and Pāṇḍura,
there was a region thirty yojanas wide and ninety yojanas long.
A region that is smooth, consisting of a single stone surface, devoid of trees and creepers, easy for the feet to traverse, and free from depressions and elevations. (1.38.50)
In the middle of that lake, however, was a beautiful land-lotus grove,
adorned with thousands of blossoming petals as large as parasols.
With white lotuses, great lotuses, beautiful and fragrant ones, with hundred-petaled blossoms, and with blooming blue-lotuses of dark leaves. ||52||
With the sounds of intoxicated honey-bees and bumblebees, and with the cries of the Kinnaras whose throats were soft and warbling; ||53||
The vast terrestrial lotus-pond was enriched with clusters of singing lotuses,
frequented by yakṣas and gandharvas, and served by siddhas and cāraṇas.
And in the center of that lotus-pond was a banyan tree with a circular canopy five yojanas in extent,
possessing a massive trunk and adorned by many climbing plants.
There, the glorious Candraprabha, whose face resembles the full moon, is a thousand-faced deity clad in blue garments, the slayer of the enemies of the gods. (56)
In the region of Mālyadhara, the illustrious Aparājita is worshipped by yakṣas,
gandharvas, and hosts of vidyādharas.
In that sacred abode, Hari himself, who is without beginning or end,
is worshipped in person by Siddhas and Cāraṇas with various offerings of lotuses.
It was renowned in all the worlds by the name Tadanantasada,
and it was adorned with garlands hanging down like rows of lotuses.
Likewise, within the interior of Sahasraśikharakumuda,
there was a lake fifty yojanas in length and thirty yojanas in width,
its peaks rising as high as a discharged arrow, frequented by various birds.
It was surrounded on all sides by great trees that possessed intense fragrances and exquisite flavors, bore fruits resembling the bodies of elephants, and exuded honey.
There, the highly meritorious hermitage of Śukra, the performer of holy deeds, was renowned and frequented by hosts of celestial rishis; it was radiant and famous.
Between Mount Śaṅkukūṭa and Vṛṣabha lies the delightful Parūṣaka plateau, extending for many yojanas.
The earth becomes saturated with auspicious, highly flavorful, and fragrant fruits, the size of bilva fruits, which have become rough as they fall from their stalks.
Kinnaras, uragas, and virtuous ones subsist upon that land;
there, the cāraṇas are intoxicated by the juice of the parūṣaka fruit and are full of pride.
Between Mount Kapiñjala and Mount Nāgaśaila,
it is two hundred yojanas in length and one hundred yojanas in width.
For that land was enchanting, adorned with various forests, endowed with diverse flowers and fruits, and frequented by kinnaras and uragas. ||67||
Delightful groves of grapes, as well as groves of *nāga* trees,
clusters of date-palm forests, and groves of blue *aśoka* trees.
And there were forests of sweet pomegranates and walnut trees, as well as groves of linseed, sesame, and plantains. (69)
And there were groves of sweet jujube trees on all sides,
beautified by rivers filled with delicious, cool water.
Likewise, between Mount Puṣpaka and Mahāmegha,
that land is sixty yojanas wide and one hundred yojanas long.
It was level like the palm of a hand, hard, pale, and dense;
it was entirely devoid of trees, shrubs, creepers, thickets, and even grass.
Constantly devoid of various beings and without any refuge,
that place called Kānanasthalī is dreadful and hair-raising.
Likewise, there were great lakes and great trees,
as well as all the vast forests, all of which bore delightful names in every respect.
There is that lake and forest of Prajāpati, and there is no counting the number of small ponds found therein. ||75||
The plateaus, valleys, lakes, and forests are renowned for their dimensions of ten, twelve, seven, eight, twenty, and thirty yojanas.
There are some regions that are most terrible, dark, and mountain-wombed;
untouched by the networks of sunbeams, they are perpetually cold and difficult to approach.
For thus, O best of the twice-born, there are hundreds and thousands of lakes heated by fire, situated within the interior of mountain clefts. (78)
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Worlds," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Henceforth, I shall describe upon which mountain peaks the various excellent abodes of the gods are situated.
Therein lies that great mountain Śītānta, of manifold extent, variegated with hundreds of diverse mineral veins, and the source of many mines of jewels. ||2||
With hips that were the support for flowers, he was the abode of many virtuous qualities;
he was adorned with golden pillars variegated with highly precious jewels.
With slopes resounding with the humming of bees, adorned with sprouts variegated by gold, and strewn with flowers while echoing with the cries of intoxicated bees; ||4||
It was adorned with peaks that hung down like creepers, variegated and painted, honored with hundreds of minerals,
and embellished with jewel-studded surfaces rich in flowers.
It was endowed with many springs of pure and sweet water, and adorned with numerous groves strewn with flowers. ||6||
It was adorned on all sides by streams carrying flowers and moon-like foam,
and by caves frequented by kinnaras.
It was adorned with many caves inhabited by yakṣas and gandharvas, which were beautiful, pleasant to dwell in, and variegated yet dense with thickets. ||8||
It was adorned with trees laden with various flowers and fruits, providing pleasant shelter and excellent water, and crowded with throngs of diverse beings;
it was filled with many caves and mountain clefts that served as dwellings.
It was the pleasure grove of Mahendra, endowed with all objects of desire and sensory qualities.
There, that great Pārijāta grove of the king of the gods is celebrated throughout the three worlds according to the conclusions of the Vedas.
With flowers resembling the rising sun, possessing great fragrance and captivating the mind,
that best of mountains shines as if ablaze on all sides.
A wind carrying the fragrance of Pārijātaka flowers issued forth from Mahendra’s grove and blew over that entire hundred yojanas.
With lotuses of vaidūrya and sapphire, with golden stalks and diamond filaments,
endowed with every fragrance and power, and resonant with the humming of intoxicated bees.
There, the ponds were adorned with charming hundred-petaled lotuses, both in full bloom and blossoming, as well as with great-leaved lotuses accompanied by their mud.
Thousands of schools of fish, adorned with golden jewels, shone within the water, their eyes constantly darting about. 16.
With tortoises of various forms, adorned with gold and jewels, moving about in the waters, it shines wonderfully on all sides. ||17||
And with birds of various colors, whose feathers were made of diverse jewels, and with many twice-born birds that had golden flowers and beaks of gems. ||18||
With those sweet-voiced, ever-intoxicated birds swooping down from all sides,
that delightful forest of the wise thousand-eyed Indra shone with splendor.
With the humming of intoxicated bees and the warbling of birds,
that great pleasure grove was perpetually filled with joy.
And with mountains having golden flanks, adorned with jewels and pearls, possessing clusters of jeweled peaks, falling down on all sides; ||21||
It was crowded with monkeys of variegated limbs whose body hair was like various jewels,
and with other creatures of diverse colors and kinds.
And there, the young creepers and trees,
shaken by the gentle breeze, release a rain of flowers, including those of the pārijātaka tree.
O twice-born ones, the auspicious pleasure grounds there in Śakra’s grove are provided with beds, seats, and porticos strewn with jewels;
the sun there is always temperate, being neither cold nor hot.

There blows a wind, born of the spring months of Madhu and Mādhava, which constantly produces intoxication; it is perfumed with various flowers, eternally delighting through the pleasure of contact, and destroying fatigue and exhaustion. (25)
In that beautiful Indra-vana dwell the gods, dānavas, and pannagas; as well as yakṣas, rākṣasas, guhyakas, and gandharvas of immeasurable power. ||26||
The Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and Kinnaras were filled with joy, as were the throngs of Apsarases, who were constantly devoted to play. ||27||
On the eastern side of that king of mountains is the great and worthy Mount Kumuda,
the king of peaks, with its many waterfalls and caves.
Upon its peaks, variegated with minerals, there are eight vast and exalted cities belonging to the high-souled Dānavas.
And on Mount Vajraka, with its many peaks and caverns,
there were exalted abodes of Rākṣasas, teeming with men and women.
Those terrible Rākṣasas named Nīlakas, who can assume any form at will and possess great strength and prowess, always take delight there.
On Mahānīla, the lord of mountains, there are fifteen cities belonging to the renowned,
high-souled Kinnaras who have the faces of horses.
The mighty-armed Devasena, as well as Indra and the other gods, and fifteen proud kings of the Kinnaras were there. ||33||
With its golden slopes, that lord of mountains was adorned with cities consisting of entrances to caves, which were mostly filled with various kinds of foliage.
Indeed, there were hundreds of great serpents there, subservient to Suvarṇa, whose venom was in their very gaze, who were as fierce as fire in their wrath, and difficult to approach. ||35||
Even on the great mountain Sunāga, there were thousands of abodes for the Daityas,
crowded with mansions and palaces, and featuring lofty walls and gateways.
On the great mountain Veṇumān, there are three cities of the Vidyādharas,
thirty yojanas in width and fifty yojanas in length.
Ulūka, Romaśa, and the powerful Mahānetra—these excellent Vidyādharas there possessed prowess equal to that of Śakra. ||38||
On a peak of the Vaikaṅka mountain, within mountain caves and waterfalls,
on a beautiful and lofty summit variegated with gems and minerals.
There dwells forever the son of Garuḍa, the invincible enemy of serpents,
the fierce and powerful one named Sugrīva, who possesses the speed of a great wind.
Indeed, the entire mountain, along with its peaks, was covered by birds, the enemies of serpents, who were of great size, possessed of heroic strides, and endowed with great strength and prowess.
The Lord, the Master of Beings, Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, the bull-bannered master of yogins, is eternally delighted in the Karañja tree. ||42||
All the mountain peaks were strewn on every side by bhūtas and invincible pramathas wearing various disguises at Karañja.
