O Vasudhare, they say that there are eight sacred shrines for the worship of the high-souled ones, who possess immeasurable splendor and are masters of the earth and wealth.
On that excellent mountain, Ratnadhātu, there are seven meritorious hermitages belonging to high-souled sages, which are inhabited by perfected beings (siddhas). ||45||
On that best of mountains is the abode of Mahāprajāpati, the golden-peaked mountain, which is saluted by all beings and belongs to the four-faced god. ||46||
On Gajaśaila, the Rudras are eternally delighted, surrounded by various hosts of beings, and honored by all creatures. ||47||
O wise one, on this lord of mountains, which is richly adorned with various minerals, resembles a cloud, and is graced by many caves, valleys, peaks, and groves; (48)
There, the arrangements of the abodes of the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Rudras of immeasurable luster, as well as those of the Aśvins, are truly delightful.
On that best of mountains, abodes were established by the Siddhas for the gods;
there, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras are constantly devoted to worship.
On Hemakakṣa, the best of mountains, there was a prosperous city of the Gandharvas, resembling eighty cities of the gods, with great walls and gateways. (51)
For there are indeed Gandharvas known as the Apattanās, who are skilled in battle;
their lord is the divine Kapiñjala, the king of kings. (52)
In Anala dwell the rākṣasas, and on Pañcakūṭa also reside the dānavas—
powerful enemies of the gods, possessed of great strength and prowess.
In Śataśṛṅga is the city of the Yakṣas of immeasurable splendor, numbering one hundred;
and in Tāmrābha is the preeminent city of Takṣaka, the son of Kadrū.
On Viśākhā, the best of mountains, auspicious with its many peaks and caves,
there is the great abode of Guha, who dwells constantly within the mountain caverns.
On the great mountain Śvetodara, adorned with magnificent palaces,
is the city of the high-souled Sunābha, the son of Garuḍa.
On that excellent mountain Piśācaka, there was a great palace of Kubera, adorned with mansions and towers,
frequented by Yakṣas and Gandharvas.
On Harikūṭa dwells the god Hari, who is saluted by all beings;
by his power, this great mountain shines forth as Mahānābha.
In Kumuda dwell the Kinnaras; in Añjana, the Mahoragas;
and in Kṛṣṇa, the Gandharva cities, which possess magnificent palaces.
There, upon a beautiful white peak with great walls and gateways,
stood a city of the Vidyādharas, adorned with rows of magnificent palaces.
On the mountain with a thousand peaks, there were a thousand flourishing cities belonging to the Daityas of fierce deeds, who wore golden garlands.
In his crown dwell many excellent mountains that serve as abodes for serpents;
indeed, in the Puṣpaka chariot, hosts of sages are always filled with joy.
On the excellent mountain Supakṣa, there are four shrines belonging to Vaivasvata, Soma, Vāyu, and the Lord of the Nāgas.
In those places, he is always desired and worshipped by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Nāgas, the highest Vidyādharas, and Siddhas.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Worlds," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Learn now of Devakūṭa on the auspicious boundary mountain;
it is upon the broad summit of that foremost of mountains.
Extending for a hundred yojanas in every direction, it was adorned with great palaces;
it was the birthplace of the wise Vainateya, the son of Suparṇa.
It was filled with many flocks of great birds of the Garuḍa species, swift in their prowess,
endowed with full vigor, tamers of serpents, and enemies of snakes.
First was the palace of that great-souled king of birds,
who dwells on Śālmali Island and can withstand the entry of mighty winds.
And on the peaks of that very mountain of beautiful summits, which possess great supernatural power, and on its seven wonderful and splendid southern ridges— 5.
Resembling twilight clouds, they have risen up with golden walls and gateways;
fashioned by the gods, they are adorned with rows of great palaces.
Thirty yojanas wide and forty long,
there were seven cities of the Gandharvas, teeming with men and women.
The Gandharvas named Āgneyas possess great strength and prowess;
they are radiant followers of Kubera, and their excellent dwellings are there. ||8||
And upon the northern peaks of that great mountain of the world, there was a place adorned with palaces and mansions, and beautified by gardens and groves. ||9||
The city was filled with venomous serpents and possessed great ramparts and gateways;
the interior of the forest was made joyful by the sounds of hundreds of musical instruments.

Learn now of the city of the Saiṃhikeyas, those enemies of the gods, which is thirty yojanas in circumference, difficult for foes to withstand, and exalted on Mount Devakūṭa, where Siddhas and celestial rishis frequent. ||11||
O tiger among the twice-born, on the auspicious boundary mountain in the second [region],
it is surrounded by rows of great palaces of various colors.
It was adorned with many ornaments variegated with gold and jewels;
it possessed broad streets, was invincible, and was eternally joyful and auspicious.
It was crowded with throngs of men and women, possessed of lofty walls and gateways,
sixty yojanas in width and a hundred yojanas in length.

The city of the Kālakeya Asuras was difficult to approach, situated on the delightful slopes of Devakūṭa, and exceedingly hard to conquer; it resembled a mass of great clouds and was renowned by the name Sunāsa. ||15||
On its very southern peak,
twenty yojanas in width and sixty-two yojanas in length, there was a golden wall and gateway.
The great city of the delighted Rākṣasas, the Autkaṭas, was a dwelling place for those who were joyful, well-nourished, arrogant, and able to assume any form at will. ||17||
On the middle peak of the mountain Devakūṭa,
which is variegated with smooth and auspicious stones of gold and jewels, and crowded with many hundreds of thousands of branches for climbing; (18)
It was delightful, with glossy leaves and massive roots, supported by many trunks, providing dense shade, and extending for a circle of ten yojanas. ||19||
There, the famous abode of the great-souled Tryambaka Mahādeva, known as Bhūtavaṭa— a dwelling place for various hosts of spirits—
was a radiant sanctuary renowned throughout all the worlds.
With faces like those of boars, elephants, lions, bears, and tigers; with faces like those of vultures and owls; and with great faces like those of rams, camels, and goats. ||21||
With formidable, thick, and long-haired Kadamba trees, possessing various colors and forms and existing in various configurations; ||22||
It was constantly filled with many blazing beings of fierce countenances and terrible prowess,
as well as with great attendants.
There, the spirits constantly offer worship to the Lord of Beings with jharjharas,
conchs, kettledrums, bherīs, ḍiṇḍimas, and gomukhas.
There, the lords of the Gaṇas, devoted to worship, are ever delighted by hundreds of resounding, rhythmic, and unrestrained songs; those Pramathas of the Enemy of Tripura are always intent on play.
In that place, Mahādeva— Śiva himself, the source of auspiciousness for the world— is personally worshipped by Siddhas, celestial rishis, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and the lords of the Nāgas.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the World," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Kailāsa, with its solitary and beautiful peaks, covered in foliage and possessing the luster of a conch shell,
is the abode of those devoted to the gods and of those whose souls are purified by good deeds.
On its delightful central peak, which resembles a kunda flower,
it is one hundred yojanas in length and likewise fifty yojanas in width.
Adorned with many rows of great palaces, variegated with gold and jewels, it was embellished and extended over a vast area.
That city of the high-souled god Kubera, the lord of wealth,
was unassailable, endowed with prosperity, and filled with joy.
In its center was a beautiful assembly hall, adorned with various kinds of gold and jewels;
it was renowned by the name Vipula, featuring massive pillars and archways.
There, that great celestial chariot named Puṣpaka— adorned with various jewels, beautiful, and endowed with all desirable qualities— [was situated].
The vehicle of the high-souled Kubera, the king of the Yakṣas, is swift as thought, moving at will, and adorned with a golden net.
There dwelt the god Ekapiṅgala himself, the lord of Yakṣas, who was a friend of Mahādeva and was honored by all beings. ||8||
There, that high-souled Kubera, the best of gods, dwelt together with hosts of Apsarases, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas.
Therein are Pāṇḍu and Mahāpāṇḍu, as well as Makara and Kacchapa; Kumuda, Śaṅkha, and Nīla, and Nandana, the best of treasures.
These eight divine, inexhaustible great treasures of the high-souled Lord of Wealth stand in his assembly hall, filled with jewels.
Likewise, there are the dwellings of Indra, Agni, Yama, and other gods, along with hosts of Apsarases;
and there is Kailāsa, the abode of those [gods], where the Lord, the Master of Yakṣas, resides.
Having first performed service for the high-souled lord of the Yakṣas,
those who are appointed as his attendants go after him.
There, the most delightful Mandākinī flows, with its vast waters,
featuring stairs made of gold and jewels, and abounding with various profuse flowers.
With lotuses made of gold, endowed with the qualities of fragrance and touch, and with great blue lotuses having petals of lapis lazuli and possessed of scent; ||15||
Likewise, it was adorned with clusters of white water-lilies and great lotuses,
and graced by the women of the yakṣas and gandharvas, as well as by the apsarases.
The delightful Mandākinī pool likewise has its waters touched by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas.
Likewise, the Alakanandā and the Nandā, the best of rivers—
these rivers possess these very same qualities and are frequented by divine sages.
On the eastern peak of that very king of mountains,
there are regions renowned as being a thousand yojanas in length and thirty yojanas in width.
Ten cities of the Gandharvas, endowed with supreme prosperity,
were adorned with many rows of great palaces.
Subāhu, Harikeśa, and others, Citrasena, Jarā, and others—these ten Gandharva kings possess the prowess of blazing fire. ||21||
On its very western peak, which possesses a radiance like that of the kunda flower or the moon,
variegated with hundreds of diverse minerals and frequented by perfected beings and celestial rishis.
Each individual yakṣa palace is eighty yojanas in length and forty in width, adorned with garlands of great mansions. ||23||
Listen to me regarding the thirty additional great abodes of yakṣas located there, which are endowed on all sides with joy and supreme splendor. ||24||
Mahāmāli, Sunetra, and others, as well as Maṇivara and the rest—thirty such exalted kings of the yakṣas were always present there. (25)
Thus have these yakṣas been described, whose splendor is equal to that of wind and fire,
and over whom the illustrious and powerful lord Vaiśravaṇa is the sovereign.
On his very right side, on the Himavat, the best of mountains, amidst groves, waterfalls, caves, and many peaks and mountain valleys; (27)
From one ocean to another, extending from east to west between the two mountains,
hundreds of cities of the Kinnaras are situated here and there.
Within the valleys of the king of mountains, which possessed many peaks and ridges,
there were people who were joyful and contented, crowded with men and women.
There were Druma, Sugrīva, Sainya, and others led by Bhagadatta;
among them were a hundred kings, radiant and powerful.
Therein is the marriage of Rudra with Mahādevī Umā,
and where that goddess of excellent form performed her ascetic penance.
And where Rudra, in the form of a Kirāta, sported;
and where the two of them surveyed Jambūdvīpa. ||32||
There, those pleasure grounds of Rudra are filled with joy and inhabited by various hosts of beings, endowed with variegated flowers and fruits.
There, joyful, slender-waisted, and beautiful Kinnarīs with lovely eyes, dwelling in mountain caves, sported among the kunda flowers.
The large-eyed Yakṣas, as well as other hosts of Apsarases, and Gandharvas endowed with graceful limbs, were filled with joy here and there. ||35||
In that very place is the one named Umāvana, renowned throughout all the worlds,
where Śaṅkara assumed a form that was half-woman and half-man.
Likewise, there is the place called Śaravaṇa, where the six-faced one was born,
and where he exerted his prowess against the Krauñca mountain forest.
It was adorned with banners and flags, garlanded with networks of tinkling bells, where the lion-chariot of the wise Kārttikeya was stationed. ||38||
On the slope of Mount Krauñca, amidst groves of variegated flowers,
Skanda, the crusher of the enemies of the gods, released his spear.
There Guha, the enemy of the Daityas, possessing the splendor of twelve suns, was consecrated to the office of general by the foremost of gods, including Indra and Upendra.
O twice-born ones, these and other places and shrines belonging to Kumāra, strewn with hosts of spirits, are located here and there.
Likewise, on the auspicious ridge of the Himalayas, crowded with various hosts of beings, was the pleasure-garden named Pāṇḍuśilā belonging to the slayer of Krauñca. ||42||
On its beautiful eastern bank is declared to be the abode of the Siddhas, renowned by the wise by the name of Kalāpagrāma. ||43||
Of Mṛkaṇḍu, Vasiṣṭha, Bharata, and Nala;
of the brahmin-sage Viśvāmitra, and likewise of Uddālaka.
And there were hundreds and thousands of hermitages on the Himalayas belonging to other sages of fierce austerities who had cultivated their souls.
It was the abode of many hosts of perfected ones (siddhas), adorned with sacred sites and shrines, frequented by yakṣas and gandharvas, and inhabited by various tribes of mlecchas. ||46||
Filled with various mines of jewels, frequented by various beings, and the source of thousands of diverse rivers—that excellent mountain. ||47||
O twice-born ones, listen as the specific characteristics of Niṣadha, the western lord of mountains, are being described in their entirety according to their true nature. 48.
On the extensive middle peak, adorned with gold and jewels,
stands the radiant abode of Viṣṇu, frequented by hosts of perfected sages,
crowded with Yakṣas and Apsarases, and served by throngs of Gandharvas.
There, the eternal Mahādeva himself, Hari, the creator of the worlds, wearing yellow garments and bestowing boons, is served by the perfected ones (siddhas). 1.41.50.
On that very peak, adorned with various minerals,
on the slope of Mount Niṣadha where the surface of the rocks was smooth and beautiful— 51.
It had side-walks of gold and refined gold, with archways of molten gold,
crowded with hundreds of various gables, pinnacles, and balconies.
It was an incomparable palace-tower adorned with refined gold,
constructed with many palace-towers, joyful, and exceedingly vast.
Adorned with garlands of gardens and thirty yojanas in length, that city of the Rākṣasas was difficult for enemies to withstand; it was filled with joyful demons who resembled venomous serpents. (54)
On its very southern side, in a cave-dwelling within the belly of the mountain that is difficult to access, there is a city that serves as the abode for many hosts of Daityas.
Likewise, on the western peak, the mountain Pārijāta,
there are prosperous cities belonging to the portions of the gods and the Dānavas.
There, on the great slope of that mountain, is the place named Somaśilā,
where the Moon always descends during each of the lunar festivals.
Here, the ṛṣis, kinnaras, and gandharvas worship the illustrious and blameless lord Tārāpati, that very god who dispels darkness. 58.
And on that very northern peak is what is known as Brahmapārśva;
there stands the celebrated abode of Brahmā, the Lord of the Gods, in heaven. (59)
There, the perfected ones— yakṣas, gandharvas, and dānavas— worship the self-existent Great Soul with sacrifices, offerings, and prostrations.
In that very place, the abode of Fire is renowned throughout all the worlds;
there, the embodied Fire is worshipped by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Likewise, on the northern, delightful, and excellent mountain with three peaks,
frequented by sages and perfected beings and a dwelling place for various hosts of spirits,
there is that city renowned throughout the three worlds as Hemacitra.
O best of the twice-born, there are three abodes for the three foremost deities:
the abode of Nārāyaṇa is on the eastern peak,
that of Brahmā is in the middle, and that of Śaṅkara is on the western peak.
The immensely powerful gods of gods, while performing sacrifices, are worshipped by the Daityas, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas.
Likewise, there are delightful cities here and there in various regions,
belonging to the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Nāgas, upon the triple-peaked, excellent mountain.
And likewise, in the northern region, on Mount Deva, which possesses many peaks and is frequented by perfected beings and holy men, there is Cārudhā. ||66||
Of thousands of yakṣas, kiṃnaras, and gandharvas,
and of nāgas, rākṣasas, and daityas of great strength.
At its central peak, frequented by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas), delightful, traversed by celestial rishis, and adorned with jewels and minerals— (68)
It was adorned with groves of blooming red and blue lotuses, as well as thickets of fragrant saugandhika flowers,
and clusters of full-blown white water-lilies.
Resounding with the cries of flocks of birds, frequented by various creatures,
filled with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and visited by intoxicated bees.
It was crowded with multitudes of various beings, graced by birds,
filled with beautiful bathing-ghats, and measured thirty yojanas in circumference.
There is a lake of great merit named Ānandajala, whose waters have been touched by the Siddhas and are free from all defects of water. ||72||
Therein dwells the lord of the Nāgas, Caṇḍa, by name Caṇḍa, who is difficult to approach;
he has a hundred heads, is highly fortunate, and is marked with the sign of Viṣṇu’s discus.
In this manner, these eight wonderful divine mountains are to be known. (73)
With meritorious cities and abodes, with lakes that produce merit,
and with many mountains of gold as well as mountains of silver.
And with many mountain peaks of jewels shining with various gems,
as well as numerous mountains of yellow orpiment, and likewise of vermilion and gold.
With pure masses of realgar that were radiant and glowing with a reddish luster, and with many mountain-like clusters of jewels variegated by various minerals; ||76||
The entire earth was filled with mountains of manifold extent,
along with numerous rivers, caves, and peaks of variegated ridges.
Thus, by the immovable ones, by the disciplined Daityas, Rākṣasas, and virtuous beings,
and by the various Kinnaras, Uragas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas— (78)
Frequented by Gandharvas and Apsarases,
the mountains, vast in their many expanses and shaped like saffron flowers, were crowded with those who have performed meritorious deeds.
The mountain range of Meru is known as the world of the Siddhas;
it is variegated, endowed with various dwellings, and is the domain of those whose souls are purified by meritorious deeds.
The images of those who have accomplished deeds that are not excessively fierce are considered middling;
for that is known as heaven—this is the sequence proclaimed.
This earth is proclaimed to possess the four great continents.
For they possess various colors and sizes, as well as various colors and strengths. ||82||
With various kinds of foods and drinks, diverse garments and ornaments,
and many different types of livestock, along with various wonderful inhabited dwellings.
The four great continents, renowned for their various colors and other qualities,
are Bhadrāśva, Bharata, Ketumāla in the west,
and the Northern Kurus, which are the refuge for those who have performed meritorious deeds. (84)
O twice-born ones, this entire earth, consisting of the four great continents and crowded with various islands, has been described by me as being shaped like a lotus. 85.
Thus, this entire earth, vast in extent and including the intermediate islands, the mountains, forests, and groves, is designated as "Pṛthivī. (86)
The world including the abode of Brahmā, along with gods, asuras, and humans—that which is known as the triple world (triloka) and wherein beings conduct their affairs—[is all contained therein]. 87.
That which is celebrated as the world is heated by the moon and the sun;
it is endowed with fragrance, color, and taste, and possessed of the qualities of sound and touch. ||88||
That lotus of the world is designated as "Pajha" by means of the Śrutis;
this sequence is well-established in all the Purāṇas. ||89||
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Worlds," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
From the lakes have issued forth the divine rivers of meritorious waters;
hear now, in due order, those rivers of mighty currents. ||1||
That which is called Soma, belonging to the ocean of space, is the support of all beings and the source of nectar for the gods. ||2||
Therefore, that river of abundant merit, flowing through the sky with its pure waters,
has proceeded along the seventh path of the wind.
Returning toward the light and attended by hosts of luminaries, she extended through the sky as far as thousands of stars and comets. ||4||
For she, whose waters were agitated, was sported with in the inner depths by the lordly elephant Māhendra as he traveled along the path of the sky.
The auspicious river, possessing waters of great merit, had its waters touched by Siddhas as they departed for the sky in numerous throngs of celestial chariots.
Driven by the wind and moving through manifold enjoyments,
she revolves day after day just as the sun does.
Extending eighty-four yojanas all around,
she proceeded with great speed, circumambulating Mount Meru to the right.
Dividing by means of those waters, the fiery wind, and the air,
it then fell upon all four peaks of Mount Meru.
Turning back from the lofty slopes of the peaks of Mount Meru,
its waters were scattered forth as they flowed in four directions.
O illustrious one, sixty thousand yojanas of unsupported space fell down on all four sides of that Mount Meru.
That auspicious and holy great river fell indeed upon the four beautiful and great foothills on all sides, specifically to the east of Mount Mandara.
To the east was the abode of the gods and all the hosts of Siddhas, featuring golden and variegated ridges and many waterfalls and caves. (13)
Flooded Mount Mandara, with its lordly peaks and beautiful caves,
by means of her many crystal-clear waters that subdued the heat of the embankments.
Thus, flooding the beautiful Caitraratha grove and keeping it to her right,
the celestial river entered Lake Aruṇoda.
Then, at the end of the cold season, the Sugāminī river, having turned back from the Aruṇodā, fell upon a mountain abounding in lovely waterfalls and inhabited by hosts of Siddhas.
The great and highly meritorious river named Sītā is the foremost among rivers;
though obstructed by groves of trees, it flows through many expanses.
Falling from the peak of Śītānta onto the excellent mountain Sukuñja,
the highly fortunate lady descended from there as well with great grace.
Therefore, flowing from Mount Mālyavat, that excellent river reached Vaikaṅka;
from Vaikaṅka she reached Maṇiparvata,
and from Maṇiparvata she reached the great mountain Ṛṣabha, which possesses many caves.
Thus splitting thousands of mountains,
the great river then fell into the belly of a massive mountain frequented by the Siddhas.
From that mountain Mahāśaila as well, the river Devakūṭā, reaching the ocean within its belly, gradually flowed across the earth. ||21||
Thus he [traversed] thousands of plateaus, hundreds of kings of mountains,
various forests, and diverse lakes.
Flowing forth with its waves swelling in the wide expanse,
that highly blessed great river has set out, followed by thousands of streams.
The excellent river, flooding the great island of Bhadrāśva, entered the ocean in the east;
such is the great river in that eastern island.
On the southern side of Gandhamādana, the lord of mountains,
there is also a cascade where the waters are splashed in many ways by various colorful waterfalls.
Flooded with its waters, that illustrious river proceeded clockwise, passing by the Gandhamādana forest, the Nandana grove, and the Devanandana garden.
For by the name Alakanandā, she is renowned throughout all the worlds;
she enters the northern lake, Mānasa, the Lake of the Gods.
From Mānasa she went to the beautiful Mount Triśikhara;
from the mountain peak Trikūṭa she went to the peak of Kaliṅga. ||28||
Falling from the peak of Kalinga, she descended upon Rucaka;
from Rucaka she reached Niṣadha, and from Niṣadha she fell upon the copper-hued [mountain].
Falling from the copper-colored peak, she went to Mount Śvetodara;
from there, she reached the king of mountains, Sumūla, and the mountain Vasudhāra.
From there she went to Hemakūṭa, and from there she went to Devaśṛṅga;
from there she went to Mahāśaila, and from there also to Piśācaka.
From the excellent mountain Piśācaka, she went again to Pañcakūṭa;
and from Pañcakūṭa, she reached Kailāsa, the mountain-abode of the gods.
Having wandered through his many caves and mountain ridges,
that supreme river fell from Himavat, the best of mountains.
Thus that great river, swiftly flowing, split apart thousands of mountains and inundated hundreds of various dry lands.
Causing thousands of forests and hundreds of caves to flow with water, the highly fortunate river proceeded toward the southern ocean.
Delightful, extending for a yojana, and sheltered within the mountain recesses,
it was sustained by Śaṅkara, the high-souled God of gods.

O tiger among the twice-born, this great river, whose waters are doubly purifying, is holy even for the most terrible sins due to the touch of the lap of the wise Mahādeva, Śaṅkara; she is renowned throughout all the worlds. (37)
Flowing out from all sides along the mountains through many mouths,
there are thousands of rivers known by various other names.
From that Himavat mountain, the Gaṅgā, that great river, has flowed forth;
thus she is known by the name Gaṅgā, radiant from the beginning and frequented by the Siddhas.
Blessed are those most excellent lands where the great river Gaṅgā flows— her glorious waters cherished by Rudra, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and the Ādityas.
I shall describe Mahāpāda, which lies indeed to the west of Meru;
it is auspicious, possessing the forms of various jewels, and is frequented by those who perform meritorious deeds.
Vast is the king of mountains, with caverns as its expansive belly,
its interior adorned by ridges, groves, and pure slopes.
Moreover, this river of Tryambaka, whose waters are frequented by the gods, has been whirled around like a creeper, its expanse now diminished by the force of the wind. (43)
Falling from the slopes of Meru’s peak, its waters tasted by those who struck it, its flow spreading wide, it resembled a pure white garment. ||44||
On its peak flows the celestial river, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas; having circled it clockwise, that river then falls downward.
The highly fortunate river, filled with various flowers, fruits, and water, flows along, flooding Devabhrāja, Mahābhrāja, Savaibhrāja, and Mahāvana.
Performing circumambulations, adorned by various forests,
she entered the western lake, Sitoda, which possessed pure water.
Emerging from the Sitodā, it flows to Mount Supakṣa;
from Supakṣa, it proceeds to Puṇyodā, where it is frequented by celestial sages.
From there, flowing along the slopes of the Supakṣakūṭa ridge with its waters firmly restrained, the highly blessed river fell toward the delightful Śikhī mountain. 49.
From Śikhin he went to Mount Kaṅka; from Kaṅka to the Vaiḍūrya mountain;
from the Vaiḍūrya to Mount Kapila; and from there to Gandhamādana.
From that mountain Girivara they reached the excellent mountain Piñjara;
from Piñjara they went to Sarasa, and from there to Mount Kumuda.
Having passed through Madhumanta and Jana, and the mountain Mukuṭa,
she went from the peak of Mount Mukuṭa to the great mountain Kṛṣṇa.
From Kṛṣṇa she fell again upon the great white mountain frequented by mighty serpents;
from Śveta, she fell upon the lord of mountains with a thousand peaks. ||53||
With its waters nourished by many flowing streams,
that auspicious great river, thus wearing away thousands of mountains,
fell with swift motion upon the great mountain Pārijāta.
With its many waterfalls and rivers, it shines upon the mountain peaks and caves;
within its many hollows flows a surging river with wandering waters. (55)
Its flow obstructed in many places by boulders,
its waters becoming scarce, it reached the surface of the earth.
Flooding the great continent of Ketumāla, which is filled with various hosts of mlecchas,
the illustrious river proceeded toward the western ocean.
On the northern mountain Supārśva, whose flanks are variegated with gold, which has wonderful great foothills, and which is frequented by great beings; (58)
Falling from the slope of the peak of Mount Meru, driven by the wind,
her body curved in many coils as she was cast through the expanse of the sky.
In the auspicious sky, sixty thousand yojanas above and without support,
the great river fell like a scattered garland.
Thus, falling from many peaks frequented by celestial sages,
she scatters her waters and has the foam of her waves for her floating flowers.
The highly fortunate river, flooding the forest of the Sun— which contains groves of various jewels—
circumambulates the great forest.
The auspicious lady, whose waters were white, entered that most meritorious lake, frequented by highly fortunate beings, which was exceedingly beautiful.
Indeed, the great river named Bhadrasomā, which is of great breadth,
great speed, great merit, and exceedingly auspicious, has issued forth.
On the slope of Śaṅkhakūṭa, rich with many waterfalls and embankments,
that swift-moving river fell down upon that peak on the mountain side.
Falling from the slope of Śaṅkhakūṭa, she descended upon Vṛṣaparvata;
from Vṛṣaparvata she went to Vatsagiri, and from there she reached Nāgaśaila.
From there, the river reached the Nīla, the best of mountains, a boundary range;
and from the Nīla, she flows through Kapiñjala and Indranīla.
After that, she went to Mahānīla and Hemaśṛṅga;
from Hemaśṛṅga she went to Śveta, and from Śveta she went to Sunaga.
Having flowed from Sunaga, that great river reached Śataśṛṅga;
from the great mountain Śataśṛṅga, she reached Puṣkara, which was adorned with flowers.
From Puṣkara he reached the great mountain Dvirāja, possessed of immense strength;
from there, Varāha-parvata, and then the mountain peak Mayūra.
Moving with great speed, she descended upon the peak of Mount Jārudhi, which was adorned with a single summit and embellished by the interior of its caves.
Thus, splitting thousands of mountains,
the great river reached Triśṛṅga, a boundary mountain thick with peaks.
Falling from the slopes of Mount Triśṛṅga and frequented by those of great fortune,
its waters are driven by the wind as it descends from the ridges of Meru’s peak.
The river of pure water fell upon that excellent mountain, Viruddha;
flooding it, the illustrious stream proceeded toward the western ocean.
On the side of the Suvarṇabhū mountain, and also on the northern mountain Supārśva.
On Mount Meru, at the great white foot, frequented by great beings. ||75||
Falling from the interior of that very mountain's caves, the river—
possessing manifold enjoyments and with its foam-crests appearing like variegated flowers— descended to the earth.
Flooded with joy, that auspicious river, flowing through the northern Kurus,
proceeded through the middle of the great island toward the northern ocean.
Thus those four great rivers, with their pure waters,
having fallen from the slopes of the great mountain, flow forth in the four directions.
Thus, this very earth, which has been described at great length and is strewn with the great mountain Meru, entered [the mouth] from every direction. ||79||
It possessed four great continents, four pleasure groves,
four great wish-fulfilling trees at its gates, and four rivers of excellent speech.
She possesses the four great mountains, she is the refuge of the four serpents, she contains the one hundred and eight great mountains, and likewise the eight excellent peaks. 81.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Worlds," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
On the side of Gandhamādana, however, there is a prosperous ridge above;
it measures thirty-two thousand yojanas from east to west. (1)
Its length is thirty-four thousand [yojanas] in measurement;
there dwell those of auspicious deeds known as the Ketumālas.
There, all the men were dark-complexioned, great beings of immense strength;
and all the women had the luster of lotus petals and were lovely to behold.
There stands a divine great tree, a jackfruit tree (*panasa*) that is the source of the six flavors.
It is the lord, the son of Brahmā, who moves at will with the speed of thought.
By drinking the juice of its fruit, beings indeed live for ten thousand years.
And on the eastern side of Mālyavat is the eastern Gaṇḍikā;
its length and breadth are exactly like those of the western Gaṇḍikā.
There, the Bhadrāśvas are to be known as those whose minds are ever joyful;
there is the auspicious Sāl forest and great trees of the Kālāmra.
There those men were white, great beings of immense strength;
the women had the luster of white water-lilies, beautiful and lovely to behold. ||7||

The women were radiant like the moon, possessed the complexion of the moon, and had faces resembling the full moon; their limbs were as cool as the moon, and they bore the fragrance of the blue lotus.
Their lifespan, free from disease, lasts ten thousand years;
having drunk the juice of the Kālāmra fruit, they remain forever in the bloom of youth.
The sages said:
The dimensions, the colors, and the lifespans of all four continents have been described according to their true nature, in summary rather than in detail.
Sūta said:
O increasers of fame, listen now in its entirety to the signs of the Bhadrāśvas as they have been proclaimed by the ancient perfected ones.
That which is beyond all the famous Devakūṭa mountains here has been duly proclaimed in all directions to the east.
Of the five principal mountain ranges and especially of the rivers,
as well as of the various provinces, exactly as they were seen and heard.
Śaivāla, Varṇamālāgra, Korañja, Acalottama, Śvetavarṇa, and Nīla—these five are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas). ||14||
From them, other mountains of great extent were also produced; they should be known as numbering in the hundreds and thousands of millions upon millions on the earth. (15)
Interspersed with those [mountains] were the inhabited lands, teeming with various kinds of beings, consisting of many different species, and protected by numerous kings. ||16||
The provinces, inhabited by illustrious and eminent men who have departed with their glorious names, are both worthy of praise and radiant with beauty.
Their names and various kingdoms are situated among mountains, on level ground, and in rugged terrain.
Likewise, there were the Sumaṅgalas, the Śuddhas, the Candrakāntas, the Sunandanas, the Vrajakas, the Nīlaśaileyas, the Sauvīras, and the Vijayasthalas. ||19||
They had broad chests, were full of desire, possessed great hair and beautiful heads;
they were as swift as the wind, equipped with side-locks, and were wanderers who traveled abroad.
The Sambhavas, Mahānetras, Śaivālas, Stanapas, Kumudas, Śākamuṇḍas, and the Uraḥsaṅkīrṇabhaumakas. ||21||
The Sodakas, Vatsakas, some Hāravāmakas, those called Śaṅkhas, the Bhāvisandras, and the northern Haimabhaumakas; ||22||
The Kṛṣṇabhaumas, Subhaumas, and Mahābhaumas have been proclaimed;
these and other famous regions of various peoples have been described by me. ||23||
Those of great merit drink from the Great Gaṅgā, the great river, which is renowned throughout the three worlds and flows with cool waters. 24.
Likewise, there are Haṃsavasati, the Mahācakrā river, Cakrā, Vakrā, Kañcī, Surasā, and the excellent Apagottamā. ||25||
The Śākhāvatī, Indranadī, Meghā, Maṅgāravāhinī, Kāverī, Haritoyā, Somāvartā, and Śatahradā; ||26||
Vanamālā, Vasumatī, Pampā, the auspicious Pampāvatī, Suvarṇā, Pañcavarṇā, and likewise the meritorious Vapuṣmatī. ||27||
Maṇivaprā, Suvaprā, Brahmabhāgā, Śilāśinī, Kṛṣṇatoyā, Puṇyodā, and the auspicious Nāgapadī. ||28||
The Śaivālī, the Maṇitaṭā, the Kṣārodā, the Cāruṇāvatī, as well as the Viṣṇupadī, which is a most meritorious great river. ||29||
The Hiraṇyavāhinī, the Nīlā, the Skandamālā, the Surāvatī,
the Vāmodā, the Patākā, the Vetālī, and the Mahānadī.
These great rivers, headed by the Gaṅgā, have been proclaimed as the principal ones;
however, there are innumerable minor rivers by the hundreds and thousands.
The women of the eastern continent are proclaimed to be meritorious and auspicious;
it is my conviction that one becomes purified even by the mere recitation of their names. (32)
It was a prosperous kingdom, flourishing and crowded with various districts,
filled with regions of diverse trees and forests, and beautifully encircled by many kinds of mountains.
It was crowded with throngs of men and women, eternally joyful and auspicious;
it was endowed with abundant grain and wealth, protected by various kings, filled with hundreds of temples of praise, and possessed mines of diverse jewels. (34)
In that region are renowned men who are bulls among men, possessing the luster of gold and conch shells, with massive bodies and great prowess.
O highly fortunate ones, the people there indeed engage in conversation, sight, and association with the gods while remaining on equal footing. (36)
Their lifespan is proclaimed to be ten thousand years;
moreover, among those great-souled ones, there is no distinction between righteousness and unrighteousness, for non-violence and truthful speech exist in them by their very nature. (37)
With devotion, they constantly perform sacrifices, worship, and prostrations before the god Śaṅkara and Gaurī, the supreme devotee of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Worlds," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
This is the well-known natural disposition of the Bhadrāśvas, as it truly is;
now hear the detailed proclamation concerning the Ketumālas.
To the west of the great-souled Niṣadha, the lord of mountains,
there is that which is celebrated throughout all directions.
You ought to hear in detail about the seven mountain ranges, the rivers in particular, and likewise the various regions.
Viśāla, Kambala, Kṛṣṇa, Jayanta, Hariparvata, Aśoka, and Vardhamāna—these seven are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas). ||4||
From their offspring, other mountains of great extent are also to be known by the hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of millions upon millions. ||5||
Interspersed with those [mountains] were the inhabited lands, crowded with various castes, diverse in their characteristics, and protected by many kings. ||6||
They were renowned on earth by various names, distinguished and celebrated; they were inhabited by provinces and adorned with their own praises.
Their various kingdoms, bearing those same names,
were situated among mountains, on level plains, and in rugged terrains.
Just as the city-dwellers here were described as cattle, humans, and pigeons,
so too are the bees— their swarms— as well as those from the earth and the mountain peaks.
The Sumaulas, the Stāvakas, the Krauñcas, those with black bodies and heaps of jewels,
the Kūṭakambalas, the Mauṣīyas, and likewise the Samudrāntarakas— [all these are the tribes of the Mlecchas].
The breasts were like balls of parched grain, white and adorned with beautiful golden bracelets;
the birds had white bodies, black feet, and tawny-colored ears. ||11||
There were extremely terrifying bulls with blazing horns, lowing and committing offenses against the forest; and buffaloes with the luster of white water-lilies, along with Karavaṭas and Hotsakas.
Śunakā, Kanāsā, Mahānāsā, Vanāsā, Gajabhūmikā, Karañja, Mañjamā, Vāhā, Kiṣkindhī, and Pāṇḍubhūmikī. ||13||
The Kuberās, Dhūmajas, Jaṅgas, Vaṅgas, Rājīvakokilas, Vācāṅgas, Mahāṅgas, Madhureyas, and Surecakas. ||14||
The Pittalas, the Kācalas, the Śravaṇas, the Mattakāsikas, the Godāvas, the Bakulas, the Vāṅgas, the Vaṅgakas, the Modakas, and the Kalas. ||15||
Those highly fortunate ones drink first from the great river, which has beautiful banks, sacred waters, and is frequented by mighty serpents. ||16||
Kambalā, Tāmasī, Śyāmā, Sumedhā, the river Bakulā, Vikīrṇā, Śikhimālā, and likewise Darbhāvatī. ||17||
The Bhadrā river, the Śukanadī, the Palāśā, and the great river;
the Bhīmā, the Prabhañjanā, the Kāñcī, and the holy Kuśāvatī. ||18||
The Dakṣā, the Śākavatī, the meritorious Mahānadī, the Candrāvatī, the Sumūlā, and the Ṛṣabhā, the best of rivers. ||19||
[Namely] the Nadī, the Samudramālā, as well as the Campāvatī;
the Ekākṣā, the Puṣkalā, the Vāhā, the Suvarṇā, and also the Nandinī.
And also the Kālindī of holy waters, the great river Bhāratī, the Sītodā, the Pātikā, the Brāhmī, and the great river Viśālā. ||21||
Pīvarī, Kumbhakārī, Ruṣā, and the excellent Apagā;
Mahiṣī, Mānuṣī, Daṇḍā, and likewise the auspicious Nadanadī.
These and many other excellent rivers are drunk—rivers frequented by gods, sages, and perfected beings, which are auspicious, purify sins, and bestow merit. (23)
It was prosperous with various provinces, adorned by great rivers,
filled with floods of diverse jewels, eternally joyful, and auspicious.
Abounding on all sides with wealth, grain, and riches, and filled with human dwellings,
this great island situated to the west belongs to those of virtuous soul;
thus has this natural disposition of the Ketumālas been described to you.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Worlds," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Śaunaka said:

O Lord, you have described to us the two regions, the eastern and the western, in their entirety— both those of the northern lands and those of the southern lands. Now tell us truly about those who dwell in the mountains.
Sūta said:
To the south of Śveta and to the north of Nīla is the region named Ramaṇaka; there the human beings are born. ||2||
Sentient beings there grant all desires throughout every season; they are free from old age and foul odors, endowed with purity and noble birth, and all are pleasing to behold. (3)
There too is a very great, divine, and vast banyan tree named Rohiṇa;
having drunk the juice of its fruit, they subsist by drinking it.
Those highly fortunate and best of men live for ten thousand, one hundred, and fifteen years, always joyful.
To the north of Śveta and to the south of the peak named Sāhva is the region called Hiraṇvat, where the river Hairaṇvatī flows.
The human beings born there are possessed of great strength and radiant splendor;
they are beings who provide for all seasonal desires, wealthy, and pleasing to behold.
Those of immeasurable splendor live for eleven thousand years,
and their lifespan measures fifteen hundred years.
In that region there is a great tree, a lakuca, which is the source of the six tastes;
by drinking the juice of its fruit, the humans there live. ||9||
Mount Śṛṅgavān has three peaks that are lofty and great;
one of them is made of jewels, another is made of gold,
and the third consists of all kinds of gems and is adorned with celestial mansions.
At the edge of the northern ocean and on the southern shore of the sea lies that sacred region, Kuru, inhabited by the Siddhas. ||11||
There, the trees always bear sweet fruit and are laden with flowers and fruit;
they produce garments, and within their fruits are found ornaments.
There, in some places, there are delightful trees that yield the fruits of all desires;
attended by Gandharvas and Apsarases, they exude the finest honey.
There are other delightful trees there called Kṣīriṇas, which constantly exude milk that possesses the six flavors and is like nectar. ||14||
The entire ground consists of jewels and fine golden sand;
it is everywhere pleasant to the touch, free from mud, free from disease, and auspicious.
Falling from the world of the gods, auspicious men are born there;
they are endowed with pure lineage, and all possess perpetual youth. ||16||
Pairs are born, including women who are exceedingly beautiful;
they drink from that milky tree, which is like nectar.
A pair is born at once and grows up equally;
they possess equal character and appearance, and they die together as well. (18)
Mutually devoted like ruddy geese,
they were indeed free from disease and sorrow, constantly enjoying happiness.
Thirteen thousand one hundred and fifty of those great heroes live, and none among them have ever served another woman.
Now listen in detail concerning these Kurus as well. To the north of Jārudhi, the king of mountains, learn all that is being proclaimed regarding everything situated in every direction.
Adorned with many caves, ravines, grottoes, and waterfalls, they were filled with numerous groves and forests and embellished with variegated minerals. ||22||
They were variegated with many elements, adorned with all kinds of minerals,
endowed with flowers, roots, and fruits, and frequented by perfected beings and celestial singers.
Both of these are exceedingly great and lofty mountain ranges;
that island is graced by hundreds of peaks belonging to them both.
Between the moonstone mountain and the sunstone mountain,
which possessed lofty peaks, that great river Bhadrasomā did not flow.
And there are thousands of other rivers with clear, divine waters,
possessing sufficient abundance for the Kurus’ bathing, drinking, and immersion.
Likewise, there are thousands of other great rivers carrying milk,
as well as those carrying honey-wine (maireya) and clarified butter (ghṛta).
There were others of curd and lightning-bolts; then a mountain of sweet food, and various fruits possessing a flavor like that of nectar.
The roots and fruits there are rich in fragrance, color, and flavor;
they extend for five yojanas in every direction and possess a magnificent scent.
Thousands of flowers of various colors and kinds,
as well as thousands of auspicious and magnificent articles of enjoyment.
They were rich in fragrance, color, and flavor, and possessed every kind of pleasant touch;
there were also forests of sandalwood trees and the scent of tamāla and aguru.
The forests were always delightful, filled with blossoming trees, shrubs, and creepers, and resounded with the songs of bees.
O best of the twice-born,
there were also thousands of lakes, rich with beds of red and blue lotuses, which were celebrated by bees and other birds.
Abounding in edible offerings and garlands, and richly adorned with many wreaths and ointments,
they resounded with the warbling of various flocks of birds with enchanting faces.
There are also beds, seats, and articles of enjoyment, expanded with manifold virtues;
delightful grounds for dwellings that provide comfort in all seasons. (35)
The pleasure gardens were prosperous on all sides, adorned with jewels and gold;
they contained excellent stone dwellings, tree-houses, and plantain-blossom houses.
There were thousands of vine-cottages, most pleasant on all sides,
as well as hundreds of ground-dwellings with the pure luster of conch shells.
There were windows made of refined gold and lattices of jewels, variegated with gold and gems, and they were vast everywhere.
Thousands of excellent great trees of every kind, as well as garments of various forms, fine and very comfortable. ||39||
Hundreds and thousands of kalpavṛkṣa trees bear fruit in great abundance, including mṛdaṅgas, flutes, drums, lutes, and other instruments. (1.45.40)
Everywhere there were likewise gardens, and everywhere indeed those cities,
filled with men and women, rejoicing throughout all the continents;
and there the breeze blew, perfumed with various flowers.
In that island which removes all fatigue, there is the constant joy and refreshment of bodily pleasure;
for men who have fallen from heaven are always born there.
Indeed, even that terrestrial realm is heaven, and it is the most excellent of places in its qualities.
The best of men born on the eastern shore are moon-lovers (candrakānta), with dark complexions;
those who are sun-lovers (sūryakānta) have a fair-dark complexion and are happy subjects.
In that region, the men were excellent, possessing the nature and prowess of gods; they all lived perpetually, radiant and acting according to their desires.
Adorned with bracelets, armlets, upper-arm ornaments, necklaces, and earrings, they wore garlands and variegated crowns, and were clothed in diverse garments. ||45||
Possessing undiminished youth, very dear, and pleasant to behold,
the subjects live for many thousands of years.
They do not possess the nature of giving birth, nor is there a rule for the extinction of their lineage;
rather, pairs are born from the tree, appearing in a manner unlike this [human] one.
All possess the power of universality and are entirely free from the sense of "mine";
therein neither dharma nor adharma exists, nor do they function. 48.
There is neither disease nor old age there, neither lack of intelligence nor exhaustion;
when their time is fulfilled, they perish like bubbles upon the water.
Thus, those who are excessively happy and devoid of all suffering do not perceive the Dharma; for it is from suffering that the Dharma is born.
To the south of the Northern Kurus, one should know there is an ocean rich with garlands of waves and adorned with various sounds. (51)
Having passed beyond the abode of the gods for five thousand yojanas, there is the place known as Candradvīpa, which is shaped like the lunar disc. ||52||
It is a thousand yojanas in circumference all around,
endowed with various flowers and fruits, and possessed of supreme prosperity;
it is a hundred yojanas in width and rises to the same height.
In its center stands a preeminent mountain, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
possessing beautiful and auspicious peaks shaped like the moon and radiant with a luster equal to that of the moon.
Variegated with white beryl and water-lilies, that mountain Kumudaprabha possesses many wonderful gardens and numerous waterfalls and caves;
it is beautifully adorned with various great plateaus, valleys, and groves.
From that mountain of great merit flows the supreme river Candrāvartā, wavy with waves and possessing water as pure as the rays of the moon.
Therein is the excellent abode of the Moon, the lord of the constellations;
there the Moon, the leader of the planets, always descends.
There, the mountain known by the name Candramas is celebrated;
it is the great island of Candradvīpa, radiant both in heaven and here on earth.
There, all the subjects resemble the moon, with faces like the full moon; they are as pleasing as the moonstone, stainless, and have the moon as their presiding deity. ||59||
The subjects there were exceedingly righteous, gentle, true to their word, and full of splendor;
they were of virtuous conduct and lived for a thousand years.
To the west of the western continent,
it is proclaimed that [the city] lies beyond the great ocean at a distance of four thousand yojanas.
Ten thousand yojanas in circumference all around, the island named Bhadrākara is adorned with various flowers. ||62||
Abounding in vast wealth and grain, protected by many kings, ever-joyful, flourishing, and adorned with great mountains. (63)
There, the Bhadrāsana of Vāyu is adorned with various jewels;
there, Vāyu in embodied form is always worshipped on the sacred festival days (parvan).
Having the luster of refined gold and adorned with refined gold, those who resemble immortals shine there, wearing variegated garments and garlands.
Those subjects were energetic, highly fortunate, and lived for five hundred years; they were true to their word, filled with joy, and had Vāyu as their presiding deity.
Sūta said:
In this very same way, this seasonal pattern of the rains in the age of Bhārata was observed by those who know the supreme truth; what more shall I tell you? 67.
When this had been narrated by the wise Sūtaputra, the Ṛṣis,
desiring to hear more, questioned him further immediately thereafter.
The sages said:
"This is the land of Bhārata-varṣa, wherein these fourteen Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, appear for the creation of progeny."
"O best of men, we wish to know this; explain it to us. Having heard these words of theirs, Lomaharṣaṇa spoke.
Then the Sūta, the knower of ancient lore, being composed,
spoke this matter at greater length to those seers of purified souls.
Sūta said:
This well-known origin of the Kurus has been told according to the facts;
now listen as I describe the origin of the Bhāratas. 72.
O best of the twice-born, at this meritorious tirtha on the southern mountain of the Himalayas, which extends from east to west, it is located to the south of this [range].
Likewise, you ought to hear the detailed account of the provinces;
herein I shall describe to you the subjects in this land of Bhārata.
But this middle region is variegated, yielding both auspicious and inauspicious fruits;
it lies north of the ocean and south of the Himalayas.
That region which is named Bhārata, where this Bhāratī progeny resides—
Manu is called Bharata because he supports (bharaṇāt) the subjects;
and according to the statement of etymology, that region is remembered as Bhārata.
From that, heaven, liberation, and the intermediate state are reached;
indeed, for mortals, no other action is ordained on earth than this.
Nine divisions of this land of Bhārata have been proclaimed;
separated by oceans, they should be known as inaccessible to one another. (78)
Indradvīpa, Kaseru, Tāmravarṇa, Gabhastimān, Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gandharva, and Vāruṇa. ||79||
Among them, however, the ninth island is surrounded by the ocean;
this island extends for a thousand yojanas from south to north.
For it extends from the Kumārī river to the source of the Gaṅgā;
its width, measured from side to side toward the north, is exactly nine thousand [yojanas].
For this island is inhabited by Mlecchas at its borders;
the Kirātas are known to dwell at its eastern edge, and the Yavanas at its western. (82)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were established in their respective places in the midst [of society], subsisting through sacrifice, warfare, and trade. 83.
Among them, this mutual social interaction proceeds,
joined with virtue, wealth, and pleasure, within the respective duties of the castes.
Among the four stages of life, with the fifth being mental resolve (saṅkalpa), human activity therein proceeds according to rule for the sake of attaining heaven and liberation in this world. 85.
As for this ninth island which is said to extend horizontally, he who conquers it in its entirety is celebrated here as a universal monarch (samrāj). ||86||
This world, O Emperor, is indeed Samrāj; the intermediate space (antarikṣa) is known as Virāj;
the other world is known as Svarāj; I shall speak further in detail. ||87||
And in this [land], there are seven renowned principal mountain ranges with beautiful peaks:
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, Ṛkṣaparvata, Vindhya, and Pāriyātra; these are the seven principal mountain ranges. 88.
Thousands of other mountains, noble in every quality, vast and with variegated peaks, are situated near them. ||89||
Mandara, the best of mountains, Vaihāra, and Dardura; Kolāhala, Surasa, Maināka, and likewise Vaidyuta.
The mountain named Pātandhama, as well as the White Mountain (Pāṇḍuraparvata), Gantuprastha, Kṛṣṇagiri, and the mountain Godhana. ||91||
Puṣpagiri and Ujjayanta, the mountain Raivataka, Śrīparvata, Kāru, Kūṭaśaila, and likewise Giri; ||92||
Others than them are those who have full knowledge, who are short-lived and subsist on very little;
they are constantly mixed with the Jatapadas, both Aryas and Mlecchas. (93)
By whom these rivers are drunk: the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Sarasvatī, the Śatadru, the Candrabhāgā, the Yamunā, and likewise the Sarayū. (94)
The Irāvatī, Vitastā, Vipāśā, Devikā, Kuhū, Gomatī, Dhutapāpā, Bāhudā, and Dṛṣadvatī. ||95||
The Kauśikī is the third, as well as the Niścīrā and the Gaṇḍakī;
the Ikṣu and the Lohita—these flow forth from the foothills of the Himavat.
Vedasmṛti, Vedavatī, Vṛtraghnī, and Sindhu; Varṇāśā, Candanā, Satīrā, and likewise Mahatī. ||97||
The Parā, Carmmaṇvatī, Vidiśā, and also the Vetravatī,
as well as the Śiprā and Avantī, are remembered as those that take their refuge in the Pāriyātra mountains.
So too are the Śoṇa, the Mahānada, the Narmadā, and the Sumahādrumā.
The Mandākinī, the Daśārṇā, and likewise the Citrakūṭā. ||99||
The Tamasā, Pippalā, Śroṇī, Karatoyā, Piśācikā, Nīlotpalā, Vipāśā, Jambulā, and Vāluvāhinī; ||1.45.100||
Sītērajā, Śuktimatī, Makuṇā, and Tridivā—these rivers, whose waters resemble jewels, were born respectively from Ṛkṣapāda. (101)
The Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Nirvindhyā, Madrā, Niṣadhā river, Venvā, Vaitaraṇī, Śitibāhu, and Kumudvatī. ||102||
Toya, Mahāgaurī, Durgā, and Antaśilā, as well as the rivers of auspicious and merit-bestowing waters that originate from the foothills of the Vindhya mountains. ||103||
The Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇā, Vaiṇyā, Vañjulā,
Tuṅgabhadrā, Suprayogā, and the river Kāverī—
these are the rivers of the southern region that have issued forth from the foothills of the Sahya mountains.
The Kṛtamālā, the Tāmravarṇā, the Puṣpajā, the Utpalāvatī, and those rivers born from the Malaya mountains—all of them possess auspicious, cool waters. 105.
Trisāmā, Ṛtukulyā, Ikṣulā, Tridivā, Lāṅgulinī, and Vaṃśadharā are known as the daughters of Mahendra. ||106||
The Ṛṣīkā, Sukumārī, Mandagā, Mandavāhinī,
Kūpā, and Palāśinī are known as those originating from the Śuktimat mountain.
All sacred Sarasvatīs, all Gaṅgās flowing to the ocean—all are remembered as mothers of the universe and removers of the sins of the world. (108)
Of those rivers and tributaries, there are hundreds and thousands;
and here dwell these Kurus, Pañcālas, Śālvas, and the Jāṅgalas. (109)
The Śūrasenas, Bhadrakāras, Bodhas, and lords of the Śatapathe; the Vatsas, Kiṣkindhas, Kulyas, Kuntalas, and the people of Kāśī and Kośala. || 1.45.110 ||
Now, the Tilangas and Magadhas on the flanks, along with the Vṛkas—these are generally proclaimed as the Janapadas of the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa). ||111||
On the northern slope of the Sahya mountain, where the river Godāvarī flows,
that region is the most delightful in all this entire earth.
There, the mountain named Govardhana was created by the king of the gods;
for the sake of Rāma's pleasure, this heaven, as well as its trees and medicinal herbs, was established there. (113)
Brāhmaṇa Bharadvāja brought them down for the sake of his beloved;
by him, that region of the inner apartments was made delightful. (114)
The Vāhlīkas, the Vāḍadhānas, the Ābhīras, the Kālatoyakas, the Aparītās, the Śūdras, the Pahlavas, and the Carmakhaṇḍikas. ||115||
The Gāndhāras, the Yavanas, the Sindhus, the Sauvīras, and the Bhadrakas; the Śakas, the Hradas, the Kulindas, the Paritas, and the Hārapūrikas. ||116||
The Ramaṭas, the Raddhakaṭakas, the Kekayas, the Daśamānikas, the settlements of Kṣatriyas, and the families of Vaiśyas and Śūdras. ||117||
The Kāmbojas, the Daradas, the Barbaras, the Priyalaukikas, the Pīnas, the Tuṣāras, the Pahlavas, and the Bāhyatodarās. ||118||
The Ātreyas, the Bharadvājas, the Prasthalas, the Kaserukas, the Lampākas, the Stanapas, the Pīḍikas, together with the Juhuḍas. ||119||
The Apagas, the Ālimadras, the various tribes of Kirātas,
the Tomaras, the Haṃsamārgas, the Kāśmīras, and likewise the Taṅgaṇas.
The Cūlikas, the Āhukas, and likewise the Pūrṇadarvas—these are the northern countries; now learn of the eastern countries.
The Andhravākas, Sujarakas, those dwelling within the mountains and those outside the mountains, as well as the Pravaṅgas, Vaṅgeyas, Māladās, and Mālavartins; ||122||
The Brahmottaras, Pravijayas, Bhārgavas, Geyamarthakas,
Prāgjyotiṣas, Muṇḍas, Videhas, Tāmaliptakas,
Mālas, Magadhas, and Govindas are recorded as the eastern provinces. ||123||
Then there were other peoples dwelling in the southern region:
the Pāṇḍyas, the Keralas, as well as the Caulyas and the Kulyas. ||124||
The Setukas, the Mūṣikas, the Kumanas, the Vanavāsikas, the Mahārāṣṭras, the Māhiṣakas, and the Kaliṅgas from all sides; ||125||
The Abhiras along with the Eṣīkas, the Āṭavyas and the Varas, the Pulindas of the Vindhya foothills, the Vaidarbhas together with the Daṇḍakas; ||126||
The Paunikas, Maunikas, Asmakas, Bhogavardhanas, Nairmikas, Kuntalas, Andhras, Udbhidas, and Nalakālikas. ||127||
Now learn of those other southern regions:
Śūrpākāra, Kolavana, and Durga, along with the Kālītakas. 128.
The Puleyas, the Surālas, along with the Rūpasas and the Tāpasas, as well as the Turasitas and all the Parakṣaras. ||129||
Those who dwell in Nāsikya and other such places, as well as those who live between the Narmadā and Bhānukaccha,
are to be avoided with haste, even by those who are eternally steadfast.
The Kacchīyas, the Surāṣṭras, and the Ānartas along with the Arbudas—these are the surrounding peoples;
now hear of those who dwell in the Vindhya mountains. ||131||
The Mālavas, Karūṣas, Mekalas along with the Utkalas, the Uttamarṇas, Daśārṇas, Bhojas, together with the Kiṣkindhakas; ||132||
The Tośalas, the Kosalas, the Traipuras, the Vaidikas, the Tumuras, the Tumburus, and the Ṣaṭsuras, together with the Niṣadhas. (133)
The Anupās, Tuṇḍikeras, Vītihotras, and Āvantayas—all these are the peoples who dwell upon the ridges of the Vindhya mountains. ||134||
Therefore, I shall describe the countries and those who dwell in the mountains:
the Nigarharas, the Haṃsamārgas, the Kṣupaṇas, the Taṅgaṇas, and the Khasas. ||135||
The Kuśaprāvaraṇas, the Hūṇas, the Darvas along with the Hūdakas, the Trigartas, the Mālavas, and the Kirātas, together with the Tāmasas; ||136||
Sages know that there are four ages (yugas) in the land of Bhārata:
Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—this is the quartet.
I shall describe their nature hereafter; listen attentively. 137.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Worlds," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Having heard this, those sages, desiring to hear more and filled with joy, again questioned Lomaharṣaṇa for a further reply. ||1||
The sages said:
And as for the region of Kimpuruṣa and likewise Harivarṣa—
explain those to us according to their true nature, just as the Bhārata region has been described by you.
Just as this was asked by the Brahmins, and especially according to their questions,
he spoke that which was ordained in the Purāṇa as directed by the Sage.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, listen with joy to that which you wish to hear:
in the Kimpuruṣa region, there is a vast forest tract resembling the Nandana grove.
In Kimpuruṣa, the lifespan is recorded as ten thousand years;
the men are golden-hued, and the women are like apsarases.
For all those humans born there are free from disease and sorrow, pure-minded, and possess the luster of refined gold.
In the meritorious Kimpuruṣa Varṣa, there is the auspicious Plakṣa tree that flows with honey;
all the Kimpuruṣas drink its excellent juice.
Beyond this, what is described as being to the east of Puruṣa?
There, the human beings are born resembling great silver. ||8||
Having descended from the world of the gods, all those who possess celestial forms in every respect— indeed,
all the men in Harivarṣa— drink the auspicious juice of sugarcane.
In Harivarṣa, all those people live for eleven thousand years filled with joy and with delighted minds;
neither does old age afflict them there, nor do those men grow decrepit.
The middle region which I have described by the name Ilāvṛta—
there the sun does not scorch, nor do human beings age.
When the sun and moon, along with the stars, are shrouded in darkness and obscured,
human beings are born there with the color of lotuses, the luster of lotuses, eyes resembling lotus petals, and the fragrance of lotus leaves. (12)

Subsisting on the fruit of the Jambūrasa tree, they were motionless and fragrant; being high-minded, they had experienced worldly enjoyments and now partook of the fruits of their own virtuous deeds. ||13||
Having descended from the world of the gods, all those best of men were born free from old age and death, living for thirteen thousand years at the end of that period. ||14||
They live for a lifespan of one hundred years in Ilāvṛta;
these regions extend nine thousand [yojanas] in each direction from Meru.
Its width is twenty-six thousand yojanas;
it is square on all sides and shaped like a shallow bowl. ||16||
To the west of Meru, extending for nine thousand [yojanas],
lies the Gandhamādana mountain, measuring thirty-four thousand [yojanas].
Extending from north to south between the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains,
it increases forty thousand yojanas above the surface of the earth;
it is submerged one thousand yojanas and stands elevated by that same amount.
To the east, the Mālyavat mountain is proclaimed to be of that same measure;
it lies to the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha.
Among them, Mahāmeru is proclaimed to be of perfect proportions,
such that it is deeply embedded within all the mountains.
Its width is said to be one million [yojanas], while its length is remembered as ten million;
because of its circular nature, it encompasses the entire circle of the earth within the ocean. ||21||
The lengths decrease on all sides for those that are square;
those situated in the middle are divided by the fourfold [measure] without being enclosed. ||22||
The river Jambūrasavatī, resembling crushed collyrium,
flows on the southern side of Meru and to the north of Niṣadha.
There is a great, eternal jambū tree named Sudarśana, which is perpetually endowed with flowers and fruit and frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas. ||24||
In Jambūdvīpa there is a lord of the forest known by his name;
that great tree, a thousand and a hundred yojanas in height, touches the heavens in every direction. ||25||
The sages who perceive reality have calculated the measurement of the fruit to be eight hundred and sixty-one aratnis.
Falling upon the earth, they produce a great sound;
the juice of that jambu fruit flows forth, becoming a river.
Having circumambulated Meru, they enter below the Jambu tree;
there, ever joyful, they drink the juice of the Jambu fruits.
Having drunk the juice of the jambūrasa fruit, they do not undergo old age,
nor indeed fixed [decay], nor disease, nor likewise such death.
There, the gold known as Jāmbūnada, which serves as an ornament for the gods, is produced; it resembles the Indragopaka insect and is intensely radiant.
The auspicious juice of the fruits of all the rain-trees becomes that semen which is gold, the ornament of the gods.
Their urine and excrement were scattered in all directions;
by the grace of the Lord, the earth swallowed those dead bodies.
The Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and Yakṣas are all known to dwell on Himavat;
on Hemakūṭa, however, the Gandharvas together with the hosts of Apsarases are to be found.
All the Nāgas—Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka—are on Niṣadha;
on Mahāmeru roam the thirty-three gods who perform sacrifices;
and on Nīla, which is made of beryl, dwell the Siddhas and Brahmarṣis.
The Śveta mountain is said to belong to the Daityas and Dānavas;
the excellent Śṛṅgavān mountain is the place of assembly for the Pitṛs. ||35||
In these nine regions, situated according to their respective portions,
all beings— both mobile and immobile— are established.
Their great increase among both gods and humans is seen;
it cannot be fully enumerated, yet it should be believed in by one who desires to prosper.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Worlds," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
On the eastern side of the Himavat stands the mountain named Kailāsa;
there dwells the illustrious Kubera together with the Rākṣasas, and as the lord of Alakā, he rejoices in the company of hosts of Apsarases. ||1||
From the foot of Mount Kailāsa arose the auspicious, cool water known as Manda; it was pure and resembled an autumnal cloud. ||2||
From that [lake] flows forth the divine and auspicious river Mandākinī;
and there, upon its bank, is the great and celestial Nandana forest.
To the northeast of Kailāsa, toward the mountain of divine beings and medicinal herbs,
he went to the variegated golden mountain composed of celestial minerals.
There is a mountain named Candraprabha, pure and resembling a jewel;
at its foot is that great, divine lake named Acchoda.
From that [lake] flows forth the divine river named Acchodā;
on its bank is the great and divine forest known as Caitraratha.
On that mountain dwells Maṇibhadra with his followers,
the commander of the Yakṣas, surrounded by cruel Guhyakas.
The auspicious Mandākinī and the river Chodakā likewise entered the great ocean through the middle of the earth's surface.
To the southeast of Kailāsa, toward the divine, tawny mountain composed of realgar—the teacher who is the medicinal herb of Śiva’s essence—[he went]. (9)
The great mountain Lohita has golden peaks and the splendor of the sun;
at its foot lies that great, divine lake named Lohita.
Therefore, the great and holy Lauhitya flows forth;
on its bank is the forest of Devāraṇya and the great grove Viśoka. ||11||
On that mountain dwells the self-controlled Yakṣa Maṇivara,
surrounded by gentle and highly righteous Guhyakas.
To the south of Kailāsa is the mountain Añjana, a source of fierce medicinal herbs;
it is said to have arisen from the body of Vṛtra and resembles Mount Trikakud.
There stands a vast mountain of lightning, composed of all the elements;
at its foot is the sacred Lake Mānasa, frequented by the Siddhas.
From that [mountain] flows the meritorious Sarayū, the benefactor of the world;
on its bank is a divine forest, renowned by the name Vaibhrāja. ||15||
There dwells the Rākṣasa Pāpa, a follower of Kubera and the son of Praheti, who possesses self-control and infinite prowess;
he is surrounded by hundreds of terrible Yātudhānas who roam through the atmosphere. ||16||
By another [route], however, they went from Kailāsa toward the mountain Aruṇa, the best of peaks, which is composed of golden minerals and is the primary abode of living beings and medicinal herbs.
The glorious mountain, beloved of Bhava, resembles a cloud and is covered with networks of auspicious rocks made of gold.
With its hundreds of golden peaks as if scraping the very heavens, that great and divine mountain Muñjavān, difficult to access, was covered with snow. ||19||
On that mountain dwells the mountain-dweller (Giriśa) Dhūmralohita;
from his foot flows forth that lake named Śailoda.
From that [lake] flows forth the divine river named Śailodā;
it enters the salt ocean between the Cakṣus and Śīta [oceans]. 21.
On its bank is a divine forest renowned as Surabhi;
to the north of Kailāsa lies the mountain Śivasattvauṣadha.
There is a beautiful mountain named Gaura, consisting of yellow orpiment;
there is also a very great, divine mountain made of jewels with golden peaks.
At its foot is a great, divine, and auspicious lake named Bindusaras, with beautiful golden sands, where Bhagīratha went.
For the sake of the Gaṅgā, the royal seer lived for many years, thinking:
"My ancestors shall go to heaven, drenched by the waters of the Gaṅgā. (25)
There, the goddess Tripathagā was first established;
having been produced from the Soma tree, she divided herself into seven streams.
There the sacrificial posts were made of jewels and the altars were made of gold;
having performed a sacrifice there, Śakra went to Śarva along with all the gods.
That which is seen at night as a luminous path of divine light, following the circle of the constellations— that, O Goddess, is the triple-pathed river.
Nourishing both the intermediate space and the heavens, she descended to the earth;
having fallen upon the head of Bhava, she was restrained by his yogic power (yogamāyā).
Some drops of hers, falling upon the earth while she was enraged, formed there the Bindu-saras; therefore, it is known as Bindu-saras.
Then that goddess, having been restrained by Bhava with a smile,
reflected in her mind regarding the casting away of Śaṅkara.
Having understood the cruel intention of the goddess that she desired to accomplish, I shall pierce Pātāla and seize Śaṅkara by means of my current. ||32||
He set his mind upon making that river disappear from his limbs;
perceiving that pride of the river, Śaṅkara became enraged, and having blocked her,
he cast her, as she fell with force, onto the earth at his feet.
At that very time, however, he saw the king before him,
emaciated with veins protruding, wasted away, and his senses overcome by hunger.
"I was indeed previously gratified by him for the sake of the river;
however, having learned of this granting of a boon, he has restrained his anger. (35)
Having heard the words of Brahmā regarding the fulfillment of his vow, he,
being gratified by Bhagīratha’s fierce asceticism, then released the river that had been restrained by his own splendor for the sake of Bhagīratha.
Then, as it was being released, that stream divided into seven branches:
three indeed flowed toward the east, and three toward the west.
The stream of the Gaṅgā then divided into seven branches:
Nalinī, Hrādinī, and Pāvanī flowed toward the east.
The Sītā, the Cakṣu, and the Sindhu occupy the western quarter;
the seventh among them is the Bhagīrathī, which flows toward the south.
Therefore, that Bhāgīrathī which has entered the salt ocean nourishes these seven [rivers] here in the region called Himavat.
From that Bindusaras, seven auspicious rivers have issued forth,
nourishing various regions that are for the most part inhabited by Mlecchas.
They all approached him from wherever the rain-cloud poured down:
from the Sirindhras, the Kuntalas, the Cīnas, the Barbharas, the Yavanas, and the Druhas.
Having divided the Sindhu and Maru rivers, she passed through the lands of the Ruṣas, the Kuṇindas, and those who are the best among the people of Aṅga, and reached the western ocean via the Sītā.

Then, causing these regions to flow with tears— the Cīnas, the Marus, the Naṅgaṇas, the Sarvamūlikas, the Sādhras, the Ṣārās, the Tampakas, the Pahlavas, the Daradas, and the Śakas— she reached the ocean.
He dismissed the Daradas along with the Kāśmīras, the Gāndhāras, the Varapas, the Hradas,
the Śivapauras, the Indrahāsas, and the Vadātīs.
The Saindhavas, the Randhrakarakas, the Bhramaras, the Abhiras, and the Rohakas, as well as the Śunāmukhas and the Anūs, who were shaded by Siddhas and Cāraṇas; ||46||
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas; as well as the Kalāpagrāmakas, Pāradas, Sigaṇas, and Khasas. ||47||
And the Kirātas and Pulindas, as well as the Kurus and Bharatas,
the Pañcālas, Kāśis, Mātsyas, and likewise the Magadhas and Aṅgas.
The auspicious Gaṅgā nourishes these noble regions: Brahmottara, Vaṅga, and likewise Tāmalipta. ||49||
Then, repelled by the Vindhya mountains, she entered the southern ocean;
thereafter, the auspicious Ahlādinī turned and flowed toward the east.
The various tribes of Niṣādas,
as well as Dhīvaras, Ṛṣikas, and Nīlamukhas, cause the waters to overflow and enjoy them.
He saw the Keralas, the Anuṣṭrakarṇas, and indeed the Kirātas;
the Kālodaras and the pale-complexioned Kumāras adorned with golden ornaments.
She vanished gradually within the circle of the ocean;
thereafter, she became the purifying river and flowed toward the eastern direction.
In this world, they cultivate the *apathas*, as well as the Indradyumna-saras, the Kharatha paths, and the Indraśaṅku paths. 54.
Passing through the midst of the garden, she went forth wearing a garment of skins;
then she entered the salt ocean at Indradvīpa.
Then Nalinī also came swiftly toward the eastern direction,
creating here the paths of swans along with the hūhukas while scattering tomara-spears.
Flowing through eastern regions, she split many mountains,
and having reached the Karṇaprāvaraṇas as well as the Aśvamukhas, she continued her course.
Having gone to the mountains of sand and the deserts, she went to the Vidyādharas;
then, entering the enclosure of the wheel-rim, she entered the great ocean.
To them flow hundreds and thousands of rivers and tributaries,
all of which come from wherever Indra sends down rain.
On the bank of the Vasvokasā, renowned for its fragrant waters,
dwells the wise and self-controlled Kaubairaka at Hariśṛṅga.
Accompanied by sacrifice, that great one of immeasurable luster and excellent prowess was there,
surrounded by learned Brahmarākṣasas of the Agastya lineage;
for these four are known as his attendants, equal to him.
In this very way, however, the supernatural power (ṛddhi) of those dwelling on the mountain should be understood:
it is twofold compared to one another, by virtue of their dharma, their desire, and their purpose.
On the back of Hemakūṭa is that lake named Sāyana;
from it flow the Manasvinī and the Jyotiṣmatī.
For, having plunged into both oceans, the eastern and the western,
there is a lake named Viṣṇupada on Niṣadha, the best of mountains.
From that, indeed, two daughters were born: Gāndharvī and Alī;
and behind Mount Meru there arises a great lake called Candraprabha.
Therein lies the auspicious Jāmbūnadī, from which the beautiful Jāmbūnada gold originates; and on Mount Nīla is the lake Payoda, exceedingly bright and filled with white lotuses.
From that [lake] flow forth two rivers, the Puṇḍarīkā and the Apayodā;
from the Śveta mountain originates the meritorious lake Uttaramānasa.
From that [lake] were born two [rivers], Jyotsnā and Mṛgakāntā;
and [from it came] the holy Madhumatsara, which was filled with lotuses, fish, and birds.
It was filled with wish-fulfilling trees and was pleasant in every respect like honey;
known as Rudrakānta, it was created by Bhava himself.
And there are others also well-known here, crowded with lotuses, fish, and birds; they are named Rudrājaya, twelve in number, resembling the ocean.
From them two rivers were produced: the Śāntā and the Mādhvī;
in those regions, such as Kiṃpuruṣa and the others, the god does not rain.
There, other excellent rivers flow, breaking through the earth;
there also are the great mountains Ṛṣabha, Dundubhi, and Dhūmra.
The illustrious river Pūrvāyatā flows toward the salt waters;
likewise, Candrakaṅka, Prāṇa, Mahānagni,
and Śiloccaya extend northward, reaching the northern limits and plunging into the great ocean.
Somaka, Varāha, Nārada, and Mahīdhara—
these indeed extend toward the west and have entered the salt ocean.
Cakra, Balāhaka, and the mountain Maināka—
these great mountains extend toward the southern ocean;
they lie between Candra and Maināka, facing the southern intermediate direction.
