There, that fire named Saṃvartaka drinks up that water;
he is the glorious Aurva, known by the name Samudrapa, the Mare’s Mouth.
Indeed, these twelve mountains,
terrified by the fear of Mahendra and fearing the severing of their wings, entered the salt ocean at that time;
it is this which is seen in the moon as the white form of the black hare.
These nine divisions of the land of Bhārata have been proclaimed;
they are seen here as described, while others are not mentioned elsewhere. (78)
Each subsequent one of these is described as superior in its qualities, in terms of health and lifespan, and according to dharma, pleasure, and wealth. (79)
Endowed with their respective portions of the qualities and the seeds,
beings of various species dwell within those regions;
thus this earth, remaining as the universal world, supported everything.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Worlds," in the Great Purāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Now listen concerning the southern region of Bhārata:
having crossed ten thousand yojanas of the great ocean. ||1||
It is three thousand yojanas in length and one-third of that in width,
abounding with various flowers and fruits.
There is a great mountain there, a Kulaparvata named Vidyutvant,
by whose many peaks and slopes that island is beautifully adorned.
There, thousands of rivers with clear and sweet water flow,
and from that island, ponds of pure water have issued forth.
In the many extensive and long fissures of that mountain, there were,
in every respect, numerous and abundant objects of various forms.
Filled with men and women, joyful and vast,
there were hundreds and thousands of their underground chambers.
The cities were established both within the mountains and elsewhere;
they were well-connected to one another and each had but a single gate.
There, the people were born with long beards, dark blue in color, and with a radiance like that of clouds;
their maximum lifespan was eighty years from birth.
Those who share the nature of monkeys, subsisting on fruits and roots; those who follow the ways of cattle, being uninitiated and devoid of purity and proper conduct. ||9||
That island was filled with such men who were like common mortals;
thus have these intermediate islands been described in their proper order.
Twenty, thirty, fifty, sixty, eighty,
a hundred, and even a thousand yojanas are said to extend all around.
Extensive and indeed long, they are crowded with various living beings;
there are mountain ranges on Barhiṇadvīpa and thousands of minor islands.
Beyond the region of Jambūdvīpa, six other islands of various forms are proclaimed here on earth as repositories of diverse jewels. (13)
Aṅgadwīpa, Yamadwīpa, and Malayadwīpa;
Śaṅkhadwīpa, Kuśadwīpa, and Varāhadwīpa as well. ||14||
Learn now of the island of Aṅga, crowded with various assemblies and filled with diverse tribes of Mlecchas; that island is of great extent. (15)
It was a terrestrial mine of gems filled with gold and coral,
variegated with rivers, mountains, and forests, resembling the salt ocean.
There is a mountain named Cakragiri, possessing many waterfalls and caves; there, moreover, is its cave, which serves as a refuge for various creatures.
In the midst of the land of the Nāgas, that great mountain was not situated in a single spot;
having reached the lord of rivers with its two peaks, it became the abode of the Nāgas.
It is called Yamadvīpa, adorned with various mines of jewels;
there also stands a mountain named Dyutimat, embellished with minerals,
which is the source of rivers flowing to the ocean and the origin of gold.
In the very same way, the island of Malaya was likewise well-enclosed,
a vast source of precious gems and a mine of gold.
It was a source of sandalwood and likewise a source of oceans;
it was crowded with various tribes of Mlecchas and adorned with rivers and mountains.
Therein lies the glorious Malaya mountain, a mine of silver;
it is renowned as Mahāmalaya, an excellent mountain. ||22||
The second, renowned on earth as Mandara, is the abode of Agastya, which is honored by both gods and asuras. (23)
Likewise, there was the hermitage of Kāñcanapāda and another, Malayā, which was frequented by the meritorious and adorned with groves of grass and soma plants.
Endowed with various flowers and fruits, it excels even heaven;
there, heaven itself descends on every auspicious festival day.
Likewise, in the abode of Trikūṭa, adorned with various minerals, rising many yojanas high, with its variegated peaks serving as a mountain-like dwelling; ||26||
On its delightful peak stood a city with golden walls and arches,
adorned with various turrets and balconies, and lined with rows of mansions and palaces.
A hundred yojanas in width and thirty yojanas in length, there is a great city named Laṅkā, ever-joyful and prosperous. (28)
One should know that city to be the abode of the high-souled Rākṣasas who can assume any form at will,
the residence of those arrogant in their strength, and the dwellers of the gods' enemies;
for that great city is unassailable and inaccessible to human beings.
On the eastern shore of that island, the lord of rivers and streams,
there is the great abode of Śaṅkara known by the name Gokarṇa.
Likewise, one should know that there is a single kingdom situated on Śaṅkhadvīpa, extending for a hundred yojanas and serving as the abode of various hosts of mlecchas. ||31||
Therein lies the mountain named Śaṅkhagiri, possessing the luster of polished conch shells;
it is a source of various jewels, meritorious, and frequented by those who perform virtuous deeds. ||32||
The Śaṅkha Nāgas are of great merit, from whom this river originates, where the Nāga king named Śaṅkhamukha has made his abode. ||33||
In the same way, there was the auspicious Kumudadvīpa, adorned with various merits, filled with various villages, and containing various mines of jewels. ||34||
The highly fortunate one named Kumudā, who destroys evil intentions, is the sister of Mahādeva; she is worshipped by those very splendors.
Likewise, on Varāhadvīpa, which is crowded with various hosts of mlecchas, filled with various guilds, and contains various cities and settlements; (36)
It was abundant, filled with wealth and grain, crowded with righteous people, and variegated with rivers, mountains, and forests abounding in many flowers and fruits. ||37||
There is a delightful mountain there named Varāhaparvata, a mass of rock adorned with many caves, ravines, caverns, and waterfalls. ||38||
Therefore, this great river named Vārāhī, which bestows boons, flows forth from it— a stream of holy pilgrimage sites with water as sweet as nectar.
There, the brahmins, having no other deity, pay homage to that powerful Viṣṇu who has assumed the form of a boar. 1.48.40.
Thus have these six sub-continents been described all around;
indeed, the region of Bhāratadvīpa is very extensive in the south.
Thus, this single continent is said here to have many islands;
it is traditionally held to be a single landmass divided into sections by the waters of the ocean.
Thus, the extent of Jambūdvīpa is fully described, consisting of the four great continents adorned with intermediate islands and accompanied by the secondary islands. ||43||
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the World," in the Great Purāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
I shall describe Plakṣadvīpa correctly and in brief;
listen, O best of the twice-born, as I speak this according to the truth. 1.
Its width is twice that of Jambūdvīpa; its circumference all around is three times its width. This salt-water ocean is surrounded by that island.
There, the provinces are meritorious and the people die only after a long time;
for how could there be famine, and whence could there be the fear of old age and disease? (3)
There too, there are seven bright mountains adorned with jewels; likewise, there are oceans and rivers—their names, O friend, I shall now declare. (4)
In each of those seven [sub-continents] beginning with Plakṣadvīpa,
there are always mountains situated straight and extended in every direction.
Now I shall describe the seven great mountain ranges in Plakṣadvīpa.
Here, the first mountain is Gomeda, which resembles a cloud;
indeed, the region is known by its name as Gomedaka.
The second mountain was Candra, endowed with all medicinal herbs;
there the herbs were situated for the sake of the nectar by the two Aśvins.
The third is named Nārada, a formidable mountain of great height;
on that mountain, the two mountains Nārada and Parvata were formerly born.
There, indeed, is the fourth mountain, known by the name Dundubhi. In ancient times, Death in the form of Sound was struck upon that mountain with a drum by the gods.
It is made of rope, consists of ropes, and is a Śālmalī tree that brings about the end of the Asuras.
The fifth was named Somaka, where in ancient times the nectar of immortality was collected and carried away by Garuḍa for the sake of his mother.
The sixth, however, named Sumanas, was called Ṛṣabha;
he was slain by Varāha on that mountain along with Hiraṇyākṣa. ||11||
The seventh there is Vaibhrāja, a great, radiant crystal mountain;
because it shines with rays of light, it is known as Vaibhrāja.
I shall describe their regions in order by name:
the first region is Gomeda, known by the name Śāntabhaya. (13)

The peak of Candra is named Sukhodaya; that of Nārada is Ānanda; that of Dundubhi is remembered as Śiva; that of Somaka is Kṣemaka; that of Ṛṣabha is Vaibhrāja; and likewise, that of Dhruva is Dhruva.
In these [places], gods, gandharvas, and siddhas, together with the cāraṇas, sport and take delight, being visible to those [beings]. (15)
Each of those regions has seven rivers flowing toward the ocean;
I shall state their names, beginning with the great river Saptagaṅgā.
Those rivers flow into it, as do thousands of others—
abounding in water and surging with currents— from wherever Vāsava sends down rain.
Those people of yours always drink from those rivers—the auspicious ones, those with tranquil currents, those that bring delight, and those that are propitious. ||18||
Then, among them all, the subjects were endowed with the conduct appropriate for their castes and stages of life; they were joyful, steadfast, secure, and accompanied by auspiciousness. (19)
All beings were free from disease, possessed great strength, and were devoid of illness;
for them there was neither the aeon of decline (avasarpiṇī) nor the aeon of increase (utsarpiṇī).
There is no state of the Yuga-periods created by the four ages anywhere there;
at all times, a period equal to the Tretā Yuga prevails there.
In all five of these, beginning with Plakṣadvīpa, it should be known that the divisions of time are recorded according to the specific characteristics of each region. ||22||
Human beings live for five thousand years in those [ages];
they are handsome, well-attired, free from disease, and likewise strong. (23)
Happiness, long life, strength, beauty, health, and indeed righteousness are to be known as existing in the islands beginning with Plakṣadvīpa and ending with Śākadvīpa. (24)
Plakṣa-dvīpa is vast and glorious, abounding on all sides with wealth and grain;
it is endowed with divine medicinal herbs and fruits, as well as every kind of herb and forest tree.

O best of the twice-born, it is surrounded by thousands of all kinds of animals from both villages and forests; in its center stands a great tree known as the Jambū tree, and because of that, it is called by its name.
There, that Sthāṇu is indeed worshipped in the midst of the country;
and that region of the sugarcane juice ocean is surrounded by Plakṣadvīpa.
And here, regarding the extent and breadth of Plakṣadvīpa: [27]
Thus has this configuration of Plakṣadvīpa been described to you in due order and in brief; now learn of Śālmala [dvīpa].
Next, the third among the islands is the excellent Śālmala island;
the ocean of sugarcane juice surrounds this Śālmala island with a breadth twice that of Plakṣa island.
Therein, seven mountain ranges are to be known as the sources of jewels,
and likewise, there are rivers that serve as mines of gems within those seven regions.
The first mountain, resembling the sun, is named Kumuda; its peaks, composed of all kinds of minerals, rise up like masses of rock.
The second mountain of that [range] is renowned by the name Unnata;
it stands covering the heavens with its peaks composed of yellow orpiment.
The third mountain of that [range] is known as Balāhaka;
it stands covering the heavens with its peaks made of pure collyrium.
The fourth mountain is Droṇa, where there are medicinal herbs of great power,
such as the Viśalyakaraṇī and the Mṛtasañjīvanī.
The fifth mountain there is Kaṅka, which brings great prosperity;
it is endowed with divine flowers and fruits and is covered with trees and creepers.
The sixth mountain there is Mahiṣa, resembling a cloud,
upon which that fire named Mahiṣa, born of water, resides.
The seventh mountain there is called Kakudmat;
there Vāsava himself rains down many jewels.
This ordinance belongs to the Prājāpatya region, beginning from Prajāpati.
Thus, these are the seven mountains on Śālmala, adorned with jewels. I shall now describe their seven auspicious regions:
from Kumuda comes the first, Śveta; and that of Unnata is Lohita. (38)
The [weapon] of Balāhaka is remembered as Jīmūta; that of Droṇa is Harita; that of Kaṅka is named Vaidyuta; and that of Mahiṣa is Mānasa. (39)
Kakuda is named Suprabha; these are the seven regions, each divided into seven parts.
Now learn of the mountains and the rivers within them.
Pānītā, Vitṛṣṇā, Candrā, Śukrā, Vimocanī, and Nivṛtti as the seventh—these are traditionally taught to occur once every year. ||41||
There were hundreds and thousands of others who approached them,
impossible to enumerate in full, yet worthy of faith by one desiring prosperity.
Thus has this configuration of Śālmaladvīpa been described to you;
in its center stands a great tree, reckoned as the Plakṣa tree.
There is a śālmali tree with massive trunks, and it is named after that;
the śālmali is surrounded on all sides by the Suroda ocean, which is equal in extent to the śālmali itself on every side. ||44||
But listen, O subjects, as I speak according to what has been heard and according to the right principle regarding the northern continents, you who know the dharma. ||45||
I shall now describe Kuśadvīpa, the fourth, in brief:
it is surrounded on all sides by the ocean of excellent wine (suroda), which is itself encircled by Kuśadvīpa.
Understand now that there are exactly seven mountains described therein, each being double the extent of Śālmala on all sides. ||47||
In Kukṣadvīpa, however, the mountain known as Vidrumoccaya is to be understood;
it is the first mountain of that island, and the second is the Hemaparvata.
The third mountain is named Dyutimat, resembling a cloud;
the fourth is named Puṣpavat, and the fifth is Kuśeśaya.
The sixth is named Harigiri, and the seventh is remembered as Mandara;
for "manda" is a name for waters, and Mandara is so called because it cleaves the waters.
The intervening space between them is twice as wide and is surrounded [by mountains];
the first region is Udbhida, and the second is Veṇumaṇḍala.
The third is Svairathākāra, the fourth is known as Lavaṇa;
the fifth is the Dhṛtimat-varṣa, the sixth is the Prabhākara-varṣa,
and the seventh is named Kapila— these are the seven mountain ranges of the regions.
In these [regions], the gods and Gandharvas, the lords of the world,
dwell and take delight, being visible for many years.
In those regions there are no bandits, nor are there tribes of Mlecchas;
all the people are predominantly fair-skinned, and they likewise die in due order [of age]. (54)
There too, there are exactly seven rivers: Dhutapāpā, Śivā, Pavitrā, Santati, Dyutigarbhā, and Mahī. (55)
Hundreds and thousands of others besides them, having been fully understood,
all approach from wherever Vāsava sends down rain.
Kuśadvīpa is surrounded on the outside by the Ghṛtoda ocean;
it should be known that this ocean is equal in extent to Kuśadvīpa itself.
Thus has this configuration of Kuśadvīpa been described to you;
hereafter, I shall speak of the extent of Krauñcadvīpa.
That [ocean] is indeed remembered as being twice the extent of Kuśadvīpa;
it is the ocean of clarified butter (ghṛtoda), surrounded by Krauñcadvīpa. ||59||
On that island, the first mountain is the best of peaks, Krauñca;
beyond Krauñca is Vāmanaka, and beyond Vāmanaka is Andhakāraka.
Beyond Andhakāra is the mountain named Divāvṛt;
beyond Divāvṛt is the mountain called Divinda.
Beyond Divinda is the great mountain Puṇḍarīka;
and beyond Puṇḍarīka, it is said, is Dundubhisvana.
These seven mountains of Krauñcadvīpa consist of jewels;
they are endowed with many trees and fruits, and are covered with various kinds of trees and creepers.
The mountain ranges are each double the width of the preceding one;
I shall now describe the regions there by name—listen.
The region of Krauñca is Kuśalin, and that of Vāmana is Manonuga;
beyond Manonuga, the third region is called Uṣṇa.
Beyond Uṣṇa is Prāvaraka; beyond Prāvaraka is Andhakāraka;
and beyond the region of Andhakāraka, the region of the Munis is traditionally taught.
Beyond the region of the Munis is said to be Dundubhisvana;
it is known to be crowded with Siddhas and Cāraṇas, and its people are mostly fair-skinned.
There too, seven auspicious rivers are recorded for each region:
Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Sandhyā, Rātri, Manojavā, Khyāti, and Puṇḍarīkā; thus the Gaṅgā is said to be sevenfold.
All those other rivers that flow toward the ocean and join them— vast and carrying abundant water— follow after them.
The glorious Krauñcadvīpa is surrounded on all sides by an ocean of curd-cream water, which is equal in extent to Krauñcadvīpa itself.
These islands, beginning with Plakṣadvīpa, have thus been briefly described;
such is the entire natural arrangement of those islands in their successive order.
It is not possible to describe this in detail even in hundreds of years—neither this natural disposition of living beings nor the dissolution that occurs among them. (72)
Henceforth I shall proclaim the rule concerning Śākadvīpa;
I shall describe the entirety of Śākadvīpa here according to its true determination.
Listen indeed to me as I speak the truth exactly as it is. 73.
Twice the extent of Krauñcadvīpa is its own breadth;
it stands surrounding the ocean whose waters are like the scum of curdled milk.
There, the regions are meritorious and people die only after a long time;
how then could there be famine, and whence could there be the fear of wild beasts and disease? (75)
There too, there are seven bright mountains adorned with jewels;
likewise, there are mines of gems and rivers—listen to their names from me. (76)
The first mountain, joined by celestial sages and gandharvas, is called Meru;
extending toward the east, it is the golden mountain named Udaya.
There, the clouds arise and depart for the sake of rain;
beyond that is another very great mountain, Jaladhāra.
Therefore, Vāsava constantly takes up the supreme water;
from that, rain arises here for all creatures during the rainy season.
Beyond that is Raivataka, where the constellation Revatī is eternally established in the sky; it is a mountain created by the Grandfather (Brahmā).
To its west was a very great mountain named Śyāma;
it is said that from this mountain these present subjects formerly acquired their dark complexion.
Beyond that is known the great mountain Asta, made of silver;
beyond that is the Ambikya mountain, difficult to access and covered with snow. Beyond the Ambikya is a beautiful mountain, endowed with all medicinal herbs.
And he alone is called Keśarin, from whom the wind blows. ||83||
Listen to those names in their proper order according to tradition:
the region of Udaya’s birth is the famous Varṣa known as Jalada.
The second [tīrtha] of Jaladhāra is known as Sukumāra;
that of Raivata is Kaumāra, and that of Śyāma is Maṇīcaka. ||85||
The auspicious year of that [king] should be known as Kusumottara;
[the years] of Āmbikeya are Modaka and Mahādruma among the Kesaras. 86.
The measurement of the continent, as well as its breadth and length, is renowned through Śākadvīpa; in its center stands a great tree named Śāka, which they worship. (87)
By this [means], the gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas sport and take delight, being seen together with them.
Therein lie meritorious provinces inhabited by the four castes;
know that in each of those regions there are exactly seven rivers flowing to the ocean,
all of which are known by the name Gaṅgā and are traditionally reckoned as sevenfold.
The first is Sukumārī, and likewise Gaṅgā with its auspicious waters;
thereafter, the river is celebrated by the name Anutaptā.
The one named Kumārī is established as the second;
furthermore, that virtuous one is Nandā and Pārvatī, who is proclaimed as the third. ||91||
Śivetikā should be the fourth, and Tridivā is likewise remembered;
Ikṣu is to be known as the fifth, and likewise Kratu again. ||92||
And Dhenukā is indeed dead; she is proclaimed as the sixth.
These seven great Gaṅgās, possessing auspicious waters every year, nourish all the people dwelling in Śākadvīpa. ||93||
Thousands of other rivers and streams with abundant flowing waters follow those [rivers] from wherever Vāsava sends down rain.
But their names and likewise their dimensions cannot be fully enumerated; those excellent rivers are all meritorious. The people of those regions always drink from those rivers with great joy.
O Śaṃśapāyana, this island is vast, circular in shape,
covered with river waters and mountains resembling clouds.
And with cities of various forms adorned with gems and corals of all kinds of colors, as well as flourishing provinces.

Śākadvīpa is surrounded on all sides by trees endowed with flowers and fruits, and it is rich in wealth and grain; it is encircled everywhere by the Ocean of Milk, and its extent is equal on all sides. (98)
In that region, situated amidst mountains, there are seven auspicious and holy provinces, filled with people of all castes and stages of life; these are indeed remembered as the seven lands. ||99||
There was no confusion among them anywhere caused by caste or stage of life;
and because their dharma was never deviated from, the subjects were exclusively happy.
In them there is no greed or deceit, nor envy, malice, or lack of fortitude; in them there is no error, for this is known to be their innate nature. 101.
Among them there is no production of karma, no punishment, and no punishers;
knowing the dharma, they protect one another solely by means of their own dharma.
This much indeed is possible for those dwelling on that island;
now I shall describe the seventh island, Puṣkara—listen. (103)
Surrounded on the outside by the Puṣkara island,
the Sea of Milk extends all around with a circumference twice the width of Śākadvīpa.
In Puṣkara, there is a single, glorious mountain of great rock, with variegated peaks made of jewels and lofty crags. ||105||
On the eastern half of that continent stands the great Citrasānu,
extending twenty-five thousand yojanas in circumference.
And extending upwards for thirty-four thousand [yojanas], the mountain Mānasottama forms the outer boundary of half the continent. 107.
Standing near the shore like the newly risen moon, it rose fifty thousand yojanas into the sky. ||108||
At that very time, that extensive and perfectly circular mountain Mānasa stands thus in the southern half of the continent.
This single great mountain range is divided into two parts by its configuration;
it is surrounded on all sides by the ocean of sweet water.
This [continent] is as extensive as Puṣkaradvīpa on all sides.
On that island, two auspicious and meritorious regions are recorded,
situated on both sides of the circular range of Mount Mānasa.
That region which lies outside of Mānasa is called Mahāvīta;
that which lies within it is known as Dhātakīkhaṇḍa.
There, human beings live for ten thousand years,
abounding in health and happiness, and established in mental perfection.
During those two years, their lifespan and physical form remained equal;
among them there were neither low nor high, for they were identical in appearance and character. ||114||
Therein there is no deceiver, no envy, no thief, nor likewise any fear;
there is neither restraint nor punishment, neither greed nor possessiveness. (115)
There, neither truth nor falsehood exists, nor likewise merit or demerit;
nor is there any mention of the castes and stages of life, nor agriculture, cattle-rearing, or trade.
The threefold knowledge, the science of government, service, and even surgery—all this is not found among the Puṣkaras within two years. (117)
There are no rivers there, nor does rain exist, nor is there cold or heat; here the waters are springing forth from the mountain cascades.
And the people of Uttarakuru always exist at the same time;
everywhere there they are exceedingly happy, free from old age and fatigue. (119)
Thus has this Dhātakīkhaṇḍa been described, as well as Mahāvīta;
in this same sequence, the entire arrangement of Puṣkara has been proclaimed.
Puṣkara is surrounded by the ocean of sweet water;
its extent and circumference are exactly like those of Puṣkara itself.
In this way, the continents are surrounded by seven oceans;
each ocean extends all around the continent that immediately precedes it. (122)
In this way, the increase of the continents and oceans should be understood relative to one another;
they are designated as "oceans" because of the overflowing of water. (123)
Because the sages and the fourfold classes of progeny dwell herein, it is therefore called a "Varṣa" (region); may that be a source of happiness for all beings. 124.

"Ṛṣi" means "seers" (ṛṣayaḥ); "vṛṣa" refers to the act of raining down power (śaktiprabandhane). Thus, because of this act of raining down, their status as "rainers" (varṣatva) is established, and that [status] belongs to them. ||125||
When the moon waxes during the bright fortnight, the ocean then fills up;
when the dark fortnight diminishes and the bird [the moon] has set, it ebbs away.
When the ocean is being filled, it is filled by itself;
likewise, when it is diminishing, it is depleted by its own nature.
Just as water contained in a cauldron overflows due to contact with fire, so too does the water situated in the great ocean overflow from it. 128.
Neither diminished nor increased,
the waters of the ocean rise and fall through the rising and setting of the moon during its bright and dark fortnights;
thus, the waxing and waning of the ocean occurs again in accordance with the increase and decrease of the moon.
An increase and decrease of exactly five hundred and ten finger-breadths is observed in the waters of the oceans during the changes of the moon's phases.
They are called "dvīpas" (islands) because they are surrounded on all sides by water;
and because it is the receptacle of water, it is therefore called the "udadhi" (ocean).
Mountains that lack joints are known as *girayaḥ*, while those with joints are called *parvatāḥ*;
in Plakṣadvīpa, however, there is a mountain named Gomeda, and for that reason it is so called.
In Śālmaladvīpa, the great tree Śālmali is worshipped;
in Kuśadvīpa, there is a clump of Kuśa grass, and it is named after that.
In Krauñcadvīpa, there is a mountain named Krauñca in the center of the region;
in Śākadvīpa, there is a Śāka tree, and it is called by that name.
Nyagrodha is on Puṣkaradvīpa; there he was saluted by them.
But Mahādeva is at Puṣkara, while Brahmā is the lord of the three worlds. ||135||
In that place dwells Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, together with the Sādhyas;
there the thirty-three gods, along with the great seers, pay him homage.
There, that most excellent of the best of gods is indeed worshipped by the deities.
Various kinds of jewels originate from Jambūdvīpa;
indeed, throughout all those islands, there are successions of living beings here.
Through complete celibacy, truthfulness, and self-restraint, one's lifespan and measure of health shall indeed be doubled on all sides. ||138||
In this Puṣkaradvīpa, regarding the two regions that have been described, he himself protects the subjects there, who are adorned by virtuous people. (139)
The Lord Brahmā, the sovereign of the three worlds, together with Viṣṇu, the god Śiva, the Pitṛs, and the Grandfather (Pitāmaha), raised their staffs.
And there, food endowed with the six flavors and great potency appeared spontaneously before them without effort, which the subjects always consumed. (141)
Beyond Puṣkara,
moreover, stands the great ocean of sweet water, which is surrounded on all sides by an enclosure.
Beyond that, a vast world-structure is seen;
the golden ground there is twice as large, and it is entirely like a single solid rock.
Beyond that, at the boundary of the limit, is the mountain range Maṇḍala;
it is called Lokāloka because it is both illuminated and unilluminated. ||144||
It is luminous on its near side, but devoid of light beyond that;
its height is recorded as ten thousand yojanas.
Its extent on earth was equal to that, and it moved at will;
the word "world" (loka) applies to the realm of light, while "salokatā" refers to the state of being in the lightless realm.
The world is considered for the sake of the worlds, yet it is lightless on its exterior.
The light extends everywhere outside the extent of the world;
it is delimited on all sides and covered by water,
and beyond that darkness stands the cosmic egg, enveloping it.

Within this egg are these worlds: the earth with its seven continents, as well as the world of the physical (bhūrloka), the atmospheric world (bhuvarloka), the celestial world (svarloka), and likewise the world of great light (maharloka).
Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka—this much constitutes the collection of worlds;
it should be understood as being essentially one, and beyond that lies the end of the worlds.
Just as the moon appears when it first stands in the pitcher-like sign (Kumbha) in the western direction at the beginning of the bright fortnight, such was the form of the Egg.
Thousands of millions of such eggs are to be known as existing horizontally,
upwards, and downwards from the imperishable Self who is the Cause;
for there, it is enveloped by sevenfold layers of primordial causal elements.
They support one another with an increase of tenfold;
all are mutually enveloped and have arisen from one another.
Surrounding this egg on all sides is the ocean of solid water (ghanodadhi), by which it is supported and remains in its place on every side.
On the outside, the circular mass of dense water, being supported on all sides by dense fire, remains stable both horizontally and vertically. (154)
The fire, resembling a glowing iron ball and circular in shape, remains supported on all sides by the dense wind (ghanavāta);
likewise, the dense wind remains supporting space (ākāśa). ||155||
The source of the elements (bhūtādi) is likewise space, and that great one (mahat) is also the source of the elements;
for the Great One is pervaded by and sustained by the infinite Unmanifest (avyakta). 156.
It is infinite, unmanifest, and subtle in ten ways;
it is infinite, uncreated, and without beginning or end.
Having passed beyond that other terrible [realm], which is without support, free from disease, extending for many thousands of yojanas, remote, and shrouded in darkness; 158.
It is indeed darkness—devoid of light, without boundaries, without a guide, unknown even to the gods, and devoid of all worldly activity. ||159||
At the end of darkness and at the end of space, it is renowned as radiant;
beyond that boundary lies the great abode of Śiva.
According to sacred tradition, that divine place is inaccessible even to the thirty gods;
it is situated within the boundary of the Great God of Gods. 161.
Those worlds which are illuminated by the moon and the sun and are renowned by the wise are called "the worlds" (loka), and there is no doubt that they belong to the world-system (jagat). ||162||
O twice-born ones, from the bottom of the netherworld (rasātala) there are seven layers above it on the earth;
likewise, there are seven columns of wind, including the abode of Brahmā.
From the netherworld (Pātāla) up to heaven, there are five types of destinies here;
this is the extent of the world, this ocean of saṃsāra. ||164||
Thus, beginningless and endless, arising from many births, that manifold activity of the world indeed proceeds in an unstable manner. 165.
Just as this so-called material world, though naturally vast in extent, is not perceived even by the great-souled Siddhas who possess super-sensory faculties. ||166||
O best of the twice-born, [he is likewise the essence] of the earth, fire, wind, and great darkness, as well as of the divine Lord Ananta.
Neither exhaustion, nor measure, nor even an end is found;
he is recited as infinite everywhere and in all places. And this was previously stated by me in that enumeration of names. ||168||
That which has indeed been proclaimed to you in its entirety under the name of Śiva is he who has gone everywhere and is worshipped in all places. (169)
On the earth, in the subterranean realm, in the sky, in the wind, in the fire,
in all the oceans, and even in heaven— of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, in the practice of austerity, this very one of great splendor is to be known;
the Great Yogin, Maheśvara, whose limbs are divided into many forms, the Lord of all worlds, is worshipped in many ways as the Sovereign throughout all the worlds. ||171||

Thus, these modifications, arising from one another, are supported by one another; they exist as the relationship between the container and the contained within that which undergoes modification. (172)
The modifications, such as earth and the rest, are limited to one another,
mutually superior, and indeed interpenetrated by one another.
Because they have entered into one another, they have attained stability;
for previously they were indeed without distinction, but through mutual entry they became distinct. And those three, beginning with earth and ending with air, are limited.
The discernment of the remaining [qualities] is particularly characterized by the diminution of their attributes;
however, because of their subtlety, they are not clearly distinguished here.
For beyond those elements, light is traditionally held to exist;
and within space, the elements and the light are all entirely delimited.
Just as various vessels placed within a large vessel exist without being distinct from one another,
owing to their mutual dependence,
so too are the various divisions considered to be contained within the light in space. ||177||
All these four are complete, yet each is superior to the others; as long as these elements exist, so long is their arising proclaimed. (178)
In this world, the formative predispositions (saṃskāra) of living beings are considered to be included within the primary elements;
and apart from the primary elements, the production of any effect is not observed.
Therefore, those limited distinctions are known as being of the nature of effects;
likewise, those distinctions such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest are of the nature of causes.
Thus, O twice-born ones, this arrangement of the seven islands and oceans has been declared by me to you in its various divisions according to their true nature.
Indeed, through its expansion, its contraction, and its enumeration,
the manifold form of Pradhāna is characterized by a limited measure.
The Blessed One is the foundation upon which this entire world rests;
thus are the seven classes of beings established in relation to one another.
"O King, regarding this arrangement, only this much can be explained by me; indeed, only this much is to be heard concerning the arrangement. (184)
These seven primary natures (prakṛtis) sustain one another;
among them, an enumeration is here stated by way of illustration, for the primary natures that exist transversely, upwards, and downwards are innumerable. (185)
The arrangement of the stars and the divine sphere,
as well as the configuration of the earth's boundaries and its corresponding mandala—
beyond this, O best of the twice-born, I shall indeed describe that which pertains to the earth.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Worlds," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Now, listen as the measurement below and above is described:
earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth—these are indeed proclaimed as the infinite elements that are all-pervasive. (1)
The earth is the mother of all beings and the sustainer of all beings;
she is filled with various provinces and possesses various capitals and cities.
The goddess Earth, vast in extent and infinite, is sung of as being filled with various mountains and rivers, and teeming with many species of beings. (3)
Those situated in rivers, streams, and oceans, as well as those dwelling in small reservoirs; those located on mountains and in the sky, and those that have entered beneath the earth. (4)
The waters are to be known as infinite, and likewise fire is common to all the worlds;
it is recited as being infinite, pervasive, and the source of all things. ||5||
Likewise, space is known to be without support, delightful, the locus of various things, infinite, and all-pervading; and wind is born from space.
The waters are upon the earth, and the earth stands above the water;
the sky is below that, and again there is earth, and again water. (7)
Thus, there exists no end to the infinite material world;
listen now to that which was declared by the gods of old and is established as certain. (8)
Earth, water, and space—this is to be known as the succession;
this is to be understood as the state of existence within this seventh subterranean realm, Rasātala.
The netherworld (rasātala) consists of ten thousand yojanas and is a single level;
it is renowned among the virtuous as being each one vast in extent.
First is Atala, and after that Sutala;
beyond that, one should know Vitala, which is very extensive.
Beyond that is the region named Gabhastala, and further still is Mahātala; they say Śrītala follows after that, and Pātāla is remembered as the seventh.
The first portion of ground is proclaimed to be black soil;
the second is white soil, and the third is red clay. ||13||
The fourth is the yellow earth, the fifth is the layer of gravel,
the sixth consists of stone, and the seventh layer is made of gold.
On the first level, however, is renowned the palace of the lord of the asuras, the abode of Namuci, Indra’s enemy, and Mahānāda. (15)
And he saw the city of Śaṅkukarṇa and the palace of Kabandha,
as well as the city of Niṣkulāda, which was crowded with joyful people.
And [he went to] the abode of Rākṣasa and Bhīma, and of Śūladanta; as well as the city of Lohitākṣa and that of Kaliṅga and Śvāpada.
And the city of Dhanañjaya, and that of the high-souled Mahendra,
as well as the cities of the nāga Kāliya and of Kalaśa.
In this manner, thousands of cities belonging to the Nāgas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas are to be known as being on the first level, the black ground; of this there is no doubt. (19)
On the second level as well, O Brahmins, were the cities of the lord of Daityas, Surakṣas, and likewise that of Mahājambha, the first.
The palace of Hayagrīva, of Kṛṣṇa, and of Nikumbha;
and the city and town of the one named Śaṅkha, and of Gomukha.
And [he destroyed] the city of the Rākṣasa Nīla, as well as that of Megha and Krathana,
and the abode of Purañjaya and Mahoṣṇīṣa.
And the city of the Naga Kambala, and the city of Aśvatara, and the city of the high-souled Takṣaka, the son of Kadrū. ||23||
In this same way, O brahmins, there are thousands of cities of the nāgas, dānavas, and rākṣasas on this second level, the Pāṇḍubhūmi; of this there is no doubt.
On the third level, however, the city of the high-souled Prahlāda is depicted, as well as the city of Anuhlāda, the great-souled lord of the Daityas. ||25||
And there was the city named Tāraka, as well as the city of Triśiras,
and the city of Śiśumāra, crowded with joyful and well-fed people.
And one must know the abode of Cyavana, as well as the residence of the Rākṣasa,
the city of Kumbhīla the lord of Rākṣasas, and that of Khara.
And [he conquered] the city of the cruel Virādha and of Ulkāmukha, as well as that of the nāga Hemaka and likewise of Pāṇḍuraka. ||28||
The city of Maṇimantra and the palace of Kapila;
the abode of Nanda and the residence of Viśāla, the lord of serpents.
In this same way, O brahmins, there are thousands of cities belonging to the Nāgas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas on this third level, the yellow earth; of this there is no doubt.
In the fourth [region] are the cities of the great-souled Kālanemi, the lion among Daityas,
as well as Gajakarṇa and Kuñjara.
And [he saw] the very extensive city of Sumāli, the lord of the Rākṣasas;
as well as the abode of Muñja, the protector of the world, and that of Vṛkavaktra.
In this fourth subterranean realm (rasātala), there is the city of Vainateya, extending for many thousands of yojanas and teeming with many birds.
In the fifth subterranean realm, Śarkarābhūmi, which extends for many yojanas,
lies the city of Virocana, the wise lion among the Daityas.
He went to the abode of Agnijihva Vaiḍūrya and Hiraṇyākṣa, as well as to the city of the wise Rākṣasa Vidyujjihva. ||35||
And [the cities] of Mahāmegha, the lord of Rākṣasas Śālina, of the Nāga Karmāra, and of Svastika and Jaya. ||36||
In this same manner, thousands of cities of the nāgas, dānavas,
and rākṣasas are always to be known as existing in the fifth layer, Śarkarānilaya.
On the sixth level is the excellent city of Kesari, the lord of the Daityas;
the cities of Suparvan and Suloman; and the city of Mahisha;
and the city of the high-souled Utkrosha, the lord of the Rakshasas. ||38||
There dwells the son of Surasā, the illustrious king of serpents named Vāsuki, the hundred-headed son of Kaśyapa, filled with joy.
In this same way, there are thousands of cities belonging to the Nāgas, Dānavas,
and Rākṣasas on this famous sixth level, the rocky ground of Rasātala.
In the seventh layer, in the very last subterranean realm (pātāla), one should know the city of Bali, which is exceedingly joyful and crowded with men and women. ||41||
There, indeed, was the great city of the Daitya Mucukunda, filled with Asuras who were like venomous serpents and had been uprooted by the enemies of the gods.
By many great cities of the sons of Diti that had risen up,
and likewise by thousands of powerful cities of the Nāgas.
It was crowded with the great cities of the Daityas and Dānavas that had flourished there,
as well as with many flourishing abodes of the Rākṣasas.
And at the end of Pātāla, O best of Brahmins, in a vast expanse extending many yojanas,
dwells that great-souled one with eyes like red lotuses, who is indeed free from old age and death.
With a body like the interior of a polished conch shell, clad in blue garments, long-armed,
possessing great coils, radiant, wearing a variegated garland, and powerful.
With his thousand faces, which shine with radiant mouths as bright as gold-adorned horns, that lord, wearing earrings, truly shines forth.
With his tongue like a garland of flickering flames of fire, the god, encircled by a wreath of flames, appears like Mount Kailāsa. ||48||
With his two thousand shining eyes,
which were copper-red like the rising sun, he appeared beautiful with his smooth, radiant orb.
Upon him, who has the complexion of a jasmine flower or the moon, his rosary shines resplendent, like a garland of young suns upon the summit of the White Mountain.
Resplendent with matted locks, he was seen upon his bed as if he were a vast mountain with a thousand peaks spread across the earth. ||51||
The Lord of Great Nagas himself, possessed of great splendor, is personally attended by those of great enjoyments, great fortune, great serpents, and great strength.
That king of all the Nāgas, named Śeṣa, possessed of great splendor,
was indeed that body of Viṣṇu established as the boundary.
Thus, these seven habitable netherworlds (rasātala) have been described, which are constantly inhabited by gods, asuras, great nāgas, and rākṣasas. 54.
Beyond this is that which cannot be seen, which is inaccessible even to perfected beings and holy men,
unknown even to gods and humans, and devoid of worldly activity.
O best of the twice-born, the greatness of earth, fire, water, wind, and space is thus described by the sages; there is no doubt in this matter.
Henceforth, I shall describe the motion of the sun and the moon;
for as long as these two, the sun and the moon, revolve, they illuminate by their own natures, established in their respective orbs. ||57||
The extent of the seven oceans and the continents is equal;
half of that extent belongs to the earth, while the remainder lies outside. ||58||
The extent of the circumference is illuminated by the moon and the sun;
by that measure of the circumference, heaven is recorded as being equal to the earth.

Because the sun, revolving around these three worlds, protects them, he is known as the "Protector" (Avadhātṛ) due to his illumination; indeed, from this act of protection (avana), he is remembered as Ravi.
Hereafter, I shall declare the dimensions of the moon and the sun;
for because of its greatness, the word "mahī" (earth) is applied to this continent.
Now learn of the very extensive diameter of this Bhāratavarṣa, which is equal to the orb of the sun in yojanas. 62.
The diameter of the sun is nine thousand yojanas; its circumference, which is the circle of its orb, is three times its diameter. The moon’s diameter is twice that of the sun. (63)
Therefore, I shall describe the measurement of the earth in yojanas,
as well as the extent and circumference of the seven continents and oceans.
Thus has this Purāṇa been enumerated here according to its extent; I shall now state that same number by calculating it in terms of the current units of measure.
Those who have transcended the presiding deities (abhimānin) are here equal to those of the present; for those gods who have passed away are identical [to the current ones] in both form and name.
Therefore, I shall describe the surface of the earth as it is now,
for the entire arrangement of heaven is indeed according to its present state.
The entire earth is recorded as being five hundred million [yojanas] in extent;
the space between the four boundaries of Meru is equal to half its measure.
The extent of the earth's diameter is proclaimed to be one hundred million yojanas;
from the center of Meru, it is recorded as eleven crores in each direction.
Likewise, the extent of the earth's diameter is eighty-nine thousand nine hundred and fifty thousand [yojanas]. (1.50.70)
Learn from me the entire extent of the earth in yojanas:
its width in the four directions is reckoned at three crores. (71)
Likewise, seventy-nine less one hundred thousand [yojanas] is said to be the extent of the earth consisting of seven continents and oceans. (72)
The circumference of the sphere ending at the earth is three times its diameter;
in calculation, it is recorded as eleven crores of yojanas.
Likewise, there are one hundred thousand and thirty-seven [yojanas];
this indeed is reckoned as the extent of the circle ending with the earth.
For as great as the sphere of the arrangement of stars is in the sky, so great is the sphere of the arrangement of the earth below. (75)
The heaven is remembered as being equal in circumference to the earth;
this is proclaimed to be the measurement for all seven worlds. (76)
By virtue of its perfect roundness and its conformity to the circle, it is circular like a parasol above all the worlds. ||77||
The entire arrangement within which living beings reside has been established;
this is proclaimed to be the measurement of the shell of the cosmic egg.
Within this egg are these worlds: the earth with its seven continents, as well as the realms known as Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, and the third, Svarloka;
furthermore, Maharloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka is the seventh.
These seven worlds are arranged like umbrellas,
each supported separately by its own subtle covering.
And being held outside by those primary elements increased by ten parts,
as well as by the specific qualities produced through their mutual interaction.
And surrounding this egg on all sides is the dense ocean;
the entire terrestrial sphere is supported by that thick water.
Then, beyond the ocean of clouds, it is supported by the mass of fire;
the sphere of the mass of fire extends outward, sideways, and upward.
It was supported on all sides by the forest wind and established there;
likewise, the sky was supported by the dense wind, and the Great Self (Mahātman) supported the sky. 84.
Everything is enveloped by the "beginning of beings" (bhūtādi); the "great one" (mahat), which is the source of beings, is enveloped by that;
and the great one is enveloped by the infinite Pradhāna, whose nature is imperishable.
I shall describe, in due order, the cities of the world-protectors;
the measurement of the movement of the hosts of luminaries will also be fully explained.
In the eastern direction of Meru, likewise upon the summit of Mānasa,
lies the holy city of Vasvokasārā belonging to Mahendra, adorned with gold.
Furthermore, to the south of Mount Meru, upon the very summit of Lake Mānasa,
Yama, the son of Vivasvat, dwells in the city of Saṃyamanī.
Furthermore, on the western summit of Mount Meru, upon the very peak of Mānasa,
is the delightful city named Sukhā, belonging to the wise Varuṇa.
In the northern direction, upon the summit of Mount Mānasa on Meru,
the city of Soma, Vibhāvarī, is equal to that of Mahendra.
On the ridge of the Mānasottara mountain, however, the world-protectors (lokapālas) stand in the four directions for the sake of establishing righteousness and for the protection of the world. ||91||
Now learn of that course of the sun when it has reached its furthest limit during the southern solstice, which lies above and on all sides of the world-protectors. (92)
In the southern course, the sun glides like an arrow shot;
taking up the wheel of luminaries, he constantly revolves.
When the sun is situated in the middle of Amarāvatī,
its rising is said to occur there at Saṃyamana, the abode of Vaivasvata.
When the sun is situated in the middle of the *sukhā* at midnight,
it is seen rising in the *sukhā* or the *vāruṇī*.
When it is half-light at midnight and the moon sets in the northeast,
then the afternoon is prescribed for those in the southeast.
For those residing in the south-western regions, the forenoon is proclaimed [as the auspicious time];
and for those people who are in the northern path, it is the latter part of the night. (97)
Those regions which lie to the northeast, toward them the sun shines during the first watch of the night;
in this very same manner, it shines upon the northern celestial mansions. 98.
When the sun rises at midday in Sukhā, Vāruṇī, Āryyamā, Vibhāvarī, or Somapurī, [it is the time for the offering]. ||99||
When it is midnight in Amarāvatī and in the city of Yama, the sun sets;
when it is midday in the city of Soma, the sun shines with great brilliance.
When the sun rises in Amarāvatī of Mahendra,
it is midnight in Saṃyamana, and it sets in Vāruṇī.
Moving swiftly, the sun, the maker of light, revolves like a whirling firebrand;
indeed, the sun moves while the stars in the sky remain stationary. ||102||
Thus it glides along the southern edge of the four continents;
by its rising and setting, it emerges again and again.
In the forenoon and in the afternoon, he shines from two celestial abodes each;
but at midday, he alone shines with those very same rays.
Having risen, the sun blazes until the delightful midday with increasing rays; thereafter, he goes to his setting with rays that diminish.
For when sunrise and sunset are not remembered, the directions—east and west—are lost;
as much as the sun shines in front, so much does it shine behind and on both sides. (106)
Wherever the rising sun is seen, that is considered their sunrise; wherever it goes to its disappearance, that is called their sunset. (107)
Mount Meru is to the north of all [the continents], while Lokāloka is to the south.
Because of its great distance from the sun, as well as from the earth which is encircled by a rim, the rays [of the sun] are obstructed; therefore, it is not seen at night.
The appearance of the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, as well as that of the sun, and their rising and setting, are to be known by means of the measurement of their elevation. 109.
The fire and water have white radiance, while the earth has black radiance.
Due to the great distance from the sun, there is an absence of rays when it has risen;
because of this absence of rays and because they are red, there is also an absence of heat.
Wherever the sun is seen situated in its written course, it is seen at a height of one thousand yojanas. ||111||
For when the sun sets, its solar radiance departs by one quarter and enters the fire at night; therefore, it shines from afar. ||112||
Having risen again, the sun entered the south-eastern quarter;
joined with fire, the sun then heats the day.
Luminosity and heat are the two splendors of the sun and fire;
through their mutual interpenetration, they nourish one another day and night.

When the sun rises over the northern half of the earth and likewise over that southern half, night enters the waters; therefore, the waters become copper-colored due to the entry of night during the day.
When the sun sets again, the day indeed enters the waters;
therefore, the waters become white due to the entry of the day at night.
By this sequential process, at the rising and setting of the sun on the southern and northern halves of the earth,
the day and night enter the waters.
Day is called the light of the sun, while night is said to be characterized by darkness (tamas).
Therefore, night is established as that [time] when the sun is not visible, and day is remembered as that which is observed by the sun.
Thus, when the sun moves through the middle of Puṣkara, [it is day].
He traverses thirty yojanas of the earth in a mere moment. ||119||
Learn this number of yojanas for one muhūrta:
it is recorded as being exactly thirty-one hundred thousand.
Furthermore, there are fifty thousand additional [yojanas];
this is indeed prescribed as the hourly speed of the sun. ||121||
By this course of motion,
when the sun reaches the southern limit, it indeed arrives at that very limit during the month of Māgha.
Listen now to that which extends toward the southern quarter:
it is measured at ninety million yojanas in circumference. (123)
Likewise, forty-five hundred thousand [leagues]—this is ordained as the daily course of the sun. ||124||
When the sun, having turned back from the south, stands at the equinox and moves toward the northern direction of the Ocean of Milk, [it is the time for the offering]. (125)
Understand that the Maṇḍala extends as far as the Viṣuvat;
it is recorded as being three crores of yojanas in width.
Likewise, when Citrabhānu (the Sun) reaches the eighty-first hundred-thousand [yojanas] and attains the northern limit in the constellation Śravaṇā,
he moves toward the northern direction at the sixth continent, Śākadvīpa.
And in the northern quarter,
the extent of the mandala is calculated by the twice-born to be exactly one koṭi yojanas.
It is eighty million yojanas here,
and likewise fifty-eight yojanas more.
The Nāgavīthī is the northern path, while the Ajavīthī is the southern;
likewise, Mūla and the two Āṣāḍhas constitute the three risings of the Ajavīthī.
Abhijit and Svāti are the three risings of the Nāgavīthī.
Furthermore, I shall state the distance between the two poles in yojanas:
it is one hundred and thirty-one lakhs [one hundred and thirty-one hundred thousand]. (131)
The distance between the two poles is established at thirty-three plus another thirty-three yojanas from the tip of the yojana.
Between the two wooden stakes and the two lines, from south to north—I shall state their measurements in yojanas; listen to that. 133.
Between each [of these], there are seventy-one million, seven hundred thousand, and seventy-five additional [yojanas]. (134)
It is taught that [the sun] moves between two lines and two wooden boards, both externally and internally;
during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), it revolves internally through the circles.
Externally, on the right and likewise continuously in due order, there is a full hundred mandalas plus eighty more to the north. ||136||
The sun likewise moves along the southern path for that same duration;
now learn the measurement of its orbit in terms of yojanas. ||137||
In brief, twenty-one thousand and two hundred yojanas are proclaimed [as its extent]. (138)
Indeed, with twenty-one additional yojanas,
that mandala's measurement is declared to be [one hundred] yojanas.
This is the diameter of the mandala, established as its transverse extent;
indeed, the sun moves through those mandalas in succession every day.
Just as the rim of a potter's wheel turns rapidly,
so the sun turns rapidly during its southern course.
Therefore, by means of twelve swift muhūrtas, the sun traverses the superior path in the south and north in a short time. ||142||
The sun moves through thirteen and a half constellations during the day,
and likewise it traverses those same constellations at night in eighteen muhūrtas.
Just as [the clay] moves slowly in the middle of a potter's wheel, so the sun moves with slow progress during its northern course (udagayana). ||144||
The sun moves through half of thirteen constellations in half [a day];
therefore, it reaches the earth with great slowness over a long period of time.
The final day of the northern course consists of eighteen muhūrtas,
and during that time, he moves with slow gait.
The sun traverses half of thirteen constellations by means of half [a day];
likewise, moving at night through eighteen constellations, it traverses them by means of as many muhūrtas.
Then the wheel indeed revolves more slowly than those two;
just as a lump of clay situated in the middle, so indeed does Dhruva revolve.
Dhruva, revolving, describes a day and night consisting of thirty muhūrtas;
he revolves through the circles situated between the two poles.
Just as the hub of a potter’s wheel remains fixed right there, so indeed should the Pole Star (Dhruva) be understood to revolve right there. ||1.50.150||
The circles described by the sun as it revolves between the two poles (kāṣṭhā) during day and night constitute its slow and swift motions respectively. ||151||
O Indu, it is traditionally held that during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), the movement of the sun is slow by day;
likewise, at night, the movement of the sun is indeed swift. ||152||
During the day, the movement of the sun is prescribed as swift when it is in its southern course;
at night, indeed, it is likewise recorded as slow.
Thus, distinguishing between nights and days according to the specific state of his journey,
he travels along the path, whether it be even or uneven.
Those world-protectors who are stationed in the Lokāloka mountain in the four directions—
Agastya moves above them with great speed,
traversing day and night with such specific modes of motion.
To the south of the Nāgavīthī and to the north of the Lokāloka mountain,
this [region] is indeed the deliverer of the world, situated outside the path of Vaiśvānara.
As far as the solar radiance shines behind it, so far does the light of Lokāloka shine on both sides and behind it, in every direction. (157)
The mountain rises ten thousand yojanas high;
it is both luminous and non-luminous, and is perfectly circular on all sides.
The constellations, the moon, the sun, and the planets, together with the hosts of stars,
shine within the Lokāloka mountain.
The world is indeed only this much; beyond this, it is without light.
Lokāloka is one, but that which is without light is manifold.
Because the sun connects the light of the world with its surrounding darkness, they call that interval between night and dawn "Sandhyā.
The learned know "uṣas" to be night, and "vyuṣṭi" is known as the day. (161)
Indeed, by the command of Prajāpati, a curse was pronounced upon those evil-minded Rākṣasas who seize the sun at the time of twilight:
that their bodies shall be indestructible, yet they shall likewise meet with death. ||162||
There are three crores of well-known Rākṣasas named Mandehas; every day at sunrise, those evil-minded ones seek the thousand-rayed sun,
scorching it as they desire to devour him.
Then a most terrible battle took place between Sūrya and them;
thereafter, Brahmā, the gods, and the most excellent Brāhmaṇas, performing their twilight worship (sandhyā), caused that great mass of water to subside. ||164||
Conjoined with the Brahman of the syllable Oṃ and consecrated by the Gāyatrī, those Daityas are consumed by that water which has become like a thunderbolt. 165.
Then again, that one of great splendor, possessing immense brilliance and prowess,
rose upwards for hundreds of thousands of yojanas.
Then the Blessed One proceeded, surrounded by Brahmins and by the Vālakhilya sages, who were successful in their aims and endowed with the power of rays.
Fifteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty *kāṣṭhās* should be counted as one *kalā*.
Thirty *kalās* constitute one *muhūrta*, and thirty of those [muhūrtas] make up a day and night combined. (168)
The decrease and increase of the days occur respectively through the portions of the day;
the twilight (saṃdhyā), however, is traditionally held to be one muhūrta in duration, remaining equal during both decrease and increase.

When three muhūrtas have passed from the time of sunrise, beginning from the *lekhā* (the first appearance of the sun), that period is known as the morning; it constitutes the fifth division of the day.
From that morning time, the period of *saṅgava* lasts for three muhūrtas;
and from that *saṅgava* time, the period of *madhyāhna* (midday) likewise lasts for three muhūrtas.
Therefore, the period following midday is known as the afternoon;
it consists of exactly three muhūrtas from that central time.
In the afternoon, when the Vyatīpāta yoga occurs, it is called Kālasāyāhna;
it consists of fifteen muhūrtas and indeed three muhūrtas.
On the equinox, the day is indeed known to consist of fifteen muhūrtas;
likewise, the night and day together are known to consist of fifteen muhūrtas. ||174||
It increases and decreases during the southern and northern solstices;
the day swallows the night, and the night swallows the day. (175)
Between autumn and spring, the equinox is perceived;
there, for a day and night, the moon partakes equally in the seven digits.
Likewise, fifteen days are designated as a *pakṣa* (fortnight);
two *pakṣas* constitute a *māsa* (month), and two months form a season (*ṛtu*).
Three seasons make an *ayana* (solar transit), and two *ayanas* are called a year (*varṣa*). ||177||
Time measured from a blink of an eye consists of fifteen *kāṣṭhās* for one *kalā*;
thirty *kāṣṭhās* constitute a *mātrā*, which is composed of two morae (*mātrā*).
One hundred and twenty-nine śataghnīs, three hundred and six mātrās, and twenty-three mātrās divided by sixty-two would constitute the moving [portion]. (179)
Know that Vidyut has forty-eight thousand and eight hundred [years],
and likewise seventy and ninety in Nisvaya.
They say that four hundred [breaths] constitute a vidyuta in the conjunction of the divisions of time;
for this is to be known as a carāṃśa, and the nālikā is the cause therein. ||181||
The five [periods] beginning with the year are divided into four parts;
this determination of all time is designated as a *yuga*. (182)
The first is the *saṃvatsara*, the second is the *parivatsara*, the third is the *idvatsara*, and the fourth is the *anuvatsara*; the fifth among them is designated as *kāla*. ||183||
A full cycle of the sun's conjunctions (yuga) consists of one hundred and twenty lunar phases;
these constitute thirty-eight risings of the sun.
The sun consists of thirty seasons, ten solstices, one hundred and thirty-five months, and sixty [fortnights]. 185.
Thirty such days and nights constitute a month for the Sun;
sixty-one days and nights are considered to be one day and night for Danu.
One hundred and eighty-three is to be known as the measure of the day of Citrabhānu, as well as that of the world. ||187||
The solar, the lunar, the stellar, and likewise the civil—these are the four names by which the Purāṇa is understood. (188)
To the north of that very lake is a mountain named Śṛṅgavān;
its three peaks seem to touch the surface of the sky. (189)
And by them also, Śṛṅgavān was celebrated as being renowned in every respect; its extent was proclaimed to be a single path, and it was also described as having a wide span.
Its central peak indeed extends everywhere;
it is made of gold, while the southern peak is silver and has the luster of crystal.
And there is one northern peak, supreme and made of all kinds of jewels;
thus, by virtue of these three mountain summits, it is renowned as Śṛṅgavān.
When the sun reaches that peak known as the equinox, situated between autumn and spring, it assumes a middle course;
then the dispeller of darkness makes day and night equal. (193)
And those divine green horses yoked to the great chariot shine as if they were anointed by the red rays of the lotus. 194.
At the end of Aries and at the end of Libra, fifteen muhūrtas are recorded from sunrise; the day and night are likewise of that same duration. (195)
When the sun has entered the first division of the Kṛttikās,
the moon should likewise be known to be in the fourth division of the Viśākhās.
When the sun moves into the third degree of Viśākhā, one should know that the moon is situated at the head of Kṛttikā. ||197||
At that time, one should know it as the equinox; thus have the great seers declared.
One should know the equinox by means of the sun and observe the time by means of the moon.
When night and day are equal, that is the equinox (viṣuvat);
at that time, as well as during the equinox, gifts should be given to the ancestors.
Especially to the Brāhmaṇas; for they are the foremost among the deities. 199.

The deficient nights and intercalary months, as well as the units of time— kalās, kāṣṭhās, and muhūrtas— should be known, along with the full moon day (paurṇamāsī) and likewise the new moon day (amāvāsyā),
as well as Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumati.

Tapa and Tapasya, Madhu and Mādhava, Śukra and Śuci constitute the northern course (uttarāyaṇa). Nabhas and Nabhasya, Iṣa and Ūrja, Sahas and Sahasya constitute the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana). ||201||
From that, the years are to be known; the five-year periods are the sons of Brahmā.
From those, the seasons are to be known, for the seasons are recorded as being intermediate. ||202||
Therefore, the new moon (amāvāsyā) should be known as the face of this lunar festival (parvan);
therefore, the equinox (viṣuva), which is always beneficial for the ancestors and the gods, should be known. ||203||
Knowing this, a person should not be deluded regarding rites for the gods and the ancestors;
therefore, the Smṛti declares that the Viṣuvat is always all-pervading for all creatures.
The world is known to extend as far as the edge of light; that which is beyond the world is called the end of the world.
The guardians of the world are stationed there, in the middle of the Lokāloka mountain.
These four high-souled ones remain until the dissolution of all beings:
Sudhāman, Vairāja, Kardama, and Śaṅkṛpa; as well as Hiraṇyaloman, Parjanya, Ketumān, and Jātaniścaya.
Free from duality, free from pride, independent, and without possessions, these guardians of the world stand in the four directions at the boundary between the inhabited and uninhabited worlds.
That which lies north of Agastya’s region and south of the Ajavīthī is indeed the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāṇa), situated outside the path of Vaiśvānara.
There dwell sages endowed with offspring who maintain the sacred fire;
they ensure the continuity of the world and stand upon the path of the ancestors.
The officiating priest is said to be one who performs action initiated by the elements and accompanied by blessings;
those who desire worldly existence undertake such rites, and their path is the Southern Path (dakṣiṇa).
Furthermore, they establish the Dharma again in every age through continuity,
austerity, the observance of boundaries, and sacred revelation.
Indeed, those who were born previously are born in the houses of those born later,
and those born later are likewise born even upon the deaths of those born previously;
thus revolving, they remain until the dissolution of all beings.
Eighty-eight thousand sages who were householders,

having resorted to the southern path of the sun, remain there as long as the moon and stars exist; those practitioners of ritual action, beyond counting, have taken their place in the cremation grounds.
Through worldly conventional usage, through the production of beings, through the nature of desire and aversion, and through the pursuit of sexual union. ||214||
Likewise, by practicing the objects of the senses through physical acts in this world,
the siddhas indeed resorted to cremation grounds for these various reasons;
those sages seeking progeny were born here during the Dvāpara ages.
That which lies north of the Nāgavīthī and south of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) is the northern path of the Sun; it is known as the Devayāna. ||216||
Where those perfected ones dwell—pure and practicing celibacy—they constantly hold [the world] in contempt; therefore, death has been conquered by them.
Eighty-eight thousand of those who maintain their vital energy upwards (ūrdhvaretas) indeed resort to the northern path of Aryaman until the dissolution of all beings.
By these pure causes, they indeed attained the state of immortality; for that immortality is understood as a state lasting until the dissolution of all beings. (219)
This duration of the stability of the three worlds belongs to those who do not proceed upon the path of non-return.
For those who perform meritorious acts such as the horse sacrifice or sinful acts such as the killing of a Brahmin, there is no other [result] than this;
however, at the end of the dissolution of all beings, those whose vital seed is drawn upward (the perpetual celibates) indeed reach exhaustion [of their karma].
Above the Ṛṣis, where Dhruva is indeed remembered to be, is this divine third station of Viṣṇu, radiant in the sky. ||221||
Having gone there, they do not grieve; that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, where Dharmadhruva and others, the perfectors of the world, reside. ||222||
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Movement of the Luminaries," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
In the creation of Svāyambhuva, however, the subsequent [ages] have already been explained;
I shall now state their sequence, including all those yet to come.
Having heard this, the sages questioned Lomaharṣaṇa regarding the movements of the sun and the moon, as well as those of all the planets.
The sages said:
How do these luminaries revolve in their circles in the sky—all of them arranged horizontally and likewise without confusion? Who causes them to revolve, or do they revolve of their own accord? (3)
O best of beings, we wish to know this;
please explain it to us, for a desire to hear this which deludes all creatures has arisen within us. (4)
Sūta said:
Understand this which I am saying, for it deludes all beings:
even that which is directly perceived and visible causes the delusion of living creatures. (5)
He who is situated at the tail of the porpoise facing the four quarters is Dhruva,
the son of Uttānapāda, who stands as the central pivot in the sky.
For as he revolves, he causes the moon and the sun, along with the planets, to revolve;
and the constellations follow him as he turns like a wheel.
By the power of Dhruva’s mind, this circle of stars (bhagaṇa) moves of its own accord—the sun and the moon, the fixed stars, and the lunar mansions, together with the planets. (8)
Bound indeed to the Pole Star by bonds consisting of the hosts of winds,
their conjunctions, their separations, and likewise their movement through time [are described].
The rising and setting of the stars, as well as the portents occurring during the southern and northern solstices,
and the colors of the planets at the equinoxes— all these proceed from the Pole Star.
Rain, heat, cold, night, twilight, and likewise day—all that is auspicious and inauspicious for living beings proceeds from Dhruva. ||11||
Having turned away from those regions presided over by Dhruva, the Sun remains there;
thus, this maker of day, with his blazing rays, is that very Fire of Time.

O best of the twice-born, as the sun turns through its course, illuminating the quarters with its rays, it draws up the water of the entire world from all sides by means of its web of rays joined with the wind. 13.
The water drunk by the Āditya enters the Soma of the sun-fire;
through the channels joined with the wind, the sustenance of the world proceeds.
That which flows from the moon as the sun stands at its head, the clouds release that water upon the earth by the force of the wind. ||15||
One [wave] is lifted up and then falls back into the water;
the water itself thus revolves in various ways. ||16||
This illusion, fashioned as the universe, exists for the sake of sustaining all beings;
by this illusion, the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, are pervaded. 17.
The Lord of All, the god who created the worlds, the thousand-rayed one, the Lord of Creatures;
the Ordainer of the entire universe, the Sovereign Viṣṇu, the Maker of Day. (18)
All worldly water indeed flows from the sky of Soma;
it is proclaimed as a truth that this entire world has Soma as its support. 19.
Heat flows forth from the sun, and cold proceeds from the moon;
these two, possessing the powers of cold and heat respectively, sustain the world when joined together.
O best of the twice-born, there is the river Gaṅgā, the support of Soma, pure with stainless waters; and there are the great rivers preceded by the daughter of Soma (Sarasvatī).
For the waters that are present within the bodies of all beings—
among those moving and stationary creatures being consumed by fire—
those waters emerge here from every side in the form of smoke.
From that, clouds are produced; this is considered the place for the waters.
For the solar heat indeed draws up water from the elements by means of its rays. (23)
From the ocean, by the conjunction with the wind, the rays carry forth the waters;
and because of the power of the seasons, the maker of day undergoes his revolution at the proper time,
for he draws up the white waters from the clouds with his white rays.
The waters, impelled by the winds from all sides, fall from the clouds driven by the wind for the sake of the welfare of all living beings.
Then it rains for six months for the growth of all living beings;
[it produces] the wind, the thunder, and the lightning born of fire.
And because they manifest the state of being a cloud from the verbal root *mih* (to sprinkle), yet the waters do not fall [from it], the wise know that as *abhra* (a cloud). 27.
Furthermore, the threefold origin of clouds is said to be their womb:
those born of fire, those born of Brahmā, and various kinds born of birds.
Clouds are thus declared to be of three types; I shall now describe their production.
Those [gems] originating from fire are said to be born of gold; therefore, their manifestation occurs [there].
Those which possess the qualities of cold, cloudy weather, and wind are established as such. ||29||
Becoming buffaloes, boars, and those with the gait of rutting elephants, they descend to the earth, wander about, and take their delight.
Those clouds named Jīmūtas are the source of living beings;
they are devoid of the quality of lightning and are characterized by their suspension of streams of water. ||31||
Dumb, dense, and massive in body, they follow the force of the current;
they rain down from a distance of one krośa, or even from half a krośa. (32)
Upon the peaks and slopes of the mountains, they rain down and take their delight;
there are those who bear the embryos of cranes, as well as those who carry the embryos of cranes within themselves.
O clouds, we know you to be born of Brahmā, having arisen from the breath of Brahmā;
for endowed with the quality of lightning, you thunder, delighting in sound.
At the sound of their clamor, the earth, with its hair of sprouts bristling upward, attained a renewed youth as if consecrated by the king;
for she was devoted to them with a love that is the very source of life for all beings. (35)
Those clouds are named Jīmūtas; from them arises the birth of living beings.
Those clouds, moreover, are supported by the second wind, Pravaha.
Even when they have emerged from a distance of one and a half yojanas,
the discharge of rain from them is proclaimed as torrents of falling water;
these clouds, born from their wings, are named Puṣkarāvartakas.
Śakra, desiring the welfare of all beings, severed the wings of those mighty mountains that were capable of moving at will and possessed great power.
Those great clouds, which are full of water and are eager for it, are called Puṣkara by name;
for that reason, they are designated here as Puṣkarāvartakas.
Assuming various forms, they are exceedingly terrible;
they are the creators of the rains at the end of a kalpa and the controllers of the fire of universal destruction.
These rain during the ends of the ages; they are proclaimed as the third [type].
Having various forms and appearances, they fill the surface of the earth.
Carrying a supreme wind, they are the supporters who bring about the dissolution of the kalpa.
Those which were the two shell-halves of that primordial egg from which the four-faced Brahmā, the self-born,
emerged— those very halves of the egg-shell are proclaimed to be all the clouds. ||42||
Smoke is the nourishment for all of them without distinction;
however, among them, Parjanya and the four elephants of the quarters are the most excellent.
Of elephants, mountains, and clouds, together with serpents, the lineage is one though they have become distinct; their single source is known as water.
In the winter season, Parjanya and the elephants of the quarters, arising from the cold, pour down showers of frost for the growth of all crops. 45.
The best among them, named Parivaha, is the wind upon which he relies—
that blessed one who supports the divine Gaṅgā as she courses through the sky,
possessing abundant waters, meritorious, and established on the path to heaven like a sacred lore. ||46||
The elephants of the quarters, with their broad trunks, release the spray from that motionless water;
this is known as mist (nīhāra). ||47||
To the south of that mountain known as Hemakūṭa,
situated north of the Himavat range and south of the northern region,
there is indeed a city celebrated by the name Puṇḍra. ||48||
The rain that falls there, originating from frost,
is then carried up by the wind blowing from the snowy mountain; wafting it by its own power, the wind pours it down upon the great mountain.
