Having crossed the Himavat, the remainder of the rain proceeds further from there;
thereafter it comes here to increase the waters in the western regions.
All this has been proclaimed as being both vast and extensive;
indeed, the Sun alone is taught to be the creator of the rains. (51)
Enveloped by Dhruva, the sun revolves; through those two, rain is set in motion. Enveloped by Dhruva, the wind again withdraws the rain.
Having emerged from the planets and the sun, it enters the entire circle of constellations at the end of the week and enters the sun, which is encircled by Dhruva.
Therefore, learn now of the structure of Sūryaratha,
which is established with a single wheel that has five spokes and three hubs.
The Blessed One proceeds upon his chariot with a golden,
highly effulgent wheel; it has six parts, a single rim, dispels the darkness from lost paths, and is radiant like the sun.
It is recorded as being ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
its pole is twice that measure, according to the dimensions of the chariot-box and the shaft.
That chariot, created for him by Brahmā according to his purpose,
was golden, divine, and unimpeded, yoked with the most excellent horses.
Because he was composed of the meters in the form of horses, Śukra remained wherever he was;
moreover, he resembled Varuṇa’s chariot in its characteristics.
Thus, that sun-like Śukra did not move through the sky like the radiant Divākara.
Now, these parts of the sun's chariot are fashioned according to their sequence by means of the constituent members of the year.
The navel of that sun is known as the single wheel;
its spokes are the five seasons, and its rim is said to be the six seasons.
The year is known as the seat of the chariot, and the two solstices are its two poles; the muhūrtas are its wooden frame, and the sixty-fourth part of a day (kalā) is known as its yoke-pin.
Its poles are said to be the ghoṇās; its shaft is the kṣaṇas;
its axle-pins are the nimeṣas; and its yoke-pole is known to be the lavas.
The night is its fender, the sun is its banner raised high aloft;
both worldly gain and desire are known as its two ends of the yoke-pole.
The meters, in the form of seven horses, carry [the chariot] from the left side of the pole:
Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Anuṣṭubh, and likewise Jagatī. (64)
The *paṅkti*, the *bṛhatī*, and the *uṣṇih* as the seventh—let these bind the wheel to the axle; the axle is firmly fixed in the nave.
The wheel revolves together with the axle; the fixed pin revolves together with the axle;
and that axle, impelled by the fixed pin, revolves together with the wheel. (66)
Thus, by the power of its purpose, the arrangement of that chariot was established;
in this way, through the principle of conjunction, the radiant chariot was fully perfected.
Therefore, that divine Sun moves swiftly through the sky;
for two reins of his chariot are indeed fastened to the end of the axle of the yoke.
As the two wheels and yoke-poles revolve with Dhruva,
the circles traced by the chariot of the sky-traveler likewise come into being.
The two ends of its axle, at the rear of that chariot,
are indeed held fast by Dhruva, like two white ropes attached to a double-wheeled vehicle.
Both of those [poles] follow Dhruva as he revolves;
the two ends of the axle of the yoke are its wind-waves for the chariot.
Just as a rope attached to a pivot revolves in every direction,
so too do those two rays shorten within the circles during the northern course [of the sun].
As they revolve in their orbits, both increase in the southern region;
held fast by Dhruva, the two reins indeed lead the Sun.
When those two, being presided over by Dhruva, are drawn together,
then the sun revolves within its orbits.
Moving through one hundred and eighty circles between the two poles,
it is released again by the two rays fixed at the pole.
In the same way, the sun revolves externally through its orbits;
winding itself around with great speed, it traverses those circular paths.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Movement of the Luminaries," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
That chariot was occupied by the gods, the Ādityas, and likewise by the ṛṣis,
as well as by the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Grāmaṇīs, Sarpas, and Rākṣasas.
These indeed dwell in the sun for two months each in succession:
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Pulastya, and the progenitor Pulaha. (2)
The two serpents Vāsuki and Saṅkīrṇāra, as well as Tumburu and Nārada, the two best of Gandharvas who sing—[these were present]. ||3||
Kratusthalī and the Apsaras Puñjikasthalī, as well as the two Grāmaṇīs, Rathakṛt and Rathacitra, and both Tapas and Yaśas. (4)
Rakṣas, Heti, and Praheti are declared to be Yātudhānas;
this host dwells in the sun during the months of Madhu and Mādhava.
The two months of spring and summer, Mitra and Varuṇa, the sages Atri and Vasiṣṭha, Takṣaka and Rambha; ||6||
Menakā and Sahajanyā, the two Gandharvas Haha and Huhu, and both Rathasvana and Rathacitra were the Grāmaṇīs. ||7||
Pauruṣeya and Dhava are declared to be the two Yātudhānas;
these indeed dwell in the sun during the months of Śuci and Śukra.
Then, when the sun had returned, other deities dwelt here once more:
Indra, Vivasvat, Aṅgiras, and Bhṛgu.
Elāparṇa, as well as the serpent Śaṅkhapāla— both of them—
and Viśvāvasu, Ugrasena, and Aruṇa of the morning.
Pramlocā, who is renowned, and Nimlocā— these two,
as well as the Yātudhāna, the serpent, and both the tiger and the white one;
this host dwells in the sun during the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya.
Furthermore, in the autumn season, the pure sage-deities dwell there:
Parjanya, Pūṣan, Bharadvāja, and Gautama. ||12||
And Viśvāvasu among the Gandharvas, as well as Surabhi;
and both Viśvācī and Ghṛtācī, who possess auspicious marks. (13)
The nāgas Airāvata, the renowned Dhanañjaya,
Senajit, and Suṣeṇa— these two being the commanders and leaders of the hosts.
Water and wind—these two are both remembered as Yātudhānas;
they indeed dwell in the sun during the months of Īṣa and Ūrja. ||15||
When the sun dwells in the two months of the winter season,
those two are Aṃśa and Bhaga, and Kaśyapa and Ṛtu as well.
And Bhujaṅga, Mahāpadma, the serpent Karkoṭaka, the Gandharva Citrasena, and both of those [known as] Ūrṇāyu. ||17||
Urvaśī and Vipracitti were likewise two auspicious Apsarases;
Tārkṣya and Ariṣṭanemi were the Senānī and the Grāmaṇī respectively.
And those two fierce Yātudhānas are declared to be Vidyut and Sphūrja;
they dwell in the sun during the months of Sahas and Sahasya.
Then, during the two months of the dewy season (śiśira),
Tvaṣṭṛ, Viṣṇu, Jamadagni, and likewise Viśvāmitra indeed reside there.
Likewise, both Kambala and Aśvatara, the two Nāgas who are sons of Kadrū;
and the Gandharva Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as well as Sūryavarcas. ||21||
The celestial nymph Tilottamā, and the goddess Rambhā, who is enchanting;
and Ṛtajit and Satyajit, the two world-renowned leaders of the hosts.
Likewise, he is remembered as being accompanied by Brahmā and accompanied by Dakṣa when joined with the sacrifice;
these gods dwell in the sun for two months each in succession.
For these twelve groups of seven, who possess pride in their respective stations,
nourish the sun with their splendor— that most excellent of splendors.
With those celebrated words, the sages praise the Sun;
and the Gandharvas and Apsarases likewise worship him with songs and dances.
The Yakṣas and Bhūtas who are village chiefs cause a terrifying gathering;
the serpents carry the Sun, and the Yātudhānas follow him.
The Vālakhilyas lead him to his setting, having attended upon the Sun at his rising.
Whatever energy these very gods possess, according to their austerity, according to their application, according to their truth, according to their dharma, and according to their strength; ||27||
Just as that sun shines by their splendor,
so indeed do these dwell here in the sun for two months each.
Sages, gods, gandharvas, hosts of pannagas and apsarases, as well as village chiefs, yakṣas, and numerous yātudhānas. ||29||
These, as they are celebrated here, scorch, rain down, shine, blow, and create; they dispel the inauspicious karma of living beings in this world.
For these [trees] take away the merit of men who are evil-minded, and they occasionally dispel the misfortune of those who move about. ||31||
Abiding in divine celestial chariots that move at will and possess the speed of the wind,
these wander together with the sun, following the course of the day.
Raining, heating, and indeed gladdening all creatures,
they protect all beings here until the end of the aeon.
This is indeed the station of those who pride themselves on their status throughout the past and future Manvantaras, as well as for those who exist at present.
Thus, those seven groups indeed dwell in the sun in the four directions,
throughout the fourteen creations and during the Manvantaras.

Releasing heat in summer, cold in winter, and rain during the monsoon; day and night, it moves according to time through the power of the seasons, its rays revolving, truly gratifying the gods, the ancestors, and human beings.
The Sun, having increased the Soma with the *suṣumna* ray, gratifies the gods with nectar;
it becomes full during the bright fortnight through the course of the days, and the wise gods drink it during the dark fortnight. //37//

The Pitṛs drink that nectar and ambrosia which remains for two periods after the Soma has been drunk, as it flows out through the rays at the end of the dark fortnight; and likewise, the gentle deities drink the Kavya.
Mortals overcome hunger through food and drink— by means of waters drawn up by the sun with its rays, drawn up once again, and then increased by rain, which in turn nourishes the medicinal herbs.
The gods are satisfied with nectar for half a month, and the ancestors are satisfied by the *svadhā* offering for half a month;
he constantly sustains mortals with food, and the Sun himself supports that [food] through the rays of light.
This Savitṛ, who is called Hari because he takes away with those horses (haribhiḥ) and who draws back the bow with his reins (raśmibhiḥ),
constantly supports the world of moving and non-moving beings while releasing them again at the time of release.
Hari is carried away by his bay horses; then he drinks water with his thousand bay steeds;
thereafter, that Hari releases them again, becoming bewildered by those bay horses.
Thus, with his single-wheeled chariot drawn by those auspicious and unwounded horses, this Sun moves swiftly through the sky in his abode.
Traversing in a single-wheeled chariot throughout the day and night,
he revolves around the seven continents and oceans with seven horses for each.

By those horses in the form of meters, which were stationed wherever the wheels were, which could assume any form at will, which were yoked all at once, and which were infinite and swift as thought; ||45||
Those horses, green, inexhaustible, tawny, lords, and exponents of Brahman,
complete one hundred and eighty circuits in a year.
The outer and inner mandalas,
joined together at the beginning of the kalpa, flow throughout until the dissolution of all beings;
enveloped by the Vālakhilyas, they revolve through nights and days.
Praised by great sages with foremost and celebrated modes of speech,
and honored by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsaras with songs and dances,
the Lord of Heaven (Indra) moves about on his winged steeds like a bird.
The moon moves through the constellations that rest upon its path;
likewise, its waning and waxing of rays are traditionally held to be like those of the sun.
The chariot of the Moon should be known as standing on both sides of the triple wheel;
born from the womb of the waters, it is a chariot equipped with horses and a charioteer,
joined with three white wheels each having a hundred spokes, and yoked to the finest of white steeds.
Indeed, when that chariot is yoked once with those ten divine, lean, unattached horses that possess the speed of thought, they carry it until the end of the age.
When that chariot was prepared, white horses with ears like those of a dog,
all of one color and possessing the luster of a conch shell, indeed drew it.
And they were Yaya, Trimanas, Vṛṣa, Rājīvala, Haya, Asva, Vāma, Turaṇya, Haṃsa, Vyomī, and Mṛga. (53)
Thus, all these ten horses of the Moon, by their respective names,
carry the divine Moon from the end of the day.
Surrounded by the gods and the ancestors, the gentle Soma proceeds;
at the beginning of the bright fortnight of the moon, with the sun stationed in front,
the interior of his city becomes filled continuously as the days progress.
The Sun, by means of a single ray, constantly replenishes the Soma that was drunk by the gods during the fifteen days of its waning.
Filling each successive portion by means of the *suṣumṇā* in the sequence of the days,
the white digits indeed increase as the *suṣumṇā* is being nourished.
Therefore, they indeed wane during the dark fortnight and wax during the bright fortnight;
in this way, the body of the moon is replenished by the power of the sun. (58)
On the full moon day, he is seen white with a perfectly full orb;
thus is Soma replenished during the bright fortnight, following the sequence of the days.
Then, from the second day until the fourteenth of the waxing moon, the gods drink that essence of water, the Soma consisting of pure flavor, which is honey-like, gentle, and nectar.
Having been gathered over half a month by the splendor of the sun,
they partake of that gentle nectar for the sake of food on the full moon day.
For one night, at the beginning of the dark fortnight of the moon, all the gods, ancestors, and great seers [worship] the sun as it faces toward the east.
The digits within the city [of the moon] are gradually drunk away;
therefore, they wane during the dark fortnight, while during the bright fortnight they are replenished.
Thus, when the sequence of days has passed, the wise and most excellent of gods,
having drunk [the moon] for half a month, go to the new moon;
and the ancestors likewise attend upon the moon on the day of the new moon.
Then, when fifteen parts remain, with a small portion of the *kalā* still left, he is attended by the hosts of ancestors during the afternoon as the lowest [of the three periods]. ||65||

The remaining portion of that [moon] which consists of two kalās is the nectar of *svadhā* that has issued forth from the rays of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). Having drunk that *svadhā* for the satisfaction of their ancestors during the month, they go to the state of immortality (*amṛta*).
The Saumyas, the Barhiṣads, and likewise the Agniṣvāttas—
all those who are called Kavyas are indeed the Pitṛs.
The Kavyas are indeed the years, those which are remembered by the twice-born as the five-year cycles;

the Saumyas are to be known as the seasons, and the Barhiṣads are remembered as the months. O twice-born ones, the Agniṣvāttas are likewise the intermediate seasons, for such is the creation of the Pitṛs.
Of that which is being drunk by the ancestors on the fifteenth day,
as long as its portion does not diminish, that indeed is the fifteenth digit.
Then, at the end of the new moon (amāvāsyā), its ultimate limit is reached;
indeed, the waxing and waning of the moon are traditionally held to occur at the beginning of the fortnights and on the sixteenth day.
Thus, this waning and waxing of the moon occurs through the influence of the sun;
now I shall describe the chariot of the stars, the planets, and likewise of Rāhu.
The bright chariot of the son of Soma is indeed composed of water and fire;
it is yoked to eight tawny horses possessing the speed of the wind.
The divine chariot was great, equipped with a protective fender and a chassis;
it possessed side-seats, banners, and a standard, and resembled a dark cloud.
The chariot of Bhārgava was filled with splendors and resembled the sun in brilliance;
it was yoked to the finest horses of various colors, born from the earth.
White, tawny, dappled, blue, yellow, crimson,
black, green, spotted, and speckled— by these ten highly fortunate steeds, which were not lean and possessed the speed of the wind. ||75||
The glorious golden chariot of Soma also had eight horses;
with those unimpeded, crimson steeds born of fire that traverse all places,
Kumāra indeed moves about, his wheels following both straight and curved paths.
Then the learned Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods and a descendant of Aṅgiras,
proceeded forth on a golden chariot drawn by ruddy horses.
Yoked with eight divine horses equal to the wind,
he dwells in the constellation Anurādhā and travels with great speed by means of that [chariot].
Then Śanaiścara also, mounting a chariot made of black iron, proceeds slowly with dappled horses born from the sky.
Likewise, Svarbhānu had eight black horses, swift as thought;
yoked once, they carry his chariot which is composed entirely of darkness.
Emerging from the sun, Rāhu approaches the moon during the lunar nodes;
he returns to the sun from the moon again during the solar nodes.
Then the horses of Keturatha were eight times eight in number, possessing the speed of the wind;
they resembled the smoke of straw, dappled and reddish-brown like donkeys. ||82||
These vehicles of the planets have indeed been described by me along with their chariots;
they are all bound to Dhruva and are fastened by cords of wind.
These, indeed, being set in motion, revolve according to their respective connections,
bound by invisible aerial rays belonging to the wind.
Bound to that [pole], the moon, sun, and planets revolve in the sky;
following its rotation, the hosts of luminaries move around Dhruva. (85)
Just as a boat on the water of a river is carried along with the current,
so too these abodes of the gods are borne by the rays of the wind;
therefore, all those hosts of gods are seen in the sky.
As many as there are stars, so many are the reins of wind;
all of them, fixed to Dhruva, revolve and cause him to revolve.
Just as a revolving oil-press wheel causes the oil-seeds to whirl,
so too do the luminaries, bound by the wind, revolve in every direction.
Driven by the Pravaha wind, the luminaries move like a whirling firebrand; therefore, it is known as the Pravaha (the "Flowing" wind). 89.
Thus bound to the Pole Star (Dhruva), this host of luminaries moves;
it is to be known as that very Śiśumāra (the Sea-monster) composed of stars in the sky.
Whatever sin one commits by day, one is released from it upon seeing him at night.
As many stars as there are in the sky resting upon the Śiśumāra,
for so many years, or even more, do they live.
This eternal Śiśumāra is to be understood through its various divisions;
furthermore, Uttānapāda is to be known as his upper jaw.
The sacrifice is to be known as the lower part, while Dharma is seated upon the head;
Nārāyaṇa, who is to be attained, is in the heart, and the Aśvins are in the two forefeet. 93.
Varuṇa and Aryaman are situated on his two buttocks in the west;
the Year is his penis, and Mitra is established in his anus. (94)
In its tail are Agni, Mahendra, Marīci, Kaśyapa, Dhruva, the stars, and Śiśumāra; this quartet never sets.
The lunar mansions, the moon, the sun, and the planets, together with the hosts of stars, all turned their faces upward and toward him, forming a circle as they took refuge in the sky. 96.
Presided over by Dhruva, all these move in a clockwise direction around Dhruva alone, who is the most excellent and preeminent pole established in the sky. 97.
Among the Dhruvas, Agnis, and Kaśyapas, this Dhruva is remembered as the most excellent;
he alone revolves upon the summit of Mount Meru.
For this wheel of luminaries, always facing downwards, draws [the earth] toward itself;
it moves here in a clockwise direction while gazing at Meru.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Conduct of Dhruva," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Śaunaka said:
Having heard this, those sages, again filled with doubt,
then questioned Lomaharṣaṇa further for an answer.
The sages said:
Regarding that which was said by you: "These houses are scattered about; how could they be temples? Describe the luminaries. (2)
"Explain all of this, as well as the definitive nature of the luminaries.
Having heard their words, the Sūta then became composed.
In this matter, I shall fully declare to you what has been stated by those of great wisdom and enlightened intellect regarding the origin of the Sun and the Moon,
and how the abode of the Sun and the Moon here is like the dwellings of the gods.
Henceforth, I shall describe the origin of the three kinds of fire:
the divine fire, the elemental fire, and the terrestrial fire.
When the night had passed for Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest,
this world was indeed unevolved and enveloped by the darkness of night.
When this [body] remains consisting only of the four elements, it is called the earthly fire;
and that which first heats within the sun is known as the pure fire.
Now I shall describe the characteristics of those [fires] known as the Vaidyuta (the lightning fire);
for there are three fires: the Vaidyuta, the Jāṭhara (the digestive fire), and the Saura (the solar fire).
Therefore, drinking the waters with its rays, that sun blazes forth in the sky.
A fire in a tree entered by lightning is not extinguished by water;
likewise, the fire dwelling within the bellies of men is not quenched by water. (9)
That supreme fire is known as Arcciṣmān, the source of the digestive fire (Jāṭhara);
and that which appears as a white orb, shining yet devoid of heat, is also he.
For when the sun goes down by a quarter [of its course], its solar radiance enters the fire at night;
therefore, it shines from afar. ||11||
Furthermore, as the sun rises, the heat of fire enters it;
therefore, that fire within the solar orb causes the sun to burn.
Likewise, light and heat in the solar and igneous energies nourish one another day and night through their mutual interpenetration. ||13||
When the sun rises again in the northern half of the earth and likewise in this southern half,
the night enters the waters;
therefore, the waters become copper-colored due to the entry of the night during the day.
When the sun sets again, the day indeed enters the waters;
therefore, at night, the white waters enter the sun once more. ||15||
By this sequential process, at the midpoint of the southern and northern courses,
it enters the waters constantly during day and night at sunrise and sunset.
And that which heats the sun, drinking up water with its rays, is known as the divine and pure [fire], for it is a mixture of the earthly and the celestial. ||17||
That fire has a thousand feet; it is circular, pot-shaped, and pure.
It draws up that [water] from all sides with its thousand rays.
The rivers of the land, those of the sea, those of the wells, and those of the forests;
the stationary and the moving; and that golden sun whose thousand rays emit rain, cold, and heat. (19)
From them, four hundred channels of diverse forms pour forth rain;
they are named Vandanas, Vandya, Ritanas, Nūtanās, and all the Amṛtas— these are the rays that discharge the rain.
Furthermore, there are three hundred other rays besides those, which carry snow;
they are visible, pure, external, joyous, and the producers of frost.
All these rays are named after the moon; they are yellowish in luster, as well as white, Kakubhas, Gāvas, and Viśvabhrts.
All those three hundred [rivers] are known by name as the Śuklas, the creators of heat;
through them, he sustains equally men, ancestors, and gods.
In this world, he satisfies humans with herbs, the ancestors with the ancestral offering (svadhā),
and all the gods with nectar— thus satisfying all three classes by means of these three.
In both spring and summer, O Lord of Beings, he draws [the breath] with three hundred;
and likewise in the rainy season and autumn, he draws it with four hundred.
In the winter and the dewy season, he emits cold with three [rays];
he bestows strength upon the plants and satisfies the ancestors with their due portion (svadhā).
The Sun, the sustainer of the three worlds, ordains immortality among the immortals.
In this way, that thousandfold solar ray, which accomplishes the welfare of the world, becomes divided upon reaching the seasons, emitting water, cold, and heat. (27)

This white and radiant orb, known as the sun, is indeed the foundation and source of the constellations, planets, and the moon; all stars, moons, and planets are to be understood as originating from the sun. ||28||
Soma is the lord of the constellations, and Divākara is the king of the planets;
the remaining five planets should be known as lords who can assume any form at will. ||29||
It is recited that fire is the sun and water is remembered as the moon; now listen correctly as the nature of the remaining elements is being described.
Skanda, the commander of the celestial army, is recited as the planet Aṅgāraka;
those who know wisdom recognize the god Budha as Nārāyaṇa. (31)
Rudra Vaivasvata is Dharma himself, the lord in the world;
he is the great planet Śanaiścara, the slow-moving one, O best of the twice-born. (32)
These two great planets,
Śukra and Bṛhaspati, sons of Prajāpati, are both brilliant and the preceptors of the gods and the asuras;
Mahendra and the Daitya were established as their respective sovereigns.
The entire three worlds have their root in the Sun; of this there is no doubt.
This whole universe, including gods, asuras, and humans, comes into being through him. (34)

The entire splendor of Rudra, Indra, Upendra, and Candra, as well as that of the foremost of Brahmins and the inhabitants of heaven, and the universal radiance of all luminous beings—[all this constitutes] your luster. (35)
The soul of all, the lord of all worlds, the root, the supreme deity—from him everything is born, and into him alone it is dissolved. (36)
For in ancient times, the existence and non-existence of the worlds issued forth from the Sun;
O Brahmins, the radiant Sun is the world to be known, the planet that is difficult to grasp. (37)
Therein they go to their destruction and are born again and again—moments, muhūrtas, days, nights, and all the fortnights;
months, years, seasons, and the ages of the world. ||38||
Therefore, apart from the sun, no reckoning of time exists for them;
without time, there is neither Vedic recitation, nor initiation, nor the sequence of daily rites.
How could there be the division of the seasons, or flowers, roots, and fruits? How could there be the production of grain, or the multitude of medicinal herbs and their qualities? (1.53.40)
There would be an absence of all worldly activities for the gods both in heaven and here on earth,
were it not for the Sun, who heats the world and draws up the waters.
He alone is Time, he is Fire, and he is Prajāpati, the twelvefold soul;
O best of the twice-born, he scorches the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
This entire mass of splendors, common to all the worlds,
having taken its place upon the highest path, heats this universe on every side— with its sides, above, and below— by means of the rays of the wind.
Of those thousands of rays of the sun that were previously described by me, seven rays are preeminent; they are the sources of the planets. (44)
Suṣumna, Harikeśa, and likewise Viśvakarman;
then another, Viśvaśravas, and after that Sampadvasu;
and yet another, Arvāvasu—these are proclaimed here along with Umā. ||45||
The Suṣumṇā, however, is a solar ray that nourishes the waning moon;
because its influence extends both horizontally and upwards, it is celebrated as the Suṣumṇā.
Harikeśa, the first, is proclaimed as having his origin in the bears (Ṛkṣas);
Viśvakarman, however, on the south, increases Budha with his ray. 47.
Viśvaśravas, who was later known by the wise as Śukrayoni, is the radiance (raśmi) Sampadvasu; she is the womb of Lohita. 48.
The sixth ray, however, is Arvāvasu; it is the womb of Bṛhaspati.
Furthermore, the self-ruling ray Āpyāyana is Śanaiścara. 49.

Thus, by the power of the sun, all the planets, lunar mansions, and stars increase; this entire universe and the world are known [to do so]. They do not perish, and because of that, they are remembered as "nakṣatras" (stars/lunar mansions). || 1.53.50 ||
These fields were indeed first reached by his rays;
then, having attained the state of a constellation, the Sun took possession of those fields. ||51||

For those who have crossed over by means of their good deeds in this world, these stars are indeed "tārakās" because they serve as supports for the planets at the end of their merit; and they are called "tārakās" also because of their whiteness.
By constantly absorbing all divine, earthly, and nocturnal darknesses from every side with his splendor, the great Sun is so called. (53)
This verbal root is understood in the sense of "impelling" (spandana);
because he impels (savana) both heat and water, he is therefore considered Savitṛ.
This word "candra" has many meanings; it is held to derive from the verbal root *cand*, meaning "to delight.
It is conceived [to signify] whiteness, immortality, and coolness. (55)
In the two divine, radiant, and moving orbs of the sun and moon—blazing with splendor, white, auspicious, and resembling rounded jars. ||56||
Therein, the orb of the moon is known to consist of condensed water, while the white orb of the sun consists of condensed light. (57)
All the gods, taking refuge in the stars, the sun, and the planets, enter all these stations in their entirety throughout all the Manvantaras.
Those very temples are known by those names;
the solar temple is the abode of Sūrya, and likewise the lunar temple is the abode of Soma.
Śukra’s station is Śaukra; he is the powerful one with sixteen rays.
Bṛhaspati’s is Bṛhat, and Lohita’s is Lohita.
Likewise, Śanaiścara’s station is Śānaiścara, and his deity is Śanaiścara himself.
Through contact with the rays of the sun, they are known to be of the nature of light;
the diameter of the sun is recorded as nine thousand yojanas.
Its diameter and circumference are three times that [of the sun];
the diameter of the moon is recorded as being twice the diameter of the sun.
But Svarbhānu, having become equal to those two, moves below them;
having drawn up the shadow of the earth, he is fashioned in the form of a disk.
The vast abode of Svarbhānu, which was fashioned out of darkness,
issues forth from the Sun and reaches the Moon during the lunar nodes (parvan).
He goes from Soma to Āditya, and again from Āditya to Soma during the lunar phases;
because he drives away the light (svar-bhās), he is therefore called Svarbhānu.
And Bhārgava is situated as the sixteenth part of the moon,
both in terms of its diameter and its circumference, measured in yojanas.
Bṛhaspati should be known as one-quarter less than Bhārgava;
both Kuja and Saura are recorded as being one-quarter less than Bṛhaspati.
In both width and circumference, Budha is one-quarter less than those two.
Those constellations which indeed possess their own radiance here, appearing in the form of stars,
are equal to Budha in both extent and orb.
The knower of reality should generally recognize the lunar conjunctions and the asterisms according to their true nature;
yet, the forms of the stars and constellations may sometimes be deficient in relation to one another.

The circles of stars, drawn out from east to west, measure five hundred, four hundred, three hundred, and two hundred yojanas; those that are half a yojana in size are the smallest, and nothing smaller than these exists.
Above those are three planets which move at a great distance;
they are Saura, Aṅgiras, and Vakra, to be known as slow-moving.
Below them, moreover, are four other great planets:
Sūrya, Soma, Budha, and Bhārgava, who move with great speed.
As many as there are millions of stars, so many are the constellations in every direction;
and by the fixed arrangement of their paths, the course of the constellations is thus established.
The courses of the sun are indeed those very same [orbits], varying in their low and high positions according to the sequence of the solstices.

When the moon is at the nodes during the parvan days while situated on the path of the northern solstice, then the lunar planet Mercury occupies the station of Mercury, and likewise Rāhu occupies the station of Rāhu. (74)
All the stars enter into the stars,
and all those houses are the luminaries of those whose souls are virtuous.
These places, created by the Self-Existent One at the beginning of the eon,
endure until the dissolution of all beings.
In all the Manvantaras, the presiding deities indeed remain in their respective abodes until the dissolution of all beings.
The past abodes exist together with the past gods and asuras, both those who have been cultivated and those who have not;
likewise, they exist with the present gods of their own respective realms.
And in this very Manvantara, the planets are known to be celestial-dwellers;
Vivasvat, the son of Aditi, is the Sun in the Vaivasvata interval.
Tviṣimān, the son of Dharma, is remembered as the Vasu Somadeva;
Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, is to be known as the divine king of the Asuras.
The god Bṛhattejā is remembered as the teacher of the gods (Devācārya), the son of Aṅgiras;
he is also known as Budha, Manohara, and the son of Tviṣi. ||81||
From Agni was born Vikalpa, that youth who is the lord of the red [flames].
Those daughters of Dakṣa are remembered as the ones who move among the stars and constellations.
Svarbhānu, the son of Siṃhikā, is the Asura who torments all beings;
these are proclaimed as the presiding deities (abhimānins) over the moon, the lunar mansions, the planets, and the sun. ||83||
These locations have been declared, as well as the deities who preside over them;
the white location belongs to Vivasvat, the thousand-rayed Agni. (84)
The abode of the thousand-rayed sun is watery and white;
however, the dwelling of the five-rayed, mind-pleasing one is remembered as dark blue.
The watery abode and residence of Śukra also possesses sixteen rays;
however, the watery abode of Lohita belongs to the youth Navaraśmi.
The house of the twelve-rayed Bṛhaspati is said to be golden and vast; that of Mercury is black and composed of water.
The abode of Svarbhānu is composed of darkness and is a place that torments all beings; all the stars should be known as consisting of water and possessing but a single ray.
The supports of merit and fame, which are exceedingly white in color, should be known as consisting of condensed water, created by the Vedas at the beginning of the kalpa. (89)
Because of its height, it is seen quickly with its rays fully manifested;
likewise, situated on the southern path, it is beheld by those dwelling in the Nīvi-vīthī.
Likewise, when the sun is covered by the markings on the earth during the full moon and the new moon,
it is not seen at the proper time and sets prematurely.
Therefore, while situated on the northern path, the moon is seen on the new-moon day;
it is seen on the southern path by necessity, and not otherwise.
By the movement and conjunction of the luminaries, both the sun and the moon have simultaneous settings and simultaneous risings during the equinoxes.

In the northern paths, the setting and rising of the Vyantara deities should be understood as following the movement of the celestial sphere, occurring on the full moon and new moon days respectively. ||94||
When the sun is situated on the path of the southern solstice,
then that sun moves beneath all the planets.
Having formed a vast mandala, the moon moves above it;
the entire mandala of the stars traverses above the moon.
Above the constellations is Mercury; above Mercury is Jupiter;
above him is Saturn; above him is the circle of the Seven Sages;
and above the seven sages, Dhruva is established.
The distances between the stars and the planets above [the sun] are, in order, two thousand and one hundred yojanas.
The planets and the moon and sun, by means of their divine splendor in the sky,
are constantly joined with the constellations and move according to the order of fixed laws.
The planets, lunar mansions, and suns, situated at their lowest, highest, or middling positions,
behold all living beings simultaneously, both in their conjunction and in their separation.
For these exist in mutual dependence and are joined with one another; their conjunction, moreover, should be understood by the wise as being without confusion. ||101||
Thus, this is the arrangement for you of the earth and of the celestial sphere, as well as of the continents, the oceans, and the mountains. (102)
In those very regions where the rains and rivers dwell, these planets indeed first arose within the lunar mansions. ||103||
Vivasvān, the son of Aditi, was indeed the Sun during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara;
he was born under the Viśākhā constellation as the foremost of the planets. ||104||
The radiant Dharmaputra, Soma, Viśvāvasu, and Śītaraśmi—the Maker of Night—were thus born among the Kṛttikās. ||105||
Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, possessing sixteen rays, arose in the lunar mansion Tiṣya immediately after the Sun; he is the foremost among the stellar planets. ||106||
Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the world, the planet and son of Aṅgiras who possesses twelve rays, was born under all the Phālgunī constellations. ||107||
The planet Lohitāṅga, whose flames are new, is the son of Prajāpati;
according to the sacred tradition (śruti), he was born here under the Pūrvāṣāḍhā constellation. (108)
In the Revatī asterism appeared Saptārchi, as well as Saura and Śanaiścara;
in Rohiṇī were born the two planets who oppress the Moon and the Sun.
These, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets beginning with Bhārgava, should be understood as such;
because they undergo a state of dysfunction during afflictions of the birth asterism,
they are therefore touched by that defect within their respective planetary divisions.
Among all these planets, the Sun is said to be the first;
among the star-planets (tārāgrahas), Venus is the first, and among the comets (ketus), the one with smoke (Dhūmaketu) is the first. ||111||
The fixed time for the planets divided according to the four quarters is such that Śraviṣṭhā is [the first] among the lunar mansions, and likewise the northern solstice among the solstices.
Of the five-year cycle, he is remembered as the first year;
of the seasons, the cool season (śiśira); and of the months, Māgha itself. ||113||
Of the fortnights, it is the bright fortnight; likewise, of the lunar days, it is the first day (pratipad);
and of the divisions of day and night, it is proclaimed to be the day. ||114||
Likewise, among the muhūrtas, the first muhūrta has Rudra as its presiding deity;
and among the divisions of time, those who know time consider the first moment to be the blink of an eye.
The five-year cycle, beginning with Śraviṣṭhā and ending with Śravaṇā, revolves like a wheel according to the specific motion of the sun. ||116||
Therefore, Divākara is known as Time; know him to be the Lord, the initiator and the terminator of all beings who are established in the four stages of life. ||117||
Thus, this very arrangement of the luminaries was fashioned by the Lord for the sake of worldly convention, based on the determination of objects. (118)
It is established that this [universe] arises from hearing, is contracted at the center, and is expanded toward all its extremities, having the form of a tree. (119)
At the beginning of the kalpa, this was proclaimed by the Blessed One with prior intelligence;
it has a substratum and possesses self-conceit, consisting entirely of light.
This is the wonderful transformation of Pradhāna, which takes the form of the universe. (1.53.120)
It is not possible for anyone with the physical eye to calculate, according to their true nature, the coming and going of the luminaries among men. ||121||
Having examined it skillfully through scripture, inference, direct perception, and reasoning, the wise person should have faith in it with devotion. (122)
Obeisance to those of supreme intelligence!
These five—astronomy, scripture, water, writing, and calculation—are to be known as the means for investigating the host of celestial luminaries. (123)
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Configuration of the Luminaries," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
The sages said:
In what land did this most excellent and highly meritorious narrative take place?
At what time, O one of great splendor, did it occur among those led by Brahmā?
Tell us this correctly, exactly as it happened, O you whose wealth is asceticism.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, this is what was previously heard by me as it was being told by Vāyu, the life-breath of the world, during a thousand-year sacrificial session.
I shall proclaim that by which the throat of the trident-bearing God of gods became blue; listen, you who are firm in your vows! (3)
To the north of the king of mountains, there are lakes, rivers, and pools;
in sacred groves, at holy fords, and in temples of the gods;
upon lofty mountain peaks, and in deep caves and forest thickets.
There, high-souled sages devoted to the gods and firm in their praised vows praise Mahādeva according to the prescribed rites.
With the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and with dance, song, worship, and so forth,
they constantly worship Śiva with the syllable Om and prostrations.
While the wheel of the luminaries was in motion and the sun occupied the meridian,
all the self-restrained deities remained engaged in that conversation;
then, committed to their observances, they stood with only their vital breath remaining.
"Salutations to you, O Blue-throated One," thus spoke Sadāgati.
Hearing that, the sages of purified soul and firm vows, renowned as the Vālakhilyas, who travel in the company of the sun, [spoke]. ||8||
Eighty-eight thousand sages,
whose vital energies are drawn upward and who subsist on air, leaves, and water, indeed inquire about Vāyu from him.
The sages said:
"O best of the wind-gods, that which was spoken by you as 'Nīlakaṇṭha'—this is the most secret among purifiers, meritorious, and supreme among those who perform merit. (1.54.10)
O Wind-god, through your grace we wish to hear that by which the throat of the Lord of Ambikā has become blue. (11)
We desire to hear correctly from your mouth, especially those meaningful words that proceed as long as they are uttered by you. (12)
When the wind has reached the locations of the phonemes, the production of speech proceeds;
O Vāyu, from you first arises knowledge and then enthusiasm.
But when you are motionless, all other activities of the phonemes cease.
Where words turn back, and even the bonds of the body are difficult to find. ||14||
Even there, O Wind, your existence is ever-present; you are all-pervading.
O Samīraṇa, there is no other god who is all-pervading except for you.
O Wind, this world of living beings is indeed manifest to you on all sides;
you know the Lord of Speech, the divine one who is the leader of the mind and the sovereign.
"Tell me, what has caused this transformation of the appearance of his neck?
Having heard these words of those sages of purified souls, the immensely radiant Vāyu, who is honored by the worlds, replied: ||17||
Vāyu said:
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, there was a brahmin named Vasiṣṭha, a righteous soul devoted to the determination of the Vedas, who was indeed the mind-born son of Prajāpati.
He indeed questioned Kārttikeya, whose vehicle is the preeminent peacock,
who steals the collyrium from the eyes of the women of Mahiṣāsura.
To the great-souled Mahāsena, whose voice resounded like the thundering of clouds,
who brought joy to the heart of Umā, and who appeared as a child in the form of a boy.
Vasiṣṭha, with devotion, questioned the mighty Kārttikeya— the taker of Krauñca’s life and the delighter in the heart of Pārvatī.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Salutations to you, the delight of Hara; O you who are the womb of Umā, let there be salutation to you!
Salutations to you, whose womb is Agni; O you who are the womb of Gaṅgā, let there be salutation to you! 22.
Salutations to you who are born from the fire-weapon; salutations to you, the son of the Kṛttikās!
Salutations to the twelve-eyed one; let there be salutations to you, the six-faced one! 23.
"Salutations to you, who hold a spear in hand and possess a divine bell and banner.
Having thus praised Mahāsena, he questioned the one whose vehicle is the peacock.
This beautiful color that is seen, shining with the luster of white collyrium—why has it arisen upon your throat, which possesses the radiance of a kunda flower or the moon? (25)
Speak this to one who is trustworthy, devoted, self-controlled, and inquisitive—
a narrative endowed with auspiciousness, purifying, and destructive of sins.
O highly fortunate one, for the sake of my pleasure, you ought to relate it in its entirety.
Having heard those words of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha,
the immensely radiant slayer of the hosts of the enemies of the gods replied.
Listen, O best of speakers, to these words being spoken by me,
just as they were previously heard by me while seated upon Umā’s lap.
O great sage, for your benefit, I shall now proclaim that dialogue between Pārvatī and the high-souled Śarva.
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, variegated with various minerals, filled with diverse trees and creepers, and adorned by ruddy geese; || 1.54.30 ||
Abounding with the songs of six-legged bees, resounding with the falling of rain-showers, and with its caves echoing with the cries of intoxicated cranes and peacocks. (31)
It was crowded with throngs of Apsarases, graced by Kinnaras,
and adorned with the Jīvañjīvaka birds and various creeping plants.
Sweet with the warbling of cuckoos, frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas,
rich with the sound of fragrant breezes, and resonant with the rumbling of thunder below.
In a cave frequented by elephants agitated by the fear of Vināyaka, [the place resounded] with the sounds of lute music, delightful to the sense of hearing. ||34||
In that place where swings were suspended for the gathering of women,
and which resounded with the tinkling of bells from the hanging swings adorned with banners.
The palace was filled with the sounds of mouth-organs, mṛdaṅga drums, and musical instruments, as well as the bursting cheers of the strong and the various playful cries of those engaged in sport.
With laughter that produced terror, with mouths distorted in various ways,
and with diverse bodily odors, the attendants of Gaṇeśa sported there.
With staircases of diamond and crystal, and with variegated slabs of stone featuring the faces of tigers and lions, as well as other faces such as those of elephants and horses.
With faces like those of cats, fierce, and with forms shaped like jackals;
short, tall, thin, and stout; with protruding bellies and large bellies. (39)
With short shanks, with hanging lips, and others with shanks like palm trees;
with ears like those of cattle, with single ears, with large ears, and with no ears at all.
With many feet, with great feet, with one foot, or without feet; with many heads, with great heads, with one head, or without heads. ||41||
The Lord of Beings was surrounded by such great yogis who were beings with many eyes, large eyes, a single eye, or no eyes at all. (42)

Seated comfortably upon a delightful golden rocky surface adorned with pure pearls, gems, and jewels, the daughter of the King of Mountains addressed these words to the destroyer of the god of love: 43.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, whose teaching is marked by the bull!
O Mahādeva, that which resembles a dark cloud shines upon your neck.
"O Lord, destroyer of the body of Kama, what is this that shines upon your neck—neither excessively brilliant nor exceedingly white, resembling a mass of black collyrium? (45)
What is the cause, what is the reason, and why is there blueness in the throat? O Lord, tell me all this according to the truth; I have great curiosity, O Hima. (46)
Then, having heard those words of Pārvatī, Śaṅkara, the beloved of Pārvatī, recounted a narrative filled with auspiciousness.
Formerly, when the nectar was being churned in the Ocean of Milk by the gods and the dānavas,
a poison arose first from it, possessing the brilliance of the fire of universal destruction.
O lady of excellent countenance, having seen him, the hosts of gods and the Daityas all became dejected in face and went into the presence of Brahmā.
Seeing the hosts of gods terrified, the immensely radiant Brahmā spoke these words:
"O highly fortunate ones, for what reason are you afraid and agitated in mind?"
The eightfold sovereignty has been bestowed upon you by me;
O best of gods, by whom indeed has your sovereignty been revoked? (51)
"You are all indeed the lords of the three worlds, free from all affliction;
in this creation of beings, there is no one who can turn back my command. (52)

All of you travel in celestial chariots, all of you move according to your own will; through the ripening of your past actions, you are eternally capable of proceeding within the realms of the self, the elements, and the divine. 53.
Therefore, for what reason are you agitated by fear like deer tormented by a lion?
What is the sorrow, by whom has this torment been caused, or from where has this danger come?
You ought to relate all of this quickly and according to the facts.
Having heard those words of the high-souled Brahmā,
the lords of the gods, daityas, and dānavas, together with the sages, spoke.
While the ocean was being churned by the high-souled gods and asuras,
a terrible poison appeared— resembling a serpent or a bee, like a dark cloud, and possessing a radiance equal to the fire of universal destruction.
Like Time and Death incarnate, possessing the splendor of the sun at the end of an eon,
it scorched the three worlds, shone like the sun, and quivered on all sides.
As the poison rose up, possessing a brilliance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction,
Janārdana— whose body was once fair with the hue of blood— was scorched and turned black.
Having seen Janārdana, whose limbs were once fair-red but now made black, all of us gods became terrified and have come to you alone for refuge. (59)
Having heard the words of both the gods and the asuras, the Grandfather,
endowed with great splendor, replied out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Listen, all you deities and sages whose wealth is asceticism,
to that which arose at the beginning when the great ocean was being churned.
The poison, resembling the fire of universal destruction and renowned as Kālakūṭa,
was such that by its mere emergence, Janārdana turned black.
Neither Viṣṇu, nor I, nor all those foremost of gods,
nor any others besides Śaṅkara, are able to withstand his impetuosity.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, who is born from a lotus yet not born from a womb and who possesses the luster of the interior of a lotus, then began to offer praise.
Salutations to you, O Virūpākṣa; salutations to you who possess many eyes.
Salutations to the one with the Pināka bow in hand; indeed, salutations to the one with the thunderbolt in hand.
Salutations to the Lord of the three worlds; salutations to the Master of all beings.
Salutations to the destroyer of the enemies of the gods, the ascetic with three eyes.
Salutations indeed to Brahmā, to Rudra, and to Viṣṇu;
salutations indeed to Sāṃkhya, to Yoga, and to the multitude of beings. ||67||
Salutations indeed to the Death of Death, who destroys the limbs of my mind;
salutations to you, Rudra, the Lord of Gods, the God of gods.
Salutations to the one with matted hair, the Terrifying One, Śaṅkara, and the bearer of the skull.
To the one who is multiform and yet of a single form, to Śiva, and to the giver of boons. ||69||
Salutations to the destroyer of Tripura, to the one worthy of praise, to the lord of the Mothers; salutations to the awakened one, the pure, the liberated, and the absolute.
Salutations to the one who holds a lotus in his hand, to the sky-clad one, to the wearer of a crest-lock;
to the one for whom the three worlds are an offering, and to the moon and Varuṇa.
To the foremost and the fierce one, to the wise one with many eyes;
to Rajas, Sattva, and Tamas, whose source is the unmanifest.
Salutations indeed to the eternal and to that which has an impermanent form, to the eternal and the impermanent;
salutations indeed to the manifest and to the unmanifest, and to the manifest and the unmanifest. ||73||
Salutations indeed to the one who is conceivable, the inconceivable, and both conceivable and inconceivable; salutations to Nara-Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of the afflictions of devotees.
Salutations to Śarva, the beloved of Umā, who is marked by the Nandi and the discus;
salutations to the fortnight, the month, the half-month, and to the year.

Salutations to the one of many forms, to the shaven-headed, to the bearer of the staff, and to the one clad in armor; salutations to the one with a skull in hand, to the one clothed in the directions, and to the wearer of a topknot.
O God, salutations be unto you who possess the banner, who ride the chariot, who are the restrainer, and the celibate student;
who are the Rig, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and the Supreme Person (Puruṣa) and the Lord (Īśvara);
salutations to you through such deeds as these. ||77||
Śrī Mahādeva said:
Having been thus praised by the gods, O lady of beautiful countenance, he then prostrated himself.

But having recognized my devotion, the God of gods—whose head is bathed by the waters of the Gaṅgā, who is subtle, inconceivable due to the excellence of his supreme yoga, and who is indeed not submerged—manifests clearly. ||79||
Thus was I previously praised by the Blessed One, by Brahmā the creator of the world, with various hymns originating from the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Then, being pleased with that high-souled Brahmā,
I addressed the Grandfather in a subtle voice.
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, Protector of the world, Master of the universe!
O Brahmin of noble vows, tell me what task must be performed by me for you. 82.
Having heard those words, the lotus-eyed Brahmā then replied:
"O Lord of the past, future, and present, O Sovereign of Causes, please listen."
O Lotus-eyed Lord, while the ocean was being churned by the gods and the asuras,
[there appeared] one resembling a cloud, like a dark rain-cloud.
A most terrible poison appeared, possessing a radiance like the fire of universal destruction;
it arose like Time and Death, with the splendor of the sun at the end of an eon.
In that [space], there arose before him the Sun-like one, who illuminates the three worlds, blazing forth on all sides with a radiance like the fire of universal destruction.
Seeing that, we were all terrified and our minds were bewildered;
therefore, O Mahādeva, drink it out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. You are indeed the foremost enjoyer, and you alone are the excellent Lord. (87)
O Mahādeva, there exists no one other than you who is able to endure this poison;
it is proclaimed that there is no man capable of it throughout the three worlds. (88)
Having heard these words of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, O fair-faced one, she accepted his speech, saying, "So be it. (89)
Then I began to drink the poison that resembled the God of Death;
as I drank that most terrible poison which caused a foul stench,
my throat quickly turned black, O lady of excellent complexion.
Seeing Takṣaka, the king of the nāgas, who resembled the petals of a blue lotus, clinging as if to his throat and standing there with his tongues flickering, [he was struck with fear]. (91)
Then the immensely radiant Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, said:
"O Mahādeva of noble vows, you shine with this throat."
Then, O daughter of the mountain king, having heard those words of his in the presence of the hosts of gods and the Daityas, O fair-faced one, I [spoke]. (93)
The terrible poison was held in the throat by the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas; therefore, I am indeed Nīlakaṇṭha (the Blue-throated One). 94.
O daughter of the mountain king, when that Kālakūṭa poison of fierce potency was being placed upon my throat by me, the hosts of gods and demons beheld it and were struck with supreme wonder. (95)
Then all the hosts of gods, together with the Daityas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, stood with palms joined in reverence and spoke to her who moves with the gait of an elephant in rut.
Oh, what strength, vigor, and prowess you possess! Oh, how great indeed is your power of yoga!
Oh, what sovereignty you have, O God of gods, with your hair disheveled and struck by the waters of the Gaṅgā! 97.
You alone are Viṣṇu and you are the four-faced Brahmā; you alone are Death and you alone are the Giver of Boons.
You alone are the Sun and you are the Moon; you alone are the Earth and you alone are Water. (98)
You alone are the sacrifice, you alone are the discipline; you alone are what has been and what will be.
You alone are the beginning and the end; you alone are the gross and the subtle—the Puruṣa yourself. 99.
You alone are the subtle essence of the supreme subtle; you alone are fire, and you alone are wind.
You alone are the creator of the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, and its protector at the time of dissolution.
Having spoken these words, the lords of the gods took hold of Soma, bowed their heads in prostration,
and all those great-souled ones departed on their celestial chariots with unrestrained speed, reaching Mount Meru.
This is the supreme secret, more meritorious than merit itself;
that which is called "Nīlakaṇṭha" is renowned and celebrated throughout the world. 102.

To him who constantly retains this meritorious narrative, which destroys sin, was spoken by the Self-Existent One himself and originated from Brahmā— I shall indeed declare a vast and great reward. (103)
O lady of excellent hips, O woman of beautiful form, whatever poison— whether stationary or mobile—
reaches his body, it is quickly neutralized.
It pacifies terrible evil and removes bad dreams;
one becomes beloved among women and in the assembly of the king. (105)
In dispute one attains victory, and in battle one gains valor;
on the journey one finds safety, and at home there is constant prosperity. (106)
O fair-faced one, I shall describe his destiny after the dissolution of the body:
he will have a blue throat, greenish-brown whiskers, and hair marked by the crescent moon. (107)
Three-eyed, with the trident in hand, riding upon the bull and wielding the Pināka bow;
he was glorious, possessing strength equal to Nandin and prowess equal to Nandin. ||108||
By my command, he shall roam through all the worlds in an instant;
his movement cannot be obstructed, just like that of the wind in the sky.
Having become equal in strength to me, he shall remain until the dissolution of all beings.
O lady of excellent hips, I shall declare the destination of those men who are my devotees and those who listen [to this], both in this world and in the next.
A Brāhmaṇa attains the Veda, a Kṣatriya conquers the earth, a Vaiśya gains profit, and a Śūdra shall obtain happiness. ||111||
The diseased is freed from illness, and the bound is released from bondage.
The pregnant woman obtains a son, and the maiden finds a virtuous husband.
One recovers everything lost, both in this world and in the next. 112.
Whatever fruit results from the proper gift of a hundred thousand cows, that same fruit is obtained by hearing this divine narrative of the Lord. 113.
Whether it be a quarter-verse, or even half a verse, or a single verse, or even half a verse—whosoever constantly retains [this] goes to the world of Rudra. ||114||
Having related this tale, which is endowed with the fruits of merit and other virtues, the Lord whose hair is bound by the moon,
accompanied by Umā upon the back of his bull, went to the cave of Kiṣkindhā, for he is fond of mountain retreats.
Having taught them that sin-destroying *Mahāpadam*, the Wind-god bestowed it upon them;
and having studied all of it in its entirety, the best of the twice-born, endowed with auspicious marks, departed for the path of the sun. (116)
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Nīlakaṇṭha," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
The sages said:
"O best among speakers, who is superior by virtue of his qualities, actions, and powers?
We wish to hear correctly this wonderful expansion of his attributes."
Sūta said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient legend concerning the majesty and sovereign power of the great-souled Mahādeva.
Formerly, after having bound Bali, the one of great power who was the sovereign of the three worlds in ancient times, this was proclaimed by Viṣṇu during the conquest of the three worlds.
When the Daityas had been utterly destroyed and the Lord of Śacī was overjoyed,
then all the gods, together with Indra, came to see the Lord.
There, near the Ocean of Milk, dwells the Soul of the Universal Form,
where Siddhas, Brahman-sages, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and hosts of Apsarases reside.
The Nāgas, the divine sages, the rivers, and all the mountains,
having approached that Great-Souled One, praise the Person Hari.
You are the sustainer and you are the creator of this world; O Lord, you create the worlds.
And through your grace, the imperishable threefold universe has attained prosperity;
all the asuras have been conquered and Bali has indeed been bound by you.
Thus addressed by the gods, the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis, Viṣṇu,
the Supreme Person, then replied to all those deities.
Listen, O best of gods, I shall declare the cause:
he who is the creator of all beings, Time, the Lord who brings about the end of time.
For by whose grace alone the worlds were created along with Brahmā through his illusory power (māyā),
it was by that very same grace that he attained the state of perfection in the beginning.
Formerly, when darkness was unmanifest and the three worlds were swallowed by me,
while all beings resided within my belly, I then lay within that world.
Having become thousand-headed, thousand-eyed, and thousand-footed,
with the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, he lay upon the pure waters.
In the meantime, from afar I beheld one of immeasurable splendor,
resembling a hundred suns and blazing with his own radiance.
That Supreme Person, the great yogin with four faces, possessing a golden luster,
wearing a black antelope skin, and adorned with a water-pot—
He, that Lord, was reached by him in merely the blink of an eye. 14.
Then Brahmā, who is saluted by all the worlds, said to me:
"Who are you, from where have you come, and why do you stand here? Tell me, O Lord. (15)
"I am the creator of the worlds, self-existent and facing in all directions.
When I was addressed in this way by the god Brahmā, I then spoke to him.
"I am the creator of the worlds and their destroyer again and again"—
as they spoke thus, each desiring victory over the other,
a flame was seen stationed, having taken its stand in the northern direction.
Then, beholding her within that mass of flames, the two of them were struck with wonder;
and by that very splendor, all the water was turned into light.
Then, as that fire grew exceedingly wonderful, both Brahmā and I quickly ran toward that flame. ||19||
Supporting both heaven and earth, he stands as a circle of flames;
and in the midst of those flames, we behold one of vast radiance.
The subtle sign (liṅga), measuring a span, is supremely illuminated;
it is neither golden in its center, nor made of stone, nor of silver.
Inexpressible and inconceivable, again and again both perceptible and imperceptible,
possessed of great power and exceedingly terrible, it was then swelling greatly,
extended with garlands of flames, and cast down, causing fear to all beings.
He who indeed reaches the end of this linga, the source of mantras—
[a form] exceedingly terrible in appearance, as if splitting asunder heaven and earth.
Then Brahmā said to me: "Go downwards without weariness;
let us discover the end of this great-souled Liṅga."
"I shall go upwards as far as its end can be seen.
Then, having made this agreement, the two of them departed—one upwards and one downwards.
Then, for a thousand years, I went further down again;
yet I did not see its end, and I was undoubtedly terrified. ||26||
Likewise, Brahmā was exhausted, yet he did not perceive his own limit;
he came together with me right there in that great expanse of water.
Then both of them were filled with wonder at that great-souled one.
Deluded by that illusion, they remained there with their consciousness lost.
Then, having entered into meditation there, he beheld the Lord who faces all directions,
the source and the repository, the imperishable sovereign of the worlds.

With palms joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, we offer our salutation to that Śarva, the wielder of the trident, who possesses a terrifying roar, a fearsome form, and fangs; to the unmanifest, the great one. (1.55.30)
Homage be to you, O God, Lord of the world and gods; homage be to you, the Great One, Lord of beings.
Homage be to you, the eternal source of perfection; homage be to you, the foundation of the entire universe. ||31||
You are Parameṣṭhin, the Supreme Brahman, the Imperishable, and the Highest State;
you are the Most Excellent, Vāmadeva, Rudra, Skanda, Śiva, and the Lord.
You are the sacrifice; you are the exclamation *vaṣaṭ*; you are the syllable *oṃ*, the supreme state;
you are the utterance *svāhā* and the salutation *namaḥ*; you are the consecration of all ritual acts.
The utterance of *svadhā*, the recitation of mantras, vows, and likewise restraints;
the Vedas, the worlds, and the gods—the Blessed One alone is all these in every respect. (34)
You are the sound of space, the origin and dissolution of the elements;
you are the fragrance of the earth, the taste of the waters, and light-form, O Maheśvara.
O Lord of Gods, the touch of wind, the form of the deity, the body of the moon, wisdom, knowledge, and the seed within primordial nature (prakṛti). ||36||
You are the creator of all beings, Time, Death, Yama, and the Ender;
you sustain the three worlds, and you alone create them, O Lord.
With your eastern face, O Lord, you manifest the state of Indra;
and with your southern face, you consume the worlds.
With your western face, you indeed exercise the nature of Varuṇa;
with your northern face, your state as Soma is established.
O God, you shine manifoldly as the imperishable source of the worlds;
you are the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Maruts, and the two sons of the Aśvins.
The Sādhyas, Vidyādharas, Nāgas, and Apsarases rich in asceticism;
the high-souled Vālakhilyas, who have attained perfection through austerity and are firm in their vows. ||41||
O Lord of Gods, those others of restrained vows who were born from you—Umā, Sītā, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, and Gāyatrī as well. (42)
O Lord of Gods, Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Dhṛti, Medhā, Lajjā, Kṣānti, Vapuḥ, Svadhā,
Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Kriyā, and the goddess Sarasvatī of speech—
these were all born from you, as were Sandhyā and Rātri. 43.
Homage be to you, whose radiance is like ten million times ten thousand suns; homage be to you, whose range is that of a thousand moons!
Homage be to you who assume the form of mountains; homage be to you, the mine of all virtues! 44.

Salutations be to you who bear the form of the *paṭṭiśa* spear; salutations be to you who bear the majesty of the shield. Salutations be to you, O Rudra, who hold the *pināka* bow in hand; salutations be to you who bear the arrow and the discus. ||45||

Homage be to you, whose limbs are adorned with ashes; homage be to you, the destroyer of the body of Kāma. Homage be to you, O God clad in golden raiment; homage be to you, O God with golden arms. ||46||
Homage be to you, O God of golden form; homage be to you, O God of golden navel.
Homage be to you, wondrous with a thousand eyes; homage be to you, O God whose seed is gold. 47.

Homage be to you, O God of golden hue; homage be to you, O God, the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha). Homage be to you, O God clad in golden raiment; homage be to you, O God, the Bestower of gold. ||48||
Homage be to you, O God, wearer of golden garlands; homage be to you, O God, bearer of golden weapons;
homage be to you, O God, clad in golden bark; homage be to you, who utters the terrible roar. ||49||
Homage be to you, O Bhairavavegavega; homage be to you, O Śaṅkara, O Nīlakaṇṭha! Homage be to you, O divine one with a thousand arms; homage be to you, O lover of dancing and instrumental music!
Being thus praised, the high-minded one became manifest;
the god, the great yogi, shone with a splendor equal to ten million suns. ||51||
Then Mahādeva Maheśvara, delighted,
addressed him as if swallowing the other with thousands of millions of mouths.
He had a single neck and a single matted lock of hair; he was adorned with various ornaments, his limbs were variegated with diverse paintings, and he was anointed with various garlands and unguents.
The Blessed One, Pinākapāṇi, who has the bull as his seat and bears the trident;
who carries the staff and the black antelope skin, and who wears a skull and assumes a terrible form. ||54||
Wearing a serpent as his sacred thread and bestowing fearlessness upon the gods,
he let out a laugh that resembled the roar of a kettledrum and the thundering of a rain-cloud;
released by him, it then filled the entire sky.
Terrified by that great sound of the Great-Souled One, we then spoke;
the Great Yogi replied, "I am pleased, O best of gods."
Behold this Great Illusion, and let all fear be abandoned;
you two were born from my limbs as ancient ones of old.
"This right arm of mine is Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds;
and my left arm is Viṣṇu, who stands ever-present in battles.
I am well-pleased with you both; I grant you a boon according to your desire."
Then, with delighted minds, those two sinless and high-souled ones bowed again at his feet and spoke once more.
If affection has arisen [in you], and if a boon is to be granted to us two,
O God, Lord of the Suras, may we have eternal devotion toward you.
The Blessed One said:
"Let it be so, O illustrious ones; create various offspring.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there.
Thus have I described to you the power of that yogin;
by him all this was created, while we here are merely the instruments.
For this form is unknown and unmanifest, designated as Śiva;
it is inconceivable and invisible, yet those with the eye of knowledge behold it.
Let him offer salutation to that Lord of the Gods, by whom those with the eye of knowledge behold the subtle and the inconceivable. (64)
O Mahādeva, homage be unto you; O Maheśvara, homage be unto you!
O best and most excellent among gods and asuras, O Haṃsa of the mind, homage be unto you! (65)
Sūta said:
Having heard this, all the gods went to their respective abodes,
offering salutations to the high-souled Śaṅkara.
Whoever should recite this hymn to the Great-Souled Lord obtains all his desires and is liberated from sins.
All this eternal Brahman was spoken by that powerful Viṣṇu through the grace of Mahādeva. Thus,
I have related to you all of this power of Maheśvara.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Hymn to the Emergence of the Liṅga," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, how did King Purūravas, the son of Ila, go to heaven month after month on the new moon day,
and how did he satisfy the ancestors?
Sūta said:
And I shall proclaim his power, O Śāṃśapāyana—
the conjunction of Aila with the Ādityas and with the high-souled Soma.

The waning and waxing of the moon, which consists of non-essence, during its bright and dark fortnights, as well as the determination of the fortnight belonging to the ancestors (the dark fortnight), [are explained]. ||3||
From Soma alone comes the attainment of immortality as well as the satiation of the ancestors;
it is also the vision of the ancestors who have partaken of the funeral offerings (kavya) and consumed the Soma.
Just as Purūravas, the son of Ilā, gratified the ancestors—
all this I shall relate, along with the chapters, in their proper order.
But when the moon and the sun, having come together with a lunar mansion, dwell for one night in a single orb on the new moon day; ||6||
He then goes to behold the sun and the moon,
and on every new-moon day, he visits his maternal and paternal grandfathers;
having paid his respects there, he awaits the proper time.
From the Soma that was being offered, which flowed for the sake of the ancestors, the wise Purūravas, son of Ila, with great effort, worshipped him month after month;
he, remaining in the celestial realm, honored him who possessed the Pitṛs along with Soma. ||8||
Having deliberated upon both of those—the two *lava*s and the measure of *kuhu*—the worshiper of Sinīvālī [should follow] the standard of Sinīvālī. ||9||
Having understood the digit (kalā) that is merely Kuhu, he worships Kuhu again;
then, observing the time, he perceives her alone as the radiant one.
From where would the nectar of immortality flow from the moon for the satisfaction of a month, by means of ten and five streams of that nectar? (11)
Then, having drunk from the dark fortnight while it was being milked by the rays [of the sun],
he was immediately gratified by that gentle nectar flowing from the fortnight.
Having offered the oblation according to the ritual prescribed by his father for the purpose of pacification, that lord of kings,
O monarch, truly gratified the ancestors with nectar and ambrosia—
the Saumyas, the Barhiṣads, the Kāvyas, and likewise the Agniṣvāttas.
That which is called Agni the Season (Ṛtu) is considered to be the year;
for from him the seasons were born, and from the seasons those things that belong to the seasons.
For the Pitṛs, known as the half-months, are the sons of the Year;
the Seasons are the Grandfathers (Pitāmahas), and the Months are both the Seasons and the sons of the Year. ||15||
The Prapitāmahas are indeed the gods; the five-year-old ones are the sons of Brahmā. Those born of Soma are to be known as Saumyas, and those born of Kavi are to be known as Kāvyas. ||16||
The gods born of Soma and likewise the Soma-drinkers are known as those who have been invited;
the Kavyas, known as the ghee-drinkers, are the classes of ancestors who are satisfied. ||17||
The Kavyas, the Barhiṣads, and the Agniṣvāttas—these are the three classes;
those householders who are performers of sacrifices are certainly the Barhiṣads of the seasons.
Furthermore, the householders who perform sacrifices, the Agniṣvāttas, the Ārtavās, the lords of the Aṣṭakās, and the Kāvyas—know them to be the five classes of Pitṛs. ||19||
For these, the Saṃvatsara is indeed Agni, the Parivatsara is Sūrya,
the Iḍvatsara is said to be Soma, and the Anuvatsara is Vāyu.
Rudra, however, is the year for those five-year periods that constitute the Yugas;
they are remembered as the Leśas, the Uṣmapās, and the Divākīrtis. ||21||
These drink the nectar in heaven month after month on the new moon day;
he gratified them with that [offering] as long as Purūravas remained.
Understand that from the Soma it flows forth month after month;
therefore, there is the nectar of immortality for the ancestors who drink the Soma.
Thus, that nectar is gentle, being both ambrosia and honey;
just as the fifteen digits of the moon appear in succession during the dark fortnight.
The thirty-three gods born of the Vedic meters drink these waters;
having drunk them for a month, they go on the fourteenth day to the nectar of immortality.
Thus being drunk by the deities, the maker of night reached the new moon (amāvāsyā),
remaining in the fifteenth part.
And having been nourished by the *suṣumnā* ray, he [reappears] at the new moon in due order.
Those ancestors drink the nectar of immortality at two times during the day.
Then, when the Soma had been consumed, that very Sun, with his single ray named Suṣumna,
caused it to swell for the sake of the Soma-drinking ancestors.
When the digit is entirely exhausted, he replenishes the moon once again;
as it is being replenished by the *suṣumṇā* ray, its portions are restored in succession through its splendor.
Thus, the dark digits wane, while the bright ones are replenished.
Thus, by the power of the sun, the body of the moon is replenished;
on the full moon day, it is indeed seen bright with its orb complete. In this manner occurs the manifestation of the moon during the two fortnights, the bright and the dark.
Thus, this Soma, possessing the Pitṛs, is traditionally known as the Idvatsara;
it has traversed [the year] together with the fifteen streams of nectar flowing from the dead.
Therefore, I shall describe the joints and the junctions of the joints,
just as the knotted joints are found in sugarcanes and bamboos.
Likewise, they know the half-months and the lunar phases (parvan) as being both bright and dark;
the knots and the junctions (sandhi) are distinguished by the full moon and the new moon. The half-months are indeed the parvans, beginning from the third day.

Since the rite of establishing the sacred fires (agnyādheya) is performed at the junctions of the lunar phases, that time—consisting of the evening and the first day of the lunar fortnight—is the time for the full-moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsika). ||34||
When the sun is situated at the Vyatīpāta yoga, one should [offer] above the line during the interval between the ages (yugāntara);
and likewise, when the moon has risen during that same interval between the ages, one should [offer] above the line in due order.
If they gaze at each other during a full moon on a Vyatīpāta day,
at whatever time that occurs at the boundary, it is indeed a Vyatīpāta.
Having observed the instruction regarding the time of the sun, the calculation proceeds;
indeed, that is the path of the time for action, which is immediately ordained from time.
On the bright fortnight of the full moon, at the junctions of night, it is the full moon (pūrṇimā);
because the ancestors together with the deities behold it, therefore the first full moon is remembered by the name Anumati. ||38||
Because the moon shines exceedingly on the night of the full moon, and because it delights [the world], the poets know that night as Rākā. (39)
When the moon and the sun dwell together in the same constellation,
that single fifteenth night is known as the new moon (amāvāsyā).
Then, on the full moon day, the moon was clearly visible to them;
when they saw it at midday during a Vyatīpāta conjunction, with both the sun and the moon full, that was indeed the full-moon day (Pūrṇimā) at the afternoon hour. ||41||
When the moon and the sun, having come together, behold that severed new-moon day, it is called *darśa*.
The time consisting of two *lava*s at each of the new moon conjunctions (*parvasandhi*)—
which is two syllables and a mere *kuhū* measure— is known as that specific time.
Although the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is devoid of the moon, it is joined with the central sun.
Having reached the sun for half a day and half a night,
the moon suddenly attains liberation from the sun;
thus there are two times of celebration at dawn, while the sun emerges at midday during their conjunction.
On the first day of the bright fortnight, the moon indeed emerges from between those two orbs,
the orb of the sun and its own.
For at that time, it is the hour for the oblation and the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance of the New Moon sacrifice;
