this should be known as the beginning of the season, the festival (*parvan*) of the Amāvāsyā.
On the day of the full moon and on the new moon (amāvāsyā), when the moon has waned during the dark fortnight,
for that reason the sun is indeed seized by day on the amāvāsyā; therefore,
it is called amāvāsyā because the [moon] is seized by day in the sky by those who observe its disappearance.
Indeed, out of great respect for those very digits (kalās), the names of the lunar days (tithis) have been designated by the wise, who are not of dull nature. ||48||
Then both the sun and the moon would show themselves to one another;
thereafter, he would gradually emerge from the solar disc by that very same path.
For two lavae of the day and night, the moon touches the sun;
that is indeed the time for the oblation and the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance of the New Moon sacrifice.
The time which was designated by Kokira when he said "kuhu," is therefore known as Kuhu, because the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is named after that time. 51.
When the moon has its remaining portion diminished to the measure of Sinīvālī, it enters the sun on the new-moon day; therefore, that [lunar phase] is known as Sinīvālī.
The time for the parvan is indeed equal to the time of the vaṣaṭ-utterance;
both the conjunction of the moon and sun (vyatīpāta) and the full moon are traditionally remembered as such. ||53||
The time of the festival (parva) at the new moon and full moon is two mātrās;
the time of the kuhū and sinīvālī phases is traditionally held to be an ocean (four mātrās), consisting of two lavas.
In the solar and lunar mandalas, the time of the lunar nodes (parva) rests upon the digits (kalā);
thus indeed occurs that bright fortnight during the junctions of the lunar nights.
The glorious moon, though its orb is full, becomes eclipsed;
for it is on the fifteenth day that the Soma is replenished at the full moon.
By means of ten and five digits (kalās) respectively according to the sequence of the days, there is therefore no fifteenth digit nor a sixteenth digit in the moon;
consequently, for the moon, there occurs a great waning on the fifteenth day. ||57||
Thus these Pitṛs are gods who drink Soma and cause Soma to increase;
they are the seasonal ones (Ārtavas) because they, as gods, bring about the seasons (Ṛtus). ||58||
Therefore, I shall describe the ancestors who partake of the monthly śrāddha,
as well as their destination and nature, and indeed the destiny of the śrāddha itself.
The destination of the dead, nor their return, can be known even by means of well-established ascetic power, let alone by the eye of flesh. (1.56.60)
These Pitṛs, who are the deities of the Śrāddha rites, are known as the worldly ancestors (laukika-pitaraḥ).
The gods are gentle, performers of sacrifice, and all are indeed not born from a womb (ayonija). ||61||
All those gods are also the ancestors (pitṛs), and the gods indeed nourish them;
likewise, humans are also ancestors, while others are known as the worldly ones (laukikas). ||62||

The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—those who have performed soma sacrifices are remembered as "Soma-sacrificers," while those who have not are known as "non-Soma-sacrificers. (63)
Those who are remembered as performers of sacrifices are indeed known as the Barhiṣads;
engaged in these rites, they remain satisfied until the birth of another body.
Those who perform oblations and those who officiate at sacrifices are known as the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs;
so too are those who are established in the various stages of life according to the duties of their respective āśramas.
And they do not falter at all, through action endowed with faith,
through celibacy, austerity, sacrifice, and indeed through progeny.
Those who are engaged in these seven types of actions— through faith, through knowledge, and through generosity— remain so until they fall from the world of the gods.
Together with those gods, the subtle Pitṛs who drink the Soma,
they rejoice in heaven after having gone there, and they wait upon the one who possesses the Pitṛs.
For those who possess offspring and perform ritual acts, praise alone is considered the perfected result;
for them, the food offered as a funeral libation is received by their kinsmen and relatives.
The inhabitants of the world of Soma obtain satisfaction for a month from those who partake in the Śrāddha;
these are the human ancestors who partake in the monthly Śrāddha.
But others besides them, who are of mixed origin from wombs of action,
have fallen away from the duties of their stages of life and are deprived of the utterances of *svadhā* and *svāhā*.
With their bodies shattered, having become ghosts in the abode of Yama, those evil-minded ones,
having arrived at the place of torment, grieve only for their own deeds.
Long-lived yet exceedingly emaciated, discolored and naked,
and overcome by hunger and thirst, they flee hither and thither.
Desiring water, they run here and there trembling toward rivers, lakes, ponds, and reservoirs, yet they long for the food of others. (74)
And they are being cooked in those various places of transit,
indeed in the Śālmalī, in the Vaitaraṇī, and in those Kumbhīpākas.
And in the Karambha-vālukā [sand], likewise in the Asipatravana [sword-leaf forest],
and in the crushing between rocks, they are cast down by their own actions.
In that regard, their locations—though like those of suffering—are indeed like the sky;
for those who dwell in other worlds, they are distinguished by various names and lineages. (77)
Having offered three pindas upon the darbha grass spread on the ground in a counter-clockwise direction,
they indeed satisfy those ancestors who are established in the realms of the deceased.
Those who have not reached the places of torment, but are created fivefold upon the earth among beings ranging from animals to stationary objects, [are engaged] in those activities of living beings.
In various forms of birth and among the diverse animal wombs,
whatever food these beings consume in those respective births,
that very food, when offered in a śrāddha ceremony, reaches them.
When food obtained by righteous means is offered at the proper time and according to the prescribed rite to a worthy recipient,
it reaches that kinsman upon whom the giver depends for support.
Just as a calf finds its mother when the cows have been lost,
so does the mantra at a śrāddha ceremony bring the ancestors to those for whom it is intended.
Thus, Sanatkumāra, perceiving with his divine eye, declared that the Śrāddha rite performed with faith and according to the mantras is complete;
for the mantra, knowing the coming and going of the departed spirits, causes it to reach the ancestors. (83)
They are known as the Bahvṛcas, the drinkers of heat (Oṣmapas), and the Divākīrtis;
for them, the dark fortnight is the day and the bright fortnight is the night, which is their sleep. 84.

Thus, these ancestors are indeed gods, and the gods are indeed ancestors; they are manifold according to the seasons and the intermediate periods, and are remembered as being fathers to one another. ||85||
These indeed are the divine ancestors and those who are human ancestors;
when they are gratified by an act endowed with faith, they in turn grant gratification.
Thus have the Pitṛs of the Soma-drinkers been described;
for this is the established doctrine regarding the nature of the Pitṛs as recognized in the Purāṇa. (87)
Thus occurred the meeting of the Sun, the Ancestors, and the Moon,
as well as the attainment of the nectar of immortality and the satiation of the ancestors.
The time of the full moon and the new moon, as well as the abode of the ancestors, has been briefly proclaimed to you; this is the eternal creation. ||89||
The manifold nature of everything has been described only partially;
it is impossible to enumerate it in its entirety, yet it must be accepted by one who desires prosperity.
This creation of Svāyambhuva has indeed been traversed by me here in detail and in its proper sequence; what more shall I describe? 91.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pitṛs," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
The sages said:
I desire to hear in detail the creation and the essential nature of those four yugas that existed previously during the interval of Svāyambhuva Manu.
Sūta said:
In connection with the earth and other elements, I have previously set forth [this matter]; now listen as I explain the cycle of these four yugas. (2)
Having calculated here by number and having explained in detail from every perspective,
[he spoke of] the Yuga, the divisions of the Yugas, and likewise the duties of the Yugas.
I shall now explain here, according to the truth, the junction-period (sandhyaṃśa) and the junction (sandhāna) of the Yugas, as well as the sixfold description of the Yugas.
A human year is known by worldly means of measurement;
calculating by that year, I shall here describe the four yugas.
[The divisions of time are] the blink of an eye (nimeṣa), the kāṣṭhā, the kalās, and also the muhūrtas.
For one should know that whatever syllable is short is equal in duration to the time of a blink of an eye.
Fifteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*, and one should count thirty *kāṣṭhās* as one *kalā*.
Thirty *kalās* constitute one *muhūrta*, and thirty of those [muhūrtas] make up a day and night combined.
The sun divides day and night for both humans and gods;
therein, the day is intended for the performance of action, and the night for sleep.

For the ancestors, a month constitutes a day and a night; furthermore, their division of these two is such that the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) is their day and the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) is their night for sleep.
Thirty human months are known as one month of the ancestors (pitrya).
Indeed, three hundred and sixty human months are reckoned as one year of the ancestors. || 1.57.10 ||
That which constitutes one hundred years by human calculation is indeed reckoned here as three years and four additional months for the ancestors (pitṛs). ||11||
That which is known as a human year by worldly calculation is considered in this scripture to be one divine day and night; this is the settled conclusion.
A divine day and night constitute a year; furthermore, their division is as follows:
the northern course (udagayana) is the day there, and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is the night.
Those two divine days and nights, when reckoned together, constitute thirty such years; that is remembered as one divine month. (14)
Know that one hundred human years are equal to three of those divine months;
likewise, ten such days constitute a divine month—this indeed is remembered as the divine rule.
Three hundred assemblies for sixty years each—this indeed is declared to be one divine year by human reckoning. ||16||
Three thousand years by human reckoning constitute thirty years, which is considered one year of the Seven Seers (Saptarṣis). ||17||
Nine thousand human years,
plus another ninety, are recorded as one year of Krauñca.
Thirty-six thousand human years are to be known as one hundred [divine] years; for this is remembered as the rule for the celestial [reckoning]. (19)
Three hundred thousand and sixty thousand human years— those who know calculation say that this is reckoned as one thousand divine years. (1.57.20)
Thus has it been sung by the sages, endowed with divine calculation; the determination of the duration of the ages is indeed according to divine measure. 21.
Sages know that there are four ages (yugas) in the land of Bhārata:
first, that which is named Kṛtayuga; after that, Tretā is ordained;
and Dvāpara and Kali—these are the ages one should reckon. ||22||
They say that the Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts for as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
And during these three twilights and the three periods of twilight,
hundreds and thousands [of years] proceed by a decrease of one.
The Tretā age is proclaimed to have a duration of exactly three thousand years;
its dawn (sandhyā) consists of three hundred years, and its twilight (sandhyāṃśa) is of the same measure. ||25||
The wise say that the Dvāpara age consists of two thousand years;
its dawn is two hundred years, and the twilight period is equal to the dawn.
The wise say that Kali consists of one thousand years;
its dawn lasts for one hundred years, and the twilight is equal in duration to the dawn.
This period of twelve thousand years is proclaimed as the cycle known as a Yuga;
it consists of the four ages: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali. (28)
Herein, the years have been created according to human measurement;
I shall now describe the duration of the Kṛta age according to its own measure.
In number, there are one hundred fourteen thousand;
indeed, forty thousand years constitute the Kali age.
Thus, the measurement of time has been specifically described here;
in this manner, the period of four yugas is reckoned without the transitional periods (sandhyāṃśaka). ||31||
The four yugas, together with their transitional periods (sandhyās) and sub-periods (sandhyāṃśas), amount in number to thirty-four million, twenty thousand, and one hundred and eighty years. (32)
Thus, seventy-one such cycles of four yugas,
including the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages, are called an *antara* of Manu.
Now learn the number of years for a Manvantara according to the human reckoning:
it is proclaimed to be thirty crores of years. (34)
Furthermore, this period consists of sixty-seven million, twenty thousand, and some additional years. (35)
This is the number of a Manvantara as recorded by the twice-born who are experts in calculation;
this duration of a Manvantara is proclaimed along with its associated Yugas. ||36||
The first age, Kṛtayuga, consists of four thousand years;
I shall now describe Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali as well.
The meaning of these two [ages] occurring simultaneously cannot be expressed in two ways;
for this pair of ages has been told by me to you in sequence, due to the complexity arising from the context of the lineage of the sages. (38)
There, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, Manu and those seven ṛṣis [established] the dharma based on revelation and the dharma based on tradition, as impelled by Brahmā. (39)
The seven seers declared the Vedic dharma characterized by such [injunctions] as the union with wife and the sacred fire, and that which is designated as the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. (1.57.40)

Manu, the son of Svayambhū, has declared the Dharma that has come down through tradition, characterized by the Smṛtis and right conduct, and endowed with the practices of the castes and stages of life.
Indeed, by means of truth, celibacy, sacred learning, and austerity,
and through the lineage of those who had performed well-refined penances, they proceeded in due order.
In the first Tretā Yuga, however, that of the Seven Sages and Manu, it occurred without prior conscious intent and indeed without any deliberate action on their part. (43)
Those mantras were indeed manifested through examples such as the Tāraka and others;
however, in the first kalpa, they appeared spontaneously to the gods.
Furthermore, even upon the disappearance of these accomplishments (siddhis), their continued practice proceeds;
those mantras which existed throughout thousands of past kalpas indeed reappear for them through the arising of intuitive inspiration (pratibhāsa). ||45||
The Ṛg-verses, Yajus-formulas, Sāman-chants, and Atharvan mantras were proclaimed by the seven seers; Manu, however, proclaimed the Dharma based on tradition (Smārta).
At the beginning of the Tretā age, the Vedas existed as mere collections (saṃhitās) with dharma as their supplement;
however, due to the contraction of the lifespan, they were divided into separate branches during the Dvāpara ages.
The ṛṣis by their austerity and the gods during the Kali and Dvāpara ages—
these divine beings, without beginning or end, were created in the past by the Self-born One.
Possessing the same dharma, together with their progeny and their constituent parts, the declarations of the Vedas play out according to the dharma of each respective age,
having common goals as they adapt to the particular yuga.
Sacrifices involving physical exertion are for the Kṣatriya; sacrifices of oblations are for the lord of the people (the Vaiśya);
sacrifices of service are for the Śūdra; but the best of the twice-born have the sacrifice of silent recitation (japa).
Likewise, in the Tretā age, the castes were joyful, protected by righteousness, devoted to ritual action, possessed of offspring, prosperous, and happy. (51)
The Kṣatriyas follow the Brāhmaṇas, the Vaiśyas follow the Kṣatriyas, and the Śūdras follow the Vaiśyas; thus they are devoted to one another in succession. ||52||
Their auspicious activities, as well as the duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life,
were performed with a mind resolved through its own nature and expressed by speech; thus,
in the Tretā Yuga, the undertaking of ritual actions was accomplished without deficiency.
Longevity, intelligence, strength, beauty, health, and virtuous conduct—
indeed, all these are common to everyone during the Tretā age.
Brahmā established the system of castes and stages of life for them;
however, those subjects, out of delusion, did not observe those duties.
Due to their mutual conflict, the descendants of Manu again followed [the path of discord].
Having perceived the true state of affairs, Svāyambhuva Manu, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), [acted accordingly].
Dhātṛ, however, begot from Śatarūpā two sons,
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, who were the first lords of the earth.
From that time forward, kings arose as wielders of the rod;
and because they delighted the subjects, these sages became known as "rājan. (58)
Those men on earth who are hidden evildoers and impossible to conquer—
even for them, I have performed penance in this scripture for the purpose of establishing righteousness.
The divisions of the social classes were proclaimed during the Tretā age;
thereafter, those sages, who were like bulls among Brahmins, compiled the mantras into collections.
And at that very time, the sacrifice was set in motion by the deities,
by the Yāmas, and by the Śuklas, through prayers accompanied by all necessary materials.
Together with Viśvabhū and the lord of gods (Indra) of great splendor,
those sacrifices were first set in motion by the deities during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
In the Tretā age, truth, recitation, austerity, and charity are said to be dharma;
however, as ritual action (kriyā-dharma) declines, the dharma of truth (satya-dharma) prevails.
From that, heroes are born— long-lived, possessed of great strength,
noble-minded as they have laid aside the rod of punishment, performers of sacrifices, and exponents of the Veda.
With eyes as broad as lotus petals, broad chests, and well-knit frames,
they were like lions at the end of an age, possessed of great strength, and moved with the gait of elephants in rut.
And in the Tretā age, there were universal emperors who were great archers,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and whose proportions were like those of the banyan tree.
Those two arms are known as *nyagrodha* when they are equal to the span (*vyāma*); this is called the *nyagrodha* [proportion].
When the height of an embodied being from the base is equal to his outstretched arms, that is known as the *samucchraya-pariṇāha*, the circular proportion of a *nyagrodha*. ||67||
The wheel, the chariot, the jewel, the queen, the treasury, the elephant, and likewise the horse—
these are the seven extraordinary jewels belonging to all universal monarchs.
The discus, the chariot, the jewel, the sword, and the bow-jewel as the fifth,
the banner, and the treasure— these seven are proclaimed to be devoid of life.
The wife, the domestic priest, the commander of the army, the chariot-maker, the counselor, the horse, and the elephant calf—these are proclaimed to be living beings. ||1.57.70||
These fourteen divine jewels, perfected by the great-souled ones, are to be possessed by all universal monarchs.
By a portion of Viṣṇu, universal emperors are born upon the earth throughout all the past and future Manvantaras. (72)

Those who were in the past and those who will be in the future, as well as those who exist in the present—these are the universal monarchs (cakravartins) born here in the Tretā Yuga and the other ages. ||73||
For those rulers of the earth, these four wonderful and auspicious things indeed come to pass here: strength, righteousness, happiness, and wealth.
Indeed, wealth, virtue, pleasure, fame, and victory are all attained by kings together, without mutual conflict. (75)
By means of sovereignty such as the power of atomization (aṇimā) and so forth,
as well as by their lordly power and other ascetic merit (tapas), they surpass even the sages;
and by both strength and ascetic merit, they surpass the gods, dānavas, and humans.
They were also born with superhuman characteristics residing in their bodies:
tufts of hair on their heads and eyebrows on their foreheads, tongues capable of wiping their faces,
copper-colored luster on their lips, teeth, and lips, the Śrīvatsa mark, and hair growing upwards.
Their arms reached down to their knees, their hands were webbed, and they were marked with the sign of the bull;
they possessed the girth of a banyan tree, shoulders like those of lions, and excellent testicles; they had the gait of lordly elephants and possessed large jaws. (78)
On their feet there are wheels and fish, and on their hands there are conchs and lotuses;
those kings shall live for eighty-five thousand years, free from old age.
The four unobstructed movements of those wheel-turning monarchs were in the atmosphere, in the ocean, in the netherworld, and upon the mountains.
Sacrifice, charity, austerity, and truth are said to be the dharma of the Tretā age;
at that time, dharma proceeds according to the divisions of social classes and stages of life.
And the science of government (daṇḍanīti) is set in motion for the purpose of establishing the boundaries of conduct;
indeed, all subjects are then healthy, well-nourished, free from disease, and full of heart's content.
In the ordinance for the Tretā Yuga, the Veda is remembered as being one with four quarters;
at that time, human beings live for three thousand years. ||83||
Crowded with sons and grandsons, they nevertheless die in due course;
this is the dharma in the Tretā Yuga—learn now of the junction of the Tretā. (84)
The nature of the Tretā Yuga exists only during the first quarter of its twilight; indeed, the nature of the twilight persists for one quarter of the Yuga. (85)
Śaunaka said:
Tell me correctly how the commencement of the sacrifice took place at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, and previously during the Svāyambhuva creation. 86.
When the twilight period had vanished along with the Kṛta Yuga,
and when the age called the Kalā had begun and the Tretā Yuga had arrived,
they indeed established the system of social classes and stages of life once again.
"And having gathered those provisions, how was the journey undertaken?
Having heard this, the Sūta said: "Listen, Śaunaka. (88)
Just as at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga there was the commencement of sacrifice,
when plants had grown, when the release of rain had begun,
and when the means of livelihood were established in householders' dwellings and cities.
Having established the system of the castes and stages of life, and having composed the mantras and the Saṃhitā,
he then joined those mantras to rituals pertaining to this world and the next.
Likewise, Viśvāmitra, the lord of sages, then commenced the sacrifice,
accompanied by all the deities and provided with every necessary material.
Then, while the horse sacrifice was being performed, the great seers assembled;
having all come together, they sacrificed with pure animals after offering oblations.
While the officiating priests were constantly engaged in the sacrificial rites and those sacred texts were being chanted, he then moved with great haste.
When the swift Adhvaryu bulls had moved about,
and when the sacrificial herds of animals had indeed been bound for the offering, ||94||
While the oblation was being poured into the fire by the divine hotṛ-priests for the gods,
and while the high-souled gods, who partake in the sacrifice, had been summoned.
Those gods who consist of the senses and likewise those who partake in the sacrifice—they worship them at that time; they are the gods who exist at the beginnings of the kalpas.

When the great sages, who had risen at the time of the Adhvaryu's summons, saw those herds of animals standing there in distress, they gathered together and asked Indra: "What is this sacrificial rite of yours? (97)
This unrighteousness of yours is indeed powerful, born from your desire for the practice of violence;
O best of gods, this slaughter of animals in your sacrifice is not desired.
Unrighteousness has been undertaken by you, who follow the path of righteousness, through these sacrificial animals.
This is not dharma; this is indeed adharma, for violence is never said to be dharma. ||99||
"O best of gods, if you so desire, perform a sacrifice here according to the sacred tradition (āgama),
by means of a sacrifice prescribed by rule which is a cause for imperishable merit,
using sacrificial seeds in which no violence is found."
O Indra, this great dharma was ordained of old by the Self-existent One: that [roots] which have not sprouted again after being left for a period of up to three years [are fit for use]. ||101||
Thus, since Viśvabhuk is Indra, by whom—whether by mobile beings or immobile things—is it said that he should be worshipped here by sages who perceive the truth? (102)
But those great seers, weary of their dispute and intent upon the truth,
reached an agreement with Indra and questioned the Lord Vasu.
The sages said:
O King of great wisdom, how was the ritual of sacrifice seen by you?
O Lord, speak to Uttānapāda and sever our doubt.
Having heard their words, the king then, without deliberating upon their relative strengths and weaknesses, recalled the Vedic scriptures and spoke the true nature of sacrifice;
he said, "One must sacrifice according to what has been taught. (105)
"One should sacrifice with pure animals, as well as with seeds and fruits"—this [statement] shows me that the very nature of sacrifice is violence. (106)
Just as here in this world, the Saṃhitā mantras containing marks of violence were [revealed] by the great seers endowed with long austerity through their insights such as Tāraka and others;
since it is on the authority of those [seers] that I have spoken, you ought not to hold me in contempt. 107.
"O twice-born ones, if those very mantra-sentences are indeed authoritative, then let the sacrifice proceed; otherwise, our word would be false.
Thus were those self-controlled ascetics, whose wealth was their austerity, deprived of an answer.
Having seen his palace, keep it hidden and remain silent regarding that matter;
for because of speaking falsely, the king entered the netherworld.
As soon as this was said, the king entered the subterranean realm (rasātala);
having been a dweller above, he became a wanderer in the depths.
By those words, he became a dweller upon the surface of the earth;
King Vasuratha arrived as one who cuts through doubts regarding the dharmas.
Therefore, even by one who is highly learned, it should not be said that there is doubt;
for when the dharma has many points of departure, its subtlety remains far beyond reach. (112)
Therefore, no one— not even the gods or the sages, starting from Svāyambhuva Manu himself— is able to declare the Dharma with absolute certainty.
Therefore, the great seers have declared that violence is not the gateway to dharma;
for thousands of millions of seers have ascended to heaven by means of their own actions. 114.
Therefore, the great seers rich in asceticism do not praise either gift-giving or sacrifice;
rather, they consider even meager roots, fruits, vegetables, or a vessel of water as sufficient.
By giving thus according to their means, they are established in the heavenly world.
Absence of malice, absence of greed, self-control, compassion for all beings, austerity,
celibacy, truthfulness, kindness, and fortitude—
this is the unassailable root of the eternal dharma. 116.
Sacrifice consists of the mantras of the Dharma, and austerity consists of fasting;
through sacrifice one attains the gods, and through austerity, moreover, one attains detachment.

The state of a Brahmin [attains] dissolution through the renunciation of action and through dispassion; through knowledge, one attains absolute liberation (kaivalya). These five are recorded as the destinies. ||118||
Thus, in the former Svāyambhuva Manvantara, there arose a very great dispute between the sages and the deities regarding the performance of the sacrifice. 119.
Then those sages, having seen that wondrous path created by Bala,
disregarded the words of Vasiṣṭha and departed just as they had come.
When the hosts of gods have departed, the deities shall obtain the sacrifice;
for it is heard that kings consist of the essence of Brahman and Kṣatriya, perfected through austerity.
Priyavrata, Uttānapāda, Dhruva, Medhātithi, Vasu, Sumedhas, Virajas, Śaṅkhapāda, and Rāja; Prācīnabarhis, Parjanya, Havirdhāna, and other kings. ||122||
These and many other kings, royal sages of great being whose fame is established, have attained perfection and gone to heaven. ||123||
Therefore, austerity is superior to sacrifice for all reasons;
by means of austerity, Brahmā created this entire universe in the beginning. 124.
Therefore, he did not transcend that sacrifice; this is remembered as having penance as its root.
For it was thus that the commencement of sacrifice occurred during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara;
from that time forward, this sacrifice proceeded along with the Yugas.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Commencement of Sacrifice," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Henceforth, I shall again declare the ordinance of the Dvāpara age;
when that Tretā Yuga has declined, the Dvāpara age begins.
The perfection that existed for living beings at the beginning of the Dvāpara age,
however, completely perishes when that age has passed away.
Then, in the Dvāpara age, there arises again among those creatures greed, lack of fortitude, trade, warfare, and uncertainty regarding the true principles.
The division of the castes, the determination of duties,
the sacrificial herb, the animal victim, punishment, intoxication, hypocrisy, intolerance, and force—
the activity of these characterized by rajas and tamas is recorded for the Dvāpara age. ||4||
In the Kṛta age, Dharma exists in its entirety; in the Tretā, it is established in three-quarters;
in the Dvāpara, it becomes disordered; and in the Kali age, it perishes.
In that age, the confusion of the social classes is proclaimed, as is the [confusion] of the stages of life;
and a twofold division arises regarding both the revealed scriptures (śruti) and the traditional law (smṛti).
Because of the duality of both the revealed scriptures (śruti) and the traditional codes (smṛti), no certainty can be attained.
Due to this lack of certainty and the resulting confusion, the true nature of dharma is said to be obscured;
indeed, among men who differ on the true nature of dharma, there arises a diversity of opinions. ||7||
Due to those mutually conflicting views and the confusion of perspectives, no certainty is reached as to whether "this is the Dharma" or "this is not. (8)
Due to the deficiency of causes and the uncertainty regarding the cause itself, as well as the divergence of their opinions, there would indeed be a confusion of views. ||9||
Then, by those divided by their views, this family of treatises was composed;
in the Tretā ages, the one Veda here is ordained as four-footed.
Due to the shortening of the lifespan, [the Veda] is seen to be divided into four parts by the Vedavyāsas during the Dvāpara ages and those following.
Furthermore, the Vedas were divided by the sons of the sages due to errors of vision, through the rearrangement of mantras and brāhmaṇas, and by the inversion of accents and phonemes. ||12||
The *saṃhitās* of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman [Vedas] were compiled by the seers who heard them, through both commonality and variation, as their perspectives differed here and there. (13)
The Brāhmaṇas, the Kalpasūtras, and the Mantrapravacanās—others have been dispatched by the Tīrthas, while some remain stationed against them. ||14||
In the Dvāpara ages, the twice-born, whose conduct and stages of life have become divided, engage [in various practices];
formerly there was only one Ādhvaryava rite, but thereafter it became twofold.

This family of treatises has been rendered confused by those whose meanings are contrary to the general consensus; it has been made disordered in many ways by the introductory discourses on the duties of the Adhvaryu priest.
Likewise, in the divided Dvāpara age, the Atharva, Ṛg, and Sāma Vedas are rendered confused by various inexhaustible alternatives and by those with divergent views.
Their divisions and sub-divisions, as well as their conceptual variations, are inexhaustible;
they flourish in the Dvāpara age, but perish again in the Kali age.
Furthermore, in the Dvāpara age, the opposites of these occur:
drought, death, as well as diseases and calamities.
Furthermore, weariness arises from the sufferings born of the actions of speech and mind;
from that weariness, there arises in them a contemplation on liberation from suffering. (1.58.20)
From reflection comes dispassion; from dispassion, the perception of defects;
and from the perception of defects, the arising of knowledge occurs in the Dvāpara age. ||21||
And among those proud ones, in the first, primordial interval of Svāyambhuva, opponents of the scriptures indeed arise during the Dvāpara age. (22)
The various branches of Āyurveda, those of the auxiliary sciences and of Jyotiṣa, the various branches of Arthaśāstra, and the various branches of Hetuśāstra; ||23||
In the Dvāpara ages, the various divisions of the Smṛti scriptures and their distinct systems of doctrine arise, as do the differing opinions of men.
In the Dvāpara age, success for all beings is achieved through mental, physical, and verbal effort, preceded by bodily austerity.
Lack of steadfastness in greed, war between merchants, uncertainty regarding the principles of reality, the composition of Vedic scriptures, and likewise the confusion of dharma-s. ||26||
In the Dvāpara ages, disease, greed, and slaughter prevail,
as do the destruction of the social classes and stages of life, as well as desire and hatred.
The maximum lifespan of humans is two thousand years when the Dvāpara age is complete;
at the end of that Dvāpara, its twilight period lasts for one quarter of that duration.
Devoid of qualities, that Dharma of the Dvāpara age subsists;
likewise, it remains through its remaining portion, the Sandhyāṃśa.
Learn now of that which belongs to the Dvāpara and the Tiṣya ages;
for when the remaining portion of Dvāpara has passed, the Kali age begins from that point.
Violence, envy, falsehood, deceit, and even the killing of ascetics—
these are the inherent characteristics of the Tiṣya age, and they indeed bring about the ruin of living beings.
This entire dharma has been established, yet dharma is being neglected;
whether through thought, action, or praise, success in one's livelihood may or may not be achieved.
In the Kali age, there will indeed be destructive diseases, constant fears of hunger,
the terrible fear of drought, and the perception of things in a distorted manner.
In the Kali age, memory has no authority in every epoch;
some die while still in the womb, others while in youth,
and indeed the people in the Kali age die in old age, middle age, or childhood.
In the Tiṣya age, people are indeed born who are unrighteous, lacking in proper conduct, prone to fierce anger, deficient in luster, and constantly speaking falsehoods. (35)
Through ill-performed sacrifices, poorly studied texts, wicked conduct, and false scriptures—through these defects of action by the Brahmins, fear arises for the subjects. (36)
Violence, deceit, envy, anger, malice, intolerance, and falsehood—these, as well as passion and greed in every way, prevail among living beings during the Tiṣya age. (37)
Upon the arrival of the Kali Yuga, extreme agitation arises;
at that time, the twice-born do not study the Vedas nor perform sacrifices,
and men, along with Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, gradually perish.
In that Kali age, there will be social relations between those of low birth and the last caste and the Brāhmaṇas, through sharing beds, seats, and meals. (39)
The kings will consist mostly of Śūdras and will be promoters of heretics;
the subjects there will be killers of embryos, and thus the subjects will conduct themselves.
Lifespan, intelligence, strength, physical form, and lineage itself are all diminished;
Śūdras adopt the conduct of Brāhmaṇas, and Brāhmaṇas adopt the conduct of Śūdras.
When the end of the age has arrived, thieves abide by the conduct of kings, kings adopt the conduct of thieves, and servants lose their sense of friendship.
When the end of the age has arrived, women will be devoid of virtue and vows, fond of liquor and meat, and will become mere deceit.
One should know that in that Kali Yuga there will be an increase in wild beasts, a decline of cattle, and the disappearance of the virtuous.
At that time, when the four stages of life have become lax, dharma will waver; thus, even that subtle dharma which yields great fruit will be difficult for worldly enjoyers to attain.
For then the goddess Earth will yield little fruit,
and when the end of the age has arrived, Śūdras will practice ascetic penance.
For that which was a one-day rite in the Kṛta age, and a monthly one in the Dvāpara,
and a yearly one in the Tretā, exceeds [the former] by a single day.
At the end of the ages, kings will become non-protectors and seizers of the tribute; they will be solely intent upon protecting themselves.
O best of the twice-born, at the end of the Yuga, there will be kings who are not Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas who live like Śūdras, and all who offer salutations to Śūdras. (49)
And there will be many kings in this Kali age;
indeed, the god will then rain down wonders when the destruction of the age is at hand.
Moreover, in that debased age, all merchants will for the most part engage in the sale of goods using false measures and deceitful means.
When the end of the age has arrived, there will be an abundance of immoral conduct and false sects of empty appearance; men will be few and women many.
The world will become full of mutual begging;
it will consist of flesh-eaters, harsh in speech, neither upright nor free from malice. (53)
There will be no one to return a favor for what has been done, and the world will become exhausted;
moreover, there will be no fear when someone falls—these are the signs of the end of that age.
The earth will become empty of men and truly desolate;
here, in various regions and cities, there will arise fragmented territories.
The earth will have little water and yield few fruits;
and those who should be protectors will become non-protectors, lacking authoritative command.
They were stealers of others' treasures and violators of others' wives;
they were lustful, evil-minded, unrighteous, and fond of reckless violence.
At the end of the Yuga, men will be born with their consciousness unimpaired, yet with disheveled hair and topknots, and they will be less than sixteen years of age.
When the end of the age has arrived, Śūdras will practice the dharma— possessing white teeth, having conquered their senses, shaven-headed, and clad in saffron robes.
There will be thieves of grain and likewise those who steal clothing;
there will be thieves who rob other thieves, and indeed those who rob even the slayers.
When knowledge and ritual action have ceased in the world and it has fallen into a state of inactivity,
insects, mice, and snakes will prey upon human beings.
Abundance of food, security, health, and capability will be difficult to find;
the Kauśikas will dwell in regions afflicted by the fear of famine.
For those overwhelmed by suffering, the maximum lifespan shall be one hundred years;
and in the Kali age, the Vedas will be seen and yet not seen in their entirety.
In that same way, sacrifices perish, as do those who are oppressed by mere formal dharma,
as well as the Kaṣāyins, the Nirgranthas, and the Kāpālikas.
Others were sellers of the Vedas, others were sellers of sacred fords,
and there were others who were heretics and adversaries of the castes and stages of life.
When the Kali age has arrived, they indeed arise in that manner;
at that time, the Vedas are not studied, yet Śūdras become experts in dharma and artha.
Kings born of the Śūdra caste will perform sacrifices instead of the Aśvamedha;
having committed the murder of women, the slaughter of cows, and having killed one another,
they will then strike each other down and thus bring about the ruin of their subjects.
In the Kali age, it is recorded that there is the prevalence of suffering, short lifespan, the destruction of countries, disease,
delusion, exhaustion, unhappiness, and conduct characterized by darkness.
Furthermore, the destruction of embryos begins to prevail among the people;
therefore, upon reaching the Kali age, lifespan, strength, and beauty decline.
For men overwhelmed by suffering, the maximum lifespan is indeed one hundred years.
In the Kali age, all the Vedas are neither seen nor perceived;
at that time, sacrifices perish, being rendered powerless and oppressed by unrighteousness.
Then, O best of the twice-born, at the end of the age, men shall attain perfection in a short time; they will be blessed and practice righteousness.
Those who, free from envy, practice the dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti—
the dharma that lasts for a year in the Tretā age and is recorded as lasting for a month in the Dvāpara—
shall obtain in a single day during the Kali age by practicing it according to their capacity, O wise one.
This is the condition in the Kali Yuga; now learn from me regarding the transitional period (sandhyāṃśa).
In each successive age, the spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) diminish by three-quarters.
Due to the inherent nature of the Yugas, these Sandhyās remain for one quarter;
and due to the inherent nature of the Sandhyās, they are established for one quarter in each of the [subsequent] portions.
Thus, when the twilight period at the end of the age had arrived,
he who arose from the destruction of the Bhrigus became the teacher of those wicked ones.
By lineage he is indeed of the Moon, and by name he is called Pramiti;
he was born from a portion of Mādhava in the previous Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
Having wandered indeed over the earth for twenty full years,
he maintained his army consisting of horses, chariots, and elephants.
Then, surrounded by hundreds and thousands of Brahmins with uplifted weapons,
he slew the Mlecchas by the thousands.
Having slain all those kings born of Śūdra origin,
that omnipresent lord then rendered all the heretics completely extinct.
He utterly destroys all those who are excessively righteous,
as well as those born from the confusion of castes and those who subsist upon them.
[He conquered] the people of the north, the Middle Country, and likewise those of the mountains;
as well as those of the east and the west, and those dwelling on the ridges of the Vindhya and in the western regions.
In the same way, he [conquered] the Southerners and the Dravidas along with the Siṃhalas, as well as the Gāndhāras, the Pāradas, the Pahlavas, and the Yavanas. ||82||
The Tuṣāras, Varvaras, Cīnas, Śūlikas, Daradas, Khaśas, Lampākas, Ketas, and the various tribes of Kirātas; ||83||
The powerful and all-pervading lord, whose wheel was set in motion and who brought about the end of the Mlecchas,
roamed the earth, unassailable by any living beings.
Indeed, he was born from a portion of the god Mādhava;
known by those who understand the rites of previous births as Pramiti, he was full of valor.
In the previous Kali age, the lord [Pradyumna] was born from the lineage of Candra;
when he had reached his thirty-second year and twenty years of his reign had passed. ||86||
Slaying all beings by the thousands,
he rendered the earth devoid of heroes through his exalted deeds,
driven by a sudden and mutual wrath.
Having brought about the destruction of those mostly unrighteous Śūdras,
he reached his end together with his followers in the region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Then, after that minister Satyasainika had passed away,
he [the king] exterminated all the kings and thousands of Mlecchas.
Then, when the twilight hour had arrived at the end of the age, and the living beings remaining here were few and scattered in various places; 1.58.90.
Then, indeed, those worldly activities, being unrestrained, act in groups;
they harm one another and fall upon one another.
When the state of anarchy arose due to the influence of the age and uncertainty presented itself, all those subjects were indeed afflicted by fear of one another. ||92||
Agitated and exhausted, having abandoned their wives and homes,
they have reached their end, deeply distressed as they gaze upon their own lives.
When the dharma of the Śruti and Smṛti had perished, they then struck one another;
they were without restraint, without refuge, devoid of affection, and shameless. (94)
When the rain had ceased, those short-lived ones, numbering twenty-five,
their faculties agitated by despair, abandoned their wives and sons.
Afflicted by drought and having abandoned their livelihoods, they become miserable and, leaving their own districts, take refuge in those border regions. (96)
Then they resort to rivers, oceans, wells, and mountains;
deeply distressed, they subsist on honey, meat, roots, and fruits. 97.
Wearing garments of bark and deerskin, devoid of possessions and free from worldly attachments,
they have fallen away from the duties of their castes and stages of life, and have entered into a terrible state of social confusion.
These subjects, having reached this ultimate limit and with but little remaining, were possessed by old age, disease, and hunger; through their suffering, they attained a state of world-weariness.
From discernment comes detachment; from discernment, the state of equanimity;
from the state of equanimity, awakening; and from awakening, the nature of righteousness.
When those [ages] have arrived and are joined together, remaining as a single unit, then a yuga of them revolves throughout a day and night. ||101||
Having caused a delusion of mind in them, that seventh [act] was performed by them;
then, through the power of a future event, it proceeded accordingly.
When that Kṛta Yuga had indeed set in again,
the offspring remaining from the Kali age were then born as those belonging to the Kṛta age.
Those perfected ones who dwell here move about in full view;
the Seven Sages also always remain established there.
Those who were known here as Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras for the sake of their seed—all of them then became indistinguishable from those born in the Kali age. 105.

Among them, the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) discourse on Dharma; and among others as well, that [Dharma] is twofold: consisting of the conduct of the social classes and stages of life, and being either revealed (śrauta) or traditional (smārta). ||106||
Then, while those [beings] were engaged in ritual action during the Kṛta age,
the dharma of the Kṛtas— both Śrauta and Smārta— was indeed established as revealed by the Seven Sages.
Among them, for the sake of establishing the Dharma, they remain here until the end of the age;
indeed, the sages remain during the periods of the Manvantaras.
Just as in this world, during the summer season when the grasses have been scorched by a forest fire, you first observe their emergence at the roots of those very same plants. (109)
In this manner, from age to age, there exists here a mutual succession that proceeds without interruption until the end of the Manvantara.
Happiness, longevity, strength, beauty, dharma, wealth, and even desire—these all decline by one-third in each successive age. (111)
During the transitional periods [between ages], the accomplishments of dharma in the Yugas decline.
Thus, O twice-born ones, this transition has been described by me to you. (112)
By this alone is the establishment of all the four yugas accomplished.
This cycle of the four yugas proceeds for a period of one thousand [such cycles].

That is declared to be the day of Brahmā, and his night is remembered to be of equal duration. During this period, until the end of the age (yuga), there occurs a state of rigidity and insentience among living beings.
This indeed is recorded as the characteristic of all the Yugas;
seventy-one such cycles of these four Yugas, revolving in succession, are called an interval of a Manu (Manvantara). ||115||
Just as it occurs here in a single cycle of four ages according to what has been heard, so too does it occur again in other cycles in that same sequence. 116.
Just as distinct entities arise in each creation, so too are they exactly twenty-five in number—neither fewer nor more. (117)
Likewise, together with the ages of the Kṛta Yuga, they possess identical characteristics;
this indeed is the characteristic of all the Manvantaras. ||118||
Likewise, the revolutions of the ages have proceeded for a long time according to the inherent nature of the ages;
likewise, the world of living beings does not remain stationary, revolving through decline and rise. ||119||
Thus has the definition of the ages been declared in brief,
as well as all the intermediate periods of those both past and future.
Likewise, a wise person should apply this same reasoning to all past and future Manvantaras in the future. 121.
Know that by means of a single Manvantara, all intermediate periods (Antaras) are indeed explained; and likewise, by means of one Kalpa, [all Kalpas] are explained.
All these possessors of egoity exist indeed through names and forms;
they are the eightfold classes of gods who are the lords here in this Manvantara.
The sages and the Manus are all equal in their purposes;
likewise, the classification of the social orders and stages of life is established in every age.
Moreover, the Lord always ordains [the world] according to the inherent nature of the yugas;
the division of castes and stages of life, as well as the yugas themselves, exist for the sake of the accomplishment of the yugas.
The secondary consequence has been fully explained; now learn of the creation and emanation.
I shall describe here, in detail and in proper sequence, the maintenance of the world throughout the ages.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Four Yugas," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Learn now of those offspring who are born in the various ages:
the female of the horse, the serpent, the cow, the bird, the piśāca, the yakṣa, and the rākṣasa;
in which age each is produced and for how long their life lasts. ||1||
Piśācas, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
and pannagas live for only a single yuga, except for those who have slain Death.
The lifespan of humans, beasts, birds, and stationary beings—all of these has completely passed away throughout the various ages (yugas). ||3||
In the Kali age, indeed, the instability of the lifespan of living beings is observed;
for humans in the Kali age, the maximum lifespan is recorded as being one hundred years.
From the measure of the gods and asuras, however, it decreases by seven times seven finger-breadths;
thus, it is a full hundred and fifty-eight finger-breadths.
The height of that [image] is said by those born in the Kali age to be equal to the measure of a Deva or an Asura;
it is recorded by those of the Kali age as being eighty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
From the feet to the head, measured by one's own finger-breadths, such is the height of humans; here, at the end of the age, it diminishes.
In all ages, past and future, here in this world,
a man is traditionally held to be eight tālas in height according to the measure of his own finger-breadths.
He whose height from the feet to the head is nine tālas,
and whose arms reach his knees when held straight, is honored even by the gods.
In this same sequence and by this same method, there is a gradual decrease and increase in the lifespan of cows, horses, elephants, buffaloes, and stationary beings in each successive age.
The hump of cattle is indeed seventy-six finger-breadths in height;
the height of elephants is recorded as a full eight hundred finger-breadths.
The height of horses is recorded by the Śākhins as fifty thousand finger-breadths, minus forty finger-breadths.
Whatever the configuration of a human body may be,
that same characteristic is seen in the bodies of the gods through the vision of reality.
The body of the gods is said to be endowed with excellence of intellect;
and the human body is said to surpass even that of the gods. ||14||
Thus, these indeed have been described as the states belonging to gods and humans;
now learn of those belonging to beasts, birds, and even immobile beings. 15.
For cows, goats, buffaloes, horses, elephants, birds, and trees—
all these are employed here in every way for sacrificial rites.

They are born again in the abodes of the gods, possessing forms exactly like those [gods]; however, they enjoy the same pleasures as the gods according to their own inclinations, though their physical bodies are auspicious. (17)
Indeed, they attained happiness through those pleasing objects— both stationary and moving— which corresponded to their forms and proportions, and which were known for their true nature.

Therefore, I shall describe the refined (śiṣṭas), the virtuous (santas), and likewise the good (sādhus). "Sat" is a word for Brahman; those who possess it are called "santas. Because they attain ultimate union with Brahman, they are designated as "santas. ||19||
Those who neither become angry nor rejoice regarding the tenfold objects of the senses and the eightfold causes are known as those who have conquered themselves.
Because the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are devoted to both general and specific duties, they are therefore called the twice-born (dvijātayaḥ). ||21||
For one who is engaged in the duties of the castes and stages of life, who moves through the gates of heaven,
and who possesses knowledge of the dharma prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti— that is called dharma.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) is called virtuous because he accomplishes learning and is devoted to the welfare of his teacher;
likewise, a householder (gṛhastha) is said to be virtuous because he accomplishes ritual duties. ||23||
A virtuous man who practices austerities in the forest is known as a Vaikhānasa;
one who strives through the practice of yoga is known as a virtuous Yati.
Thus, by the practice of the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma), they are remembered as the virtuous:
the householder, the student, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant. ||25||
Neither gods, nor ancestors, nor sages, nor men—seeing with undivided vision—say, "This is dharma," or "This is not. (26)
In this context, these two terms "dharma" and "adharma" are declared to be of the nature of action (kriyā).
Wholesome and unwholesome karma are traditionally known as dharma and adharma respectively. (27)
Dharma is proclaimed as the quality derived from the root *dhṛ* (to hold), meaning "retention" or "support. Conversely, that which lacks retention and lacks greatness is called *adharma*.
In this regard, the teachers instruct on those dharmas that lead to the attainment of what is desired.
For those who are aged, free from greed, self-possessed, devoid of deceit, properly disciplined, and upright—them they call "teachers. (29)

Because he practices good conduct himself and establishes it [in others], and because, endowed with proper restraints and observances, he gathers the meanings of the scriptures through his efforts; || 1.59.30 ||
Having informed the ancestors here, the Seven Sages spoke of the Śruti:
the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman verses, as well as the limbs of the Veda. (31)
Having recalled the conduct of the past Manvantara, he sang it once again;
therefore, the dharma arising from the divisions of caste and stage of life is known as Smārta (based on tradition). ||32||

This very twofold Dharma is here called the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra). From the word "remainder" (śeṣa) comes the term "learned" (śiṣṭa), and thus it is designated as the conduct of the learned.
Those righteous ones who remain here during the various Manvantaras—
namely Manu and the seven Ṛṣis— for the sake of the continuity of the world,
and those who are truly learned, explain the truth exactly as it is for the sake of dharma.
And those cultured ones such as Manu and others whom I have previously mentioned—
they, being cultured, practiced dharma perfectly in age after age.
The three Vedas, commerce, the science of government, sacrifice, as well as the castes and stages of life—
because these are practiced by the learned and have been enjoined again and again by Manu,
and because they were established by the ancients of old, that conduct of the learned is eternal. (36)
Generosity, truthfulness, austerity, freedom from greed, knowledge, sacrifice, procreation, and compassion—these eight are the practices that characterize the conduct of the virtuous. (37)
Because the learned (śiṣṭas), as well as Manu and the seven sages, follow this in all the Manvantaras, it is therefore remembered as the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra). ||38||
That which is to be known from hearing is called Śrauta; that which is known from recollection is called Smārta.
Śrauta consists of sacrifice and the Vedas; Smārta consists of the duties of the castes and stages of life.
Furthermore, I shall here describe the characteristics of Dharma along with its constituent parts.
He who, upon seeing great wealth, does not conceal it when questioned, but speaks exactly as it is—this is the characteristic of truth. (1.59.40)
Celibacy, recitation, silence, and even fasting—this is the root of austerity; it is most formidable and difficult to master. ||41||
The conjunction of the sacrificial animals, the material offerings, the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus verses, as well as the officiating priests and the sacrificial fees, is called Yoga. 42.
He whose vision operates with equality toward all beings, regarding their welfare and non-welfare as he does his own—this entire state is indeed remembered as compassion. (43)
Whether reviled or even struck, he who does not revile in return nor strike back through speech, mind, or action—this patience and endurance is known as forbearance (kṣamā). 44.
The non-appropriation of others' property— whether it be guarded by its owner, abandoned, or even found in the earth— is proclaimed here as non-greed.
The non-practice of sexual intercourse, indeed, is the absence of thought and the absence of conceptualization;
that cessation is celibacy (brahmacarya), which, when unbroken, is called self-control (dama). ||46||
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, the fact that one's senses do not function erroneously in this world— that indeed is the characteristic of tranquility.
He who does not become angry when obstructed regarding objects consisting of the ten [faculties] or the eightfold cause is considered one who has conquered his self. 48.
Whatever object is most beloved and has been acquired through righteous means—that very thing should be given to one who possesses virtue; this is the defining characteristic of giving.

This gift is of three kinds: inferior, superior, and middling. Among these, that which leads to the highest good is superior; that for the sake of achieving one's own purpose is inferior; and that which is distributed with compassion toward all beings and among kinsmen is middling. (1.59.50)

Dharma is that which is ordained by the Śruti and Smṛti, consisting of the system of castes and stages of life; it is also that which is not contradicted by the conduct of the learned and is associated with the virtuous and the good. ||51||
For non-aversion toward the undesirable, as well as non-rejoicing in the desirable, and the turning away from joy, heat, and dejection—this is detachment. (52)

Renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is the laying down of action; it is the abandonment of deeds performed along with those not yet performed, and the relinquishing of both the auspicious and the inauspicious. This is called renunciation (tyāga). ||53||

In this insentient world, there is a transformation beginning from the unmanifest and proceeding through the non-specific stages; the discernment of the difference between the sentient and the insentient is called knowledge. (54)
This is the definition of the dharma of the individual limbs as it was remembered by the sages, who knew the true nature of dharma, in the former Svāyambhuva interval. (55)
In this regard, I shall describe to you the rule for a Manvantara,
pertaining both to the mutual duties of the individual castes and to the fourfold order as a whole;
for in every Manvantara, a different sacred revelation (Śruti) is ordained.
The Ṛg-verses, Yajus-formulas, and Sāman-chants, according to their respective deities, remain even until the dissolution of all beings;
however, the Śatarudriya alone is excluded. (57)
The ritual procedure, the *hotṛ*-priest's office, and likewise the hymn of praise proceed as before.
There is the hymn of praise concerning substances, the hymn of praise concerning qualities, and likewise the hymn of praise concerning actions;
this fourth is the hymn of praise concerning lineage—thus the hymn is fourfold. (58)
In all the Manvantaras, whatever gods there may be,
he indeed causes their fourfold Vedic hymns to proceed;
likewise, the fourfold origin of the qualities of the mantras occurs.
Then, among the Atharva, Yajus, and Sāman Vedas, the sages performed here separately and intensely,
the most difficult and supreme penance.
Indeed, in former Manvantaras here, the mantras manifested in five ways: from satisfaction, from fear, from suffering, from happiness, and from grief.
I shall here describe by their characteristics that which constitutes the true state of being a seer (ṛṣi) among seers— whether through the totality of their asceticism, through vision, or by chance.
The Sage (Ṛṣi) is said to be fivefold with respect to the past and the future;
therefore, I shall explain the origin of the Sages and of the Ṛṣicompiled [text].
When the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) prevails during the universal dissolution,
there occurs the transgression of the gods and the transfer of authority between those two [principles], just as it is described.
That [unconscious matter], though devoid of prior intelligence, proceeds for the sake of consciousness;
for it is indeed preceded by non-intelligence, yet it is presided over by consciousness. ||65||
And just as those two, the fish and the water, exist together,
so too does reality proceed by means of the qualities (guṇas), presided over by consciousness.
Thus, because it is the instrument, the effect then proceeds from it;
likewise, because it possesses the nature of the subject with respect to the object, and because it possesses desire for the purpose. ||67||
When the time for attainment arrives, the distinctions consisting of causes become fully established; then the manifest principles, beginning with Mahat, emerge in due order.
From the Mahat arises ego (ahaṅkāra), and from that, the elements and the sense organs;
the various modifications of the elements arise from those [elements] through mutual interaction.
The effect, which is the cause of perfect accomplishment, manifests instantaneously.
Just as sparks flying upward from a firebrand proceed at one and the same time,
so does the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), when manifested, act through a single impulse of time and karma.
Just as a firefly suddenly becomes visible in the darkness, so indeed has this [Self] emerged from the unmanifest, like a shimmering firefly. (71)
That great one, still possessing his body, remained right where he had first been stationed;
the wise one stayed fixed in that very place, positioned at the entrance of the gate-hall.
But that which is beyond darkness is perceived as distinct;
the scripture states that the wise one established in that very place is "at the end of darkness. (73)
As the intellect undergoes transformation, a fourfold set emerges:
knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and virtue—this is the tetrad. (74)
These [powers] of his, indeed, are innate and well-manifested;
because they are irreversible even while he possesses a body, they are called "perfection" (siddhi). //75//

Furthermore, because he lies within this city [of the body], or else because he is the knowledge of the field (kṣetra), he is called the Puruṣa on account of lying in the city, and the Kṣetrajña on account of being the knowledge of the field. (76)

The Lord is called the Knower (kṣetrajña) because of his knowledge of the field (kṣetra); he is called the Intellect (mati) because by means of the intellect (buddhi) he indeed lies within it; therefore, he is truly of the nature of consciousness. That which is composed of the manifest and the unmanifest, as well as the insentient, is encompassed for the sake of perfect accomplishment.
Thus, cessation is brought about by the Knower of the Field when it is directed toward the Knower of the Field;
for this object of experience is fully understood as "this is the field of enjoyment" by the Knower of the Field. (78)
The root *ṛṣ* signifies movement toward hearing, truth, and austerity;
when one is established in these through Brahman, he is remembered as a *ṛṣi*. (79)
At the very moment of cessation, the Sage himself perceives the Unmanifest through his intellect;
because he perceives that which is supreme, he is therefore remembered as the Supreme Sage (Paramarṣi). ||1.59.80||
The formation of the name [of the first Manu] arose from the root *dṛś* in the sense of "seeing" (*gati*) from the beginning;
because he was self-born (*svayambhū*), his status as a seer (*ṛṣitā*) is recorded.
These lords, born of their own accord, were the mind-born sons of Brahmā. (81)
Because one who is great and surrounded by [wisdom] is not struck down by conceits,
and because the wise behold the Great One on every side through his virtues, therefore those seers of the supreme state of awakening are called "Great Seers" (Maharṣis). ||82||
For those lords, they were auspicious, consisting of mind and inner essence;
having abandoned both ego and darkness, they attained the state of being sages.
Therefore, those seers indeed were perceivers of reality at the beginning of the elements;
but the sons of the seers, known as the Ṛṣīkas, were born from embryos through sexual union.
Those of great power perceive both the subtle elements (tanmātras) and truth;
therefore, they are indeed the Truth-Seers (satyarṣis), supreme perceivers of reality. ||85||
Those who are the sons of the sages (ṛṣis) are to be known as the "sons of sages" (ṛṣiputrakas).

Because they indeed hear (ṛṣanti) the sacred revelation (śruta) and its specific details according to their true nature, they are therefore called "sages by hearing" (śrutarṣis), for they are the revealers of that which has been heard. ||86||

The unmanifest self, the great self, likewise the ego-self, the elemental self, and the sensory self—this is said to be their knowledge. Now hear these five classes of sages according to their names. 87.
Bhṛgu, Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu,
Manu, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, and Pulastya—
these ten were the mind-born sons of Brahmā, born as lords in their own right. ||88||
Because they proceed from the Great Sage (Maharṣi), they are called Maharṣis;
know that these sages are the sons of the lords. 89.
Kāvya, Bṛhaspati, Kaśyapa, and Uśanas; likewise Utathya, Vāmadeva, Apojya, and Aiśija.
Kardama, Viśravas, Śakti, Vālakhilya, and Dharā—these are declared to be the sages who attained the status of ṛṣis through their knowledge. ||91||
Now learn of the sons of sages and the female sages born from the womb:
Vatsara, Nagraha, and likewise Bhāradvāja.
Bṛhaduttha, Śaradvān, Agastya, and likewise Auśija;
the sage Dīrghatamas, as well as Bṛhaduktha and Śaradvata. ||93||
Vājaśravas, Suvitta, Suvāgveṣaparāyaṇa,
Dadhīca, Śaṅkha, Āṃśu, and King Vaiśravaṇa—
these are declared to be the Ṛṣikas, who attained the status of Ṛṣis through truthfulness. ||94||
The Īśvaras, the Ṛṣikas, and those others who are likewise remembered—all these are creators of mantras; learn of them all in their entirety. ||95||
Bhṛgu, Kāvya, Pracetas, Dadhīci who was indeed self-possessed, Aurva, Jamadagni, and likewise Divasārasvata; ||96||
Advīṣeṇa, Arūpa, Vītahavya, Sumedhas,
Vainya Pṛthu, Divodāsa, Praśvāra, and Gṛtsamānabha—
these nineteen were seers who proclaimed the mantras. ||97||
Aṅgiras, Vedhas, Bhāradvāja, Bāṣkali, as well as Amṛta, Gārgya, Śenī, and Saṃhṛti. ||98||
Then Purukutsa, Māndhātṛ, and likewise Ambarīṣa;
Āhārya, Ajamīḍha, Ṛṣabha, and Bali as well. ||99||
Pṛṣadaśva, Virūpa, Kaṇva, and Mudgala;
Yuvanāśva, Paurukutsa, Trasadasyu, and Sadasyumat.
Utathya, Bharadvāja, as well as Vājaśravas, Āyāpya, Suvitti, and likewise Vāmadeva; ||101||
Aujasa, Bṛhaduktha, the seer Dīrghatapas, and Kakṣīvān—these thirty-three are remembered as the eminent Aṅgirasas. All of these are composers of mantras; now learn of the Kāśyapas. ||102||
Kāśyapa, Vatsāra, Vibhrama, Raibhya, Asita, and Devala—these six were exponents of the Veda. ||103||
Atri, Arcīṣaṇa, Śyāmāva, Niṣṭhura,
the wise sage Valgūtaka, and he who was Pūrvātithi—
these are declared to be the Atris, the great seers and authors of mantras. ||104||
Vasiṣṭha, Śakti, and likewise Parāśara;
the fourth was Indrapramati, and the fifth was Bharadvāja. ||105||
The sixth was Maitrāvaruṇa, and the seventh was Kuṇḍina;
Sudyumna was the eighth, and Bṛhaspati was the ninth;
the tenth was Bharadvāja—these were the authors of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. ||106||
For these very ones are the agents who destroy the dharma;
this is the characteristic of Brahmins ordained for all those who follow the Vedic branches.
The word *hetu* is traditionally derived from the root *hi*, meaning "to strike down" (*nihanti*) what has been asserted by others;
or else, it is derived from the root *hi* in the sense of "going" (*gati*), because it reaches the full extent of the meaning [of the thesis]. (108)
Likewise, one should state the etymological derivation (nirvacana) for the determination of the meaning of the sentence.
The teachers say that it is "censure" (nindā) when a word is censured because of its defect. (109)
From the verbal root *śaṃs* preceded by the prefix *pra*, "praśaṃsā" means praise on account of possessing good qualities;
however, when one does not reach a certainty, thinking "this is it," "that is it," or "this is not it," that state is doubt (*saṃśaya*). (1.59.110)
"This alone must be performed"—this is called an injunction (vidhi). When something other than that is stated, it is recorded by the wise as the "action of another" (parakṛti). (111)
For that which is spoken of as being extremely remote is called the "Purākalpa" (Ancient Account).
Because it speaks of deeds performed in the past, the conceptualization of it is termed "Purākalpa. (112)

They say that a conceptualization based on restrictive determination is that which is made without having ascertained [the truth] through the Mantras, Brāhmaṇas, Kalpas, and the pure, extensive Nigamas. ||113||
"Just as this is, so indeed is that; and just as that is, so indeed is this. This, indeed, is the instruction for the tenth [chapter] of the Brāhmaṇa. ||114||
The wise have declared this to be the primary definition of a Brāhmaṇa;
his conduct has been indicated by the twice-born, and its explanation follows immediately thereafter. (115)
And the formulation of mantras in rites prescribed by rule:
[the word] *mantra* is derived from the verbal root *mantr*, and *brāhmaṇa* from *brahman* because of its protection (*avana*). (116)

Those who know the sūtras understand a sūtra to be that which consists of few syllables, is free from ambiguity, is substantial, is comprehensive in all its aspects, is devoid of filler words, and is irreproachable. (117)
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Sages," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
The sages said:
Having heard those words, the sages said to Sūta, who was difficult to overcome:
"O high-minded one, tell us how the Vedas were divided in ancient times. (1)
Sūta said:
When the Dvāpara age had returned during the interval of Svāyambhuva Manu, Brahmā spoke this to Manu; I shall relate that, O high-minded one. (2)
When the age has turned, O dear one, the twice-born have all become diminished in strength due to the defects of the age, in their respective order.
Indeed, this Kṛta age and the others are seen to have fallen away through the power of the Yugas, with only a small portion remaining;
for of this [Kṛta], only one ten-thousandth part remains.
One's vigor, splendor, strength, and speech—all of these utterly perish;
therefore, the Vedas must indeed be performed [in ritual], lest there be the destruction of the Veda.
When the Veda meets with destruction, the sacrifice will go to ruin;
when the sacrifice is lost, the gods perish, and thereafter everything perishes.
The original Veda consisted of four quarters and was known as the Śatasāhasra;
it was indeed the entire sacrifice, ten times greater, which grants all desires.
Having been addressed thus, Manu, who is devoted to the welfare of the world, said "So be it," and the Lord divided the single Veda, which has four quarters, into four parts.
O dear one, at the word of Brahmā and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, this arrangement of the Vedas was made by you while you were present here. 9.
I shall describe the calculation of the past Manvantaras;
O best of beings, understand that which was beyond perception through direct perception. 1.60.10.
In this age, Vyāsa Pārāśarya, the scorcher of foes, was born;
he is celebrated as Dvaipāyana and is proclaimed to be an incarnation of Viṣṇu. ||11||
Urged by Brahmā, he began to arrange the Veda therein;
then, for the sake of the Vedas, he took four disciples.
Jaimini, Sumantu, and Vaiśampāyana; Paila was the fourth among them, and Lomaharṣaṇa the fifth. ||13||
He duly accepted the twice-born Paila as the reciter of the Ṛgveda, and likewise Vaiśampāyana as the expounder of the Yajurveda. (14)
He approached Jaimini, the reciter of the meaning of the Sāmaveda,
and likewise Sumantu, the best of sages, for the Atharvaveda.
The Lord, the Blessed Īśvara, the Master, indeed properly received me as a teacher of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
There was originally only the Yajurveda; he divided it into four parts.
Within it arose the Caturhotra; by means of that, he fashioned the sacrifice. ||17||
He performed the duties of the Adhvaryu with the Yajus formulas, likewise the Hotṛ's duties with the Ṛks,
the Udgātṛ's duties with the Sāmans, and the office of the Brahman priest with the Atharvan verses;
indeed, he performed the office of the Brahman at the sacrifice by means of the Atharva Veda.
Then, having extracted the Ṛcas, he fashioned the Ṛgveda;
by means of it, the office of the Hotṛ priest was established, which carries the sacrifice for the welfare of the world. ||19||
With the Sāman chants he caused him to delight in the Sāmaveda as the Udgātṛ priest;
and with the Atharvaveda, he performed all the rites for the king.
Skilled in the meaning of the Purāṇas, he composed collections of Purāṇas through narratives, episodes, verses, and accounts of the deeds of noble lineages.
Whatever remained in the Yajurveda, with that he then joined the sacrifice;
"While joining [it] in the Yajurveda"—such is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures. ||22||
Because the words [of the mantras] had been extracted, the sacrificial formulas (yajūṃṣi) were indeed disordered.
Thus, with his potency extracted by those officiating priests who had mastered the Vedas, the Aśvamedha sacrifice was performed; or rather, he himself was bound by it.
Having taken up the Ṛgveda, Paila divided it again into two parts;
having made them two, the master gave them to his two disciples.
Having composed four Saṃhitās— one for Indrapramati and a second for Bāṣkala— that best of the twice-born, Bāṣkali,
taught them to his devoted and beneficial disciples. (25)
May they study the first branch, the second the Agnimāthara, the third the Pārāśara, and then the other, the Yājñavalkya. ||26||
Indrapramati, the best of the twice-born, taught the Saṃhitā to the illustrious and highly fortunate Mārkaṇḍeya.
That highly illustrious brahmin, Satyaśravas, taught his son Agrya,
and Satyaśravas in turn taught Satyahita.
That powerful lord further instructed his even more truthful son,
the high-souled Satyaśrī, who was devoted to truth and righteousness.
He indeed had three disciples of great majesty;
they were wise, possessed of the glory of truth, and devoted to the mastery of the scriptures.
Śākalya was the first among them; other than him were Rathāntara, Bāṣkali, and Bharadvāja—these are the founders of the branches. ||31||
But Devamitra Śākalya, arrogant with the pride of his knowledge,
met his destruction at the sacrifice of Janaka, O twice-born one.
Śaunaka said:
How did that sage, who was arrogant in his knowledge, meet his destruction?
And how did the debate with Janaka take place during the horse sacrifice?
"For what purpose did the debate take place, and with whom?
Tell me all this exactly as it happened, for everything is known to you.
Having heard the words of the sages, he then spoke this reply. (34)
Sūta said:
At Janaka’s horse-sacrifice, however, there was a great gathering;
thousands of sages arrived there in great numbers,
desiring indeed to behold that sacrifice of the royal sage Janaka.
Seeing that the brahmins had arrived, he then felt a desire to know:
"Who among these is the most excellent brahmin? How may I reach a certain conclusion?
Having thus resolved in his mind, O lord of men, he applied his intellect. (36)
Taking a thousand cows along with abundant gold, villages, jewels, and servants, the lord of men spoke to the sages:
"I seek refuge before you all with my head bowed; you are the recipients of the most excellent portion. (37)
"O best of the twice-born, this wealth which has been brought here shall indeed be presented to whichever among you is the most excellent; for this is the wealth of knowledge. (38)
Having heard the words of Janaka, those sages, who were capable of hearing [the truth],
seeing that wealth of great value, and desiring to seize it through the increase of their riches,
placed their faith in one another, though they were not arrogant in their knowledge of the Vedas. (39)
"Has this wealth gone to my mind? Is this wealth mine? "It is mine alone; it is not yours.
Thus, due to the fault of greed for wealth, they engaged in many such disputes. (1.60.40)
Likewise, another learned man was there, the wise son of Brahmavāha,
