Yājñavalkya, who possessed great splendor, was an ascetic, and was the foremost among those who know Brahman.
Born from the limb of Brahmā, he, the best among the knowers of Brahman, spoke these words in a melodious voice to his disciple: "O, take this wealth! (42)
"Lead him to my home, my child; of this there is no doubt.
I am the speaker of all the Vedas, and there is no other equal to me.
Or, if that brahmin is not pleased, let him protect me without delay. (43)
Then Brahmārṇava was agitated like the ocean during a universal deluge;
thereafter, Yājñavalkya, composed and as if smiling, spoke to them.
"O wise ones, do not be angry; you are speakers of truth.
Desiring to know one another, we speak what is appropriate. (45)
Then, their debates proceeded in manifold ways,
branching out a thousandfold with auspicious meanings arising from subtle insight.

In that place, debates concerning worldly affairs, the Vedas, and spiritual science took place among high-souled men, who were adorned with the branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), endowed with the power of supreme curses, and honored by throngs of kings, all for the sake of wealth. (47)
On one side were all the sages, and on the other side was Yājñavalkya;
when all those munis were questioned one by one by that wise Yājñavalkya, they could not provide an answer.
Having completely conquered all those sages, the immensely radiant mass of Brahman spoke directly to Śākalya, the proponent of the debate: 49.
"Śākalya, speak! What is it that you are meditating upon as you stand there?
You are filled with dull-headed pride, like a leather bag inflated by wind. (1.60.50)
Thus insulted by him, his face and eyes copper-red with rage,
he spoke to that man Yājñavalkya in the presence of the sages.
Having cast us aside like blades of grass, as well as these best of the twice-born,
you yourself desire to seize for yourself this highly precious wealth of knowledge that is to be taken by one's own effort.
Yājñavalkya, who had not been addressed by Śākalya, spoke thus:
"Know that the strength of those most devoted to Brahman is the vision of the true meaning of the principles of knowledge. (53)
Desire is connected with wealth; therefore, we desire wealth.
With desire as our guide, O Brahmins, we speak these questions of desire.
"This is the wager for this royal seer; therefore, I have taken his wealth.
Having heard these words of his, Śākalya, overwhelmed with anger, then spoke these words to Yājñavalkya for the purpose of asking a question at will.
"Now, speak according to the truth regarding the questions concerning desire that I have proposed.
Thereupon, a great debate arose between those two knowers of Brahman.
Śākalya then posed more than a thousand questions to him;
Yājñavalkya answered them all while the sages were listening.
During the debate with Śākalya as well, Yājñavalkya said to him:
"O Śākalya, you answer even a single question of mine that you desire.
A curse shall be the wager for this debate; he who fails to answer shall go to his death. (58)
Then, if Śākalya did not understand that question posed by the wise Yājñavalkya, he would immediately meet his death. (59)
Thus Śākalya died, oppressed by the explanation of the questions;
and such was the great dispute between them, who were seekers of wealth,
and Yājñavalkya, along with the ṛṣis and munis.
O Sage, having explained by the hundreds and thousands all the questions asked by them,
the one of great course (Mahāgati) revealed the essence of their inquiries.
Having accepted the wealth and having proclaimed his own glory, Yājñavalkya,
self-controlled and composed, went to his home surrounded by his disciples.
But the high-souled Devamitra Śākalya, the best of the twice-born,
wise and most skilled in the knowledge of words, composed five Saṃhitās.
His disciples were five:
Mudgala, Golaka, Khālīya, Matsya, and Śaiśireya as the fifth.
Śākapūṇi Rathītara, that best of the twice-born, proclaimed three Saṃhitās and further composed the Nirukta as a fourth.
He had four disciples:
Ketava, Dālaki, Dharmaśarman, and Devaśarman; all were twice-born brahmins who observed their religious vows.
When Śākalya had died, they all became slayers of Brahmins;
then, overcome by great anxiety, they went into the presence of Brahmā.
Having known this with his mind, Brahmā sent Pavana to the city of Pavana;
"Go there, and your sin shall be instantly destroyed."
Having paid homage to Dvādaśārka and likewise to Vālukeśvara,
as well as to the eleven Rudras and especially to the Son of the Wind (Hanumān),
you shall cross over the sin of killing a Brahmin after bathing in the four pools.
All of them, having become even swifter, arrived at that city;
they performed their ablutions according to the prescribed rites and beheld the gods.
Having paid homage to Uttaresvara, by the grace of the Vāḍavas,
they were all liberated from sin and went to the solar orb.
From that time forward, that sacred ford became a destroyer of sins;
it is the city of Vāyu, pure and fashioned of old by Vāyu himself.
When Hanumān, the son of the Wind-god, born from the womb of Añjanā,
was produced as Mahādeva— that Hanumān of true prowess—
then this very Tīrtha was created by Vāyu, whose source is Brahman.
Those Śūdras born on the earth who were designated for the service of Brāhmaṇas—for the sake of their livelihood and for the sake of the Brahmayajña—a great tax was imposed upon them. (74)
By this method, a great teaching has been produced for the Brahmins:
even one who is a killer of a cow, ungrateful, a drinker of liquor, or a violator of the teacher’s bed—by bowing to Vāḍāditya, he is liberated from all sins. (75)
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "Description of the Great Pilgrimage Sites," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
The sages said:
Bhāradvāja, Yājñavalkya, Gālaki, Sālaki, the wise Śatabalāka, and Naigama, the best of the twice-born. ||1||
Bāṣkali Bharadvāja taught three Saṃhitās;
Rathītara, moreover, composed the fourth, the Nirukta.
He had three disciples who were high-souled and endowed with virtues:
the wise Nandāyanīya, the intelligent Pannagāri, and the third, Āryavata; they were all praised for their vows through ascetic penance.
Free from passion, possessed of great luster, and having reached the further shore of the knowledge of the Saṃhitās—these are declared to be the Bahvṛcas, by whom the Saṃhitās were set forth. ||4||
Belonging to the Vaiśampāyana lineage, he arranged the Yajurveda;
there were eighty-six variations of its Saṃhitās.
He gave them to his disciples, and they received them according to the prescribed rules;
however, one among them, the great ascetic Yājñavalkya, was excluded.
Furthermore, there were eighty-six variations of the Saṃhitās belonging to him as well.
Indeed, for all of them, threefold divisions have been proclaimed;
these threefold divisions have been declared in this auspicious ninth division.
The people of the North, the Middle Country, and the East were of various kinds;
among those of the North, Śyāmāyani became the preeminent one.
For those established in the Middle Country, Āruṇi is praised as the first;
for those of the East, Ālambi and others are the first, beginning with the thirteenth [generation]. 9.
"Thus have these Carakas, the twice-born exponents of the Saṃhitā, been described.
Having heard those words, the sages, desiring to know more, spoke to Sūta.
"O Carakas and Adhvaryus, tell me the truth:
for what reason and by virtue of what deed did they come to possess the status of reciters?
Being thus addressed, he spoke to them concerning how their state as Carakas came to be. (11)
Sūta said:
O best of Brahmins, there was a certain task for the sages;
having reached the summit of Mount Meru, they then deliberated thus.
"O best of the twice-born, whoever among us does not return here within seven nights shall indeed commit the murder of a Brahmin; this is the covenant we have proclaimed. (13)
Then all of them, together with their attendants— with the exception of Vaiśampāyana—
proceeded for seven nights to where the truce had been established.
At the word of the brahmins, he committed the murder of a brahmin;
then, having summoned his disciples, that Vaiśampāyana said to them: (15)
"O best of the twice-born, perform the discourse on Brahman for my sake;
all of you, having assembled together, speak those words that are beneficial to me. (16)
Yājñavalkya said:
I alone shall proceed; let these sages remain here.
Inflamed by my own ascetic power, I shall summon my strength.
Thus addressed, he then became enraged and spoke to Yājñavalkya:
"Return to me everything that has been learned by you. (18)
Thus addressed, that best of those who know the Veda vomited forth the sacrificial formulas (yajūṃṣi) consisting of forms, smeared with blood, and gave them to his preceptor. ||19||
Then, O twice-born ones, having resorted to meditation, he propitiated the Sun—
that Brahman which, when severed, remains established in the sky.

Then, being pleased, Sūrya indeed gave those Yajus-mantras which had gone upward to the solar orb to that wise Yājñavalkya, the son of Brahmarīti, who was in the form of a horse; Mārtaṇḍa [gave them] to him. ||21||
Those sacrificial formulas (yajūṃṣi) which were recited by the Brahmins in whatever manner possible were given to him in the form of a horse; therefore, they became known as the Vājins.
Those by whom the killing of a Brahmin was committed are known as Carakas because of their conduct;
those disciples of Vaiśampāyana are declared to be the Carakas.
Thus these Carakas have been described; now learn of those Vājins.
They were the disciples of Yājñavalkya, namely Kaṇva, Vaidheya, and Śālīna. ||24||
Madhyandina, Śāpeyī, Vidigdha, Āpya, Uddala, Tāmrāyaṇa, Vātsya, as well as Gālava and Śaiśirī, Āṭavī, Parṇī, Vīraṇī, and Parāyaṇa. ||25||
Thus these fifteen Vājins have been proclaimed;
they are remembered as the one hundred and one complete alternatives for the Yajus formulas.
Then Jaimini taught his son Sumantu;
the lordly Sumantu, in turn, taught his son Sutvan;
and the lordly Sutvan taught his son Sukarman.
Having quickly mastered a thousand Saṃhitās,
Sukarman then spoke to those thousand [pupils], who were as radiant as the sun.
Śatakratu struck them down as they were studying during forbidden times;
thereupon, he undertook a fast unto death for the sake of his disciples.
Seeing him enraged, Śakra then granted him another boon:
"Your two disciples shall be of great heroism and possess the splendor of fire."
These two highly wise and illustrious gods are studying together as a pair;
do not be angry with them, O best of the twice-born.
Having spoken thus, the glorious Vāsava,
seeing that the twice-born one was illustrious for his good deeds and that his anger had been pacified, vanished right there.
O best of the twice-born, his disciple was the wise Pauṣyañji;
the second was Hiraṇyanābha, a descendant of Kuśika and a lord of men.
Pauṣyañji, however, taught five hundred Saṃhitās;
by him were produced the other auspicious disciples of Pauṣyañji, who were Sāmavedins of the North.
The powerful Hiraṇyanābha had five hundred disciples who were masters of the Kauśika Saṃhitās; they are remembered as the Prācyasāmagas.
Lokākṣī, Kuthumi, Kuśītī, and Lāṅgali were the four disciples of Pauṣyañji; learn now of their divisions. (36)
The Rāṇāyanīya was indeed the son of Taṇḍi; from him came another, the very learned Mūlacārī.
The son of Sakati and the son of Sahasāti—know these to be the branches of Lokākṣi. (37)
The three sons of Kuthumi were Aurasas, Rasapāsara, and the radiant Bhāgavitti; these are known as the three types of Kauthumas. ||38||
Śauridyu and Śṛṅgiputra—these two were observers of their vows;
Rāṇāyanīya and Saumitri were both experts in the Sāmaveda. (39)
The son of Śṛṅgin, a man of great asceticism, composed three Saṃhitās;
they were Caila, Prācīnayoga, and Surāla, O best of the twice-born.
Pārāśarya, however, taught the six Saṃhitās to Kauthuma,
Āsurāyaṇa, and Vaiśākha, who were both devoted to the Veda-vṛddhas.
Prācīnayogaputra, the wise Patañjali, Lāṅgali, and Śālihotra—these six branches of Kauthuma are recorded as belonging to Pārāśarya; he taught these six Saṃhitās. (42)
Bhāluki, Kāmahāni, Jaimini, Lomagāyin, Kaṇḍu, and Kolaha—these six are known as the Lāṅgalas;
they were the disciples of Lāṅgali by whom the Saṃhitās were established. ||43||
Then, having become a disciple of Hiraṇyanābha, that prince,
the best among men, composed twenty-four Saṃhitās;
and he taught them to his disciples— listen now to who they were.
Rāḍha, Mahāvīrya, and the fifth, Vāhana; Tālaka, Pāṇḍaka, Kālika, and likewise Rājika; Gautama, Ajabasta, and Somarāja fell there after that. ||45||
Pṛṣṭhaghna, Parikṛṣṭa, and Ulūkhalaka;
Vaiśāla, who was younger, and Aṅgulīya of Kauśika. ||46||
Sālimañjarisatya, Kāpīya, Kānika,
and the righteous Parāśara— these are the renowned chanters of the Sāman hymns.
Among all the chanters of the Sāmaveda, two are proclaimed as the most excellent:
Pauṣyañji and Kṛti, who are the arrangers of the Saṃhitās. 48.
O twice-born ones, Sumantu divided the Atharvaveda into two parts and gave them to Kabandha; he, in turn, learned the whole in its proper sequence.
Kabandha, having divided [the Veda] into two parts, gave one back to Pathya;
he then divided the second into four parts for Vedasparśa.
Moda, Brahmabala, Pippalāda, and likewise Śaukāyani,
the knower of dharma—
these four are recorded as the disciples of Vedasparśa, all firm in their vows. ||51||
Furthermore, know that there is a supreme threefold division of those who follow the wholesome path:
Jājali, Kumuda and others, and the third is remembered as Śaunaka.
But Śaunaka, having divided [the text] into two parts, gave one to Babhru;
the wise one gave the second Saṃhitā to the one known as Saindhavāyana. (53)
The Saindhava [Kalpa] for Muñjakeśa was split again into two parts:
the Nakṣatrakalpa, the Vaitāna as the third, the Saṃhitānidhi,
the Aṅgirasakalpa as the fourth, and the Śāntikalpa as the fifth.
These are indeed the most excellent variations of the Saṃhitās of the Atharvans;
having divided them into six, O best of sages, I have also spoken the Purāṇa.
Ātreya Sumati, the wise Kāśyapa Akṛtavraṇa,
Bhāradvāja Agnivarṇa, Vasiṣṭha Mitrayu, Sāvarṇi, Somadatta, Suśarman, and Śāṃśapāyana. ||56||
O Brahmin, these disciples of mine, firm in their vows regarding the Purāṇas,
have indeed divided the three collections (saṃhitās) into three groups of three once again.
Kāśyapa was the author of the Saṃhitā, followed by Sāvarṇi, Śāṃśapāyana, and Sāmika as the fourth; this is that ancient Saṃhitā.
For all of them consist of four quarters and all express the same meaning;
they are distinct in their various recensions just like the branches of the Veda,
and all are four thousand [verses] long, with the exception of that which was composed by Śāṃśapāyana.
Then there were the Lomaharṣaṇikas, followed by the Kāśyapikas;
the third were the Sāvarṇikas, who were experts in the meaning of the Yajurvedic sentences.
Furthermore, there are eight thousand and six hundred other verses belonging to the Śāṃśapāyanikas, adorned with injunctions and explanatory passages. 61.
These fifteen, as well as another ten and yet another ten,
along with all the Vālakhilyas together with the Sāvarṇas, have been proclaimed.
The chanters of the Sāman sing eight thousand Sāmans, fourteen Sāmans, and the Āraṇyaka together with the Homa.
Twelve thousand verses are recorded as the Chandas for the Adhvaryu priest,
according to how Vyāsa arranged them among the Yajus formulas and the Brāhmaṇas.
That [narrative] may be both village-based and forest-based, as well as accompanied by ritual mantras;
beyond this, the stories are characterized by the designation "former" (pūrva). 65.
The Grāmya, Āraṇyaka, and the Mantras are recorded as the Ṛk, Brāhmaṇa, and Yajus;
likewise, there are the Khilas and Upakhilas of the Hāridravīyas, and similarly, the Parakṣudras are recorded as belonging to the Taittirīyas. (66)
In the Vājasaneyaka Veda, the collection of Ṛks is calculated to be two thousand less one hundred; the Brāhmaṇa, however, is four times that amount. (67)
Eight thousand, eight hundred, eighty-four, and an additional quarter—this is the measure of the Yajus and Ṛcs, including the Śukriya and the entire Śākala collection, according to Yājñavalkya. (68)
Likewise, hear the measure of the Caraṇa-vidyās as stated in the Saṃhitā:
six thousand Ṛks are mentioned, and furthermore, twenty-six Ṛks;
this much more of the Yajus they desire to declare. (69)
Eleven thousand, ten more, and ten in excess;
ten thousand verses, and three hundred and eighty. (1.61.70)
One thousand mantras of the Ṛgveda have been stated according to their measure;
such is the extent of the Bhṛgu [portion], and there is much more belonging to the Atharva.
The definitive number of Ṛgvedic verses is five thousand;
another thousand, excluding twenty, is to be known by the sages.
This Āraṇyaka of theirs was further proclaimed by Aṅgiras;
thus has the enumeration been calculated, as well as the divisions of the branches.
The authors of the branches and likewise the cause for their division—
thus, in all Manvantaras, the divisions of the branches are recorded as being the same.
The Vedic revelation pertaining to Prajāpati is eternal, whereas these Smṛtis are known as its variations;
because of the impermanence of the gods, the production of mantras occurs again and again.
The determination of the names of the Manvantaras and the gods is made;
furthermore, in the Dvāpara ages, the various divisions of the revealed scriptures are proclaimed.
Then the Blessed One, the best of sages, having likewise given this Veda to other disciples, went to the forest to perform austerities;
and by his disciples and grand-disciples, these various divisions of the branches were established.
The auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, Nyāyavistara, Dharmaśāstra, and Purāṇa—these are the fourteen branches of knowledge (vidyās). ||78||
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda— these three,
together with Arthaśāstra as the fourth, constitute the eighteen branches of knowledge.
The Brahmarṣis are to be known as preceding them, and after them, the Devarṣis;
then the Rājarṣis—these are the three classes of sages (ṛṣiprakṛti). Among these, the Rājarṣis are [honored] by the Munis who are firm in their vows. (1.61.80)

Among the Kaśyapas, the Vasiṣṭhas, as well as the Bhṛgus, Aṅgirases, and Atris—within these five lineages, those who discourse upon Brahman are born. Because they perceive Brahman, they are remembered as Brahmarṣis. ||81||
Then [the sacrifice] of Dharma, of Pulastya, of Kratu, and of Pulaha;
and again that of Pratyūṣa, of Prabhāsa, and of Kaśyapa.
The sons of those [sages] were the celestial rishis; learn their names:
both Nara and Nārāyaṇa were the celestial rishis and the two sons of Dharma. (83)
The Vālakhilyas are the sons of Kratu; Kardama is the son of Pulaha;
Kubera is the son of Pulastya; and Acala is recorded as the son of Pratyūṣa.
Both Parvata and Nārada were the two sons of Kaśyapa;
because they delight the gods, they are therefore remembered as Devarṣis (divine sages). ||85||

Those kings who belong to the lineage of Manu, the Vaiṣaya dynasty, and the Aila dynasty—namely the descendants of Aila, Ikṣvāku, and Nābhāga—they are to be known as the royal sages (rājarṣis). ||86||
Because the subjects delight in them, they are therefore called royal sages (rājarṣis);
those who are established in the world of Brahmā are remembered as and considered to be brahmin sages (brahmarṣis). 87.
The auspicious celestial sages (devarṣis) are to be known as those established in the world of the gods;
all the royal sages (rājarṣis), however, are considered to be established in the world of Indra.
By birth, by austerity, and likewise by the recitation of mantras,
those who are thus described as Brahman-sages are also the divine royal sages.
I shall likewise describe the characteristics of the celestial sages and others:
their knowledge of the past, the future, and the present, as well as their speech that is always truthful.

Those who are perfectly awakened ones (sambuddhas) by themselves, those who are indeed awakened by themselves, those who are renowned here for their asceticism (tapas), and those by whom the embryo was impelled—[all these have been described]. 91.
Those who utter mantras, those who are all-pervading through their sovereignty—
these are the ones joined with the status of seers (ṛṣis), as well as gods, the twice-born, and kings.
Those who study these principles and those who are considered to be the seers—these seven are remembered as the Seven Seers (Saptarṣis) because of their seven respective qualities. ||93||
Those who are long-lived, creators of mantras, lords, possessed of divine vision, Buddhas who have directly realized the Dharma, and those who establish the lineages. //94//
Constantly devoted to the six duties, those virtuous householders conducted their affairs with equals, based on unseen causes of action. ||95||
The prosperous householders, dwelling both within and outside the city, sustained themselves with refined flavors prepared by their own hands. 96.
In all the ages known as Kṛta and the others, the establishment of the system of castes and stages of life is indeed performed again and again at the very beginning.

When the beginning of the Tretā Yuga arrives once again, those same Seven Sages appear here and establish the social classes and the stages of life in every respect; it is from their very lineage that heroes are born again and again.
When a son is born to a father, and likewise a father to a son,
they thus meet in succession without interruption and continue this way until the end of the age;
eighty-eight thousand such householders have been proclaimed.
Those who have taken refuge in the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāṇa) are the followers of Aryaman;
they are indeed those who maintain a wife and the sacred fire, and are remembered as the causes of progeny.
And those who were householders resort to cremation grounds in numbers that can be counted;
eighty-eight thousand of them are deposited during the northern course of the sun.
Those sages who are heard to have reached heaven, possessing sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) and being the authors of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, are indeed born again at the end of the Yuga.
Thus revolving again and again during the Dvāpara ages,
at the end of the Kalpas, they became authors of various treatises on the commentaries and sciences.
In the future Dvāpara age, the son of Droṇa, Dvaipāyana, will once again become Vedavyāsa; indeed, he shall be a man of great asceticism in this [age] that has passed.
In the future, there will indeed be the transmissions of the branches among those yet to come;
that imperishable Brahman was obtained by him through the austerity of Brahman.
Through austerity, action is attained; from action, indeed, fame arises.
Through fame, truth is reached; and through truth, the Imperishable is attained.
From the imperishable comes the immortal, the pure; indeed, from the immortal everything arises.
This eternal, single-syllabled [reality] is established within its own self.
Because of its vastness and because it causes growth, it is designated as Brahman. ||107||
Furthermore, that which abides in the Praṇava is known as Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ;
salutations to Brahman, whose form consists of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas. (108)
Salutation to that Subrahman, who is designated as the cause of the dissolution and origin of the world, and who is the supreme secret beyond the Great Principle (mahat). ||109||
It is unfathomable, supreme, and inexhaustible; it is the abode that deludes the world, and its purpose is the fulfillment of the aims of man through both illumination and activity.
The culmination and goal for those possessing the knowledge of Sāṅkhya is that which is the immortal, unmanifest, primordial nature (prakṛti), the eternal Brahman. ||111||
He is called Pradhāna, Ātmayoni, Guhya, Sattva, Avibhāga, Śukra, Akṣara, and Bahu; to that Supreme Brahman, let there be eternal salutation after salutation. 112.
Once it has been done, there is no further action; how much less so for an unperformed action?
For everything that is done or left undone in the world is accomplished all at once.
Indeed, that which is to be heard or already heard, as well as the goodness or badness [of things],
must be known; furthermore, that which is to be reflected upon, touched, eaten,
seen, heard, or known in any way whatsoever.
Whatever knowledge was shown by him alone belongs indeed to the celestial sages;
who indeed is capable of seeking out that which he has revealed?
That Blessed One alone spoke of all things, all [beings], and all [aspects]. ||115||
When something is done by someone, then that person identifies with it;
yet that by which this was previously performed has been rendered distinct by another.
But whenever something verbal is produced by someone anywhere, it indeed appears to the authors as having been created by that very person previously. (117)
Dispassion and attachment, knowledge and ignorance,
the pleasant and the unpleasant, merit and demerit, happiness and suffering, death and immortality,
as well as the regions above, across, and below— all these have that very [Self] as their unseen cause. ||118||
Then, in each Tretā age here, the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara] of the eldest Brahmā Parameṣṭhin occurs again and again.
For that single Vidyā was divided again and again during the Dvāpara ages;
Brahmā spoke this at the beginning of that Vaivasvata interval.
The sages, revolving again and again throughout the periods called yugas, compose these collections (saṃhitās) as they are born from one another.
Indeed, eighty-eight thousand seers of revealed knowledge are recorded;
these very collections (saṃhitās) recur again and again. ||122||
Those who, resorting to the southern path, frequented the cremation grounds—by them those branches were repeatedly expanded again and again in age after age. ||123||
Just as in all the Dvāpara ages, the Saṃhitās were [compiled] by the ṛṣis of revealed knowledge;
in their lineages, these branches arise here again and again. Due to the end of the Yuga, those authors of the branches appear here once more.
In this very same way, it should be understood that in all the past and future Manvantaras here, there will indeed be the promulgations of the Vedic branches.
Those [events] that occurred in the past, those that are occurring in the present, and those that will be in the future are described even in relation to the future [lives]. (126)
The past is to be known by means of the future, and both are known by means of the present;
by this sequential method, the determination of the Manvantaras is established.
In this way, the gods, the ancestors, the sages, and those who are Manus,
go upwards together with the mantras, and indeed they return along with them.
From Janaloka, all the gods repeatedly descended from Paśukalpa;
yet when the time was fully arrived, they were not truly born [there].
But when they are connected with that which is necessarily destined to happen,
they then perceive their birth as being fraught with defects and preceded by passion.
Then their activity ceases because they perceive faults;
thus, O Lord, the ages here cease after being repeated ten times.
From Janaloka they go to Tapoloka, from which there is no return;
thus thousands of divine yugas have passed here,
as they have gone to their end in the world of Brahmā along with the sages.
It is not possible to describe them in detail in their proper sequence,
because time is beginningless and entirely incalculable,
including all the past Manvantaras along with the Kalpas that preceded them.
Together with the ancestors, the sages, the gods, and the seven seers, there is indeed the recurrence of the ages that are created again by Time. 134.
By this sequential process,
hundreds and thousands of kalpas and manvantaras, along with their inhabitants, have passed away.
At the end of a Manvantara occurs the dissolution, and at the end of that dissolution occurs the re-manifestation of the deities, the sages, and the host of Manu's ancestors.
It is not possible to describe in full detail, even in hundreds of years,
the successive order of the creation and the dissolution in their entirety;
however, learn now the calculation of a Manvantara according to human reckoning.
By the twice-born who were experts in calculation and the determination of meaning, thirty full crores of deities and sages were enumerated by means of their reckoning.
The duration of time, excluding the additional years, is sixty-seven million, twenty thousand, and [one hundred] more by calculation. (139)
This number of a Manvantara has been proclaimed according to human reckoning;
now I shall describe the interval between Manus according to divine years.
Eight hundred thousand according to divine reckoning,
and additionally fifty-two thousand more, is what is recorded.
This period of fourteen guṇas, known as the dissolution by invocation (āhūtasaṃplava), constitutes a full thousand yugas; that is recorded as one day of Brahmā.

There, all beings, having been consumed by the rays of the sun and placing Brahmā at their head, enter along with the celestial sages and the Dānavas into Maheśvara, the god of gods and the foremost of the Suras. 143.
He is the creator of all beings again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas;
such indeed is the period of stability for Manu together with the divine seers.
Understand indeed the transition between all the Manvantaras,
which were previously described by me to you in this context as being designated by the term "Yuga."
The four ages, beginning with Kṛta and Tretā, are known as a *caturyuga*.
When that [cycle] has revolved seventy-one times and more, the Blessed Lord, the Master, declared it to be one *manvantara*, the period of authority for a single Manu. (146)
Thus, the characteristics of all the Manvantaras—both those past and those yet to come—have been proclaimed by means of the present one. 147.
Thus has this creation of Svāyambhuva Manu been described;
now I shall indeed speak of the transition to his next [period].
Just as in former times a Manvantara, together with the sages and the deities, necessarily comes to an end by the power of inevitable destiny, so indeed does this one pass away.
In this Manvantara, those who were formerly the lords of the three worlds—
the seven ṛṣis, the gods, the ancestors, and likewise the Manus—
were the practitioners when the period of the Manvantara was complete.
Realizing that their office had come to an end and understanding their own destiny,
they all turned their faces upward toward Maharloka and set out on that path.
Then, at the end of that Manvantara, when the period of stability is complete, those deities perish and only one Kṛta Yuga remains.
There arise those who will be the future lords of the Manvantaras, as well as the deities, the ancestors, the sages, and Manu himself. (153)
But when a Manvantara is complete, if indeed another Kṛtayuga arises even among those remaining in the Kali age, then it truly becomes a Kṛtayuga for them. ||154||
Just as the continuity of what has been done is considered by the wise to be preceded by the Kali age,
so too at the ends of Manvantaras is the beginning of a new Manvantara.
When the previous Manvantara has perished and another has begun again,
at the commencement of the Kṛtayuga, those who are then remaining as the learned elite (śiṣṭas) [are the progenitors].
The seven ṛṣis and Manu, who abide awaiting the proper time, remain established in austerity while they await the end of the manvantara; thus they gradually wane.
Once the release of rain has begun, all things proceed as before for the sake of establishing the order of the Manvantaras and for the sake of continuity in every respect.
When dualities had fully set in, when medicinal herbs had appeared, and when living beings were established in their dwellings here and there; (159)
When the discourse on the true Dharma cultivated by the seers had ceased, and when the world had become joyless, with all things mobile and immobile having perished; (1.61.160)
In that former Manvantara, when there were neither villages nor cities and the system of castes and stages of life had ceased to exist, those who remained here as righteous ones—
the Seven Sages and Manu— remained established for the sake of procreation.
While they perform most difficult penance for the sake of the subjects,
all things here arise from their destruction in every way.
The gods, asuras, hosts of ancestors, sages, and likewise Manus;
serpents, spirits, piśācas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas. ||163||

Then, among those who remained, it was the Seven Sages and Manu who, at the beginning of the Manvantara, proclaimed the rules of proper conduct; and from that time, human beings began their ritual activities together with the deities.
At the beginning of a Manvantara, even prior to the onset of the Tretā Yuga, the gods first existed; indeed, they remained present in every respect as long as Dharma was established.
Having discharged his debt to the sages through celibacy, he likewise discharges his debt to the ancestors through progeny, and to the gods through sacrifice. (166)

For a hundred thousand years, remaining established in the dharma consisting of the [four] castes, they— having established the three Vedas, the means of livelihood, the science of government, the duties of the castes and stages of life,
and the hermitages themselves— set their minds upon heaven. (167)
Formerly, among those very gods who were foremost in heaven, the gods themselves previously remained entirely established in dharma. ||168||
When the Manvantara has passed away, they abandon all their abodes and,
together with the mantras, ascend to the healthy Maharloka.
With their transformations ceased, established in mental perfection,
and self-controlled, they remain observing [the world] until the dissolution of all beings.
Then, when all those [former] gods had passed away forever,
and all those abodes of the gods throughout the three worlds were entirely empty,
other gods who dwell in heaven arrived right here.
Then, endowed with ascetic power (tapas) and possessed of truthfulness, celibacy, and sacred learning (śruta), they indeed fill their respective stations.
The deaths of the seven ṛṣis, of Manu, and of the gods, together with the ancestors—of those who have passed away here, as well as of the primordial ones and those yet to be—[are all recounted]. 173.
Their absolute cessation occurs here at the end of a Manvantara;
thus, this state of affairs remains unstable through the successive sequence of all Manvantaras until the dissolution of all beings (ābhūtasaṃplava).
Thus, the characteristic of the transition between the past and future Manvantaras has been proclaimed by Svāyambhuva.
The means for those yet to come in the past manvantaras is thus completely severed until the dissolution of all beings.
The transitions of the Manvantaras are exclusively situated in Maharloka;
and Maharloka, as well as Janaloka and Tapoloka, are exclusively present in Satyaloka.
But for those destined for that state, by seeing [the truth] therein and through the cognition of diversity,
those [faculties] remain established in the truths here at the time of dissolution, when transformation has been reached.
Releasing the truth from the revolutions of the Manvantaras, they then, at the end of that period,
through their application, enter the very god Nārāyaṇa, who is of immeasurable magnitude.

As the cycles of the Manvantaras have been revolving for a long time, the world of living beings— by its very nature as a treasure-house— remains for but a moment in a state of flavor, being constantly buffeted by rise and fall.

Thus, having received these subsequent [sections] concerning the Manus—who were praised by the sages, whose nature was dharma, who possessed divine vision, and who were guided by Vāyu—the visible [truth] was presented through the conjunctions of expansion and condensation by means of divine power. (181)
All these [worlds] were filled with royal sages and celestial sages, as well as Brahman-sages, gods, and serpents;
they were perfectly endowed with the lords of the gods, the seven ṛṣis, the ancestors, and the progeny. 182.

For it is indeed meritorious for lords to proclaim their own renown, they who possess the splendor of noble lineage and ancestry, who are further strengthened by preeminent intelligence, and who are endowed with fame, brilliance, and glory. (183)

This is conducive to heaven, supremely purifying, and beneficial for obtaining sons; it is a supreme secret to be recited on festival days, foremost among great prayers, and it brings peace from evil dreams and bestows long life. (184)

O you who are foremost among the lords of creatures, divine seers, and Manus, you who are the source of merit and renowned as the Unborn One’s progeny—may you grant me success in the realization of the supreme Mahesvara-tattva, for the sake of proclaiming and restraining myself. 185.
Thus has been described in detail and in proper sequence this interval of Svāyambhuva Manu; what more shall I relate? 186.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Genealogy of the Prajāpatis," in the *Mahāpurāṇa* proclaimed by Vāyu.
Ānandāśrama edition, Chapter 62.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Śaunaka said:
I wish to know, according to the truth, the sequence of the Manvantaras,
and which deities belong to each interval of a Manu.
Sūta said:
Listen as I describe, both briefly and in detail, those Manvantaras that have passed and those yet to come.
Svāyambhuva Manu was first, then Svārociṣa Manu; Auttama, Tāmasa, as well as Raivata and Cākṣuṣa—these six Manus have passed away; I shall now describe the eight who are yet to come.
The five Sāvarṇas, Raucya, and Bhautya, as well as Vaivasvata—
these I shall describe later, specifically in the section concerning Vaivasvata Manu.
Learn now of those five Manavas who have passed away;
I have already described to you the completed Manvantara of Svāyambhuva.
Henceforth, I shall describe in brief the creation of beings by the high-souled Svārociṣa Manu, the second.
Indeed, during the Manu-Svārociṣa interval, there were the Tuṣita gods and the learned Pārāvatas; these two groups alone are recorded.
Born in Tuṣitā were the sons of Kratu, Svarociṣ;
Pārāvatas and Śiṣṭas—these two groups are recorded as twelve each.
The Chandajas are recorded as twenty-four gods at that time. ||8||
Then Dhaivasya, Vāmanyaka, Gopā, Devāyata, the divine Lord Aja, and the very powerful Duroṇa. ||9||
Āpā, Mahābāhu, Mahaujā, Vīryavān,
Cikitvān, Nibhṛta, Aṃśu, and Paṭhyamāna—
these were the sons of Kratu, and they were drinkers of the Soma juice.
And the god Pracetas, as well as the Viśvedevas; and he who is renowned as Samāñja, and Ajihma, the crusher of enemies. ||11||
And Ajoṣa, the highly fortunate one, and Yavīyas, who possesses great strength. ||12||
Hota, Yajvan, and these others were the Parākrāntas and Parāvatas;
for these were indeed the deities during the Manvantara of Svarocis.
At that time, these twenty-four deities were indeed drinkers of Soma;
their Indra was then Vaidha, renowned throughout the world. (14)
Ūrja was the son of Vasiṣṭha, while Stambha was the son of Kaśyapa;
then Droṇa was of Bhṛgu’s lineage, and likewise Ṛṣabha was of Aṅgiras’s lineage.
Paulastya, Dattātri, Ātreya, Niścala, and Dhāvan, the son of Pulaha—these are remembered as the seven Ṛṣis. ||16||
Bṛhadguha and Nava—these are remembered as his nine sons. ||17||
These are remembered as the lineage-founding sons of Svārociṣa Manu, enumerated in the Purāṇa; this is the second interval (antara).
The seven ṛṣis, Manu, the gods, and the ancestors—these four constitute the root of a manvantara; and within their interval lie all created beings. (19)
The deities are the sons of the ṛṣis, and the ancestors (pitaras) are the sons of the gods;
the ṛṣis and the sons of the gods—such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures. From Manu came the Kṣatriyas and the Vaiśyas, and from the seven ṛṣis came the twice-born (dvijātis).
This Manvantara has been described in brief, but not in detail.
The detailed account of Svārociṣa’s [Manvantara] should be understood from that of Svāyambhuva;
its full expansion cannot be told even in hundreds of years,
due to the great abundance of repetitions regarding the various lineages of beings.
Now, furthermore, in the interval of the third Manu, Uttama, five groups are proclaimed; I shall describe them—listen.
The Sudhāmans, the Devas, and those others who are Vaśavartins—the Pratardanās, Śivas, and Satyas—these are remembered as the twelve Gaṇas. ||24||
Satya, Dhṛti, Dama, Dānta, Kṣama, Kṣāma, Dhṛti, Śuci, Īśa, Ūrja, Jyeṣṭha, and Vapuṣmān— these twelve are the Sudhāmans, pervaded by these names. (25)
The thousand-streamed one, the soul of all, the pacifier, the possessor of great wealth, the all-pervading, the creator of all, the wise, the sovereign, and the glorious one. ||26||
Jyotis, Vibhāvasu, Kīrtimān, Vaṃśakārin,
and the other Vasudhiṣṇa, the son of Vivasvat, were gods who had been propitiated by others.
Dinakratu, Sudharmā, Dhṛtavarman, Yaśasvin, and Ketumān—these are proclaimed as the Pramardanās. ||28||
Haṃsasvara, Ahihā, Pratarddana, Yaśaskara, Sudāna, Vasudāna, and both Sumanjas and Viṣa. (29)
Jantuvāhayati, Suvitta, and Sunaya— these twelve others are to be known as auspicious and worthy of sacrifice. Now,
learn from me according to my understanding the names of those who are devoted to truth.
Dikpati, Vākpati, Viśva, and likewise Śambhu. ||31||
Svamṛḍīka, Adhipa, Varcodhā, Muhyasarvaśas, Vāsava, Sadāśva, as well as Kṣema and Ānanda. ||32||
For these twelve others, who were worthy of sacrifice, were indeed perfected as truths;
these were the deities during the interval of the Manu Auttama. (33)
Aja, Paraśu, Divya, Divyauṣadhi, Naya, Devānuja, the peerless Mahotsāha, and likewise Auśija; ||34||
Vinīta, Suketu, Sumitra, Subala, and Śuci—
these were the thirteen sons of the high-souled Auttama Manu.
These were the leaders of the Kṣatriyas during this third interval.
The creation by Svārociṣa has been enumerated as the most excellent;
now learn from me that [creation] of Tāmasa in detail and in its proper sequence.
Then, in the fourth period, during the interval of the Manu Tāmasa,
there were four groups of Satyas, Svarūpas, Sudhiyas, and Haris.
The son of Pulastya was Śīrṣyaṇya, and Tama was the eighth;
these are remembered as the gods of the senses during that Manvantara of his.
The sages declare that there were one hundred senses;
the vital breaths (prāṇas) were the head-senses, and darkness (tamas) was the eighth.
During the interval of that Manu, these were known as the gods of the senses.
And during the reigns of those Prabhūdevas, the powerful Śibir was Indra;
likewise, there were the Seven Sages. Know them, O best of beings:
Kāvya, Harṣa, Kāśyapa, and Pṛthu.
Ātreya is indeed Agni, and Jyotirdhāman is Bhārgava. ||41||
Paulaha, Vanapiṭha, and Vāsiṣṭha by lineage,
as well as Caitra and Paulastya— these were the sages in the Tāmasa Manvantara.
Januṣaṇḍa, Śānti, Nara, Khyāti, Bhaya,
Priyabhṛtya, Avakṣi, Pṛṣṭaloḍha, Dṛḍhodyata,
Ṛta, and Ṛtabandhu were the sons of the Manu Tāmasa.
Now, in this fifth section concerning the wandering mind, learn of the well-proclaimed hosts of deities. 44.
The sons of the Prajāpati Vasiṣṭha were Amṛta, Bhā, Bhūtarajas, Vikuṇṭha, and Sumedhas; they were auspicious and mobile. These radiant ones formed fourteen groups of four each.
Svatravipra, Gninibhāsa, Sva, Pratyetiṣṭhā, Amṛta, Tathā, Sumati, Vāvirāva, Vācinoda, and Srava. ||46||
Pravira, Āśī, Vāda, and Prāśa—these fourteen gods, possessing the luster of nectar, are remembered as having existed during the Ariṣṇu Manvantara. (47)
Mati and Sumati, as well as Ṛta and Satya; likewise Āvṛti and Vivṛti, and Mada and Vinaya. ||48||
Jetā, Jiṣṇu, Sahas, Dyutimān, and Sravas—these are known here as the names of those who have transcended the quality of passion (rajas). ||49||
Vṛṣabhettā, Jaya, Bhīma, Śuci, Dānta, Yaśas, Dama,
Nātha, Vidvān, Ajeya, Kṛśa, Gaura, and Dhruva—
these are indeed proclaimed as the Vikuṇṭhas; now learn of the Sumedhas.
Medhā, Medhātithi, and likewise Satyamedhās; Pṛśrimedhā, Alpamedhās, Bhūyomedhās, and the lord [Medhātithi]. (51)
Dīptamedhā, Yaśomedhā, Sthiramedhā,
as well as Sarvamedhā, Aśvamedhā, and he who is remembered as Pratimedhā;
Medhāvān and Medhahartṛ— these are proclaimed as the Sumedhasas.
At that time, Indra was their sovereign, possessing valorous prowess;
there were Paulastya Vedabāhu and Yajurnāman of the lineage of Kaśyapa.
Hiraṇyaroman Aṅgiras, Vedaśrī Bhārgava,
Ūrdhvabāhu Vāsiṣṭha, Parjanya Paulaha,
and Satyanetra Ātreya were the sages during the Raivata Manvantara. (54)
Mahāpurāṇasambhāvya, Pratyaṅgaparahā, Śuci,
Balabandhu, Nirāmitra, Ketubhṛṅga, and Dṛḍhavrata—
these are the sons of Cariṣṇu; this is the fifth interval.
Svārociṣa, Uttama, Tāmasa, and likewise Raivata—these four Manus belong to the lineage of Priyavrata. (56)
Now, in the sixth section, those gods who existed during the Cākṣuṣa interval—
the Ādyas, Prasūtas, Bhāvyas, Pṛthukas, and Mahānubhāvalekhas— are recorded as the five classes of celestial beings.
This creation of the celestial dwellers is proclaimed by the names of their mothers.
They are the grandsons of the Prajāpati Āraṇya, the son of Atri;
and those hosts of gods are traditionally recorded as having eight members each.
Antarikṣa, Vasuhaya, Atithi, Priyavrata, Śrotṛ, Mantṛ, and Sumantṛ—these are proclaimed as the primordial ones. ||59||
Śyenabhadra, Paśya, the highly renowned Pathyanetra,
Sumanas, Suvetas, Raivata, Supracetas,
and Dyuti— these are proclaimed as the great beings born [from her]. (2.1.60)
Vijaya, Sujaya, as well as Manodyāna,
Sumati, Supari, and he who is known as Arthapati—
these are indeed remembered as the Bhāvyas; now learn of the Pṛthukas.
Ajiṣṭha, Śākyana, Deva, Vānapṛṣṭha, as well as Śāṅkara, Satyadhṛṣṇu, Viṣṇu, Vijaya,
and the highly fortunate Ajita— these are the Pṛthukas, the inhabitants of heaven.
I shall likewise declare the Lekhas; listen as I speak.
Manojava, Praghāsa, and the highly illustrious Pracetas—these are they. (63)
Vāta, Dhruvakṣiti, the heroic Adbhuta, Avana, and Bṛhaspati are celebrated as the Lekhās. ||64||
Manojava, the son of Atri, was then their Indra;
Unnata, the descendant of Bhṛgu, and Haviṣmat, the son of Aṅgiras, were also there. (65)
Sudhāmā Kāśyapa, Vāsiṣṭha Virajas, Atimāna Paulastya, Sahiṣṇu Paulaha,
and Madhura Traiya— these seven indeed [were the ṛṣis] in the Cākṣuṣa interval.
Ūru, Pūru, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavāk, Kṛti, Agniṣṭut, Atirātra, and Sudyumna—these are the nine. (67)
And Abhimanyu was the tenth; these are the sons of Manu who should not be disparaged.
These indeed were the sons of Cākṣuṣa, and that was the sixth interval.
O twice-born ones, the creation of that high-souled one has been enumerated by Vaivasvata; it has indeed been recounted by me in detail and in due order.
The sages said:
But the heir of Cākṣuṣa was Sambhūta, born in the lineage of Kaśyapa; tell us truly who else there were in his lineage. Sūta said:
You should now hear in brief the lineage of Cākṣuṣa;
in his dynasty was born the powerful Pṛthu, son of Vena.
There were other lords of creatures as well, such as Dakṣa Prācetasa;
and the patriarch Atri took Uttānapāda as his son.
The son of this Prajāpati Dakṣa was indeed a king,
who was granted [the kingdom] by Svāyambhuva Manu for the sake of Atri.
O twice-born ones, having reached the future Manvantara of Cākṣuṣa,
which is the sixth, I shall now describe it by way of introduction.
From Uttānapāda was born the clever Sūnṛtā, the possessor of wealth,
who arose through Adhirdharma; she was the auspicious mother of Dhruva, that woman of pure smiles born indeed from Lakṣmī, the wife of Dharma.
Uttānapāda begot Dhruva, Kīrttimat, Ayasmant, and Vasu, as well as two daughters of pure smiles;
Manasvinī and Svarā are proclaimed to be the three sons of these two.
For ten thousand divine years, the valiant Dhruva,
abstaining from food, performed austerities while seeking great renown.
In the first Tretā Yuga, that grandson of Svāyambhuva,
maintaining himself through yoga, sought after great renown.
To him, Brahmā, being pleased, granted the supreme station among the luminaries—
a delightful place that lasts until the dissolution of all beings and is devoid of rising or setting.
Beholding his extraordinary supernatural power and majesty, Uśanas, the preceptor of the Daityas and Asuras, even sang this verse:
"Aho! The power of his asceticism! Aho! His sacred learning! Aho! His sacrificial offerings!"
Having placed him above as the Pole Star (dhruva), the Seven Sages remain fixed;
that Lord, the master of the day, has the celestial sphere attached to the Pole Star.
That Bhūmi gave birth to two kings, Dhruva and Puṣṭi;
and Puṣṭi said to her own shadow, "Become a woman," and the Lord made her so.
As soon as he uttered the word "Truth," she immediately became a woman, possessing a divine luster and adorned with celestial ornaments. (83)
In the shade, Puṣṭi gave birth to five sinless sons:
Prācīnagarbha, Vṛṣaka, Vṛka, Vṛkala, and Dhṛti.
The wife of Prācīnagarbha, Bhūvarcā, gave birth to a son, a king named Udāradhī, who had been Indra in a previous birth. (85)
At the end of a thousand years, he would take food only once;
thus, the omnipresent Lord attained the status of Indra for the duration of a Manvantara.
Bhadrā gave birth to a son, Divañjaya, for Udāradhi;
and Varāṅgī bore Ripuñjaya to that Divañjaya. (87)
Bṛhatī bore to Ripu a son named Cākṣuṣa, who possessed all splendor.
Cākṣuṣa begot Manu upon Puṣkariṇī, the daughter of Varuṇa and the high-souled Prajāpati Āraṇya.
O highly fortunate one, ten auspicious sons were born to the daughter of the patriarch Vairāja by Danū. (89)
Ūru, Pūru, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavāk, Kavi,
Agniṣṭut, Atirātra, and Sudyumna— these nine,
along with Abhimanyu as the tenth, were the sons of Manu born of Nadvalā. (2.1.90)
From her thighs, the daughter of Agni gave birth to six sons of great splendor:
Aṅga, Sumanas, Svāti, Kratu, Aṅgiras, and Śiva.
From Aṅga, Sunīthā gave birth to a single son, Vena;
due to the misconduct of Vena, a very great wrath arose.
For the sake of the subjects, the sages churned the right hand of Vena;
when Vena’s hand was churned, there arose a great king, the protector of the earth known as Pṛthu, who is celebrated by the name Vainya. (93)
Armed with a bow and wearing armor, blazing as if with fiery energy,
Pṛthu, the son of Vena and the first of the Kṣatriyas, protected all the worlds.
For the purpose of praising him, two skillful bards and panegyrists appeared. ||95||
Thus, O Great King, this cow was milked by the wise one for the sake of the crops, together with the gods and hosts of ṛṣis who desired a means of livelihood for their subjects. 96.
By the Pitṛs, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, the hosts of Apsarases, by all the Puṇyajanas, as well as by the plants and the mountains; ||97||
As the earth was milked into those various vessels, it yielded milk according to each one's desire; with that, he sustained the worlds.
The sages said:
O high-minded one, relate in detail the birth of Pṛthu, and how the earth was formerly milked by that great-souled one. (99)
Just as in the past by the gods and the *nāgas*, by the celestial sages (*brahmarṣi*), and by the *yakṣas* along with the *gandharvas* and *apsarases*,
[he saw] their various vessels, the milker, and the milk itself.
Likewise, please tell us who are asking you about the specific types of calves.
And tell us everything regarding the reason why, in the past, the hand of Vena was formerly churned by the enraged great seers. 102.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, I shall describe to you the origin of Pṛthu, the son of Vena;
listen with one-pointed attention and self-restraint, O best of the twice-born. (103)

I shall not describe this meritorious [teaching] to one who is impure, nor to one who is wicked, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who seeks harm; nor under any circumstances to one who does not observe the vows.
He who listens without malice to this secret, proclaimed by the seers—which leads to heaven, brings fame and long life, is meritorious, and is equal to the Vedas—[attains these rewards]. (105)
That mortal who, having paid homage to the Brahmins, causes others to hear this account of the origin of Pṛthu, the son of Vena, shall not grieve over what has been done or left undone.
That lordly king was a protector of dharma, equal to Atri. (106)
Born in the lineage of Atri was a Prajāpati named Aṅga,
whose son was Vena, who was not particularly righteous.
That Prajāpati Vena, the son of Kālātmajā, was indeed born of Sunīthā, the daughter of Mṛtyu; yet, due to the fault of his maternal grandfather, he became such. (108)
Having cast dharma behind him, that king turned toward desire and greed; he established a system devoid of dharma.
Transgressing the Vedic scriptures, he became devoted to unrighteousness. While he ruled, the subjects ceased their Vedic study and the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call;
and the deities did not drink the *soma* offered in sacrifices.
"One must neither sacrifice nor offer oblations"— this was the cruel vow made by that Prajāpati when destruction was imminent.
I am the one to be sacrificed to and the one to be honored by the twice-born in all sacrifices;
sacrifice is to be ordained unto me, and it is also to be offered into me.
As he was acting improperly, transgressing all bounds of propriety, all the great seers, headed by Marīci, spoke to him as follows: (113)
"We shall enter upon initiation for many hundreds of years;
do not commit unrighteousness, O Vena, for this is not the eternal dharma. You were born for the sake of destruction, yet you are undoubtedly a Prajāpati. (114)
"I shall protect the subjects"—this was previously promised by you.
To all those Brahman-sages who were speaking thus, he then replied: 115.
Laughing, that evil-minded man, skilled in speech, said:
"Who else is the creator of dharma? Whose words indeed should I listen to? (116)
"Who on earth is my equal in heroism, learning, austerity, and truth?
Know me truly to be a great-souled one, lacking in nothing. (117)
I am the source of all worlds and especially of all phenomena;
if I so desired, I could burn the earth or flood it with water,
or I could create or swallow it— there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
When King Vena could not be persuaded because he was utterly deluded by arrogance and obstinacy, the great seers became enraged.
Having seized that mighty-armed one as he writhed like a fire,
they, provoked to intense anger, then wrung his left hand. From that hand, as it was being wrung, there was indeed born the one previously celebrated.
O twice-born ones, the man was exceedingly short in stature and likewise dark-complexioned. ||121||
Terrified, with his senses agitated, he stood with palms joined in reverence;
seeing him thus distressed and overwhelmed, they indeed said to him, "Sit down. (122)
He of infinite prowess became the founder of the Niṣāda lineage;
he also begot the fishermen who were born from the impurity of Vena.
And others, such as the Vindhyanilayas, the Tumburus, the Ātubaras, and the Khasas—
those who delight in unrighteousness— were also born from the impurity of Vena.
Furthermore, the great sages, their indignation aroused, vigorously churned the right hand of Vena as one churns a fire-drill, filled with wrath.
Pṛthu was born from him through the power of the clapping of his hands;
or rather, because he was born from the palm of Pṛthu’s hand, he was therefore named Pṛthu.
Blazing with his own body, he was like a fire manifest in its brilliance. (126)
Taking up his first bow, named Ājagava, which produced a great roar, and bearing arrows and a highly lustrous armor for the sake of protection, [he set forth]. (127)
When he was born, all living beings were filled with joy on every side;
and when that great night had arisen, Vena ascended to the third heaven.
By that wise and virtuous son who has been born, the royal sage—like a tiger among men—is thereafter rescued from the hell named Put. (129)
Then the rivers and the oceans, having brought all kinds of jewels from every quarter and having assembled together, consecrated that son of Vena as the lord of men—
the great king of great splendor— with the vast sovereignty of kings.
Thus was the powerful Pṛthu, son of Vena, the first king and great monarch, consecrated as a great king by the gods, the sons of Aṅgiras. 131.
His subjects were not won over by his father, but they were won over by him;
therefore, the name "Rāja" (King) arose for him because of their affection. 132.
As he set out toward the ocean, the waters solidified for him;
even the mountains crumbled away, yet his banner did not break. (133)
The earth yields crops without being ploughed; foods are accomplished by mere thought;
cows grant all desires; and there is honey in every leaf-cup.
At that very time, during the auspicious sacrifice of the Grandfather (Brahmā),
the high-minded Sūta was born from the *sūti* vessel on the day of the *sūtyā*;
and at that same great sacrifice, the wise Māgadha was likewise born.
Having offered an oblation mixed with the oblation of Bṛhaspati by means of an oblation dedicated to Indra, he sacrificed to the god Indra; from that, a son was born.
In that regard, negligence arose concerning the sacrificial rites;
for the oblation of the preceptor, when mixed with the offering of the disciple, was overwhelmed by the inversion of the upper and lower positions, resulting in a corruption of the castes. (137)
And he who is born from a Kṣatriya father by a Brāhmaṇa mother, being of inferior birth, is proclaimed as a Sūta; he shares the same characteristics and duties as the former [the Māgadha]. ||138||
For this is the middling duty of a Sūta: subsisting by the profession of a Kṣatriya;
the management of chariots, elephants, and horses is the lowest, as is the practice of medicine. 139.
The two of them were summoned there by the celestial rishis for the purpose of praising Pṛthu.
All the sages said to them, "Let this king be praised;
this deed is worthy of you both, and he is indeed a fit recipient for your hymn."
Then the Sūta and the Māgadha said to all those ṛṣis:
"We two please both the gods and the ṛṣis by means of our own duties. (141)
"O twice-born ones, we do not know his deeds, nor his characteristics, nor his fame, by which we might offer praise for this radiant king. (142)
The sages then appointed them both, saying, "Let him be praised for his future deeds.
He was constantly devoted to the duty of giving, truthful, and one who had conquered his senses; he was wise in character, generous, and undefeated in battles. (143)
Whatever deeds the exceedingly powerful Pṛthu performed,
those were bound by his virtuous character as they were being praised by the bards and panegyrists.
Then, at the conclusion of the hymn, the well-pleased Pṛthu, lord of subjects, bestowed the Anūpa region upon Sūta and the Magadha region upon Māgadha.
At that time, the protectors of the earth were indeed praised by *sūtas* and *māgadhas*, and they were awakened with benedictions by *sūtas*, *māgadhas*, and bards. ||146||
Seeing him, the subjects and the great sages were exceedingly joyful and said: "This son of Vena shall be the provider of livelihood for you; let him be your lord of men. (147)
Then, at the command of the great seer, "Provide us with a means of livelihood," the subjects flocked to the illustrious Vainya;
thus pursued by the subjects, he acted out of a desire to promote their welfare.
Taking up his bow and arrows, the powerful one tormented the earth;
terrified by the fear of his tormenting, the earth fled, having assumed the form of a cow.
Pṛthu took up his bow and pursued her as she fled;
having gone through the worlds beginning with the world of Brahmā out of fear of Vainya,
she then saw Vainya before her, bearing his bow raised and ready.
With blazing arrows and shafts, he [assailed] Acyuta, who was radiant with splendor,
a great yogin, a high-souled being, and invincible even by the immortals.
Finding no protection there, the goddess—who is always worthy of worship by the three worlds—then sought refuge with Vainya alone, with her palms joined in reverence. (152)
He said to the son of Vena: "Do you not perceive the unrighteousness in the killing of a woman?
O King, how will you sustain the subjects without me? (153)
O King, the worlds are established in me; by me this universe is sustained. Without me, O best of monarchs, all creatures would perish.
"You ought not to kill me, O protector of the earth, if you desire to act for the welfare of your subjects; listen to these words of mine:
all undertakings succeed when they are commenced through the proper means. (155)
"O King, even after killing me, you will not be capable of protecting your subjects. (156)
"I shall become food; abandon your anger, O one of great luster!
They say that women are not to be slain, even among hundreds of animal births.
Considering this, O protector of the earth, you ought not to forsake righteousness. (157)

Having heard these various words, the high-minded and righteous king restrained his anger and spoke thus to the Earth: evam bahuvidhaṃ vākyaṃ śrutvā rājā mahāmanāḥ | krodhaṃ nigṛhya dharmātmā vasudhāmidamabravīt ||158||
Whoever would kill even a single living being—whether for his own sake or for the sake of another—whether it be one or many, he certainly incurs the sin of a transgression. (159)
"But when that one who is slain, O auspicious lady, many obtain happiness;
in the slaying of such a virtuous person, there is neither sin nor secondary sin.
"Therefore, O Earth, for the sake of the subjects, I shall slay you."
If you do not carry out my word today for the benefit of the world, [the consequences will follow]. (161)
Having slain you today with an arrow for turning your back on my command,
I shall establish myself here and sustain the subjects by manifesting my own power.
Therefore, O best among the upholders of dharma, having accepted my word, restore the subjects to life constantly; for you are indeed capable of this, there is no doubt.
"O you of terrible appearance, become my daughter; let this great boon be so. I shall restrain you for the sake of dharma."
Then the Earth, having been addressed thus, replied to the son of Vena:
"It is even so, O King; I shall do this, there is no doubt. (165)
"Give me that calf so that, out of affection for it, I may flow with milk;
and make me level everywhere, O best of the upholders of dharma, so that my overflowing milk may nourish all things. (166)
Then the son of Vena cleared away the masses of rocks in every direction; by means of the tip of his bow, he caused the mountains to be split apart.
In the past manvantaras, the earth was uneven; by its very nature, it possessed both level and rugged places. (168)
For indeed, in the primordial creation, when the surface of the earth was uneven, there existed no division of cities or even of villages. ||169||
In former times, during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, it is said that there were no crops, no cattle-rearing, no agriculture, and no trade routes; however,
in this Vaivasvata Manvantara, the origin of all these things has occurred.
Wherever there was a greater degree of equanimity, there indeed did those subjects always dwell. (171)

It is said that in ancient times, food consisted only of fruits and roots for all living beings; however, from the time of Vainya onwards, the production of all these [other foods] came into existence in this world.
When the medicinal herbs had indeed perished, that lord Pṛthu, with great difficulty,
fashioned Cākṣuṣa Manu as the calf and then milked the earth for crops upon his own surface.
Having made Manu Cākṣuṣa the calf and the earth the vessel, that son of Vena milked the crops from the Vasundharā; by means of that food,
those subjects were then constantly sustained.
Furthermore, the Earth was milked again by the sages;
Soma became their calf, and Bṛhaspati was the milker. (175)
The Vedic meters, beginning with the Gāyatrī, were entirely the vessel;
their milk was austerity and the eternal Brahman. (176)
Having praised her again by the hosts of gods led by Purandara,
they then took a golden vessel and milked the nectar;
with that very [nectar], the gods, headed by Indra, subsist.
Then the Earth was milked by the Nāgas; milk became poison for them, and Vāsuki, the son of Kadrū and possessed of great power, was their milker. 178.

O best of the twice-born, the fierce, large-bodied, and exceedingly formidable nāgas and serpents of every kind subsist entirely upon that [poison]; they have that as their food, that as their conduct, that as their strength, and always take refuge in that. (179)
Furthermore, this earth was milked into an earthen vessel (śrāma-pātra) by the Yakṣas,
those beings of merit, who made Vaiśravaṇa the calf;
Jatunābha, the father of Maṇivara, was the milker.
"The son of a Yakṣa, possessed of great splendor, self-controlled, and endowed with immense strength—
by him they are sustained," so said the supreme Ṛṣi.
The earth was milked again by the Rākṣasas and Piśācas;
Kubera, accompanied by Brahmā, was indeed their milker. ||182||
The powerful Rākṣasa Sumālī milked blood into a skull-bowl, and the Rākṣasas attained invisibility; by that milk, the Rākṣasas sustain themselves here in every way. (183)
Furthermore, the Gandharvas and hosts of Apsaras milked [the cow] into a lotus vessel, having made Citraratha the calf and using pure fragrances as well. (184)
For them, the milk-cow was Viśvāvasu, the pure son of the sage;
he was a Gandharva king of great power, high-souled, and resplendent like the sun. (185)
And even by the mountains was the goddess Vasundharā milked;
there, the medicinal herbs in embodied form and various kinds of gems [were obtained]. (186)
Among them, Himavat was the calf, the great mountain Meru was the milker, and the mountain itself served as the vessel;
thus was the mountain established.
The earth, having been milked again, is praised by trees and creepers; taking a vessel of *palāśa* leaves, she yields milk that causes the regrowth of what was severed. (188)
The mountain is the wish-fulfilling cow in full bloom; the Plakṣa tree is the calf, and the Earth—the source of all beings—is the illustrious milch-cow that yields all desires. (189)
This very Earth is the supporter, the creator, the sustainer, and the bearer of wealth;
we have heard that she was milked by Pṛthu for the benefit of the worlds,
serving as the foundation and the source of the world of both the moving and the unmoving.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Milking of the Earth," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu. ||2.1||
Sūta said:
This earth was renowned as extending to the edge of the ocean;
because it holds wealth (*vasu*), it is therefore called *Vasudhā*. (1)
Formerly, it was completely saturated with the fat of Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
thereafter, through the acceptance of King Pṛthu, the son of Vena, who was wise. ||2||
And this earth, formerly renowned as extending to the ends of the ocean, attained the status of being his daughter; therefore, she is called Pṛthivī. (3)

The earth was made famous, well-ordered, and beautiful by that wise king; it abounded in crops and mines, was adorned with garlands of cities and ports, and was filled with the four social orders, all protected by him. (4)
Such was the power of that king Vainya, the best of monarchs;
he was to be saluted and honored by the entire multitude of living beings from every side.
And by the highly fortunate Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
Pṛthu alone— being the eternal source of the Brahman— is to be saluted.
Even by highly fortunate kings seeking great glory,
the majestic Pṛthu, son of Vena and first of monarchs, must be honored.
Moreover, even by warriors seeking victory in battle,
Pṛthu alone is indeed to be saluted, for he was truly the first creator among men.
For whatever warrior goes to battle after having praised King Pṛthu, he,
being renowned, crosses through the terrible conflict safely.
Even by the Vaiśyas who abide in the conduct of Vaiśyas,
Pṛthu alone— the giver of livelihoods and the one of great fame— is to be saluted.
These are the specific calves, the milkers, and the milk itself.
And all the vessels have been described by me in their proper sequence.
In ancient times, the high-souled Brahmā first milked the earth,
making the wind the calf and placing the seeds upon the surface of the ground.
Then, during that previous Svāyambhuva Manvantara,
the Earth was indeed milked by Grīṣma, having made Svāyambhuva his calf.
In the past, during the Svārociṣa Manvantara, the wise Caitra milked the earth,
having made Svārociṣa Manu the calf, and [obtained] the grains.
The supreme [cow] was milked by the wise Devabhūti, who used the unsurpassed Manu as the calf, and all the crops [were obtained]. (15)
Furthermore, during the interval of the Tāmasa Manu, this earth was milked by Balabandhu, having made Tāmasa the calf. (16)
When the interval of the god Cāriṣṇava arrived during the Manvantara,
the earth was milked by the Ancient One (Purāṇa) with Cāriṣṇava as the calf.
And when the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara had arrived once again,
the Earth was milked by the Ancient One (Brahmā), having made Cākṣuṣa the calf.
When the interval of Cākṣuṣa had passed and the Vaivasvata [Manvantara] had arrived again,
this earth was milked by Vainya, just as has been described to you by me.
In former ages that have passed away, this earth was indeed milked by gods and others,
as well as by humans and beings such as the *bhūtas*;
thus it should be understood to have been done by all [beings] here in both past and future times.
Hear now of the gods and the subjects of this Pṛthu during the Manvantaras.
Two valiant sons, Antardhi and Pālin, were born to Pṛthu;
from Antardhi, Śikhaṇḍinī gave birth to Havirdhāna.
From Havirdhāna, Dhiṣaṇā Āgneyī gave birth to six sons:
Prācīnabarhis, Śukra, Gaya, Kṛṣṇa, Vraja, and Ajina. (23)
The venerable Prācīnabarhis was a great Prajāpati;
by virtue of his strength, learning, austerity, and heroism, he was the sole sovereign on earth.
Because his *kuśa* grass blades were pointed toward the east (*prācīnāgra*), he was therefore called Prācīnabarhis.
Having taken Samudratanayā as his wife,
that lord indeed [lived] beyond the great darkness; and Savarṇā, the daughter of the Prajāpati Samudra, bore ten sons to Prācīnabarhis.
All were named Pracetas, masters who had reached the further shore of the science of archery; practicing their religious duties without deviation, they performed great austerities,
remaining submerged in the waters of the ocean for ten thousand years.
While the Pracetasas were performing austerities upon the earth, trees began to devour it as it remained unprotected, and consequently, there occurred a destruction of living beings.
When that [wind] was thus repelled within the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu,
the wind was unable to blow; the sky became covered with trees,
and for ten thousand years the creatures were unable to move.
Having heard that, all the Pracetasas, endowed with ascetic power and filled with wrath,
emitted wind and fire from their mouths.
Then the wind uprooted those trees and dried them out;
the fire consumed them, O terrible one—thus occurred the destruction of the trees.
Then, perceiving that the trees were being exhausted when only a few branches remained,
King Soma approached those wise ones and spoke to them.
Having seen all the purpose for the sake of ending the suffering of the world, the kings [of the lineage] of Prācīnabarhis abandoned everything. 32.
Trees shall grow upon the earth, and fire and wind shall be stilled;
for this girl of excellent complexion is a jewel among trees.
"Knowing the future, I have indeed caused this woman to be nourished by cows;
she is named Māriṣā, fashioned from trees themselves.
Let her, who has been nurtured by the womb of Soma, become your wife. (34)
"By half of your splendor and by half of my own splendor, a wise Prajāpati named Dakṣa shall be born from her. (35)
He, being himself like fire, shall further cause all creatures to flourish with this fire of yours which consists of fiery energy and has largely consumed this earth. ||36||
Then, at the word of Soma, those Pracetasas withdrew their anger from the trees and, according to dharma, accepted Māriṣā as their wife.
Then they indeed conceived a child in Māriṣā by means of their mind;
from the ten Pracetas, Prajāpati [was born] in Māriṣā.
The highly energetic and powerful Dakṣa was born from a portion of Soma;
at first, Dakṣa created offspring through his mind, and thereafter through sexual union.
Having mentally emitted both the immobile and the mobile, as well as bipeds and quadrupeds, Dakṣa afterwards created women.
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa, and twenty-seven, who were engaged in the guidance of time, to the Moon. (41)
Having given these to them, he then gave four others to Ariṣṭanemi,
two to Bahuputra, and likewise two to Aṅgiras;
and one daughter to Kṛśāśva— learn now of the offspring born from them.
The sixth intermediate period (antara) of this Manu Cākṣuṣa,
as well as that of the seventh Prajāpati, Vaivasvata Manu, is now passing away.
From them were born the gods, birds, cattle, serpents, sons of Diti and the Dānavas, Gandharvas, Apsarases, and other species as well. ||44||
From that time forward, the progeny in this world were born from sexual union;
it is said that the creation of the ancestors occurred through intention, sight, and touch.
The sages said:
The auspicious origin of the gods, the dānavas, and the celestial sages,
as well as that of the high-souled Dakṣa, has been previously recounted.
The birth of Prajāpati Dakṣa from Prāṇa has been described by you;
how did that one of great asceticism again obtain the state of being a Pracetas? (47)
O Sūta, you ought to explain this doubt of ours here:
how did he, the grandson of Soma, come to become his father-in-law? (48)
Sūta said:
O best of beings, arising and cessation are constant among all creatures;
the sages and those men who possess true knowledge are not deluded in this regard. (49)
In every age, all these twice-born ones, beginning with Dakṣa, come into being;
and again they are dissolved. A wise man is not deluded by this.
O best of the twice-born, neither seniority nor juniority existed among them from the beginning.
Austerity alone became more important, and spiritual power was indeed the cause.
He who knows this creation of Cākṣuṣa, including all that is moving and unmoving, transcends the lifespan of living beings and is glorified in the heavenly world. ||52||
This creation of the virtuous Cākṣuṣa has been fully described.
Thus, these six creations, consisting of the Manvantaras, have been recounted in brief, beginning with Svāyambhuva and ending with Cākṣuṣa, in their proper order. (53)
O best of the twice-born, these creations have indeed been described according to my understanding;
however, their full detail should be known through the account of the Vaivasvata creation.
All the creations of Vivasvat are infinite and not redundant,
whether in terms of health, lifespan, measure, or in accordance with dharma, desire, and wealth.
He who reads this without malice attains these very same qualities.
I shall now describe the creation of the high-souled Vaivasvata Manu;
listen as I speak of it both in brief and in detail. 56.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Genealogy of Pṛthu," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu. ||2.2||
Sūta said:
Now, in the seventh period of Vaivasvata Manu, the gods, who were supreme rishis, were born from Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci. (1)
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, the hosts of Maruts, the Bhṛgus, and the Aṅgirases—these are remembered as the eight classes of gods. ||2||
The Ādityas, Maruts, and Rudras are to be known as the sons of Kaśyapa;
the Sādhyas, Vasus, and Viśvedevas are the three groups who are the sons of Dharma. (3)
The divine Bhārgava was the son of Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras was the son of Aṅgiras;
indeed, in this Vaivasvata Manvantara, those gods are eternally born from the Vedas (chandas).
This present auspicious creation of Mārīca should be known;
the radiant one among them is now Indra by name, Mahābala. (5)
Those who have passed, those who are yet to come, and those who exist now—
all these Indras of the Manvantaras should be known as possessing identical characteristics.
The Lord of the past, future, and present; the thousand-eyed Purandara;
and all those Maghavans—horned and holding the thunderbolt in hand—all have performed a hundred sacrifices, each one a hundredfold more than the last.
Whatever beings there are in the three worlds who possess movement and are weak, they remain overcome by him through causes such as the Dharma and others. (8)

In splendor, ascetic power, intellect, strength, learning, and valor—just as those lords of the past, future, and present are all-powerful—I shall declare all of this; listen with focused minds as I speak. (9)
The past, the present, and the future—these are known as the three worlds by the twice-born.
This earth is known as Bhūrloka; the intermediate space is known as Bhuvar; and heaven is indeed known as Bhavya. I shall now describe the means for attaining them.
While meditating, Brahmā, desiring a son, first uttered the sacred syllable;
"Bhūḥ" was pronounced first, and at that time this world became Bhūrloka.

Regarding this [element], Brahmā spoke again, "Let it be" (bhavat); because of its state of becoming (bhavatva) and because of its visibility, this became the Bhūrloka. Therefore, because of its state of having come into being (bhūtatva), this first world is remembered by the twice-born as Bhūḥ. ||12||
Regarding this "being" (bhūta), the second [term] "becoming" (bhavat) was spoken by Brahmā;
furthermore, this word "time" (kāla) is said to refer to that which is in the process of arising (bhavati). ||13||
The world of Bhuvar is defined by those who know the etymologies as the intermediate space (antarikṣa);
therefore, it is called the second world. ||14||
But when the Bhuvarloka had arisen, Brahmā uttered "Bhavya" once more; because of that, the world then became Bhavya.
In the future, this word "bhavya" (fortunate/destined) will be fully realized; therefore, that world is indeed called "Bhavya," while by name it is remembered as "Diva. (16)
When "Svaḥ" was uttered, another world, the third, came into being;
for the verbal root *bhū* (to become) signifies that which is yet to be manifested at a future time. ||17||
"Bhūḥ" is remembered as this earth; "Bhuvaḥ" is remembered as the intermediate space (antarikṣa);
and "Svaḥ" is remembered as heaven—this is the summary of the three worlds. ||18||
Through utterances associated with the three worlds, the three *vyāhṛtis* came into being.
Indeed, this verbal root *nāth*, known by those who understand roots, is recorded as signifying protection. (19)
Because they were the lords of the past world, the future world, and the present world— of the three worlds at that time— they are therefore remembered as Indras by the twice-born.
The lords of the gods are indeed the primary [beings], and likewise those who are subordinate;
