for they are the gods who partake in the sacrificial offerings during the various Manvantaras.
Yakṣas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, piśācas, uragas, and dānavas—these are indeed recorded as the various classes of great beings belonging to the lords of the gods. (22)
For you, O best of gods, are indeed lords of the gods, teachers, protectors, kings, and fathers;
you shall guard all these subjects here by means of righteousness. (23)
Thus has the description of the lords of the gods been declared in brief;
now I shall fully describe the seven ṛṣis who currently abide in heaven.
The wise Viśvāmitra, son of Gādhi and descendant of Kuśika, of great ascetic power;
and Jamadagni of the Bhṛgu lineage, the powerful son of Ūru. ||25||
And there was also the son of Bṛhaspati, Bhāradvāja, of great asceticism;
and the learned Gautama, the son of Utathya, the righteous one named Śaradvat. ||26||
The venerable Atri was the son of Svayambhū; the fifth was Brahmakośa;
and the sixth was Vasumān, the son of Vasiṣṭha, renowned throughout the world. ||27||
Vatsāra and Kāśyapa—these seven are esteemed as holy;
these are the perfected Seven Sages who exist in the present interval.
Ikṣvāku, Nābhāga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti, the renowned Nariṣyanta, and Nābha have also been mentioned. ||29||
Karūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, and Vasumān is recorded as the ninth;
these are proclaimed as the nine sons of Vaivasvata Manu.
Indeed, these have been recounted by me, along with this seventh interval (Manvantara).
Thus, O twice-born ones, this second quarter has indeed been recounted by me in detail and in its proper sequence; what more shall I describe? (31)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Vaivasvata Creation," in the *Śrī Mahāpurāṇa* spoken by Vāyu. [End of] the Introductory Section (*Upodghātapāda*).
The Sages said:
Having heard the second quarter recited by the wise Sūta, Śaunaka then asked for the third quarter. ||1||
"This second quarter has been traversed by you through its connection;
now proclaim the third quarter in detail, along with its introductory context.

Being thus addressed, Sūta spoke with a delighted inner soul: 2. "This second quarter has been traversed by you through its connection; now proclaim the third quarter in detail, along with its introductory context. Being thus addressed, Sūta spoke with a delighted inner soul.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, I shall proclaim the third chapter in detail, along with its introductory context; understand from me as I speak this quarter [of the teaching] concerning the origin of suffering. (3)
O twice-born ones, hear in detail and in proper sequence this account of the creation of the high-souled Manu Vaivasvata, the present one.
He was already reckoned [as such] by seventy-one cycles of four yugas,
together with the hosts of gods, the sages, and the dānavas.
Together with the Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and likewise the hosts of Rākṣasas and Bhūtas,
as well as humans, animals, birds, and even the stationary beings.
Having paid homage to Vivasvat, I shall describe in great detail, through various narratives, the creation beginning with Manu and ending with the future, specifically the Vaivasvata creation.
In the first Manvantara, those creations that had passed away and those that were setting in motion;
those seven great sages who existed previously in the Svāyambhuva interval;
and when the Cākṣuṣa interval had passed and the Vaivasvata interval had arrived once again— ||8||
And due to the curse of Maheśvara, there was the manifestation of the high-souled Dakṣa and the sages of great power, such as Bhṛgu and others. 9.
Furthermore, those seven sages were born as the seven mind-born [sons]; they were indeed appointed by Svayambhū himself to the status of sons.
By those high-souled beings who were born as the progenitors of the human race,
creation was set in motion again, just as before and in due order.
I shall describe the progeny of those whose actions are purified by knowledge,
according to their sequence and in proper order, through both concise and detailed treatments.
By those born of their lineage, this world of moving and non-moving beings was filled once again; that creation was adorned with planets and constellations. (13)
Having heard these words of his, a doubt arose among the sages.
Then, filled with that doubt, those sages of celebrated vows, having honored Sūta for the sake of resolving their uncertainty, questioned him. (14)
The sages said:
"How were the seven sages first born as the seven mind-born ones, and how were they conceived as sons? Tell us that, O best of beings.

Thereupon, the highly effulgent Sūta, the knower of the Purāṇas, spoke these auspicious words: [Note: The provided text contains only the question and the introduction to the answer; the actual narrative follows in the subsequent verses.]
How did the seven sages who were perfected during the Svāyambhuva interval come to attain it again upon reaching the Vaivasvata Manvantara? (16)
For, due to the curse of existence, their consciousness was impaired and they did not attain that austerity at that time;
having been reborn in the world of men, they are now once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin). ||17||
Then all those great seers in Janaloka spoke to one another;
indeed, those illustrious ones spoke thus while the sacrifice of Varuṇa was being performed.
"We shall all be born during the interval of Manu Cākṣuṣa; we are all the sons of Pitāmaha. Therefore, it will be for our welfare. (19)
In the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, those seven were cursed by Bhava for a certain purpose;
they indeed returned to birth from Janaloka and ascended to heaven.

We have heard that at the great sacrifice of the Lord Varuṇa, while he was assuming a body and offering his own pure essence into the fire out of a desire for progeny, the Ṛṣis were first born; this is said to be the second [creation]. (21)
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Atri, and Vasiṣṭha— these eight are the sons of Brahmā.
Likewise, at his extensive sacrifice, all the gods assembled,
as did all the constituent parts of the sacrifice and the Vaṣaṭ-call personified.
And the Sāman and Yajus mantras by the thousands appeared there in embodied form, as did the Ṛgveda, adorned with the Pada and Krama recitations.
And the Yajurveda stood there, rich in its meters, radiant with the syllable Oṃ upon its face,
endowed with hymns, Brāhmaṇas, and mantras, and intent upon the purpose of sacrifice.
And the Sāmaveda, rich in meters and preceded by all that is to be sung, was gathered together with the Gandharvas, such as Viśvāvasu and others. ||26||
The Veda, namely the Brahman, accompanied by terrible rites of sorcery (kṛtyā-vidhi) and the applications of the Praty-aṅgirasa mantras, became the head of his second body. (27)
The characteristics, the vowels, the stobhas, the etymological explanations, and the divisions of the vowels; the basis, the *vaṣaṭ*-call, as well as suppression and extension. (28)
Dīptā, Dīpti, and the goddess Ilā; the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the lords of the quarters; the daughters of the gods, their wives, and likewise the Mothers. (29)
These very forms of longevity are present on every side in the mouth of the sacrificing god; they are Varuṇa’s embodied manifestations, bearing his own form and essence. (2.4.30)
But when the Self-Existent One saw them, his semen fell upon the earth;
this was due to the disposition of the Brahman-sage who had come into being, and there is no doubt regarding the divine ordinance. (31)
Having prepared it and taken hold of it with the two *sruk* ladles and the *sruva* spoon,
the Grandfather offered oblations of clarified butter with the appropriate mantras.
Then that Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) produced the multitude of beings;
from his splendor arose the luminous [nature] in the worlds during the sacrifice,
as well as the pervasiveness of non-existence through darkness (tamas), and likewise goodness (sattva) and passion (rajas).
From the luminous energy (tejas) endowed with qualities, darkness (tamas) is eternally situated in space;
and from that darkness becoming luminous energy, all beings were born.
When no sons born of his own actions were produced at that time,
he took his own semen and offered it as an oblation into the vessel of clarified butter.
Then, when that oblation of clarified butter was offered, seven great sages appeared, blazing and endowed with bodies possessed of the qualities of their progeny.
When the semen was offered once into the fire, the Sage emerged from the flame.
Seeing him emerge by piercing through the flame, Hiraṇyagarbha said, "You are Bhṛgu"; because of that, he indeed became Bhṛgu. (37)
Having seen him thus born, Mahādeva spoke to the Brāhmaṇa: "O Lord, this one has been born for me who am consecrated and desirous of a son;
therefore, O divine Bhṛgu, let him be my son. (38)
Having been thus authorized by the Self-born One with the words "So be it," Mahādeva likewise adopted Bhṛgu as his son;
therefore, the Bhṛgus are the offspring of Varuṇa, and he, the Lord, became their progenitor.
Then the Lord cast his second seed into the embers;
from those embers, O Aṅgiras, the limbs were joined together, and thus he became Aṅgiras.
Seeing that manifestation of his, Vahni said to Brahmā:
"I am the depositor of seed for you alone; let this second one be mine. (41)
"Let it be so," said Brahmā to that lord of the assembly;
therefore, we have heard that the Aṅgirases also belong to Agni.
Furthermore, when the six rites were offered by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, into Śukra,
the sacred tradition (śruti) states that six Brahmās were born there.
Marīci was the first among them; from Marīci he arose, and in that sacrifice a son was born, and because of that, he is indeed called Kratu.
Because he was "I am third" (ahaṃ tṛtīya), he is therefore celebrated as Atri;
and because he was produced from sharp hair (keśa), he is remembered as Pulastya.
Because he was produced from long hair (keśa), he is therefore remembered as Pulaha;
born from the midst of the Vasus, he is Vasumān, the refuge of the earth (vasudhā). 46.
He is called Vasiṣṭha by the knowers of reality, the exponents of Brahman. Thus, these six great sages are the mind-born sons of Brahmā. ||47||
These sons of Brahmā, who cause the continuity of the world and by whom these subjects have been increased, are recited as the "Prajāpatis" (Lords of Creatures).
Others known as Pitṛs were produced by these very great seers; they are the groups of seers renowned throughout the seven worlds. ||49||
The Mārīcas, the Bhārgavas, and likewise the others, the Aṅgirasas;
the Paulastyas, the Paulahas, and the renowned Vāsiṣṭhas;
and the Ātreyas—these are declared to be the world-renowned groups of the Pitṛs. 2.4.50.
In brief, my dear, these three qualities were already renowned as the unprecedented, the luminous, and the radiant. (51)
Of them, the god Yama is the king; listen attentively to those other lords of creatures who have had their sins ordained by the Yamās. (52)
Kardama, Kaśyapa, Śeṣa, Vikrānta, and likewise Suśravas;
Bahuputra, Kumāra, Vivasvat, and he who is Śuciśravas. (53)
Pracetas, Ariṣṭanemi, Bahula, Prajāpati, and many other such lords of creatures as well. (54)
From the heaps of kusha grass were born the Valakhilyas, supreme rishis;
they became as swift as thought, all-pervading, and sovereign over the entire earth.
Born from Bhasmavyapohinī, the hosts of Vaikhānasa sages, esteemed by the assembly of Brahman-sages,
were devoted to austerity and sacred learning.
And from his two nostrils were born the Aśvins, equal in beauty to him;
they knew themselves to be born from the dust of the Imperishable, stainless and produced from the eyes. 4.57
The lords of creatures were born from his vital channels as the eldest;
likewise, the seers were born from the pores of his skin, arising from the sweat and impurities.
For the months, the exudations, the junctions of the fortnights, and those years which are the days and nights are indeed terrible; so too is the ancestral light, which is dreadful. (59)
They say that the fierce (raudra) is red; red is known as gold.
That should be understood as friendly (maitra), and smoke is known as the sacrificial animals (paśu).
Those who were his flames became the Rudras, and likewise the Ādityas;
from the glowing coals there arose the celestial and human luminaries.
"Brahmā is the beginning of this world, born from Brahmā;
they say that there he grants all desires," saying this, they presented a maiden there.
There Brahmā, the preceptor of the gods, was highly pleased by the deities:
"These lords of creatures shall indeed procreate all beings."
All the lords of creatures and all the ascetics shall,
by his grace, sustain these worlds and these ritual activities.
He caused the pair to increase, which augmented your splendor;
likewise, all the gods who were knowers of the Vedas and all the royal sages [did so].
All are devoted to the Vedic mantras, born from the qualities of Prajāpati;
they are the infinite Brahman, truth, and the supreme austerity on earth.
For all of us and these others, O Lord, are indeed your own offspring;
so too are Brahmā, the Brahmins, and the worlds, both moving and unmoving.
Beginning with Marīci, the gods together with the sages, having reflected upon their offspring here, said: "We desire offspring. (68)
In that sacrifice, the highly fortunate gods, together with the sages, were born of this lineage; they were the presiding deities of the respective positions and times.
They would not establish these creatures in that very same form;
rather, they would establish these creatures according to the beginning and the end of the Yugas.
Then the Teacher of the World spoke, without further deliberation:
"Thus, having reached this conclusion, these gods were created by me; there is no doubt.
Furthermore, these great seers (maharṣis) are born from your own lineage. (71)
Of them, I shall proclaim the lineage of the first great-souled Bhṛgu,
that of the primordial Prajāpati, in detail and in proper sequence.
The wife of Bhṛgu was born of incomparable and most excellent lineage;
she was the auspicious daughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu, renowned by the name Divyā,
and also the daughter of Puloman, Paulomī, a woman of beautiful complexion.
The divine wife of Bhṛgu gave birth to Kāvya, the best among those who know the Vedas,
Śukra, the son of Kavi, the preceptor of the gods and asuras, and a planet.
He was known as Śukra and Uśanas, and was also remembered by the name Kāvya.
The illustrious Aṅgī, the mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs who drink Soma,
became the wife of Śukra and gave birth to four sons.
Endowed with Brahmanic splendor, he was therefore the foremost among the knowers of Brahman;
moreover, four sons were born to Śukra by that very same woman.
Tvaṣṭṛ and Varūtrī—these two, as well as both Śaṇḍa and Marka—were like the suns in appearance, equal to Brahmā by virtue of their power. ||77||
Rañjana, Pṛthuraśmi, the learned Bṛhadgirā, and Varūtriṇa—these were indeed the sons of [Varuṇa], most devoted to Brahman and performers of sacrifices for the gods. ||78||
They approached Manu and incited him to destroy the dharma of sacrifice;
seeing that dharma being cast aside, Indra spoke to Manu.
"However, by these very means I shall surely bring you to the performance of the sacrifice.
Having heard those words of Indra, he departed from that place.
When they had vanished, Indra, having released both Dharmapatnī and Cetanā from his grasp,
then pursued her.
Then, seeing those wicked ones who were striving and exerting themselves for the destruction of Indra as they arrived there once more,
Indra slept upon the southern altar of the God of Gods.
As they were being devoured there by the jackals,
their heads fell down and subsequently became date-palms.
Thus, in former times, the sons of Vṛṣaparvan were slain by Indra;
and Devayānī, the daughter of Śukra, was born of Yajñā.
The great Triśiras Viśvarūpa was the son of Tvaṣṭṛ;
and the younger brother of Viśvarūpa was Viśvakarmā, who is remembered as Yama. (85)
Twelve divine sons were born to Bhṛgu as the Bhṛgus;
the lord Kāvya likewise begot all of them upon the goddess.
Bhuvana, Bhāvana, and another, Anyāyatas; Kratuśravas, Mūrdhan, Vyajaya, and he who is Vyaśruṣas; Prasava and Aja—these are remembered as the twelve Adhipatis. ||87||
Thus, these twelve Bhṛgu gods are remembered as performers of sacrifice.
Paulomī gave birth to a son who was most devoted to Brahman, self-controlled, and all-pervading.
In the eighth month, he was afflicted by a cruel fetal malady;
then, from Cyavana came Cyavāna, and from Pracetas came Pracetasa. From the wrath of Cyavana, the Unborn One (Aja) traversed the path of men.
And Bhārgava begot two sons upon Sukanyā:
the self-possessed Dadhīca; both of them were highly esteemed by the virtuous.
Sārasvata was born from Dadhīca through Sarasvatī;
his wife was the highly fortunate Ruci, the daughter of Nahuṣa, who was self-possessed.
From his thighs was born the highly illustrious seer Aurva, having split open his thighs;
and there was also Ṛcīka, whose splendor was like a blazing fire.
Jamadagni was born to Ṛcīka from Satyavatī;
and likewise, [he was born] from Bhṛgu during the succession of Ruci, as well as from Rudra and Viṣṇu.
From the Vaiṣṇava fire, Jamadagni was born;
and from Jamadagni, Reṇukā gave birth to Rāma, who possessed immeasurable splendor, whose prowess was equal to that of Indra, and who was composed of both Brahmanical and Kṣatriya natures. (94)
Aurva had a hundred sons, including Jamadagni;
from among them, there were thousands of descendants of Bhṛgu born of one another.

Among the other Ṛṣis, many Bhārgavas are indeed recorded as being outsiders (bāhya). Vatsa, Viśva, Aśviṣeṇa, Pāṇḍa, Pathya, and Śaunaka—these seven are to be known as the Bhārgava clans according to their lineages (gotra). ||96||
Listen to the lineage of the wise Aṅgiras, the son of Agni, in whose family were born the Bhāradvājas and the Gautamas;
and from whom arose the principal Aṅgirasas, the gods, radiant and of great power. (97)
Surūpā, Mārīcī, Kārddamī, Svarāṭ, Pathyā, and the maiden Mānavī—these six were the wives of Atharvan.
These were the wives of Aṅgiras; among them, I shall describe the progeny.
The heirs of Atharvan were born from them as upholders of their lineage;
they were produced through the great ascetic power of those whose selves were purified by austerity. 99.
Bṛhaspati begot Svarāṭ upon Surūpā; and Gautama begot Avandhya, Vāmadeva, Utathya, and Uśija.
Dhiṣṇu was the son of Pathyā, and Saṃvarta was her mind-born son;
likewise, Vicitta, Ayasya, and Śaradvat were the sons born of Utathya.
Aśija, Dīrghatamas, Bṛhaduktha born of Vāmadeva,
Dhiṣṇu, and the sons of Sudhanvan— namely Ṛṣabha and the others—
are known as the Ratha-kāras (Chariot-makers) among the gods and sages who are celebrated. 4.102.
From Bṛhaspati was born Bharadvāja, who was renowned and possessed of great fame. ||103||
From Aṅgiras came Saṃvarta; now hear of the divine Aṅgirases.
Those gods who were younger than Bṛhaspati are indeed remembered as the divine Aṅgirases. (104)
The ten sons of Aurasa-Aṅgiras were born of Surūpā: Audārya, Āyu, Danu, Dakṣa, Darbha, Prāṇa, as well as Haviṣmān, Haviṣṇu, Kratu, and Satya. (105)
Ayāsya, Utathya, Vāmadeva, and Uśija;
the Bhāradvājas, Śāṅkṛtikas, Gārgyas, Kāṇvas, and Rathītaras. (106)
The Mudgalas, Viṣṇuvṛddhas, Haritas, Vāyavas, as well as the Bhākṣas, Bharadvājas, Ārṣabhas, and Kimbhayas; ||107||
These fifteen branches of the Aṅgirasas are indeed to be known;
among the other sages, many external Aṅgirasas are recorded. ||108||
I shall describe the lineage of Mārīca, a line of supreme beings, in whose progeny the entire world— both the stationary and the moving— was born.
Marīci desired the waters, meditating upon them with the wish for progeny:
"May there be a son endowed with all virtues, possessed of offspring, radiant, and worthy of praise; may the Lord be conceived in mind within that which is most excellent. 2.4.110.
Then the Lord summoned all the waters and settled within them;
having fixed his self within them, that one Lord brought forth [the world].
The Prajāpati Ariṣṭanemi begot a son named Apratima,
and Vadhūveśa begot a son, Marīci, who was radiant like the sun.
For, desiring a son, he remained in the water meditating upon the words of the virtuous for seven thousand years; thereafter, he became peerless.
Kaśyapa is the knower of Savitṛ; therefore, he is equal to Brahmā.
In all the Manvantaras, he is born as a portion of the Brahman.
When Dakṣa spoke thus regarding the maiden, the subjects became enraged; they then drank the *kaśya*, which is here called *madya* (liquor). 115.
Indeed, *hā* is to be understood as the singular [vowel], while *kaśya* is said to belong to Brahmā.
The wise have recorded that *kaśya* means wine; and because he was born from Kaśyapa, he is called Kaśyapa. (116)
Because he uttered a cruel word against the speech of Vāc, Kaśyapa became angry and cursed Dakṣa; by that act, he [Dakṣa] came to be as such.

And because he was so addressed by Kaśyapa, who had been commanded by the Supreme Brahmā, Dakṣa bestowed those maidens upon Kaśyapa; they were all exponents of the Veda, and all of them were mothers of the world. (118)
He who knows this meritorious creation of the Ṛṣis belonging to Varuṇa becomes long-lived, virtuous, and pure, and attains unsurpassed happiness;
by retaining it in memory and by hearing it, he is liberated from all sins. ||119||
Then all the sages spoke again to Romaharṣaṇa:
"When the creation of subjects by Cākṣuṣa had indeed ceased during the sixth [manvantara],
this creation of Vaivasvata Manu has now commenced."
Sūta said:
Commanded by the Self-born One himself to "create progeny," Dakṣa created all beings, both moving and stationary,
during this present Vaivasvata Manvantara.
Then Dakṣa proceeded to create the fourfold progeny:
those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from a sprout, and likewise those born from sweat. 122.
Having performed severe and great penance for ten thousand years,
he was especially endowed with the powers of yoga, such as *aṇimā* and the others.
The illustrious one divided himself into humans, serpents, and rākṣasas;
and into gods, asuras, and gandharvas— beings of divine constitution—
who were lords equal to himself in form, wealth, and splendor.
In the same way, being delighted and desiring to create various offspring, he [created] other beings of mental origin that were moving and stable. (125)
The sages, gods, along with the gandharvas; humans, serpents, and rākṣasas; as well as yakṣas, bhūtas, piśācas, birds, domestic animals, and wild beasts. ||126||
When those creatures created by his mind did not multiply,
they were looked upon with displeasure by the wise Lord Mahādeva.
And with a mind intent on sexual union, desiring to create various offspring,
he took Asiknī, the daughter of the patriarch Vīraṇa, as his wife.
She was born endowed with great ascetic power, the sustainer of the worlds, by whom this entire universe—both the stationary and the moving—is upheld. (129)
In this regard, they cite these two verses concerning Prācetasa:
"When Dakṣa was taking as his wife Asiknī, the supreme Vīriṇī... (2.4.130).
The skillful Lord, creating millions of wells filled with ghee along with their presiding deities upon the rivers and mountains, followed behind them.
Seeing him, the sages declared: "The subjects shall indeed be established here;
this is the first [creation], while the second belongs to Dakṣa, the Lord of Progeny. (132)
Thus he proceeded at the proper time toward the million wells where Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, had carried away Asiknī, the daughter of Virocana.
Then the lord Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, endowed with immeasurable splendor, begot a thousand sons upon Vairiṇī, the daughter of Aśvini.

Seeing them desiring to increase the population, the great-splendored celestial sage Nārada, the son of Brahmā who speaks so pleasantly, spoke these words for their destruction and for his own curse: tāṃstu dṛṣṭvā mahātejāḥ sa vivarddhayiṣūn prajāḥ | devarṣiḥ priyasaṃvādo nārado brahmaṇaḥ sutaḥ || nāśāya vacanaṃ teṣāṃ śāpāyaivātmano'bravīt ||135||
He who is indeed called the artificial Brahmin Kaśyapa is a brahmarṣi who, out of fear of Dakṣa’s curse, became so through that very action.
Then Parameṣṭhin, who was born as the mind-born son of Kaśyapa, was born again here from Kaśyapa out of fear of Dakṣa’s curse.
Therefore, he then became the second mind-born son of Kaśyapa;
for that Nārada had previously arisen from Parameṣṭhin.
By him those sons of Dakṣa, renowned as the Haryaśvas, were all destroyed for the sake of censure and brought to ruin; of this there is no doubt. (139)
Then, as he was raising [his weapon] for the destruction [of Dakṣa], the powerful and enraged lord,
having placed the Brahman-sages at his head, was entreated by Parameṣṭhin.
Then Dakṣa was directed by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) with the intention:
"Let Nārada be born as my son through your daughter. (141)
Then Dakṣa gave his beloved daughter to Parameṣṭhin;
from him was born Nārada, the sage who was once again tranquil through fear.
Having heard that, those brahmins, their curiosity aroused once more, questioned Sūta, the best of speakers and seer of the true meaning of reality. (143)
The sages said:
How were those sons, the offspring of Prajāpati and the progeny born of Pracetas, destroyed by the high-souled Nārada? 144.
Having heard those truthful words, which were auspicious and born of a desire for knowledge, he spoke sweet speech endowed with all virtues to them. (145)
And the sons of Dakṣa, the Haryaśvas, being desirous of increasing their progeny, assembled together; those of great prowess were addressed by Nārada.
"You are indeed childish and lacking in strength; you do not know the surface of the earth, nor its end, nor what is above or below. How then will you create living beings? (147)
What is the measure of the earth, and likewise what things are to be created?
Without knowing this, how will you create otherwise?
Whether it be small or great, a fault is seen in that case. (148)
Having heard those words, they departed in all directions;
but upon encountering the wind, they indeed met with defeat.
"Even now they do not cease, wandering driven by the wind;
thus, having reached the path of the wind, those great sages continue to wander. When his own sons had perished, Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas,"
The Lord begot a thousand sons upon Vairiṇī alone.
Then those Śabalāśvas, desiring to increase their progeny,
were made to hear once again the words previously spoken there by Nārada.
Having heard those words, all those immensely powerful princes said to one another, "The great seer has spoken correctly;
we must indeed follow the path of our brothers, there is no doubt about this. (153)
"Having ascertained the extent of the earth, we shall create offspring for our own happiness.
They too set out in every direction along that very path;
even today they have not returned, like rivers flowing into the oceans. (154)
From that time on, a brother indeed becomes intent on searching for his brother; he sets out and perishes in that manner. Therefore, a wise man should not do such a thing. 155.
When the dappled horses had vanished, the powerful Dakṣa became enraged and said, "Go to destruction, Nārada! You shall dwell in a womb! (156)
Likewise, it is said that in ancient times, when those great-souled ones had perished,
Dakṣa produced sixty daughters, renowned as the Vairiṇīs.
Then the lord Kaśyapa accepted them for the sake of wives, as did Dharma, the blessed Soma, and likewise other great seers. ||158||
He who knows this entire creation of Dakṣa according to its true nature becomes long-lived, famous, and prosperous, and moreover, he gains offspring. ||159||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Genealogy of the Prajāpatis," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
The sages said:
Tell me here in detail the origin of the gods, the Dānavas, and the Daityas in every respect during this Vaivasvata interval.
Sūta said:
First, I shall declare the nature of Dharma; listen to it:
Arundhatī, Vasu, Yāmī, Lambā, Bhānu, and Marutvatī. (2)
Saṅkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and likewise Viśvā—
Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave these ten as wives to Dharma.

The Sādhyas begot twelve sons of Dharma, known as the Sādhyas—highly fortunate beings born of the Vedic meters and partakers of the sacrifice. Those who know the gods describe them as gods superior even to the [other] gods. ||4||
Indeed, the Jaya deities were created from the mouth of Brahmā out of a desire for progeny;
they are all remembered here as being composed of mantras throughout the Manvantaras.
The New Moon sacrifice and the Full Moon sacrifice, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara [Sāmans], as well as perception and discernment, intention and action. ||6||
The knower and the known, as well as the mind and the sacrifice—
these are recorded as their names, which are celebrated among the Jayas.
By the curse of Brahmā, they were born again; they were the Jitas in the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara], the Tuṣitas in the Svārociṣa, and the Satyas again in the Uttama.
In the interval of Raivata, the Tāmasas were known as the Vaikuṇṭhas; and in the Cākṣuṣa period, the Sādhyas were born as gods known by the name Chandajas.
The highly fortunate sons of Dharma, who are the twelve gods to be propitiated,
were formerly known as the Anusūyas during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu.
In the past Svārociṣa Manvantara, those gods of great power who were known as the Tuṣitas spoke thus to one another during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara.

When only a small portion of that [time] remained, the highly fortunate Tuṣita gods indeed said to one another: "By entering the Sādhyas, we shall indeed exist during the Manvantara; that will be for our welfare. (12)
Having spoken thus, they all [received] from that Svāyambhuva Manu, during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu, those twelve dharmas which had arisen from him once again.
Indeed, Nara and Nārāyaṇa were born there once again;
they were those two who had previously been the gods Tuṣita during the Svārociṣa Manvantara—namely Vipaścit and Indra, as well as Satya and Hari. (14)
Regarding the Tuṣita gods, these names will be declared for their attainment:
Mano, Anumantṛ, Prāṇa, Nara, and the heroic Yāna. (15)
Citti, Hayu, Naya, Haṃsa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa, Prabhava, and Vibhu—these twelve Sādhyas were born. (16)
In the previous Svāyambhuva Manvantara, and then again in the Svārociṣa Manvantara, those were the names of the Tuṣitas; learn them once more.
Prāṇa, apāna, udāna, samāna, and vyāna;
likewise, sight, hearing, smell, touch, intellect, and mind. ||18||
Prāṇa, apāna, udāna, samāna, and vyāna—these were indeed known as the names of the Tuṣitas in former times. (19)
The Vasus are known as the sons of Vasu and are recorded as the younger brothers of the Sādhyas.
Dharma, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anala, Anila,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
The son of Dhara was Draviṇa, as well as Hutahavyavaha;
the son of Dhruva was named Bhava, who is Time (Kāla), the destroyer of the worlds. ||21||
The lord Varcas, son of Soma, and Budha, the awakener of the planets, were both born under Rohiṇī; they are renowned throughout the three worlds. (22)
The three sons of Candra were Dhārā, Ūrmi, and Kalila; and the sons of Āpa were Vaitaṇḍya, Śama, and likewise Śānta.
Skanda and Sanatkumāra were born from a portion of that splendor;
however, Agni’s son Kumāra was born within a thicket of Śara reeds. To him were born as younger brothers Śākha, Viśākha, and Naigameya.
Anila’s wife was Śivā, and her son was Manojava;
Avijñātagati was the other—these were the two sons of Anila.
The wise one knew Pratyūṣa’s son to be the sage named Devala. Devala also had two sons who were patient and wise.
The sister of Bṛhaspati, an excellent woman who observes celibacy,
has attained perfection through yoga and wanders through the entire world unattached.
The wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus,
was she from whom Viśvakarman was born, the son who is the lord of artisans.
He is the creator of all crafts and the architect of the thirty gods; he is the maker and the one who causes all ornaments to be made.
He constructs the celestial chariots for all the deities,
and human artisans subsist upon his crafts.
The Viśvedevas were born from Viśvā; they are renowned as ten:
Kratu, Dakṣa, Śrava, Satya, Kāla, Kāma, and Dhuni. (31)
Kuru, Vān, Prabhava, and Rocamāna—these ten are remembered as the sons of Dharma; these auspicious ones were born of Viśvā. (32)
From Marutvatī, the Marutvats were born; from Bhānu, the Bhānus are recorded as being born; and from Muhūrtā, the Muhūrtas were born. Lambā gave birth to Ghoṣa.
From Saṅkalpā was born Vidvān and Saṅkalpa himself;
and from Jāmī were born the Nāgavīthīs, which are situated upon the three paths.
The entire domain of Pṛthivī was born from Arundhatī.
This is declared to be the eternal creation of the wise Dharma. (35)
O you of virtuous vows, I shall declare by name the Muhūrtas and the Tithis along with their lords; listen as I speak. (36)
The division of day and night, the lunar mansions in brief, the muhūrtas, all the stars, and likewise those who know the day and night [are described]. (37)
For one who desires all the seasons through the specific movements of the sun, six hundred and sixty kalās of day and night are traditionally taught.
Therefore, those who know the Vedas desire this lunar day during the festival days;
it should be employed at all times without distinction for the offering to the ancestors.
Raudra, Sārva, Maitra, Piṇḍyavāsava, Āpya, Vaiśvadeva, and Brāhma, which is situated at midday. (2.5.40)
Likewise, the portions belonging to Prajāpati, Indra, Nīrṛti, Varuṇa, and Aryaman are also dependent upon the days. ||41||
These muhūrtas of the day, fashioned by the Maker of Day,
are to be understood according to their measure through the remainder of the shadow of the gnomon.
Aja, as well as Ahibudhnya and Pūṣan, have Yama as their presiding deity;
they should also be known as belonging to Agni and likewise to Prajāpati. ||43||
The Brahma, Saumya, Āditya, Bārhaspatya, Vaiṣṇava, Sāvitra, Tvaṣṭra, and Vāyavya—this is the summary. ||44||
There are fifteen muhūrtas in a single night, as stated in the sequence;
these are to be known as the muhūrtas of the moon’s movement at its rising, consisting of one-quarter nālikās.
These muhūrtas, which exist within the divisions of time, are remembered as deities. (45)
For all the grahas, exactly three locations have been prescribed:
the southern, the northern, and the middle; one should know them in their proper order.
The *jāradgava* position is in the center, while *airāvata* is in the north;
*vaiśvānara* is specified here as being in the south according to the true principle.

Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, and Bharaṇī (Yāmyā) are known as the Nāga path; Puṣya, Āśleṣā, and Punarvasū are considered the Airāvata path. These three paths are indeed called the Northern Course (Uttara-mārga). ||48||
The two Phālgunīs, Pūrvaphālgunī and Uttaraphālgunī, as well as Maghā, are known as Āryamī;
likewise, Hasta, Citrā, and Svātī are designated as Govīthī. 49.
Jyeṣṭhā, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā are known as the Jāradgavī path;
these three paths are said to be in the middle course. Mūla and the two Āṣāḍhas are designated as the Ajavīthī.
Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Gārgī, and likewise Śatabhiṣak. ||51||
Vaiśvānarī and Revatī are proclaimed [to be in] Bhādrapada;
these three are remembered as the paths (vīthīs) on the southern course by the wise.
Dakṣa gave those twenty-seven maidens to Soma;
they are all known by the names of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) and are celebrated in the science of astronomy.
Their offspring were radiant with immeasurable splendor.
Then Kaśyapa accepted the remaining daughters;
these fourteen illustrious ones were all mothers of the world. (54)
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Ariṣṭā, Surasā, as well as Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, Irā,
Kadrū, and Muni— O knower of dharma, learn now of their offspring. (55)
When the Cāriṣṇava interval had passed, those twelve who were the leaders became known by the name Vaikuṇṭhas during the Cākṣuṣa interval.
When this interval of Vaivasvata had indeed arrived,
those who had propitiated Aditi gathered together and spoke to one another.
Having indeed entered this very Aditi of great fortune,
during this Vaivasvata interval, by means of half of his mind through yoga— (58)
"Let us go to become her sons; that will be for our welfare. By being born of Aditi, we shall attain the status of Ādityas. (59)
Having spoken thus, all those twelve Ādityas were born again from Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu;
indeed, Śatakratu and Viṣṇu were born once more.
For in this Vaivasvata interval, the two deities Nara and Nārāyaṇa [appeared].
For even for those gods, death and birth are said to occur,
just as in this world both the rising and the setting of the sun take place;
so it is for Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, and the high-souled Bhava.

Because they were capable in the supreme revealed tradition characterized by sound and the rest, as well as in the eightfold [attainment] beginning with *aṇiman*, therefore those gods became knowers. (63)
Thus, this passion for the field of sense-objects is recorded as the cause of rebirth.
By the curse of Brahmā, the Jayas, born during the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara], were defeated.
In the Svārociṣa [Manvantara], they were the Tuṣitas; in the Uttama, the Satyas;
in the Tāmasa, the gods were born as the Haris; and in the Ariṣṭa, as the Vaikuṇṭhas. In the Cākṣuṣa, they were the Sādhyas, and in the present [Manvantara], they are the Ādityas.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, Bhaga, Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is recorded as the tenth. ||66||
Then Tvaṣṭṛ, then Viṣṇu, the non-lowest, born of the non-lowest;
these are remembered as the twelve Ādityas, the sons of Kaśyapa. ||67||
From Kaśyapa, Surabhī gave birth to the eleven Rudras;
she, being purified by asceticism, did so through the grace of Mahādeva. (68)
Aṅgāraka, as well as Sarpa, Nirṛti, Sadasaspati, Ajaikapāt, Ahirbudhnya, Ūrdhvaketu, and likewise Jvara; ||69||
Bhuvana, Īśvara, Mṛtyu, and the renowned Kapāla—
these eleven gods, the Rudras who are lords of the three worlds,
Surabhi gave birth to them through that great austerity.
Then she gave birth to two other daughters, Surabhi, Rohiṇī—who was as radiant as Rudra—and the illustrious Gāndhārī. (71)
Under Rohiṇī were born four daughters renowned throughout the world:
Surūpā, Haṃsakīlā, Bhadrā, and Kāmadughā.
Kāmadughā, moreover, gave birth to two sons by Surūpā.
O King, Haṃsakīla begot the Ṛṣis from Bhadrā;
moreover, the highly fortunate Gandharvas were the sons of Vājina. (73)
Then Uccaiḥśravas was born; those sky-faring horses were as swift as thought.
White, hawk-colored, tawny, dappled, green, and pale-white—those horses, the offspring of Gandharvas, were the mounts for the Rudras and the gods.
Furthermore, from Surabhi was born the illustrious one, radiant with a splendor like the moon;
he was garlanded, humped, resplendent, and born from the abode of nectar.
With Surabhi’s consent, that banner of Maheśvara was bestowed upon him.
Thus these sons of Kaśyapa are proclaimed as the Rudras and Ādityas; the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and likewise the Vasus are remembered as the sons of Dharma.
The offspring of the wives of Ariṣṭanemi were sixteen here;
the four Vidyuts are recorded as the progeny of the learned Bahuputra.
Born of Pratyaṅgirasa, they were the preeminent Ṛks, honored by the Brahman-sages.
The divine weapons are said to belong to the celestial sage Kṛśāśva;
indeed, these are born once again at the end of a thousand yugas.
All the hosts of gods, the thirty-three classes of Brahmins born of the Vedas—for these gods as well, cessation and origination are said to occur. (79)
Just as both the rising and setting of the sun occur in this world,
so do these hosts of gods come into being age after age.
The sages said:
The Sādhyas, the Vasus, the Viśvedevas, and likewise the Rudras and Ādityas, are renowned for their noble birth, their powers, and their deeds. (81)
We wish to know the distinction between Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, and the high-souled Bhava, and which among them is superior to whom.
He from whom one originates, he in whom one is established, and among them, he who is indeed the eldest, the middlemost, and the youngest. (83)

Tell us all this—who among them was the preeminent one, and who among them was subordinate; who was great by virtue of his deeds, his lineage, and his power—for you indeed know each thing as it truly is. (84)
Sūta said:
In this regard, I shall describe to you that which is remembered within the inner and outer limits of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; listen to me as I speak.
These bodies of the Self-born One are declared to be rajasic, tamasic, and sattvic; they appear from time to time as they arise. (86)
O best of the twice-born, it is impossible to describe the interval between these [states], because they are bound by the increase of qualities and because they are linked by a twofold grace. (87)
O twice-born ones, I shall explain here, according to my ability, the occurrence and cessation, as well as the increase of the qualities of the subtle bodies; listen to that. 88.
One among them, being of the nature of *rajas*, produces all creatures everywhere; another, abiding in the ocean and being of the nature of *sattva*, bestows grace;
and one, being of the nature of *tamas*, casts down and devours the creatures at the time of destruction. ||89||
When Brahmā arises as one overwhelmed by passion (rajas),
then his sattvic designation as "Puruṣa" ceases.
When he becomes the self of time due to the excess of tamas,
then that [state] of his called Brahman ceases, being characterized by rajas.
But when the person becomes the Lord due to the predominance of sattva, that state of his is indeed called "Time" (kāla), and it does not cease to exist. (92)
Gradually, for him who exists throughout the three worlds through all acts of favor and restraint, his form, name, and activity cease. (93)
When there is Brahman, then an interval is spoken of;
and when Puruṣa is Brahman, he is indeed not Puruṣa.
Just as a gem displays various colors within a crystal, due to its purity and by the power of its substrate, it takes on that color and is colored accordingly. (95)
Then, by virtue of its qualities, there is the spontaneous coloring of that [consciousness];
this is declared to be the illustration of both unity and diversity. (96)
Just as a single cloud, having become one, remains distinct in its form and color, so too does he [the Self] abide according to the influence of the qualities (guṇas). //97//
Through the destruction of his physical form, he becomes one, then two, and even three;
these three are Brahmā, Antaka (the Ender), and Puruṣa. ||98||
These three are said to belong to the one, the Self-born;
they are Brāhmī, Pauruṣī, and Antakārī—these are the three. 99.
Among these, that which is of the nature of *rajas* is his body that produces progeny;
that which is of the nature of *tamas*, called *kāla* (Time), brings about the destruction of progeny;
and that which is of the nature of *sattva*, known as *pauruṣī* (the personal aspect), is remembered as that which bestows grace.
From the portion of Brahmā’s *rājasa* nature, Marīci and Kaśyapa arose;
and from the portion of that which is *tāmasa* and brings about the end, Bhava was born.
That which is sattvic and that which is puruṣic is said to be its luster;
these three are remembered as the bodies of the Self-born (Svayambhū) throughout the three worlds.
For Time, which brings about various states for the sake of diverse purposes,
having created beings through its aspect as Brahmā and having sustained them through its aspect as Viṣṇu,
again devours those who were sustained by the Vaiṣṇava power through its own fierce (raudra) power. ||103||
The one self-existent Time, by means of its three aspects, indeed effects the three;
it creates, sustains, and likewise withdraws all beings.
Thus, these three bodies of the Self-Existent One have been described;
they are known as the Prajāpatyā, the Raudrī, and the Vaiṣṇavī. ||105||

In the Veda, the Dharmaśāstra, and the ancient [traditions], as well as among the heroes devoted to Sāṃkhya and Yoga who perceive both difference and unity, and by the seers who perceive reality and know the power of noble birth, that single body is traditionally taught. (106)
Whether in unity or in diversity, living beings here are distinct;
they possess divergent views, asserting "this is supreme" and "that is not. (107)
Some say that Brahmā is the cause, while others say it is Prajāpati; some declare Śiva to be the supreme, and others likewise Viṣṇu.
Bound by ignorance and attached with minds full of passion and the like, they hold these views. (108)
Having truly examined the reality, time, place, and the effects, as well as the cause—it is remembered that these deities here exist for various purposes. (109)
He who censures one among them censures all of them;
he who praises one indeed praises all of them.
That man who knows the One is called a knower of Brahman.
One who possesses discernment should always maintain freedom from hatred toward the deities;
for it is impossible to fully know the Lord as he abides in his sovereign power.
He who, though being a single self, becomes threefold and deludes all creatures—
people wander within the interval between these three.
Inquiring and examining, yet attached and with their minds deluded by forms, those who perceive through duality say, "This is supreme, this is not," (113).
These [powers] enter those Yātudhānas and Piśācas;
the Self-existent One (Svayambhū) abides as both unity and multiplicity. 114.
Deluding living beings with subtle bodies composed of the mere qualities (guṇas),
he who worships one among them, at that time worships all three.
Therefore, these three gods are established in uninterrupted succession.
Consequently, regarding their distinctness, their unity, their number, their arrival and departure, whether they are one or many—who is capable of knowing them? (116)
Because he creates, favors, and indeed devours those creatures throughout the three periods of time, being composed of the [three] qualities (guṇa), he is therefore called "One. (117)
The twice-born declare that single deity Nārāyaṇa to be Rudra, Brahmā, Indra, the world-protectors, the sages, and the Danus—him who is one, though spoken of in many ways. (118)
The body that belongs to Prajāpati and the body that belongs to Viṣṇu recur again and again throughout the Manvantaras and the Kalpas. ||119||
Learn now of those who are born equal to them in splendor, fame, intelligence, sacred learning, and strength. (2.5.120)
From the portion of the Rajasik Brahmā, Marīci and Kaśyapa came into being; from the portion of his Tamasik aspect, Rudra is said to be the soul of Time (Kālātmā);
and from the Sattvic aspect, Viṣṇu then appeared at the sacrifice as a portion of Puruṣa.
In the three times, these bodies of that Brahman are born from his portions;
having become Time, he, as Rudra, again withdraws all creatures.
And when the end of the eon has arrived, the sun with its seven rays becomes the Saṃvartaka sun and then burns the three worlds.
Viṣṇu bestows grace upon all beings during the transformation of names and forms;
at that final stage, he is the cause of their respective origins. (124)

That divine and all-pervading Lord, who was described as the manifestation of Brahmā’s body characterized by an abundance of *sattva*, was born here during the *Svāyambhuva* interval as a portion of that [body], produced from Manu through Ākūti at the very beginning. (5.125)
Then, when the Svārociṣa interval had arrived, that very deity was born again in Tuṣitā, having passed away from among the Tuṣitas.
In the Auttama and Cāntara Manvantaras, he is indeed known as Tuṣita;
furthermore, Hari is born as Vaśavartin among the Vaśavartins.
When Satyā was born, he became Satya along with the best of the gods who were true;
and when the interval of Tāmasa had arrived once again,
Hari himself indeed became [Satya] together with his wives and the monkeys.
Furthermore, during the Cāriṣṇu interval,
that god Hari was born again as Vaikuṇṭha, together with the Ābhūtarajasas;
and when the Cākṣuṣa interval arrived, that god became Vaikuṇṭha once more.
Dharma was Nārāyaṇa, who existed together with the Sādhyas and the gods;
yet that Nārāyaṇa, the Sādhya, [reappeared] when the Vaivasvata interval had arrived.
From Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, Viṣṇu was born of Aditi;
having conquered these worlds three times over with his strides, Viṣṇu is known as Urukrama.
That lord bestowed [the sovereignty] upon Indra and the gods;
thus these seven sons of his passed away during the seven past Manvantaras, by whom the subjects were protected. (132)
Therefore, all this was desired by him; let him be born here as Vāmana.
Thus he is indeed remembered as Viṣṇu, from the root *viś*, meaning "to enter. (133)
Thus, the identity, the distinction, and the superiority of these—the Great-Souled Vāmana and Brahmā—have been proclaimed. 134.

Those deities who are born here as partial incarnations of the gods are born with a splendor, intelligence, learning, and strength equal to theirs; indeed, they arise through the grace of those very gods.
Whatever being exists that is possessed of glory, splendor, or even power—
know each of those to have arisen from a portion of Viṣṇu’s radiant energy.
Some men maintain that he is thus born with a partial portion (aṃśa); others, however, say that he is born from one another's portions. (137)
Seeing them thus disputing, they indeed said to them:
"Since there is no distinction between the mind (manas) and the consciousness (cetas), therefore, by virtue of that favor, they shall indeed become knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas). (138)
The Lord, indeed, by the power of his sovereignty, becomes manifold;
and having become manifold, he again becomes one once more. (139)
Therefore, from the differentiation of *sumanasa* and from *tejas*,
all beings— both stationary and moving— are born throughout all the Manvantaras.
Having been produced once at the beginning of creation, they remain here by virtue of their excellence.
At each successive end of the eon, Rudra withdraws all creatures;
yet other non-lords are born, deluding others through their power of yogic illusion.
Moving about with sovereign power, they indeed delude those who are not sovereign;
therefore, in the midst of the spread of faults, there exists neither what is appropriate nor what is inappropriate.
The corrupters of reality are wicked, while those who speak of what is real and will be are impartial;
the three Vedas are capable of refuting the proponents who distort reality. (143)
And because of firm prior learning, as well as from worldly discourse, one does not perceive reality as it truly is due to these four causes. (144)

Previously, [cognitions] were fixed upon one object; even when they have passed into another time, because of that [fixation], one does not apprehend another object that is actually present, due to aversion. (145)
He who is the substantial essence among the eight [qualities], he who is subordinate to them,
the agent of actions and thoughts, and he who is great by birth— by these four reasons known through sacred scripture, he is celebrated. (146)
One who is powerless and angry recognizes the deities individually;
and regarding this, they cite these two verses concerning the Lord of Yoga (Yogeśvara): [147]
Having attained the power of yoga, one may create thousands of forms resembling oneself and others, and act together with all of them.
He may indeed attain all objects of the senses while practicing fierce austerity,
and he may withdraw them all again, just as the sun withdraws its rays.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Creation of Progeny by Kaśyapa," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
The sages said:
Having heard these words of his, the ascetics of Naimiṣa questioned the preeminent sage regarding the sequence of his speech.
How were the gods born here during the seven Manvantaras?
Who were those Ādityas of great luster, with Indra and Viṣṇu as their leaders?
O Romaharṣaṇa, tell us all of this in detail.
Thus addressed then by those exponents of the Veda, the humble charioteer,
the best among speakers, replied as he had been questioned by the great seers.
Sūta said:
Indeed, just as the gods were created from the mouth of Brahmā out of a desire for progeny,
so too are they remembered here in these Manvantaras as having their entire bodies composed of mantras.
The New Moon sacrifice and the Full Moon sacrifice, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara;
among these, Ākūta is the first, and after it is Ākūti. (5)
Vitti and Suvitti, Ākūti and Kūti,
then Adhīṣṭa should be known, as well as Adhīti in its true essence; Vijñāti, Vijñāta, and Mānava— these are the twelve.
He who would assemble [the gods] in a year should be known as having twelve sons;
seeing him, Brahmā said, "O Jayā, you have given birth to the gods."
And [he said], "One should not undertake [the rites] falsely when joined with a wife and the household fire.
Having spoken thus to him, Brahmā vanished right there.
Then they did not approve of those words of the Supreme Lord;
for in this world, the actions of truth consist of deeds born of speech and mind.
Those very people who, having perceived the defects in ritual actions, nevertheless remain engaged in them,
do so because they see that the fruit of actions is characterized by both decay and excess.
Disgusted with rebirth, they became free from sloth and devoid of possessiveness;
longing for the eternal, they were detached and perceived the defects [of worldly existence]. ||11||
Having abandoned wealth, virtue, and pleasure, they indeed remained steadfast;
relying upon human wisdom and withdrawing their vital energy, they stood firm.
And having understood their intention, Brahmā became enraged;
then Brahmā spoke to those gods who were devoid of energy.
"For the sake of progeny, you indeed must procreate here; I am the creator of progeny, not otherwise.
'Beget and conquer,' this is what I said previously. (14)
Since you have disregarded my words and remained fixed in dispassion, you loathe your own birth and do not rejoice in your progeny. (15)
For you have deposited your karmas with the desire for immortality;
therefore, disregarding that, you shall go back seven times.
Cursed by Brahmā, those gods indeed propitiated him, saying:
"O Mahādeva, O All-pervading Lord, forgive us for that which was done through ignorance. (17)
Having prostrated with courtesy, Brahmā spoke to them again:
"In this world, who that has not been authorized by me deserves to exercise independence? (18)
Since everything has been taken possession of by me, how can living beings act according to their own will toward me, whether it be for good or for ill? (19)
Whatever exists in the world, whether established as sentient or insentient, is pervaded by me through my nature as consciousness; who in the world could surpass me? (2.6.20)
Whatever has been deliberated by living beings, whatever has been ordained for them, and likewise whatever has been investigated—all that is known to me. ||21||
This entire world, both stationary and moving, has been established by me through the reality of hope; how then can I venture to cut it off here? (22)
And since I have indeed manifested here for the sake of creation and not otherwise, who, without undertaking actions here, shall be liberated from my will? (23)
Then, having rebuked the gods who had lost their presence of mind after the victories,
Prajāpati spoke again to them as they stood firm under his rod of punishment.
"Since this renunciation was previously made by me with you in mind,
and since that which was performed is not fruitless for you— indeed, it is boundless—
therefore, O gods, let there arise among beings a result that culminates in happiness. (25)
"O best of gods, your birth shall occur according to your own will;
all of you, being deluded, shall pass through six Manvantaras. (26)
Having learned of those [beings] at the end of the Vaivasvata [manvantara] and likewise at the beginning of the Svāyambhuva and other manvantaras, Brahmā sang this ancient verse there: [Verse 27]
For those who practice the threefold knowledge, celibacy, procreation, the ancestral rites,
sacrifice, and charity— indeed, for those performing these very acts—
he, having become free from passion, dwells in the praise of others. (28)
Having seen this verse, Jayā then spoke to the gods:
"When the Vaivasvata interval has passed, you shall come here into my presence. (29)
"Then you shall attain eternal perfection along with me.
Having spoken thus to them, Brahmā vanished right there.

Then, when the Lord had vanished, the gods, endowed with the powers of yoga and possessed of the supernatural faculties such as atomization (aṇimā), sought refuge in that which is free from fear from any quarter.
Then their bodies became twelve lakes,
known as the Jayās, which were born resembling the ocean.
Then, in that Svāyambhuva creation, these gods were born:
the twelve Ajitas, the sons of Ruci, who were themselves of an unconquerable nature.
Vidhi, Muni, Kṣema, Nanda, Avyaya,
Prāṇa, Apāna, Sudhāman, Kratu, Śakti, and Vyavasthita—
these twelve are all remembered as the mental sons of Ajita. (34)
And they were then remembered as the sharers of the sacrifice along with the gods;
first in the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, and then again in the Svārociṣa [Manvantara],
they were born as the sons of Svarocis in the Tuṣita heaven.
Those gods known as the Tuṣitas were indeed called Prāṇas, subsisting on vital breath;
yet those same Tuṣita gods themselves [arose] during the supreme intermediate period.
The auspicious sons of Uttama were born of Satyā;
therefore, those gods are remembered as the Satyas during that period of the Uttama Manvantara. (37)
In the third Dvāpara interval, they were the gods who partook of the sacrifice;
but when the Tāmasa interval arrived, those same gods became the Satyas once again.
Those twelve who were born as the sons of Tamas were indeed the gods named Haris;
they likewise became partakers of the sacrificial offerings.
Then, when the Cāriṣṇava interval had arrived, those gods, the Haris,
were born as the Vaikuṇṭhas from Cariṣṇu;
those gods named Vaikuṇṭhas existed during the fifth interval of Manu.
Then those very gods, the Vaikuṇṭhas, having reached the Cākṣuṣa [Manvantara],
were born as twelve sons of Sādhyā, the offspring of Dharma.
Then those Sādhyas, when the Cākṣuṣa interval had been exhausted and the creation of Vaivasvata Manu was about to begin, were indeed reborn.
When the beginning of the first Tretā Yuga of the Vaivasvata Manvantara had arrived,
those Sādhyas were born again from Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, through a portion [of themselves] in Aditi.
The twelve Ādityas were born again during the current interval;
indeed, when these were produced during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu. ||44||
Then, from Svāyambhuva, twelve Sādhyas were born as immortals;
thus, those original Jayas indeed came into being at that time through a curse.
Whoever, endowed with faith, recites this "Sevenfold Origin" of the gods by the command of the gods, does not go to the state of rebirth. (46)
Thus, these seven prosperities, characterized by the seven types of victory, have been fully described by me today. What more do you wish to hear? 47.
The sages said:
Tell us in detail the origin and the destruction of the Daityas and Dānavas, of the Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas, as well as of all beings, Piśācas, animals, birds, and plants. 48.
Thus addressed, Sūta then spoke to the best of sages:
"We have heard that two sons were born to Diti from Kaśyapa. (49)
Those two sons of Kaśyapa are indeed remembered as being born before all others,
on the day of the *Atirātra* sacrifice during Kaśyapa’s horse-sacrifice.
First, the sacrificial seat named Hiraṇyakaśipu emerged from the womb of Diti; he sat there in that eminent assembly,
and therefore he is remembered by the name Hiraṇyakaśipu on account of that deed.
The sages said:
O Lord, tell us in detail the name and birth of the high-souled Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, as well as his power.
Sūta said:
In ancient times, there was a meritorious horse sacrifice of Kaśyapa at Puṣkara,
graced by sages, deities, and Gandharvas.
According to the most excellent rite, as prescribed for the beginning of the narration and so forth,
five golden seats were indeed prepared in due order.
In this rite, one should prepare three bundles of *kuśa* grass purified by sprinkling, as well as a seat-mat (*kūrca*) and a wooden board;
these are the primary items that the four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) must have ready.
There, the auspicious seat that was prepared for the sake of the Hotṛ priest was made of gold, divine, and spread with celestial coverings.
Diti, being pregnant, entered into the state of wifehood;
her embryo remained within her for ten thousand years.
Having then emerged from his mother’s womb, he sat upon the golden seat that had been prepared for the sake of the Hotṛ priest; seated there, he recited the hymn while still in the womb.
Just as the great seer Kāśyapa [taught] the Vedas with the Ākhyānas as the fifth, the sages, having seen him, gave him a name corresponding to that. (59)
Because of that deed, he became renowned as Hiraṇyakaśipu;
his younger brother was Hiraṇyākṣa, and his younger sister was Siṃhikā,
who became the mother of Rāhu through her marriage to Vipracitti.
The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu performed supreme austerity for a hundred thousand years, remaining without food with his head turned downwards.
Brahmā, being pleased, invited that Daitya to choose a boon;
he chose immortality from all Brahmins and from all living beings,
and having conquered the gods through yoga, he established himself as the lord of all deities.
"Let the Dānavas, the Asuras, and the gods indeed be equal;
let this boon be granted to me: that the great sovereignty belonging to Māruta be mine. (63)

Thus addressed, Brahmā then granted him whatever he desired; having bestowed those divine boons upon him, he vanished right there. The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu is celebrated in ancient verses: hiraṇyakaśipurdetyo babhūva prathitaḥ purā | trailokye nāsti tasyānyo vīryeṇa ca balena ca || 65 || He was the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, renowned in ancient times; in the three worlds, there was no other equal to him in prowess or strength. na saṃkhyeyeṣu yuddheṣu parājayaṃ sa lebhe ha | na cāpi saṃyuge kaścid dharṣayāmāsa taṃ tadā || 66 || He never suffered defeat in countless battles, nor did anyone ever overcome him in combat at that time. na devāsuragandharvā na yakṣā na ca rākṣasāḥ | na nāgāstaṃ hi śaknuvanti sma yodhayitum || 67 || Neither gods, asuras, gandharvas, nor yakṣas, nor rākṣasas, nor even nāgas were able to fight him. tasyaivaṃ vartamānasya kadācit kālaparyayāt | putratvamagamad brahmā mahiṣyāṃ tu mahābalam || 68 || While he was living in this manner, once, due to the passage of time, Brahmā entered the state of being a son to his queen, [being born as] Mahābala. tasya putro 'bhavad daityaḥ prahlādo nāma viśrutaḥ | brahmaṇā yaḥ kṛto pūrvaṃ brahmadatta iti śrutaḥ || 69 || A son was born to that Daitya, the famous one named Prahlāda, who had previously been created by Brahmā and was known as Brahmadatta. hiraṇyakaśipoḥ putraḥ prahlādo 'bhūt sudhārmika� | viṣṇubhakto mahātejāḥ sarvabhūtahite rataḥ || 70 || The son of Hiraṇyakaśipu was Prahlāda, a very righteous man, a devotee of Viṣṇu, possessed of great splendor, and devoted to the welfare of all beings. hiraṇyakaśipuḥ śrutvā putraṃ taṃ vaiṣṇavaṃ tadā | cintayāmāsa matimān vadhopāyaṃ mahāmati� || 71 || Having heard that his son was a Vaiṣṇava, the wise and high-minded Hiraṇyakaśipu then reflected upon a means for his destruction. iti śrīviṣṇudharmottare prathamakhaṇḍe dvitīyo 'dhyāyaḥ || 2 || Thus ends the second chapter in the first section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Whichever direction King Hiraṇyakaśipu turned toward,
the gods, together with the great seers, paid homage to that very quarter.
O twice-born ones, such was the power of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the lord of the Daityas;
it is said that in ancient times Viṣṇu, as Narasiṃha, became his death. He was torn apart by him with his claws, and therefore the nails are remembered as being pure.
The five sons of Hiraṇyākṣa were valiant and possessed of great strength:
Utkura, Śakuni, and likewise Kālanābha.
Mahānābha, Vikrānta, and Bhūtasantāpana—
these sons of Hiraṇyākṣa were indeed difficult even for the gods to overcome.
Their sons and grandsons, along with the Bāḍeyas and their hosts,
are recorded as numbering hundreds of thousands, all slain in the Tārakāmaya war.
Hiraṇyakaśipu had four sons of great strength: Prahlāda was the eldest among them, as well as Anuhlāda, Saṃhrāda, and Hrāda; now learn of the sons of Hrāda.
Hrada and Nisunda were the two sons of Hrada; both Nisunda’s sons, Sundopasunda, were valiant. (71)
The immensely powerful Brahmaghna was born from Hradoda;
Mārīca, the son of Sunda, became Tāḍakā.
Then Tāḍakā was slain by the mighty Rāghava,
and Mūka was also killed by Savyasācin in the Kirāta forest.
Born and personally purified by great asceticism,
those three crores of inhabitants of Maṇivarta were indeed unconquerable even by the gods, yet they were slain by Savyasācin.
Anuhlāda’s son was Vāyu, and likewise Śinīvālī;
their host, consisting of a hundred thousand, is known as Hālāhala.
Vairocana was the son of Prahlāda, and five sons are recorded as his offspring:
Gaveṣṭhin, Kālanemi, Jambha, Bāṣkala, and Śambhu; these are remembered as the sons of Prahlāda’s lineage. (76)
I shall describe their sons, who are difficult to overcome, according to their preeminence:
Śumbha, Niśumbha, and Viṣvaksena of great prowess.
For these are the sons of Gaveṣṭhin: Śatadundubhi, Dakṣa, and Khaṇḍa; these three are the sons of Jambha.
Virodha, Manu, Vṛkṣāyu, and Kuśalīmukha—these were indeed the sons of Bāṣkala. Now hear of the sons of Kālanemi.
Brahmajit and Kṣatrajit, as well as Devāntaka and Narāntaka—these were indeed the sons of Kālanemi; now hear of the offspring of Śambhu.
Dhanuka, Asiloman, Nabala, Gomukha, Gavaksha, and Gomamsha are proclaimed as the sons of Śambhu. ||81||
The son of Virocana was the powerful Bali alone;
a hundred sons were born to Bali, and all of them were kings.
Among them, four were the principal ones— valiant and possessed of great strength:
Sahasrabāhu was the eldest, Bāṇa was esteemed for his wealth,
as well as Kumbhanābha, Garddabhākṣa, Kuśi, and others.
Śakunī and Pūtanā were two daughters born of Bali;
and the sons and grandsons of Bali numbered in the hundreds and thousands.
The host known by the name Bali, possessed of heroic prowess, attained the redness of Bāṇa’s moon-like mind. (85)
Diti, whose sons had indeed been destroyed, propitiated Kaśyapa;
that Kaśyapa, his mind pleased and being perfectly honored by her, invited her to choose a boon, and she then chose a boon from him. (86)
The Lord, the Blessed One, granted her the boon she had requested;
"What do you desire from me, O auspicious one? Mārīca said to her. (87)
Then, with palms joined in reverence, she addressed her satisfied husband Mārīca Kaśyapa:
"O Blessed One, I have been deprived of my sons by your sons, the Ādityas. (88)
"I desire a son who will be the slayer of Śakra and who is endowed with long asceticism;
I shall perform penance, so you should conceive a child. (89)
Having heard those words of hers, the highly effulgent Kaśyapa Mārīca replied thus to Diti, who was deeply distressed.
"So be it; may you be blessed. Be pure, O you who are rich in asceticism!
You shall give birth to a virtuous son who will slay Śakra in battle. (91)
If you remain pure for a full hundred years, you will then give birth to a son who shall travel throughout the three worlds. (92)
Having spoken thus, the lord of great splendor dwelt with her;
embracing her, the blessed ṛṣi departed for the three worlds.
When her husband had departed, that queen Diti, filled with supreme joy,
reached a forest and performed most rigorous penance.
While she was performing her ascetic penance,
the thousand-eyed one, the best of the gods, rendered service to her with supreme excellence of character.
The thousand-eyed one offered firewood, sacrificial grass, fuel, fruit, and likewise roots, as well as whatever else there might be.
With massages of the limbs and likewise by removing her fatigue,
Śakra attended upon Diti at all times and in all places. Thus propitiated, Diti then spoke to Śakra.
Diti said:
"I am pleased with you, O best of gods; my son, ten years remain for you at the end of this auspicious period, after which you shall see your brother. (98)
"O son, having obtained such a son, I shall establish my desire for victory;
indeed, together with him, I shall attain conquest over the three worlds. (99)
Having spoken thus to Śakra, when the sun had reached the meridian, the goddess Diti was overcome by sleep, placing her head upon her knees.
Seeing her impure state with hair fallen upon her feet, Śakra,
having found that vulnerability, laughed and rejoiced.
Then Purandara entered her exposed body;
having entered and seen the immeasurable embryo of great luster, the highly illustrious Indra shattered that primary form with his thunderbolt.
Then, being split by the hundred-jointed thunderbolt, the embryo cried out with a terrible sound, trembling again and again. "Do not cry," Śakra spoke to that embryo once more. (103)
Indra split that embryo, which had become sevenfold, into seven parts again one by one with his thunderbolt; then Diti awoke.
"He must not be killed, he must not be killed"—thus Diti spoke.
Out of respect for his mother's word, the wielder of the thunderbolt emerged from her womb.
With palms joined in reverence and holding his vajra, Śakra addressed Diti. (105)
"O Goddess, you were sleeping in an impure state with your hair fallen over your feet;
having found that opportunity, I pierced this embryo of yours into many pieces—[the one] who was to be the slayer of Śakra in battle. You ought to forgive me for this. (106)
When that embryo had thus become fruitless, Diti was deeply distressed;
she then spoke these words to the thousand-eyed Indra regarding her mother's eyes.
"O Lord of Gods, O mighty son of a sage, if this embryo of yours has been rendered fruitless through my fault, it is not my fault. (108)
"There is no fault in the killing of an enemy; therefore, O sir, I do not curse you. Rather, I wish to do what is pleasing to you; perform that which will bring welfare to my child. (109)
"May there be seven stations for my sons in heaven;
let these seven winds move about as my sons. Let them be known as the Maruts, seven groups of seven."
The first section is on the Earth, the second is on the Sun, the third is to be known as being on the Moon, and the fourth is on the host of luminaries. (111)
The fifth is among the planets, the sixth is in the circle of the seven sages, and the seventh is in the Pole Star (Dhruva); beyond that is the wind-sphere (Vātaskandha).
Let these sons of mine wander through them today; becoming these masses of wind at their respective times, let my little sons move about. (113)
May those sons of mine, who brought [the first] from impurities upon the earth, move about; let them be the first to roam the courtyard. 114.
And the second Pravaha wind, which extends from the pure regions up to the sun,
is the second division of the wind, moving as the second courtyard.
Above the sun and beyond the moon is that which is known as the *udvaha*;
they call it the *vātaskandha*, the third range of those who move through the sky.
O Lord, that fourth group of my sons who wander, beginning with Soma and following the constellations, is indeed the one headed by Suvasu. (117)
Likewise, from the Yakṣas upwards as far as the crown of the head,
the fifth arm is gentle, moving about the courtyard, and constitutes the fifth shoulder.
Above the Ṛṣis, from the Grahas, there is indeed a sixth who has been struck down;
let those who belong to that sixth group wander as my sons.
Likewise, the Seven Sages are situated above up to Dhruva; let my sons dwell there in the Vāta-skandha wind called Parivaha.
"May all these sons of mine perform this at the proper times;
and by virtue of that name, may they indeed become these Maruts. (121)
Then the mother and son bestowed names upon them individually, according to their respective deeds; thus indeed were they called the Maruts.
Sattvajyotis, likewise Āditya, and another, Satyajyotis; Tiryagjyotis, Sajyotis, and another, Jyotiṣman. ||123||
The first group has been declared; now learn from me the second:
Ṛtajit, Satyajit, Suṣeṇa, and likewise Senajit. (124)
Satmitra, Abhimitra, and Harimitra—this is the second group; now learn from me the third. (125)
Kṛta, Satya, Dhruva, Dhartṛ, and Vidhāraya; Dhvānta, Dhuni, Ugra, Bhīma, Abhiyu, Sakṣipa, and Āhvaya—this is remembered as the Gaṇa. ||126||
Such as this, and likewise otherwise, and whatever the counter-form may be;
so too the assembly, the agitation, and the host. ||127||
And such is the person, arising from a mind that is otherwise;
indeed, the qualities arise from that which is similar, dissimilar, equal, unequal, and even from that which is a counterpart.
These are indeed remembered as the forty-nine Maruts by name;
they have been enumerated together with those two, namely Diti and Candrā.
Having heard their names, Diti said to Indra:
"O dear son, let these sons of mine roam with Vāta as their support;
let my offspring wander about together with the gods—may it be well with you."
Having heard those words of hers, the thousand-eyed Purandara, with palms joined in reverence, said: "O Mother, let it be so. (131)
All this that has been spoken by you shall come to pass, without a doubt.
These high-souled Kumāras, esteemed as gods, shall become divine beings;
likewise, these sons shall share in the sacrificial offerings along with the gods. (132)
Therefore, all those Maruts, as well as the gods who are the younger brothers of Indra, are to be known as immortals;
and all these sons of Diti are ascetics.
Having thus understood their resolve, the mother and son, whose wealth was their asceticism, departed for heaven in joy; Śakra too returned to the celestial realm.
Whoever hears or recites this auspicious birth-story of the Maruts shall not encounter the fear of drought and shall thereafter become long-lived. (135)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Creation of Progeny by Kaśyapa," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Henceforth I shall proclaim the sons of Danu; listen.
In his lineage there were great asuras known as the sons of Danu. (1)
Led by Vipracitti, those hundred [demons] possessed fierce prowess;
they had all obtained boons and likewise performed intense austerities.
Those Dānavas were true to their word, valiant, cruel, and deceitful;
they were possessed of great strength, yet they were non-sacrificers and hostile to the Brahmins.
Listen as I describe them all according to their principal characteristics.
Dvimūrdhan, Śaṅkuvarṇa, as well as Śaṅkunirāmaya, Śaṅkukarṇa, Mahāviśva, Gaveṣṭhi, and Dundubhi. ||4||
Then the venerable Ajāmukha, Śila, Vāmanasa, Marīci, Akṣaka, Mahāgārgya, and Aṅgiras surrounded him. ||5||
Vikṣobhya, Suketu, Suvīrya, and likewise Suhṛda; Indrajit, Viśvajit, and Asuravimardana. (6)
Ekacakra, Subāhu, and the very powerful Tāraka; Vaiśvānara, Puloman, Pravīṇa, and Mahāśiras. ||7||
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and the great asura Muṇḍaka;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sūrya, Candra, and Indra are the Tāpina [daityas]. ||8||
Sūkṣma, Nicandra, Ūrṇanābha, Mahāgiri,
Asiloman, Sukeśa, Sada, and Balaka— these are the ten.
Likewise, Gaganamūrdhā, Kumbhanābha, Mahodara, Pramodāha, Kupatha, and the powerful Hayagrīva. ||2.7.10||
And the Asura Virūpākṣa, Supatha, and the great Asura Aja; Hiraṇmaya, Śatamāyu, and Śambara. ||11||
Śarabha and Śalabha, both Sūrya and Candramas—these two are Asuras, yet these two are currently Suras. (12)
Thus have been proclaimed the principal lineages of Danu’s sons;
their offspring, including sons and grandsons, are beyond counting and infinite.
Thus have been declared these Asuras who are Daiteyas and Dānavas.
Svarbhānu is remembered as a Daitya, for he was Anubhānu, the son of Danu.
These, however, are the sons of Danu who are recorded as belonging to his lineage.
Ekākṣa, Ṛṣabha, Ariṣṭa, Prabandhana, Naraka, Indrabādhana, Keśī, Meru, Śamba, and Dhenuka. (15)
Gaveṣṭhin, Gavākṣa, and the heroic Tālaketu—these sons of Danu, possessing human-like qualities, have been remembered by me. (16)
These sons of Vipracitti, born of Siṃhikā, were endowed with terrible prowess and were born amidst the great joy of the Daityas and Dānavas. (17)
There were fourteen great asuras known as the Saiṃhikeyas:
Śatagāla, the powerful Nyāsa, and likewise Śāmba.
Anuloma, Śuci, Vātāpi, Sitāṃśuka, Hara, Kalpa, Kālanābha, Bhauma, and likewise Naraka. (19)
Rāhu was indeed the eldest among them, the crusher of the moon and the sun;
these sons of Siṃhikā were difficult to overcome even by the gods.
Those of fierce lineage, cruel, and all haters of Brahmins—ten thousand others are known as the group of Saiṃhikeyas. (21)
He was slain by the more powerful Bhārgava, the son of Jamadagni.
Furthermore, Prabhā was the daughter of Svarbhānu, while Śacī was likewise the daughter of Puloman.
Upadanavī was the daughter of Yama, while Śarmiṣṭhā was the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan;
both Pulomā and Kālikā were the daughters of Vaiśvānara.
Prabhā’s son was Nahuṣa, and Jayanta was the son of Śacī; then Śarmiṣṭhā gave birth to Puru, and Upadānavī bore Duṣmanta.
For these two, Pulomā and Kālikā, were both daughters born of Vaiśvānara;
indeed, both of those maidens became the wives of Mārīca. 7.25.
From those two were born sixty thousand sons who were the foremost of the Dānavas,
as well as fourteen others who were inhabitants of Hiraṇyapura.
The Paulomas and Kālakeyas, those Dānavas of immense strength who were incapable of being slain by other Dānavas, were all killed by Savyasācin.
The sons born to Māyā were all endowed with heroic prowess:
Māyāvī, Dundubhi, Vṛṣa, and likewise Mahiṣa. ||28||
Bālika, Vajrakaṇa, and likewise the maiden Mandodarī—this is proclaimed to be the creation of the Daityas and Dānavas. ||29||
The sons of Danāyuṣī are remembered as five of great strength: Arūru, Bāli, Jambha, Virakṣa, and Viṣa.
The cruel and great asura named Dhundhu, who was childless, was indeed slain by Kuvalāśva at the word of Uttaṅka. (31)
The two sons of Bali were both of great heroism and incomparable splendor:
Kubhila and Varma; he was Karṇa in his previous birth.
Virakṣas also had two sons, Kālaka and Vara;
and Viṣa, the performer of cruel deeds, had four sons:
Śrāddhaha, Yajñaha, Brahmaha, and Paśuha.
Learn also of the sons of Vṛtra who were overcome by Danāyu;
they were born from the terrible breath of Vṛtra as he was fighting with Indra. (34)
The immensely powerful Rākṣasas known as the Bhartṛs are said to number one hundred thousand; they are remembered as the followers of Mahendra. ||35||
All are knowers of Brahman, gentle, righteous, and subtle in form; all these highly virtuous ones dwell hidden within living beings. ||36||
