This creation of the Daityas and Dānavas has been proclaimed; Pravāha begot sons who were indeed the best of singers at the sacrifice.
Sattvaja, Sattvātman, and Kalāpa the vigorous;
Kṛtavīrya, Brahmacārī, and Supāṇḍu as the seventh. ||38||
Panasa, Taraṇya, and Sucandra as the tenth—these are to be known as the celebrated Devagandharvas. ||39||
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Creation of Progeny by Kaśyapa," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
The Gandharvas and Apsarases are proclaimed as the meritorious Mauneyas:
Citrasena, Ugrasena, Ūrṇāyu, and likewise Anagha.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pulomā, and likewise Sūryavarcas; simultaneously [were born] Kāli, Diti, and Citraratha. (2)
Trayodaśa Bhramiśiras is the thirteenth, Parjanya is the fourteenth, Kali is the fifteenth, and Nārada is the sixteenth;
these are proclaimed as the Devagandharvas who are the sons of Muni. (3)
Thirty-four younger sisters of theirs were beautiful Apsarases; among them was Priyamukhyā, the most excellent of goddesses, who dwelt between Dāravatī and [the city of] Śubhā.
Miśrakeśī, Śācī, Parṇinī, Alambuṣā, Mārīcī, Putrikā, Vidyudvarṇā, and Tilottamā. (5)
Adrikā, Lakṣaṇā, and the goddess Rambhā, Manoramā, Suvarā, Subāhu, Pūrṇitā, and Supratiṣṭhitā. ||6||
Puṇḍarīkā, Sugandhā, Sudantā, and likewise Surasā;
Hemāsarā, Sutī, Suvṛttā, and she who is Kamalā. ||7||
Subhujā, Haṃsapādā, and likewise the worldly Apsarases—these Gandharvas and Apsarases are proclaimed to be the offspring of Muni. ||8||
Listen as I proclaim the names of all those daughters of the Gandharvas who have been mentioned by me. (9)
Suyaśas was the first among them, followed by Gāndharvī;
then came Vidyāvatī, Cārumukhī, Sumukhī, and Varānanā.
Now, these sons of Suyaśas were possessed of great strength and prowess;
the Yakṣas were the sons of Pracetas—listen to their names from me. (11)
Kambala, Harikeśa, Kapila, and likewise Kāñcana—
this is declared to be the host of Yakṣas known as Meghamālī.
Suyaśā’s four daughters are known as Apsarases;
listen attentively as I correctly state their names. (13)
Loheyī was the eldest, and after her came Bharatā; then Kṛśāṅgī and Viśālā, who were likewise matchless in beauty. (14)
From them, four other hosts of yakṣas are proclaimed to have been produced by the great-souled Viśāla, who was full of valor. (15)
Lohitya, Bharateya, the renowned Kṛśāṅgeya, and Viśāla—these are the celebrated groups of Yakṣas mentioned in the Purāṇa. (16)
O best among those who know the worlds and the non-worlds, these worlds are pervaded by these terrible asuras of great strength and prowess, as well as by the worlds and the hosts of yakṣas.
Then, by the valiant and high-souled one, the Gandharvas and Vāleyas were produced—those of great heroism who are the leaders of the great Gandharvas. ||18||
Endowed with valor and magnanimity, and possessing great strength and prowess—I shall declare their names in due order and according to the facts. (19)
Citrāṅgada of great heroism, Citravarmā likewise,
the highly fortunate Citraketu, and the valiant Somadatta;
and there were also three daughters, whose names shall now be told.
The first was named Agnikā, and immediately after her was Kambalā;
likewise was she named Vasumatī, whose beauty and vigor were incomparable. (21)
Beyond them, these Gaṇas were produced by Kumāra;
they are the three foremost Gandharvas, valiant and fierce in battle. (22)
The Āgneyas, the Kāmbaleyas, and likewise the sons of Vasumatī—
this world, with all its moving and non-moving beings, is pervaded by these various hosts.
And by that very same noble-souled and valiant one, illustrious beings were produced who were masters of beauty, knowledge, and wealth. (24)
Listen as I proclaim the names of those high-souled Gandharvas who have exerted their heroic vigor. (25)
Hiraṇyaroman, Kapila, Suloma, Māgadha, as well as Candraketu, Gāṅga, and the very powerful Goda. ||26||
Of those who are pure through great knowledge, heroic, and ascetic—such is the host, O Sulocanā, as well as two others. (27)
And by those two high-souled ones, Śivā and Sumanā, [sons] who were within the scope of learning and conduct were procreated by Viśravas. (28)
The Śaiveyas, the Vikrāntas, and the Saumanasa hosts—by these three groups of Vidyādharas, this world is pervaded. (29)
From these, hundreds of groups indeed arose in the world among those who move within the intermediate space of the sky, through the activities of the Vidyādharas.
And by that very same valiant high-souled one, horse-faced beings were produced;
indeed, understand those Kinnaras to be horse-faced. 31.

nyaṅkus, śarabhas, rurus, and pṛṣatas;
the sons of Mṛgamandā were the kings of beasts (tigers), and others were the gavayas.
And [there were] buffaloes, camels, and boars, as well as those with faces like rhinoceroses and oxen. ||201||
The sons of Hari, however, were the golāṅgulas, tarakṣus, vānaras, kiṃnaras, vyāghras, and kimpuruṣas; learn that these and others as well were born of Irāvatī. (202)
Then Bhauvana, having brought together the two halves of the sun’s egg and grasped them with his hands, sang the Rathantara chant.
As soon as he was impelled by the Sāman chant, he became an elephant;
that son of Bhuvana then offered himself for the sake of a son to Śatarūpā.
Because he was the son of Irāvatī, he is known as Airāvata;
because he is the mount of the King of the Gods, he is considered the foremost among the lords of elephants.
The glorious elephant Airāvata has the luster of a white cloud and possesses four tusks. (205)
Of that auspicious six-tusked elephant, born in the water, with a single root, possessing a golden luster, and of the *aupāvāhya* breed, his strength was indeed great. (206)
His sons were Añjana, Supratīka, Vāmana, and Pajra as the fourth; likewise Hastinī and Abhravān.
And Śveta begot four swift-moving sons of long life: Bhadra, Mṛga, Manda, and Saṅkīrṇa. ||208||
The elephant Añjana, though of mixed breed, was the mount of Yama; Bhadra was the mount of Supratīka, and Harita was the mount of the Lord of the Sahya mountains.
The pale elephant that was slow-moving belonged to Ailavila; the dark elephant that served as the mount for the Pāvakas was called Mṛga.
From Pajhottra were born eight sons: Pajha, Gaja, Varuṇa, Gaṇa, Upalepana, and Eṣa.
Those born in his lineage arise endowed with a state of exaltation;
they are elephants with white hair and nails, tawny in color, and large in stature.
I shall now describe these elephants, as well as other types of *nāgas*, in due order. (212)
From them were born two sons named Kapila and Puṇḍarīka; from these two were born Sumanābha and Rathāntara, and their sons were Supratiṣṭha and Pramarddana by name. (213)

Elephants that have prominent tusks, thick bodies, well-proportioned heads and temples, pure hair and nails, and are both powerful and capable of striking with their trunks are known as *ākulikās*. (214)
Puṣpadanta, Bṛhatsāman, Ṣaḍdanta, Dantapuṣpavat, Tāmravarṇa, and his son Sahacāriviṣāṇita. ||215||
And in his lineage are born those with hanging lips who are pleasant to behold, as well as those who are dark-complexioned, handsome, fierce, afflicted by various ailments, and long-faced. (216)
Vāmadeva, dark as collyrium, was born from the Sāman; then Vāmana was born, whose wife was Aṅgadā, and his two sons were Nīla and Vallakṣaṇa.
Those elephants born in their families who have sunken foreheads, short necks, broad chests, and great speed, yet are bound by men, become deformed. (218)
Supratīka was peerless in form; there was no elephant equal to him.
His three sons were Prahārī, Sampāti, and Pṛthu, the offspring of Cittī. (219)
In his lineage, elephants are born with long palates and lips, well-proportioned heads and bellies, and they are produced from a gentle stock. (2.8.220)
Añjanā gave birth to Nāda, and Cañjanāvatī gave birth to Sāman;
thus their mother was known as Prathitāyu, and they were the two sons of Aja.

In his lineage there arose elephants with large, well-proportioned heads, resembling glossy clouds; they were handsome, well-built, radiant as lotuses, and perfectly rounded; they were robust, yellowish in hue, and possessed long faces. (222)
From Candramas, through the Sāman, was born Piṅgalā, who possessed the luster of a white lotus;
from that Piṅgalā were born two sons, Mahāpadma and Ūrmimālin.
Know that those born in his lineage are equal to the best of boar-eaters, fierce, with powerful bellies, and fond of elephant-fights.
In the war between the gods and the asuras, the gods took up these [weapons] for the sake of victory;
and once their purpose was accomplished, those previously mentioned were released by them and departed toward their respective directions.
The gods gave these well-trained elephants to Lomapāda Aṅga, the author of the Sūtras, who was born in their lineage. ||226||

He is a *dvirada* because he has two rows of tusks; a *hastin* from his trunk (*hasta*); a *karin* from his hand-like trunk (*kara*); a *vāraṇa* because he wards off others; a *dantin* because of his tusks (*danta*); and a *gaja* because he roars (*garja*). (227)
He is called *kuñjara* because he moves through thickets (*kuñja*); *nāga* because he is an adversary to mountains (*naga*);
*mātaṅga* because he originates from Mataṅga; and *dvipa* because he is remembered as having two [tusks].
He is *sāmaja* because he is born from a female elephant (*sāman*); such is the sequence of etymological derivations. ||228||

The tongue-turning of these [elephants], which arises from the curse of Agni, is like that of a snake; furthermore, the lack of testicles in Bala and the hidden scrotum of these [elephants]—both of these result from the curse of Svayambhū and Sūra. (229)
From the daughters born of the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas by the elephants of the quarters (diṅnāgas), elephants of various temperaments were thus produced.
Origin, progeny, and likewise the etymological derivation of their names—this is to be known concerning the elephants of which the Sun is the king. (231)
From the ocean [flow] the Kauśika and others, and immediately thereafter the Gaṅgā;
to the east of Añjana, who has a single root, lies that Nāgavana forest.
That forest of Supratīka lies to the north of the Vindhya and to the south of the Gaṅgā, extending from the source of the Gaṅgā to the Karūṣas. 233.
To the west of Utkala and from the Āvedis, this fifth [region] is known as the forest of Vāmana, who is the one and only Self. 234.
To the west, however, extending as far as the Lauhitya river and reaching the ocean,
this forest of Yama is said to lie along the mountain range.
Bhūti understood the beings who were the attendants of the Lord Rudra—
those who were stout and those who were lean, those who were tall, those who were dwarfish, those who were short, and those who were of equal stature.

Those with long ears, protruding lips, hanging tongues, pendulous breasts, and large bellies; those of uniform appearance and those of dual forms, as well as those with drooping buttocks and thick calves. (237)
Dwelling on the sandy banks of rivers, lakes, oceans, and other waters,
they are black, fair, blue, white, and reddish-brown.
They were tawny, brindled, smoky-colored, and dark;
they had the appearance of donkeys, hair as stiff as *muñja* grass, and were masters of the senses (*hṛṣīkeśa*), wearing serpent-skins as their sacred threads.
Those with eyes cast away, those with deformed eyes, those with emaciated eyes, and those with many eyes;
those with many heads, those without heads, those with a single head, and those who are merely heads.
Those who were fierce and hideous, hairless and hairy, blind and matted-haired, as well as those with crooked limbs, hunchbacks, and dwarfs. 241.
Those who frequent the sandy banks of rivers, lakes, oceans, and other waters—those with a single ear, those with large ears, those with spike-like ears, and those without ears at all. (242)
Those with fangs and those with claws, those toothless and those double-tongued; those with one hand, two hands, three hands, and even those without hands. ||243||
Those with one foot, two feet, three feet, and many feet;
great yogins, great beings, well-matured, and possessed of great power. ||244||
All-pervading, unimpeded, possessing the knowledge of Brahmā, and able to assume any form at will;
both terrible and cruel, yet pure, auspicious, meritorious, and sweet-sounding. ||245||
Those with kusha grass in their hands, those with large tongues, those with large ears, and those with large faces;
those who take [things] from the hand, those who take from the mouth, those who take from the head, and those carrying skulls.
They were archers bearing mallets, as well as those wielding swords and spears;
they had blazing mouths and blazing eyes, and were adorned with variegated garlands and ointments.
Those who eat food and those who eat flesh, multiform and well-formed;
those who roam at night and at twilight, terrible yet sometimes gentle, wandering by day;
those nocturnal wanderers, most difficult to behold—those indeed are the terrible night-stalkers.

O Lord, there is fear regarding their status as others; for all of them have set their minds [on liberation], none of them has a wife or a son, and they are all indeed perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas).
There were hundreds and thousands of beings who were masters of the self;
all these high-souled ones are celebrated as the sons of Bhūti.
Furthermore, Kapiśā and Kūṣmāṇḍī gave birth to the Kūṣmāṇḍas.
The pairs of Piśācas are tawny in color;
because they are tawny, those Piśācas are all eaters of flesh.
There were sixteen other pairs, their descendants living in succession;
I shall name them according to their names, as well as those who followed in their lineage, the man-eaters.
Chagala and Chagalī, Vakra and likewise Vakramukhī;
the groups of sixteen, and Sūcī as well as Sūcīmukha. (253)
Sumbhapātra, Kumabhi, Vajradaṃṣṭra, Dundubhi, Upacāropacāra, Ulūkhala, and Ulūkhalī. ||254||
Anarka and Anarkā, Kukhaṇḍa and Kukhaṇḍikā;
Pāṇipātra and Pāṇipātrī, as well as Pāṃśu and Pāṃśumatī. ||255||
Nitunda and Nitundī, Nipuṇā and Nipuṇa,
as well as Chalādī, Uccheṣaṇā, Praskanda, and Skandikā—
these are declared to be the sixteen hosts of the sixteen Piśācas. (256)
The Ajāmukhas, Vakramukhas, Pūriṇas, and Skandinas; likewise the Vipādāṅgārikas, Kumbhapātras, and Prakundakas. ||257||
The Upacārolūkhalikas, the Anarkas, the Kukhaṇḍikas, the Pāṇipātras, the Naituṇḍas, the Ūrṇāśās, and likewise the Nipuṇas. ||258||
These sixteen families are those that subsist on the remnants of a needle’s point;
indeed, these are proclaimed as the noble-born among the Kūṣmāṇḍas. ||259||

They were born as those known as the Piśācas, who were well-formed in appearance yet possessed loathsome and distorted conduct; their progeny, consisting of sons and grandsons, was infinite. Therefore, learn now the characteristics of these Piśācas.
Those with hair on all their limbs, those called vṛtta, as well as those with fangs and claws,
the animals, the man-eaters, and the piśācas— these indeed have downward-facing mouths.
For they are hairless, devoid of body hair, with skin for fat and skins for clothing;
those Piśācas are known as Kūṣmāṇḍikas, who always eat sesame seeds and raw meat.
Those with crooked limbs, hands, and feet, as well as those with crooked conduct and gait, should be known as the crooked piśācas; they move crookedly and can assume any form at will. ||263||
With protruding bellies, large mouths, short bodies, heads, and arms, those Piśācas have pendulous testicles; they are smeared with sesame paste and are fond of pleasant sounds.
They have dwarfish forms, are talkative, and move with a leaping gait;
these Piśācas are as fierce as the sun, dwell in trees, and are fond of eating.
With arms raised, hair standing on end, and dwellings likewise with trees growing upward,
those Piśācas and the Pāṃśavas cast dust from their limbs.
Those with prominent veins, emaciated, bearded, and clad in rags; those who wear sacred threads, the Piśācas, and likewise those whose dwellings are the cremation grounds. ||267||
With fixed eyes and large tongues, they were licking their lips;
they had the broad chests of mortars, heads as thick as elephants or camels, were devoid of hair, and had their limbs bound together in lumps.
Those Piśācas, who hold drinking vessels made of skulls, consume food unseen;
subtle, hairy, and tawny, they indeed move about both seen and unseen. 269.
And those skillful Piśācas enter here unobserved;
their mouths are split open to their ears, and they have long whiskers and thick noses.
The Piśācas, who frequent the maternity chamber, are short in stature, have their gaze fixed upon the earth, and remain there with their hosts trampled by hands and feet. ||271||
With hands and feet on their backs, short in stature, and possessing the speed of the wind,
those Piśācas were flesh-eaters who subsisted on blood in battle.
For they are naked, homeless, with hanging hair, and living on alms;
they are Piśācas, Skandins, and others who subsist on putrid matter. These sixteen species of Piśācas are proclaimed. ||273||
Seeing such miserable piśācas, Brahmā, out of compassion and pity for those small-minded beings, granted them a boon: invisibility and the power to assume any form at will. ||274||
He should observe the movements at both junctions, as well as the dwellings, means of livelihood,
and those houses which are broken, empty, or inhabited by few people.
And those which are ruined, those not inhabited by people of good conduct, those not smeared or plastered, and those devoid of ritual consecrations; ||276||
He likewise cleared the royal highways, side streets, crossroads,
squares, gates, watchtowers, and bridges, making them free from obstacles.
Piśācas are indeed stationed everywhere in these places: on paths, rivers, holy fords, sacred trees, and great highways. (278)

Those people are indeed unrighteous; they were established by the gods as those who subsist by improper livelihoods, as well as those who cause the intermixture of castes and stages of life, and likewise artisans and craftsmen.

Those who perform rites with wealth acquired through injustice— whether it be from beings comparable to nectar, or from thieves and betrayers of trust, or by other such means— the *piśācas* are the presiding deities in those acts. (2.8.280)
With honey, meat, and boiled rice; with curd, sesame powder, and spirituous liquors;
with incense, turmeric, and kṛśara; and with oil, auspicious jaggery, and rice. ||281||
Black garments, incenses, and likewise flowers—
having thus provided these excellent offerings at the junctions of the lunar phases,
Brahmā, their sovereign lord, granted permission to the Piśācas.
Having seen Giriśa, the wielder of the trident, the beautiful lady gave birth to sons who were all spirits and piśācas, as well as tigers and lions.
Her sons were the leopards and the flesh-eating pythons.
Now listen to the ṛṣis as they describe the creation of progeny in its entirety;
she had five daughters, hear their names from me. (284)
Mīnā, Mātā, Vṛttā, Parivṛttā, and likewise Anuvṛttā are to be known; now hear indeed of their offspring. ||285||
Thousand-toothed makaras, pāṭhīnas, tāmasas, rohitas, and so forth—this is called the vast host of aquatic creatures. (286)
The four kinds of crocodiles are to be known, as well as those that follow in seniority;
she gave birth to offspring consisting of sea-monsters and porpoises. (287)
She produced many circular forms resembling the transformations of tortoises belonging to aquatic creatures,
and likewise she produced numerous forms resembling conch shells.
She gave birth to offspring that followed the transformations of frogs, as well as those of deer and snails. (289)
Likewise, she gave birth to various products of mother-of-pearl made from cowries, as well as various products of conch-shells that had been turned over. 2.8.290.
The Kālakūṭas and the Jalaukasas are the transformations [of this lineage].
Thus, this lineage of the Sage is proclaimed to have five branches. ||291||
The origin of animals, their causes, their initial appearance, and the extensive proliferation of their lineages;
as well as the various transformations of those born from moisture—how they come to be from these sources. (292)
From bodies that have perished, the twice-born are born as progenitors;
humans are born from sweat and impurities, as are creatures named *uśanas*, various swarms of ants, insects, and those with bound legs. (293)
Conch-shells, stones, crystals, pegs, and glass—these and many other such terrestrial groups are born of moisture. (294)
Likewise, these living beings are not born from bodies of deer, nor from rains, nor even from those scorched by the heat of the summer and other seasons. (295)
Mīnakas, pippalas, daṃśas, as well as tittiraputrikās, and blue-spotted ones are born; indeed, the alakas are produced in great abundance.
These creatures are born from water and born from sweat:
the kāśātas, yañjakas, insects, naladas, and many-legged beings. (297)
The Sihalas, Romalas, and Picchalas are thus proclaimed;
this and other such groups are known as those born from moisture (svedaja) within the class of water-born beings (jalaja). ||298||
Likewise, from clarified butter arise beans and mung beans in succession;
and from fruits such as the rose-apple, the wood-apple, the mango, and the betel-nut, living beings are born.
Indeed, they arise from mudga beans, from jackfruit, and likewise from rice grains;
they also arise from those placed within hollows or dried wood,
and they are produced from other sources as well, for they do not always emerge from those [specific sources] after a long time.
Living beings [are harmed] by horses and such, and likewise by poisons and the like. ||301||
O Brahmins, when cow dung has been set aside for many days, worms arise from it;
and from wood, wood-boring insects and the like are born. (302)
In due course, various blue flies are born from trees;
likewise, female pupae arise from dried excrement.
From the *kālikā* insects, snakes are born in every way;
and from dried cow dung, scorpions are born through moisture.
For from cows and buffaloes, O Lord, various creatures are born, especially fish and others within the womb of the egg. (305)
And they are born as Caivīrikas, as well as among the families of cattle and goats;
likewise, there are other subtle species such as leeches and the like. (306)
Various transformations of flies arise, and others are born there;
for the most part, they dwell in this mire of leftover water and mud.
The various transformations of mosquitoes and likewise of bees, as well as the female and male wasps, are born from blades of grass. (308)
Likewise, the Maṇicchedas and Vyālas are proclaimed to be born from eggs;
here, the various transformations of Śataverī arise from dried cow dung.
This and other such innumerable groups of moisture-born beings have been described by me in brief; indeed, they are known to arise through the power of past karma. (2.8.310)
Likewise, other beings belonging to the Nairṛta class are known as those born from afflictions;
some are born from a womb, while others are known as those born spontaneously. ||311||
Generally, all gods are indeed to be understood as being born of spontaneous generation;
however, some gods are born from a womb, and some gods arise without a cause.
Tūlālāgha, Kola, Śivā, and likewise Kanyā;
these were the offspring of Saramā, and the Saramādya hosts indeed [arose from them]. ||313||
Śyāma, Śabala, Arjuna, Harita, Kṛṣṇa, Dhūmrāruṇa, and Tūlālāgha are the Kadrukas. (314)
Surasā then gave birth to one hundred heads, which are considered the serpents;
Takṣaka is their king, and Vāsuki is the king of the Nāgas.
This group, characterized by an abundance of *tamas*, is of the nature of Krodhavaśā. (315)
Learn now of the progeny of Tāmrā, who was the daughter of Pulaha;
many other daughters, however, were born of Tāmrā who are not well-known. (316)
Śyenī, Bhāsī, Krauñcī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Śukī were likewise the wives of Aruṇa.
Of these, Śyenī gave birth to two sons of great prowess and immense strength,
Sampāti and Jaṭāyu, the best among birds.
Sampāti begot a son and likewise a single daughter;
and the sons of Jaṭāyu were the crows, vultures, and karṇins.
The wives of Garuḍa were Bhāsī, Krauñcī, Śukī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Bhadrā; their offspring shall now be described. (319)
Śukī gave birth to six renowned sons of Garuḍa:
Triśiras, Sumukha, Bala, Pṛṣṭha, and Mahābala.
Triśaṅkhanetra, Sumukha, Surūpa, Surasa, and Bala—the sons and grandsons of these high-souled Garuḍas—[are as follows]. (321)
There were fourteen thousand of those cruel serpent-eaters;
indeed, the expansion of their lineage resulted from the procreation of sons and grandsons.
I shall describe in due order those regions that are pervaded:
the entire Śālmalidvīpa and the Devakūṭa mountain. (323)
And likewise the lord of mountains Maṇimant with its thousand peaks, Parṇamāla, Sukeśa, and the mountain Śataśṛṅga.
The mountain Kauraja with its five peaks and Mount Hemakūṭa were illuminated by lotus-hued rays produced by fierce winds.
The mountain ranges were pervaded by those high-souled descendants of Garuḍa;
the sons of Bhāsī are known as the bhāsas, owls, crows, and cocks. (326)
Peacocks, sparrows, pigeons, quails, and partridges;
female curlews, cranes, hawks, ospreys, and cranes; and herons. ||327||
And other such carnivorous creatures as well as birds,
and Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, O beautiful lady, along with the haṃsas and kalahaṃsas.
He then produced the cakravāka birds, all water-birds, and the twice-born; from these alone, he brought forth an infinite succession of sons and grandsons.
The offspring of Garuḍa have been described; now hear of the progeny of Irā.
Irā gave birth to three lotus-eyed daughters. (2.8.330)
They are the mothers of the lords of the forest, of trees, and of creepers;
indeed, they are known as *latā*, *vallī*, and *vīrudh*. (331)
A creeper indeed brings forth those forest trees that were previously without flowers, standing on the riverbanks;
the creeper truly causes the trees to be endowed with both flowers and fruit.
Now, creepers, shrubs, trees with bark-fiber, and species of grass—
these are the offspring of the *vīrudh*, and here the category of *vaṃśa* (bamboo/thicket) is concluded.
These descendants of Kaśyapa, both stationary and moving, have been described;
their sons and grandsons by whom this world is filled. (334)
Thus, this single portion of the creation has been described by me as a part;
this creation of progeny by Mārīca has been proclaimed in brief,
O twice-born ones, for it cannot be told in detail even in hundreds of years.
Aditi is known as being of virtuous character, Diti as being of powerful character;
Surabhi is known as being of ascetic character, and Danu as being of illusory character. ||336||
Kadrū was of cruel disposition, while Krauñcī was renowned for her learning; Irā was inclined toward grasping, and Danāyuḥ delighted in devouring.
Vinatā is indeed of a nature to carry burdens, while Tāmrā is possessed of nooses;
such are the dispositions of the Mothers of the World in every respect. (338)
By their nature, conduct, intellect, forbearance, strength, and appearance,
those characterized by passion, goodness, and darkness are indeed righteous or unrighteous.
The noble offspring born of Kaśyapa were like his own mother;
they were the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
and pannagas, as well as piśācas, domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, and plants.
Since these were born here among human women of the lineage of Dakṣa throughout all the Manvantaras, therefore human beings are indeed the most excellent.
Human beings are indeed the achievers of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
below that, the gods and asuras are born from the downward-flowing stream.
They are born again and again among human beings for the sake of accomplishing their tasks;
thus has the origin of the lineage of these ascetics been fully recounted.
Of the gods and the asuras, as well as the gandharvas and apsarases;
of the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas, and of the suparṇas, uragas, and birds. ||344||
Of beasts of prey and peacocks, and of all medicinal herbs;
of worms, insects, moths, and small creatures born in water;
of animals and of the illustrious Brahmins—[he perceived] their marks of merit. (345)
It bestows long life, brings prosperity, is glorious, and confers welfare and happiness; it should be constantly heard and grasped by one who is free from envy. (346)

Whoever recites this lineage of the great-souled ones with discipline in an assembly of Brahmins and learned scholars shall indeed obtain abundant progeny, as well as fortune, wealth, and an auspicious state after death. (347)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Creation of Progeny by Kaśyapa," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Thus, when all creatures had been created by the high-souled Kaśyapa, both the stationary and the moving, they were firmly established.
Having consecrated them in their respective positions of authority, Prajāpati, the foremost among them,
then proceeded to assign the kingdoms in due order.
He consecrated Soma in the sovereignty over the twice-born, the plants, the lunar mansions along with the planets, as well as sacrifices and ascetic penances.
He appointed Bṛhaspati, the lord of the Aṅgirases, as the leader of the Viśvedevas,
and he consecrated Kāvya, the sovereign of the Bhṛgus, in his kingdom.
Furthermore, among the Ādityas he is Viṣṇu, among the Vasus he is Pāvaka,
among the Prajāpatis he is Dakṣa, and among the Maruts he is Vāsava.
Then [he saw] Prahlāda, the son of Diti, as the king of the Daityas;
Nārāyaṇa as the lord of the Sādhyas; and the bull-bannered one (Śiva) as the lord of the Rudras.
Then he appointed Vipracitti as the king of the Dānavas;
Varuṇa as the king over the waters; and Vaiśravaṇa as the lord over kings, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, earthly rulers, and wealth.
He consecrated Vaivasvata Yama in the kingdom of the ancestors,
and Giriśa, the wielder of the trident, as the lord of all beings and piśācas.
Then he made Himavat the lord of mountains, the ocean the lord of rivers,
and Citraratha the lord of the Gandharvas.
He consecrated Uccaiḥśravas as the king of horses,
the tiger as the king of wild beasts, and the bull as the king of quadrupeds.
Among all birds, he is Garuḍa, the best of flyers;
among fragrances, he is Mātulaṅga; and among bodiless beings, he is the wind.
Among sound, space, and strength, he chose the wind as the best among the powerful;
among all fanged creatures, Śeṣa; and among serpents, Vāsuki.
Among the reptiles, he consecrated Takṣaka as king of the serpents and nāgas;
among the oceans, rivers, clouds, and rain, he consecrated Parjanya as king;
and among the Ādityas, he consecrated one of them [Vivasvat] as king. (13)
And likewise Kāmadeva, the lord of all the hosts of Apsarases;
as well as the seasons, the months, and the monthly periods. (14)

He established the Lord Saṃvatsara as the master of the fortnights and their opposites, of the muhūrtas and the lunar nodes (parvan), of the measures of kalās and kāṣṭhās, of the passing of the two solstices (ayanā), and of calculation and the conjunctions [of planets]. ||15||
In the eastern direction of the realm, Prajāpati consecrated his son, renowned by the name Sudhāman, as king. ||16||
In the western direction, he consecrated the high-souled King Ketumān, the son of Rajas, as the unshakable sovereign. ||17||
And he made Manu his son the sovereign lord of human beings;
by them this entire earth, with its seven continents and its cities, is protected according to their respective regions through righteousness even today. ||18||
In the past, during the Svāyambhuva interval, these kings were consecrated by Brahmā; indeed, those who become Manus are likewise consecrated.
Indeed, the kings who passed away during the elapsed Manvantaras have gone;
likewise, others are consecrated when a new Manvantara arrives.
All those of the past and future are remembered as the lords of the Manvantaras.
And Pṛthu, having been consecrated in the Rājasūya sacrifice by these best of men according to the procedure seen in the Vedas, became a powerful king. (21)
Having produced these sons for the sake of the continuity of progeny,
the illustrious lord and master of creatures once again [proceeded].
Kaśyapa, desiring a lineage, performed supreme austerity;
he thought, "May there be two sons who will establish my lineage. (23)
As that high-souled Kaśyapa was thus meditating,
two sons of great splendor, who were portions of Brahmā, subsequently manifested.
Vatsāra and Asita were both exponents of the Veda;
from Vatsāra was born Nidhruva, and that highly illustrious Raibhya.
The sons of Raibhya are to be known as the Raibhyas; learn now of the sons of Nidhruva.
To Cyavana, through Sukanyā, Sumedhas was born.
The wife of Nidhruva was indeed the mother of the Kuṇḍapāyins;
from her, Asita’s son Ekaparṇā, the most devoted to Brahman, was born.
Having heard the words of the Śāṇḍilyas, the highly illustrious Devala said:
"The Nidhruvas, the Śāṇḍilyas, and the Raibhyas—these three are indeed Kaśyapas. (28)
Vara and the others were the gods; these were the progeny of Devala. When the four yugas had passed in the eleventh Manvantara, and that [period] was yet remaining, the Dvāpara age commenced.
The son of Mānasa was indeed Dama;
his heir, the son of Mānasa, was known as Tṛṇabindu.
At the beginning of the third age, the Tretāyuga, a king was born; he had a daughter named Iḍaviḍā, who was peerless in beauty. That royal sage gave his daughter in marriage to Pulastya.
From the Ṛṣi Ṛcīka and Iḍaviḍā, Viśravas was born;
he had four wives who increased the lineage of Paulastya. (32)
He married the daughter of Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, who was renowned for his great fame; her name was Devavarṇinī.
Puṣpotkaṭā and Vākā were born to Mālyavat;
Kaikasī was the daughter of Mālin—now hear of their offspring.
Devavarṇinī gave birth to his eldest son, Vaiśravaṇa,
who was endowed with divine rites, as well as those prescribed by the seers and heard in the scriptures,
and possessed of the form of a Rākṣasa and the strength of an Asura. (35)
He had three feet, a very large body, a thick head, and a massive frame;
he possessed eight tusks, greenish-yellow whiskers, spike-like ears, and was deep red in color.
With short arms and long forearms, tawny-hued and most terrifying, he is the Perfectly Awakened One, endowed with the knowledge of the turning back [of saṃsāra] and rich in the wealth of wisdom. (37)
Seeing his son thus, bearing such a universal form,
the father himself looked upon him there and said, "This is Kubera."
This word "kvi" is used in the sense of contempt; the body is called *bera*.
Because his body was deformed (*ku-śarīra*), he was named Kubera, and by that name he is marked. (39)
Because he is the offspring of Viśravas and resembles Viśravas,
he shall therefore be known by the name Vaiśravaṇa in the world.
Through his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), Kubera begot the renowned Nalakūbara;
likewise, Kaikasī gave birth to these four sons: Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā as a daughter, and Vibhīṣaṇa as the fourth. (41)
Śaṅkukarṇa, Daśagrīva, Piṅgala, and Raktamūrdhaja—four-footed, twenty-armed, with massive bodies and great strength. ||42||
Jātyāñjananibha, Daṃṣṭra, and Lohitagrīva, as well as Rājasena, were endowed with victory, beauty, and strength. (43)
Rāvaṇa was one whose intellect was fixed on truth and whose body was firm;
though naturally fierce and cruel, he was called "Rāvaṇa" because he caused even Rākṣasas to flee.
In his previous birth, that king was Hiraṇyakaśipu;
as a Rākṣasa, he reigned here for thirteen cycles of four yugas.
Those fifty million years are declared by number by the twice-born;
sixty-one hundred thousand (niyuta) more are proclaimed by those who know calculation. (46)
For six million years, that Rāvaṇa kept the gods and the sages awake with his terrifying deeds.
In the twenty-fourth Tretā Yuga, Rāvaṇa, due to the exhaustion of his ascetic merit,
met his destruction along with his hosts upon encountering Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
Mahodaya, Prahasta,
and Mahāpāṃśukhara were the sons of Puṣpotkaṭā, and Kumbhīnasī was her daughter.
Triśiras, Dūṣaṇa, the Rākṣasa Vidyujjihva,
and the maiden Asalikā are known as the offspring of Vākā.
Thus, these ten Rākṣasas of cruel deeds are the descendants of Pulastya.
All of them were of fierce seed and were difficult to approach even for the gods. ||51||
All of them had indeed obtained boons and were accompanied by sons and grandsons; so too were all the Yakṣas and those Rākṣasas who were descendants of Pulastya.
Of the cruel Brahmarākṣasas of the lineages of Agastya and Viśvāmitra, who were devoted to the study of the Vedas and practiced austerities and vows; ||53||
Among them, Aiḍaviḍa was the king; he was a descendant of Pulastya, left-eyed and tawny-hued.
The other three groups of Rākṣasas were indeed the "Yajñamukhas. (54)
The Yātudhānas, the Brahmadhānas, the Vārttas, and those who roam by day—these four classes of night-roaming beings are recorded by the poets. (55)
The Paulastyas, the Nairṛtas, the Āgatsyas, and the Kauśikas—these are indeed known as their seven classes of Rākṣasas. ||56||
I shall describe their form as it is established by its own nature:
they have round eyes, are tawny, possess massive bodies, and have large bellies.
They had eight fangs, spike-like ears, and hair standing erect;
their mouths were gaped open as far as their ears, and their smoke-colored hair rose upward like muñja grass.
They had thick heads and a white luster, were short in stature, and prone to drooling;
they had copper-colored faces, long tongues and lips, pendulous bellies, and thick noses.
With blue limbs, red necks, deep-set eyes, and terrifying, they possessed most dreadful voices; they were hideous and had thick-set calves.
They are large-bodied with prominent noses, firm with a skeletal structure like stone;
they are of fierce lineage, cruel, and generally performers of afflicted deeds.
Wearing earrings, armlets, and head-ornaments, and bearing crowns and turbans; adorned with various garments and jewels, and anointed with diverse garlands and unguents.
They are known as eaters of food, eaters of flesh, and even eaters of men;
this is considered by the wise to be the similarity of form among the Rākṣasas.
However, their entire strength is not understood [to be real], for that is indeed produced through illusion.
The sons of Pulaha were all deer, as well as fanged beasts of prey, spirits, piśācas, serpents, bees, and likewise elephants. (64)
The monkeys, the kinnaras, as well as the yamas and kimpuruṣas,
and others who had wandered about, were all under the sway of illusion and anger.
In that Vaivasvata interval, Kratu was remembered as being childless;
neither his son nor his grandson remained, for he had withdrawn his vital energy and stayed [in a state of dissolution].
I shall now proclaim the lineage of Atri, the third Prajāpati;
he had ten beautiful wives who were devoted to their husbands.
To Bhadrāśva, by Dhṛtācī, ten Apsarases indeed gave birth as their sons:
Bhadrā, Śūdrā, Madrā, Śaladā, and likewise Maladā; 68.
Velā, Khalā, and these seven, along with that which is known as Gocapalā, as well as Mānarasā and Ratnakūṭā—these are the ten. (69)
Their husband, Prabhākara, a founder of the lineage of Atri, begot upon Bhadrā a glorious son named Soma. (2.9.70)
When the sun was struck by Svarbhānu and [the light] fell from heaven, he caused radiance to proceed in this world while it was overwhelmed by great darkness. (71)
When he was told, "May it be well with you," the Sun-god, as he was falling here,
did not fall from heaven to the earth due to the word of that Brahman-sage.
He of great asceticism, who established the Atri clans as the most excellent,
and who was indeed the bestower of wealth in sacrifices, was set in motion by the gods.
She, her splendor purified by great asceticism, bore sons to them who were equal to himself and unnamed— ten sons in those very wives.
There were sages known as the Svastyātreya, who had reached the further shore of the Vedas;
among them were two of celebrated fame, most devoted to Brahman, and possessed of great luster.
Dattātreya was his eldest [son], and Durvāsas was his younger brother;
his youngest daughter was Abalā, a knower of Brahman.
Regarding this, the experts in the Purāṇas cite this verse from of old: 76.
Those who know the Purāṇas declare that Dattātreya—the high-souled son of Atri, whose mind was tranquil and free from blemish—was an incarnation of Viṣṇu. (77)
In his lineage were born four renowned clans on earth:
the Śyāmas, the Mudgalas, the Balārakas, and the Gaviṣṭhiras.
These are remembered as the four lineages of men of great power.
From Kaśyapa were born Nārada, Parvata, and likewise Arundhatī; O best of beings, learn now of those who were born from Arundhatī.
Nārada, however,
of great luster and with vital energy drawn upward, bestowed Arundhatī upon Vasiṣṭha due to the curse of a tree.
Formerly, during that Tārakāmaya war between the gods and the asuras,
when the world was struck by drought and Śakra along with the gods was distressed,
the wise Vasiṣṭha indeed sustained all creatures through his ascetic power.
There, employing roots, fruits, and medicinal herbs as medicine,
he brought them back to life by means of that compassionate remedy.
O twice-born ones, Vasiṣṭha begot Śakti upon Arundhatī;
and from Śakti, Adṛśyantī gave birth to Sāgara and Parāśara.
Kālī gave birth to the lord Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana from Parāśara;
and from Dvaipāyana, Śuka, endowed with all virtues, was born to Araṇī.
And from Pīvarī these six sons of Śuka were born:
Bhūriśravas, Prabhu, Śambhu, Kṛṣṇa, Gaura as the fifth, [and Ṣaṭsaṃjña]. ||85||
Kanyā Kīrtimatī, firm in her vows, was the mother of Yoga and the wife of Brahmadatta and Sattvaguha. (86)
The Śvetas, Kṛṣṇas, Gauras, Śyāmas, Dhūmras, Samūlikas,
Ūṣmapās, Dārakas, Nīlas, and Parāśaras—
these eight divisions of the high-souled Parāśaras have been declared. (87)
Henceforth, learn of the birth of one equal to Indra:
he was produced by Vasiṣṭha through Kapiñjalī, who was Ghṛtācī.
He is celebrated as Kuśīti and is said to be equal to Indra. (88)
From the daughter of Pṛthu was born a son, Vasu;
his son was Upamanyu, from whom these Upamanyus are descended.
Those known as the Kuṇḍinas of Mitrāvaruṇa,
as well as others renowned by the name Vasiṣṭhas who have a single Ṛṣi ancestor—
these are recorded as the eleven branches of the Vasiṣṭhas.
Thus these eight sons of Brahmā, born of his mind, are renowned;
they were highly fortunate brothers, and their lineages became firmly established.
They uphold these three worlds, which are crowded with hosts of gods and sages;
their sons and grandsons are by the hundreds and thousands,
by whom the entire earth is pervaded, just as by the rays of the sun.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Genealogy of the Sages," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Śaunaka said:
Having heard these words of his son, who was self-realized,
the twice-born ones questioned the Sūta’s son for a further reply.
How was Bhavānī born as the second [wife]?
And how did she who was formerly Satī become Dākṣāyaṇī, and how was Umā born? (2)
The mountain-dweller begot [him] upon Menā, the daughter of the Pitṛs.
And who indeed were these Pitṛs, of whom Menā was the mind-born daughter? (3)
And Maināka was his daughter’s son, as were Umā, Ekaparṇā, and likewise Ekapāṭalā. ||4||
The Gaṅgā is indeed the best of rivers and likewise the first-born of them all;
listen to everything I have previously declared regarding her. (5)
And where do the many ancestors reside?
O auspicious one, I wish to hear from you the supreme ritual for the śrāddha offering. (6)
Whose sons are they remembered to be, and how are they your fathers?
How were the Pitṛs born, whose sons are they, and what is their essential nature? (7)
"But as for the other ancestors in heaven who are even the deities of the gods—
I truly wish to hear in this manner about the supreme creation of the Pitṛs, and how the Śrāddha duly offered by us indeed gratifies them. (8)
For what purpose are they seen by him? What is considered the reason for that? Who indeed are those who dwell in heaven, and who are those in hell? (9)
Intending [the offering] for his father, his father’s father,
and likewise his father’s grandfather, he should name them in the three funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
What śrāddhas are to be given, and how indeed do they go to the ancestors? And how are those residing in hell able to bestow fruit in return? (11)
Who indeed are those called "fathers" here, whom we should worship again?
For we have heard that even the gods worship their sons in heaven. (12)
O learned one, I truly desire to hear this in detail;
you ought to explain its meaning with clear expression. (13)
Having heard the words of the sages, the charioteer, who perceived the true meaning of things,
then explained the intention of the sages in accordance with their questions.
Sūta said:
In this regard, I shall describe for you according to my wisdom and as I have heard it:
in the various Manvantaras, the ancestors are born as the sons of the gods. (15)

Among those of the past and the future, they are respectively the elders and the juniors. Those ancestors who formerly dwelt together with the gods in the past ages, and those who exist at present—I shall describe them to you with certainty. (16)
For these humans, the ancestral rite (śrāddha) indeed proceeds as a śrāddha.
Brahmā created the gods, saying, "They shall not sacrifice.
Then, desiring the fruits [of their actions], they abandoned him and created themselves. (17)
Cursed by Brahmā, those fools were deprived of their consciousness;
they understood nothing at all, and consequently, the world became bewildered.
Bowing down once more, they all entreated the Grandfather;
for the sake of favoring the worlds, the Lord spoke to them again.
"Perform indeed an expiation for the transgression that has been committed;
ask your own sons, and from them you shall obtain knowledge. (2.10.20)
Then, with their minds restrained and desiring to undertake expiatory rites, they questioned one another in accordance with the prescribed rules regarding their own sons.
To them, those sons of self-restrained minds, who were knowers of dharma, declared various atonements for the faults arising from speech, mind, and action.
Having regained their consciousness, those delighted inhabitants of heaven said to their sons:
"You are indeed our fathers, you by whom we have been awakened!
Since you possess knowledge of dharma, what desire and what boon shall be granted to you? (23)
Brahmā spoke to them again: "You are indeed speakers of truth;
therefore, what has been spoken by you is so, and not otherwise."
And it has been said: "They shall indeed become our fathers; they are our own sons. Let this boon be granted to them. (25)
By that very word, the sons of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin attained the state of fathers,
and the fathers, in turn, attained the state of sons.
Therefore, those fathers are sons, and their status as fathers is established in them.
Having thus remembered the fathers as sons and the sons as fathers, Brahmā spoke again to the fathers for the sake of his own progeny. (27)
For whoever performs any ritual action in a śrāddha ceremony without first having offered to the ancestors,
the Rākṣasas and Dānavas shall obtain the fruit of that act.
And the ancestors, nourished by the faithful, will in turn nourish the imperishable Soma;
being thus nourished by you, they shall cause him to increase eternally. (29)
Soma, nourished by those who perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha), shall nourish the entire world—
including its mountains and forests, and all that is mobile and immobile.
Those men who perform ancestral rites (śrāddha) while desiring prosperity, to them the ancestors will always grant prosperity as well as progeny. ||31||
To those whom they shall offer three rice-balls at the *śrāddha* ceremony according to name and lineage—
those ancestors, wherever they may reside, including the great-grandfather,
will indeed cause their progeny to prosper through the gift of that *śrāddha*. (32)
Thus was the command formerly issued by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord;
by that, this—charity, study, and austerity—has been accomplished in every way.
They are indeed the givers of knowledge, your ancestors; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, these ancestors are gods, and gods are again ancestors;
for they are mutually both ancestors and gods.
Having heard these words of Brahmā from the self-disciplined Sūta,
the sages questioned him further regarding that which was the subsequent answer.
The sages said:
How many indeed are the classes of ancestors, and at what time do those classes exist?
O best of gods, they are the gods who increase the soma of the deities. (36)
Sūta said:
I shall now declare to you this unsurpassed account of the creation of the Pitṛs,
which Śaṃyu formerly asked of his father Bṛhaspati.
Seated before Bṛhaspati, who was skilled in the meaning of all branches of knowledge, his son Śaṃyu, endowed with humility, asked him this question. (38)
Who are these known as the *pitṛs*, how many are they, and what are their names?
How did they originate, and how did they attain the status of being *pitṛs*? (39)
And why is it that they always join the father first at a sacrifice?
For all the rites of the great-souled ones proceed, preceded by the *śrāddha*.
To whom should the śrāddhas be given, and what gift yields great fruit? In which sacred fords (tīrthas) and rivers does the śrāddha become inexhaustible? ||41||
In whom indeed does the best of the twice-born obtain everything by performing a śrāddha? What is the proper time for the śrāddha, and what procedure is to be followed? (42)
O Blessed One, I desire that this which was mentioned by me be explained in detail, exactly as it is, and in its proper sequence. (43)
Thus questioned correctly, the high-minded Bṛhaspati,
the best among those who know how to answer questions, explained the matter in due order.
Bṛhaspati said:
I shall explain to you, my dear, that which you ask of me—the profound and supreme question—in accordance with discipline and as is right. (45)
The heavens, the intermediate space, the earth, the stars, as well as the directions, the sun and the moon, and likewise day and night. ||46||
At that time, O dear one, this world did not exist; it was enveloped in darkness.
There, Brahmā alone performed supreme austerity, difficult to practice.
Śaṃyu spoke again to his father, the most eminent among those who know Brahman,
who was always purified by his vows and the foremost among those who possess all knowledge.
"What kind of austerity did Prajāpati perform for the sake of all beings?
Being thus addressed, Bṛhaspati, possessed of great luster, spoke to him. 49.
Then the Blessed One, meditating upon that unsurpassed yoga of austerity— the application of all austerities— created by means of it the worlds,
the past and future, the sciences, and the Vedas in their entirety.
Having entered into yoga, he beheld with the eye of yoga that which had been created by Brahmā.
The worlds named Sāntānika, where radiant beings dwell, are known as the Vairājas; they are the deities among the gods in heaven. (52)
Then, at the very beginning, the Lord Brahmā, endowed with yoga and austerity, having applied himself to eternal yoga, created the gods.
Known as the primordial gods (ādidevas), these beings of great essence and great majesty bestow all desires; they are worthy of worship by gods, dānavas, and humans alike. (54)
Seven groups of them are proclaimed, worshipped throughout the three worlds;
three of them are formless, while four possess excellent forms.
Above them, three exist as substantial forms;
below them, four exist as subtle forms. ||56||
From them come the gods, from them the earth; such is this succession of worlds. For they exist within this world, and from them arises Parjanya (the rain-god).
From them comes rain, and through that rain, the birth of the worlds occurs once again. ||57||
Because they nourish both Soma and food through their yoga,
those best of worlds called them "Pitṛs" (Fathers) for the sake of the worlds.
Swift as thought, subsisting on *svadhā*, with all their desires and requisites provided, they are free from greed, delusion, and fear; resolute and devoid of sorrow. (59)
Having abandoned their yoga, these great-souled ones have attained the worlds of Sudarśana; indeed, they become divine, meritorious, and free from sin.
Then, at the end of a thousand yugas, those who discourse on Brahman are born;
having regained yoga once more, they, being formless, proceed to liberation.
Having abandoned both the manifest and the unmanifest through the power of great yoga,
they vanish like a meteor in the sky or like the fading radiance of a spent lightning bolt.
Having cast off their bodily births by the power of great yoga,
they attain a state beyond description or definition, just as rivers do when they reach the ocean.
And those who constantly perform ritual actions and worship of the guru—by means of these, the ancestors, who increase their yoga, are nourished. ||64||
Satisfied by the śrāddha, the ancestors, established in yoga,
nourish the moon through their yogic power, by which the three worlds live.
Therefore, offerings for the ancestors should always be given with effort to yogis;
for yoga is indeed the strength of the ancestors, and from yoga the moon proceeds.
One should indeed feed thousands of Brahmins, as many as have arrived.
But listen to this: a single person who knows yoga and is devoted deserves all of them. ||67||
That which is eaten by a single teacher of yoga protects from great fear more than [that eaten] by a thousand consecrated *snātakas* and a hundred [ordinary teachers]. (68)
A single yogī indeed excels over a thousand householders, a hundred forest-dwellers, and a thousand celibate students. (69)

Whether one is an atheist, a practitioner of forbidden acts, of mixed caste, or even a thief—Prajāpati has declared that there is no other cause for attaining the yogas than the practice of giving. (2.10.70)
His ancestors are gratified, just as farmers are by a timely rain;
for whether it be a son or a grandson, he shall feed one absorbed in meditation. (71)
If meditative monks are not available, one should feed those who observe the celibate life;
if even they are unavailable, one should feed a neutral householder as well. (72)
One who might stand on one foot for a hundred years subsisting only on air is surpassed by the practitioner of meditation; such is the instruction of Brahmā. (73)
For perfected beings (siddhas) indeed wander this earth in the form of brahmins;
therefore, one should approach an arriving guest with palms joined in reverence. ||74||
One should worship them with an offering vessel, with a dwelling, and with food. These lords of yoga, the gods, always range over the earth as far as the oceans upon their thighs,
moving in various forms while protecting the subjects through righteousness.
Therefore, a man should indeed give gifts to a Brahmin guest;
I shall now describe the various gifts as well as their respective fruits. (76)
A dwelling among yogis is better than a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred royal consecrations, and a thousand lotus-sacrifices.
This first host of the ancestors of immeasurable splendor has been described;
indeed, this host remained then, manifesting itself throughout the seven periods of time.
Henceforth, I shall again declare all the groups of ancestors (pitṛgaṇas), as well as their lineage, their abode, and their meditative dispositions, in due order.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Commencement of the Śrāddha Procedure," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Seven groups of ancestors (pitṛgaṇas) are recorded as the best among the wise, residing in heaven;
four of them possess form, while three of them are formless. I shall now proclaim their creation of the worlds; listen to it. ||1||
Those who are their daughters, and those who are remembered as their grandsons—among them, there are three supreme groups who bear the very form of Dharma. ||2||
I shall briefly state their names and the creation of the worlds, wherein the radiant ones known as the Virajas dwell. (3)
The formless hosts of Pitṛs were indeed the sons of Prajāpati Viraja, O best of the twice-born; they are renowned as the Vairājas. This is proclaimed as the first kalpa of the Vairājas.
Their mental daughter was named Menā,
the auspicious wife of Himavat, the great mountain, from whom Maināka is said to have been born.
Born as the bearer of all medicinal herbs and possessing the nature of a mine of all jewels, there was a preeminent and meritorious mountain; Krauñca was his son.
The king of mountains begot three daughters upon Menā:
Aparṇā, Ekaparṇā, and the third, Ekapāṭalā.
Two of them, however, being without leaves and without a fixed abode, practiced austerities:
Ekaparṇī at a banyan tree and Ekapāṭalā at a trumpet-flower tree.
For a hundred thousand years, they performed that penance which is difficult even for gods and dānavas to practice.
One who subsists on a single leaf should practice as an *ekaparṇī*; likewise, one who subsists on a single *pāṭala* flower should act as an *ekapāṭalā*.
Every two thousand years, indeed, Prajāpati would take food;
there was one among them who remained without food, and her mother addressed her.
For her mother, pained with affection, was restraining her by saying "Um," yet the goddess,
acting with perverse conduct, spoke thus to her mother.
That highly fortunate woman, renowned throughout the three worlds, was called "Umā" by him because of her conduct; thus was that auspicious lady etymologically defined.
This world, consisting of these three maidens, shall endure eternally;
for as long as the earth endures, it shall remain proud of their ascetic power.
All those three goddesses were embodiments of austerity, endowed with the power of yoga; they were highly fortunate and possessed perpetual youth. ||14||
All were expounders of Brahman and all were perpetual virgins; among them, Umā was the most excellent, the best, and possessed of the fairest complexion.
Endowed with the power of great yoga, she attended upon Mahādeva;
her son was Dantakaṇva Uśanas, the delighter of Bhṛgu.
Asita’s wife was Ekaparṇī, a virtuous woman firm in her vows;
she was given by Himavat to that wise teacher of yoga.
She bore him a mind-born son, Devala, who was most devoted to Brahman.
And among these maidens, the third, Ekapāṭalā,
attended upon Jaigīṣavya, the son of Śataśilāka.
Śaṅkha and Likhita were also his two sons, born not from a womb;
these indeed were the illustrious and auspicious daughters of Himavat. (19)
She is Rudrāṇī, preeminent and surpassing all others by her own virtues; the mutual affection between these two, Umā and Śaṅkara, is such as no other can equal.
Having learned of the union of those two who were joined together, the slayer of Vṛtra became suspicious;
fearing the birth of offspring from those two who were engaged in sexual intercourse,
Indra dispatched the bearer of oblations (Agni) to their presence.
"O Consumer of Oblations, bring about this obstacle to our pleasure;
since you are omnipresent, no fault shall then be found in you. (22)
When he had spoken thus, Agni acted accordingly;
having cast off the body of Umā, the semen was discharged upon the ground. (23)
Then, O Śāṃśapāyana, the goddess, being enraged, cursed Agni and spoke these words to the Fire-god with a voice faltering from anger: ||24||
"O Fire-god, since you have created this obstacle to pleasure while I was still unsatiated, you have done what ought not to be done; therefore, you are evil-minded. (25)
"Since you have thus borne this embryo—terrible, pure, and of great splendor—bear this embryo indeed; such is your bearing of the staff. (26)
O twice-born ones, due to that curse, the Fire-god, having become the internal embryo of Rudrāṇī,
indeed carried the fetus for many groups of years.
Having approached the Gaṅgā, he said: "Listen, O best of rivers!
I have experienced very great exhaustion on account of bearing the fetus. (28)
"Therefore, O river, bear this fetus for my benefit;
and by my grace, your exhaustion shall indeed become slight. (29)
Having said, "So be it," that great river, greatly delighted,
then bore that embryo with a burning heart.
She too, the great river, being distressed by great hardship,
remained intent on bearing the embryo for an exceedingly long period of time.
The auspicious womb within her, which had been taken up by her in the beautiful Himalayas,
released that embryo— blazing like a fire— into the lovely and wondrous grove of reeds known as Śaravaṇa, where the trees were in full bloom.
There was born the son of Rudra, Agni, and Gaṅgā, possessing a ruddy luster, resembling a hundred suns, endowed with great splendor and majesty. ||33||
When that illustrious prince, the son of Jahnavī, was born,
the sky was filled with celestial chariots as if by birds.
Divine drums resounded in the sky with sweet tones, and the Siddhas and Cāraṇas moving through the air released a rain of flowers. ||35||
The chief Gandharvas sang here and there on all sides, as did the Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and Kinnaras everywhere. ||36||
Thousands of great serpents and the most excellent of birds attended upon the illustrious son of Śaṅkara, who was like Agni;
at that time, by his power, the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas [were overcome].
At first, he saw the fire born of the wives of the Seven Sages as they were proceeding to perform their ablutions, with the exception of Arundhatī.
Surrounded by them— who were exceedingly affectionate toward him as if they were his own mothers— that lord, fierce and resembling the rising sun, shone resplendent.
Desiring to see all the goddesses simultaneously, the illustrious and highly resplendent son of Jahnavi, who possesses six faces, emitted them out of affection for them.
The glorious one, with eyes like lotus petals, resembling the rising sun;
by whose birth the worlds were eclipsed by his splendor. (41)
Because the hosts of Dānavas were unable to endure him when he was born and were routed by him,
the powerful one is therefore called Skanda.
Because that ancient one was reared by the Kṛttikās, the slayer of asuras is therefore renowned as Kārttikeya. (43)
Then, as that enemy of the Daityas yawned, his own power Aparājitā emerged from his mouth, which was filled with garlands of flames. 44.
And for the sake of Skanda’s sport,
the powerful Viṣṇu indeed created two birds from Garuḍa, who were the Prabhadrakas.
A peacock and a cock were given by Vāyu, as was a banner;
Sarasvatī gave him a great lute of loud sound;
Aja was given by Svayambhū, and a ram was given by Śambhu. (46)
O brahmins, when Māyā was sporting on Mount Krauñca, and when Tāraka, the preeminent among the Asuras who had risen up, was struck down; ||47||
The illustrious and powerful lord, the enemy of the Daityas and son of Agni, was consecrated as the commander-in-chief by the highly fortunate gods, including Indra and Upendra.
Thus is the Lord of the Divine Army recited: the leader of men, Skanda, the crusher of the enemies of the gods, the sovereign lord of all the worlds. 49.
She saw various *pramatha* spirits, as well as *dāva* beings, hosts of *bhūtas*,
diverse *mātṛ*s, and likewise the hosts of *vināyakas*;
she beheld these while falling from the celestial realm, descending from the sky.

In those [atoms], he beheld his ancestors, fallen in numbers equal to motes of dust—extremely subtle, yet not having abandoned their fires, like consecrated fires within the sacrificial hearths. Then, falling headlong, he cried out to them, "Save me! (51–52).
Addressed by them with the words "Do not fear," she became reassured;
then, indeed, she propitiated those ancestors with a piteous voice.
The ancestors said to the maiden: "O girl of pure smiles, you have fallen from your sovereignty due to transgression; having lost your power through your own fault, you must now perform penance. (54)
And by those very bodies with which the deities perform actions here in this world,
those same deities experience the fruit of those actions in this world.
Actions bear fruit immediately in the state of divinity or after death as a human;
therefore, you shall obtain the fruit of being childless after death.
By saying this, the ancestors were indeed propitiated;
having meditated, they showed favor to her out of compassion. (57)
Having perceived that this event was inevitable, the gods, the Soma-drinking ancestors, and the daughters of King Amāvasu spoke thus. (58)
"But when that great-souled one is born upon the earth in human form, you shall become his daughter and regain these worlds of yours. (59)
"In the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, you shall be born from the womb of a fish as the daughter of this very king Amāvasu by Adrikā;
you will give birth to the heir of the sage Parāśara."
That brahmin seer shall indeed divide this single Veda into four parts.
"You yourself shall procreate two sons for Śantanu, the son of Mahābhiṣa, who will increase his fame— namely Vicitravīrya, the knower of dharma."
"O King, having produced these sons— Citrāṅgada and yourself, endowed with the qualities of splendor and strength— you shall regain your own worlds."
Due to your transgression against the ancestors, you shall undergo a contemptible birth;
you will become the daughter of that very king by Adrikā.
"Having become a maiden, you shall then attain these worlds.
Thus addressed, that daughter of the fisherman was born as Satyavatī.
The sons of Adrikā were born among the Matsyas from Amāvasu;
they were born of the union of the mountains and the Matsyas at the confluence of the Gaṅgā.
For that king, indeed, that maiden [was born] from his own valor;
those worlds named Virajas always shine for him, and those hosts [of gods] in heaven.
There, the ancestors known as the Agniṣvāttas are remembered as possessing radiant splendor;
them the hosts of Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Bhūtas, serpents, and Piśācas propitiate, seeking their rewards. (68)
These are declared to be the sons of the Prajāpati Pulaha;
these three auspicious groups are said to be the bearers of the forms of Dharma.
Their daughter, renowned by the name Pīvarī,
will become a Yoginī, a consort of Yoga, and likewise a mother of Yoga,
when the twenty-eighth divine age, the Dvāpara, arrives.
Born in the lineage of Parāśara was one named Śuka, a man of great asceticism. ||71||
The illustrious Yogī Mahāyogī was born from Vyāsa in Araṇyā, O best of the twice-born, like a smokeless fire. (72)
In that daughter of his father, he begot Kṛṣṇa, Gaura, Prabhu, Śambhu, and likewise Bhūriśruta— all of whom were well-versed in the teachings of the Yogācāryas.
[He gave] the maiden Kīrtimatī, a yoginī and mother of yoga, who was the mother of Brahmadatta and the queen of Aṇuha. (74)
Having produced these sons who were embodiments of Dharma, and having attained mastery in yoga,
as well as through the asceticism of great yoga, he established himself in the state of non-returning,
endowed with the rays of the sun, and reached the stage of no-more-rebirth (apunarbhava).
The Great Sage will become all-pervading and liberated. ||76||
Those Pitṛs who are formless and those who bear the form of Dharma—these are three groups; learn now of four others besides them.
O best of the twice-born, those whom I shall mention—embodied beings of great splendor—were born from Svadhā; they were indeed the daughters of Agni and the sons of Kavi.
O twice-born ones, the Pitṛs, radiant and luminous, dwell in the divine worlds that shine with light and abound in all desired objects; indeed, they cause those worlds to flourish.
Their daughter was Mānasī, renowned in heaven by the name Gau;
she was Dattasenā, the beloved queen of Śukra by the prince [Bhṛgu].
Thus, thirty-one [descendants] of the Bhṛgus are celebrated as increasers of their fame.
Those worlds, filled with rays of light, remain situated in the sky, completely surrounding it. ||81||
For these sons of Aṅgiras, who were nurtured together with the Sādhyas,
are remembered as the radiant Pitṛs invited in heaven;
beholding those hosts of Kṣatriyas, they bring them prosperity for the sake of their rewards.
The mental daughter of these [gods], renowned by the name Yaśodā, was the wife of Viśvamahat and the daughter-in-law of Viśvaśarman. (83)
The queen was the mother of the great-souled royal sage Khaṭvāṅga, at whose sacrifice in ancient times this verse was sung by the great seers in song: [84]
Having thus witnessed the birth of the fire from the high-souled Śāṇḍilya,
those who behold the sacrificer Dilīpa with well-composed minds—
that great-souled one devoted to truth— become immortal conquerors of heaven. (85)
The ancestors named Ājyapās are the sons of the Prajāpati Kardama; they were born from Pulaha, who was himself born of him (Kardama). 86.
These birds dwell in these worlds that move at will;
indeed, those seeking rewards cause these hosts of Vaiśyas to be honored in the Śrāddha ceremony.
Among these, the eldest was the virtuous and renowned Sannati, free from passion,
who was the mother of Yayāti and the wife of Nahuṣa.
The Pitṛs named Sukālas are the progeny of the Prajāpati Vasiṣṭha;
they are the sons of Hiraṇyagarbha, and the Śūdras indeed nourish them. 89.
Those worlds where they dwell in heaven are called Mānasa; their mind-born daughter is Narmadā, the best of rivers. Flowing toward the southern region, she nourishes all living beings.
For the mother of Trasadasyu was indeed the consort of Purukutsa. ||91||
By accepting these [principles], the Lord of the Manvantara becomes the progenitor of the mother;
at the beginning of the Manvantara, he causes the Śrāddha rites to proceed in every respect.
O best of the twice-born, because [the ancestors] belong to all [classes] in their respective order,
one should therefore offer the śrāddha here with faith according to one's own dharma.
Whatever is given by all [the ancestors] using silver vessels, or those adorned with silver,
while placing the word "svadhā" before it, truly gratifies the ancestors.
Having performed the replenishment of Soma and of Agni Vaivasvata,
and having sung the Udgītha facing north toward the fire, one would then obtain the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
One indeed pleases the ancestors through devotion, and the ancestors in turn please him;
for one who desires prosperity or offspring, the ancestors bestow prosperity, progeny, and heaven—of this there is no doubt. (96)
The rite for the ancestors always takes precedence even over the rite for the gods;
for it is traditionally taught that the nourishment of the ancestors precedes that of the deities. (97)
For the subtle course of yoga and the satisfactions of the ancestors are not seen even by the fleshly eye, except through well-established ascetic power. 98.
Thus, these are indeed the Pitṛs, the worlds, the daughters, the grandsons, and the sacrificers who are said to sustain them. (99)
Four of them possess form, while three of them are formless;

with devotion, all the gods, including Indra, with palms joined and minds fixed upon them, diligently perform *śrāddha* rites for them with great care. (2.11.100) 73.60 All of them, with palms joined and their minds absorbed in him, are his devotees.
And the Viśvas, the Sikatās, the Pṛśnijās, and likewise the Śṛṅgiṇas. ||101||
Furthermore, the black, the white, and the goats worship according to the prescribed rites;
so too do those people who wear garments of air and the Divākirtyas.
The Lekhas and the Maruts, as well as the celestial dwellers beginning with Brahmā, and all the sages beginning with Atri, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras. ||103||
The Yakṣas, Nāgas, Suparṇas, and Kinnaras, together with the Rākṣasas, all constantly worshipped the Pitṛs, seeking their rewards. (104)
Thus, when these great-souled ones are honored and worshipped at a śrāddha ceremony,
they bestow all desires by the hundreds and thousands.
Having abandoned the cycle of existence in the three worlds as well as the fear of old age and death,
the ancestors bestow liberation and the sovereignty consisting of yoga.
Furthermore, the Grandfathers bestow the means to liberation, sovereignty, subtle bodies, the deities, complete dispassion, and infinity. (107)
Sovereignty is ordained through yoga; sovereignty is the supreme wealth.
Without the sovereignty of yoga, liberation can in no way be attained. (108)
Just as the flight of a wingless bird in the sky is impossible, so too liberation is the most excellent among all dharmas, the eternal dharma. (109)
The Grandfathers bestow thousands of celestial chariots, yoked with throngs of Apsarases and fulfilling all desires.
Wisdom, nourishment, memory, intelligence, sovereignty, and even health— these they grant.
For it is through the grace of the ancestors that this is attained by one of great soul. ||111||
Grandfathers bestow pearls, lapis lazuli, garments, tens of thousands of horses and elephants, and even crores of jewels.

The ancestors always joyfully bestow upon men vehicles yoked with swans and peacocks, adorned with pearls and lapis lazuli, draped with networks of tinkling bells, and ever-blooming with flowers and fruits. (113) 73.73
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for Śrāddha," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu. ||11||
Bṛhaspati said:
A vessel made of gold, silver, or copper is said to be the vessel for the ancestors; likewise, a vessel made of silver or coated with silver is said to be the vessel for the ancestors. (1)
Likewise, the sight of silver and its gift are said to be an infinite,
inexhaustible, and heavenly offering for the ancestors;
by this gift, virtuous sons indeed deliver their ancestors.
For indeed, O dear one, the *svadhā* (offering) milked by the ancestors in former times shines within this vessel;
when it is given to those who seek the gift of *svadhā*, that [merit] becomes inexhaustible.
The proximity to, the sight of, or even the gift of a black antelope skin destroys demons, bestows Vedic luster, and carries those [offerings] to the ancestors. ||4||
Gold, silver, copper, a daughter's son, a woolen blanket, sesame seeds, cloth, and likewise a triple staff and a yoga-mat are purifying objects. (5)
This is the supreme, eternal Vedic injunction for the rite of ancestral offerings (śrāddha);
it increases longevity, fame, progeny, wisdom, and the continuity of one's lineage.
In the south-eastern direction, specifically at the intermediate point,
there is a square space measuring one cubit on all sides, well-proportioned and firmly constructed.
At the command of the Pitṛs, I shall duly describe the sacred site,
which bestows wealth, health, and long life, and increases strength and complexion.

There, three pits should be made and three staffs of Khadira wood; they should be made one cubit (ratni) long and adorned with silver. They should be made one span (vitasti) in length and four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula) wide on all sides. ||9||
Facing the east or the south, remaining on the ground and likewise free from perforations,
one who is pure should constantly drench them with water purified by strainers.
Indeed, purification is achieved through cow's milk and speech alone;
for by constant libation in this manner, eternal satisfaction arises.
In this world and the next, he shall be illustrious and endowed with all accomplishments;
thus, he who always worships the ancestors while bathing at the three periods of the day,
properly and according to the rules with the mantra, shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
One should place that [fire] in a pit four finger-breadths deep on the new moon day;
those sacrifices known as the twenty-one-fold (triḥ-sapta) indeed sustain the three worlds.
For him, nourishment, sovereignty, long life, and progeny flourish;
he enjoys manifold prosperity and attains liberation in due course. (14)
It removes evil, it is purifying, and it likewise yields the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Indeed, this which yields the fruit of the horse-sacrifice has been honored and worshipped by the twice-born;
therefore, I shall declare the mantra, which is nectar-like and fashioned by Brahmā. (15)
Salutations to the deities, to the ancestors, and indeed to the great yogis; salutations also to Svadhā and Svāhā, which are ever-present. ||16||
One should always recite this three times at the beginning and the end of the Śrāddha;
one should also recite it with a concentrated mind during the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa).
Thus, the ancestors arrive quickly and the Rākṣasas flee.
Furthermore, this mantra always saves the ancestors in the three worlds when it is recited during a śrāddha ceremony by those who speak of Brahman with self-restraint. (18)
One who desires sovereignty should always recite this mantra without indolence;
it increases valor, purity, wealth, courage, prosperity, longevity, and strength. (19)
I shall proclaim the auspicious *Saptārciṣ*, which grants all desires and by means of which the ancestors are gratified through recitation and observance. 2.12.20.
I always pay homage with the eye of yoga to those ancestors of radiant splendor, both formless and embodied, who are absorbed in meditation. (21)
I bow to those bestowers of desires, who are the progenitors of Indra and the other gods, as well as of Bhṛgu and Mārīci, of the Seven Sages, and of the Pitṛs. 22.
Having paid obeisance to Manu and the other lords of the gods, as well as to the Sun and the Moon, and indeed to all the ancestors who bestow welfare; ||23||
Then, with palms joined in reverence, I bow to the ancestors and grandfathers of the stars, such as Carā and the others, as well as to Heaven and Earth. (24)
I bow with palms joined in reverence to those who are the progenitors of the celestial sages, who are honored by all the worlds, and who are the constant granters of fearlessness.
With palms joined in reverence, I bow to Prajāpati Kaśyapa, to Soma, to Varuṇa, and to the Lords of Yoga.
Salutations to the seven groups of ancestors in the seven worlds;
salutations likewise to the Self-Existent One, to Brahmā, who possesses the eye of yoga.
Thus has been spoken this which is worshipped by the hosts of Brahmarṣis along with the Seven Sages;
for it is supremely purifying, glorious, and the destroyer of Rākṣasas. (28)
A man who is joined with this rite obtains three boons;
the ancestors on earth bestow food, long life, and sons. (29)
Endowed with supreme devotion, full of faith, and having conquered his senses, he who,
being constantly composed, recites the *Saptārciṣ* mantra will become the sole sovereign of the earth with its seven continents and oceans.
Whatever is cooked in the house, whether it be solid food (bhakṣya) or soft food (bhojya), one must never eat it in that sanctuary without first offering it. 31.
Hereafter, I shall describe in due order the vessels for the bali offering;
listen as I speak of what fruit is declared for each of them. 32.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Śrāddha," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Bṛhaspati said:
The *pālāśa* wood brings the splendor of the Brahman; the desire for sovereignty resides in the *aśvattha*;
and lordship over all beings is always proclaimed to be in the *plakṣa*.
