The Nyagrodha tree is said to bring nourishment for one desiring growth; it bestows intelligence, wisdom, fortitude, and mindfulness.
The Kāśmarya vessel is declared to be a destroyer of demons and a source of fame.
The highest good fortune in the world is said to reside in the Madhuka tree;
one who makes offerings in a vessel of Phalgu wood shall attain all desires. ||3||
Furthermore, there is supreme splendor and especially manifest renown for the performer;
likewise, in the *bilva* tree reside prosperity, intelligence, and eternal longevity. (4)
For one who makes bamboo vessels, the rain-cloud shall indeed rain incessantly upon their fields, gardens, ponds, and all their crops.
For those who give the first-fruits of the harvest to these very same worthy recipients,
it is said that they obtain the fruit of all sacrifices here, even if only once.
He who always offers garlands and fragrant substances of every kind to the ancestors shines forth endowed with prosperity, like the sun.
He who offers incense such as guggulu and other fragrances to the ancestors,
combined with honey and clarified butter, shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
One who offers incense endowed with the quality of fragrance, which is pleasing and dedicated to the ancestors,
obtains offspring through women both in this world and in the next;
therefore, one should indeed always offer it to the ancestors without weariness.
He who, being self-restrained, always offers a lamp to the ancestors, obtains in this world an incomparable and ever-auspicious vision. ||2.13.10||
Through splendor, fame, beauty, and strength,
he becomes renowned upon earth and shines in the third heaven;
surrounded by Apsarases, he rejoices at the forefront of his celestial chariot.
Being self-restrained and pure, one should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, and oblations of clarified butter; with fruits, roots, and prostrations, one should worship the ancestors.
Having first honored the twice-born, one should afterwards worship them with an abundance of food. 12.
At the time of the ancestral rite (śrāddha), the ancestors, having become like the wind, constantly enter the twice-born upon seeing them; therefore, I say this to you.
Having honored the best of the twice-born with garments, food, gifts, as well as various kinds of edibles and drinks, and likewise with cows, horses, and villages; ||14||
The ancestors become pleased when the twice-born are honored;
therefore, one should worship the best of the twice-born with food according to the prescribed rule. 15.
With his right and left hands, the twice-born man,
remaining vigilant, should perform the drawing of lines and likewise the sprinkling of water during the śrāddha rite.
The wise man should offer darbha grass, rice-balls, as well as various kinds of food, flowers, the gift of fragrance, and ornaments— one of each for every recipient.
Having properly nourished his people, the twice-born man should become superior like Vaiśravaṇa;
he should perform an oil massage according to the rule with three tufts of *darbha* grass.
One should offer excellent food to the ancestors with the sacred thread over the right shoulder;
then, having uttered his name, one should likewise offer thread for the sake of clothing for all of them.
Cutting, nourishing, and likewise scraping—these are said to be performed for the gods once, and for the ancestors three times. (2.13.20)
Having offered a single purifier (pavitra) with his hand to all the ancestors, one by one, using the *caila* mantra, he obtains the benefit arising from the sight [of the offerings]. (21)
Devoted to the ancestors, he should place three balls of rice mixed with ghee and sesame seeds upon the ground,
having placed his left knee upon the earth.
Having summoned the fathers, grandfathers, and likewise the great-grandfathers—

the ancestors facing east— he should diligently offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) with the *pitṛ-tīrtha* of his hand, properly circling them while keeping his sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*) and remaining alert.
Some men desire that for the maternal grandfathers there should be separate offerings of food, water, flowers, and various kinds of edibles.
One should carefully offer three balls of food in succession, using the thumb and increasing their size, placing the balls between the knees in the proper order. ||25||
With his right and left hands, there is a reversal regarding both the Dharma and the Mantra;
"Homage to you, O Pitṛs," [he says] with subtle [mantras], always indeed thus unwearied. (26)
First, he should offer the first ball of rice with both hands toward the south, reciting without weariness: "Homage to you, O gentle Pitṛs. (27)
With both hands, the right over the left, one who is entirely free from sloth should perform the service of the mortar's line and the water-vessel for Dharma. 28.
One should give new linen thread, as well as red cotton thread, silk from leaves, and the thread of the ancestors; however, one should avoid silk from silkworm cocoons.
One should avoid that [thread] at a sacrifice, even if it comes from unwashed cloth;
for these do not please [the ancestors], and thus the prosperity of the giver would be diminished.
They say that the collyrium from Mount Trikakuda is always the best;
likewise, oil that has been carefully preserved from black sesame seeds is excellent.
Both sandalwood and agallochum, tamāla, uśīra, and lotus, as well as the finest guggulu incense and turuṣka incense. ||32||
The finest white jasmine flowers, as well as red and blue lotuses, and whatever other fragrant blossoms there are in their entirety— 33.
The *japā*, *sumanasa*, *bhaṇḍīra*, *upakā*, *makuṭa*, and *kuṇḍaka* flowers should always be avoided in the performance of *śrāddha* rites. (34)

Those flowers which are devoid of fragrance, those that have an unpleasant odor, and those that are otherwise unsuitable—all such flowers should be avoided by one seeking prosperity at that time. (35)
Likewise, the twice-born, having fasted and being self-restrained, should face the north;
the patron, however, should worship according to the rules while facing the south.
Facing them, one should diligently offer *darbha* grass and funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
By this procedure, one should directly worship one's own ancestors. (37)
Indeed, the green *sapiñjalī* trees, glossy with flowers and well-composed, stand established at the *pitṛtīrtha* by means of a gift measuring a *ratni*. (38)
Likewise, those that are blue at the base, such as the *prastara* and others arising from the *yakula*,
as well as the *śmāmāka* and *nīvāra* grains, are declared to be difficult to ward off.
The excellent Prajāpati, who had been previously celebrated, then appeared;
his hairs fell upon the earth from the path of the sky.
Therefore, those regions which are pure and as vast as space are honored in the rite of Śrāddha;
one who desires prosperity should perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) upon them.
They possess the nourishment of progeny, splendor, fame, and are endowed with the beauty of their offspring;
they are ever radiant, free from sin, and devoid of evil.
Facing south, he should spread darbha grass only once for the sake of the pindas;
being disciplined, with the tips of the grass pointing east and south, he will also declare the ritual procedure.
Neither dejected nor angry, and certainly not with a distracted mind, a wise man should always perform the śrāddha, having fixed his mind in one-pointed concentration. 44.
I shall destroy everything that is impure; all the gods and dānavas have been slain by me, as well as the hosts of rākṣasas, yakṣas, piśācas, and all the yātudhānas. (45)
Thus, all the asuras avoid that person for whom food has been seen by the father;
and in whatever place this mantra is recited, the rākṣasas indeed avoid that place. ||46||
By this method, a twice-born man should always perform the Śrāddha rite constantly;
whatever is desired in his mind, that very thing the ancestors shall grant.
When the Śrāddha has been performed with constant effort, the ancestors become joyful in mind and the Rākṣasas become dejected. (48)
In a Śrāddha rite, one should always avoid grasses such as the śūdrā, kṣīravāśu, balvaja, tarava, vāraṇa, lava, and lavavarṣa, as well as other similar types of grass. 49.
Likewise, the application of collyrium, ointments, perfumes, and unguents,
as well as all rites performed with *kāśa* grass that has been reborn, shall yield their full fruit.
Furthermore, the Kāśas, the Punarbhavas, the Barhaṇas, and the Upabarhaṇas—these are the Pitṛs who are gods, and the gods who are again the Pitṛs. (51)
This mantra has been proclaimed for flowers, perfumes, incense, and the like;
having procured them with effort from a Brahmin for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa) at the conclusion of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 52.
"To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, Svadhā! To Aṅgiras, obeisance!
For the sake of accomplishing the rite, one may offer oblations that are either non-heavenly or worldly. (53)
Having thus placed a fuel-stick within, the oblation is prescribed.
With a concentrated mind, he should carefully tend the sacrificial fire with great effort. ||54||
Saying, "To Agni Kavyavāha, svadhā! Obeisance to Aṅgiras! And to Yama Aṅgiras, svadhā! Obeisance! [he offers]. (55)
These indeed are the oblation-mantras for the mantras in their proper sequence:
always for Agni from the south, and likewise for Soma from the interior.
One should constantly offer oblations to Vivasvat between these two [rites], as well as the ritual service (upacāra), the utterance of *svadhā*, and whatever scraping (ullekhana) may be required.
Homage, recitation of mantras, salutation, and especially sprinkling with water;
likewise, the application of collyrium and ointment, as well as the scattering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas). ||58||
That is said to be equal to the fruit of the horse-sacrifice when preceded by the mantras;
one should perform all the rites as prescribed with great care. 59.
Especially in a well-kindled fire that is smokeless and flickering, one should offer many oblations for the successful accomplishment of the ritual act.
If one offers oblations into a fire that is unkindled and full of smoke, we have heard that the sacrificer will become blind and childless. (61)
Whether it has little fuel, or is dry, or emits sparks in every direction, or is attended by flames and smoke—that fire does not lead to success. //62//
Where the ground is particularly foul-smelling, blue, or black, one should know that defeat is imminent.
Radiant, with a compact crest of flames, originating from ghee and gold,
smooth, and moving clockwise— such a fire portends the accomplishment of one's purpose.
He receives eternal worship from hosts of men and women;
by him, the imperishable and immutable ancestors become honored.
Vessels made of udumbara wood, bowls, fruits, and likewise sacrificial fuel—
these are especially pure and fit for use at a śrāddha ceremony.
Or, O best of the twice-born, for the sake of purification during rites of birth and other ceremonies, the fruit that has been declared by me regarding vessels in the rite of Śrāddha is the same. 67.
All that should be known in its entirety, as well as the sacrificial fires in their proper order—having composed my mind, I indeed perform this for the sake of the Supreme. (68)
Having been granted permission with the words "Do so" by those best of the twice-born,
he should take his wife and sons and offer oblations into the fire.
The *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, *plakṣa*, *aśvattha*, and *vikaṅkata* trees, as well as the *udumbara*, *bilva*, and *candana*, are fit for sacrifice. (2.13.70)
The Sarala, Devadāru, Śāla, and Khadira—these trees are especially recommended for the purpose of sacrificial fuel. (71)
Village-grown trees, as well as thorny ones, are fit for sacrifice by whatever means;
they are honored for the purpose of sacrificial fuel—such is the word of the ancestors.
Listen as I declare to you the fruit of that action which belongs to one who offers oblations into the fire with fuel-sticks made of *kalkaleya* wood. (73)
That which is made of iron fulfills all desires, for it indeed yields the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Likewise, the śleṣmātaka, naktamāla, kapittha, and śālmali [trees are used]. ||74||

One should avoid the *nīpa* and *vibhītaka* trees, as well as climbing vines; one should also avoid trees that serve as dwellings for birds, and those trees which are traditionally considered unfit for sacrifice. ||75||
At the end of the mantra, "svadhā" is the word used for the ancestors,
while "svāhā" is prescribed for the gods in the sacrificial rite.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Śrāddha," in the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa* proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
"The gods and the ancestors, as well as other ancestors besides them—this is the Atharvaṇa injunction," Bṛhaspati replied. (1)
One should worship the ancestors first, and especially the gods as well;
for in this world, one should diligently honor the ancestors even before the gods. ||2||
The daughter of Dakṣa, known in the world by the name Viśvā, was given to Dharma according to the sacred law and in accordance with righteousness, O knower of dharma;
her sons were the high-souled Viśvedevas, so says the Śruti. (3)
Renowned throughout the three worlds and honored by all people, those great-souled ones together performed severe and mighty penance. ||4||
On a delightful peak of the Himalayas, frequented by gods and gandharvas, [there was a place] traversed by all the apsarases and served by gods and gandharvas. ||5||
Then the ancestors, pleased by their pure minds, said to them: "Choose a boon; we are gratified. What desire shall we fulfill for you?"

When the ancestors had spoken thus, Brahmā, the creator of the three worlds and lord of creatures, then spoke these words to Viśvāmitra: evamukte tu pitṛbhistadā trailokyabhāvanaḥ | prajānāmadhipo brahmā viśvāmitramidamabravīt ||7||
Brahmā said:
Mahādeva, possessed of great splendor, was heated by their austerity; being well-pleased by that austerity, he said: "What desire shall I grant you? (8)
Thus addressed then by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds,
they all together spoke to Brahmā, the progenitor of the worlds.
"May we have a share in our *śrāddha*; this is the boon we desire.
Then Brahmā replied to those who are honored in the three heavens:
"Whatever boon has been desired by you shall indeed come to pass in this very way;
having said 'So be it' to the ancestors, it shall be thus, without a doubt. (11)
"You must be with us in whatever is performed here;
indeed, in the Śrāddha rite prepared by us, you shall have the seat of honor. (12)
This shall come to pass among men; I tell you this as the truth: he will honor you with garlands, perfumes, and likewise with food. (13)
And because he is the giver to you, he will give to us;
therefore, our dismissal shall be first, and that of the deities afterwards. (14)

Protection of the Śrāddha and hospitality—these are the two rites [to be performed] toward living beings, deities, and ancestors during the Śrāddha ceremony. When performed according to this rule, all of this will be perfectly accomplished. (15)
Having thus granted this boon to them, Brahmā, together with the hosts of ancestors, [departed].
The God, who bestows favor upon all beings, moved about according to his pleasure.
The Vedas declare that five great sacrifices have been prescribed for men;
a person should constantly perform these five great sacrifices. (17)
Listen to the destination where the givers shall go:
they attain the abode of Brahmā, which is free from fear, free from ego, free from sorrow, and devoid of pain or fatigue, and is preceded by the fulfillment of all desires. 18.
These five [rites] must also be performed by a Śūdra, excluding the mantras;
however, he who eats otherwise incurs perpetual debt.
The evil-minded man who cooks food for his own sake alone consumes only debt;
therefore, a wise man should always perform the five great sacrifices.
Some desire that an offering of food (naivedya) be made with effort even while [the person] is still alive;
likewise, one should offer a bali-oblation toward the north, as well as a water-pot.
One should prepare the oblation well-known [to tradition] and cast it higher and higher;
first, one should skillfully toss the oblation toward the horns of another's cow.
The funeral cake (piṇḍa) intended for the ancestors should not be given to one who is still living;
rather, he should be fed with desired food and edibles according to the rule.
I shall now explain with care this procedure ordained by the Vedas. (23)
For these high-souled ones—the gods of gods and even the ancestors—desire that the teachers receive some offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) afterwards. ||24||
Indeed, the constant worship of Brahmins in every respect is for that very purpose;
so spoke Bṛhaspati, who is skilled in the matters of dharma and artha. ||25||
One should first offer the piṇḍa and afterwards feed the brāhmaṇas.
The great-souled ancestors, whose nature is yoga and who are born of yoga, being established in yoga, cause the moon to swell. ||26||
Therefore, one who is pure and devoted to that [practice] should offer rice-balls to the yogis;
for this becomes for the ancestors like an oblation actually poured into the fire. (27)
If a yogi is seated upon the foremost seat even among thousands of Brahmins, he shall ferry both the patron and the eaters across [the ocean of existence], like a boat upon the water. (28)
Where there is the favoring of the wicked and the humiliation of the virtuous,
there the rod of divine punishment falls instantly and violently.
Having abandoned the traditional teaching that accords with the Dharma, if one should feed a fool there—neglecting the primary ritual—the donor perishes therein. (2.14.30)
One who desires enjoyments should always diligently offer the *piṇḍa* into the fire;
one who desires progeny should offer it to the ancestors, with the former being the first among them. (31)
Seeking supreme splendor, he constantly bestows it upon cows;
he constantly bestows wisdom, honor, fame, and renown upon cows. (32)
Seeking long life, he offers [food] to the crows;
and seeking delicacy, he offers it to the cocks. (33)
Thus has been declared the fruit resulting from the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
One should offer them either toward the sky or remain facing the auspicious south; for the sky is the abode of the ancestors, and the southern direction is likewise theirs. (34)
The Brahmins spoke again: "First, let there be the extraction of the funeral cakes";
and when those Brahmins gave their permission, they said, "Let it be raised up. (35)
Having set aside the first portion of all flowers, fruits, and edible foods as well as the rice, one should offer them into the Jātavedas fire.
Having offered into the fire food fit for eating, as well as drinks and excellent fruits, he should then offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) while facing the south.
One should satisfy [the deity] with unctuous, fragrant foods and likewise with savory juices;
with a one-pointed mind, self-restrained, standing with palms joined in reverence, intent upon that and full of faith, a person attains their desires. (38)
From their lack of meanness, their gratitude, their courtesy, and their hospitality, the ancestors bestow upon them sacrifices and gifts. (39)
Henceforth, listen as I describe to you, in due order and according to rule, the gentle rite to be performed after the twice-born have finished their meal. 2.14.40.
Then, having sprinkled the ground and first dug it up, one devoted to the ancestors should there perform the scattering of food (vikirana) according to the rite prescribed by rule.
Then, having pronounced "svadhā," the Brahmins should be given abundant sacrificial fees according to the rules;
having requested permission regarding the remainder of the food and having honored those best of the twice-born,
one should follow them for a short distance with palms joined in reverence and, being self-restrained, bid them farewell.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Śrāddha," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Bṛhaspati said:
The ancestors, who are distinct from others—those whose nature is yoga, who are great-souled, free from sin, and possessed of great splendor—become pleased when worshipped even once. (1)
And for the sake of attaining heaven after death, they bestow upon them vast sovereignty over all desires; and furthermore, they favor those who follow the sequence for the attainment of liberation.
I shall describe them to you, O gentle ones: the lakes and the rivers, as well as the holy pilgrimage sites, the regions, the mountains, and the hermitages.
Meritorious is that mountain Amarakaṇṭaka in the three worlds;
it is a preeminent and holy mountain, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas. ||4||
Where, in ancient times, the venerable Aṅgiras performed most difficult austerities for thousands, millions, and billions of years.
Where there is no passage for Death, nor likewise for the Asuras and Rākṣasas,
and where there is neither fear nor misfortune as long as the earth shall endure.
That best of mountains shines eternally with splendor and fame,
like the Saṃvartaka fire upon the peak of Mālyavat.
Soft, fragrant, golden-hued, and pleasing to behold, these blades known as *kuśa* grow tranquil along the southern bank of the Narmadā. (8)
In former times, the venerable Aṅgiras, possessed of great splendor, beheld a staircase to heaven at his Agnihotra sacrifice, made of excellent kuśa grass intended for the sacrificial strewing.
I shall describe the fruit that accrues to that wise man who, even once, offers funeral cakes upon those Darbha grasses on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka.
That ancestral offering (śrāddha) becomes inexhaustible and increases the satisfaction of the ancestors;
moreover, having reached that sacred field, they always attain invisibility [liberation].
There, the meritorious Jvālārasa is seen even today in every respect;
it is a river that removes the arrows from sentient beings who are pierced by them. (12)
To the southeast of that most excellent mountain is a pond with clockwise whirlpools;
situated on the edge of the Kalinga country, it increases the satisfaction of the ancestors.
O best of sages, regarding that which was declared as the supreme field of accomplishment on earth, even Uśanas, esteemed by both gods and daityas, sang this verse: [14]
Blessed are those men in the world who, having reached Amarakaṇṭaka, being devoted to their ancestors, shall gratify their forefathers with śrāddha offerings. (15)
By practicing austerities there, they will undoubtedly attain perfection;
even if worshipped but once, they shall go to heaven at Amarakaṇṭaka.
On the delightful Mahendra mountain, which is holy and frequented by Śakra, one shall find joy upon ascending it, and a śrāddha performed there yields great fruit. ||17||
When one is disciplined at the lower peak of the Bilva tree, divine vision arises;
invisible to all beings, one traverses the earth like a god. ||18||
At Saptagodāvara, Gokarṇa, and Tapovana, a person obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice by bathing there. ||19||
Having reached Dhūtapāpasthala, a man becomes purified by bathing there;
it was there that Rudra, the God of gods, Maheśvara, performed his austerities.
At Gokarṇa, the brahmins have described the illustration of atheists:
the Sāvitrī of one who is not a brāhmaṇa perishes as he recites it. (21)
Having ascended that peak, the abode of celestial rishis frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, they then go to heaven through their disciplined observance.
It was adorned with divine sandalwood trees and other plants, from which waters mixed with delicious flavors flowed constantly. (23)
From those two, a river flows forth by the name Tāmraparṇī;
like a woman greatly distressed, it flows toward the southern ocean.
The waters of that river, as they mingle with the great ocean, become shells, and from them pearls are born; thus they are known as "shell-pearls. (25)
Having performed the water-offering accompanied by conch shells and pearls,
they are liberated from both mental afflictions and physical diseases and go to Amarāvatī.
According to the sacred tradition, offerings made with sandalwood, conch shells,
and pearls deliver even those ancestors who have committed sins.
At Candratīrtha, at Kumārī, at Kāverī, at the inexhaustible Prabhasa, at the holy sites of Śrīparvata, and likewise on Mount Vaikṛta; ||28||
On Mount Ośira, indeed, trees are seen gathered together in one place:
palāśas, khadiras, bilvas, plakṣas, aśvatthas, and vikaṅkatas. ||29||
O best of the twice-born, this is indeed the perfected sacrificial mandala;
having cast off his limbs within it, a person swiftly goes to Amarāvatī.
Actions performed by oneself succeed at the end of their power; however, those performed for one's ancestors, even if undertaken with difficulty, may also bear fruit.
The sacred Narmadā, the daughter of the Pitṛs and the best among rivers, is there;
indeed, the śrāddha offerings given there become inexhaustible.
In the holy forest of Māṭhara, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
living beings do not vanish on that great mountain.
And on the holy Vindhya mountain, there is a demonstration of dharma and adharma:
the wicked do not see the stream of evil, while the virtuous see the stream. (34)
In that [river], the sin of certain evildoers is not seen;
for those of generally virtuous deeds, that current becomes clearly visible. (35)
In Kauśalā is the tank of Mataṅga, which destroys all sins;
those who bathe therein go to heaven, moving through the air like birds at will. (36)
At the Kumāra-kośala tīrtha, on Mount Pālapañjara, on the bank of the Pāṇḍu river at the edge of the ocean, and likewise in the Paṇḍāraka forest. ||37||
And always at Vimala, Vipāpa, Satkṛtya, Prabhasa, Abhaya, Bhīṣaṇa, Gṛdhrakūṭa, and Jambūmārga. ||38||
At that holy site of the wise teacher Asita, who was a master of yoga,
there too, and especially at the Asitā river, a śrāddha offering performed perpetually yields infinite merit.
At Puṣkara, a śrāddha offering is inexhaustible, and asceticism yields great fruit;
the same should be declared regarding Mahodadhi and Prabhāsa.
On the Devikā is a well named Vṛṣa, frequented by the Siddhas;
its waters always rise up at the sound of cows. 41.
I shall describe the fruit for him who offers a śrāddha at that place, which is always frequented by the lords of yoga who are free from all sins. ||42||
The Śrāddha performed there is inexhaustible and fulfills all desires; it truly gratifies the ancestors.
There, the Jātavedas stone is the eternal, manifest form of Agni himself.
He who enters the fire there rejoices upon the vault of heaven;
when the fire has been extinguished and is born again, what is given therein becomes inexhaustible. 44.
At the holy ford of Daśāśvamedhika and at each of the fifty horse-sacrifice sites, one obtains the fruit of those sacrifices as prescribed; there is no doubt in this matter. ||45||
The sacred ford named Hayaśiras is renowned as the bestower of boons immediately;
by performing a śrāddha there, that offering becomes inexhaustible, and one rejoices in heaven. 46.
The Śrāddha performed at Kumbha is known as the destroyer of sins;
the Śrāddha there is declared to be inexhaustible, as are the recitations, burnt offerings, and austerities.
One should constantly offer libations to the ancestors at the auspicious Ajhatuṅga tīrtha,
where the shadow of the celestial dwellers is always seen on the holy days; there,
what is given becomes inexhaustible on earth, and where the Pāṇḍavas were freed from disease.
I shall declare the fruit that belongs to him who offers a śrāddha at that place, which is always frequented by the lords of yoga who are free from all sins. (49)
By him, the ancestors indeed become personally honored at all times;
he who is self-controlled in this world rejoices in heaven after death.
There is generally a preeminent and meritorious lake named Śiva;
there also is the meritorious Vyāsasara and the divine Brahmasara.
The sacred mountain Ujjanta belongs to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha;
it is the head of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, known as Kāpota and named Puṣpa;
for these were created by Brahmā within them as the fifth Veda.
Having gone there, the twice-born man is liberated from sin, just as the eternal fire is.
An ancestral offering (śrāddha) performed for these [ancestors], as well as recitation, fire-oblations, and ascetic penances, yield infinite results. ||53||
At the great pilgrimage site of Puṇḍarīka, one obtains fruit equal to that of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice;
at the great pilgrimage site of Brahmatīrtha, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Then, at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean, at Pañcanada, there is the inexhaustible [merit];
thereafter, the holy Kīrakātman is at Maṇḍavā on the mountain. (55)
A śrāddha ceremony should be offered at Saptahrada, and especially at Mānasa;
likewise at Mahākūṭa, Vanda, Giri, and Trikakuda. (56)
And at twilight, a great marvel is seen upon the great altar:
it does not approach those who lack faith, yet it approaches those who are firm in their vows.
There, the eternal Jātavedas stone is the manifest presence of Agni;
one should perform śrāddha rites and fire-rituals there, and they shall be eternally inexhaustible.
Resorting to that single [tīrtha] alone every evening,
one who desires the inexhaustible [merit] for the ancestors should always offer the śrāddha there.
Whether one has disciplined the self or not, wherever that man is known,
there is the sacred ford named Svargyamārgaprada, which instantly bestows boons;
having cast aside all enmities there, the Seven Sages went to heaven.
Even today those enmities are seen, yet they have indeed passed away;
by bathing in that most excellent of holy places, a man attains heaven.
There is a famous sacred site frequented by Nandisiddha,
where the form of Nandīśvara is not seen even by those difficult to conquer.
Golden sacrificial posts are seen blazing at the rising of the sun;
having circumambulated them, they depart, vanishing into the sky.
And Kurukṣetra is meritorious in every respect, especially its excellent holy sites; it is proclaimed as the field of the high-souled Sanatkumāra, the Lord of Yoga,
where by giving sesame seeds, one always attains inexhaustible merit for the ancestors.
An inexhaustible śrāddha was offered for the sake of vital energy in the abode of Dharmarāja;
the śrāddha was given on the new moon day according to the prescribed rite and in due order.
Furthermore, especially at Kurukṣetra where the ancestors are present, a virtuous son should worship them there; thus he becomes free from debt.
At Vinaśana on the Sarasvatī, likewise at Plakṣapraśravaṇa, at Vyāsatīrtha on the Sarasvatī, and especially at Brahmakṣetra. ||67||
One who desires that their *śrāddha* be inexhaustible should perform it while reciting the syllable *oṃ* at every point along the Gaṅgā and at Maināka, the best of mountains. (68)
And by [bathing] at the source of the Yamunā, one is liberated from all sins;
the evidence for this is that the waters there are both extremely hot and extremely cold.
The auspicious sister of Yama, likewise the daughter of Mārtaṇḍa, is there;
it was previously proclaimed by the ancestors that a śrāddha performed there becomes inexhaustible.
Having bathed in the Brahmānugraha lake, one immediately becomes a Brāhmaṇa;
for in that place, the Śrāddha rite, as well as recitation, burnt offerings, and austerities, yield infinite results. (71)
There, the great ascetic Vasiṣṭha moved about like a pillar;
even today, the trees there are seen adorned with jewels.
But where the balance scale is seen, which demonstrates righteousness and unrighteousness, by that indeed the supreme fruit of sacred fords is weighed by the Brahmins. (73)
The daughter of the Pitṛs, renowned as Gandhakālī through her yoga, and the fourth portion of Brahmā, the upholder of the lineage of Parāśara; ||74||
Having divided the Veda into four parts, that wise and great sage will beget Vyāsa,
the high-souled one of great yoga.
There is a lake named Acchodaka where the Acchodā river rises; there, by the command of Vāraṇa, she was born again from the womb of a fish. (76)
At her holy hermitage, frequented by those who perform meritorious deeds,
it is declared that even a single Śrāddha offering becomes inexhaustible.
When performed there with the mind fixed in Yoga, the merit arises simultaneously.
At Kubera-tuṅga, at Vyāma-ucca, and likewise at Vyāsa-tīrtha,
that meritorious Brāhmaṇa shall offer a śrāddha that is infinite and inexhaustible.
It is constantly frequented by the Siddhas, but it is not seen by those of undisciplined soul.
At Nandā, in the northeastern direction on the altar, there is the point of no-return.
Indeed, this is a field of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra) frequented by the wise Mahādeva, who, having set his foot upon it at Mahālaya, does not return.
Having performed penance on the peak of Umā for a divine age with one foot, Īśvara and Nīhāra remained there as water. (81)
At Umā-tuṅga, Bhṛgu-tuṅga, Brahmatuṅga, and Mahālaya;
at Kādravatī, Śāṇḍilī, and the cave of Vāmana. ||82||
Having gone there, one becomes purified; the śrāddha offering becomes truly inexhaustible, as do whatever recitations, fire-offerings, meditations, and other meritorious deeds may be performed. (83)
Those devoted to their gurus indeed practice celibacy for a hundred years;
by bathing in this [tirtha], one immediately obtains the true fruit of such deeds and others like them. //84//
Right there, the Kumāradhārā is seen, which destroys all sins;
and right there, whatever vehicle or seat is seen appears immediately.
In the vicinity of Śailakīrtipura, one obtains abundant desires;
invisible to all beings, one wanders the earth like a god. (85)
The great sacred site of Kāśyapa is known as Kālasarpis; one who desires imperishable merit should always offer Śrāddha ceremonies there. (86)
The great sacred site of Kāśyapa is known as Kālasarpis; one who desires imperishable merit should always offer Śrāddha rites there. (87)
A śrāddha performed in the vicinity of a śālagrāma becomes inexhaustible;
yet it is not perceived there by one of unrefined self through direct vision.
For this is the rejection of the unrefined and the establishment of the refined;
and it is there, in that holy lake, because the divine king of the nāgas resides.
He accepts alms from the virtuous, but he does not accept them from the wicked;
for food cannot be consumed by snakes that are excessively inflamed with venom. (2.15.90)
The Dharma is visibly seen in these two holy places;
you should also observe that illustration in the Devadāru forest.
But those whose nature is virtuous are seen to have shaken off their sins;
at Prayāga on the Bhāgīrathī, it is said that [the merit] is eternally inexhaustible. 92.
At Kālañjara, Daśārṇa, Naimiṣa, Kurujāṅgala,
and in the city of Vārāṇasī, the śrāddha should be offered with great effort.
In that [river], what is given to the Lord of Yoga (Yogeśvara) is eternally inexhaustible;
and by giving [there] in these [places], one becomes purified, and the śrāddha becomes truly infinite.
Whatever austerity, fire-oblation, meditation, or any other meritorious deed one may perform at Lauhitya, at Vaitaraṇī, and likewise at Svarṇavedī— ||95||
It is seen only once at the edge of the ocean by those of meritorious deeds,
as well as at Gayā, on the Dharmapṛṣṭha, and likewise in the lake of Brahmā.
A śrāddha offered at Gayā and Gṛdhrakūṭa yields great fruit;
there, snow falls on all sides for five yojanas. ||97||
In the holy hermitage of Bharata, the forest is remembered as most sacred;
there, the footprint of Mataṅga is visible even to the physical eye. (98)
The entire essence of the Dharma has been proclaimed as an illustration for this world.
Thus, the meritorious Pañcavana is frequented by those who perform virtuous deeds;
therein lies the sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Pāṇḍuviśālā, which is an immediate manifestation [of that merit]. 99.
Likewise, those people who are evildoers emerge from their sins through scales, measures, bows, and various scriptures at the moment of their birth.
Likewise, a Śrāddha offered on the third lunar day at Pāda, at Niḥsvara, at Pāpamaṇḍala, at Mahāhrada, or at Kauśikī, yields great fruit. (101)
The wise Mahādeva set his foot upon Muṇḍapṛṣṭha after performing intense and extremely difficult penance for many divine ages.
Even by a short time here, a man devoted to dharma quickly casts off his evil, just as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin. (103)
It was guarded day and night by those with great coils who were licking [their lips], causing joy to the Siddhas and instilling fear in sinners.
To the north of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is the sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Kanakanandī, frequented by hosts of celestial sages;
having bathed there, birds go to heaven, moving at will. (105)
Likewise, a śrāddha offering given there is declared to be inexhaustible;
having bathed, that best of men then discharges his three debts. (106)
On the shore of that lake is a great temple of the God;
having ascended it and recited [the mantra] there, one becomes perfected and goes from there to heaven. ||107||
Having gone to Uttaramānasa, one attains unsurpassed success;
having gone there, a great wonder is seen in that best of cities. (108)
One should perform the śrāddha rite therein according to one's capacity and according to one's strength;
thus one obtains divine desires and the means to liberation eternally. ||109||
In the excellent Mānasa lake, a great marvel is seen:
that highly fortunate lady, having descended from heaven, shines resplendent in the mid-air.
The goddess Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths, descended from the foot of Soma to the earth;
there she is seen in the sky, and there is an archway resembling the sun.
Made of divine Jāmbūnada gold, it was as long as the gateway to heaven, from which [the river] flows once more toward the western ocean. 112.
The Candrabhāgā and the Sindhu both purify all beings, especially those who possess knowledge of the Dharma; like the Mānasa lake,
this supreme river, a divine stream, flows toward the western ocean.
There is a mountain named Himavat, adorned with various minerals;
it is said to extend for eighty thousand yojanas.
Crowded with Siddhas and Cāraṇas and frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, there is a beautiful lotus pond there, renowned by the name Suṣumnā. ||115||
One born there lives for ten thousand years;
a śrāddha performed there becomes infinite and brings great prosperity.
Furthermore, when a śrāddha is offered there, it delivers ten ancestors and ten descendants.
All merit belongs to the Himavat, and the Gaṅgā is meritorious everywhere;
all rivers flowing to the ocean and the oceans themselves are meritorious on every side. ||117||
In all such cases as these, a wise man should perform the *śrāddha* ceremony;
having bathed, he becomes purified, and likewise by giving and giving again. ||118||
On the lofty mountain ridges, in the ravines and caves, on the slopes and in the valleys, as well as at the waterfalls. ||119||
On the banks of rivers, as well as at their sources, in the ocean, in cow-pens, at confluences, and in forests; ||| 2.15.120 ||
In houses that are uncluttered, smeared with cow dung, pleasant, fragrant, and secluded. ||121||
Then, those desiring to accomplish all their wishes should always perform the śrāddha rite according to the rules in these directions, having proceeded toward them in a clockwise direction. ||122||
Thus, one should perform acts of faith toward all these without weariness;
in this very way, the wise man shall attain the perfection of Brahman. 123.
When one abides in the place ordained for the three castes, as well as in the dharma of caste and stage of life,
the worship of the ancestors is attained through the abandonment of occasions for anger.
A wise man who visits sacred fords with faith and has conquered his senses shall be purified even if he has committed sin; how much more so one who performs virtuous deeds? (125)
He shall not go to the womb of an animal, nor shall he be born in an evil land;
indeed, the Brahmin becomes a dweller in heaven and finds the means to liberation.
Those who lack faith, the sinful, the nihilists, those whose doubts remain unsettled,
and the mere logician— these five do not attain the fruit of the sacred ford.
In the sacred ford of the Guru lies supreme accomplishment, the highest state among all sacred fords;
meditation is the highest of sacred fords, and therefore the eternal sacred ford is Brahman. (128)
Meditation is superior to fasting; it is the withdrawal of the senses.
For through fasting, one is repeatedly bound here by the vital breaths.

Having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal, as well as the sense objects and the senses, and having restrained the intellect within the mind, there is the cessation of all [mental fluctuations]. (2.15.130)

Furthermore, know that withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is undoubtedly the means to liberation; it is the restraining of the mind, which is fierce, and the turning back of the senses, intellect, and so forth. (131)
Through non-nutrition, it goes to destruction; know that fasting is austerity. Through the restraint of the intellect and the mind, a beautiful wisdom is born. 132.
When all evils have been exhausted and the sense-faculties themselves have likewise ceased,
the pure self enters final nirvana, just as a fire goes out when its fuel is spent.
Then, by means of yoga, the knower of yoga completely disunites the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) from the causes, which are the guṇas, as well as from the manifest and the unmanifest. 134.
He has no place of going or staying; he is neither manifest nor unmanifest, there is no doubt.
He is near, yet neither existent nor non-existent; he does not abide as anything at all.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Pilgrimage," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa* proclaimed by Vāyu.
Bṛhaspati said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the gifts and their fruits, as well as those Śrāddha rites that are pure and those which are to be avoided. ||1||
During the falling of snow, one should either perform the fire-sacrifice or fetch it from a place where it is cold;
therefore, the Agnihotra is remembered as the supreme merit.
One should avoid performing a śrāddha at night, except when there is the sight of Rāhu;
indeed, it must be performed immediately even at the cost of one's entire wealth during the appearance of Rāhu.
He who does not perform [this] during an eclipse sinks like a cow in the mud;
but by performing it, he delivers others from sin, just as a boat rescues those submerged in the ocean.
The sacrificial offering for Viśvedevas and Soma, which consists largely of meat,
should indeed avoid the horn of a rhinoceros for the sake of destroying malice.
Indeed, Tvaṣṭṛ, being restrained by the high-souled Lord of the Gods while drinking the Soma of the Lord of Śacī, fell upon the earth in ancient times.
Likewise, śyāmāka grains were produced and offered for the sake of the ancestors;
and in that same manner, drops [of water] issued from his two unobstructed nostrils.

Phlegmatic substances are cooling, pleasing to the heart, and sweet; likewise, śyāmāka grain and sugarcane are beneficial for the ancestors. He who performs the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice with these attains success swiftly. ||8||
Śyāmāka, hastin, paṭola, the fruit of bṛhatī, and the sharp crest of agasti—all these are indeed astringent. (9)
Likewise, other such foods that are savory and sweet should be given here,
as well as ginger and long radish.
Vaṃśīkarīra, surasa, sarjaka, and bhūstṛṇa—these are to be avoided; I shall now describe those things that must always be excluded from the rite of Śrāddha. (11)
Garlic, leeks, onions, and radishes, as well as other inferior substances deficient in taste and smell, such as karambha and the like. (12)
The things to be avoided at the time of the Śrāddha rite and the reason for this will now be explained.
Long ago, in the war between the gods and the asuras, Bali was conquered by the gods. (13)
Indeed, drops of blood that have fallen, spurting from wounds—these must always be avoided in the performance of the śrāddha rite. ||14||
Furthermore, resinous exudations mentioned in the Vedas, salts, saline soils, and women who are menstruating are to be avoided at the performance of a Śrāddha rite. (15)
Water that is foul-smelling, frothy, or from a stagnant pool, where a cow cannot find satisfaction, or that which is taken at night—[these are not to be used]. (16)
The milk of sheep, of camels, and all that which has only one hoof, as well as that of buffaloes and yaks, should be avoided by one who possesses discernment. (17)

Henceforth, I shall carefully declare the regions that are to be avoided, as well as those by whom the *śrāddha* should not be witnessed, and the entirety of what constitutes purity and impurity. (18)
One should perform the śrāddha with faith, subsisting on wild roots and fruits;
thus one attains a beloved kingdom, as well as heaven, liberation, and fame. (19)
One should avoid for the performance of a śrāddha rite ground that is filled with unpleasant sounds, or infested with living creatures, or likewise possesses a foul odor. 2.16.20.
The rivers extending as far as the ocean constitute the gateway to the southeast;
one should avoid the entire region of Triśaṅku for twelve yojanas.
To the north of the Mahānadī and to the south of Kaikaṭa,
there is a region named Traiśaṅku, which is excluded from the performance of śrāddha rites.
The Karankaras, the Kalingas, and those regions even further north of the Indus, where the duties of the stages of life have perished—these lands should be avoided with great effort. (23)
Naked ascetics and others shall not see the Śrāddha once it has been offered;
even if they look upon it, those [impure persons] do not reach the ancestors or the grandfathers.
Śaṃyu said:
O Blessed One, foremost among the best of the twice-born, please explain in detail and according to the truth to me, who am now questioning you correctly regarding the naked ascetics and others. (25)
Thus addressed, the highly resplendent Bṛhaspati said to him:
"The triple Veda is remembered as the protective covering for all beings. (26)
Those best of the twice-born who, out of delusion, abandon you shall indeed become naked;
so too shall perish that man who is without support, as well as he who is a bull. (27)
He who abandons the Bull and seeks liberation elsewhere, and he who does not truly perceive the Bull, which is the Veda itself—[these two are lost]. (28)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras alike— all of them—
[were present] when, in the past, during the war between the gods and the asuras, the asuras were utterly defeated.
This creation was not fashioned by the Self-Existent One in a place of heretical deformity:
neither the Dviśrāddhakas, nor the Nirgranthas, nor the Śākyas, nor the Puṣṭikalāṃśakas. (2.16.30)

Those who do not follow the Dharma are indeed people such as the naked ones; for a twice-born man who wears matted hair in vain, bears sacred marks in vain, or remains naked in vain, is likewise so. (31)
Those who observe vows in vain and those who mutter prayers in vain—these are indeed people such as the naked ones (nagnas) and others;
they are the Kulaṃdhamas and Niṣādas, as well as destroyers of prosperity.
These evil paths are proclaimed to be those where deeds are performed and [their fruits] are exhausted;
by these, men go to the Śrāddha that has been prepared or witnessed. (33)
Killers of Brahmins, ungrateful persons, atheists, those who violate the teacher’s bed, robbers, and the cruel—these are to be avoided even by sight alone. (34)
One should avoid all others who perform evil deeds, and especially those who take delight in reviling the gods and the celestial sages. (35)
Furthermore, it is seen that by these [beings], asuras and yātudhānas also go [to those realms].
The Kṛta Yuga is declared to belong to the Brāhmaṇas, while the Tretā is remembered as belonging to the Kṣatriyas. (36)
They say that the Vaiśya is the Dvāpara age, and the Śūdra is remembered as the Kali age.
The ancestors said:
In the Kṛta age, the Vedas are to be honored, while in the Tretā age, the gods likewise.
In the Dvāpara age, wars are constant; in the Kali age, there are heretics, as well as those who are disrespectful, impure, and [the presence of] the village cock and the village pig. (38)
A dog destroys the śrāddha by its mere sight; there is no doubt about this.
So too does one who has been touched by a corpse or by those in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), as well as those suffering from chronic diseases. (39)
It must never be seen by those who are impure or fallen;
if they should see the food, it would certainly not be fit for offerings to the gods or the ancestors.
That which has been touched by such [an impurity] becomes a defilement for the primary purpose;
however, in the case of sacrificial oblations that have been gathered together, they are discarded beforehand, and sprinkling with water mixed with clay is prescribed. ||41||
Or one should perform the scattering of white mustard seeds and black sesame seeds, or else diligently seek the sight of a guru, the sun, fire, or a sacred object. (42)
That which has been stepped upon by one mounted on a seat, that which is struck by the feet, that which is seen by impure moving beings, and that which is dry or stale; ||43||
That which is stale, or thoroughly spoiled, or likewise licked by the tip of the tongue;
that which is contaminated by sugar, hair, stones, or insects; (44)
Likewise, oil-cakes, pressed sesame seeds, and grains such as sesame and barley; and those foods that are fit to be eaten which have been seasoned with visible salt. (45)
Those who have shaken off [their impurities] with a garment should be excluded from the rite of Śrāddha;
there are some who, in contradiction to the Vedas, consider themselves possessors of true knowledge. (46)
Those known as *ajājñapatis* are like dust for the sake of a *śrāddha*;
likewise, curd and vegetables are unfit for consumption, and anything turned sour (*śukta*) is strictly forbidden.
One should avoid eggplant, yet one may offer all types of fermented liquors,
as well as rock salt and that which originates from Lake Mānasa.
For this is indeed the supreme purifier, even though it is directly perceptible;
having cast it into the fire, one should diligently bind it after dipping both hands. 49.
One should cause the water to reach the very top of the head; that indeed is remembered as the Brahma-tīrtha.
Likewise, the sprinkling of ritual materials (dravyas) should be performed, and furthermore, their scattering (āvapana).
Having placed [the items] there, one should sprinkle them with water; likewise, their immersion in water [is prescribed].
In the midst of the *ariṣṭa* and *tumula* [trees], one should also place *bilva*, *iṅguda*, and *śvadanī*.
For all objects made of split bamboo, purification is prescribed by means of fire;
likewise for those made of ivory, bone, wood, and horn, it is by scraping. (52)
For all objects made of clay, re-burning is prescribed;
likewise for gems, diamonds, corals, pearls, and conch-shells.
Furthermore, the purification of all woolen cloths and those made of sheep's wool may be accomplished by means of a paste of white mustard seeds or a paste of sesame seeds. (54)
For all [parts] above the navel, purification is prescribed with earth and water;
however, at the beginning and end of these purifications, there must again be washing with water alone. (55)
Likewise, it is declared that for cotton products, purification is by means of ashes;
and for fruits, flowers, and stalks, immersion in water is prescribed.
Having gone outside the village, one should perform the sweeping, sprinkling, and smearing of the ground; thus purified by the wind, the earth becomes clean. (57)
For those who carry bows and for birds, purification with earth is prescribed.
Thus has this supreme rule for purifications been fully described;
hereafter I shall declare it further—listen to me as I speak. (58)
In the morning, to the southwest of the house, at a distance of five arrow-throws and the measure of an axle, one should void excrement;
having covered the head, one must not touch the head with the hand there.
Having covered the earth with dry grass, or wood, or leaves, or bamboo strips, or even with earthen vessels; 2.16.60.
Having taken up water from which impurities have been removed, as well as earth,
one who is restrained in speech should perform the rite facing north during the day, and indeed facing south at night.
One should indeed hold the water-pot with the right hand;
for purification, one should use the left hand, applying three applications of clay to the anus.
Furthermore, one should give ten [applications] again by means of the sequence of the left hand;
or again, one should give five applications of clay with both hands.
Having washed his feet with clay and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules,
he should likewise offer three oblations of water to Sūrya, Agni, and Pavana.
A wise man should always keep a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) near him at a sacred site; with these [implements], he should properly perform his duties and the washing of the feet.
The sipping of water (ācamana) is performed with the second [finger], and thereafter the rite for the gods;
however, fasting for three nights is prescribed when the hand is defiled.
A penance has been declared for a distant [transgression] that is difficult to perform:
having touched a dog or an outcaste (śvapāka), one should practice the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
Having touched human bones, one must fast for three nights as the cause of purification; it is said that if they are smeared with fat, the fast is for one night, otherwise than that.
The Kāraskaras, Pulindas, as well as the Andhas, Śabaras, and others,
having drunk from the bow and gone to the Yugaṃdhara mountain in the abode of Bhūti, [attained their goal].
As far as the northern limit of the ocean, and likewise a hundred yojanas within the sky,
there are whatever sinful lands exist that are inhabited by people of evil deeds.
Those who are shunned by the learned and by Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, having gone to unholy regions, incur the full measure of sin. (71)
The manifestation of the mind, fire, time, and the act of smearing; the proclamation of purifications, and constant ignorance [of these]. (72)
But he who, out of delusion, should act otherwise and cause a confusion of purifications, undoubtedly reaps the fruit of becoming a piśāca or a yātudhāna. (73)
One who lacks faith in purity is born among the Mleccha tribes;
likewise, one who does not perform sacrifices or is sinful may even be born into the animal realm.
A man who attains liberation through purity shall become a dweller in heaven;
for the gods indeed desire purity—this has been declared by the gods.
The gods always avoid that which is loathsome and impure;
those of auspicious deeds perform the three purifications according to the rule. (76)
O twice-born ones, [this should be given] to one who is devoted to Brahman, hospitable, endowed with purity, wise, devoted to his ancestors, self-controlled, and compassionate. (77)
Pleased by these various [offerings], the ancestors, who increase one's spiritual power (yoga),
grant the desires wished for in the mind, even those originating from the three worlds.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Śrāddha," in the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa* spoken by Vāyu.
The sages said:
"Oh, how wise you are, O Sūta! You have proclaimed the ritual for the Śrāddha ceremony.
Indeed, we have heard this ritual for the Śrāddha as it was fully described by the sages. (1)
Since his life has been recounted with such great detail and distinction,
O highly wise one, please tell us the remainder of that sage's story according to your understanding.
Sūta said:
O brahmins, I shall proclaim to you that opinion of that ṛṣi regarding the śrāddha; O highly fortunate ones, listen to it from me in detail. (3)
I have previously described the śrāddha and the procedure for the śrāddha rite; now I shall explain the supplementary details regarding the Brāhmaṇas in their proper order. (4)
Brahmins are never to be scrutinized, for they are the supreme purifiers;
yet, in rites for the gods and the ancestors, their examination is indeed constantly enjoined.
One should diligently avoid that person in whom faults are clearly visible, or who is shunned by the virtuous, or whose character one learns through living together with him.
A wise man should always examine an unknown twice-born guest at a śrāddha;
for perfected beings (siddhas) wander this earth in the form of brahmins.
Therefore, one should go out to meet a guest who is approaching with palms joined in reverence;
one should also honor him with water for the feet, anointing for the feet, and food.
Likewise, these gods, who are masters of yoga, roam across the vast earth bounded by the ocean in various forms, protecting their subjects according to dharma.
Having thus honored them, a man should then give side-dishes, foods to be chewed, and fruits to a brahmin guest; such shall be their reward.
One should indeed obtain the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice by means of milk, as it is heard in the scriptures;
by means of clarified butter, one obtains auspicious vision and the fruit of the Ṣoḍaśī sacrifice;
and by means of honey, one shall fully attain the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice. ||11||
A man who possesses faith shall indeed attain that [fruit] who feeds the Brahmins with all their desired objects;
he who provides for all needs and honors all Brahmin guests constantly enjoys the fruit of the Sarvamedha sacrifice.
But he who, having received a guest at a rite for the ancestors or even at a rite for the gods, treats him with contempt—
the gods indeed abandon him, just as a Hotṛ priest abandons a patron who has reached the end of his wealth.
For the gods, the ancestors, and indeed the fire-god enter those twice-born ones and consume [the offerings], for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world. (14)
If not honored, these burn [the host]; if honored, they grant all desires.
Therefore, one should always honor guests even with one's entire possessions. 15.
A forest-dweller, a householder, or one who has come to his home;
children, the weary, and an ascetic—one should always recognize these as guests. (16)
A beggar who arrives is a guest, while one who does not beg is a true guest;
the guest of a guest is the most excellent, and such a guest is called Yoga. 17.
He is neither fierce nor confused, neither ignorant nor a knower of distinctions;
he is neither virtuous nor prosperous, neither a servant nor a guest who observes [proper conduct]. ||18||
To one who is thirsty, weary, wandering, and extremely hungry, one who desires the fruit of sacrifice should give with due honor. 19.
Having ascended the peaks of Bhṛgutuṅga and gone to the holy Sarasvatī,
as well as the sacred Āpagā river and the goddess Gaṅgā, the great river.
The rivers originating from the Himavat, as well as others honored by the sages,
those known for their lakes and sacred bathing places, and likewise the newly flowing rivers— [all these he saw].
Having gone [to them], one is liberated from sins and is eternally honored in heaven.
Indeed, impurity (aśauca) is declared to last for ten nights in the case of death or birth (sūtaka). ||22||
For a Brāhmaṇa, purification is specifically prescribed as twelve days; for a Kṣatriya, it is remembered as half a month; for a Vaiśya, it is a month; and a Śūdra becomes pure after one month. 23.
A woman in her courses becomes pure after three nights for all castes.
[One should avoid] a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, a dog, and an outcaste (antyāvasāyin). 24.
Upon touching those who are naked and the like, or those carrying the dead, impurity is prescribed;
having bathed with one's clothes on, one becomes pure by means of twelve applications of clay.
This alone shall be the purification after sexual intercourse; likewise, having washed both hands with earth, a man should perform the rite of purification with nine [applications]. (26)
Having washed his hands with water and bathed again with clay,
the wise man should then apply clay twice to the private parts, and once more to the anus.
Thus is the rule for purification seen as always applicable to all castes:
one should apply three applications of earth and perform the sprinkling of the hands and feet. (28)
This is the purification pertaining to the forest; hereafter I shall describe that which pertains to the village.
There are three applications of clay for the feet and likewise three for the hands.
Fifteen applications of clay are required for purification from impurity; these are distributed among the hands and other limbs respectively.
One should apply clay until it is no longer perceptible, but at the end, one should use water alone.
Having covered one's neck or head, or while walking on the road, or having failed to perform the purification of the feet—even if one has sipped water (ācamana)—one remains impure. (31)
Having washed the vessel and discarded [the water], and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should again perform the sprinkling (abhyukṣaṇa);
likewise, one should again perform the sprinkling for any other substance. ||32||
The sprinkling of flowers and the like, as well as of grasses and sacrificial oblations, and likewise the sprinkling of materials brought from elsewhere after they have been set down. ||33||
One should take some of the sprinkled [food] for the ancestral rite (śrāddha) and likewise for the divine rite;
one should take it from the north side of the altar and dismiss it on the south side.
In the case of an error regarding the rite for the gods or likewise for the ancestors, the ritual would be interrupted;
therefore, one should draw a line on the southern altar with the right hand.
With both hands, one should perform the auspicious *vikara* rite for the gods and the ancestors, as well as after agitated dreams and likewise after voiding urine or excrement. (36)

As [one becomes impure] upon spitting when it is manifest, or after eating, or after changing one's clothes, or upon contact with one who is defiled by food remnants, so too is one [impure] upon the washing of the feet. (37)

For one who has released [the breath], for one who is about to speak, for one who is impure, for one who is striving [in ritual purity], and in all cases of doubt, as well as when the topknot is loosened—[in these instances, one should not recite]. //38//

If, out of delusion, one should sip water without the sacred thread, or if there is contact between the lips and the teeth, or upon seeing those who dwell outside the pale (antyavāsins), [one must perform purification]. (39)
Having touched with his tongue what was stuck to his teeth, and likewise [what was stuck] there,
he looked down while making a sound with his fingers and bowing.
And whoever, out of delusion, stands in unrighteousness, shall become impure even while approaching;
having sat down in a clean place, he should remain bowed, facing either the east or the north. (41)
Having washed his feet and hands, he should touch [the organs] while keeping his hands between his knees;
being self-restrained and well-composed, he should drink water three times with a serene mind.
One should perform the wiping twice and then the sprinkling once;
[this applies to] the apertures, the head, oneself, the hands, and likewise the feet. (43)
Likewise, if his sprinkling (abhyukṣaṇa) has not been examined, so too his sipping of water (ācamana), as well as the Vedas, sacrifices, and austerities [are rendered fruitless]. ||44||
Likewise, acts of charity and the practice of celibacy become fruitful for that nihilist who,
out of delusion, performs a ritual action without having sipped water for purification.
Furthermore, his ritual actions will undoubtedly be in vain—even if they are purified by purity of speech and intention, faultless, or beyond reproach. (46)
These are to be known as pure; the opposite of these is considered defiled.
A Brahmin who is hungry and possesses nothing should never be addressed [harshly]. (47)
If one should give to him with due honor, that sacrifice is called a "non-sacrificial post" (ayūpa);
it consists of unburnt food and cooked food given to one who is of meager means and does not beg. (48)
One should always feed those who possess exclusive virtue and modesty among the faithful;
he who gives [only] to the last [of these] is a slayer of Brahmins and evil-minded. (49)
Even after passing through a hundred births, that man who feeds Brahmins unequally in a single row shall not be released from his sin. (2.17.50)
Whether appointed or unappointed, one who takes food from the row incurs the misdeed;
he is quickly seized by sin, and his merit from sacrifices and charitable works perishes. (51)
Among all Brahmins, the ascetic is the foremost at the festival—he who is the best of the twice-born and recites the Vedas, with the Itihāsas as the fifth. ||52||
Immediately thereafter, one who understands should appoint them as is appropriate:
after him [the king] comes the knower of the three Vedas, and after him the knower of two Vedas. (53)
Likewise, one who knows a single Veda, and thereafter one who studies the Nyāya;
for the sake of purification alone, I shall indeed declare those [who sanctify] a row—listen! (54)
All those who have been previously described, indeed, in their proper sequence, are the masters of the six limbs, the disciplined ones, the yogis, and likewise the masters of all tantras. ||55||
The Yāyāvara—these five should be known as purifiers of the row (paṅktipāvana).
Also, one who has mastered even a single one of the eighteen branches of learning (vidyā) [is such]. //56//
And all those who abide according to their station are purifiers of the assembly:
one who knows the three fires, one who is learned in the three Vedas, and the twice-born who recites the Dharmas. (57)
Likewise, the twice-born who has reached the further shore of the Bārhaspatya Śāstra—all these Brāhmaṇas are declared to be purifiers of the rows [of diners]. ||58||
But that twice-born man who, having been invited to a śrāddha, has sexual intercourse with a woman—his ancestors lie within his semen for that entire month. (59)
If one engages in sexual intercourse after having given or partaken of a śrāddha feast, his ancestors will remain in his semen for that entire month; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, one should give to a guest and feed a celibate student;
that which is righteous should be given to one who is devoted to meditation and is compassionate. 61.
In the performance of a śrāddha rite, one should feed either ascetics or the Vālakhilyas;
a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) who is still a student (upakurvvāṇa) is satisfied by mere honor.
He who feeds a householder has the Viśvedevas honored; by feeding a forest-dweller, one honors the Ṛṣis and the Vālakhilyas, as well as Purandara. ||63||
In the worship of ascetics (yatis), Brahmā himself is indeed worshipped directly.
The five stages of life (āśramas) are purifying; those who lack these stages are [tainted] by their underlying motives (upadhās).
The four stages of life (āśramas) are to be honored in both the ancestral (śrāddha) and divine (daiva) rites;
one should never cause the śrāddha to be offered to those who stand outside the four stages of life.
Whether he remains there or, being hungry, stays outside the four stages of life (āśramas),
both he who lacks self-restraint and he who preaches liberation are defilers of the row.
One should avoid those who wear shaven heads in vain, those with matted hair, and likewise all mendicants; as well as those who are merciless, those of broken conduct, and those who eat everything.

One should exclude from offerings to the gods and ancestors those who follow the livelihoods of artisans and the like, those of improper conduct, those excluded from all the Vedas, singers, and those who subsist on the service of deities.
One should always avoid performing [these acts] even toward Brahmins during the performance of a Śrāddha rite. ||69||
He who eats with all these castes present, and he who eats together with a Śūdra—all of them are defilers of the row. (2.17.70)
Killing, the destruction of power, agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, or even service to a master in secret—none of these activities is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa. (71)

But those Brahmins who are eternally established as possessors of knowledge and likewise practitioners of meditation, or all those twice-born ones who harbor false intentions or are of evil conduct; ||72||
Those who know the truth falsely, as well as those who are hypocritical and malicious, should be avoided,
especially those associated with minor offenses (upapātaka) and major sins (pātaka).
Those who give commands regarding the Vedas, those who seek the fruits of greed and delusion,
and those who sell the Veda— these are excluded from the śrāddha rite.
There is no injunction for the Vedas; he who imposes one is a doer of evil.
Such a person falls away from the fruit of the Vedas, and likewise, the giver falls away from the fruit of his gift.
He who teaches for a fee and he who is taught by one for a fee—
neither of these two is worthy of the Śrāddha, nor is the seller of the Veda.
Those who buy and sell for the sake of livelihood are censured;
this, however, is the proper occupation of a Vaiśya, but for a Brāhmaṇa it is a sin.
Those who know the Vedas declare that one who lives by the Vedas is also a knower of the Vedas.
Neither of these two deserves to partake in the Śrāddha: the husband of an appointed daughter (putrikā) and [the son of a remarried woman]. //78//
He who approaches his wife in vain, he who performs sacrifice at a futile rite, and the twice-born man who is an atheist—none of these are worthy of the śrāddha offering. (79)
He who cooks food for his own sake, and does not offer it to the gods or guests—even those two are unworthy of the *śrāddha* rite; they are outcasts, *brahmarākṣasas*. (2.17.80)
One should not feed at śrāddha ceremonies those who consort with women at night, those who take pleasure in the wives of others, and those who are devoted solely to wealth and sensual desire. (81)

Those who act contrary to the duties of the castes and stages of life, those who are hostile toward the rite of ancestral offerings (śrāddha), thieves, and those who officiate at sacrifices for all types of people— all these are defilers of the assembly (paṅktidūṣaka).
The ancestors do not eat the food of one who eats like a pig, nor of a twice-born man who eats from the palm of his hand, nor of one who eats with his left hand. (83)
One should not cause the remnants of a *śrāddha* to be given to a woman, a *śūdra*, or one who has not been initiated (*anupeta*).
If one should give them out of delusion, that [offering] shall never reach the ancestors.
Therefore, in the performance of a śrāddha rite, no leftover food should be given, except for curd and clarified butter; nor [should it be given] to a disciple or a son, and not otherwise.
Food should especially be given without being left over;
they attain satisfaction even with flowers, roots, and fruits, but most certainly through food.
As long as the foods remain pure, as long as they do not release their heat, and as long as the offerers remain silent, for that long the ancestors eat. (87)
Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, eating, and even the offering of oblations—these should be performed with the thumb so that they do not belong to the Asuras. (88)
All these [practices], beginning with giving, should especially be performed with the hands between the knees; likewise, the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) should be done in that same manner. 89.
One should avoid those with shaven heads, those with matted hair, and those wearing saffron robes even at the time of a śrāddha;
instead, one should diligently cause the śrāddha to be offered to those with topknots or to those who carry the triple staff.
But those who are ever established in their vows, who are wise and meditative, great-souled devotees of the gods—they purify even by their mere sight. (91)
The entire three worlds are indeed pervaded without interval by the masters of yoga;
therefore, they all see whatever exists within the world. ||92||

Having mastered both the manifest and the unmanifest, as well as that which is beyond all, those great-souled ones have perceived both the existent and the non-existent, as well as that which is both existent and non-existent. (93)
All the forms of knowledge, such as liberation and the like, have been seen to belong to the great-souled ones;
therefore, one who is always devoted to them attains unsurpassed auspiciousness. 94.

He who knows the *Ṛgveda* knows the Vedas; he who knows the *Yajus* formulas knows the sacrifice; he who knows the *Sāmans* knows the Brahman; he who knows the mind knows all. (95) Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Examination of Brāhmaṇas," in the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa* spoken by Vāyu. 2.17.
Bṛhaspati said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the gifts and their fruits—the means of deliverance for all beings, which leads to heaven and brings happiness. (1)
Whatever is most excellent in the world, whatever leads to heaven, and whatever is dear to oneself—all that should be given to the ancestors by one who desires their inexhaustible [merit]. (2)
The giver of food obtains as his fruit a divine celestial chariot made of Jāmbūnada gold, radiant like the sun, and filled with divine apsarases. (3)
He who gives a new garment at the time of the Śrāddha rite obtains long life, abundant sovereignty, beauty, and a son. ||4||

Furthermore, the knower of dharma who provides the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and drink to all the Brahmins during the times of *śrāddha* obtains the fruit that results from the gift of the Veda (*brahmadāna*). ||5||
If one gives a water-pot to Brahmins at the time of a śrāddha ceremony,
a cow that flows with honey and milk attends upon the donor.
He who gives a water-pot pierced with a wheel at the time of a śrāddha ceremony obtains a divine cow that yields milk at will.
But he who gives a full bed adorned with flower garlands, an excellent palace indeed follows after him as he departs. (8)
Having given to ascetics at a funeral rite (śrāddha) a residence filled with jewels, along with beds, seats, and food, he rejoices in the heights of heaven.
Pearls, lapis lazuli, garments, and various kinds of jewels,
as well as tens of thousands and hundreds of millions of divine vehicles.
He obtains an imperishable, divine celestial chariot (vimāna), resembling a great blazing fire, endowed with jewels and objects of desire, and possessing the splendor of the sun and moon. ||11||
Surrounded by apsarases, traveling at will and with the speed of thought, he dwells at the forefront of a celestial mansion while being praised from all sides.
They sprinkle [him] with divine perfumes and with showers of flowers;
there the gandharvas and apsarases sing and play instruments. 13.
Preeminent maidens and young women, together with hosts of Apsarases, constantly awaken him with their ever-delightful and melodious voices. (14)
By the gift of a thousand horses, a hundred chariots,
and a thousand elephants, a man dwells with a Yoginī.
That man who offers illumination for the yogic ancestors in the water obtains the fruit of a thousand gold coins. ||16||
Indeed, no gift excels the granting of life;
therefore, with every effort, one should provide protection for living beings. 17.
Non-violence is the most sacred of all things for all gods and is the giver of everything;
for the wise have said that the gift of life is the supreme gift for living beings. (18)
One should cause vessels of excellent quality and auspicious marks to be given at a śrāddha;
thus the flavors attend upon him, as does the prosperity of cattle.
One should indeed give a beautiful vessel made of metal at the Śrāddha meal;
such a vessel becomes the source of all desires, as well as beauty and wealth.
One should give silver or even gold at the śrāddha rite;
by giving, the donor obtains his heart's desire as well as merit itself. ||21||
He who gives a cow at a śrāddha ceremony, along with a rain-pitcher and a milking vessel,
will find that cows attend upon him, as well as the prosperity of cattle.
Likewise, he who provides fire with plenty of wood and fuel to the twice-born at the onset of the cold season; (23)
He is eternally victorious in battle, endowed with prosperity, and shines with splendor;
likewise, he possesses fragrant and sweet-smelling garlands.
Having honored the vessels at the śrāddha ceremony, one should respectfully cause them to be given away, along with fragrant scents, great rivers, and various comforts. (25)
To the giver attend beautiful young women, as well as delightful beds and seats, grounds, and vehicles. (26)
Whoever should offer these even at a śrāddha ceremony shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
and when the Darśa-śrāddha has arrived, these should be presented at the time of the śrāddha.
He obtains the memory and intelligence of virtuous Brahmins;
one should respectfully cause vessels filled with clarified butter to be given at the Śrāddha.
One shall obtain the fruit of many cows that yield pots of milk;
in this world, one rejoices with chariots and excellent vehicles.
Having given whatever is desired at a śrāddha ceremony, one obtains the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice;
by giving a beautiful dwelling, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
By giving a forest endowed with flowers and fruits, one enjoys a fragrant scent;
likewise by providing wells, gardens, tanks, fields, cow-pens, and houses. (31)
Having given these, one rejoices in heaven eternally as long as the moon and stars endure;
likewise, by giving a bed spread with jewels at a śrāddha ceremony.
His ancestors are satisfied with this, and he enjoys infinite heaven;
he is honored by kings and increases in wealth and grain. (33)
Woolen garments, silken cloths, as well as excellent blankets; skins, gold, fine cloth, woven rugs, and deer-hair wool.
Having bestowed these other gifts upon the Brahmins and fed them according to the prescribed rite, the faithful person indeed obtains the fruit of a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices. (35)
Many beautiful women, sons, servants, and attendants remain under one's control; all beings abide in subjection, and in this world there is freedom from disease. (36)
Whoever gives these—silk, linen, cotton, and likewise fine silk cloth—at śrāddha ceremonies, obtains abundant fulfillment of his desires. (37)
He quickly dispels misfortune, just as the rising sun dispels darkness;
he shines at the front of his celestial chariot like the moon among the stars. (38)
For clothing is sacred to all the deities and is praised by all the gods;
in the absence of clothing, there is no ritual action—neither sacrifice, nor the Vedas, nor ascetic penances. (39)
Therefore, garments should especially be given at the time of a Śrāddha;
by that, one obtains all those [benefits], as well as sacrifices, the Vedas, and penances.
