He who, being self-restrained and devoted to that supreme goal, constantly gives at ancestral rites (śrāddha), attains all desires as well as the entire kingdom. ||41||
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled:
various foods, parched grains, parched flour mixed with curds, cakes, clarified butter, and sugar. (42)
Whoever offers kṛśara, honey, karka, milk, and even milk-rice (pāyasa), as well as oily cakes, obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. ||43||
Cow's curd that has not been mixed [with other things], as well as various kinds of edible foods—such food offered at a śrāddha during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism brings grief. (44)
One should feed the Brahmins with ghee and pour ghee upon the ground;
by giving even an elephant at Gayā during a Śrāddha, one does not grieve.
By giving boiled rice, milk-rice, clarified butter, honey, roots, fruits, and various kinds of edible foods, one rejoices both in this world and after death. 46.
Whoever, out of affection, daily offers *pṛthuka* mixed with sugar and milk, as well as *kṛsara* and *masūra*, for a full year, [attains inexhaustible merit]. (47)

One should feed the guests at the śrāddha with groats, parched grain, cakes, and boiled beans with condiments; likewise, one should offer delicious and savory preparations mixed with ghee and barley-meal with curd.
He who gives these offerings at the śrāddhas obtains a treasure of lotuses.
He who, having honored them with effort, gives fresh grains at a śrāddha, attains all enjoyments and, having gone to heaven, is honored there. (49)
The man who gives the most excellent foods—those to be chewed, eaten, sucked, drunk, and licked—shall himself become the most excellent of all. (2.18.50)
The Vaiśvadeva and the Soma offerings consist of the supreme oblation of rhinoceros meat;
one should avoid the horn of the rhinoceros, for we destroy all malice.
With palms joined in reverence, one should offer the first portion of food to guests;
such a person obtains the unsurpassed fruit of all sacrificial rites. (52)
One should promptly give food that is very hot and pure to one who desires to eat, as well as condiments that are likewise unctuous, having honored them with devotion and effort. (53)
The giver of food obtains for thirty million kalpas a celestial chariot resembling the rising sun and drawn by swans.
There exists no gift whatsoever in this world superior to the gift of food;
from food all beings are born and they live by it, of this there is no doubt. (55)
There is no gift whatsoever found here superior to the gift of life;
for the three worlds subsist on food, and such indeed is the fruit of food. (56)
All worlds are established upon food; that is the fruit of the gift of food. Food is Prajāpati himself; by it all this [universe] is pervaded.
Therefore, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to the gift of food.
Whatever jewels exist upon the earth, as well as vehicles and women—a man devoted to his ancestors quickly attains all of that. (58)
One should always offer shelter to guests with palms joined in reverence;
for the gods wait by the thousands for such divine hospitality. (59)
He who should give all of these would become the sole sovereign of the earth;
yet by three, two, or even one gift, one becomes happy. (2.18.60)
Giving is the supreme dharma, honored with reverence by the virtuous;
indeed, sovereignty over the three worlds is established through giving alone. (61)
A king indeed obtains a kingdom, and a man without wealth obtains supreme wealth; a man who is always devoted to his ancestors recovers even a life that has been exhausted.
Whatever desires he may long for in his mind, those his ancestors know.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Fruit of Giving," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Bṛhaspati said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim that which is honored in the rite of Śrāddha—namely, the optional, occasional, and perpetual rites, performed constantly in the Śrāddha ceremony. (1)
The three Aṣṭakās have their root in sons, wives, and wealth;
indeed, the bright fortnight is superior, and the constellation Citrā is declared to be the best.
The second [offering] should be dedicated to Prajāpati, and the third indeed to the Viśvedevas;
the first should always be performed with cakes, while the other should always be performed with [other] seasonal offerings.
Another [offering] with vegetables shall be the third; such is the rule regarding the substances.
Indeed, the Anvaṣṭakā rite for the ancestors is ordained as a constant obligation. (4)
If there should be another fourth [lunar day], one should especially observe it;
on those days, a wise man should perform the śrāddha rite even at the cost of his entire wealth, doing so constantly.
In both the next world and this one, in all circumstances, he shall always be happy;
for those who worship [the deity], there is constant prosperity, while for the atheists, there is a downward path.
The ancestors at all times, and the deities on the days of the lunar calendar—all approach a man like cows to a watering hole. (7)
May the Aṣṭakā rites, honored by the gods, never fail you;
otherwise, his world would become futile and whatever he has acquired would perish.
Those who give go to the gods, while those who do not give go among the animals;
[the former attain] progeny, nourishment, memory, intelligence, sons, and even sovereignty.

By performing [the sacrifice] on the full moon day, one attains complete fulfillment beforehand; by performing it on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), there is the gain of wealth, and what has been gained does not perish for him.
He who performs [the vow] on the second day shall become a lord of bipeds;
the third, however, is the destroyer of enemies and the annihilator of sins for one seeking boons.
Performing the śrāddha on the fourth day, one perceives the vulnerabilities of the enemy;
performing it on the fifth day, one indeed attains great prosperity.
Furthermore, the twice-born honor that man who performs the ancestral rites (śrāddha) on the sixth day; and the man who constantly performs the ancestral rites on the seventh day. (13)
The man who performs [this rite] on the eighth lunar day attains a great sacrifice, becomes a leader of hosts, and achieves complete prosperity.
One performing a śrāddha on the ninth day obtains sovereignty; by performing it on the tenth day, a man attains the glory of Brahmā and his desired wife. ||15||
One shall obtain all the Vedas as well as the destruction of one's sins;
likewise, on the eleventh day, there is supreme charity and constant sovereignty.

By performing [the fast] on the twelfth day, one obtains a kingdom, victory, and wealth; likewise, by performing it on the thirteenth day, one attains progeny, intelligence, cattle, wisdom, independence, supreme nourishment, long life, and sovereignty. (17)
One should cause [the rites] to be performed for those who died in whose house young men perished;
and for those who were indeed slain by a weapon, one should give [the offerings] on the fourteenth day.
Likewise, for those born under inauspicious conditions and for twins in every respect, one who is pure should always diligently perform the Śrāddha on the new moon day (Amāvāsyā). ||19||
He obtains all desires and enjoys eternal heaven;
on the new moon day, he should offer the Truth, which is the great nourishment of the Soma.
Thus nourished, Soma shall sustain the three worlds, being constantly praised by the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas. ||21||
With hymns, beautiful flowers, and all kinds of desirable articles, as well as with thousands of apsarases performing dance, instrumental music, and song. ||22||
The gods, Gandharvas, and hosts of Siddhas always praise that man who is devoted to his ancestors and firm in his vows, even as they sport upon their celestial chariots.
Devoted to his ancestors, he shall obtain all desires on the new moon day;
by him, the ancestors are always worshipped as if visibly present.
Since the ancestors and gods [dwell] in Maghā, therefore it is remembered as "Akṣaya" (the inexhaustible) during those [days];
on that day, the wise especially perform ancestral rites.
Therefore, the ancestors always desire the Maghā constellation;
even those who are devoted to the ancestors as their deity attain the supreme goal.
(26) Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Fruits of Śrāddha on Specific Lunar Days," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the *Śrī Mahāpurāṇa* proclaimed by Vāyu. (2.19)
Bṛhaspati said:
Listen to me in its entirety regarding those śrāddhas which Yama proclaimed to Śaśabindu, categorized individually according to the lunar mansions (nakṣatras). (1)
The man who constantly performs the *śrāddha* rite during the conjunction of Kṛttikā, having established the sacred fires, becomes free from affliction and is born with offspring. (2)
One desiring offspring should perform the śrāddha under Rohiṇī; through Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), one becomes endowed with vigor.
Generally, however, one who performs cruel deeds should perform the śrāddha under Ārdrā.
One who performs the *śrāddha* on the Punarvasu [nakṣatra] shall become a possessor of fields and a father of sons;
he will be filled with wealth and grain and crowded with sons and grandsons. (4)
Furthermore, a person desiring contentment should perform ancestral rites during the asterism Tiṣya;
by worshipping the ancestors under Āśleṣā, one obtains heroic sons. (5)
By performing a śrāddha under the Maghā constellation, one becomes the most excellent among kinsmen;
by honoring the ancestors under the Phalgunī constellations, a man obtains good fortune.
He who performs the rite under the Uttarās while possessing excellent character and offspring becomes preeminent among the virtuous— he who offers libations with his own hand to the ancestors.
He who performs [the rite] under Citrā shall see handsome sons;
and he who performs it under Svāti shall obtain gain, provided he is wise.
A man seeking a son should endeavor to perform a śrāddha under Viśākhā;
performing it under Anurādhā, a man may set the wheel of sovereignty in motion.
He who always performs [rites] under Jyeṣṭhā shall obtain sovereignty and preeminence;
under Mūla they desire health, and under the Āṣāḍhās, great fame.
By means of the Uttara-āṣāḍhās, a man shall become free from sorrow;
under Śravaṇā, he shall attain the supreme goal among the auspicious worlds. (11)
One who performs a śrāddha under Dhaniṣṭhā indeed becomes a sharer of the kingdom and shall obtain abundant wealth;
however, performing a śrāddha under Abhijit, one obtains the fruit of goats and sheep.
Performing [the rite] under the constellation Vāruṇa, a physician shall obtain success;
performing it under the two Pūrvaproṣṭhapadas, one obtains the fruit of goats and sheep.
Without transgressing the *Uttarās*, one shall indeed obtain [wealth] by the thousands;
performing the rite under *Revatī*, one obtains wealth consisting of many forms.
One joined with *Aśvinī* obtains horses, and under *Bharaṇī*, one obtains the highest lifespan. (14)
By performing this rite of ancestral offerings (śrāddha), Śaśabindu obtained this entire earth;
and having gained it all, he praised him [the sage].
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Fruits of Śrāddha on Specific Lunar Mansions," in the glorious *Vāyuprokta Mahāpurāṇa*.
Śaṃyu said:
O best of speakers, what gift given to the ancestors truly satisfies them?
What indeed leads to long-lasting results, and what conduces to infinity? (1)
Bṛhaspati said:
Listen to me regarding all those oblations which those who know the śrāddha rites recognize as appropriate for the time of a śrāddha, and hear also their fruits according to one's capacity. ||2||
By the offering of sesame seeds, rice, barley, mung beans, water, roots, and fruits at a śrāddha ceremony, the ancestors remain gratified for one month. (3)
With fish they satisfy [the ancestors] for two months; with the meat of the black antelope (hāriṇa), for three months;
with the meat of the hare (śāśa), for four months; and the meat of birds (śākuna) satisfies them for five months.
The boar-skin [vessel] lasts for six months, the goat-skin for seven months, and it is said that the one made from the hide of a spotted deer lasts for eight months. (5)
The grandfathers are pleased for nine months by means of the raurava meat;
however, satisfaction from the meat of the gavaya lasts for ten months.
One should know that with the meat of a tortoise, the śrāddha lasts for exactly eleven months; with beef, it shall last for a full year.
Likewise, milk-rice prepared with cow's products, honey, and clarified butter,
along with the meat of the Vadhrīṇasa, provides satisfaction for twelve years.
Offerings of rhinoceros meat on the anniversary of the ancestors' death lead to infinity;
likewise, the black goat and the monitor lizard are conducive to infinity itself. (9)
Regarding this, those who know the past recite the verses sung by the ancestors (*pitṛgītā*);
I shall proclaim them to you exactly as they are—listen attentively.
"May there be born in our own family one who would offer food on the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*)."
One should consume milk-rice with honey and ghee in the shade of an elephant.
With a sacrifice of all metals (ājya) during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism, one should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā;
or he may marry a Gaurī bride, or release a dark-colored bull. || 83.12-13 ||
Śaṃyu said:
O dear one, tell the fruit of Gayā and other such places to me who am asking;
and tell me in its entirety whatever merit belongs to the ancestors.
Bṛhaspati said:

O son, at Gayā, the ancestral rite (śrāddha), as well as recitations, burnt offerings, and ascetic penances, become inexhaustible on the anniversary of the ancestors' passing; therefore, it is remembered as inexhaustible there.
Furthermore, a son born of a Gaurī wife purifies twenty-one generations.
The merit of her [giving] is recorded as being sixfold for the maternal grandfathers.
(15) I shall describe the fruit of the bull; listen to me as I speak.
The one who releases a bull purifies ten generations past and ten generations yet to come. (16)
Whatever is touched by the waters with which one has emerged from the water onto the earth during the rite of Vṛṣotsarga is declared to be inexhaustible for the ancestors.
Whatever water he touches, even with his tail or other parts of his body, all of that becomes inexhaustible for his ancestors; of this there is no doubt. (18)
If a bull constantly scratches the earth with its horns or hooves, streams of honey flow for his ancestors, and they indeed become inexhaustible. (19)

Just as it is heard in the scriptures that satisfaction for the ancestors is obtained through a pond measuring a thousand nalvas, the satisfaction from a bull is said to be even greater than that. He who gives sesame seeds mixed with jaggery during the performance of a śrāddha ceremony [attains great merit].
Whether with honey or mixed with honey, all of that indeed becomes inexhaustible.
Bṛhaspati said:
A man should never examine Brahmins when a gift is to be given;
however, it is indeed heard in the tradition that examination is required for rites concerning the gods and the ancestors.
The twice-born who have bathed after completing all Vedic vows and are purifiers of the assembly rows—those who are preeminent knowers of the Bhāṣyas and those who are devoted to grammar. (23)
He studies the Purāṇas as well as the Dharmaśāstras;
he is one who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, maintains the five sacred fires, knows the Trisuparṇa hymn, and is a knower of the six Vedāṅgas.
The son of a Brahmadeya, a Chandoga, and a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāman—those who have performed their vows by bathing in sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas). ||25||

Those for whom the ritual purificatory baths (avabhṛtha) are prescribed in the principal sacrificial sessions (sattra), those who always observe their vows immediately, and those who are constantly devoted to their own duties; ||26||
One should indeed invite those who are free from anger, devoted to peace, and who are always established in the ten virtuous deeds at the śrāddha ceremony. (27)
What is given to these is inexhaustible; indeed, these are the purifiers of the row—those Brahmins who are worthy of trust and devoted to the practice of yoga. (28)
They are the most excellent among those who have taken refuge in the Dharma; they are the best recipients for offerings to gods and ancestors.
Thus, all three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—were honored by him. (29)
The man who honors these worlds together with the ancestors—
[he honors] the purifier of purifiers and the auspiciousness of all auspicious things. Yoga-dharma is declared to be the foremost of all dharmas.
Now I shall declare those who are unworthy of the company; listen as I speak. ||31||
A gambler, a drunkard, one afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, an outcaste, a village servant, a usurer, a singer, and likewise a merchant; ||32||
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats from a sacrificial vessel (kuṇḍāśī), a seller of Soma, one who travels by sea, one with a skin disease, an oil-presser, and a forger; ||33||
One who quarrels with his father, one in whose house there is a paramour, one who is accused of a crime, as well as a thief, and one who subsists by mechanical arts; ||34||
One who is a slanderer, one who performs ritual knots for others, one who betrays friends, one who begs from a group, an atheist, and one who has abandoned the Vedas; ||35||
The insane, the eunuch, the deceitful, the killer of an embryo, the violator of the guru’s bed, one who lives as a physician, a messenger, and he who goes to another's wife; ||36||
And he who sells the Veda, as well as vows and ascetic penances—
for one who gives to such an atheist, or to an ungrateful person, or to a slanderer, that gift is as good as lost.
And that which belongs to a usurer shall exist neither in this world nor in the next;
the same applies to one who misappropriates a deposit, a gambler, and a reviler of the Vedas. (38)
Likewise, he buys merchandise while reviling the merchant who is devoid of dharma, and he praises it while selling it himself. (39)
One who dwells in falsehood is no merchant and does not deserve a *śrāddha* offering;
it is like an oblation poured into ashes, or a gift given to a twice-born man born of a remarried woman.
A one-eyed man sees for sixty paces, a eunuch for a hundred, and one with white leprosy for as far as he can see.
One afflicted by a foul disease destroys the fruit of a thousandfold gift. ||41||
The donor from whom a foolish person eats—
whether that person eats with their head wrapped or while facing south— is deprived of the fruit of that gift.
Brahmā ordained that whatever one eats while wearing shoes, and whatever one gives with contempt, all of that belongs to the lords of the Asuras. (43)
Dogs and Yātudhānas should not look on in any way whatsoever;
therefore, one should provide a surrounding enclosure while scattering sesame seeds.
Sesame seeds are said to belong to the Rākṣasas, as is the surrounding area;
a pig destroys [the merit] by its mere sight, and a cock by its flapping of wings.
He who gives in anger after touching a woman in her menses,
and he whose offerings of *śrāddha* and oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are given to unworthy recipients—
such a man does not gratify the ancestors or the gods, nor does he go to heaven. (46)
The ancestors, gratified by what is given here, take delight in beautiful riverbanks, in streams, in lakes, and in secluded places. (47)
One should never shed tears, nor utter words that are improper;
while eating, one should not harbor mutual envy toward another. 48.

When the rite has been performed by him according to rule with the sacred grass (darbha) held in the left hand, the ancestral rite (pitrya) must be carried out until its conclusion; in this way, he truly gratifies the ancestors.
One should duly honor the Brahmins, beginning with Anumati, in the fire;
one should offer to the ancestors on the ground, or in a winnowing basket, or upon a bed of Darbha grass.
A wise man should perform the Śrāddha during the forenoon of the bright fortnight.
During the afternoon of the dark fortnight, one must not cross the Rauhiṇa [line].
Thus, these great-souled ones, who are great yogis of immense power,
are indeed always to be worshipped as the Pitṛs, for they are the perceivers of place and time.
One who is constantly devoted to filial piety attains unsurpassed yoga;
through meditation, they reach liberation, having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma.
For the sake of the sacrifice, having extracted and deluded the world at that time,
the high-souled Kaśyapa deposited the Yoga within a cave.
O best among those who know yoga, Sanatkumāra has proclaimed that great and eternal dharma, having extracted the secret nectar of yoga. ||55||
It is the supreme secret of the gods and the ultimate refuge of the sages;
it should be practiced constantly with effort by those devoted to the ancestors out of filial devotion.
And one who is devoted to his father shall, through effort, obtain that yoga in its entirety and in brief; there is no doubt that everything therein will be attained. ||57||
To whom the śrāddhas should be given, that which when offered yields great fruit,
those holy places and rivers where a śrāddha becomes inexhaustible,
and those through which one attains heaven— all this has been declared to you in summary. (58)
Bṛhaspati said:
But that man who, having heard this ritual for the ancestral offerings (śrāddha), harbors malice, shall sink into a terrible hell—an atheist enveloped in darkness. (59)
But he whose mind is restrained,
who has liberated his heart from the stages of life (āśramas) prescribed by the Vedas, does not fall into the Kumbhīpāka hell;
nor do thieves, having undergone the severing of their tongues, reach that very place.
Those enemies of yoga will sink like clods of earth in the ocean and remain there as long as the earth endures;
therefore, this dharma prescribed for the faithful must always be practiced by a man of faith.
One should not engage in slander, especially against yogins;
by slandering them, one becomes a worm and revolves right there.
He who speaks ill of yoga, which is the cause of liberation for those engaged in meditation,
shall go to a terrible hell— this is certain for both he and whoever hears it.
All of hell, which is terrible to behold, is shrouded in darkness;
yet through the discourse of the Lord of Yogins, a human being arrives at certainty.
He who hears the abuse of the masters of yoga who are self-restrained shall undoubtedly sink for a long time in the Kumbhīpāka hell.
One should avoid hatred toward yogis in thought, deed, or speech;
for after death one experiences the fruit of that [hatred], and even in this world there is no doubt. ||66||

One who has not reached the further shore does not find the shore of the Self; wandering within the three worlds by means of one's own actions, even one who has mastered the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences, perishes indeed without attaining the state beyond transformation.

He has reached the further shore of transformation and the further shore of primordial nature; he has reached the further shore of the three qualities and the further shore beyond the three qualities.
He has reached the further shore of the twenty-four principles and the further shore of Yoga; he is one who has reached the further shore of the end of the [solar] transit.

Just as he brought about the entire emission of his own self according to reality, so too, the knower of yoga—whose range of action transcends all others—should again withdraw that dissolution of his true self by the power of yoga. (69)
He who is the knower of the Veda, who as a master of yoga finds that which is to be known—
he indeed they call a knower of the Veda, him they call one who has reached the further shore of the Veda.
Having truly understood, according to the prescribed rule, both that which is to be known and that which is to be realized...
Thus others, who are thinkers on the Vedas, have declared one who knows the Vedas. ||71||
One who is devoted to the ancestors obtains sacrifices, the Vedas, as well as desires, various forms of knowledge, long life, progeny, and wealth.
He who recites this final Śrāddha-kalpa with discipline during a śrāddha ceremony obtains all these rewards as well as the fruits of giving at sacred fords (tīrtha). //73//
He shall indeed become a purifier of the assembly and the foremost diner among the twice-born;
or, by teaching all the twice-born, he shall attain all his desires. (74)
And whoever should hear this constantly attains infinite heaven—provided they are free from malice, have conquered anger, and are devoid of greed and delusion. (75)
It yields the entire fruit of sacred fords (tīrthas) as well as that of gifts and other meritorious acts.
Indeed, this is the most excellent means to liberation and the supreme means to heaven; it brings the highest satisfaction even in this world. Therefore, one should practice it with diligent effort.

Whoever recites this ritual procedure with vigilance and concentration during assemblies on the junctions of the lunar phases shall obtain offspring and, through supreme splendor, attain the same world as the inhabitants of heaven.
Salutation to that Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) by whom this ritual manual was proclaimed;
and I am forever bowed down before the Great Lords of Yoga.
These, O dear one, are the Pitṛs, the deities even of the gods;
in these seven locations, the Pitṛs always abide free from distress.
For all these are indeed the sons of Prajāpati and belong to the Great-Souled One;
the first group belongs to the Yogas, which is eternal and increases Yoga.
The second belongs to the Devas, and the third belongs to the enemies of the Devas.
But the remaining [stages] are to be known as belonging to the social classes; thus all have been proclaimed. ||81||
The gods indeed worship these [deities], being established within all of them;
likewise, the four stages of life (āśramas) worship these in their proper order. 82.
Furthermore, these four castes perform sacrifices according to the prescribed rules;
likewise, those born of mixed unions and even the Mlecchas indeed perform sacrifices.
The ancestors honor him who worships them with devotion;
furthermore, for one desiring prosperity or desiring progeny, the grandfathers bestow prosperity, progeny, and heaven. (84)
Even more important than the rites for the gods are the rites for the ancestors;
for the ancestors themselves are the primary source of nourishment for the deities. (85)
For the subtle course of yoga and the supreme state of the ancestors cannot be seen with the fleshly eye, even through extensive asceticism. (86)
For all [offerings], a silver vessel or one adorned with silver is declared to be the most excellent and purifying for the gods as well as the ancestors. (87)

To those for whom the kinsmen shall offer three morsels of food according to their names and lineages, upon the ground covered with *kuśa* grass and according to the rite of the *apasavya* (leftward) orientation. ||88||
These balls of food, offered everywhere, truly gratify the ancestors;
whatever be the food of a living being, that very food becomes theirs. (89)
Just as a calf finds its mother who has wandered lost in the cow-pen, so does the mantra lead that person to wherever he dwells. 90.
His name, his lineage, the mantra, and the food offered—these lead him there.
Even when they have attained hundreds of wombs, satisfaction follows after them. ||91||
Thus was this arrangement established by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin:
the primary creation of the ancestors for the sake of those worlds seeking imperishability. 92.
Thus, these Pitṛs are gods, and gods are again Pitṛs; O sinless one, I have also declared that grandsons and sacrificers are likewise [Pitṛs]. 93.
The worlds, daughters, grandsons, and likewise sons, as well as gifts along with purity, sacred fords, and their fruits—[all these arise from this]. (94)
The imperishability [of the lineage], the twice-born, and likewise the ritual procedure of the Yāyāvara—all this has been declared according to the rule, just as Brahmā spoke it in the past. (95)
Bṛhaspati said:
Thus Aṅgiras spoke while the sages were listening;
questioned regarding the entire doubt, he explained it in the assembly of the ancestors.
Indeed, when that thousand-year sacrificial session was first extended, Brahmā was the presiding householder and the lordly deity. (97)
"Furthermore, according to the sacred tradition (śruti), they remain there for hundreds of years;
and in this regard, verses were sung of old by the seers who discourse on Brahman. (98)
Then, at that very place during the sacrificial session (*sattra*) of the consecrated Brahmā, the Supreme Self,
an exceedingly fierce [being] was born by the Supreme Creator Brahmā, who desired the imperishability of the ancestors and for the welfare of the worlds. (99)
Sūta said:

Thus was Bṛhaspati previously questioned by his wise son; he then proclaimed that lineage of the ancestors which has been related. Hereafter, I shall declare the lineage of Varuṇa; listen to it. 2.21.100. 83.129.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Examination of Brāhmaṇas and the Fruits of Śrāddha at Gayā, as well as the Specific Substances that Serve as Means for Satisfaction at Different Times," in the Śrāddhakalpa of the *Śrī Mahāpurāṇa* proclaimed by Vāyu. 2.21.
The sages said:
When the sages had been addressed in this manner, they attained supreme joy; desiring to hear more, they immediately asked further.
Tell us, who are questioning you, about the successive lineages of these kings of immeasurable splendor— their stability and their power.
Thus addressed, that Sūta Lomaharṣaṇa,
who was skilled in speech, then expressed his desire to listen to the further narrative from the sages.
Skilled in narration, he spoke further words:
"Listen to me as I relate what the sage said to me. (4)
Listen as I describe, in their successive order, the dynasties and kings of immeasurable splendor, as well as their stability and power.
The wife of Varuṇa, the daughter of the ocean, is celebrated as Śunodevī;
her sons were Kali and Vaidya, and her daughter was Surasundarī.
Kali had two sons of great heroism, Jaya and Vijaya;
and the sons of Vaidya were Ghṛṇi and Muni, both of great strength.
Desiring to eat living beings and devouring one another, they both met their destruction after having devoured each other. (8)
Kali was born from Surā; his son is known as Mada.
Hiṃsā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, was the wife of Kali; she is remembered as the eldest, Nikṛti.
From Asūta were born four man-eating sons of Kali:
Vighna, the famous Nāka, Sadrama, and likewise Vidhama.
The obstacle (Vighna) of those two was headless, and Nāka was bodiless;
Sadrama had one hand, and Vidhama is remembered as having one foot.
Likewise, the wife of Sadrama is known as Pūtanā, who is of the nature of darkness (tāmasī); Revatī is the wife of Vidhama, and they have thousands of sons.
Nākasyaśakuni is the wife of Vighna, and Ayomukhī is the wife of Rākṣasa;
these great-headed Rākṣasas roam about during both twilights.
The sons of Revatī and Pūtanā are known by the name Nairṛtas;
all those grahas are Rākṣasas, especially [dangerous] to children. Skanda is their overlord, the powerful one, acting with the approval of Brahmā. (14)
The sister of Bṛhaspati, an excellent woman who observes celibacy, perfected in yoga, wanders forever through the entire world unattached. (15)
She was the wife of Prabhāsa, the eighth of the Vasus;
from her was born Viśvakarman, the son who is the lord of artisans.
Tvaṣṭṛ, the grandson of Dharma, possessed noble intellect; he was the fashioner of the forms of Virāj, the creator of thousands of arts, and the architect for the thirty gods.
He who indeed fashioned the celestial mansions for all the gods, and upon whose craftsmanship human beings depend for their livelihood—[that high-souled one]. (18)
The renowned Prahlādī was the wife of that Tvaṣṭṛ;
she was the sister of Virocana and the mother of Triśiras.
He is known as the son of the great and wise Viśvakarman, the preceptor of the gods;
indeed, he is considered to be composed of the very essence of Viśvakarman.
His younger sister was renowned as Sureṇu; she was the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, the wife of Savitṛ, and was further known by the name Saṃjñā. (21)
O Sūta, through her ascetic penance, she [gave birth] to Manu, the eldest son of Vivasvat;
furthermore, that same woman gave birth to Yama and Yamunā. ||22||
Having gone to the Kurus, that goddess, assuming the form of a mare, [pierced] those two [nostrils] with the nostrils of Savitṛ, who was in the form of a horse; thus they are remembered.
O Sūta, that illustrious lady indeed saw in the intermediate space both Nāsatya and Dasra, the two sons of Mārtaṇḍa, the Aśvins. 24.
The sages said:
Why is this Vivasvat called Mārtaṇḍa by the wise?
For what reason was she indeed born from his nostrils in the form of a mare?
We wish to know this; O Vibhu, explain the truth to us who ask. (25)
Sūta said:
Having seen the eggshell split and torn open by Tvaṣṭṛ, Kaśyapa, whose mind had long since been set upon it, became distressed and filled with fear that the embryo might be destroyed.
When the egg was split in two, having seen the egg, he spoke to Tvaṣṭṛ:
"This is certainly not an egg; O sinless one, you shall indeed become Mārtaṇḍa."
"Indeed, he is not dead, even though he is in the egg," the father said out of affection;
hearing those words of his, [the son] uttered a name that was true to its meaning. (28)
Because he was told by his father, "Become Mārttaṇḍa," when the egg was indeed split in two,
he is therefore called Vivasvān Mārttaṇḍa by those who know the Purāṇas.
Next, I shall describe the progeny of Vivasvat Mārtaṇḍa;
in ancient times, Saṃjñā, the wife of Savitṛ, gave birth to a triad.
Manu Sāvarṇi the youngest, Saṃjñā, and likewise the two Aśvins, as well as Śanaiścara—these seven are remembered as the sons of Mārtaṇḍa. ||31||

The highly illustrious Vivasvān was born from Kaśyapa through Dākṣāyaṇī. The wife of that Vivasvān was the great goddess, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, who was renowned as Sureṇu and also celebrated as Saṃjñā. (32)
But that wife of the Blessed Mārtaṇḍa,
though endowed with beauty and youth, was not satisfied with the appearance of her husband, who possessed exceeding splendor.
For that form of the Sun, Mārtaṇḍa, being obstructed by the splendor of the lineages, indeed did not appear very radiant.
Out of affection, Kaśyapa, being ignorant, said to him, "He is not dead, for he is within an egg"; and because of that affection, he is called Mārtaṇḍa.
The splendor of that son of Kaśyapa, Vivasvat, was always exceedingly great, by which he scorched the three worlds.
The Sun indeed begot three offspring upon Saṃjñā:
two sons of great prowess and a daughter, Kālindī.
Manu, the eldest son of Vivasvat, was the Prajāpati Śrāddhadeva;
from him were born Yama and Yamī as twins.
Seeing that form of Vivasvat’s wife to be of such a tranquil appearance, Saṃjñā, unable to endure her own wife Savarṇā, created another [form] for herself. (39)
But that woman, made of earth, having emerged from her shadow,
stood with palms joined in reverence and, becoming composed, spoke again with consciousness restored.
"Tell me, what must be done by me? Saṃjñā then said to her:
"Blessings upon you; I shall go to my own father's abode. (41)
"You must dwell here in my house without any hesitation;
and these two children of mine, as well as this maiden of excellent complexion. (42)
"This must certainly not be told by you to your husband, the Blessed One.
Thus addressed, that earthly woman spoke to Saṃjñā. (43)
"O Goddess, because of my grasp upon the sky, I shall never disclose my intention; I shall explain my thought to you [later]. Go, O Goddess, to your own abode. (44)
Having composed herself and agreed to that designation with "So be it," she,
like a distressed woman overcome with shame, went into the presence of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Seeing her returned, the father became enraged and said to Saṃjñā:
"Go to your husband; do not despise the Sun. (46)
Thus addressed by her father and urged again and again,
she lived indeed in her father's house for a thousand years.
"Go to your husband's presence, for you have been repeatedly commanded. Having said this, the blameless woman, concealing her form and becoming a mare,
went to the northern Kurus and there began to graze upon the grass.
Regarding the second name, let it be considered that this is the name of the one to be named:
Āditya begot two sons who possessed the splendor of the sun. (49)
Those two lords were equal to their elder brother Manu in appearance;
they were Śrutaśravas, the knower of dharma, and Śrutakarmā.
Śrutaśravas will be that Manu Sāvarṇi;
and Śrutakarman is to be known as the planet Śanaiścara.
He indeed became Manu Sāvarṇya; thus he is known.
That was the name given by the daughter of the Earth (Pārthivī) to her own son at that time.
Manu indeed showed greater affection for him than for his elder brothers;
Manu tolerated all of that, but Yama did not tolerate it at all.
Though he was repeatedly oppressed and deeply distressed by the rivalry of his co-wife,
he [spoke] to her out of anger, childishness, and the force of destiny yet to come.
Then Yama himself threatened Saṃjñā with his foot;
she, in turn, out of anger, cursed her mother Savarṇā.
"Since you have threatened the illustrious wife of your father with your foot, therefore this foot of yours shall fall; of this there is no doubt. (56)
But Yama, his mind deeply afflicted by that curse, reported everything to his father along with Manu, he who is righteous in soul. ||57||
Greatly agitated by the fear of a curse and overcome by the words of Saṃjñā, you ought to save me, whether out of compassion for my youth or because of your own delusion. (58)
O Lord of the World, O best among those who radiate heat, I have been cursed by my mother;
may your grace protect us from this great danger. (59)
Thus addressed, the lord Vivasvat spoke to Yama:
"O son, there is no doubt that a great destiny awaits; therein lies the cause."
That anger which has taken possession of you— you who know the Dharma and speak the truth—
it is impossible to make this word of your mother false.
Worms shall take your flesh and go to the earth;
thereafter, O one of great wisdom, you will again obtain comfort in your foot.
In this way, the word of your mother will become true;
and by averting the curse, you shall be her savior.
The Sun then said to Saṃjñā: "Why indeed is greater affection shown by you toward one among your children, even though they are all equal? (64)
Seeking to avoid it, she did not tell Vivasvat;
instead, having composed herself through yoga, she perceived the truth within her own soul.
Desiring to curse her, the Lord, the powerful master, became enraged for the sake of her destruction;
she then related everything to Vivasvat exactly as it had happened.
Then Vivasvat, having heard that, went in anger to Tvaṣṭṛ;
but Tvaṣṭṛ, having honored that Vibhāvasu according to custom, [honored him].
Desiring to pacify him who was burning with rage, he spoke gently:
"This form of yours, endowed as it is with excessive brilliance, does not look well. (68)
Unable to endure that perception, she wanders in the grassy forest;
today you shall behold her, your own wife of auspicious conduct.
O Lord of Rays, having resorted to yoga, you should favor this praiseworthy woman endowed with youth,
if it be your considered time.
O subduer of enemies, at the end he transformed his form;
that first and most excellent form of Vivasvat was likewise horizontal, upward, and downward. (71)
Because of that, the god who was the lord of heaven was ashamed of his form;
therefore, Tvaṣṭṛ, of great asceticism, highly esteemed that discus.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ was authorized for the creation of the form;
thus, by the acceptance of Vivasvat Mārtaṇḍa, Tvaṣṭṛ [proceeded].
Having placed that splendor upon a lathe, he indeed whetted it;
and that splendor was rendered lusterless by being stripped of its brilliance through his own splendor.
Then, desiring to see something more beautiful than the beautiful, he beheld an auspicious sight;
employing his yogic power, he likewise saw his own wife in the form of a mare.
Invisible to all beings by virtue of his splendor and ascetic discipline,
Mārtaṇḍa, in the form of a horse, infused her with vital energy through his mouth.
Striving for sexual union out of suspicion that he was another man,
she discharged Vivasvat’s semen through her two nostrils.
From him were born two gods, the Aśvins, the best among physicians;
they are known as the two Aśvins, namely Nāsatya and Dasra. ||78||
These two were the sons of Mārtaṇḍa, the eighth Prajāpati;
the Sun-god revealed himself to them in his beautiful and radiant form.
Upon seeing him, his wife then rejoiced and was overcome with passion;
Yama, however, his mind deeply tormented by that curse, [fell into a swoon].
Then that Dharmarāja delighted [his subjects] through righteousness;
by virtue of that auspicious action, he attained supreme splendor.
He shall possess sovereignty over the ancestors and the status of a world-protector;
he is Manu Prajāpati Sāvarṇi, possessed of great fame.
He is to be manifested when that Sāvarṇika Manvantara has arrived;
for even now, the Lord continues to move about upon the beautiful summit of Mount Meru.
His brother Śanaiścara obtained the status of a planet there;
Tvaṣṭṛ, by means of that form, fashioned for Viṣṇu a discus that was great and irresistible in battle for the purpose of warding off the Dānavas.
The younger of the two was the illustrious Yamunā;
she became the Yamunā, the best of rivers, who brings prosperity to the world.
I shall now describe in detail the lineage of Vaivasvata Manu, who is the eldest and most illustrious, and whose creation is current at this time.
Whoever should hear or recite this account of the birth of the seven sons of Vaivasvata, who possess great majesty,
shall be liberated from calamity upon encountering it and shall attain great renown. (87)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Varuṇa," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Then, when the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara had passed, together with the deities,
he assigned the sovereignty of the earth to the great Vaivasvata.
O brahmins, listen as I describe in due order the lineage of that great-souled Vaivasvata Manu, who is current in this age. ||2||
Now, taking up the current creation of Manu Vaivasvata here, he had nine sons born first from Manu who were equal to him. (3)
Ikṣvāku, Nahuṣa, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti,
Nariṣyanta, Prāṃśu, Nābhāga, Ariṣṭa,
Karūṣa, and Pṛṣadhra— these nine are remembered as the sons of Manu. (4)
Listen now: having been previously impelled by Brahmā, Manu set about creating;
however, his desire proved to be fruitless. (5)
Then Prajāpati, desiring sons, performed a supreme sacrifice;
Manu offered an oblation into the portion of Mitra and Varuṇa.
In that regard, the sacred tradition (śruti) states that Iḍā was born wearing divine garments, adorned with divine ornaments, and clad in divine armor.
Then Manu, the wielder of the rod of punishment, said, "She is known as Tāmilī.
"I shall follow her; may it be well with you," Tāmilī replied. (8)
"O best among speakers, this which is consistent with dharma should be said to Prajāpati, who desires a son: 'I was born from the portions of Mitra and Varuṇa. (9)
"I shall go into their presence so that Dharma may not destroy us.
Having spoken thus, the goddess once again approached the vicinity of those two.
Approaching them, the lady of noble form spoke these words with palms joined in reverence:
"O gods, I am born from a portion of you both; what shall I do? (11)
"I have been told by Manu himself: 'Follow me.
Thus did the virtuous woman speak, and both of them took refuge with Iḍā. (12)
And the two gods, Mitra and Varuṇa, spoke these words:
"O knower of dharma, because of this humility and self-restraint of yours," (13)
"O lady of beautiful hips, O woman of excellent complexion, we are both pleased by your truthfulness; O highly fortunate maiden, you shall attain renown among us. (14)
He became renowned as Sudyumna, honored throughout the three worlds; beloved by the world, virtuous in character, he was the one who caused the lineage of Manu to flourish. ||15||
That lord Sudyumna, though a human being, attained the state of a woman;
and that goddess, having obtained the boon, returned toward her father.
Having approached Budha, she was invited for sexual union;
from Budha, the son of Soma, Aila Purūravas was born to her. (17)
Having given birth to Sudyumna from Budha, she returned once more;
and Sudyumna had three sons who were supremely righteous.
Utkala, Gaya, and likewise Vinatāśva;
Utkala’s kingdom was Utkala, and that of Vinatāśva was in the west.
In the various directions were the cities of the royal sages Vāta and Gaya, namely Gayā. (19)
When Manu had been thus dismissed, the Maker of Day, having created the progeny, divided this earth into ten portions and established that as his field. ||2.23.20||
Ikṣvāku alone shall obtain ten other heirs;
however, because Sudyumna was in the state of a maiden, he shall not receive this share.
And by the word of Vasiṣṭha, there was the highly resplendent Pratiṣṭhāna,
which became the capital of the high-souled Sudyumna, the king of dharma.
Having obtained the kingdom, that highly illustrious one gave it to Purūravas; meanwhile,
O fortunate ones, regarding the characteristics of men and women among human beings,
that Sudyumna, the son of Manu, again attained the state of womanhood.
Having heard this, the ṛṣis immediately asked:
"How did that Mānava, Sudyumna, attain the state of a woman? (24)
Sūta said:
For the sake of her beloved, the dear goddess spoke these words:
"O Lord, whatever man shall enter my hermitage, he will certainly become a woman, auspicious and equal to the Apsarases. (25)
There, all beings—whether Piśācas or animals—as well as those who have become women, sport together with Rudra and the Apsarases. (26)
Having entered Umāvana, that king went out on a hunt;
accompanied by Piśācas, Bhūtas, and Rudras, he assumed the form of a woman.
Therefore, that King Sudyumna regained his female state,
and by the grace of Mahādeva, he attained the rank of a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya).
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Account of the Creation of Vaivasvata Manu," in the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa* told by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Learn in detail the natural disposition of the sons of Manu:
Pṛṣadhra, having caused injury, ate the cow of his preceptor.
Having attained the status of a Śūdra due to the curse of the high-souled Cyavana,
he became Karūṣa’s son, Kārūṣa, a Kṣatriya fierce in battle.
He indeed became one who surpassed a thousand hosts of kṣatriyas;
the son of Ariṣṭa was the learned Nābhāga, and his son was Bhalandana.
Bhalandana had a son named Prāṃśu, who was possessed of great strength.
Prāṃśu had an only son, renowned as Prajāni. (4)
Prajāni had a son named Khanitra, who was full of valor;
his son was the illustrious and highly renowned Kṣupa. ||5||
Kṣupa had twenty sons, but there was no one among them who was his equal;
the son of Viṃśa was the righteous Kalyāṇa, named Viviṃśa.
The son of Viviṃśa was the righteous and powerful Khaninetra;
his son Karandhama appeared at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga.
The son of Karandhama was the heroic one named Āvikṣita;
Āvikṣita surpassed his father in virtue.
A righteous king named Marutta, equal to a universal monarch,
was led to heaven by Saṃvarta along with his friends and kinsmen.
A great dispute arose here between Saṃvarta and Bṛhaspati;
having seen the prosperity of his sacrifice, Bṛhaspati became enraged.
When the sacrifice was carried away by Saṃvarta, he then became exceedingly enraged;
for he was intent on the destruction of the worlds, though he was eventually pacified by the deities. (11)
Marutta was a universal monarch (cakravartin); he obtained Nariṣyanta as his son.
The heir of Nariṣyanta was King Dama, the wielder of the staff of punishment.
His son was the valiant King Rāṣṭravardhana;
Sudhṛti was his son, and Nara was the son of Sudhṛti.
Kevala’s son was Bandhumān, the son of Kevala;
then the son of Bandhumān was the righteous King Vegavān.
Budha was the son of Vegavat; Tṛṇabindu was the son of Budha;
he became the king at the beginning of the third age, the Tretā Yuga. ||15||
His daughter was Draviḷā, for she was the mother of Viśravas;
and his son was Viśāla, a most righteous king.
To Viśāla was born Viśālā, created by Naya;
the son of Viśāla was King Hemacandra, who possessed great strength. ||17||
After Hemacandra, there was the one renowned as Sucandra;
Sucandra’s son was the king celebrated as Dhūmrāśva. (18)
The learned Dhūmrāśva’s son was Sṛñjaya;
Sṛñjaya’s son was the illustrious and powerful Sahadeva. (19)
Kṛśāśva was the son of Sahadeva and was supremely righteous;
Kṛśāśva’s son was the highly effulgent and powerful Somadatta.
Janamejaya was the son of the royal sage Somadatta;
and the son of Janamejaya was the renowned Pramati.
By the grace of Tṛṇabindu, all the kings of Vaiśālī were long-lived, high-souled, heroic, and very righteous. ||22||
Śaryāti had a pair of children: a son renowned by the name Ānarta, and a daughter named Sukanyā, who became the wife of Cyavana. (23)
The heir of Ānarta was the heroic one named Reva;
his domain was Ānarta, and his city was Kuśasthalī.
Reva’s son was the righteous Raivata, named Kakudmin;
having obtained Kuśasthalī, he became the king of a hundred brothers as their eldest. ||25||
Having heard from Brahmā that the Gandharva marriage had taken place with the maiden,
[he understood] that for the Lord of gods, a single moment is for mortals like many eons, O All-pervading One.
And the youth returned to his own city, which was surrounded by the Yādavas—the beautiful Dvāravatī by name, possessing many gates. ||27||
Having heard that account exactly as it happened from the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas, who were protected by Vasudeva and led by him, Raivata, the subduer of enemies, [acted accordingly].
Having given his daughter Revatī, named Suvratā, to Baladeva,
he went to the peak of Mount Meru and remained there established in asceticism.
The righteous-souled Rāma, accompanied by Revatī, was indeed sporting;
having heard that story, the sages then questioned him further.
The sages said:
O son of a Sūta, how is it that after so much time has passed through many ages, Revatī has not grown old? And why, O Lord, does she have no grey hair? (31)
How did the lineage of that Śaryāti, who had gone to Mount Meru, remain on earth even until today? I wish to hear this according to the truth. (32)
How many hosts of gods and what kind of Gandharvas are there, hearing of whom Raivata considers long periods of time to be like a mere moment? (33)
Sūta said:
For one who has reached the world of Brahmā, there is indeed no old age, nor hunger or thirst, nor fear of death; nor does disease prevail. (34)
Furthermore, O best of sages, regarding that which you have asked concerning the Gāndharva [Veda], I shall explain it to you exactly as it is, O you of excellent vows. (35)
There are seven notes, three scales (grāmas), twenty-one melodic modulations (mūrchanās), and forty-nine time-measures (tālas); this is the circle of notes (svaramaṇḍala). //36//
Ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, madhyama, pañcama, as well as dhaivata, and likewise niṣāda are to be known. (37)
Sauvīrī, Madhyamagrāma, and likewise Hariṇāsyā; the fourth is Śuddhamadhyamā, which is endowed with *kalā* and *upabala*. (38)
Śārṅgī, Pāvanī, and Dṛṣṭākā are known respectively as belonging to the Madhyama-grāma; now learn of the Ṣaḍja-grāma. (39)
One should know that the seventh [mūrcchanā] is Uttaramandrā, Rajanī, as well as that which is Uttarāyatā, and likewise Śuddhaṣaḍjā. (2.24.40)
Learn now of other [sāmans] belonging to the Gāndhāra scale as they are being proclaimed:
the first is the Āgniṣṭomika, and the second is the Vājapeyika. ||41||
The third is declared to be Pauṇḍraka, the fourth the Aśvamedhika;
the fifth is the Rājasūya, and the sixth the Cakrasuvarṇaka. ||42||
The seventh is called Gosava; the eighth is the Mahāvṛṣṭi-karma;
the ninth is Brahmadāna; and immediately after that is Prājāpatya.
One should know the Nāgapakṣāśraya, and likewise the Gotara;
also the Hayakrānta, the Mṛgakrānta, and the charming Viṣṇukrānta. 44.
The Sūryyakrānta, the Vareṇya, the Mattakokilavādin, the Sāvitra, the Ardhasāvitra, and the Sarvatomadra. ||45||
Suvarṇa, Sutandra, both Viṣṇu and Vaiṣṇava, Sāgara, and Vijaya—all of whom are enchanting to all living beings. ||46||
We recognize Haṃsa as the eldest, as well as Tumburupriya,
Manohara, Madhātṛ, and he who is followed by the Gandharvas.
Alambuṣeṣṭa and likewise Nāradapriya were also mentioned by Bhīmasena as being dear to the citizens.
Karopanīta, Vinatā, and Śrīrākhyo are dear to Bhārgava;
there are twenty [tunes] in the Madhyama-grāma and fourteen in the Ṣaḍja-grāma. ||49||
Likewise, they maintain that there are fifteen notes established in the Gāndhāra scale;
for the Gāndhārī, together with the Sauvīrī, is indeed sung by Brahmā.
Furthermore, Brahmā is the presiding deity here of the very first note, Uttara.
Born in the region of Hari, she was born with a deer-like face;
her musical mode (mūrcchanā) was indeed Hariṇāsyā, and Indra was her presiding deity. (51)
In the circle of notes (svaramaṇḍala), it is extended by the winds brought forth by effort;
therefore, it is brought to perfection by that [effort], and the wind is the presiding deity here. 52.
The *mūrcchanā* arising from the region of Manu is Śuddhamadhyamā;
here the note Madhyama is pure, and the deity here is Gandharva. (53)
Because she wanders with deer while showing the path to the Siddhas, she is known as Mārgī; and the Lord of Beasts (Siṃha) is her presiding deity. //54//

And that [melody], joined with the *āśrama* [scale], possesses many *paurava* notes; for this is indeed a *mūrcchanā* consisting of a union [of notes], and it is thus a night (*rajanī*) due to its passion (*rajas*). (55)
They know that Tāla has Uttara-mandra as its primary part and Ṣaḍja as its presiding deity;
therefore, they know that the first [measure], Svāyata, belongs to Uttara-tāla;
hence this is Uttara-mandra, and Dhruva is certainly its deity.
And because it follows after Apāna, this mūrcchanā is indeed the Uttarāyaṇa;
thus, the Pitṛs are the deities of the Śrāddha.
Since the great seers perform their worship of the fire after producing the pure Ṣaḍja note,
one should therefore know that [note] as the pure Ṣaḍjika.
That which, having formed the *mūrcchanā* of the virtuous, becomes the fifth note (*pañcama-svara*), is the *mūrcchanā* of the *yakṣīs*; it is known as the *yākṣikā-mūrcchanā*. ||59||
The poisonous glances of the serpents do not approach when this melody is sung;
for these serpent-deities are as if seized by Brahmā.
This is indeed the "fainting" (mūrcchanā) of the snakes, and Varuṇa is the presiding deity here.
Having made a comparison with birds, the Kinnaras attain the highest *mūrcchanā*;
therefore, the king of birds is the presiding deity here.
By the term *gāndhāra-rāga*, one holds (*dhārayate*) the earth (*gām*) in its true sense;
therefore, she is the Pure Gāndhārī, and the Gandharva is her presiding deity. (62)
Since this mūrchanā was created after going immediately following Gāndhārī, it is therefore called Uttaragāndhārī; and the Vasus are the presiding deities here.
Indeed, O Grandfather, this great element has approached you;
therefore, this *mūrcchanā* of the note Ṣaḍja is remembered as having the god of fire as its deity. (64)
This [jāti] is divine and extensive; therefore, it has a weak sixth note in the *mūrcchanā*, and here the fifth note is called *nivṛtta-guṇa* while the *dhaivata* is present.
Thus, the *mūrcchanās* are proclaimed to be complete with all seven notes (*svaras*),
including the various *sādhāraṇas* and the six *anuvits*.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of the Gāndharva Mūrcchanās in the Lineage of Vaivasvata Manu," in the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa* spoken by Vāyu.
Having understood the doctrine of the former teachers, I shall explain the thirty ornaments in their proper sequence; listen as I proclaim them to you. (1)

The ornaments, which serve as the causes [of their application], should be described according to their respective phonemes, as well as through the application of metrical structures and by examining the arrangement of the quarters. (2)
The completion of the ornament is achieved through the meaning of the sentence and the meaning of the word-connections;
they say that the words [of the ornament] may appear either before or after the song. (3)
One should know there are three locations: the chest, the throat, and likewise the head.
In these three locations, the supreme method is set in motion. (4)
The gods know that there are four castes in nature, fourfold discernment, eightfold conceptualization, and sixteenfold [perception]. ||5||

Those who know the *varṇas* recognize that the first is the stationary (*sthāyin*) *varṇa*, the second is the passing (*prasaṃcārī*), the third is descending (*avarohaṇa*), and the fourth is ascending (*ārohaṇa*). (6)
Therein, one [note] moves through the stationary [notes], becoming both moving and stationary;
then one should indicate the descent (avaroha) of the notes of the *rohaṇa* scale.
Those who know the colors understand the color of the ascent by means of the ascent;
now learn the ornaments of these very colors.
The ornaments, however, are fourfold: Sthāpanī, Krama, Rejinī, Pramāda, and Apramāda; I shall explain their characteristics. (9)
The Visvaroṣṭra-kalās, having moved from their place by one interval, are two in number according to their measure, produced in succession within the Āvarta. ||2.25.10||
One should know another youth as having gone to extensive vomiting;
he indeed possesses the apāṅga [lineage], and Kutāreka is superior in his artistic skill (kalā). ||11||
The Śyena, however, is born at an interval of one [mātrā] and remains at an interval of a mere *kalā*;
in that very tone, an increase exists that is distinct from it. (12)
The hawk (śyena) is proclaimed as the lower hand, while the other is the upper; by the measure of a sixteenth part (kalā), it is known by the name Bindu.
The single digit of the drop (bindu) should be fashioned so that it remains at the end of the phoneme;
even if its vowel is reversed, it shall not be difficult to accomplish.
The intervals between the notes should be one step apart; the supreme note begins from *ṣaḍja*.
One should perform the "seizing" and "leaping" movements with a loud resonance like that of a crow. (15)
Those two, however, are to be moved as *santāra* notes, whether as effect or cause;
likewise, they may be projected (*ākṣipta*), descended (*avarohya*), sprinkled (*prokṣa*), or even at the beginning or end. 16.
And the twelfth is the place of the *kalā*; then, moving at intervals of one, there is the ornament called *preṅkholita*, thus endowed with the musical notes (*svara*). (17)
Then, that which is called "puṣkala" is indeed proclaimed as having its own inherent transfer;
it occurs when a quarter-measure is added to each of the other two feet. 18.
Or, that which has been diminished according to its true nature during two moments is called "reduced" (hrāsita);
likewise, it arises from the utterance mounted upon the vowels, up to the end of the eighth vowel.
Whether it be a descent from high to low or from low to high, these [notes], being devoid of any interval, ultimately resolve into that very same note. (2.25.20)
The four-syllable gaṇa is known as *makṣipracchedana*.
These thirty ornaments that have been proclaimed exist through the application of syllables and positions, according to the measure of *kalā* and *mātrā*. ||21||
Configuration, measure, modification, and likewise characteristic—these four are to be known as the purposes of poetic ornamentation. 22.
For just as an ornament misplaced on oneself is highly censured, so too is it improper to use one's own caste for the sake of adorning it, since it originates from oneself. (23)
Just as a woman's adornment consists in the combination of various ornaments, so too the ornamentation of a caste is highly censurable when it is misplaced. (24)
Just as an earring is not seen on the foot nor a girdle on the neck, even so an ornament placed out of its proper position is censured. (25)
Even when being performed, an ornament which reveals passion is prescribed for the path that has been indicated as the task to be accomplished. ||26||
I shall explain, according to reality, the characteristics, the manifestations, and the modes of occurrence of those born from the mouth of Māsedbhava. (27)
Twenty-three and eighty—that is the reverse of those [values].
Even in the Ṣaḍja-pakṣa, the middle tone becomes a low tone at the beginning of the principles (tattva) and so forth. (28)
Likewise, there are six [notes] for the Śuddha-Ṣaḍja and Śuddha-Madhyama scales, as well as for the Mārgī-Uttaramandra and the Avikṛta [scale]. (29)
The conviction in one's own voice is indeed considered the conviction for all;
having followed the external song, the five deities are thus understood. ||2.25.30||
The middle portion, however, is the transition occurring before the cow-figures;
the division between those two is established within the path of aesthetic charm (*lāvaṇya*) of the songs. 31.
I have indicated the *anuṣaṅga*, the *svasāra*, and the *svarāntara*;
the *paryāya* proceeds according to the sequence of the seven notes (*saptasvara*).
The four *mandraka* notes are sung with the *gāndhāra* partial note (*aṃśa*).

We recognize that the fifth (*pañcama*) and the middle (*madhyama*) [notes] are produced by the *dhaivata* and *niṣāda* [partial notes], respectively; however, among the *mandraka* notes themselves, there is no interval (*antara*) [between them]. (33)
One should know that there are two [notes] belonging to the future limit (apara-anta) for the eight syllables of *dhayaśulla*;
these are indeed employed in the *prākṛta* and *vaiṇava* [modes] within the *gāndhāra* division.
The *pada* has three forms, while the *kauśika* has seven;
the rule for the variation is traditionally held to be by means of the *gāndhāra* partial note (*aṃśa*) in its entirety.
And thus, in the sequence specified, the *madhyama* [jāti] belongs to the *madhyamāṃśa*.
Those songs which have been proclaimed, especially by way of form,
should be performed with seven notes and seven forms, O Kauśika.
They call it "the vision of the limbs"; likewise, there are two equal measures (mānas). The practice of the second state is the measure established at the navel. ||37||
And in the subsequent [state], it dissolves into the measure (mātrā) by its very nature;
thus, the slayers [of the senses] do not transcend that measure wherein the body (piṇḍaka) resides. ||38||
When one foot is missing from the measure, it is called *pādonā* or *vīraṇā*;
the reduction of the number [of feet] therein is traditionally known as *yāna*.
The second [foot] is a *pādabhaṅga* established by a *graha*;
the first occurs at the eighth and third [syllables], while the second occurs at the [eighth and] twelfth. (2.25.40)
By half [of the measure], there is equality with a quarter; and from a fifth part of the quarter-measure, there is a quarter-measure plus a quarter, which is likewise established in the *prakṛti*.
In Uttara, as well as in Madravatī and Madraka, it is the fourth;
and in Madraka, even in the south, the aforementioned kalā prevails. 42.
The subsequent inquiry is intended as the second cognition;
the bringing of the feet and our reaching the further shore is not prescribed here. (43)
O best of the twice-born, when there is a unity of function between two [characters], it is called *patākā*; however, when there is a combination of many, it is known as *hariṇa*. (44)
And of the three modes of conduct (*vṛtti*), the *dakṣiṇā* is the conduct;
there are eight musical combinations (*samavāya*), as well as the *sauvīra* scale (*mūrcchanā*).
Kuśa is unsurpassed, and truth is that which is the sevenfold tone of being (*sattvasvara*). (45) 87.46
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ornament of the Gītā," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu. 2.25.
Sūta said:
When Kakutstha had departed for the realm of Raivata,
that entire city of Kuśasthalī was destroyed by the Puṇyajanas and Rākṣasas.
Then that hundred of brothers of that righteous, high-souled one,
being bound by the Rākṣasas, fled in all directions out of fear.
Overcome by fear of them, those Kṣatriyas fled here and there;
however, O best of the twice-born, their lineage there became very great indeed.
Renowned in all directions as righteous, they were known as the Prayatas;
the Kṣatriya clan of Dhṛṣṭa became indeed bold in battle.
The three thousand great-souled kṣatriyas along with their clans [were his followers];
and the heir of Nabhaga was the powerful one named Nābhāga.
Ambarīṣa was the son of Nābhāgi, and Virūpa was his son;
Pṛṣadaśva was the son of Virūpa, and Rathītara was his son.
These, born from Kṣatriyas and Sūtas, are indeed remembered as Aṅgirasas;
they are the foremost among the Rathītaras, twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas.
As Manu was sneezing, Ikṣvāku first emerged;
that Ikṣvāku had a hundred sons who gave profuse sacrificial fees.
Their three eldest sons were Vikukṣi, Nemi, and Daṇḍa;
his other sons, headed by Śakuni, numbered fifty.
The protectors of the land of the Northern Path were forty-eight kings, and likewise, there were [the same number] in the southern direction.
Those twenty leaders were indeed the protectors of the southern region;
then, on the occasion of the Aṣṭakā rite, Ikṣvāku appointed Vikukṣi.
The king said:
"O mighty one, having slain deer, bring meat for this ancestral rite (śrāddha);
today the śrāddha must indeed be performed on the occasion of the Aṣṭakā, of this there is no doubt. (12)
Having gone out on a hunt at the command of that wise king,
the valiant Vikukṣi, after killing thousands of deer, became exhausted;
while engaged in the hunt, he ate a hare there.
When Vikukṣi had arrived with his army and the meat, he urged Vasiṣṭha, saying, "Let the meat be consecrated! (14)
Having been thus commanded by the king, he approached according to the prescribed rites;
seeing that the meat had been spoiled, he became enraged and spoke to the king. (15)
O King, O one of great splendor, meat defiled by a Śūdra is unfit to be eaten; indeed, your own meat is as unfit to be eaten as that of a rabbit-eater. 16.
O sinless one, O best of kings, that rabbit was previously devoured by a wicked soul in the forest; therefore, this meat is impure for the ancestors.
Then Ikṣvāku, filled with anger, spoke thus to Vikukṣi:
"Appointed by me for the ancestral rites, you have been hunting;
yet today, being merciless, you have eaten a hare in the forest even before [the sacrifice]. (18)
"Therefore, I renounce you; go according to your own karma.
Thus was the son abandoned by Ikṣvāku at the word of Vasiṣṭha.
When that Ikṣvāku had passed away, Śaśin,
whose soul was supremely devoted to dharma, obtained this earth and became the sovereign of Ayodhyā.
Urged by Vasiṣṭha, he indeed ruled that kingdom;
thereafter, the king’s state of sovereignty was filled with thieves.
Having arrived there at the proper time and perceiving that his state was one of extreme deficiency, he understood this narrative; indeed, the Creator himself would not consume him.
"He who eats my flesh here shall have his flesh eaten by me in the next world;
the wise declare this to be the 'meat-ness' (māṃsatva) of meat. (23)
The heir of Śaśāda was the heroic one named Kakutstha;
in ancient times, Kakutstha was born from Indra when he had taken the form of a bull.
In the former Āḍīvaka war, he was remembered as Kakutstha by him;
Anenas was the son of Kakutstha, and he is remembered as Pṛthuromā.
Vṛṣadaśva was the son of Pṛthu; from him came the heroic Andhra.
Āndhra’s son was Yavanāśva, and Śrāvasta was his offspring.
From him was born King Śrāvastaka, by whom Śrāvastī was founded;
the heir of Śrāvastaka was the highly illustrious Bṛhadaśva.
It is heard that Bṛhadaśva’s son was Kubalāśva, who, because of his slaying of Dhundhu, became known as King Dhundhumāra. (28)
The sages said:
O highly wise one, I wish to hear in detail the account of the slaying of Dhundhu,
and for what purpose that Kubalāśva attained the status of Dhundhumāra.
Sūta said:
Bṛhadaśva had twenty-one thousand sons,
all of whom were proficient in the sciences, powerful, and difficult to overcome.
All became righteous, performers of sacrifices, and givers of abundant sacrificial fees;
[they honored] the highly heroic, brave, and most virtuous Kubaḷāśva.
Bṛhadaśva, the lord of men, consecrated him in that kingdom;
having transferred his royal fortune to his son, the king indeed entered the forest.
As the great king Bṛhadaśva— a hero and most virtuous man—
was setting out, the brahmin seer Uttaṅka stopped him.
Uttaṅka said:
Your protection must be ensured; therefore, you ought to perform that first.
O King, I am indeed unable to practice asceticism while free from anxiety.
O King, near my hermitage, in the level desert lands, there stands an ocean filled with sand. (35)
Invulnerable to the gods, possessed of a massive body and great strength,
that great being remained there within the earth, hidden amidst the sands.
His son, the cruel and most terrible one named Dhundhu,
undertook a harsh penance for a hundred years in order to destroy the world.
At the end of each year he releases a breath;
whenever that occurs, the earth, together with its forests, trembles there. (38)
By the wind of his breath, a great cloud of dust is raised, obscuring the path of the sun for seven days, while the earth trembles. (39)
"O King, because it is accompanied by sparks, flames, and smoke, and is exceedingly terrible, I am unable to remain in my own hermitage there."
Restrain him, O mighty-armed one, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
the Great Viṣṇu will augment your great splendor with his own splendor. (41)
"May the worlds be at peace today now that this asura has been slain;
for you alone, O lord of the earth, are capable of his destruction today."
And previously, O sinless one, a boon was granted to me by Viṣṇu:
"Indeed, Dhundhu, who possesses great heroism, cannot be overcome by one of little splendor. (43)
O protector of the earth, even in hundreds of years it would be impossible to burn him here;
for his prowess is truly immense and difficult even for the gods to withstand.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Uttaṅka, the royal sage gave his son Kubalāśva for the purpose of warding off Dhundhu.
"O best of the twice-born, I am a king who has laid down my weapons; however, this son of mine will undoubtedly become Dhundhumāra. (46)
Having instructed his son, who was intent upon the slaying of Dhundhu, he,
firm in his vows, departed for the mountain to practice asceticism.
The righteous King Kubalāśva, abiding by the word of his father,
set out together with twenty-one thousand sons and accompanied by Uttaṅka to repel that Dhundhu.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu entered him with his own splendor, at the command of Uttaṅka and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. 49.
As that invincible one set forth, a great sound arose in the sky:
"From this day forward, this king shall be known as Dhundhumāra."
The gods honored that wonder with divine flowers;
then that tiger among men, the valiant one, went there together with his sons.
The royal sage caused the inexhaustible ocean of sand to be dug,
for he had been empowered by the splendor of Nārāyaṇa.
He became exceedingly powerful once more, yet remained under the control of Uttaṅka;
meanwhile, while his sons were digging, he was hidden beneath the sand.
There, Dhundhu, having taken his stand in the western direction, was enraged; with the fire issuing from his mouth, he seemed as if he were overturning the worlds.
O best of Soma-drinkers, he heard the water [of his voice] through yoga, like the great ocean agitated by waves and currents at the rising of the moon. 55.
His sons, the Rākṣasas, were burnt, being three fewer [than a full number];
then that exceedingly powerful king, the destroyer of Dhundhu’s kinsmen, [proceeded].
That lord of men drank up his watery torrent;
like a yogi who by means of yoga extinguishes fire with water, he quelled it.
Having forcibly cast away that water-demon of massive body,
the king, having accomplished his task, revealed himself to Uttaṅka.
And Uttaṅka granted a boon to that high-souled king:
he bestowed upon him inexhaustible wealth and invincibility against his enemies.
Constant delight in the Dharma, as well as an imperishable residence in heaven,
and for those Rākṣasas slain in heaven, imperishable worlds for their sons.
Three of his sons remained; Dṛḍhāśva is called the eldest, while Bhadrāśva and Kapilāśva are remembered as the two younger ones. (61)
Dhundhumāri’s son was Dṛḍhāśva, and Haryaśva was his son;
Haryaśva’s son was Nikumbha, who was always devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya.
Saṃhatāśva, renowned as an expert in battle, was the son of Nikumbha;
and both Kṛśāśva and Akṣayāśva were the sons of Saṃhata.
His wife was Haimavatī, also known as Dṛṣadvatī, who was esteemed by the virtuous and renowned throughout the three worlds; her son was Prasenajit.
His son was Yuvanāśva, who possessed exceeding splendor throughout the three worlds;
he was exceedingly righteous, and Gaurī was his devoted wife.
But having been cursed by her husband, she became the Bāhudā river;
her son was Gaurika, who indeed became a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva, was indeed a king who conquered the three worlds;
regarding this, O twice-born ones, the reciters of the Purāṇas cite these two verses: [Verse 1] [Verse 2] (These verses follow.)
From where the sun rises until it sets, all that is called the domain of Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva. (68)

Regarding this, those who know the lineage recite this verse concerning the high-souled Yauvanāśva, the performer of sacrifices of immeasurable luster: "The ancient knowers declare that Māndhātṛ was indeed a portion of Viṣṇu. (69)
Caitrarathī, the daughter of Śaśabindu, became his wife;
she was a virtuous woman named Bindumatī, peerless on earth in her beauty.
She was a devoted wife and the eldest of ten thousand brothers;
upon her the lord Māndhātṛ begot three sons.
Purukutsa, Ambarīṣa, and the renowned Mucukunda;
the heir of Ambarīṣa is remembered as another, Yuvanāśva. (72)
Harita was the son of Yuvanāśva; the Hāritas are remembered as heroic.
For these were the sons of Aṅgiras, twice-born ones endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas.
The illustrious Trasadasyu was the heir of Purukutsa;
he was born of the Narmadā, and Sambhūta was his son.
The son born of Sambhūta was the powerful Anaraṇya,
by whom Rāvaṇa was formerly slain during his conquest of the three worlds.
Trasadasyu was the son of Anaraṇya, and Haryaśva was his son.
From Haryaśva, through Dṛṣadvatī, was born the king Vasumān.
His son was the righteous king named Tridhanvan;
and from Tridhanvan was born the learned Trayyāruṇa, a lord in battle.
He had a son, a prince named Satyavrata, who possessed great strength;
by him, having slain the gods, the wife of the King of Vidarbha was carried off.

Having reached the final consummation here through the mantras of marriage, his son was Viṣṇuvṛddha, for he is remembered as Viṣṇuvṛddha. These sons of Aṅgiras, endowed with the qualities of the Kṣatriya order, took up their residence here. (79)
Out of desire, strength, delusion, and the power of Saṅkarṣaṇa,
and by the force of destiny, that was done by that wise one.
His father, Trayīguṇa, abandoned him who was joined with unrighteousness;
filled with anger, he said to him many times, "Be gone! (81)
Being alone, he repeatedly asked his father, "Where shall I go?
And then the father said to him, "Live together with the outcaste dog-cookers."
"I do not desire a son through you, O defiler of my lineage!"—thus addressed, O Lord, he departed from the city because of those words. (83)
The venerable sage Vasiṣṭha did not accept him; however,
the wise and heroic Satyavrata, released by his father, lived near the dwellings of the dog-cookers, while his father departed for the forest.
But in that region, Pākaśāsana did not send rain for twelve full years because of that unrighteousness.
But having entrusted his wife to the care of Viśvāmitra in that region,
the great ascetic [Gādhi] practiced intense penance on the shore of the ocean.
His wife, having tied her own middle biological son by the neck with her hair,
sold him for ten cows for the sake of sustenance.
But seeing him bound by the neck and sold, that best of men, the righteous-souled one of noble vows, liberated the son of the great seer. (88)
The highly intelligent Satyavrata provided for his maintenance, both to please Viśvāmitra and out of compassion. (89)
He became known by the name Ghālava, a great ascetic with a rope tied around his neck;
by that very act of valor, his father, the great seer Kauśika, was liberated.
Abiding in discipline, he supported Viśvāmitra’s wife through his vow, devotion, compassion, and promise. (91)
Having killed deer, boars, and wild buffaloes,
he then cooked that meat in the vicinity of Viśvāmitra’s hermitage.
Having undertaken a twelve-year initiation and observed the vow of silence,
he remained devoted to his father’s command after the king had retired to the forest.
The sage Vasiṣṭha protected both Ayodhyā and the kingdom, as well as the inner apartments, by virtue of his relationship with the sacrificer and the preceptor. (94)
But Satyavrata, due to his youth and by the force of destiny, maintained an even greater resentment toward Vasiṣṭha out of his own wrath. (95)
At that time, the sage Vasiṣṭha did not prevent his own son from being abandoned by his father and departing from the kingdom while weeping, for there was indeed a specific reason.
"The completion of the marriage mantras occurs at the seventh step;
Satyavrata, indeed, performed them at the seventh step. (97)
"Though he knows all dharmas, Vasiṣṭha does not desire the mantras here.
Thus did Vasiṣṭha harbor anger toward Satyavrata in his mind. (98)
At that time, the venerable Vasiṣṭha performed it with his mind, but Satyavrata did not mentally observe this vow of silence. ||99||
And when he had passed away, Pākaśāsana did not send rain for twelve years because of that high-minded son of his.
"Therefore, now that initiation has been performed in many ways on this earth, let this act serve as an expiation for my own family. (101)
Then the venerable Vasiṣṭha restrained him who had been abandoned by his father, saying,
"I shall consecrate him in the kingdom hereafter," O Lord.
But he, the powerful one, having carried out his initiation for twelve years,
found no meat available for the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
The prince beheld a cow that grants all desires;
