yet, overcome by anger, delusion, fatigue, and hunger, he [treated her thus]. (104)
Seeing that he had adopted the conduct of a bandit, the best of the strong killed him;
he then ate the meat himself and also gave some to the sons of Viśvāmitra.
Having heard that, Vasiṣṭha then caused him to be fed and abandoned him;
and the venerable Vasiṣṭha spoke thus to that prince.
"O cruel one! O cruel one! I shall cause your iron stake to fall [upon you], if indeed you do not have three stakes, O lowest of men! (107)
"Through the dissatisfaction of your father, the killing of your guru's milch cow, and the consumption [of her milk] without his permission, you have committed a threefold transgression. (108)
Thus, having seen those three stakes, that great ascetic said, "He is Triśaṅku";
by that he is remembered as Triśaṅku.
When Viśvāmitra had been provided with the maintenance of his wives,
he was then pleased and granted a boon to Triśaṅku.
Then, being invited to choose a boon, the prince said to the preceptor:
"Now that this twelve-year fear of drought has passed... (111)
Having consecrated him in the paternal kingdom,
the sage Kauśika, while the gods and Vasiṣṭha looked on,
caused that lord to ascend to heaven in his physical body.
While Vasiṣṭha looked on, that appeared as if a miracle;
regarding this, people learned of the Purāṇas cite these two verses: (113)
By the grace of Viśvāmitra, the highly effulgent Triśaṅku shines in heaven together with the gods, through the favor of that wise one.
In winter, the lovely night passes slowly, adorned by the moon and decorated with three phases, embellished by the planet Rāhu. 115.
His wife, named Satyarathā, born of the Kekaya lineage, gave birth to a sinless prince named Hariścandra. (116)
That king Hariścandra was known as Traiśaṅkava;
he was celebrated as a sovereign emperor who performed the Rājasūya sacrifice. ||117||
The son of Hariścandra was the powerful Rohita;
the son of Rohita was Harita, and the son of Harita is called Cañcu Hārīta.
Vijaya and Sudeva were the two sons of Cañcu;
because he was the conqueror of all the kṣatriyas, he is remembered as Vijaya. ||119||
There, Ruruka’s son was the king who was skilled in dharma and artha;
from Ruruka was born a son named Dhṛtaka, and from him Bāhu was born.
The king, being addicted to vice, was expelled by the Haihayas and the Tālajaṅghas,
as well as by the Śakas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Pāradas, and Pahlavas.
In that Satya Yuga, he was not excessively devoted to righteousness;
however, Sagara was born as the son of Bāhu along with poison (gara).
Having reached the hermitage of Bhṛgu, he was protected by Tūrva.
Having obtained the Āgneya weapon from Bhārgava, King Sagara went forth and slew the Tālajaṅghas along with the Haihayas throughout the earth.
The infallible one, who knew the dharma, abolished the religious practices of the Śakas and the Pahlavas, as well as those of the Kṣatriyas and the Pāradas. 124.
The sages said:
How was that King Sagara born with poison?
And for what reason did the steadfast king, filled with wrath, abolish the duties appropriate to his lineage belonging to the Kṣatriyas of great power, such as Śakra and others? (125)
Sūta said:
It is said that in former times, the kingdom of that king Bāhu was seized by the Haihayas and Tālajaṅghas who had arrived together with the Śakas. (126)
Then these five tribes—the Yavanas, the Pāradas, the Kāmbojas, the Pahlavas, and the Haihayas—exerted their prowess for his sake. (127)
The kingdom was seized by these powerful bulls among Kṣatriyas.
Then, his sovereignty having been taken away, King Bāhu, that righteous soul, renounced the world and, entering the forest with his wife, practiced austerities. 128.
Then, after some time, the king set out for the sake of water; however, due to his old age and weakness, he died along the way. (129)
His Yādava wife, who was pregnant, followed behind him;
however, her co-wife had administered poison to her with the intent to destroy the fetus.
Having prepared her husband's funeral pyre, she ascended it into the fire;
but Aurva Bhārgava, seeing her, turned her back out of compassion.
In that hermitage, she then gave birth along with Sagara to a righteous son of mighty arms named Sagara.
But Aurva, having performed for that high-souled one the birth-rites and other ceremonies,
and having taught him the Vedas and the Shastras, then bestowed upon him the divine weapons.
Then, from Jamadagnya, he obtained the Agneya weapon, which was unbearable even for the Asuras.
Endowed with both the power of that missile and his own physical strength,
he, filled with rage, slaughtered the Haihayas as Rudra slaughters herds of animals.
Thereupon, the king resolved to exterminate without remainder the Śakas, the Yavanas, the Kāmbojas, the Pāradas, and the Pahlavas as well. ||135||
Being slaughtered by the heroic and high-souled Sagara, they all, seeking refuge, approached Vasiṣṭha for protection. ||136||
The great sage Vasiṣṭha, having said "So be it," granted them safety and restrained Sagara by means of a formal agreement.
Having heard his own promise and the command of his preceptor,
Sagara indeed destroyed their dharma and caused them to change their appearance.
Having shaved half the heads of the Śakas, he released them;
but he shaved the entire heads of the Yavanas and likewise those of the Kāmbojas.
The Pāradas have their hair disheveled, and the Pahlavas wear beards;
deprived of the study of the Vedas and the utterance of the vaṣaṭkāra, they were made so by that high-souled one.
The Śakas, Yavanas, and Kāmbojas, along with the Pahlavas and Pāradas;
the Kelisparśas, Māhiṣikas, Dārvās, Colas, and likewise the Khasas. ||141||
All those groups of Kṣatriyas had their dharma cast aside by the high-souled Sagara, following the previous words of Vasiṣṭha. 142.
That king, victorious through righteousness, having conquered this earth, being initiated for the horse sacrifice, set out a horse for its search. ||143||
As he was driving it, that horse was carried away near the shore in the south-eastern ocean and made to enter the earth.
That king had all his sons dig up that region,
and then they reached it within that great ocean.
To that primordial Person, the divine Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Prajāpati,
Viṣṇu in the form of Kapila, the Swan, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord.
Having reached his eye, that splendor entered it;
at that time, all his sons were consumed, with only four remaining. (147)
Barhiketu, Saketu, and likewise Dharmarata—these three, as well as Śūra and Pañcavana, O Lord, were the perpetuators of his lineage. ||148||
And the Blessed Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa granted him boons:
the imperishability of his own lineage, a hundred horse-sacrifices, a powerful son named Samudra, and likewise eternal residence in heaven. (149)
Taking the horse, that ocean, the lord of rivers, paid him homage;
and by that very act of his, he indeed attained the state of being the ocean (Sāgara).
Having recovered that horse intended for the horse-sacrifice from the ocean,
the king performed a hundred horse-sacrifices again and again.
Sixty thousand sons who followed the horse were consumed by fire; we have heard that those great-souled sons, having entered the splendor of Nārāyaṇa, numbered sixty thousand. (152)
The sages said:
"How were the sixty thousand sons of King Sagara born so exceedingly powerful and valiant? Tell us, by what ritual or means did this come to pass? (153)
Sūta said:
Sagara had two wives whose sins were burnt away by ascetic penance;
the elder was the daughter of Vidarbha, known by the name Keśinī.
But his younger wife was most virtuous, the daughter of Ariṣṭanemi, peerless on earth in her beauty. (155)
Propitiated by their ascetic penance, the Lord Aurva granted them a boon:
"One shall give birth to a desired son who will be the founder of a lineage;
the second shall give birth to sixty thousand sons. (156)
Having heard the words of the sage, Keśinī, the excellent lady, accepted her only son as the cause for the continuation of the lineage in the assembly of kings.
Likewise, O King, the noble-minded Sumati took charge of the nourishment of the sixty thousand sons and Suparṇabhaginī.
Then, after some time had passed, Jyeṣṭhā gave birth to her eldest son, the descendant of Kakutstha and son of Sagara, known as Asamañja. (159)
The illustrious Sumati also gave birth to a gourd-shaped embryo;
from the midst of that gourd, sixty thousand sons emerged.
Then the king placed those embryos in jars filled with clarified butter, and he assigned a nurse for each one to nourish them. ||161||
Then, after nine months, those illustrious princes, who increased the joy of Sagara, emerged at their ease. (162)
After a long time, those sixty thousand sons who were following the horse reached their youth. (163)
That eldest son of Sagara, O tiger among men, was known as Asamañja; he possessed a peacock banner and was endowed with great strength. (164)
The son of that Aṃśumat, who was formerly devoted to the welfare of the citizens and had been exiled by his father, was the powerful one named Asamañjas. 165.
His son was the righteous-souled one renowned as Dilīpa;
from Dilīpa was born the heroic and highly resplendent Bhagīratha.
By him, through this sacrifice, the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, adorned with celestial chariots, was indeed brought forth from the ocean and adopted as his daughter.
Regarding this, people learned in the Purāṇas cite this verse: 167. [The verse follows.]
Bhagīratha brought that Gaṅgā down through his ritual acts;
therefore, she is called Bhāgīrathī by those most learned in the genealogies. 168.
The son of Bhagīratha was indeed named Śruta;
his heir was Nābhāga, who was eternally devoted to righteousness.
Ambarīṣa was his son, and from him Sindhudvīpa was born;
thus it is heard that those who know the ancient chronicles of the lineage sing.
Protected by the two arms of Ambarīṣa, the earth under Nābhāga became exceedingly free from the three types of suffering. 171.
The valiant Ayutāyu was the son of that Sindhudvīpa;
the highly illustrious Ṛtuparṇa was the heir of Ayutāyu.
This powerful king, a friend of Nala, was skilled in the knowledge of divine dice;
they are both renowned in the Purāṇas as two Nalas of firm vows. (173)
The son of Vīrasena, who was the upholder of the Ikṣvāku lineage, became the lord of men named Sarvakāma, the son of Ṛtuparṇa. ||174||
The son of that Sudāsa was King Haṃsamukha;
the son of Sudāsa is said to be the monarch named Saudāsa. (175)
He was indeed known by the name Kalmāṣapāda and also as Mitrāsaha.
Then the highly resplendent Vasiṣṭha begot Aśmaka in the wife of Kalmāṣapāda for the sake of increasing the Ikṣvāku lineage. (176)
The son of Aśmaka was Urakāma, and his son was Mūlaka;
regarding this King Mūlaka, they cite this traditional account. (177)
For that king, out of fear of Rāma, lived surrounded by women;
indeed, the lord, seeking protection, had taken women as his armor and remained unclothed.
The righteous King Śataratha is also recorded as the son of Mūlaka;
from that Śataratha was born the powerful King Caiḍibiḍa.
There was indeed the illustrious and powerful Kṛtaśarman, son of Viśvamahat; from him was born a daughter, Putrikā. (2.26.180)
Dilīpa was his son, renowned as Khaṭvāṅga;
by him, having come here from heaven and obtained life for but a moment, the three worlds were indeed secured through both wisdom and truth. (181)
Dīrghabāhu was his son, and from him Raghū was born; Aja was the son of Raghū, and from him that heroic one was born—the king named Daśaratha, the delighter of the Ikṣvāku lineage. ||182||
The heroic Rāma, son of Daśaratha, who knows the dharma and is world-renowned, as well as Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, and the mighty Śatrughna. ||183||
Having slain Lavaṇa and Mādhava and gone to that Madhuvana forest,
Śatrughna established his city, Mathurā.
Both Subāhu and Śūrasena, together with Śatrughna, protected the two sons of Vaidehī in the city of Mathurā. (185)
Both Aṅgada and Candraketu were the two sons of Lakṣmaṇa;
their two flourishing provinces were located near the Himalayan mountains. (186)
In the region of Kārapatha, there is the city of Aṅgadīyā belonging to Aṅgada;
and the auspicious city of Candravaktrā belongs to the wrestler Candraketu. (187)
The two heroic sons of Bharata were Takṣa and Puṣkara;
the cities of those two high-souled ones were established in the region of Gāndhāra. (188)
The delightful city of Takṣaśilā is renowned in all directions as belonging to Takṣa;
likewise, Puṣkarāvatī is famous as belonging to the hero Puṣkara. (189)

And those who are learned in the Purāṇas sing a verse here concerning Rāma, which is devoted to the welfare of all beings and arises from the majesty of that wise one: "Even when he was a child, he did not act contrary to righteousness; even as a youth, he did not abandon his father's command. Even when he was a king, he did not abandon dharma; even now, though fallen into calamity, he does not abandon truth. (2.26.190)
Dark-complexioned, youthful, with red eyes, a radiant face, and measured speech;
his arms reach down to his knees, he has a handsome countenance, lion-like shoulders, and mighty arms. (191)
Rāma ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years;
there was the sound of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajur Vedas, along with the great resonance of the bowstring.
In the kingdom, the cry "Let it be given! Let it be enjoyed! became uninterrupted;
dwelling in Janasthāna, he performed the work of the gods.
Seeking the track of Sītā, that bull among men, the highly illustrious one, slew the descendant of Pulastya who had previously committed an offense against him. (194)
Endowed with courage, perfected in virtues, and blazing with his own splendor,
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, shone more brightly than the sun and the fire.
In this very manner, the mighty-armed and powerful lord, the joy of the Ikṣvāku dynasty,
having slain Rāvaṇa along with his hosts, ascended to heaven.
The son of Śrī Rāma was born known by the name Kuśa;
the other was the highly heroic Lava. Learn now of their two kingdoms. (197)
Kuśa established the kingdom of Kośala and the city of Kuśasthalī;
he settled that delightful place upon the slopes of the Vindhya mountains. (198)
The kingdom of Uttarakośala belongs to the high-souled Lava, and Śrāvastī is world-renowned; now learn of the lineage of Kuśa. 199.
Kuśa’s son was the righteous-souled Atithi, who was exceedingly fond of guests;
from Atithi was born the renowned king named Niṣadha.
Nala was the son of Niṣadha, while Nabha was the son of Nala; Puṇḍarīka was the son of Nabha, and Kṣemadhanvan is recorded as his successor.
The powerful King Devānīka was the son of Kṣemadhanvan;
the lord named Ahīnagu was the son of Devānīka. (202)
The heir of Ahīnagu was the highly illustrious Pāriyātra;
his son was Dala, and from him was born King Bala.
That righteous-souled son of Bala was indeed named Auṅka;
Vajranābha was his son, and Śaṅkhaṇa was his offspring.
The learned son of Śaṅkhaṇa was known as Dhyuṣitāśva;
and the son of Dhyuṣitāśva was indeed King Viśvasaha. (205)
Hiraṇyanābha was from Kauśala; Vasiṣṭha became his son.
He is remembered as the disciple of Jaimini’s grandson among all those who possess the title Śarman. (206)
After he had studied five hundred Saṃhitās,
yoga was mastered by the wise Yājñavalkya from him.
His son was the learned Puṣya, and Dhruvasandhi was his son;
Sudarśana was his son, and from Sudarśana came Agnivarṇa.
The son of Agnivarna was Śīghra, and the son of Śīghra is remembered as Manu. Having established himself in Yoga, Manu settled in the village of Kalāpa;
he was the lord who inaugurated the Kṣatriya order in the nineteenth yuga-cycle.
Prasuśruta was the son of Manu, and Susandhi was his son;
likewise, the son of Susandhi was named Amārṣa, who was also known by the name Sahasvān.
Sahasvān had a son, the king known as Viśrutavat;
Viśrutavat’s son was the king Bṛhadbala. ||211||
These kings are generally remembered as the heirs of Ikṣvāku;
those who were the preeminent ones in this lineage have been described here in detail.
By correctly reciting this creation of the radiant Āditya Vivasvat,
one becomes possessed of progeny and attains union with Manu Vaivasvata.
Of the god Śrāddhadeva, the bestower of nourishment upon all creatures,
one becomes free from sin, free from passion, long-lived, and imperishable.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Vaivasvata Manu," in the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa* proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Now learn of the lineage of Nimī, the younger brother of Vikukṣi,
who established a city resembling the city of the gods.
It was renowned as Jayanta, situated near the hermitage of Gautama;
in whose lineage, indeed, at a sacrifice, [the son] was born from Janaka, the best of sages.
There was a son of the highly wise Ikṣvāku, who possessed immense splendor, named Nemi; he was a man of pure virtue and was honored by all living beings. (3)
By the curse of Vasiṣṭha, he became bodiless (videha);
his son, named Mithi, was born from three joints [of his body]. (4)
While the fire-drill wood was being rubbed in the forest, one of great renown appeared;
he became famous by the name Mithi, and because of his birth, he was known as Janaka.
There was a king of great prowess named Mithi, after whom that city became Mithilā; he was known as Janaka, and from Janaka came Udāvasu.
From Udāvasu was born the virtuous Nandivardhana;
from Nandivardhana came the righteous Śūra, whose name was Suketu.
The son of Suketu was the righteous and mighty Devarāta;
it is heard that the son of Devarāta was the righteous Bṛhaduccha. ||8||
The son of Bṛhaduccha was the powerful and majestic Mahāvīrya;
the son of Mahāvīrya was Dhṛtimān, and his son was Sudhṛti.
From Sudhṛti was born Dhṛṣṭaketu, a righteous soul and scorcher of foes;
and the son of Dhṛṣṭaketu was the renowned Haryaśva.
Maru was the son of Haryaśva, and Maru’s son was Pratitvaka.
The son of Pratitvaka was the righteous King Kīrttiratha. ||11||
The son of Kīrttiratha was known as Devamīḍha;
the son of Devamīḍha was Vibudha, and the son of Vibudha was Dhṛti.
The son of Mahādhṛti was the powerful King Kīrttirāja;
the learned son of Kīrttirāja was renowned as Mahāroma. ||13||
From Mahāromā was born the famous Svarṇaromā;
and the son of Svarṇaromā was King Hrasvaromā.
The learned son of Hrasvaroman was known by the name Sīradhvaja, according to tradition;
it was by that illustrious king that the glorious furrow (sītā) was ploughed, [from which was born] Rāma’s virtuous queen, who was firm in her vows and exceedingly devoted to her husband. (15)
Śaunaka said:
How was the illustrious Sītā born while the field was being ploughed? And for what purpose did the king plough the field in which she appeared? (16)
Sūta said:
When the sacrificial ground of the high-souled one was being ploughed for the horse sacrifice according to the well-applied ritual, she emerged from it. 17.
From Sīradhvaja was born the Maithila named Bhānumat;
his brother was Kuśadhvaja, who was the king and lord of Kāśī.
The son of that Bhānumat was the powerful Pradyumna;
his son was Muni, and from him Ūrjavaha is remembered.
From Ūrjavāha came Sutavāja, and Śakuni was his son;
Svāgata was the son of Śakuni, and Suvarcā is recorded as his son.
Śruta was his heir, and Suśruta was his son;
Jaya was the son of Suśruta, and Vijaya was the son of Jaya.
Vijaya’s son was Ṛta; Ṛta is remembered as having Sunaya as his son.
From Sunaya came Vītahavya, and the son of Vītahavya was Dhṛti.
From Dhṛti was born Bahulāśva, and Bahulāśva’s son was Kṛti.
In him the lineage of the high-souled Janakas comes to an end.
Thus have the Maithilas been described; now learn also of Soma's [lineage]. (23) 89.23
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Lineage of Vaivasvata Manu," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
The venerable sage Atri, the father of Soma, was born as a seer;
that blessed one surpassed all the worlds by his own splendor.
Performing only auspicious deeds through action, mind, and speech,
he stood with arms raised, possessing great luster, like wood, a wall, or a stone.
There was a great austerity called Suduścara which was performed by him in the past;
indeed, we have heard that it lasted for three thousand divine years. (3)
As that man of great intelligence remained there with his vital energy drawn upward, longing for the Unblinking One, his body indeed attained the state of Soma, O twice-born one.
As his mind was thus purified, the state of being Soma ascended upward from him;
Soma flowed forth from his two eyes, illuminating the ten directions.
Then, commanded by the prescribed rite, ten goddesses took up that embryo;
having come together, they bore it, yet they were not able to sustain it individually.
Then, from those directions, that radiant embryo suddenly emerged,
illuminating the worlds like the sun with its rays, the creator of all beings.
When those women were no longer able to hold that embryo,
then he, like the cool-rayed moon, fell from them onto the earth.
Beholding Soma falling, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, placed him upon his chariot out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. ||9||
For he, O brahmins, is a god-like man, seeking righteousness and true to his promise;
we have heard that he is yoked with a thousand white horses.
When that son of Atri, the Supreme Soul, had descended, the gods—
the seven renowned mind-born sons of Brahmā— offered praise.
Right there, he was likewise the son of that Aṅgiras and of Bhṛgu;
[he was honored] with many Ṛg-verses, Yajus-formulas, and Atharvāṅgiras hymns.
Then, as he was being praised, the radiant splendor of Soma,
while increasing, nourished the three worlds in every way.
O Vipula, with his excellent chariot, he circumambulated the earth bounded by the ocean twenty-one times.
And that energy of his which entered the earth gave rise to the plants, which indeed blaze forth with that energy.
By means of them, he sustains these worlds as well as the fourfold classes of beings;
for the blessed Soma, O best of the twice-born, is indeed the nourisher of the universe.
Having gained splendor through his asceticism, those praises, and those deeds,
that illustrious one performed austerities for one hundred and ten padmas of years.
Those goddesses who are golden-hued and sustain the world by their own nature—among them, Soma became all-pervasive through his own celebrated deeds. (18)
Then, O best of the twice-born, Brahmā, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, bestowed upon him sovereignty over the seeds and medicinal herbs of the Brahmins, as well as over the waters.
Thus consecrated in the great sovereignty, that king of kings, possessed of great splendor and the best among those who practice austerity, brought welfare to the worlds by his very nature.
Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave twenty-seven daughters of Dakṣa, who were observers of great vows, to Soma; they are known as the constellations (nakṣatras).
Having obtained that great sovereignty, Soma, the lord of those who possess the Soma-plant,
performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, in which hundreds of thousands were given as sacrificial fees.
Hiraṇyagarbha was the Udgātṛ priest, and Brahmā attained the office of Brahman.
There, the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Sovereign, served as the Sadasya, surrounded by the primordial Brahmarṣis headed by Sanatkumāra. ||23||
O twice-born ones, we have heard that Soma gave the three worlds as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to those foremost brahmin-sages and to the members of the assembly.
Sinī, Kuhū, Vapuḥ, Puṣṭi, Prabhāvasu, Kīrti, Dhṛti, and Lakṣmī—these nine goddesses waited upon him. (25)
Having completed the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) without agitation, honored by all the gods and sages, that supreme king among kings illuminated the ten directions with his splendor. ||26||

Then, O brahmins, having obtained that sovereignty which is difficult to attain and praised by the seers, he— whose mind was deluded and whose humility had been destroyed— became devoid of discipline.
He indeed forcibly carried off Bṛhaspati’s illustrious wife, named Tārā, showing contempt for all the sons of Aṅgiras.
Although he was entreated by the gods as well as by the celestial sages,
he did not at that time release Tārā to Aṅgiras.
O twice-born ones, Uśanas took up the rear-guard of that Aṅgiras;
for he was the highly resplendent disciple of his father, Bṛhaspati, in former times.
Out of that affection for Bṛhaspati,
the Lord Rudra took up his Ājagava bow and became his rear-guard.
By that high-souled one, the supreme weapon was discharged at the foremost of the Brahman-sages with the gods in mind, by which their fame was destroyed.
There, that great battle took place before their very eyes, like the war between the gods and the Dānavas, causing the destruction of the worlds.
Thereupon, the remaining three classes of gods, including those known as the Tuṣitas,
went for refuge to Brahmā, the primordial god and the Grandfather.
Then, having restrained Uśanas, Rudra, and the eldest Śaṅkara,
the Grandfather himself gave Tārā back to Aṅgiras.
And seeing her pregnant, Tārā, whose face resembles the lord of stars, Bṛhaspati, the Brahmin, said: "You shall not cast off the fetus. (36)
"In some way, a fetus must be borne within my body, in my womb.
Then she did not release the thread, [conceiving] a boy who would be the greatest slayer of the Dasyus.
Having reached a stalk of reed that was like a blazing fire,
the Blessed One, as soon as he was born, eclipsed the splendor of the gods.
Then, fallen into doubt, the gods said to Tārā:
"Tell the truth; whose son is he—Soma’s or Bṛhaspati’s? (39)
When she, being put to shame, said nothing— whether good or bad— to the gods,
then Kumāra, the greatest slayer of robbers, began to curse her.
Then Brahmā, having restrained Tārā from the moon, said:
"O Tārā, tell me what is the truth in this matter: whose son is this? (41)
With palms joined in reverence, she spoke thus to the Lord Brahmā, the granter of boons,
concerning the high-souled Kumāra, the son of Soma and the greatest slayer of demons.
Then Soma, the giver and Prajāpati, having embraced that wise son, gave him the name Budha. (43)
And at the time of departure, the wise rise up to meet him;
then the princess indeed gave birth to a son. 44.
His son was the highly resplendent Purūravas, the son of Ilā.
Six sons of great prowess were born to him by Urvaśī. (45)
There, having been forcibly overcome and rendered helpless by consumption (rājayakṣman),
Soma, his orb wasted away and overwhelmed by that disease,
then went for refuge to his father, Atri himself.
The highly illustrious Atri performed that pacification of his sin;
freed from consumption, he blazed forth with prosperity on all sides.
O best of the twice-born, this birth of Soma has indeed been proclaimed;
O foremost of the twice-born, now listen as his lineage is being recounted. 48.

Having heard of the birth of Soma—which is auspicious, conducive to health and long life, meritorious, and a purifier of sins—one is liberated from all evils. (49) Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Origin of Soma," in the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa* proclaimed by Vāyu. (28)
Sūta said:
Budha was the son of Soma, and Purūravas was the son of Budha;
he was radiant, charitable by nature, a performer of sacrifices, and a giver of abundant sacrificial fees. ||1||
A proponent of Brahman, valiant and invincible by his enemies in battle,
he maintained the Agnihotra sacrifice and bestowed the earth upon those who performed sacrifices.
Truthful in speech, with a mind intent on his duties, beloved, and restrained in sexual conduct, the son became peerless in the worlds for his extraordinary beauty. (3)
The illustrious Urvaśī, casting aside her pride, chose him as her husband—he who was a proponent of Brahman, self-controlled, a knower of dharma, and a speaker of truth. (4)
The valiant king lived with her for eighteen years—
seven, six, seven, eight, ten, and eight.
In the delightful Caitraratha forest, likewise on the banks of the Mandākinī, in the vast city of Alakā, and in the supreme grove of Nandana; ||6||
At the foot of Gandhamādana, on the peak of Meru, that best of mountains;
having reached the Northern Kurus and the village of Kalāpa as well.
In these forest groves, delightful and frequented by the gods,
the king, accompanied by Urvaśī, took his pleasure with supreme joy.
The sages said:
O learned one, tell us how the celestial Gandharva lady Urvaśī came to a mortal king, having abandoned the gods. (9)
Sūta said:
Overcome by the curse of Brahmā, that woman of beautiful limbs approached a mortal; she established herself with Purūravas, the son of Ilā, according to an agreement.
For the sake of liberation from her curse, she undertook a vow:
namely, never looking at fire and never engaging in sexual intercourse even out of desire.
Two rams remain near his bed;
such is his food, O King, for only ghee, and that for but a single period of time.
"O King, if this is your firm resolve for as long as time lasts, then for that duration I shall dwell here; this is the agreement we have made. (13)
The king observed all her customs;
thus did that beautiful woman dwell with Purūravas.
Then, for sixty-four years, Urvaśī, deluded by the curse through her devotion to him, remained among mortals; meanwhile, the Gandharvas were filled with anxiety. (15)
The Gandharvas said:
"O highly fortunate ones, consider how that excellent woman, Urvaśī, the ornament of heaven, may return once more, O gods. (16)
Then Viśvāvasu, the best among speakers, spoke there:
"O sinless one, the agreement being made by her there is considered appropriate. (17)
Indeed, by transgressing her vow, she will abandon the king;
I shall tell you all of that, how she will forsake the monarch. (18)
"I shall suddenly attain union [with you] for the sake of accomplishing your purpose.
Having spoken thus, the highly illustrious one departed for Pratiṣṭhāna.
Then, having arrived at night, he indeed carried off one of the rams;
yet that sweet-smiling woman behaved toward the two rams as if they were her own mother.
Having learned of the Gandharvas' arrival while still lying on her bed, the illustrious lady spoke to the king, saying, "My son is indeed being carried away! (21)
Having been addressed thus and having reflected, the king indeed remained naked, thinking:
"If the queen sees me naked, my agreement will become false."
Then the Gandharvas brought forth a second ram;
when the second ram had been taken away, the goddess spoke to that son of Ila. (23)
"O King, O Lord, my two sons have been carried away like one who is helpless.
Thus addressed, the king then rose up and ran forth naked.
Then, O King, when the path had been blocked by the Gandharvas with two rams,
a great illusion was produced;
that vast palace was suddenly illuminated, and she beheld it as naked.
Seeing him naked, that apsaras, who could assume any form at will, vanished from sight.
Perceiving that she had vanished, all those Gandharvas abandoned the two rams right there and disappeared on the spot. (27)
Seeing the two young goats released, the lordly king returned home;
but not seeing her there, the king, deeply distressed, lamented.
He wandered over the earth, searching here and there;
then the mighty king beheld her at Kurukṣetra.
At the Plakṣa-tīrtha, she was bathing in a lotus pond filled with deep water,
sporting together with five celestial nymphs, appearing most beautiful.
Then, from no great distance, the fair-browed Urvaśī beheld the king; she said to her friends, "This is that Puruṣottama. (31)
In that very place where I had dwelt, he revealed himself to the king;
thereupon, those five-crested Apsarases appeared.
But upon seeing her, the king was delighted and uttered many words of lamentation:
"Come! Stay! O terrible one, stay in my mind; O woman, stay in my speech! (33)
They conversed with one another in such subtle ways;
but Urvaśī said to Caila, "O Lord, I am pregnant by you."
"In one year, a son shall be born to you; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, the king remained with her for but a single night. (35)
Then, filled with great joy, the highly illustrious king returned to his own city;
when a year had passed, the king came once more for Urvashi.
Having stayed with her for one night, the high-minded one, afflicted by desire, spoke in distress: "Become mine forever! (37)
Then Urvaśī said to Caila, "The Gandharvas have granted you a boon;
choose it, O great king, for you yourself must speak to them. (38)
"I choose eternal residence in the same world as the high-souled Gandharvas.
Having said, "So be it," the Gandharvas granted the boon, saying, "May it be so. (39)
Having filled a vessel with fire, the Gandharvas said to him:
"O lord of men, by sacrificing with this, you shall attain that world."
Taking that boy, he set out for the city;
having left him in the forest, he went home with his son.
Taking up the fire that was visible once more, he saw the aśvattha tree there;
having seen that aśvattha tree nearby, he was indeed struck with wonder.
Having gone to the earth with Agni to report that matter to the Gandharvas,
he heard that the purpose was already accomplished and commanded Araṇī.
"O lord of men, having made a fire-drill from an aśvattha tree and having churned out the fire according to the prescribed rite, you shall attain our world by sacrificing with it.
Having churned the fire and divided it into three parts, that lord of men indeed performed the sacrifice. (44)
Having worshipped with various kinds of sacrifices, that great chariot-warrior, the Gandharva, attained the same world as them; and for his residence during the Tretā age, he— Aila—
formerly established those three fires, which had previously been but one.
Such was the power of King Aila, O best of the twice-born,
in that most meritorious land adorned by great sages.
That highly illustrious lord of the earth ruled his kingdom at Prayāga,
on the northern bank of the Yamunā, at Pratiṣṭhāna.
He indeed had six sons, equal in splendor to Indra,
who were known in the world of the Gandharvas as Āyu, Dhīmat, and Amāvasu.
Viśvāyu, Śatāyu, and Gatāyu were the sons of Urvaśī;
and from Amāvāsya was born King Bhīma, also known as Viśvajit.
The illustrious Bhīma had a son, King Kāñcanaprabha.
The learned Suhotra, who was possessed of great strength, was the son of Kāñcana.
Jahnu, born from the womb of Keśikā, was the son of Suhotra.
Then, having returned from there, Gaṅgā [appeared] during the performance of the extensive sacrificial rite.
He caused that region to be flooded because he foresaw a future event;
seeing the sacrificial enclosure inundated on all sides by the Gaṅgā, [he was filled with wonder].
Sauhōtri, the bestower of boons, became enraged and, with eyes bloodshot, said:
"O Gaṅgā, receive immediately the fruit of this arrogance! (53)
"I shall render all this water you have drunk utterly fruitless.
Then, seeing the Gaṅgā drunk by the royal sage, the celestial ṛṣis [were struck with wonder].
The highly fortunate Jahnu brought the daughter of Yauvanāśva, Kāverī, as his own daughter; he took Jāhnavī as his daughter as well. 55.
By whose curse Yuvanāśva brought forth Gaṅgā—the blameless Kāverī, the best of rivers and the wife of Jahnu. (56)
And Jahnu begot upon Kāverī a beloved and righteous son named Suhotra; Ajaka was his son. (57)
The heir of Ajaka was the highly illustrious Balākāśva;
Gaya and Śīla were born, and Kuśa is recorded as his son.
And Kuśa had four sons, radiant with the splendor of the Vedas:
Kuśāśva, Kuśanābha, Amūrtarayas, and Yaśovasu. (59)
The excellent king Kuśastamba, desiring a son, performed austerities;
when a full thousand years had passed, he beheld Śatakratu.
Seeing him engaged in such fierce austerity, the thousand-eyed Purandara himself,
the eternal one, became capable of fathering a son for him.
Purandara himself conceived the thought of becoming his son;
the subduer of Paka, Kauśika, became the son named Gādhi.
The daughter of Purukutsa became his wife, and from her Gādhi was born.
First, a highly fortunate and auspicious maiden named Satyavatī was born;
the lordly son of Gādhi gave her to Ṛcīka, the descendant of Kavi.
In that [sacrifice], the son of Bhṛgu, the descendant of Bhṛgu, who was indeed her husband,
prepared sacrificial porridge (caru) for the sake of a son for both Gādhi and himself.
And so, having summoned Sudhṛti at that time, Ṛcīka, the descendant of Bhṛgu, said:
"O auspicious lady, this sacrificial porridge must be consumed by you and by your mother."
In her shall be born a son, radiant, a bull among Kṣatriyas,
unconquerable by Kṣatriyas in battle, and a slayer of the foremost of Kṣatriyas.
O blessed lady, this sacrificial porridge shall also provide for your son— a steadfast ascetic,
self-controlled, and the best among the twice-born.
Having spoken thus to his wife, Ṛcīka, the joy of the Bhṛgus,
entered the forest, being constantly devoted to ascetic penances.
Then King Gādhi, accompanied by his wife, went to the hermitage of Ṛcīka on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, in order to see his daughter. (69)
Having taken the two portions of sacrificial food, Satyavatī, remaining composed and joyful, reported it to her mother, in accordance with her husband’s word. (2.29.70)
But her mother, by fate, gave her own sacrificial porridge to her daughter; she, however, unknowingly took that porridge for herself. (71)
Then Satyavatī, of terrible appearance, bore with her radiant body a glorious embryo that was destined to be the end of the Kṣatriyas.
Then Ṛcīka, having seen her and having also discerned it through yoga,
spoke to his own wife of excellent complexion, O best of the twice-born.
"O blessed lady, your success will come about through the cause of exchanging the sacrificial porridge with your mother;
for you will give birth to a son who is a performer of cruel deeds and exceedingly terrible. (74)
"Or rather, a mother shall give birth to such a one rich in asceticism,
for the entire universe has been entrusted by me there through my ascetic power.
Having been addressed thus by her husband, the highly fortunate Satyavatī then [replied].
She propitiated her husband, saying, "May my son not be like this; let him be someone else, a low-caste Brahmin. When she had spoken thus, the sage replied:
"O blessed lady, this desire was not conceived by me, nor likewise by you;
that a son of fierce deeds might arise for the sake of his father and mother. (77)
Satyavatī, having been addressed with these words, spoke again as follows:
"O Sage, if you so desired, you could even create the worlds; how much more so a son? (78)
"You ought to grant me a son for my husband who is composed of tranquility and upright;
O Lord, tell me, may such a son as this indeed be mine. (79)
"O best of the twice-born, it is indeed impossible for me to act otherwise;
therefore, he granted her favor by the power of her asceticism."
O woman of excellent complexion, there is no distinction for me between my son and my grandson;
O blessed lady, it shall be exactly as you have spoken. (81)
Therefore, Satyavatī gave birth to a son of the Bhṛgu lineage, Jamadagni, who was devoted to austerity, self-controlled, and of a peaceful nature. 82.
In ancient times, due to the reversal of the sacrificial oblations (caru) for Raudra and Vaiṣṇava by Bhṛgu,
Jamadagni was born from the Vaiṣṇava fire through the act of restraint.
Having obtained Viśvāmitra as his heir, Gādhi, the descendant of Kuśika, accompanied by the Brahman-sages, departed for the world of Brahmā, surrounded by the Sun-god.
For she, the virtuous Satyavatī, who was devoted to the vow of truth, has become this great river known as Kauśikī. (85)
The highly fortunate Kauśikī, the best of rivers, flows nearby;
and in the lineage of Ikṣvāku, there was a king named Suveṇu.
His highly fortunate daughter was named Kāmalī Reṇukā. From that Reṇukā Kāmalī, Jamadagni— the son of Ṛcīka— begot the very formidable [Rāma], who was endowed with asceticism and fortitude.
Rama, the destroyer of Kshatriyas, who has reached the end of all branches of knowledge, is the most excellent master of the science of archery and is like a blazing fire. (88)
From Aurva Ṛcīka, through his prowess, Jamadagni—the best among the knowers of Brahman—was born of Satyavatī; he was high-minded. Śunaḥśepha was the middle son, and Śunaḥpuccha was the youngest. (89)
The righteous-souled Viśvāmitra, known by the name Viśvaratha, was born through the grace of Bhṛgu from Kauśika as the increaser of the lineage. (2.29.90)
The son of Viśvāmitra was the sage Śunaḥśepha;
he was indeed appointed as the sacrificial animal at the sacrifice of Hariścandra.
Because he was given by the gods, he therefore became Devarāta. (91)
Among the sons of Viśvāmitra, Śunaḥśepha is remembered as the eldest;
then Madhucchandas, Naya, Kṛtadeva, Dhruva, and Aṣṭaka. (92)
Kacchapa and Pūraṇa were indeed the sons of Viśvāmitra;
the lineages of those high-souled Kauśikas are manifold.
The Pārthivas, Devarātas, Yājñavalkyas, Samarṣaṇas, Udumbaras, Udumlānas, Tārakas, and Yamamuñcatas [were there]. (94)
The Lohiṇyas, the Reṇus, and likewise the Kārīṣavas are recorded;
as well as the Babhruvas, the Pāṇinas, and similarly the Dhyāvajapyas.
The Śālāvatyas, Hiraṇyākṣas, Syāṅkṛtas, and Gālavas are recorded; as are the Devalas, Yāmadūtas, Śālaṅkāyanas, and Bāṣkalas. ||96||
The Bādaras give [their daughters] to the wise Viśvāmitra;
these many others are known as the Śauśikas, who are distinct from other sages. ||97||
The Kauśikas, the Aśrumas, as well as others, the Saidhavāyanas—these belong to the meritorious Brahmarṣi Kauśika, the son of Purūravas. ||98||
Likewise, Aṣṭaka was born from Viśvāmitra as the son of Dṛṣadvatī;
indeed, he who is called the son of Aṣṭaka has been described by me as belonging to the lineage of Jahnu.
The sages said:
By what characteristic dharma, or by what asceticism or learning in this world,
was the status of a Brāhmaṇa attained by kings such as Viśvāmitra and others,
through which those born of Kṣatriya lineage reached the state of Brāhmaṇahood?
I wish to know the distinction [between them] through austerity as well as through giving. ||101||
Thus addressed, he then spoke these meaningful words:
"One who desires merit and performs a sacrifice with the intention of sacrificing by means of wealth acquired through unjust means does not enjoy the fruit of that merit. (102)
Having proclaimed this as the Dharma, that evil-souled and lowest of men gives gifts to the Brahmins for the sake of deceiving the world. (103)
Having performed such intense recitation, one who is unrestrained by greed for wealth and filled with passion and delusion gives [the merit] at the end for the sake of purification. (104)
The gifts given by that wicked-souled person, who is intent on violence though appearing to practice dharma, indeed become fruitless. (105)
Thus, for one who has acquired wealth through delusion and gives it away while performing sacrifices— such a person of afflicted karma and evil soul finds that his gift does not endure.
He bestows wealth acquired by righteous means upon worthy recipients; and he performs sacrifices and gives gifts without aiming for the fulfillment of desires. (107)
He obtains the fruit of giving, and that gift results in happiness;
through giving one attains enjoyments, and through truth one goes to heaven. ||108||
By means of well-performed austerity, he stands supporting the worlds;
having supported them, that radiant one enjoys infinity within the worlds.
Sacrifice is superior to charity, and austerity is superior to sacrifice;
renunciation is superior to austerity, and therefore knowledge is considered the highest teacher. (2.29.110)
For it is heard that there were twice-born ones who attained perfection through asceticism while endowed with the qualities of the kṣatriya class:
Viśvāmitra, King Māndhātṛ, Saṃkṛti, and Kapi. (111)
From Kapi were born Purukutsa, Satya, Anṛhvan, Anṛthu,
Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Amīḍha, and likewise Bhāga.
Kakṣīvat, Śijaya, and other great chariot-warriors (mahāratha), as well as Rathītara, Runda, Viṣṇuvṛddha, and other kings. ||113||
For these are remembered as being endowed with the qualities of a Kṣatriya, yet they attained the status of Ṛṣis through austerity. All these royal seers (rājarṣis) have reached supreme perfection.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the lineage of the high-souled Ayus.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Glorification of the Lunar Dynasty," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, these five high-souled and mighty sons were born as kings to Prabhā, the daughter of Svarbhānu. ||1||
Nahuṣa was the first among them; after him, Putradharma is recorded;
and then Dharmavṛddha’s son, the highly illustrious Sutahotra. ||2||
The three heirs of Suta-hotra were supremely righteous:
these two, Kāśa and Śala, as well as the lord Gṛtsamada. ||3||
The son of Gṛtsamada was also Śunaka, from whom the Śaunakas descended;
likewise, there were Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
O twice-born ones, in his lineage were born those who performed various deeds;
Śala’s son was indeed Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and Caranta was his son.
The Śaunakas and the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas were twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas;
likewise, Dīrghatapas was the son of Kāśya, the son of Kāśa, and the son of Rāṣṭra.
Then, from that wise and aged ascetic of great splendor, Dhanvantari was born through his long penance—Dhanvantari who was learned in the Dharma.

Then the Ṛṣis spoke these words again to Sūta: 7. "And Dhanvantari, the knower of Dharma, possessed of great luster through his long austerity, was born to the wise and aged one. Then the sages addressed him with this speech once more."
The sages said:
How did the god Dhanvantari take birth here among human beings?
We wish to know this; therefore, tell us what is pleasing. (8)
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, let this birth of Dhanvantari be heard here;
he was born in ancient times at the edge of the ocean while the nectar was being churned.
He was born before everything from the totality, and was encompassed by glory on all sides.
Seeing him whose body was fully perfected, [Brahmā] stood paralyzed;
he said, "You are the Unborn (Aja)," and therefore he is remembered as Aja. || 2.30.10 ||
Aja said to Viṣṇu: "O Lord, I am your son;
O best of gods, grant me a portion and a place in your world. (11)
Thus addressed, the Lord Sudṛṣṭi spoke accordingly:
"The sacrificial portions have indeed been assigned by the gods worthy of sacrifice."
And the fire-sacrifice performed according to the injunctions in the Vedas by the great seers cannot ever be equaled here by any other sacrifice. (13)
"O Lord, you are Arvāksuta; O Master, you are indeed the Name-mantra.
Through your second manifestation, you shall attain renown in the world. (14)
"Success endowed with the powers such as *aṇimā* shall belong to you while you are still in the womb;
by that very body, O Lord, you shall attain divinity.
The twice-born shall worship you with beautiful mantras, clarified butter, and fragrant perfumes. (15)
And yet, you shall indeed restore the science of Ayurveda;
for this matter was destined to happen and was previously ordained by the Lotus-born One.
Upon reaching the second Dvāpara age, you will undoubtedly become [the incarnation];
therefore, having granted him the boon, Viṣṇu then vanished from that place.
When the second Dvāpara age had arrived, that King of Kāśi, Saunahotra,
as well as King Dīrghatapas, both performed austerities desiring sons.
Desiring to propitiate Lord Aja for the sake of a son, the king indeed endeavored to please him;
and Dhanvantari, being pleased, invited the king to choose a boon.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased with me, then be my steadfast son.
Having granted permission, saying "So be it," he vanished right there.
Then, in his house, the god Dhanvantari was born as the great king Kāśirāja, the destroyer of all diseases. ||21||
Bharadvāja composed the Āyurveda, which includes the practice of medicine;
having then divided it into eight parts, he imparted it to his disciples.
The son of Dhanvantari was also renowned as Ketumān. Now, O Lord, the son of Ketumān was King Bhīmaratha, who became famous as Divodāsa and was the sovereign of Vārāṇasī. ||23||
At that very time, however, a Rākṣasa named Kṣeṇaka entered the ancient city of Vārāṇasī, which had become desolate.
"For that city was formerly cursed by the high-souled Nikumbha, who said again and again: 'It shall indeed remain empty for a thousand years. (25)
As soon as she had been cursed, Divodāsa, the lord of subjects,
established a beautiful city at the edge of his domain on the banks of the Gomatī.
The sages said:
For what reason did Nikumbha formerly curse Vārāṇasī—that righteous-souled Nikumbha who cursed the field of the Siddhas? ||27||
Sūta said:
But the royal sage Divodāsa, having reached the city, that king of great splendor dwelt there, O lord of men, in that prosperous city. ||28||
At that very time, Maheśvara,
having taken a wife and desiring to please the Goddess, was dwelling in the vicinity of the gods.
By the command of the God, the attendants, who possess universal forms and whose wealth is asceticism,
gratify the Great Goddess with the specific forms previously described.
Mahādeva rejoiced because of them, but Menā did not rejoice at all;
she constantly felt loathing for the god and likewise for the goddess.
"By my side, however, your husband Maheśvara is ill-behaved;
he is entirely destitute here, O sinless one, and he sports about without any effort. (32)
Mātrā was addressed thus with these words, but out of her feminine nature, she could not endure it;
having smiled, the bestower of boons then went to the side of Hara.
With a dejected face, the goddess said to Mahādeva:
"I will not dwell here, O Lord; take me to my own abode. (34)

Thus addressed, O best of the twice-born, Mahādeva, the one of great splendor, having surveyed all the worlds, chose Vārāṇasī on earth as his dwelling place, for it was a field of perfection (siddhakṣetra), Maheśvara.
Having learned that [the city] had been settled by Divodāsa, Bhava summoned Kṣemaka, his attendant Gaṇeśa, and spoke to him. (36)
"Go to the city of Gaṇeśvara and make Vārāṇasī empty by means of gentle stratagems; for that king is possessed of extreme prowess. (37)
Then, having gone to the city of Vārāṇasī in the past, Nikumbha appeared to him in a dream as a barber named Maṅkaṇaka.
"I shall bring you prosperity; choose a place for me, O sinless one.
Having fashioned an image in my likeness, install it within the city. (39)
O twice-born ones, having obtained permission at the gate of the city, the king caused everything to be done exactly as it had been seen in the dream, according to the prescribed rites.
Furthermore, a great worship is performed constantly with perfumes, incenses, garlands, and likewise with objects for visual delight. (41)
And with those engaged in the offering of food, it became as if most wonderful;
thus Gaṇeśvara was constantly worshipped there. 42.
Then he bestows thousands of excellent cities, as well as sons, gold, long life, and all objects of desire. ||43||
The king’s chief queen, renowned by the name Suyaśas, was a virtuous lady who had been urged by the king to come for the sake of obtaining a son. ||44||
Having performed extensive worship, the goddess came again and again many times for the sake of her sons, and she entreated him for them. (45)
But Nikumbha does not give up his sons for a specific reason;
if the king were to become angry at that, then something [dangerous] might happen. (46)
Then, after a long time, anger took possession of the king:
"This being indeed bestows [wealth] at the great gates of cities. (47)
Out of affection, hundreds of boons were granted, yet nothing at all proceeded;
nevertheless, in my very city, he is constantly worshipped by my own people.
There, for that reason, he was honored by the goddess many times;
yet that ungrateful man, who eats much, does not give me a son. (49)
Therefore, he does not deserve worship from me in any way whatsoever;
consequently, I shall destroy the abode of that evil-minded one.
Having thus resolved, that evil-minded and wicked king, a perpetrator of sin, destroyed the abode of that Gaṇapati.
Seeing the sanctuary destroyed, the Lord went to the king and said:
"Since you have demolished my abode without any offense on my part, [I shall depart]. (52)
"But suddenly, O lord of men, your city shall become empty;
thus, by that curse, Vārāṇasī likewise became desolate. (53)
Then Nikumbha brought the cursed city to Mahādeva;
Mahādeva, by means of the Supreme Self, fashioned the city as empty.
The goddess, possessing a divine splendor equal to that of the Great-Souled One, indeed delights there; and while she is rejoicing, Maheśvara likewise rejoices.
The goddess did not find pleasure there because of her longing for home;
then, for the sake of the goddess's diversion, the Lord, the God, spoke these words.
"I shall certainly not leave this dwelling, for my home is unrenounced.
Then, laughing, he said to her: "Indeed, my home is unrenounced. (57)
"O Goddess, I will not go; you may go, for I am enjoying myself here.
Therefore, this place was indeed called Avimukta by the Lord himself. (58)
Thus was Vārāṇasī cursed, and Avimukta was proclaimed [as its name],
for it is there that the righteous Maheśvara, the god adored by all gods, dwells together with his goddess throughout the three ages. (59)
In the Kali age, that city of the Great-Souled One goes into concealment;
when that city has vanished, that [other] city dwells there once again.
Thus cursed, Vārāṇasī returned once more to its habitation;
there were a hundred sons of Bhadraśreṇya, all of them excellent archers.
Having slain him, King Divodāsa established [the city] there;
the kingdom of Bhadraśreṇya was seized by that more powerful one.
The son of Bhadraśreṇya was named Durmada; because he was a child, he was spared by Divodāsa out of compassion.
From Divodāsa, a hero named Pratardana was born on the Ṛṣadvatī river.
By that son, while still a child, he indeed struck him once again.
Then, while that great king was bringing an end to hostilities, Pratardana had two sons, the renowned Vatsa and Garga. 65.
Vatsaputra was indeed Alarka, and Sannati was his son.
Regarding Alarka, there are two ancient verses sung by the royal sage: [The verses follow.]
For sixty thousand and sixty hundred years,
Alarka, the best of the Kāśīs, remained young and endowed with beauty.
Through the grace of Lopāmudrā, he attained a supreme lifespan. ||68||
At the end of the curse, the mighty-armed king, having slain the Rākṣasa Kṣemaka,
caused the beautiful city of Vārāṇasī to be inhabited once more.
The heir of Sannati was the righteous one named Sunītha;
and the heir of Sunītha was the righteous one named Suketu.
And it is heard that Suketu’s son was Dharmaketu;
Dharmaketu’s heir was the great chariot-warrior Satyaketu.
The son of Satyaketu was the lord of subjects named Vibhu; Suvibhu was the son of Vibhu, and from him Sukumāra is remembered.
Sukumāra’s son was Dhṛṣṭaketu, who was righteous;
Dhṛṣṭaketu’s heir was Veṇuhotra, a lord of subjects.
The son of Veṇuhotra was the renowned Gārgya by name;
Gārgya’s son was Gargabhūmi, and the son of the wise Vatsa was Vātsya.
The Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas were their sons, highly righteous, valiant, powerful, and possessed of prowess equal to that of lions. ||75||

Thus these descendants of Kāśyapa have been described; now learn also of those of Raji. Raji had five hundred sons of great prowess on earth, and the warrior class known as the Rājeyas became a source of terror even to Indra.
Then, when a most terrible war between the gods and the asuras had broken out,
both the gods and the asuras spoke to the Grandfather.
"O Lord of all worlds, tell us which of us two will be the victor in battle; we wish to hear it. (78)
Brahmā said:
"For whose sake the lord Raji, having taken up his weapons, will fight in battle, they shall conquer the three worlds; of this there is no doubt. (79)
Where there is royal splendor, there is prosperity; where there is prosperity, there is fortitude;
where there is fortitude, there is righteousness; and where there is righteousness, there is victory.
Then, having heard of Rāji’s victory, all the gods and Dānavas approached him,
desiring victory themselves and praising that best of kings.
All those kings, gods, and dānavas, with joyful minds, said to the king: "Take up your excellent bow for our victory! (82)
Raji said:
"I shall conquer the gods, led by Śakra, in battle;
I shall become the righteous Indra, and thereafter I will fight in the conflict. (83)
The Dānavas said:
Indra is ours; for his sake we shall conquer.
At this time, O King, you must remain here like a god of Aditi. (84)
Saying "So be it," even as he was being urged by the gods,
he was invited by the gods, saying, "Having conquered [the demons], you shall become Indra."
He, the self-controlled one of supreme glory, slew all the Dānavas in the very presence of the wielder of the thunderbolt and brought under his control the lost prosperity of the gods. 86.
Having slain all the Dānavas, the lord Raji spoke;
and there, Śatakratu, together with the gods, addressed that Raji in such a manner. ||87||
Having said, "I am the son of Raji," he spoke these words once more:
"O King, you are Indra among all the gods; of this there is no doubt.
O slayer of enemies, I shall become known as your son, Indra. (88)
Having heard Śakra’s words, the king— deceived by his illusion—
replied "So be it" to the performer of a hundred sacrifices, feeling delighted.
When that king, who resembled a god, had ascended to heaven,
the sons of R̥jiṣin seized the inheritance from Indra, following established custom.
Those hundreds of his sons and that abode of the Lord of Śacī traversed the heavenly world, Triviṣṭapa, in many directions. ||91||
Then, after a long time had passed, the mighty Śakra, deprived of his kingdom and stripped of his sacrificial share, spoke to Bṛhaspati.
O Brahmarṣi, prepare for me a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) the size of a jujube fruit, so that, nourished by its splendor, I may remain [alive]. 93.
"O Brahmin, this man is emaciated, dejected, stripped of his kingdom, deprived of food, robbed of his vigor, weakened, and bewildered by the sons of Raji; be gracious to me. (94)
Bṛhaspati said:
O Śakra, if I had been exhorted by you in this way even earlier, O sinless one, I would not have existed; for there is nothing that ought not to be done by me for the sake of your pleasure. (95)
O Lord of Gods, O one of great splendor, I shall strive for the sake of your welfare so that you may regain both your portion and your kingdom before long. (96)
"O Śakra, I shall go thus; let not your mind be distressed.
Then he performed a great rite for the increase of his splendor.
And he, the best of the wise, caused their intellects to become deluded;
when they, along with their sons, were thus bewildered, they became unrighteous due to the arising of passion.
Having become haters of Brahman and having had their vigor and prowess destroyed,
they then lost their sovereignty over the gods and likewise their supreme station as Indra.
Having slain all the sons of Raji, who were devoted to lust and anger,
he established this purifying place as the abode of Śatakratu;
whoever hears of this, whether of Raji or of him, shall not incur wickedness.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Battle with Rājī," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu. ||30||
The sages said:
How was the maiden given by the high-souled Maruta to the king?
And what were the powers of the high-souled sons born of Maruta’s daughter? (1)
Sūta said:
Desiring food, the king of great splendor worshipped that Marutsoma, the lord of progeny,
month after month for sixty years, O King.
Thereupon, those Maruts, being gratified by that Marutsoma,
joyfully bestowed upon him inexhaustible food and all manner of desired articles.
His food, cooked but once, does not diminish throughout the day and night, even as it is given away by the millions from the very time of sunrise. ||4||
Mitrā-jyotis was the daughter of the wise Maruta;
from her were born those of great being, knowers of Dharma, and seers of liberation. ||5||
Having renounced the duties of household life and attained dispassion, they reached the state of asceticism here and departed for union with Brahman.
From him was born Anapāya, who then bestowed the Dharma;
from him was born Kṣatradharma, a great ascetic who was an adversary.
And the son of Pratipakṣa was the renowned Sañjaya;
Sañjaya’s son was Jaya, and his son was Vijaya. (8)
Vijaya’s son was Jaya; his son is remembered as Haryaṇḍuta. From Haryaṇḍuta was born King Sahadeva, who was full of prowess.
The righteous son of Sahadeva was known as Adīna;
Adīna’s son was Jayatsena, and his son was Saṃkṛti.
Saṃkṛti, Dharmātman, Kṛtadharman, and Mahāyaśas—
learn now of these, who were the upholders of the kṣatriya dharma of Nahuṣa.
The heirs of Nahuṣa were six of great power, possessing splendor equal to that of Indra; they were born of Virajā, the daughter of the Pitṛs.
Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Āyāti, and Pañca were the five sons;
Yati was indeed the eldest among them, and Yayāti was the one born after him.
Then the ascetic Saṃyāti took the daughter of Kakutstha named Gā as his wife;
having established himself in liberation, that sage became one with Brahman.
Among those five, however, Yayāti, the lord of the earth,
obtained Devayānī, the daughter of Uśanas, as his wife.
Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of the Asura Vṛṣaparvan, and Devayānī both gave birth to sons: Yadu and Turvasu.
Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, gave birth to Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru—sons of great prowess who were like the sons of gods. (17)
Pleased, Rudra gave him a chariot that was supremely radiant,
unimpeded, golden, and divine, along with two inexhaustible great quivers.
Yoked with swift horses, he by whom the maiden was carried away conquered the earth with that preeminent chariot. 19.
Yayāti, invincible in battle by gods, dānavas, and humans,
became the chariot-warrior (the leader) of all the Paurava kings.
That chariot, belonging to King Janamejaya, the Kuru born in the lineage of Sudeva and son of King Parikṣit, came to destruction through the curse of the wise Gārgya. (21)
For that foolish King Janamejaya caused the slaughter of the son of Gārgya, the lord of men named Lohagandha. ||22||
That royal sage, smelling of iron, ran hither and thither;
abandoned by the people of the city and the countryside, he found no peace at any time.
Then, tormented by grief and finding no peace anywhere,
he, being distressed, cursed the sage Hetuka, who was his refuge.
That renowned sage of noble intellect named Indrota— Indrota Śaunaka, the best of the twice-born— engaged King Janamejaya in an Aśvamedha sacrifice for the sake of his purification. (25)
Upon entering his dwelling, that smell of iron vanished;
likewise, that divine chariot disappeared from the abode of Vasu, the lord of Cedi.
Then, from that [Indra], Bṛhadratha received it because Śakra was pleased.
Subsequently, having slain Jarāsaṃdha, Bhīma, the joy of the Kauravas, affectionately gave that excellent chariot to Vāsudeva.
Having reached old age, that royal sage Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, spoke these words to his eldest and most excellent son, Yadu: ||31.28||
O dear one, wrinkles and gray hairs have come upon me due to the curse of Kāvya Uśanas, yet I am not yet satiated with youth.
"O Yadu, accept this evil along with my old age; take my old age upon yourself. To him, Yadu replied: [30]
The alms I promised to the brahmin were not specifically defined; they must indeed be earned through exertion, and I will not accept your old age.
There are many evils in old age for one who consumes food and drink;
therefore, O King, I do not venture to accept you while you are subject to old age. (32)
Bearing white whiskers, dejected, made frail by old age, wrinkled, with drooping limbs, difficult to look upon, and of weak appearance. ||33||
"Incapable of performing actions and humiliated in my youth, and beset by great fears, I do not desire that old age. (34)
"O King, you have many sons who are dearer to you than I;
O knower of dharma, let them accept [the kingdom], or indeed, choose another son. (35)
Thus addressed by Yadu, he, the best among speakers, filled with intense anger,
spoke to his eldest son while censuring him.
What other stage of life (āśrama) is there for you, or what rule of dharma? O evil-minded one, you who are no teacher, why do you speak thus while disregarding me? (37)
Having spoken thus to Yadu, the king, filled with wrath, cursed him:
"Since you, though born from my own heart, do not yield your youth to me. (38)
Therefore, O fool, you shall not share in the kingdom; indeed, your subjects shall belong to another.
Turvasu, take upon yourself this evil along with old age. (39)
Turvasu said:
"O father, I do not desire old age, which destroys one's strength and enjoyments.
There are many defects in old age regarding the consumption of food and drink;
therefore, O King, I am not willing to accept old age from you. (2.31.40)
Yayāti said:
"Since you, who were born from my heart, do not grant me your own youth, therefore, O Turvasu, your progeny shall go to utter destruction. (41)
O fool, you will become a king whose dharma is unconfused even among those who follow the inverse order of castes, and who partakes of flesh and other such things. 42.

There is no doubt that [the teaching] will exist among those addicted to the wives of their gurus, among those born as animals, among those following the customs of cattle, and among the barbarians. ||43||
Sūta said: Having thus cursed his own son Turvasu, Yayāti spoke these words to Druhyu, the son of Śarmiṣṭhā. ||44||
"O Druhyu, accept for a thousand years this old age that destroys complexion and form; give your youth to me."
"When a full thousand years have passed, I shall restore your youth to you, and I shall take back my own sin along with old age. (46)
Druhyu said:
An old man enjoys neither elephant, nor chariot, nor horse, nor woman.
He has no attachment, nor does he desire old age because of that. ||47||
Yayāti said:
Since you, who were born from my heart, do not grant me your own youth,
therefore, O Druhyu, your cherished desire shall never be fulfilled.
There, the movement of boats and caravans will be constant;
you shall always be there as one of the lineage of kings who do not flee from battle. (49)
"Accept, therefore, your own evil along with old age;
in this way, I shall live for a thousand years with your youth. (2.31.50)
Anuru said:
An old man gives even a child his preference, for he is always impure due to old age.
He does not offer oblations into the fire at the proper time; that old age does not desire him.
Yayāti said:
Since you, who were born from my heart, do not grant me youth as food,
this defect of old age which you have mentioned shall therefore befall you.
Furthermore, your subjects who have reached the prime of youth will perish because of you;
consequently, you too shall become intent on leaping into the fire.
"O Pūra, take upon yourself this evil along with my old age;
let wrinkles and grey hair encompass me, my son. (54)
Due to the curse of the poet Uśanas, I am not yet satiated with youth; therefore, for a certain period of time, let her indeed enjoy the objects of the senses through your vital energy. (55)
"When a full thousand years have passed, I shall restore your youth to you, and I myself shall take back my own sin along with old age. (56)
Sūta said:
Thus addressed, the son immediately replied to his father:
"O dear father, I shall do exactly as you authorize."
O King, I shall take upon myself your infirmity along with your old age;
take my youth from me and enjoy all desires as you wish. (58)
Covered by old age, I have assumed the form of youth;
having given my youth to you, I shall live according to my true nature. (59)
Yayāti said:
"Pūru, I am pleased; may it be well with you. Being pleased, I grant this to you:
your subjects in the kingdom shall have all their desires fulfilled."
Sūta said:
Then, with the consent of Puru, King Yayāti transferred his own old age [to him], by virtue of the grace of the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Then, endowed with youth and vigor, Yayāti, the son of Anuṣa and best among men, moved about enjoying his own sensory pleasures with great delight.

According to his desire, according to his energy, according to the time, and according to what is pleasant—indeed, that very king of kings deserves it, provided it does not conflict with the Dharma. //63//
He gratified the gods with sacrifices, the ancestors likewise with śrāddha rites,
the wretched with favors, and the best of the twice-born with their desired objects.
He should support guests with food and drink, the Vaiśyas by means of protection,
the Śūdras through kindness, and the Dasyus by means of suppression.
And by pleasing all his subjects according to righteousness as was fitting,
Yayāti protected them like a second Indra in person.
That king, possessing the prowess of a lion and being young, moved within the range of sensory objects and enjoyed supreme happiness without contradicting the Dharma.
Seeking the defects inherent within sensual pleasures,
he took delight in the Vaibhrāja Nandana grove for the sake of attaining confidence.
When the king saw that she was indeed growing old,
he went to the presence of Pūru and took back his own decrepitude.
Having attained those desires, the king, though satisfied, became weary;
that lord of men indeed remembered the passing of time for a thousand years.
Having calculated the time, as well as the *kalās* and *kāṣṭhās*,
and considering that the duration was complete, he then spoke to his son Pūru.
O subduer of enemies, O son, I have enjoyed the objects of the senses according to my pleasure, according to my enthusiasm, and according to the proper time during my youth.
"O Pūru, I am pleased; may prosperity be yours! Take back your own youth, as well as the kingdom and King Pūru, my youngest son.
Then the castes, headed by the Brāhmaṇas, spoke these words: ||73||
King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, underwent old age,
and Pūru regained his own youth once again.
And when the king desired to consecrate his youngest son, Pūru, the social orders, headed by the Brāhmaṇas, spoke these words: [75]
O Lord, how can you bypass Śukra’s grandson, the son of Devayānī, who is the most excellent, and bestow the kingdom upon Pūru? (76)
Of you, Durjyeṣṭha was born as the eldest son; after him came Turvasu, then Śarmiṣṭhā’s son Druhyu, then Anu, and Pūru.
How can the younger brother deserve the kingdom by bypassing the elder?
Therefore, I entreat you: uphold the Dharma. (78)
Yayāti said:
"Let all the social classes, headed by the Brahmins, hear my words:
the kingdom must never, under any circumstances, be given away by me to my eldest [son]. (79)
"He alone is praised as a son who carries out the commands of his mother and father; by my eldest son, Yadu, this command was not obeyed. (2.31.80)
He who acts contrary to his father's will is not considered a son by the virtuous;
he alone is a true son who behaves toward his father and mother as a son should.
Just as I have been treated with contempt by Yadu and by Turvasu,
so too has such extreme contempt been shown by Druhyu and Anu.
The word of Pūru was indeed honored by me with special distinction;
my youngest heir, who took upon himself my old age, fulfilled all my desires and accomplished everything for me through his act of becoming my son. (83)
And Śukra, the son of Kavi, Uśanas himself, granted this boon:
"O high-minded one, he who follows you shall be your son and your king. (84)
"Even with your consent, let Pūru be consecrated in the kingdom;
for that son who is endowed with virtues and always devoted to the welfare of his parents deserves every auspicious thing—he is the lord, even if he is the youngest. (85)
"Pūru is worthy of this kingdom, for he is dear to you and does what is pleasing to you;
because of Śukra’s boon, it is not possible to give a reply [to the contrary]. (86)
Then, having been addressed thus by the contented citizens and country-folk, the son of Nahuṣa consecrated his own son Pūru in his own kingdom.
In the south-eastern direction he settled Turvasu, and in the south-western direction the king settled the preeminent Yadu. (88)
Having conquered both Druhyu and Anu in the west and the north,
King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, then divided the earth with its seven islands and its oceans into five parts for his sons. (89)
By them, this entire earth—with its seven continents and its cities—is protected according to their respective regions through righteousness by those who know the Dharma. ||2.31.90||
Having thus bestowed the earth upon his sons, the son of Nahuṣa,
the king, felt great joy, for he had transferred the royal glory to his offspring.
Having entrusted his bow, arrows, and even the kingdom to his sons,
the king became filled with joy, having placed the burden upon his kinsmen.
In this regard, a verse was sung of old by the great king Yayāti:
"He who, having set his mind upon desires, withdraws them from all sides like a tortoise its limbs. (93)
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter. (94)
Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist on earth—all that is not enough for even one person; seeing this, one is not deluded. (95)
But when one maintains a purifying disposition toward all beings through action, mind, and speech, then one attains Brahman. 96.
When one does not fear others, when others do not fear him, when he neither desires nor hates—then he attains Brahman. (97)
That craving which is difficult for the foolish to abandon, which does not decay even as one decays, and whose faults are life-ending—for one who abandons that craving, there is happiness. (98)
The storehouses decay as one decays; the teeth decay as one decays;
but the hope for life and the hope for wealth do not decay even as one decays. (99)

Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine happiness there may be—this [happiness of liberation] is not worth even a sixteenth part of that very pleasure which is the absence of craving. (2.31.100)
Having spoken thus, that royal sage departed for the forest with his wife;
and having performed austerities at Bhṛgutuṅga, the highly illustrious one, having observed hundreds of vows right there, attained heaven. (101)
These five lineages of his are meritorious and honored by the celestial rishis;
by them the entire earth is pervaded, just as by the rays of the sun.

The best of the twice-born who reads or hears the entire life-story of Yayāti shall become blessed, possessed of progeny, long-lived, and renowned. (103) Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Glorification of the Lunar Dynasty," in the *Śrī Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. (31)
Sūrya said:
Listen as I describe in detail and in proper sequence the lineage of Yadu, the most excellent and of supreme splendor, as I speak. (1)
Yadu had five sons who were like the children of gods:
Sahasrajit, Śreṣṭha, Kroṣṭu, Nīla, Jita, and Laghu. (2)
The son of Sahasrajit was the illustrious king named Śatajit; the sons of Śatajit were the three renowned and most righteous Satajits. (3)
There were Haihaya, Haya, and King Veṇuhaya;
it is heard that Dharmatattva was the heir of Haihaya. (4)
Dharmatantra was the son of Kīrti, and Saṃjñeya was his son;
the heir of Saṃjñeya was the king named Mahiṣmān.
The powerful Bhadraśreṇya was the son of Mahiṣmat;
he was indeed previously mentioned as the king who ruled over Vārāṇasī. (6)
The heir of Bhadraśreṇya was the king named Durmada;
from Durmada was born the wise and renowned Kanaka.
The heirs of Kanaka were four, renowned throughout the world:
Kṛtavīrya, Kārtavīrya, and likewise Kṛtavarman. (8)
Kṛta was born and became the fourth; from Kṛtavīrya, Arjuna was then born, a king who possessed a thousand arms and ruled over the seven continents.
For having performed most difficult austerities for ten thousand years,
Kārtavīrya propitiated Datta, who was born of Atri.
To him, Datta granted four boons of immense splendor;
first, he chose as his primary boon a thousand arms. ||11||
Therefore, the virtuous must prevent that which is being given away in violation of dharma;
having conquered the earth through dharma, one must protect it by dharma alone. ||12||
Having conquered many battles and slain enemies by the thousands, his death would come while fighting in battle, even more so in the midst of combat. (13)
Thus, by the kṣatriya method, these people [ruled] this entire earth with its seven continents and its cities, surrounded by the seven oceans.
As that wise one fought with his thousand arms,
a warrior’s banner and chariot indeed appeared through his illusory power.
It is heard that ten thousand sacrifices were performed without obstruction by that wise king on those seven islands. (16)
All the sacrifices of that mighty-armed one of vast splendor were performed with altars made entirely of gold and sacrificial posts made entirely of gold. (17)
All were adorned by highly fortunate gods stationed in their celestial chariots, and they were constantly graced by gandharvas and apsarases. ||18||
Then the Gandharva Nārada sang a verse concerning that king,
having observed the life and the greatness of that royal sage.
"Surely no men shall ever attain the state of Kārtavīrya, whether by means of sacrifices, gifts, austerities, valor, or sacred learning. (2.32.20)
Indeed, on those seven islands, that king— armed with a sword and excellent bows,
and accompanied by chariots and other attendants— was seen following after him.
No property was ever lost, nor was there any sorrow or confusion, as the great king protected his subjects with righteousness through his sovereign power. ||22||
For eighty-five thousand years,
that lord of men became a sovereign universal monarch (cakravartin) seven times over.
He himself became the guardian of the cattle and likewise the protector of the field;
through his state of yoga, he became Arjuna and Parjanya by means of rain.
With his thousand arms, hardened by the striking of bowstrings, he shone like the autumnal sun with its thousand rays. ||25||
For that lord of men, having defeated Karkoṭaka along with a thousand Nāgas at Māhiṣmatī, established his city there. ||26||
With eyes like lotuses in the rainy season, he indeed made the monsoon come forth as if in sport, though agitated by pleasure, amidst the surge of the ocean.
Agitated and played with by him, the Narmadā approaches in fear, adorned with garlands of golden flower-strings, her waves acting as frowning brows and her roar as her cry. (28)
In the past, while pursuing her, he plunged into the great ocean;
having drawn it up to the edge of the shore, that Time covered the forest with rain.
When that great ocean was agitated by his thousand arms,
the great asuras dwelling in the netherworld became motionless and cowed.
They fell into the unbearable [ocean], where great fish submerged in the Mahāvīci hell were ground to powder,
where masses of foam were pierced, and which was tossed by violent whirlpools.
The king, agitating the ocean with his thousand arms,
made it resemble the Ocean of Milk when it was surrounded by gods and asuras.
Agitated by the Mandara mountain and suspecting it to be the water of immortality,
