they were suddenly struck with fear upon seeing that most excellent of kings, Bhīma.
And the great serpents stood with their heads motionless,
like groves of plantain trees at evening when stilled by the absence of wind.
Having strung his bow and mounted his chariot,
that arrogant one, having by force bewildered Rāvaṇa along with his army in Laṅkā,
conquered and bound him, and brought him back, he imprisoned him in Māhiṣmatī.
Then, having gone there, Pulastya propitiated Arjuna;
the king released the descendant of Pulastya, who had been protected by Pulastya.
From those thousand arms arose the sound of bowstrings being struck,
like the roar of thunder when the clouds and trees burst asunder at the end of an eon.
Oh, what great prowess in battle! For Bhārgava severed his thousand arms in the fray, like a grove of golden palm trees.
Once, when he was thirsty, he was begged for alms by Agni;
the lord of the people gave the seven islands as alms to Agni.
Cities, cowherd settlements, villages, and towns in every direction.
The fire blazed within his arrows with the desire to consume him.
By the power of that lord of men, the highly illustrious one burned the mountains and forests of Kārtavīrya.
That Citrabhānu, together with Haihaya, milked the entire empty hermitage of Varuṇa’s son, as well as the sacrificial islands.
In ancient times, Varuṇa obtained an excellent and radiant son;
that sage, known by the name Vasiṣṭha, was renowned and devoted to the waters.
Then, out of anger at that calamity, the Lord cursed Arjuna:
"O Haihaya, because you did not avoid this forest of mine, [you shall suffer]. (44)
Therefore, you have performed a difficult deed; another shall slay him—the son of Kuntī named Arjuna—and he shall not become king. ||45||
O Arjuna, the mighty Rāma, the best among strikers,
having violently crushed you with his strength, indeed severed your thousand arms.
A powerful ascetic brahmin shall slay him;
for at that time, Rāma was subject to the death-curse of that wise sage.
Long ago, that king himself chose a boon;
he indeed had a hundred sons, five among whom were great chariot-warriors.
Skilled in weapons, powerful, heroic, righteous, and illustrious were Śūra, Śūrasena, Vṛṣṭimat, and Vṛṣa. (49)
And Jayadhvaja was indeed the son of Viśāṃpati among the Āvantis;
the son of Jayadhvaja was the powerful Tālajaṅgha.
It is heard that he had exactly one hundred sons known as the Tālajaṅghas;
among them, five groups of those high-souled Haihayas became famous.
For there were the Vīrahotras, the innumerable Bhojas, the Āvartayas,
the valiant Tuṇḍikeras, and likewise the Tālajaṅghas.
The son of Vīrahotra was also a king named Ananta;
his son was Durjaya, who was formidable to behold by his enemies.
Indeed, that king possessed the quality of having his wealth never lost;
by his power, O great king, he protected those subjects.
There shall be no loss of wealth for him, and he shall recover what has been lost, whoever here recounts the birth of the wise Kārtavīrya. (55)
In this very world he becomes wealthy, and his merit increases;
as the giver was, so shall he be honored in heaven, like Tvaṣṭṛ.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Account of the Birth of Kārtavīryārjuna," in the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa* spoken by Vāyu.
The sages said:
For what reason was the world, which was otherwise inviolable for great-souled beings, consumed by Kārtavīrya through his prowess? Tell that to us who ask you. (1)
We have heard that this royal sage was a protector of his subjects;
how then, having become their protector, did he destroy that penance grove? (2)
Sūta said:
The Sun-god, having assumed the form of a brahmin, approached Kārtavīrya;
desiring food, he said, "I am the Sun-god, of this there is no doubt. (3)
The king said:
"O Blessed One, tell me, O Maker of Day, by what would you be satisfied?
What kind of food shall I give? Having heard it, I shall provide it. (4)
Sūrya said:
"O best among givers, grant me all that is stationary as my food;
by that alone shall I be satisfied, O King, and not by anything else. (5)
The king said:
O best of those who shine, it is not possible for any human power to utterly consume all that is stable; therefore, I bow down to you alone.
The Sun said:
"I am pleased with you; I grant you inexhaustible arrows that are comfortable in every respect.
When discharged, they shall blaze forth, imbued with my own splendor. (7)
"Commanded by my splendor, he will dry up the ocean of clouds;
I shall reduce it to parched ashes, and by that, O lord of men, I shall be pleased. (8)
Then Āditya bestowed arrows upon Arjuna;
having obtained them, he indeed acquired everything that is vast and immobile.
Then [he saw] hermitages and villages, cowherd settlements and cities, delightful penance groves, forests, and pleasure gardens.
Thus the great eastern forest was consumed; then the earth, devoid of trees and grass, was scorched by the heat of the sun.
At that very time, however, the great seer took refuge in the waters as his dwelling, remaining within the water for ten thousand years.
When his vow was completed, that great ascetic of immense splendor arose;
seeing the hermitage burnt by Arjuna, that great ṛṣi,
out of anger, cursed the royal sage, as has been narrated to you by me.
Sūta said:
Listen to the lineage of the royal seer Kroṣṭu, which possesses the most excellent men;
in his family was born Vṛṣṇi, the upholder of the Vṛṣṇi clan.
Kroṣṭu had one son, the highly illustrious Vṛjinīvān;
they call him Vārjinīvata, the best of those who offer oblations with the Svāhā-call.
The son of Svāhi was King Raśādu, the best among the generous givers;
they desire that the foremost son of Raśādu should be born from clarified butter. 16.
He performed various great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
his son was Citraratha, who was endowed with diverse meritorious deeds.
In this manner, the heroic Citraratha performed sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees;
Śaśabindu likewise followed the supreme conduct practiced by the royal sages.
The Great Being was a universal monarch, possessed of great heroism and many offspring;
concerning him, this genealogical verse was sung in the past by those learned in ancient lore: (19)
Śaśabindu had a hundred sons,
a hundred who were wise, worthy, and possessed of great wealth and splendor.
Of them, six were the principal ones, mighty Pṛthuṣāṭka and the others:
Pṛthuśravas, Pṛthuyaśas, Pṛthudharman, and Pṛthuñjaya. ||21||
Pṛthukīrti, Pṛthu the donor, and the Śāśibindu kings praise the lineage of Pārthaśravas in the Purāṇas;
he who was formerly Antara became the son of Yajña.
Uśanas, whose soul was devoted to the dharma of the sons [of his father] and who was supremely righteous, having obtained this earth,
performed a hundred horse-sacrifices.
Marutta was his son, who followed the path of the royal sages;
the heroic Kambalabarhi is remembered as the son of Marutta.
The wise Rukmakavaca, however, was the son of Kambalavarhiṣ;
having slain armored warriors in battle long ago, he was known as Rukmakavaca.
The archer, having attained supreme glory through his sharpened arrows,
performed the highly renowned Aśvamedha sacrifice and bestowed wealth upon the Brāhmaṇas.
From King Rukmakavaca, however, five sons were born who were slayers of heroes, possessed of great being and great strength, and who did not turn back in battle. ||27||
Rukmeṣu, Pṛthurukma, Jyāmagha, Parigha, and Hari—the father established both Parigha and Hari in Videha. (28)
Brahmeṣu became king, and Pṛthu Ukmaratha was his refuge;
from among them, Jyāmagha went forth from the kingdom to the hermitage.
Having been awakened by the brahmin while dwelling in the terrible forest, he became peaceful;
then, taking up his bow, he went toward the middle of the land, mounted on his chariot with his banner.
Alone in the marshlands of the Narmadā and also in Mekalāvṛttikā,
he went to Mount Ṛkṣavān and then entered Śuktimatī.
Jyāmagha’s wife was Śaibyā, who was exceedingly powerful;
although that king was childless, he did not take another wife. (32)
He achieved victory in battle, and through that he obtained a maiden;
that king, the lord of men, said to his wife, "She is my daughter-in-law. (33)
Thus addressed, she spoke in this manner to Kāmya: "O Yantṛ, I am your daughter-in-law;
I shall become the wife of whichever son is born to you. (34)
Through that fierce asceticism, the fortunate Śaibyā, having reached maturity, gave birth to a son, Vidarbha, the descendant of Viśaṃ. ||35||
The two wise princes, Kratha and Kauśika, were the sons-in-law [of Vidarbha];
Vidarbha begot upon his daughter two heroic sons, skilled in battle.
Afterwards, the highly righteous Lomapāda was born as the third;
Lomapāda’s son was Aṣṭaka, and Rāhūta was his son.
Cidi was the son of Kauśika; from him the Caidya kings are said to have descended.
Kratha’s son was Vidarbha, and Kunti was his offspring. (38)
From Kunterdhṛṣṭa was born the powerful Purodhṛṣṭa;
Dhṛṣṭa’s son was the righteous Nirvṛti, the slayer of enemy heroes.
His son was Daśārha, possessed of great strength and prowess;
Daśārha’s son was Vyoma, from whom Jīmūta is said to have descended.
Jīmūta’s son was Vikṛti, and his son was Bhīmaratha;
now, Bhīmaratha’s son was indeed Rathavara.
He was a donor who was constantly devoted to righteousness and dedicated to virtuous conduct and truth;
his son was Navaratha, from whom Daśaratha is said to have descended.
His son was Ekādaśaratha, and his son was Śakuni;
from him came Karambhaka, the archer, and from him Devarāta was born.
Devakṣatra became the king, the highly illustrious Devarāti;
Devakṣatra’s son was born as Devana, the delighter of the Kṣatriyas. ||44||
From Madhu was born that Madhu from whom the origin of Medhātithi arose;
and from Madhu also were born the highly resplendent Manu and Manuva.
And Nandana was of great splendor; likewise, from Puru came the son Puruvasu. From Puruvasu was born Purudvān, the best of men. (46)
To Purudvata was born a son, Purūdvaha, by Bhadravatī. Aikṣākī became his wife, and from her was born Sattva.
From Sattva was born Sāttvata, who was endowed with the quality of goodness (sattva) and increased the glory of the lineage.
Having understood this creation of the high-souled Jyāmagha,
one attains progeny and union with the wise King Soma.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Account of Jyāmagha," in the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa* proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
Sātvatī gave birth to a son endowed with beauty, Kauśalyā bore Bhajina and Bhajamāna, and [the latter] begot the divine king Devāvṛdha. ||1||
And Andhaka along with Sahābhāja, and Vṛṣṇi, the delight of the Yadus—
listen indeed to their four lineages in detail.
Bhajamāna had a daughter by Śr̥ñjayī named Bāhyakā; moreover, he was an outsider (bāhya). Śr̥ñjaya, however, had two daughters, and Bāhyaka married them both.
His two wives, who were sisters, gave birth to many sons:
Nimi, Paṇava, Vṛṣṇi, and Parapurañjaya.
Those who were born from Bhajamāna at Śṛñjayī as his external offspring were Ayuta, Ayutasāhasra, Śatajit, and Vāmaka. ||5||
While those who were devoted to the sister of Bāhyakarya were known as the twice-born (Brahmins),
King Devāvṛdha performed supreme austerity.
Thinking, "May I have a son endowed with all virtues," she,
being of the same caste as him, joined herself with him and touched the water.
And by his bathing,
that river, the best of streams, brought auspiciousness to that king and to the sage.
With her limbs overwhelmed by anxiety, she then reached this conclusion:
"I do not find that woman from whom such a son could have been born. (9)
"Indeed, [the child] shall be endowed with all virtues for King Devāvṛdha;
therefore, today I myself shall become his companion in religious observances.
Then her own hand was born from her, exactly as his state had been described.
Then, having become a maiden, Sāvitrī thought of the king; that monarch desired her.
In her, that noble-minded one conceived a radiant embryo;
then, in the ninth month, that best of rivers gave birth.
Just as Devāvṛdha desired a son endowed with all virtues, so too, in that lineage, the twice-born who know the Purāṇas sing this verse: [13]
Proclaiming the virtues of that high-souled Devāvṛdha,
he hears as if from afar and sees as if from close at hand.
Babhru is the best among men; he is equal to Devāvṛdha among the gods.
Seventy thousand and sixty-five men have attained immortality through Babhru and Devāvṛdha. (15)
A performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, a hero, devoted to the Brahmins, truthful in speech, wise, illustrious, highly fortunate, and a great chariot-warrior among the Sātvatas. ||16||
In his lineage arose the very great Bhojas and the Ārtikāvalas;
furthermore, Gāndhārī and Mādrī became the two wives of Vṛṣṇi.
Gāndhārī gave birth to Sumitra, the delighter of his friends;
and Mādrī bore a son, Yudhājit, who was indeed Devamīḍhuṣa.
Anamitra and Suta—both were supreme among men.
Anamitra’s son was Nighna, and Nighna had two sons. (19)
He had two sons, the illustrious Prasena and Śakrajit;
of these, Śakrajit had a former friend who was as dear to him as his own life.
Once, at the end of the night, that best of chariot-warriors went by chariot from the water's edge to touch the waters and to offer worship to the sun.
As he was standing there, the Lord Sun, Vivasvat, stood before him—
his form indistinct, the all-pervading one, possessed of a circle of light.
Then the king spoke to Vivasvat, who stood before him:
"O Lord of Light, I behold you just as I see [the sun] in the sky. (23)
And likewise, there stands before you one who possesses a circle of radiance;
what indeed is the distinction between him and you, O Vivasvat, who have come here in person?
Having heard this, the Blessed One then removed the Syamantaka jewel from his own neck and fastened it upon the king.
Then the king beheld him in embodied form;
having seen that image, he remained thus for a moment.
As Vivasvat was about to depart once more, Śakrajit said to him,
"You must give me that jewel-gem by which you shall go to the worlds. (27)
The Sun-god gave him the jewel named Syamantaka;
having fastened it on, the lord of the earth entered the city.
The people ran after him, crying out, "This is the sun that is moving! Having thus amazed the assembly hall, as well as the city and the inner apartments, he departed.
The king, the conqueror of Śakra, out of affection gave that divine and supreme Syamantaka jewel to his brother, the King of Prasenajit.
In whose kingdom the jewel named Syamantaka remains, there the rain-cloud pours at the proper time, and there is no fear of disease at that time. (31)
Govinda desired the Syamantaka jewel from Prasena; however, though he was capable, he did not obtain it, nor did he seize it by force.
Once, while adorned with that [jewel], Prasena went out hunting;
for the sake of the Syamantaka, he met a most terrible death at the hands of a lion. (33)
Jāmbavat, the king of the bears, indeed slew that lion;
and taking the divine jewel, he entered his own cave.
Then the elders of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, desiring the jewel, suspected that very deed of Kṛṣṇa.
Unable to endure that false accusation from them, the powerful and illustrious slayer of enemies wandered through the forest.
He, however, was engaged in a hunt there, and then,
following the tracks of Prasena with trustworthy men, he [pursued him].
Exhausted from his search, that high-minded one beheld Ṛkṣavān, the best of mountains, and Vindhya, the supreme mountain.
He did not find that slain Prasena with his horse there, nor indeed the jewel;
then, near the body of Prasena, a lion [was seen]. (39)
Seeing that he had been struck down by the bear, the Yādava followed the tracks indicated by the bear's feet and searched for the cave of the bear.
O twice-born ones, in that great cave, he heard a voice uttered by Pramada;
it was the voice of the nurse, who, having taken up the son of Jāmbavān, spoke with affection while presenting him with a jewel, saying, "Do not cry. (41)
The nurse said:
"A lion killed Prasena; that lion was slain by Jāmbavān.
Do not weep, O Sukumāra, for this Syamantaka belongs to you. (42)
Having made that sound manifest, he too quickly went to the cave;
and near the entrance of the cave, he saw Prasena torn apart.
Having entered that bear-cave with ease, the Blessed One,
possessed of noble intelligence, beheld Jāmbavān, the king of the bears.
Vāsudeva, however, fought with Jāmbavān inside the cave;
Govinda fought with his two arms alone for twenty-one days.
And when Kṛṣṇa had entered the cave, those who preceded Vāsudeva returned to Dvāravatī and announced that Kṛṣṇa was slain.
Vāsudeva, having conquered the mighty Jāmbavanta,
obtained the maiden Jāmbavatī, who was highly esteemed by the king of the bears.
Overwhelmed by the splendor of the Blessed One, Jāmbavān quickly gave the jewel and his daughter Jāmbavatī to Viṣvaksena.
Having entreated the king of bears, he took the Syamantaka jewel for the sake of his own purification and then emerged from the cave.
Thus, having taken that jewel and purified himself by his own effort,
he gave that very jewel to Satrājit in the presence of the Sātvata.
Then Madhusūdana spoke again to the maiden Jāmbavatī;
thus Janārdana was liberated from that false accusation.
He who knows how this false accusation against Kṛṣṇa was dispelled here shall never again be falsely accused because of a false accusation. (52)
From his ten sisters, who were his wives, Śatrājita begot one hundred sons.
Among them, three were famous; Bhaṅgakāra was the eldest, followed by Vīra, Vratapati, and the very dear Apasvānta. (53)
Then, in Dvāravatī, Suprajā, the wife of Bhaṅgakāra, gave birth to three daughters endowed with beauty and virtue. (54)
Satyabhāmā was the most excellent of women, firm in her vows like a female ascetic;
thus, Kṛṣṇa’s father gave her to him as one who was truly devoted to penance.
That jewel-gem Syamantaka which Kṛṣṇa had given to Satrājit was then seized by Bhoja Śatadhanvan.
For at that time, Akrūra, seeking a jewel, requested the blameless Satyabhāmā for the Syamantaka gem.
Then, having killed Bhadraka, the mighty Śatadhanvan took that jewel at night and gave it to Akrūra.

When dharma had perished, Viṣṇu himself was then born in the Vṛṣṇi clan to establish the order of dharma and to bring about the destruction of the asuras.
At that time, the maiden Rukmiṇī was brought [as a wife], as were Satyā, the daughter of Nagnajit;
Satyabhāmā, the daughter of Satrājit; and also Jāmbavatī and Rohiṇī.
Śaibyā, Sudevī, Mādrī, and another named Suśīlā; Kālindī, Mitravindā, Lakṣmaṇā, and Jālavāsinī. ||234||

Thus, sixteen thousand gods and the fourteen classes of Apsarases who are proclaimed to be in heaven— having been considered by the gods and Śakra, these most distinguished ones have been sent here. (235)
Born in royal palaces for the sake of being the wives of Vāsudeva,
these highly fortunate women are renowned as the consorts of Viṣvaksena.
Pradyumna, Cārudeṣṇa, Sudeṣṇa, and Śarabha;
as well as Cāru, Cārubhadra, and another named Bhadracāru. ||237||
Cāruvindhya was born of Rukmiṇī, as was the daughter Cārumatī;
likewise Sānu, Bhānu, Akṣa, Rohita, and Mantraya. (238)
Jarāndhaka, Tāmravakṣas, Bhaumari, and Jarandhama were born; from him whose banner is Garuḍa, four sisters were also born. (239)
Bhānu, Bhaumarika, Tāmraparṇī, and Jarandhamā—these were the sons of Satyabhāmā; now hear of the offspring of Jāmbavatī.
Bhadra, Bhadragupta, and likewise Bhadravindra;
the renowned Saptabāhu, and the maiden Bhadrāvatī; and the famous Sambodhanī—these are to be known as the sons of Jāmbavatī. (241)
Saṃgrāmajit, Śatajit, and Sahasrajit—these sons of Sudevi are proclaimed as the offspring of Viṣvaksena. ||242||
Vṛka, Vṛkāśva, Vṛkajit, and the celestial maiden Vṛjinī;
Mitrabāhu and Sunītha—these were the offspring of Nāgnajitī here on earth. (243)
Understand that there were thousands of sons beginning with these;
those who were the sons of Vāsudeva are said to number one million.
Likewise, there were eighty thousand heroes skilled in battle;
thus has this lineage of Janārdana been recounted to you exactly as it is.
Bṛhatī was the daughter of the high-souled Śauneya Bṛhaduccha; she was a dancer skilled in the Ānīya style, and she was thus united with Sunaya. ||246||
Her sons were three famous ones who graced the assembly:
Aṅgada, Kumuda, and Śveta; and likewise, there was a daughter named Śvetā.
Avagāha, Citra, Śūra, and Citravara;
his son was Citrasena, and likewise his daughter was Citravatī. ||248||
Tumba, Tumbabāṇa, and Janastamba—these two are remembered as the Upāṅgas; and Vajrāra and Kṣipra likewise. (249)
Bhurīndrasena and Bhūri were both sons of Gaveṣa;
Yudhiṣṭhira’s daughter was the renowned Sutanu by name.
From him was born a son by Aśvā, the highly illustrious Vajra;
Vajra’s son was Pratibāhu, and Sucāru was his son.
Kāśmā gave birth to a powerful son, Supārśva;
Sāmbā had three crores of sons who were high-souled Yādavas. (252)
Six million [beings], heroic and possessed of great strength, all portions of the gods, have here been born with immense power. ||253||

Those great ascetics among the Asuras who were slain in the war between the gods and the Asuras have been born here among men; they oppress all human beings, and for their destruction, I have been born in the lineage of the Yadavas. (254)
The eleven clans of the high-souled Yādavas all exist as one single clan within the Vaiṣṇava lineage. ||255||
Viṣṇu is established as the authority and the sovereign over them;
all human beings are bound by those who abide by his command. (256)
Thus, the lineage of the Vṛṣṇis has been proclaimed through both concise and detailed accounts;
and by this very proclamation, one attains the desired perfection of fame.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Lineage of Viṣṇu," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Learn now of the gods who are of human nature as they are being proclaimed:
Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, and Sāmba. (1)
And Aniruddha—these five are proclaimed as the heroes of the lineage;
likewise the seven ṛṣis, Kubera, and the yakṣa Maṇivara.
Śālakī, Badara, the learned Dhanvantari, and Mahādeva as Nandin—these are called the Śālaṅkāyanas;
then the primordial god Jiṣṇu was present along with these deities. ||3||
The sages said:
For what purpose was Viṣṇu born? How many past incarnations are recorded?
And how many other future manifestations of the Great Soul will there be? (4)
For what purpose is one born here again and again among human beings in this field of Brahman during the ends of the ages? Tell that to us who ask you.
We desire to hear in full detail all the deeds performed by the bodies of the wise Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of his enemies. (6)
O Sūta, you ought to tell us the sequence of actions, their manifestations, O Lord, and what their essential nature is.
How did that Blessed One Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the lords of the gods, become the wise Vāsudeva in the lineage of Vasudeva? (8)
"O Sūta, what is this merit-filled place adorned by the performers of virtuous deeds, that you have come here to the mortal world, abandoning the realm of the gods? (9)
Hari, the leader of gods and men and the progenitor of the earth and the atmosphere—why did he enter his divine self into a human form? 2.35.10
He who alone turns the mind-made wheel among men—how could that best of wheel-bearers have conceived the thought of being a mere man? (11)
How is it that Viṣṇu, the Lord who provides universal protection for all the worlds, went to the earth and acted as a cowherd? (12)

How could he, the essence of the great elements, who tore asunder and created the very self of the elements—he whose womb is auspiciousness—be held in the womb of a woman who walks upon the earth? 13.
By whom, having conquered the worlds with three strides out of a desire for the thirty [gods], the three paths of the world—the foremost among the three aims of life—were established. (14)
He who, at the time of the end, having swallowed the world and assumed a body composed of water,
made the universe a single ocean by means of his visible and invisible path.
He who is the ancient Self within the Purāṇa, the best of gods, having assumed the form of a boar, conquered and bestowed the earth upon the deities. 16.
By whom, having assumed a lion-like body and then dividing it into two parts, the former Daitya of great prowess, Hiraṇyakaśipu, was slain. (17)
He who was formerly the all-pervading Aurva, the fire of universal destruction,
dwelling in the netherworld and situated within the ocean, drank the oblation consisting of water.
They speak of that god who has a thousand feet, a thousand rays,
and a thousand heads, as the god who exists in every age.
From whose navel arose that lotus— the ancestral home of his forefathers— which remained free from mud even when the world had become a single ocean.
By him those Daityas were slain in the Tārakāmaya battle,
after he had made his body consist of all the gods and bear all weapons.
Mounted upon Garuḍa, he became exultant and struck down Kālanemi.
In the northern region of the ocean—the Ocean of Milk, the sea of nectar—he lies, having established himself in eternal yoga, dispelling the great darkness. (22)
In ancient times, Aditi bore a divine embryo through the excellence of her asceticism— that [child] who,
by the power of his presence within the womb, greatly distressed Śakra when he was besieged by the hosts of Daityas.
When the Wind-god, having seized the positions of the world-regents, made those Daityas dwellers in the waters;
and the Primordial God, having established the gods in heaven, made Puruhūta alone the lord of the deities.
According to the ritual procedure for the *gārhapatya* fire, by means of the *anvāhārya* rite,
he prepared the *āhavanīya* fire, the sacrificial altar, and the bundle of *kuśa* grass.
He likewise created the water for sprinkling, the *sruva* ladle, and the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*);
furthermore, he fashioned here the three who bestow shares of the oblation in the sacrifice.
He made the gods consumers of *havya* (sacrificial offerings) and the ancestors consumers of *kavya* (funeral offerings),
for the sake of enjoyment through the ritual procedure of sacrifice— that which is sacrifice within the act of sacrificing.
The sacrificial posts, the fuel, the ladle, the Soma, the filter, and even the enclosing sticks;
likewise, the materials fit for sacrifice and the fires worthy of sacrifice. ||28||
He who formerly shone with the office of the supreme lord (Pārameṣṭhya) by means of the Aśvamedha sacrifices—the best of rituals—along with the members of the assembly and the sacrificers. ||29||
Having fashioned the three worlds in accordance with the respective ages in their proper order,
he likewise created the moments (kṣaṇas), the twinklings of an eye (nimeṣas), the units of time called kāṣṭhās, the kalās, and the three divisions of time.
The muhūrtas, lunar days, months, as well as days and years, the seasons, the conjunctions of time, and likewise the threefold measure [of time]. ||31||
Longevity, fields of merit, accumulation of wealth, auspicious marks, excellence of form, intelligence, riches, valor, and the mastery of the scriptures—[all these result from this]. ||32||
The three castes, the three worlds, the three Vedas, the three fires, the three times, the three types of action, the three illusions, and the three qualities. ||33||
By him, through his supreme action, the worlds and the gods were created;
by him, whose self is the essence of all hosts of beings, all the multitudes of living creatures were created.
He who delights in the yoga preceded by the senses of men, who is the leader of those who come and go, and who is the sovereign over all various things; ||35||

He who is the destination for those endowed with righteousness and the non-destination for those of evil deeds; the source of the fourfold caste system and the protector of the fourfold caste system. (36)
He who knows the fourfold knowledge and dwells in the four stages of life;
the quarters of space, the sky, the earth, water, wind, and fire. (37)
He who is the light of both the moon and the sun, the Lord of the Yugas, the wanderer of the night; he who is heard of as the supreme deity, and he who is heard of as the supreme austerity. (38)
He whom they call the scorcher of enemies, he who is the supreme self-possessed one,
the deity who is the beginning of the Ādityas, and the all-pervading lord who is the destroyer of the Daityas.
He who is the Ender at the end of the ages, and he who is the destroyer of the destroyers of the worlds;
he who is the bridge for those who are bridges for the world, and he who is the purest among those whose deeds are pure.
He who is the object of knowledge for those who know the Vedas, the Lord of those whose nature is power;
he who has become the moon among living beings, and has become the fire among those with the luster of fire. (41)
He is the mind of men, the asceticism of ascetics, the humility of those satisfied with right conduct, and the splendor even of the splendid. (42)
He who is the body of all bodies and the goal even of those who possess a goal;
from space arises wind, and fire has wind as its life-breath.
During the day, the vital breaths became the fire; the life-force of the fire was Madhusūdana.
From that, essence (rasa) became blood, and from blood, flesh is said to arise.
From flesh arises fat, and from fat bone is produced;
from bone marrow comes into being, and from marrow the production of semen occurs. (45)
From the semen, the embryo was produced through action rooted in the vital essence;
therein, water comes first, and that is called the lunar mansion. (46)
The second aggregate is said to be known as arising from the heat of the womb;
one should know that the semen is of the nature of the moon, while the menstrual blood is of the nature of fire. 47.
These two states follow the flavors; the moon and fire reside in the potency (vīrya).
Semen belongs to the category of phlegm (kapha), and blood belongs to the category of bile (pitta). 48.
The heart is the seat of phlegm (kapha), and bile (pitta) is established in the navel;
the heart, situated in the middle of the body, is remembered as the seat of the mind (manas). 49.
That which is the space between the navel and the stomach is where the god Hutāśana (Fire) resides;
the mind is to be known as Prajāpati, and phlegm is perceived as Soma.
Bile is known as fire; thus the world consists of the nature of fire and moon.
Thus set in motion, the embryo develops like a cloud. (51)
The vital air (vāyu), united with the Supreme Self, performed the act of entering;
abiding within the body in fivefold ways, it exists and causes [the elements] to increase once again. ||52||
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—prāṇa, increasing the supreme self (paramātman), circulates throughout him. ||53||
Apāna moves through the posterior part of the body, udāna resides in the upper part of the body;
vyāna is that by which [the breath] is distributed throughout, while samāna is located in all the joints. (54)
From that, his attainment of the elements arises as objects of the senses:
earth, air, space, water, and light as the fifth. (55)
All the senses entered him and each performed its own function;
they called that the earthly body and the vital breath the self of life (prāṇātman). ||56||
The apertures have space as their source, and the flow of water proceeds from them; the light in the eyes is the moonlight, which is known by its name;
and the battles and the objects of the senses were set in motion by his power.
How is it that Viṣṇu, the eternal Puruṣa who created all these worlds, has attained the state of a human in this mortal world? (58)
O wise one, this is our doubt; this is indeed a great wonder:
how has he, who is the refuge of those who seek refuge, assumed a human body? (59)
We desire to hear the deeds of Viṣṇu in their proper sequence;
for Viṣṇu is said to be the supreme wonder by all the gods and the Vedas.
O high-minded one, tell us the wonderful account of Viṣṇu’s birth;
let this marvelous narrative, which brings happiness, be related.
Let the nature of Viṣṇu— the Great Soul, whose power and heroism are renowned, who has manifested in this world, and whose deeds are wonderful— be described here.
Sūta said:
And I shall proclaim the manifestation of that Great-Souled One—
how that Blessed One, of great ascetic power, was born among human beings.
It is said that there are seventy-seven types of asceticism; by the curse of Bhṛgu, one is born as a human being at the end of the ages for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
Listen as I describe to you that divine form of Viṣṇu:
when the dharma of the age has turned away and time has become lax, the Lord [acts].
The establishment of the Dharma among human beings here occurs due to the cause of Bhṛgu’s curse and through the actions of the gods and asuras. (66)
The sages said:
How might one obtain victory over the gods and asuras?
We wish to know this: how did the conflict between the gods and asuras unfold? (67)
Sūta said:
Listen as I relate how that conflict between the gods and the asuras occurred;
formerly, the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu ruled over the three worlds.
The kingdom was governed by Bali, and subsequently, throughout the three worlds,
there arose a supreme friendship between those gods and the asuras.
Indeed, that age was uncorrupted by the ten vices, and the world was free from obstruction;
both the gods and the asuras remained obedient to their commands.
Indeed, this powerful and most terrible dispute has now broken out;
it is a great conflict between the gods and the asuras that causes horrific destruction.
Indeed, for the sake of their inheritance, many battles occurred;
in this Vārāha Kalpa, twelve [kalpas] are recorded as following Ṣaṇḍa and Mārka.
Listen now, in brief, as I intend to speak of them by name:
the first is Nārasiṃha, and the second is Vāmana. (73)
The third was indeed the Vārāha battle, the fourth was the churning for nectar (Amṛtamandhana), and the fifth was the most terrible battle, the Tārakāmaya.
For the sixth among them was Āḍībaka, the seventh is remembered as Traipura;
Andhakāra was the eighth among them, and Dhvaja is remembered as the ninth. ||75||
The tenth is to be known as Vārtta; after that, Hālāhala is remembered.
The twelfth among them is remembered, and another is Ghorakolāhala. (76)
The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by Narasiṃha;
Bali was bound by Vāmana when he performed the conquest of the three worlds. (77)
Hiraṇyākṣa, who was of great strength and great courage, undefeated in battles, was slain in single combat by the gods in their dispute. (78)
When the earth was raised from the ocean by the boar with his tusk, and when Prahlāda was defeated in battle by Indra during the churning for the nectar of immortality; 79.
Virocana, the son of Prahlāda, was constantly intent on slaying Indra;
however, he was overcome by Indra himself and slain during the Tārakāmaya war.
In the sixth [chapter], Saṃjaya, having attained invincibility from Bhava, was slain by Viṣṇu, who had entered into Śakra, using special weapons and other means.
Being unable to protect the city of Tripura, which had three deities as its guardians, among the gods,
all the Dānavas were slain by Tryambaka.
In the eighth [kalpa], however, the Asuras and the darkness-bringing Rākṣasas,
having conquered the gods and humans, joined together with the Pitṛs.
All those Dānavas who had assembled together were likewise completely destroyed by Mahendra, with Viṣṇu as his ally.
His banner was struck down by Mahendra while he fought concealed by illusion;
having fixed his aim upon the banner, the mighty-armed Vipravarti fell. (85)
Raji, surrounded by the gods, defeated all those Daityas and Dānavas together in their entirety at Kolāhala; however,
Ṣaṇḍa and Mārka were conquered by the deities through the nectar of sacrifice.
These twelve battles between the gods and the asuras have indeed occurred;
they caused the destruction of both gods and asuras and brought misfortune to all creatures.
King Hiraṇyakaśipu shone for one hundred million years (an arbuda), as well as seventy-two hundred thousand and eighty thousand more; he was the lord of the three worlds. (88)
In succession, King Bali again [ruled] for a hundred crores of years, as well as sixty thousand and thirty million years.
For as long as Bali held the authority of sovereignty,
for that same length of time it was held by Prahlāda and the Asuras.
Those three Indrāstras were renowned among the Asuras of great power;
indeed, for ten yugas, this entire world remained under the dominion of the Daityas.
Consequently, for ten yugas in the past, this entire kingdom was free from rivals;
indeed, this imperishable triple world is protected by Mahendra.
Then, by the turn of time, the three worlds came to belong to Prahlāda; and when the three worlds had come to him in due succession, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, [regained them].
Then, having abandoned the Asuras, the gods approached the sacrifice.
When the gods had thus gone to the sacrifice, those Asuras spoke to Kāvya. (94)
While we looked on, our kingdom was ruined; having abandoned the sacrifice, they have departed again.
Indeed, we are unable to remain here today; we shall enter the netherworld.
Thus addressed, he spoke to them, dejected yet consoling them with his voice:
"Do not fear, O Asuras; I shall sustain you by my own splendor."
Rain, the herbs, the tastes, and whatever wealth exists—all these abide entirely within me, yet their fourth part indeed resides in the gods.
For your sake, I shall bestow all of that; it is sustained by me.
Then, seeing the gods and asuras held in check by the wise Kāvya, they,
agitated by their desire for victory, took counsel together.
"This Kāvya forcibly turns all this of ours away.
Let us go quickly; replenish those whose food is exhausted.
Having violently slain the survivors, let us indeed send them to Pātāla. (99)
Then the gods, highly incensed, rushed toward the Dānavas and slew them; being slaughtered by them, the Dānavas fled toward Kāvya himself.
Then Kāvya, seeing those sons of Diti being swiftly pursued by the gods in battle, protected them who were distressed from the gods.
Having seen the gods standing there, the god Kāvya reflected;
then, having meditated and recollecting former events, he spoke to them. (102)
The entire triple world was conquered by Vāmana with three strides;
Bali was bound, Jambha was slain, and Virocana was struck down. (103)
In twelve great battles, they were slain by the gods;
those who were most prominent were killed by various means in great numbers.
Since you indeed remain as a small remnant in these final battles, I myself shall provide you with counsel; wait for a certain time. (105)
"I shall go to Mahādeva for the sake of your victory through the power of mantras;
let the Hotṛ priest Bṛhaspati nourish the fire with mantras alone. (106)
"Therefore, O God, I shall go to the blue-and-red deity for the sake of counsel;
having returned here later, I will bestow my grace upon you once more. (107)
"Perform ascetic penance indeed, clothed in bark garments in the forest;
the gods will certainly not slay you until my return. (108)
Then, having obtained from the god Maheśvara mantras that are irresistible, we shall fight the gods again; thereafter, you shall indeed attain victory.
Then, having reached an agreement, those asuras said to the gods:
"We have all renounced our claims; you may indeed proceed through the worlds."
"Having heard those words of Prahlāda, which were a declaration of truth, we shall practice austerities in the forest, clothed in bark garments. (111)
Then the gods, indeed free from fever and joyful, withdrew;
once the Daityas had laid down their weapons, they returned each to his own place as he had come.
Then Kāvya said to them:
"Wait for some time, remaining free from anxiety, devoted to austerity, and intent on accomplishing your purpose;
for all the gods, including Vāsava, are indeed staying in my father’s hermitage. (113)
Having thus instructed the Asuras and having sought refuge with Mahādeva,
Kāvya then bowed down and spoke to the Lord, the source of the world.
"O God, I desire the mantras that exist with Bṛhaspati;
they bring fearlessness to the Asuras and lead to the defeat of the gods. (115)
Thus addressed, the god said: "O twice-born one, you truly desire the mantras;
perform the vow prescribed by me, remaining composed as a celibate student. (116)
"If you attend upon Kuṇḍadhūma with your head hanging downwards for a full thousand years—blessings be upon you—you shall obtain the mantra from me. (117)
Thus addressed by the God of gods, that Śukra of great asceticism touched the feet of the God and replied, "So be it. (118)
"O Lord, I shall perform the remaining vow exactly as I have been instructed.
Then, appointed by the God, Kuṇḍadhāra became his provider of smoke.
When Śukra had departed for the sake of the Asuras,
Maheśvara then dwelt there in celibacy for the purpose of [learning] the mantras.
Having learned that the kingdom had been laid down by the Asuras not long before,
the gods, led by Bṛhaspati and all bearing sharpened weapons, rushed toward them in that interval out of indignation.
Seeing the hosts of gods once again with their weapons raised, all the asuras suddenly sprang up and became terrified.
When victory had been granted and the weapons laid down, and while he remained firm in his vow as a teacher, those gods, desiring to slay their rival, abandoned their agreement. (123)
But those who have no teacher—blessings upon you—remain confident, established in austerity, wearing rags, bark, and skins, free from ritual action, and without possessions. (124)
"We shall certainly not be able to conquer the gods in battle by any means;
therefore, being impure, we seek refuge with the mother of Kāvya. (125)
We shall inform him of this matter until the arrival of our preceptor;
once the composition has been completed, we shall then fight those gods in battle.
Having spoken thus to the gods, they then, being terrified, sought refuge with Kāvya’s mother, who was the worthy protector and the source of fearlessness.
To those Daityas who were terrified and seeking freedom from fear, he granted [this]:
"Do not fear, do not fear! Cast away your fear, O Dānavas! (128)
"Let it be that you remain in my presence; there should be no fear for you.
Then, seeing those gods and asuras overwhelmed by fear," (129)
They attacked these [gods] by force, without considering their relative strength;
then, seeing those asuras terrified and being slaughtered by the gods.
The goddess, enraged, said to them, "I shall deprive him of his Indrahood.
Then, having quickly paralyzed Indra out of her fury, she performed rites against him.
Then, seeing Śakra paralyzed like a sacrificial pillar,
the gods fled in terror upon seeing Śakra brought under control.
When the hosts of gods had departed, Viṣṇu spoke to Indra:
"Enter me; may it be well with you; I shall carry you away, O Lord of the Gods. (133)
Having been addressed thus, Purandara then entered Viṣṇu.
Seeing him protected by Viṣṇu, the Goddess became enraged and spoke these words. (134)
"I shall burn you along with Viṣṇu, just as Maghavan [burned Vṛtra], while all beings look on; behold the power of my asceticism! (135)
Overwhelmed by her, those two gods, Indra and Viṣṇu, conversed; how might we two be released together? Viṣṇu spoke to Indra. (136)
Indra said: "O powerful one, slay her before she consumes us both;
for I am especially overwhelmed by her, and so are you—do not delay! (137)
Then, having observed her, Viṣṇu resolved to slay the woman; thereupon, the Lord, reflecting upon it, quickly took up his discus.

As she was hurrying away, Viṣṇu, the slayer of the enemies of the gods and swift-acting Mādhava, perceiving the cruel deed the goddess intended to do, became enraged; having brandished his weapon, he severed her head. (139)
Seeing that terrible slaughter of his wife, Bhṛgu, the lord, was enraged;
then Viṣṇu was cursed by Bhṛgu for the killing of his wife.
Since you, knowing the dharmas to be inviolable, have destroyed a woman, therefore you shall indeed enter among human beings seven times. (141)
Then, when dharma has been destroyed again and again by that curse,
he is born here among humans for the sake of the welfare of the entire world.
Having addressed Viṣṇu and personally taken that head, he then brought it to the body; taking up water, he spoke as follows: ||143||
I shall restore you to life, though you were slain by Viṣṇu in truth. If my entire dharma is known to have been practiced by me, by that truth do you live, if indeed I speak the truth! (144)
When the truth was uttered, the goddess was then restored to life;
having sprinkled her with cool waters, he said, "Live! (145).
Then, seeing her as if she had just awakened from sleep, all beings and the invisible voices of the quarters cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! (146).
Having seen the queen thus restored to life by Bhṛgu at that time, while all beings looked on, it was like a miracle. (147)
Then, seeing his wife restored to life by the unperturbed Bhṛgu,
Śakra found no peace thereafter due to his fear of Kāvya.
Then, while awake, the wise Indra, the subduer of Pāka, spoke these words to his own daughter Jayantī: ||149||
"For this Kāvya is performing a severe penance for the sake of one who is not Indra;
by him, my daughter, I have been made deeply agitated despite my firm resolve. (2.35.150)
Go and attend upon him with auspicious means of removing fatigue, and with various services that are agreeable to his mind, remaining ever vigilant. (151)
That goddess Jayantī, the daughter of Indra, who moves with auspicious conduct, [beheld] him—steadfast in meditation, tranquil, weak, and established in fortitude. ||152||
Then she, speaking with charming words, praised Kāvya with agreeable speech, performing exactly as her father had instructed.
Massaging his limbs at the proper times with pleasant treatments, serving him and acting in accordance with his wishes, she lived there for many years. (154)
When the terrible smoke-vow of a thousand years was completed, he,
being pleased, then invited Kāvya to choose a boon.
"Since you alone have practiced this and no one else,
therefore, by virtue of your austerity, intelligence, learning, and power," (156)
And by your splendor, O Brahmin, you shall surpass all the gods;
whatever belongs to me, O descendant of Bhrigu, shall be yours.
Along with its limbs, its secret doctrines, and likewise the Upaniṣads of sacrifice—
all that shall be revealed to you, and it shall be without beginning or end for anyone else.
"By that, you shall become a conqueror of all, O best of the twice-born.
Having thus granted these boons to that descendant of Bhṛgu again and again, [he departed]. (159)
He granted him invincibility, lordship over wealth, and indeed immunity from being slain;
having obtained these boons, Kāvya’s hair stood on end with great joy.
Out of joy, a hymn to the Great Lord (Maheśvara) manifested within him;
then, while remaining in a horizontal position, he thus praised Nīlalohita.
Homage be to the blue-throated one, the drinker of wine, the resplendent, the licking one, the devourer, the year, the Lord of the World! 162.

Salutations to the one with matted hair, to the one with upward-pointing body hair, to the horse, to the creator, to the consecrated one, to the one of excellent sacred sites, to the god of gods, and to impetuous speed.
To the one with the protuberance on the head, to the one with beautiful curves, to the thousand-eyed, to the bountiful,
to Rudra who possesses the wealth of seed, to the ascetic heat, and to the one clothed in bark.
And to Hrasva, Muktakeśa, Senānī, and Rohita. ||165||
To the poet, the elder of kings, and the plaything of Takṣaka;
to the dweller on the mountain, the sun-eyed one, and the ascetic Jāmbava;
to the one of excellent conduct, the fair-handed one, the archer, and the descendant of Bhṛgu. ||166||
To the one with a thousand arms, to the one with a thousand stainless eyes, to the one with a thousand bellies, and to the one with a thousand feet. ||167||
And to the thousand-headed one, to the multiform creator, to Bhava, to the universal-formed, to the white one, and to Puruṣa. ||168||
To the one armed with a quiver, to the one clad in armor, to the subtle one, and to the destroyer;
to the copper-colored one, to the terrible one, to the fierce one, and to the auspicious one.
And to Babhru, to Piśaṅga, to Piṅgala, and to Aruṇa;
to Mahādeva, to Śarva, and to Viśvarūpa-Śiva. ||2.35.170||
To Hiraṇya, to Śiṣṭa, to Śreṣṭha, and to Madhyama; to Pinākin, to Iṣumat, to Citra, and to Rohita. ||171||
To Dundubhya, to Ekapāda, to Arhat, and likewise to Buddha;
to Mṛgavyādha, to Sarpa, to Sthāṇu, and to Bhīṣaṇa. ||172||
To the one of many forms, to the fierce one, to the three-eyed Lord, to the tawny one, to the solitary hero, to Death, and to the three-eyed one. ||173||

O Lord of the Dwelling, for the one who is without a home, for the bringer of joy, for the auspicious one, for the forest-dweller, for the one abiding in the cave, for the ascetic, and for the student of sacred knowledge. ||174||
To Sāṅkhya, to Yoga, to the meditator, and to the initiated; to the hidden Śarva, to the venerable one, and likewise to Mālin. ||175||
To the Buddha, the meritorious, the righteous, and the auspicious;
to Rodhasa, the wise, the most devoted to Brahman, the great seer.
To the four-footed, the pure, the possessor of dharma, and the swift-moving;
to the crested one, the skull-bearer, the fanged one, and the universal sacrifice.
To the unimpeded, the radiant, the sun-like, the wise, to the fierce, the deformed, the loathsome, and to Śiva. ||178||
To the gentle one, the meritorious, the righteous, and the auspicious;
to the one who is not to be slain, whose limbs are mortal, and who is eternal and everlasting. ||179||
Salutations to the one who is like a śarabha, to the trident-bearer, to the three-eyed one;
to the drinker of soma, the drinker of clarified butter, the drinker of smoke, and the drinker of heat.
To the Pure One, to the Licking One, to the Newly Born, to Death, to the Flesh-eater, to the Dwarf, to Medha, and to the Lightning-like One. ||181||
To him who is supported by the quarters, who is the refuge of the Śraviṣṭhas, who belongs to the Bharatas, who dwells in the intermediate space;
to him who is forgiveness, who possesses endurance, who is truth, and who is the sun. ||182||
To the destroyer of Tripura, to the radiant one, to the wielder of the discus, to the hairy one;
to the one with sharp weapons, to the pure one, to the perfected one, and to Pulastya.
To Rocamāna, Khaṇḍa, Sphīta, and Ṛṣabha;
to Bhogin, Puñjamāna, Śānta, and indeed to Ūrdhvaretas.
To Aghaghna, to Makhaghna, to Mṛtyu, and to Yajñiya;
to Kṛśānu, to Pracetas, to Vahni, and to Kiśala. ||185||
To Sikatya, to Prasanna, to Vareṇya, to Cakṣus, to Kṣipraga, to Sudhanvan, to Pramadhya, and to Priya. ||186||
To the slayer of Rākṣasas, to the slayer of animals, to the obstacle-maker, and to the one who lies down;
to the bewildered, to the great, to the end-maker, and to the one difficult to traverse. ||187||
And to Dakṣa, and to Jaghanya, and to the Lord of the worlds; and to Anāmaya, and to Ūrdhva, and to him who is established by means of concentration. ||188||
And to Hiraṇyabāhu, to Satya, and to Śamana;
to Asikalya, to Māgha, to Rīriṇya, and to Ekacakṣus. ||189||
To Śreṣṭha, Vāmadeva, and the wise Īśāna;
to Mahākalpa, Dīpta, Rādena, and Hasa.
To the one who wields a drawn bow, who possesses wisdom, who is a chariot-warrior, and who has a protective shield;
to the Lord of the Bhṛgus, to Śukra, to the wise one who is cherished by Agni. ||191||

Salutations be to you, who are the destroyer of Bhaga, who are clothed in the directions and clad in animal skins, and who are both the source of misfortune and the destroyer of misfortune, both the unpleasant and the beloved. 192.
Salutations to the Lord of beasts and to the Lord of beings;
salutations to the breath, to the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and to Svadhā and Sudhā.
Salutations to you, the most worthy of the *vaṣaṭ* call, the inner self; salutations to the creator, the sustainer, the invoker, the destroyer, and the one who brings about dissolution. (194)
Salutations to you, the self of time, for the sake of the past, the future, and the present;
and salutations to the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Aśvins.
Salutations to you, O Viśva and Marut, who are the very self of the gods;
salutations to the fire, the moon, the officiating priest, the sacrifice, the sacrificial animal, the mantra, and the medicinal herb.
Salutations to you, whose essence is sacrifice, for whom the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) is the sacrificial fee; salutations to austerity, truth, renunciation, and tranquility. (197)
Salutations to you, whose self is yoga, who are non-violence, freedom from greed, beautiful attire, and supreme excellence, and who have become the very self of all beings. 198.
Salutation to you, the soul of the worlds: to the earth, the intermediate space, and the heavens; to the great realm, and to Janas, Tapas, and Satya. ||199||

Salutations to you, the unmanifest, and to the great element, and to the sense-faculty; salutations to you, the Great One, the essence of the subtle elements, whose nature is the fundamental principles (tattva). 2.35.200.
Salutations to you, the eternal self, who are constant, indicated by the purpose [of the world], subtle, conscious, pure, and all-pervading power. ||201||
Salutations to you who exist within the three worlds, from Svara down to Bhava;
salutations be to you who are present in the four [worlds], from Satya down to Mahat. 202.

"O All-pervading Lord, O Friend of Brahman, whatever has been spoken by me in this hymn of praise— whether true or false— you ought to forgive it all, for you are my devotee. Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of Śambhu’s Praise," in the Viṣṇu-māhātmya of the glorious Vāyu Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
Having thus propitiated Īśāna, the Lord of Gods, who is blue-and-red (Nīlalohita),
Brahmā bowed down before him with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words.
Having touched the body of the poem with his hand, the joyful Bhava granted him a full vision and vanished right there.
Then, when that attendant of the Lord of Gods had vanished, he stood with palms joined in reverence and spoke these words to Jayantī: ||3||
Whose [daughter] are you, O fortunate one? Or who are you that you grieve when I am grieving?
For what purpose do you conceal me, who am endowed with great ascetic power? (4)
O lady of beautiful hips, O woman of excellent complexion, I am constantly pleased by this devotion, humility, self-restraint, and affection. (5)
"What do you desire, O most excellent of women? What wish of yours may be fulfilled?
I shall fulfill it for you today, even if it should be very difficult to attain. (6)
Thus addressed, she said to him: "O Brahman, you ought to know my intention through your ascetic power, for you know it exactly as it is."
When this was said, he looked upon her with his divine eye and spoke to her:
"O lady of beautiful hips, you are the daughter of Mahendra; you have come here for my benefit."
"O lady of beautiful hips, O passionate one, you desire to enjoy union with me here for ten years, remaining invisible to all living beings. (9)
"O lady of beautiful hips and lovely eyes, possessing a complexion like that of the lord of the gods or fire,
choose this desire from me, O sweet-spoken one!"
"Let it be so; let us go home, O intoxicated one.
Then the Lord, having arrived at his own home together with Jayantī, [remained there]. (11)
He lived with that goddess for ten years, divided by portions,
invisible to all beings, then concealed by his illusory power (māyā).
Seeing Kāvya arrive having accomplished his purpose, all the sons of Diti, joyful and desiring to see him, went to his house. (13)
When they departed and no longer saw their preceptor concealed by Jayantī,
they realized his courtesy and returned the way they had come.
But Bṛhaspati, knowing that Kāvya was confined,
acted for ten years on behalf of his father, out of a desire for the welfare of Jayantī.
Then, perceiving that vulnerability and as if impelled by the Daityas themselves,
he assumed the form of Kāvya and addressed the Asuras.
Then, seeing them assembled, Bṛhaspati said to them: "Welcome! I have arrived for the benefit of my patrons. (17)
"I shall teach you, for that knowledge has indeed been attained by me.
Thereupon, with joyful minds, they approached him for the sake of learning.
Then, at that time of the ten-year [festival], Pūrṇakāma departed; and at that very same moment, Sadyotpannamati likewise set out. (19)
At the end of the sacrificial session, a daughter was then immediately born to Devayānī;
she then set her mind upon the supervision of those for whom sacrifices were to be performed.
Śukra said:
"O Goddess of radiant smiles, O virtuous lady with wandering glances and large eyes of three colors, let us go to see those for whom you perform sacrifices. (21)
Thus addressed, the goddess said: "O observer of great vows, favor your devotees!
O Brahmin, this is the duty of the virtuous; I do not cause your dharma to be violated."
Sūta said:
Then, having gone there and seen the asuras, the wise preceptor of the gods, the creator in the form of Kāvya, spoke to the asura who had been deceived: ||23||
"O dear ones, know me to be Kāvya; for I am indeed Aṅgiras on this earth.
Alas, O Dānavas, you have been deceived while I was capable! (24)
Having heard him speaking thus, the sons of Diti were then bewildered;
they gazed upon both of them there, who possessed white and dark complexions and pure smiles.
All remained utterly bewildered and attained no understanding whatsoever;
then, while they were thus confounded, Kāvya spoke to them again.
"For I am your teacher, the son of Kavi; this Aṅgiras is the teacher of the gods.
Follow me all of you, and abandon this Bṛhaspati! ||27||
When this was said, all the asuras gazed intently at those two Ṛbhus;
however, at that time, the asuras could not distinguish any difference between the two of them.
Bṛhaspati said: "O Daityas, this Aṅgiras is not bewildered; I am Kāvya, who am your preceptor. This Bṛhaspati is merely my likeness. (29)
"O Asuras, this one deludes you with my form.
Having heard his words, they indeed consulted together and spoke these meaningful words.
For ten years this lord has indeed ruled continuously;
this twice-born man is our preceptor, yet he desires our downfall. (31)
Then all those Dānavas, having prostrated and offered salutations,
accepted his words, being deluded by long-standing habituation.
All the asuras, enraged and with eyes bloodshot, said to him:
"This man is our benefactor; go away, you are not our teacher. (33)
"Let this man be either a descendant of Bhṛgu or of Aṅgiras; he shall indeed be our preceptor.
We remain under his command, so go, do not delay. (34)
Having spoken thus, all the asuras approached Bṛhaspati; when they did not accept what he had said, which was for their great benefit, [they departed]. (35)
Then Bhārgava became enraged at their arrogance, saying:
"O Dānavas, since you have been warned by me yet do not resort to me. (36)
"Therefore, having lost your senses, you shall surely meet with defeat.
Having spoken thus to them, Kāvya then departed as he had come.
Having learned that the Asuras had been cursed by Kāvya, Bṛhaspati,
having achieved his purpose, was then delighted and resumed his own form;
realizing that the Asuras were now fallen, he, having accomplished his aim, vanished from sight.
Then, when he had vanished, those Dānavas became bewildered and said to one another, "Alas! Woe! We have been deceived here. (39)
We have been turned away and struck from behind by the Creator; we have been burnt by his employment of illusion regarding our respective purposes.
Then the Asuras, terrified of the gods, fled in haste,
placing Prahlāda at their head and following Kāvya once again.
Then, having approached Kāvya, they stood facing him;
seeing them returned, Kāvya spoke again to his patrons.
Since you did not welcome me when I awakened you at the proper time,
you have therefore fallen into defeat because of that very arrogance.
Prahlāda then said to him: "O Bhārgava, abandon your pride toward those who are your own patrons, those who serve you, and especially your devotees. (44)
We have been questioned by you and deluded by that preceptor of the gods;
knowing this with your far-reaching vision, you ought to protect us, your devotees. 45.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, if you do not show us favor,
then being cursed by you today, we shall enter the netherworld.
Sūta said:
Having understood the truth as it is, Kāvya, out of compassion and pity, spoke thus;
being thus addressed, entreated, and praised, he restrained his anger. (47)
He said this: "Do not fear; you must not go to the netherworld (rasātala).
For this event was destined to happen, and it has come upon you even while I am awake."
It is not possible to act otherwise, for what has been seen is most powerful;
though your consciousness is lost today, you shall surely regain it.
"The time for the succession has arrived," Brahmā declared;
"and by my grace, you have enjoyed the powerful three worlds."
Having ascended to the heads of the gods for the full duration of ten yugas,
Brahmā likewise ruled the kingdom for that same length of time.
Furthermore, it is said that your kingdom will belong to Sāvarṇika;
moreover, your grandson Bali shall become the lord of the worlds. (52)
Thus, indeed, I was addressed by Brahmā himself: "O grandson, even though the worlds have been withdrawn in this manner, his asceticism did not cease. (53)
Since his activities were not motivated by desires,
therefore he was given [the kingdom] by the pleased Aja during the Sāvarṇika interval.
"The lord told me that Bali shall possess the sovereignty of the gods;
therefore, he remains invisible to all beings, awaiting his time. (55)
"Out of affection, immortality was indeed granted to you by the Self-born One;
therefore, why are you so despondent and agitated regarding this turn of events? (56)
"O Lord, it is not possible for me to approach you;
I have been forbidden by Brahmā, who knows what is to come. (57)
And these two disciples of mine are equal to Bṛhaspati;
they shall sustain all of you when you are provoked by the gods. (58)
Thus addressed by Kāvya, whose deeds are effortless,
the sons of Diti then departed together with those two, led by Prahlāda.
Having heard from Śukra that the matter was inevitable, the Dānavas,
placing their hope for victory solely upon what had been spoken by Kāvya, waited expectantly.
All of them, armored and equipped with weapons, then challenged the gods.
Then, seeing the gods and asuras standing ready for battle, [the Lord spoke].

Then the gods, having donned their armor, fought them. During that war between the gods and the asuras which lasted for a hundred years, the asuras defeated the gods; the vanquished gods held a consultation.
The gods said:
We do not know the power of Ṣaṇḍāmārka, even by the gods;
therefore, for the sake of the sacrifice and whatever is for our own benefit, [we must act]. 63.
"Having deprived these two of that knowledge, we shall conquer the asuras.
Then the gods entreated both Śaṇḍa and Mārka.
"O twice-born ones, we shall summon you at the sacrifice; do not abandon the Asuras!
Having conquered the Dānavas, we shall indeed seize that cup. (65)
Thus, Śaṇḍa and Mārka abandoned those Asuras;
then the gods attained victory and the Dānavas met with defeat.
Having defeated the gods and asuras, they approached Śaṇḍa and Mārka;
yet, overcome by the curse of Kāvya and deprived of their support, they were once again [defeated].
Being slain by the gods, they then entered the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Thus were those Dānavas rendered devoid of effort by Śakra through the curse occasioned by Bhṛgu. From that time forward, they remained so due to that curse.
The Lord Viṣṇu was born again and again whenever sacrifice became slackened,
in order to establish righteousness and to destroy unrighteousness.
The Lord Brahmā declared that all those Asuras who did not abide by the command of Prahlāda were to be slain by humans.
From that Dharma, Nārāyaṇa was born during the Cākṣuṣa interval;
he then set forth the sacrifice at the Caitya during the Vaivasvata interval.
At that time, upon the manifestation of another [incarnation], Brahmā alone was the domestic priest;
then, during the fourth age known as the Kali Yuga, when the Asuras had come into being.
Having arisen within the ocean for the sake of slaying Hiraṇyakaśipu,
he became the second Narasiṃha, Rudra, the leader of the gods.
When the worlds were situated in Bali and the third Yuga was in its seventh cycle,
the third incarnation, Vāmana, appeared as the three worlds were assailed by the Daityas.
Having contracted his body into his limbs with Bṛhaspati at the forefront,
the delighter of Aditi’s lineage,
having become a twice-born brahmin, formerly approached Bali, the son of Virocana and lord of the Daityas, at an auspicious time.
"You are the king of the three worlds; everything is established in you.
O King, it behooves you, as lord, to grant me three strides," [said] the Lord.
"I give," King Bali, the son of Virocana, said to him;
and having recognized him as the dwarf, he himself was then filled with joy. (77)
O best of the twice-born, that Lord Vāmana traversed this entire universe—both heaven and the intermediate space, as well as the earth—with three strides. (78)
The Greatly Renowned One, the soul of all beings, surpassed the sun with his own splendor, illuminating all the cardinal and intermediate directions. (79)
Having seized the splendor of the Asuras and the three worlds, that mighty-armed Janārdana shone forth, illuminating all the worlds;
he sent the Asuras, along with their sons and grandsons, down to the depths of Pātāla.
Namuci, Śambara, and Prahlāda—these cruel ones were slain and driven away by Viṣṇu, and they fled in all directions. (81)
Mādhava displayed there the great elements, the elemental self along with its specific qualities, time in its entirety, and the brahmins—a truly wondrous sight. (82)
He perceives the entire world within his own body;
there is nothing in the worlds that is not pervaded by that Great-Souled One. (83)
Indeed, upon seeing that form of Upendra, all the gods, dānavas, and humans were utterly bewildered, stupefied by the splendor of Viṣṇu. ||84||
Bali, along with Sili, his kinsmen, and his circle of friends, as well as the entire lineage of Virocana, was cast down into Pātāla by means of great nooses. (85)
Then, having bestowed the sovereignty over all the immortals upon the high-souled Indra,
the mighty-armed Janārdana appeared among human beings.
These three are known as his auspicious, divine births;
now learn of his seven human births, which arose from curses. 87.
In the tenth Tretā Yuga,
when Dharma had perished, Dattātreya appeared as the fourth [avatāra], preceded by Mārkaṇḍeya.
The fifth [incarnation] appeared during the fifteenth Tretā age;
he stood at the forefront of Māndhātṛ’s universal sovereignty as his counselor. ||89||
In the twenty-first [cycle], during the Tretā Yuga, there was one who became the destroyer of all the Kṣatriyas;
likewise, the sixth was the son of Jamadagni, preceded by Viśvāmitra.
In the twenty-fourth yuga, Rāma, the seventh [incarnation], was born as the son of Daśaratha with Vasiṣṭha as his domestic priest, for the sake of Rāvaṇa.
In the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, Viṣṇu became the eighth [incarnation] as Vedavyāsa, born from Parāśara,
preceded by Jātūkarṇa.
In that very same way, the ninth Viṣṇu, the son of Kaśyapa and Aditi,
[was born] from Vasudeva and Devakī, preceded by Brahmā and Gārgya.
Immeasurable and one who can be directed, yet moving according to his will as a master, the Blessed One plays in the world like a child with his toys. 94.
This mighty-armed Madhusūdana cannot be measured;
there exists nothing higher than this supreme form of the universe. 95.
Likewise, in the twenty-eighth cycle, when the remnants of the Dvāpara age had diminished and dharma had perished, the Lord Viṣṇu was born in the Vṛṣṇi clan.
In order to establish the system of dharma and to destroy the asuras,
he whose self is yoga deluded all beings by means of his yogic illusion.
Having entered a human womb, he wanders the earth in disguise for the sake of diversion among men,
with Sāndīpani at his head.
Therein [he slew] Kaṃsa, Śālva, and the great asura Dvivida;
Ariṣṭa and Vṛṣabha, Pūtanā, and the horse Keśin. (99)
The valiant one slew the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, the lord of the city of the king of wrestlers, as well as the Daityas dwelling within human bodies.
The thousand arms of Bāṇa, the performer of wondrous deeds, were severed;
Naraka was slain in battle, as was the exceedingly powerful Yavana.
All the jewels of the kings were seized by his splendor,
and those kings of evil conduct who resided in the subterranean realm (rasātala) were slain.
These manifestations of the Great-Souled One for the sake of the welfare of the world will occur when this very age has declined and is joined with the twilight period. ||103||
The tenth incarnation, known as Kalki Viṣṇuyaśas, will be born as the son of Parāśara; he will be endowed with great prowess and will be preceded by Yājñavalkya. 104.
Leading an entire army teeming with elephants, horses, and chariots, he was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of Brahmins who held weapons in their hands. (105)

Those who are excessively righteous and those who are anywhere haters of the Dharma, [as well as those from] the northern regions, the Middle Country, and likewise the areas beyond the Vindhya mountains—[all these shall be subdued]. (106)
Likewise, he [subdued] the southerners and the Dravidians along with the Siṃhalas, as well as the Gāndhāras, Pāradas, Pahlavas, Yavanas, and Śakas. ||107||
That lord [subdued] the Tuṣāras, the Barbaras, the Pulindas, the Daradas, the Khasas, the Lampākas, the Andhakas, the Rudras, and the Kirātas.
Powerful, possessing the strength of one who has set his wheel in motion, a mighty destroyer of the Mlecchas, he will wander the earth invisible to all beings. (109)
That man was born from a portion of the wise god;
he who in a previous birth was the powerful Viṣṇu named Pramiti.
In the full Kali Yuga, he indeed became equal to the moon in stature;
these are remembered as the ten manifestations of that deity. ||111||
According to each specific time and purpose, and for various reasons directed toward those ends,
he shall enter into various wombs throughout the three worlds by means of his partial manifestations.
In the twenty-fifth eon, for twenty-five years indeed,
he slaughtered all beings, including humans, in every way.
Having, through cruel deeds, reduced the earth to nothing but seeds,
he caused those mostly unrighteous Vṛṣalas to be utterly destroyed.
Then, at that time, Kalki, having accomplished his purpose, together with his army,
[will see] those who were slain by his deeds, but who were perfected ones (siddhas), [return] of their own accord.
Deluded, they will suddenly become angry with one another;
and having destroyed all those who were incited by the meaning of the *Bāvinī*, [they shall perish].
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, he shall attain his final end along with his followers;
thereafter, when Kalki has passed away, together with his ordinary soldiers.
Then, when the kings had perished, the subjects were left without a protector;
and since protection had ceased, they began slaying one another in battle.
With their mutual consolations gone, without anyone to cry out for them, and deeply distressed, they abandoned their cities and villages; like those [wanderers], they were now without possessions.
Those who have lost the sacred scriptures and the Dharma, as well as those for whom the duties and stages of life have perished,
being short in stature and short-lived— these are known as forest-dwellers (vanaukas).
Frequenting rivers and mountains, subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits,
wearing rags, leaves, and deerskins, they have entered into a terrible state of confusion.
Short-lived, their livelihoods ruined, beset by many ailments and deeply distressed—
thus did they fall into such misery during that period of the Kali-sandhyamsha.
The people will go to destruction along with the Kali age;
when that Kali age has waned and the Kṛta age has set in again.
They will attain [their goals] according to the proper rule through their own nature alone, and not otherwise;
thus has all this activity of the gods and asuras been proclaimed. 124.
"In connection with the lineage of Yadu, your great Vaiṣṇava glory has indeed been told;
now I shall proclaim [the history] of Turvasu, as well as that of Pūru, Druhyu, and Anu.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Viṣṇu," in the glorious *Mahāpurāṇa* spoken by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
The son of Turvasu was Vahni; the son of Vahni was Gobhānu;
and the son of Gobhānu was the unconquered hero Trisānu. ||1||
Karandhama was the son of Trisānu, but he had no son;
however, another King Marutta, who was previously unobserved, has been mentioned [in the Purāṇas]. ||2||
It is heard that King Marutta was indeed Anavatya;
and they all appointed Paurava as his son for the performance of difficult rites.
Thus, indeed, by means of that curse and through the transfer of old age,
[the lineage] formerly entered the Paurava dynasty of Turvasu.
The heir of Duṣkṛta was the king named Śarūtha;
from Śarūtha came Janāpīḍa, who had four sons.
The Pāṇḍyas, the Keralas, the Colas, and likewise the Kulyas—their territories are known as the Kulyas, the Pāṇḍyas, and the Colas along with the Keralas. ||6||
Druhyu had two renowned heroic sons, Babhru and Setu.
Aruddha was the son of Setu, and the son of Babhru is called Ripu.
The powerful one was slain with great difficulty by Yauvanāśva in battle;
indeed, the combat lasted for fourteen months.
The heir of Aruddha was the king named Gāndhāra,
after whose name the great region of Gāndhāra is known.
There were also horses born in the land of Gāndhāra, the best among steeds;
Dharmma was the son of Gāndhāra, and Ghṛta was his son.
From Ghṛta was born Durdamana, and Pracetas was his son.
These hundred sons of Pracetas were all kings.
All the rulers of the Mleccha kingdoms indeed took refuge in the northern direction.
The three high-souled sons of Anu were supremely righteous.
Sabhānara and Pakṣa, and likewise Parapakṣa;
Sabhānara’s son was the learned King Kālānala. (13)
The virtuous and righteous Sṛñjaya was the son of Kālānala;
Sṛñjaya’s son was the heroic King Purañjaya.
Janamejaya, a great being, was the son of Purañjaya;
and King Mahāśāla was the son of the royal sage Janamejaya. (15)
There was a king equal to Indra, whose fame was established in heaven;
his son was the high-minded and righteous Mahāśāla. (16)
The king, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) of great fame who ruled over the seven continents, begot two sons of noble mind who were renowned throughout the world. (17)
And [he begat] Uśīnara, who was knower of dharma and patient, as well as Dhārmika.
The wives of Uśīnara were five, born from lineages of royal sages. (18)

Mṛgā, Kṛmi, Navā, Darvā, and Dṛṣadvatī as the fifth—these were the five daughters of Uśīnara, through whom his lineage was carried forward. They became highly advanced through great asceticism and were all righteous. (19)
Mṛga was the son of Mṛgā, while Nava was the son of Navā; Kṛmi was the son of Kṛmi, and from Darvā was born the righteous Suvrata by name.
O twice-born ones, Śibi Auśīnara was also the son of Dṛṣadvatī;
the city known as Śivapura belonged to Śibi, while Yaudheya belonged to Mṛga.
The city of Nava was Navarāṣṭra, and that of Kṛmi was the city of Kṛmilā; likewise, Vṛṣṭā belonged to Suvrata. Now learn of the sons of Śivi.
Śiva had four sons, esteemed by the world:
Vṛṣadarbha, Suvīra, Kekaya, and Madraka. ||23||
Their prosperous territories were Kekaya and Madra, as well as Vṛṣadarbha and Sūcidarbha; now hear of the progeny of Titikṣu.
In the eastern direction there was a king renowned as Taitikṣu;
he was the mighty-armed Uśadratha, and his son was Hema.
To Hemas, Suta was born, a powerful son of great fame;
he was indeed born from a human womb when his lineage had declined, out of a desire for progeny. (26)
That great yogi was indeed Bali; though bound, he was high-minded and procreated sons who established the four castes on earth.
He begot Aṅga, Vaṅga, and likewise Suhma;
Puṇḍra and Kaliṅga, as well as Bāleya—this is called the Kṣatriya lineage.
The Bāleyas and the Brāhmaṇas were the progenitors of that lord's lineage;
for the wise Bali, boons had been granted by the gratified Brahmā. (29)
The state of being a great yogi and a lifespan measured by an eon,
invincibility in battle, and the proclamation of the Dharma itself.
Furthermore, there is the vision of the three worlds, preeminence in procreation, invincibility in strength, and the perception of the true meaning of the principles of Dharma. (31)
"And you shall indeed establish the four castes as fixed.
Thus addressed by the Lord, King Bali attained supreme peace.
After a long time, the wise one indeed returned to his own place;
their territories—the Vaṅgas, Aṅgas, and Sūhakas—were likewise prosperous.
The Puṇḍras and the Kaliṅgas likewise—declare their lineage.
All those sons of his were born of a field (kṣetraja), produced by Dīrghatamas through Sudeṣṇā; they were all possessed of great splendor.
The sages said: "O Lord, how were the five sons of Bali born as *kṣetraja* [sons begotten on another's wife] by the sage Dīrghatamas? Tell this to us who ask you. (35)
Sūta said:
In ancient times, there was a renowned and wise ṛṣi named Aśija;
that great-souled one had a wife named Samatā.
But the younger brother of Aśija, Bṛhaspati, who was the priest of the inhabitants of heaven and possessed of great splendor, obtained Mamata.
Mamatā, unwilling to grant him her favor, said to Bṛhaspati:
"I am pregnant by your elder brother; this child is his eighth. (38)
"O Bṛhaspati, this great embryo of mine weeps, even as he practices the sacred knowledge (*brahman*) and recites the Veda with its six limbs. (39)
Your seed is also infallible; therefore, you ought not to consort with me.
O Lord, let this matter remain as it is, or do as you think best.
Thus addressed by her, the great-spirited Bṛhaspati of immense luster did not restrain himself, for his mind was possessed by desire. ||41||
Bṛhaspati, whose soul was devoted to dharma, indeed united with her;
then, as he was emitting his seed, the one staying within the womb spoke to him.
A *snātaka* should not deposit [semen] here, for the union of two is not possible here; moreover, you are one whose seed is unfailing, and I too have come here previously. (43)
Thus addressed, the venerable sage Bṛhaspati, filled with anger, then cursed his brother’s son who was still in the womb as he was pronouncing a blessing.
Since you have spoken thus to me out of delusion at such a time, when all beings desire [your success], you shall enter into long-lasting darkness.
From him was born the seer named Dīrghatamas due to a curse;
