then came Aśija of great fame, who was like Bṛhaspati in his splendor.
Thereafter, with his vital energy drawn upward (a celibate), he dwelt in the hermitage of his brother;
O Lord, he learned the dharma of cattle from a bull, the son of Surabhi.
Then his brother, who was his paternal uncle, built a residence for him;
for there, Vṛṣa dwelt, having arrived by chance.
Surrounded by fragrant cows, he grazed upon the darbha grass brought for the sake of the New Moon sacrifice;
Dīrghatamas seized him as he was struggling at his two horns.
Though restrained by him, he did not move even a single step from his place;
then the bull said to him, "Release me, O best among the strong!"
"O father, nowhere have I encountered anyone as powerful as you;
for since I was born upon this earth, I have carried the god Tryambaka. (51)
"Release me, O best of the strong; I am pleased with you, choose a boon.
Being thus addressed, he said to him: "Where will you go from me while I am alive? (52)
"Therefore, I shall not release you; I am the four-footed master over another's property.
Then that bull replied to Dīrghatamas:
"O dear one, we possess neither sin nor even theft;
we know nothing at all of what may or may not be eaten, nor what may or may not be drunk. (54)
"O Brahmin, we do not indeed know what should or should not be done, nor what is to be approached or avoided; for we are not sinful, since this is declared to be the dharma of cows. (55)
Having heard the name of the cows, he indeed became agitated; having released him, he sought grace from them with devotion derived from sacred tradition.
When he had departed after being propitiated, he—being established in that and devoted to it—then mentally assumed that very nature of a cow out of devotion. (57)
Then, due to fate, that man of deluded mind became enamored with the wife of his younger brother Autathya, even as she struggled and wept. (58)
Considering that to be an insult, Śaradvat could not endure it;
regarding the strength of cows as his own dharma, he treated his daughter-in-law with contempt.
Seeing him in this contrary state, Śaradvat reflected;
and having known the future event, that great-souled one did not grieve for his death.
With eyes bloodshot from rage, he spoke to Dīrghatamas:
"Out of a cow's nature, you do not know what is proper and improper to approach, for you have solicited your daughter-in-law."
"You are ill-behaved; I am indeed abandoning you—go by your own karma!
Since you are blind, old, and difficult to maintain due to your misconduct, for that reason you have been cast out; it is my conviction that you are one of evil conduct."
Sūta said:
Then, his mind became set upon this cruel deed;
having rebuked him many times and seized him with both arms,
he threw him into the belly of the ocean and cast him into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Then, as the ocean was being carried away by the current for seven days,
a king named Bali— who was accompanied by his wife and who knew the true nature of dharma and artha—
beheld it approaching nearby while sinking in the stream.
Having taken him, that righteous Bali, the son of Virocana,
then guarded him in his inner apartments, satisfying him with various kinds of food and delicacies.
Pleased by that boon, he then invited Bali to choose a favor;
and that bull among the Dānavas chose a boon from him for the sake of a son.
Bali said:
O illustrious one, O bestower of honor, for the sake of the continuity of our lineage, you ought to procreate with my wife sons endowed with righteousness and purpose.
Thus addressed by him, the ṛṣi said to him, "So be it";
then the king sent his wife, named Sudeṣṇā, to him.
Seeing that he was blind and old, the queen did not go to him;
instead, she adorned her own nurse and sent her to him. (69)
In her, that self-controlled and righteous seer begot these two sons of great luster, Kakṣīvat and Cakṣuṣa, from that womb of a Śūdra woman.
Then King Bali, seeing those two Kakṣīvats with their eyes [wide open],
who were masters of the Vedas, well-versed in sacred knowledge, and speakers of Brahman according to the prescribed rules, [was amazed].
"Though these two, who have directly perceived dharma, are most excellent even among the wise, they are mine," so said Bali, the son of Virocana, to the seer. (72)
"No," he replied, and then said, "These two are mine. "But you two, best of gods, have been born from a Śūdra womb while disguised as me," [the other said]. (73)
Thinking me to be both young and old, your queen Sudēṣṇā sent a Śūdra woman, the nurse’s daughter, to bring me with contempt. (74)
Then the lord Bali again propitiated that best of sages,
and he indeed rebuked his wife Sudeṣṇā.
Having adorned her once more, he presented her to the Ṛṣi.
Dīrghatamas said to that lady: "O auspicious one, if you [will accept me]... (76)
With curd mixed with salt, you shall lick [your body], clearly naked as you are,
from the soles of your feet to the top of your head, without feeling any disgust.
"Therefore, O Goddess, you shall obtain sons desired by your heart.
The Goddess did everything exactly as he had said.
Having approached the *apāna*, she shrank back in disgust.
Then the sage said to her:
"O auspicious one, because you have rejected it, you shall give birth to a son who is your first-born, even without the *apāna*. (79)
Then that queen replied to Dīrghatamas:
"O highly fortunate one, you ought not to give me such a son."
The sage said:
"O Goddess, this is your own fault; it shall not be otherwise.
O lady of virtuous vows, I shall now give you a son. (81)
Without her downward breath (apāna), there will be an absence of fitness;
having touched her in the womb, that Dīrghatamas spoke these words.
"O lady of pure smiles, that curd which you have consumed today from my body has filled your womb, like the ocean on a full-moon day. (83)
Those five princes will be like sons of gods;
they will be radiant, heroic, performers of sacrifices, and likewise righteous.
From him was born Aṅga, the eldest son of Sudeṣṇā;
from him came Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Puṇḍra, and likewise Brahma. (85)
These five, who were the upholders of the lineage, were then born from the wife of Bali.
Thus, these sons were formerly given to Bali by Dīrghatamas. (86)
His offspring were destroyed by Brahmā for a specific reason:
"May there be no progeny for this great-souled one through his own wives. (87)
Then he indeed begot offspring from a human womb;
Surabhi, being pleased, spoke these words to Dīrghatamas: ||88||
"Since you have acted in this manner after deliberating upon the duty toward cows, I have been released by that very logic; therefore, I am pleased with you. (89)
Therefore, behold today as I extract from you that long-standing darkness; and whatever other sin born of Bṛhaspati remains within your body, I shall remove it.
"Having smelled this, I shall dispel for you even the fear of old age and death.
As soon as it was smelled, darkness was destroyed and he immediately beheld [the light]. (91)
Thereupon he became long-lived, youthful, and possessed of sight; then that Gautama became known as Dīrghatamas because of his cows.
Then Kakṣīvān, having gone with his father to Giriprajā,
performed extensive austerities as directed for the sake of his father.
Then, after a long time, that lordly man, permeated by darkness,
shook off his defects and attained devotion to Brahman.
Thereupon his father said to him, "O Lord, I am truly a father who has found a worthy son."
O father, I have achieved my life’s purpose through you, my illustrious and virtuous son.
For, with his soul thus disciplined, he subsequently attained the dissolution into Brahman;
having reached the state of being devoted to Brahman, Kakṣīvat begot a thousand sons.
Those Kṛṣṇāṅgas are indeed remembered as the Gautamas, the sons of Kakṣīvān; thus [ends the lineage] of Dīrghatamas, who was the son of Bali, the son of Virocana.
The meeting and the continuity of both of them have been fully described.
There, Bali consecrated those five stainless sons.
Having achieved his purpose, that lord, whose self is yoga, relying upon yoga,
became invisible to all beings and wandered about, awaiting the appointed time.
There, the son of Aṅga was the royal seer (rājarṣi) King Dadhivāhana;
from Sāparādha and Sudeṣṇā was born King Anapāna. The son of Anapāna is remembered as King Diviratha.
The son of Diviratha was the learned King Dharmaratha. ||101||
That glorious chariot of Dharma, by which the high-souled Soma was indeed drunk at the sacrifice together with Śakra on Mount Viṣṇupada.
Listen: the son of Dharmaratha was King Citraratha, renowned as Lomapāda, whose daughter was Śāntā. (103)
Indeed, his elephant was the fierce Caṇḍika, the very elephant of Śakra;
he brought that supreme mount of Mandhātṛ to the earth.
The heir of Haryyaṅga was indeed King Bhadraratha; then, the lord of subjects Bṛhatkarman was the son of Bhadraratha. 105.
Bṛhadratha was his son; from him was born Bṛhanmanas. And Bṛhanmanas, O Indra among kings, begot a son. (106)
From him was born a king named Jayadratha; from Jayadratha came R̥ḍharatha; and from R̥ḍharatha came Janamejaya, the conqueror of the universe.
O twice-born one, because Karṇa was born from his limbs as his heir, he became the king; Śūrasena was the son of Karṇa, and he is remembered as his son.
The sages said:
"How did Karṇa become the son of a charioteer, and how was he born into the lineage of Aṅga?
We wish to hear this, for you are indeed exceedingly skillful."
Sūta said:
To Bṛhadbhānu was born a son named King Bṛhanmanas;
he had two wives, both of whom were daughters of the King of Cedi.
There were Yaśodevī and Satyā; from them the lineage was divided.
Jayadratha, the lord of kings, was born of Yaśodevī. (111)
Between Brahmā and Kṣatra was the renowned Satyavijaya;
Vijaya’s son was Dhṛti, and his son was Dhṛtavrata.
The son of Dhṛtavrata was the highly illustrious Satyakarman;
the son of Satyakarman was indeed Sūta Adhiratha.
He seized Karna by the hand, and thus Karna, the son of a Sūta, was addressed.
All this that was urged regarding Karna has been told to you. 114.
All these kings born of the lineage of Aṅga have been described by me in detail and in their proper order; now hear, O subjects, concerning the progeny of Puru.
Sūta said:
The son of Pūru was the mighty-armed King Janamejaya;
his son was Aviddha, who conquered the eastern quarter. (116)
From Aviddha was born the heroic son Manasyu;
then the king named Jayada was the son of Manasyu.
His heir was the lord of the earth named Dhundhu;
Dhundhu’s son was Bahugavī, and Sañjāti was his offspring.
Now learn of the sons of Raudrāśva, who was born of Sañjāti;
indeed, ten Apsarases were the daughters born to Raudrāśva by Ghṛtācī.
Rajeyu, Kṛteyu, Vakṣeyu, Sthaṇḍileyu, Ghṛteyu, Jaleyu, and Sthaleyu as the seventh. (2.37.120)
Dharmeyu, Sannateyu, and Vaneyu—may he be the tenth.
Rudrā, Śūdrā, Madrā, Śubhā, and likewise Jāmalajā. (121)
Talā, Khalā—these seven are remembered, as well as Gopajalā;
likewise Tāmrarasā and Ratnakūṭī are of the same kind. (122)
Their husband was Prabhākara by name, a descendant of Atri;
he was a royal sage (rājarṣi), and Anādṛṣṭa was his son. 123.
The wife of Rivi was named Jvalanā, the daughter of Takṣaka;
upon that queen he, the royal sage, begot a son named Ranti.
Rantirnara begot auspicious sons upon Sarasvatī: Trasu, Pratiratha, and the exceedingly righteous Dhruva.
The auspicious Gaurī Kanyā was renowned as the mother of Māndhātṛ;
Dhurya was the son of Pratiratha, and Kaṇṭha was his son. (126)
Medhātithi was his son, from whom the Kāṇṭhāyana twice-born ones descended;
Yama’s daughter Iti bore sons to him. (127)
Then Trasu obtained four sons who were very dear to him, pure, speakers of the Veda, and givers of gifts. 128.
Then Suṣmanta, Duṣyanta, Pravīra, and likewise Anagha were born;
from them was born the emperor Dauṣyanti, the best of kings.
From Śakuntalā was born Bharata, after whose name the land is called Bhārata;
concerning King Duṣyanta, an incorporeal voice spoke.
The mother is but a skin-bag; the son belongs to the father, for he is the very same as the one by whom he was begotten.
Support your son, Duṣyanta; Śakuntalā has spoken the truth. 131.
O god among men, the progenitor of the seed leads the son from the abode of Yama;
you are the sower of this embryo, so do not disregard Śakuntalā.
Bharata begot nine sons by his three wives;
yet the king did not welcome them, thinking, "They are not worthy of me. (133)
Then those mothers, filled with rage, led their sons to the abode of Yama;
thereafter, that birth of sons for the lord of men was rendered fruitless.
Then, having been brought by the Maruts, that powerful son of Bṛhaspati,
Bharadvāja, was transferred by the Maruts through sacrificial rites.
In that very place, they recite this noble account of the wise Bharadvāja’s transition of birth, as well as [the story] of how he was indeed entrusted to Bharata by the Maruts.
While his wife was pregnant, Aśija passed away.
Seeing his brother’s wife, Bṛhaspati said:
"O auspicious one, having adorned your body, grant me sexual union. (137)
Thus addressed, she replied to him: "O Lord, I am indeed pregnant; this fetus has matured and speaks the Veda with its voice. (138)
"Your seed is not in vain, yet Dharma itself is censured.
Having been addressed thus, Bṛhaspati spoke to her with a smile: (139)
"You must not, under any circumstances, instruct me in the Vinaya.
Speaking thus, he joyfully and forcibly proceeded to have sexual intercourse with her. (2.37.140)
Then the embryo spoke to Bṛhaspati, who was filled with joy:
"O dear Bṛhaspati, I have indeed been established here first. (141)
"Your seed shall not be in vain, yet there is no room for two [beings] here.
Thus addressed by the embryo, he became enraged and replied: (142)
"Since you have forbidden me at such a time as this, which is desired by all beings, therefore you shall enter into long-lasting darkness. (143)
By his two feet, he covered the door of Bṛhaspati’s mother; that semen, however, having been obstructed between them, became a child. (144)
Then, seeing that newborn boy, Mamata said to Bṛhaspati: "I shall indeed go to my own home, O Bharadvāja. (145)
When she had spoken thus and departed, he abandoned his son at that very moment;
having been told, "Support him well," he thereafter became Bharadvāja.
Then, seeing the infant abandoned by his parents, the Maruts took him and went out of compassion to Bharadvāja.
At that time, however, Bharata, desiring a son, performed sacrifices in due order with the Maruts and with various rites, both optional and occasional. ||148||
When that powerful sacrificer could not obtain sons, he then performed the Marutsoma sacrifice again for the sake of obtaining sons. ||149||
By that Marutsoma sacrifice, those Maruts were gratified;
then [the gods bestowed] upon him a wise son, Bharadvāja, the descendant of Bṛhaspati.
Then Bharata, having obtained Bharadvāja as his son, spoke to him.
"O Lord, once the progeny has been withdrawn, I shall have accomplished my purpose through you. (151)
Indeed, his previous birth as a son had been in vain;
therefore, he became known by the name Vitatha Bharadvāja. ||152||
Therefore, the divine Bharadvāja became a Kṣatriya from his Brāhmaṇa [lineage];
he is indeed remembered as having two fathers and being named Dvimukhyāyana. (153)
Then, when Vitatha had passed away, Bharata ascended to heaven;
and the heir of Vitatha was indeed Bhumanyu.
And the four sons born of Bhuvamanyu were like the great elements:
Bṛhatkṣatra, Mahāvīrya, Nara, and the powerful Gāgra. (155)
Nara’s son was Sāṃkṛti; his two sons were of great luster, namely Guruvīrya and Trideva, who are remembered as the younger Sāṃkṛtyas. (156)
And from Śini, who was bound to Garga, there arose heirs;
therefore, these are remembered as the Gārgyas, twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas. 157.
And Bhīma was the son of Mahāvīrya; from him came Ubhakṣaya.
His wife Viśālā indeed gave birth to three sons. (158)
Trayyāruṇi gave birth to Puṣkariṇa as the third son, who was a monkey;
these three are said to be the great seers among the Kṣatravaras of the monkey lineage. ||159||
The Gāgras, Sāṃkṛtis, and Vīryas— twice-born men endowed with the qualities of kṣatriyas—
will take refuge in the faction of Aṅgiras and will proclaim the lineage of Bṛhatkṣatra.
The heir of Bṛhatkṣatra was the righteous one named Suhotra;
the heir of Suhotra was indeed Hastin by name.
By him this city was formerly built, and it was called Hāstinapura after his name.
The sons of Hastin were also three, who were supremely righteous:
Ajamīḍha, Dvimīḍha, and likewise Purumīḍha. (162)
The sons of Ajamīḍha were virtuous, upholders of a noble lineage, and righteous; they were born at the conclusion of the great asceticism of the aged king. (163)
By the grace of Bharadvāja, hear the detailed account of him:
it is said that Kaṇṭha was born to Aja-mīḍha by Keśinī. (164)
His son was Medhātithi; from him the Kaṇṭhāyanas, the twice-born, descended.
From Ajamīḍha, by Dhūminī, was born King Bṛhadvasu. (165)
Bṛhadvasu’s son was Bṛhadviṣṇu, whose son was Mahābala;
his son was Bṛhatkarman, and his son was Bṛhadratha. ||166||
Viśvajit was his son, and Senajit was his offspring;
now, Senajit had four sons who were world-renowned. (167)
Rucirāśva, Kāvya, Rāma Dṛḍhadhanus,
and King Vatsa of Avanti— these were his successive years.
The heir of Rucirāśva was the highly illustrious Pṛthuṣeṇa;
from Pṛthuṣeṇa was born Pāra, and from Pāra, Nīpa was then born.
And we have heard that he had one hundred and one sons;
all of them were kings known as the Nīpas. (2.37.170)
In their lineage was born the illustrious King Kīrtivardhana;
in Kāmpilya there was one named Samara, who was ever ready for battle. (171)
Samarasya, Paraḥpāra, and Satvadaśca—these three sons, endowed with all virtues, were born; among them, Pāraputra Vṛṣu shone forth. (172)
Vṛṣa was named Sukṛti because of his well-performed deeds in this world;
he was endowed with all virtues, and his son was Vibhrāja. (173)
The heir of Vibhrāja was the king named Aṇuha,
the highly illustrious son-in-law of Śuka and husband of Ṛcī.
The heir of Aṇuha was Brahmadatta, a man of great austerity;
his son was Viṣvaksena, who became the king known as Yogasūnu. ||175||
The kings of Vīrajāputra fell [to ruin] here by their ill-performed deeds;
however, Viṣvaksena’s son became Udaksena.
Bhallāṭa was his heir, by whom the king was formerly slain;
Janamejaya was the heir of Bhallāṭa,
for whose sake all the Nīpas were destroyed by Ugrāyudha.
The sages said:
Whose son was Ugrāyudha, and in which lineage is he celebrated? And for what reason were all those Nīpas destroyed by him? (178)
Sūta said:
The learned Yavīnara was born as the heir of Dvimīḍha;
Dhṛtimat was his son, and Satyadhṛti was his son.
Then there was the powerful Dṛḍhanemi, the son of Satyadhṛti;
and the son of Dṛḍhanemi was the king named Suvarmā.
Suvarman had a powerful son, Sārvabhauma;
known as Sārvabhauma, he shone as the sole sovereign of the earth. 181.
In his great lineage was born Mahatpaurava-nandana;
the son of Mahatpaurava was known as King Rukmaratha. (182)
Now, the son of Rukmaratha was the king named Supārśva;
and the son of Supārśva was the righteous Sumati. ||183||
Sumati was also a virtuous, humble, and powerful king;
his son was named Sanati, who was likewise well-disposed. (184)
The disciple of the high-souled Kauthuma Hiraṇyanābha proclaimed those Sāma-vedic collections in twenty-four ways. (185)
Those who were known by their ancient names were the singers of the Sāmans;
Kārti was among them, as was Ugrāyudha, that hero, the joy of the Pauravas.
By him, exerting his prowess, the mighty-armed Panchala ruler named Nila—the grandfather of Prishata—was slain. (187)
The heir of Ugrāyudha was the highly illustrious Kṣema;
from Kṣema was born Suvīra, and from Suvīra came Nṛpañjaya. From Nṛpañjaya was born Vīraratha; these are remembered as the Pauravas. ||188||
From Ajamīḍha and Nīlinī was born King Nīla;
from Nīla’s fierce asceticism, Suśānti was born. (189)
Suśānti’s son was Purujānu, and the son of Purujānu was Rikṣa.
From him came the heirs of Rikṣa, and these were his sons, the Bhedas.
Mudgala, Sṛñjaya, King Bṛhadiṣu, the valiant Yavīyas, and Kampilya as the fifth. ||191||
For the sake of protecting the five, the father addressed them:
"Know these five to be prosperous regions endowed with [resources]. (192)
They were sufficient for their protection; they were renowned as the Pañcālas, and the Maudgalyas, though twice-born brahmins, were endowed with the qualities of the kṣatriya class. (193)
For these were followers of the side of Aṅgiras;
Mudgala’s eldest son was most devoted to Brahman and possessed of great fame. (194)
From Indrasena, Badhyashva obtained a conception;
from Badhyashva a pair was born, [consisting of] Menaka—so we have heard. (195)
The royal sage Divodāsa and the illustrious Ahalyā;
and Ahalyā gave birth to a son for Śaradvat. (196)
To that best of sages, Śatānanda, was born a son of great renown named Satyadhṛti, who had reached the further shore of the science of archery.
Then, having seen the Apsaras Śukrā standing before him, Satyadhṛti’s seed spilled into a clump of reeds as he engaged in sexual union. (198)
Śaṃtanu, who had gone out hunting, took it up out of compassion;
he was indeed remembered as Kṛpa from that, and likewise Gautamī became Kṛpī.
These Śāradvatas have been declared; Ṛtadhya belongs to the lineage of Gautama.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the progeny of Divodāsa.
The heir of Divodāsa was King Mitrayu, who was most devoted to Brahman.
But Maitreya was born from him; these [others] also are remembered as having resorted to him. ||201||
These Bhārgavas, though endowed with the qualities of the Kṣatriya order, also took up his side;
and the wise King Cyavana likewise became a Pratiratha.
Then indeed, from Cyavana, the wise Sudāsa was born;
Saudāsa and Sahadeva were his sons, and Somaka was his offspring.
When his lineage had perished, Ajamīḍha was born again as that Somaka.
O Lord, when Somaka was slain, Jantu became his son, and he had a hundred sons.
Among the sons of the high-souled Ajamīḍha by Somakā,
the youngest was Pṛṣata, the grandfather of Drupada.
His son was Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and his son was Dhṛṣṭaketu;
and the queen of Ajamīḍha was Dhūminī, who longed for a son.
Furthermore, for a hundred years she performed difficult penance for the sake of a future birth;
she maintained the sacrificial fire, remained sleepless, and partook of pure, measured food. (207)
She of the great vow slept for a full day and night upon kusha grass;
and while she was of smoky hue, the heroic Ajamidha begot [a son].
He begot Ṛkṣa, who was smoke-colored and had white-tipped hair;
from Ṛkṣa, Saṃvaraṇa was born, and Kuru was born from Saṃvaraṇa.
Having traversed Prayāga on foot and ploughed Kurukṣetra,
that one of great splendor did so for many years.
As he was being dragged away at that time, Śakra appeared there as the bestower of boons [to him],
[a place] meritorious, delightful, and frequented by those who perform meritorious deeds.
His descendants were the renowned Kurus, the best of kings;
and Kuru had two beloved sons, Sudhanvan and Jahnu.
The great king Parikṣit had a son named Arimardana;
the heir of Sudhanvan was known as the wise Suhotra. (213)
His son was Cyavana, a king skilled in dharma and artha;
Cyavana’s son was Kṛta, a man of great asceticism who performed sacrifices.
The king begot a renowned son, a friend of Indra,
the heroic Vidyoparicara, known by the name Vasu, who traveled through the atmosphere.
From Vidyoparicara, Girikā gave birth to seven sons:
Mahāratha, Bhagadhara, and the renowned Bṛhadratha. ||216||
Pratyagraha, Kuśa, whom they call Maṇivāhana, Māthailya, Lalittha, and Matsyakāla as the seventh. ||217||
The heir of Bṛhadratha was the renowned Kuśāgra;
and the son of Kuśāgra was the powerful Ṛṣabha by name. (218)
The heir of Ṛṣabha was the righteous Puṣpavān;
his heir was the valiant King Satyahita, so it is remembered.
His son was Sudhanvan, and from him was born the powerful Ūrja;
Nabhas was the son of Ūrja, and from him that heroic one was born.
He was indeed born from two fragments; he was joined together by Jarā.
Thus the mighty-armed Jarāsandha was joined together by Jarā. ||221||
That Jarāsandha of great strength was the conqueror of all kṣatriyas;
Sahadeva, full of prowess, was the son of Jarāsandha. ||222||
The illustrious Somādhi, of great asceticism, was like his own son;
and Śrutaśravas is celebrated as the Māgadha of Somādhi.
Sūta said:
Janamejaya was the heir of Parikṣit;
Śrutasena’s heir was also named Bhīmasena.
Jahnu begot a son named Suratha, a protector of the earth;
the heir of Suratha was the heroic King Vidūratha.
It is heard that Vidūratha’s son was Sārvabhauma;
from Sārvabhauma came Jayatsena, and his son was Ārādhita.
The Mahāsattva was propitiated; therefore he is remembered as Ayutāyu.
Because he was free from anger, he became Ayutāyu; hence he is remembered as Devātithi. ||227||
The heir of Devātithi was indeed Ṛkṣa;
likewise, Bhīmasena was born from Ṛkṣa, and Dilīpa was his son.
The son of Dilīpa was Pratīpa; three sons are recorded for him:
Devāpi, Śantanu, and Bāhlīka—these were the three.
It should be known that King Saptabāhliśvara was the son of Bāhlīka;
and the highly illustrious Somadatta was the son of Bāhlīka.
From Somadatta were born Bhūri, Bhūriśravas, and Śala;
Devāpi, however, departed for the forest out of a desire to practice righteousness.
The sage Devāpi became the preceptor (upādhyāya) of the gods;
Cyavana was indeed the son of that high-souled one, as was Iṣṭaka.
Śāntanu became king; he was indeed the learned Mahābhiṣa.
And regarding this Mahābhiṣa, they cite here the following verse: [233]
Whichever aged man the king touched according to the agreement, he became young again;
therefore, they know him as Śantanu.
Then his name Śaṃtanu became renowned among his subjects here;
that righteous king Śaṃtanu married the daughter of Jahnu.
In her, that lord begot a son, Devavrata Bhīṣma;
he became renowned as Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Pāṇḍavas.
In due time, Śāntanu begot a son upon Vicitravīrya—
a beloved son of Śāntanu, a lord who acted for the welfare of his subjects—
and Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana likewise [begot sons] in the field of Vicitravīrya.
She gave birth to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura as well;
and from Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī bore a hundred sons.
Among them, Duryodhana was the eldest; he was the lord of all the kṣatriyas.
Queen Mādrī and Pṛthā were the two wives of Pāṇḍu. ||239||
From those two, sons were begotten for the sake of Pāṇḍu by Devadatta. Yudhiṣṭhira was born from Dharma, and Vṛkodara was born from Vāyu.
From Indra was born Dhanañjaya, whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra;
and from the two Aśvins were born the god Nakula and Sahadeva, both sons of the Mountain-Daughter.
Five sons were born to Draupadī from the Pāṇḍavas;
Draupadī gave birth to Śrutaviddha as the eldest son from Yudhiṣṭhira.
From Bhīmasena, Hiḍimbā gave birth to a son, Ghaṭotkaca;
furthermore, from Bhīmasena, Kāśī gave birth to a son, Sarvavṛka.
Mādrī gave birth to Suhotra and Vijaya from Sahadeva; and from Karamatī, the wife of Vaidya, Niramitra and Lāṅgali were born.
From Subhadrā, the charioteer Abhimanyu was born to Pārtha;
and from Uttarā, the daughter of Virāṭa, Parikṣit was born as the son of Abhimanyu.
The heir of Parīkṣit was King Janamejaya;
he indeed established the Vājasaneyika Brāhmaṇas [as officiants]. 246.
Out of indignation, Vaiśampāyana alone will not endure this word of yours on earth, O evil-minded one; it shall remain without rival.
"As long as I remain in this world, this will not be praised.
Then Janamejaya stood all around him. 248.
Having worshipped the god Prajāpati with the full-moon oblation,
he remained there, and having gained insight, he beheld that [destruction] of the Lord in the sacrifice.
Janamejaya, the son of Parikṣit and descendant of Puru,
having performed the horse sacrifice twice and having established the Vājasaneyaka,
that Janamejaya caused the Brahman [text] consisting of thirty million verses to be propagated.
Janamejaya, having three crores of horses and horse-leaders, three crores of inhabitants of Aṅga, and all the people of the Middle Country,
went to his destruction after being cursed by the Brahmins out of indignation. ||251||
His son was Śatānīka, powerful and of true valor;
then, O brahmins, they consecrated him as king.
The heroic Aśvamedhadatta became the son of Śatānīka;
indeed, Parapuraṃjaya was born from Aśvamedhadatta as his son. (253)
This present king, Adhisāmakṛṣṇa, is righteous-souled and of great renown;
while he rules the earth, this was brought by you.

O best of the twice-born, a long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra) lasting three years is indeed difficult to accomplish; likewise, a two-year session at Kurukṣetra on the Dṛṣadvatī river is difficult to perform.
The sages said:
O Great-minded One, we wish to hear about the future of the subjects;
O Sūta, you have already narrated what has passed along with the kings. ||256||
Tell me also of the deeds that shall be accomplished and those kings who shall arise, even starting from the first year; speak of those kings by their names as well. (257)

The duration of time and its measure, the future virtues and faults, and the happiness and suffering of living beings—[all these] he knows according to their nature, their causes, and their purposes. (258)
"Having reflected upon all this, tell it truly to those who ask. Thus addressed by the sages, Sūta, the best among the wise,
related exactly as it had occurred, as it had been seen, and as it had been heard.
Sūta said:
Just as everything has been narrated by me, so too have the future Kali Yuga and the Manvantaras been described by Vyāsa of wondrous deeds.
Listen as I speak of all those yet to come;
hereafter I shall proclaim those who will be the bulls [of the Śākya clan]. (261)
And likewise the Ailas, the Ikṣvākus, and the Sudyumnas—those kings in whom this auspicious field of Ikṣvāku is established. (262)
I shall proclaim all those kings who will be read of in the future, as well as others who will arise after them as rulers of the earth. (263)
The Kṣattras, Pāraśavas, Śūdras, as well as those who were twice-born (dvijātis),
the Andhas, Śakas, Pulindas, Tūlikas, along with the Yavanas— 264.
The Kaivartas, Ābhiras, Śabaras, and whatever other Mleccha tribes there may be—I shall describe those kings by name, starting from the first year. (265)
This very Adhisāmakṛṣṇa is now the king of the Pauravas;
I shall describe as many future kings who will belong to his lineage.
It is said that Adhisāmakṛṣṇaputra will become free from crookedness;
when that city named after the Nāga has been swept away by the Gaṅgā,
he will abandon that fine residence and dwell in Kauśāmbī.
His son will be Uṣṇa; from Uṣṇa, Citraratha is recorded [to descend].
From Citraratha comes Śucidratha, and from Śucidratha comes Vṛtimant.
Suṣeṇa will indeed be of great heroism and great fame;
from that Suṣeṇa shall arise a king named Sutīrtha.
From Rucya, Sutīrtha will be born; from him, Tricakṣu will be born.
And the heir of Tricakṣu will indeed be Sukhībala.
Sukhībalasuta will also be a king named Paripluta; and Paripluta’s son will be a king named Sunaya. (271)
Then Medhāvin will become a king of wise policy,
and the son of Medhāvin will be Daṇḍapāṇi.
From Daṇḍapāṇi will come Nirāmitra, and from Nirāmitra, Kṣemaka;
these twenty-five kings shall indeed be born of the former lineage. ||273||
In this regard, this genealogical verse was sung of old by Brahmins learned in the past:
"This lineage, honored by divine sages, is the source of the Brahmin and Kṣatriya orders. (274)
Having reached King Kṣemaka, he will indeed attain his final state in the Kali age.
Thus has this Paurava lineage been recounted exactly as it is. ||275||
After [the account of] the wise and high-souled Arjuna, son of Pāṇḍu, I shall hereafter proclaim the lineage of the high-souled Ikṣvākus. 276.
The heir of Bṛhadratha was the heroic King Bṛhatkṣaya;
from him came his son Kṣaya, and from that Kṣaya came Vatsavyūha.
His son was Divākara, who formed a counter-array against Vatsavyūha;
he is the king who currently occupies the city of Ayodhyā. (278)
Divākara’s son will be the highly illustrious Sahadeva;
Sahadeva’s heir shall be Bṛhadaśva. ||279||
His son shall be Bhānuratha, and his son will be Pratītāśva;
the son of Pratītāśva, moreover, will be Supratīta.
His son was Sahadeva, and his son was Sunakṣatra. ||281||
From Sunakṣatra, however, will come Kinnara, the scorcher of foes;
and Antarikṣa will be the great son of Kinnara. (282)
From Antarikṣa came Suparṇa, and from Suparṇa came Amitrajit.
His son was Bharadvāja, and his son is remembered as Dharmī.
The son of Dharmī will be named Kṛtañjaya.
The son of Kṛtañjaya was Vrāta, and his son was Raṇañjaya. ||283||
From Raṇañjaya, the hero Sañjaya shall be born as king;
the Śākya son of Sañjaya was Śuddhodana. ||284||
Rāhula is remembered as the son of Śuddhodana for the sake of the Śākyas; after him Prasenajit will arise, and after him Kṣudraka will arise. ||285||
From Kṣudraka, Kṣulika shall arise; from Kṣulika, Suratha is recorded [as the next];
Sumitra shall be the son of Suratha, and he will be the last king. (286)
These descendants of Ikṣvāku are said to be those who will arise in the Kali age;
born in the lineage of Bṛhadbala, they will exist in the Kali age—
heroes, accomplished in learning, true to their word, and masters of their senses.
Regarding this, a genealogical verse has been proclaimed by those who know the future:
"This lineage of the Ikṣvākus shall end with Sumitra;
having reached King Sumitra, it will indeed reach its conclusion in the Kali age."
Thus, this is declared to be the field of Mānava and Aila. ||288||
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the Bṛhadrathas of Magadha—
those kings who belong to the lineage of Jarāsaṃdha and the family of Sahadeva.
Those of the past, the present, and likewise those of the future—I shall proclaim them according to their importance; listen as I speak.
In that Bhārata war, Sahadeva was struck down;
his son, the royal sage Somādhi, [resided] in Girivraja.
Śrutaśravas ruled the kingdom for fifty-eight years;
his son was Ayutāyu,
who ruled the kingdom for twenty-six years after having lived for sixty-four years.
Having enjoyed the earth for a hundred years without an enemy, he passed away to heaven.
Having well-conquered the earth for fifty-six years, Bṛhatkarman ruled the kingdom for twenty-three years. ||293||
Senajit shall likewise enjoy this earth for the present years;
Śrutajaya, however, will rule for forty years. (294)
The king, who possesses mighty arms, great intellect, and most formidable prowess,
shall protect the earth for thirty-five years.
The pure one shall indeed remain in his kingdom for fifty-eight years;
Kṣema will be king for twenty-eight full years.
The valiant one shall obtain the kingdom for sixty-four years;
for five full years, he will be Dharmnetra.
The king shall indeed enjoy [the kingdom] for fifty-eight years;
the reign of Suvrata will last for thirty-eight years. (298)
Dṛḍhasena will rule for forty-eight years, and thereafter Sumati will obtain [the throne] for thirty-three years. (299)
Thereafter, Sucala shall enjoy the kingdom for twenty-two years;
then King Sunetra shall enjoy it for forty years;
and Satyajit shall enjoy the sovereignty of the earth for eighty-three years.
And having attained this, Vīrajit shall become thirty-five [years old]. ||301||
Ariñjaya, however, will obtain the earth for fifty years;
these thirty-two kings will indeed belong to the lineage of Bṛhadratha. (302)
Their sovereignty shall indeed last for a full thousand years,
after the Bṛhadrathas, the Vītahotras, and the Vartins have passed away.
Having slain his master, Mūlika will forcibly consecrate his son as king, even while the Kṣatriyas look on; for Pradyota is the son of Mūlika. (304)
Deprived of statesmanship, he will indeed become a king whose vassals are submissive; that best of men shall rule for twenty-three years. (305)
Thereafter, King Pālaka will rule for twenty-four years;
then King Viśākhayūpa will rule for fifty years.
The reign of Ajaka will last for thirty-one years;
his son, Vartivardhana, will rule for twenty years. (307)
One hundred and thirty-eight Pradyotas are to be known; five will be their sons.
Having destroyed their entire glory, Śiśunāka shall come to be.
In Vārāṇasī, his son will obtain Girivraja;
he will rule for forty years as Śiśunāka. (309)
His son will be Śakavarṇa, and he shall have thirty-six [sons];
after him, King Kṣemavarman will rule for twenty years.
The king Ajātaśatru will be for twenty-five years;
thereafter, he, possessing the vigor of a Kṣatriya, will obtain the kingdom for forty years. (311)
King Vivisāra will reign for twenty-eight years; King Darśaka, however, will reign for twenty-five years. ||312||
Therefore, Udāyin shall become king for thirty-three years. In his fourth year, that king will indeed establish the excellent city named Kusuma on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā upon this earth.
King Nandivardhana shall rule for forty-two years; Mahānandin shall likewise rule for forty-three years. (314)
Thus, these ten Śaiśunāka kings will indeed come to be;
their reigns will last for three hundred and sixty-two years. (315)
The Śaiśunāka kings will rule for that duration;
along with them, there will be other kings who are kinsmen of the Kṣatriyas. ||316||
The Aikṣvākas were twenty-four, the Pāñcālas twenty-five, the Kālakas twenty-four, and the Haihayas twenty-four. (317)
The Kaliṅgas are indeed thirty-two, the Śakas likewise twenty-five;
the Kurus are twenty-six, and the Maithilas twenty-eight. (318)
Twenty-three Śūrasenas and twenty Vītihotras—all these kings shall exist at the same time. (319)
And the son of Mahānandin, Kālasaṃvṛta, shall be born as King Mahāpadma from a Śūdra woman during the interval between all the kṣatriyas.
From that time forward, kings shall be born from the Śūdra caste;
that Mahāpadma shall become a sole monarch, ruling under a single umbrella.
Having uprooted all other kṣatriyas by the power of his destined purpose, he shall rule the earth for twenty-eight years.
His eight sons were indeed each a thousand years in age; those kings lived for twelve years.
In the lineage of Mahāpadma, kings will arise in succession. ||323||
Kauṭilya will indeed uproot all of them with eighteen [years];
having enjoyed the earth for a hundred years, he will become the moon of the Nandas.
Kautilya will establish King Candragupta upon the throne;
King Candragupta shall rule for twenty-four years. ||325||
Bhadrasāra shall be king for twenty-five years;
and King Aśoka shall indeed be king among men for twenty-six years.
His son will be Kunāla, who shall rule for eight years;
and Kunāla’s son, Bandhupālita, shall likewise enjoy the kingdom for eight years.
The heir of Bandhupālita will be Indrapālita, the tenth [king];
Devavarmā shall be the lord of men for seven years. (328)
King Śatadhara will have eight sons;
Bṛhadaśva shall indeed be the king for seven years. (329)
Thus, these nine kings who shall enjoy the earth will rule for a full three hundred and thirty-seven years; from them, Gaurī shall arise.
But Puṣpamitra, the commander-in-chief, having deposed Bṛhadratha,
shall indeed rule the kingdom for exactly sixty years.
The eight sons of Puṣpamitra will become kings of equal status;
furthermore, his eldest son shall rule for seven years thereafter.
Vasumitra shall be the son and king for ten years;
thereafter, Dhruva shall indeed be the son and king for two years.
Therefore, there will be exactly three Pulindaka kings of equal status, and Ghoṣasuta shall also be king for three years. (334)
Then indeed Vikramitras will be king for thirty-two years, and thereafter the Bhāgavata king shall likewise rule for thirty-two years.
He will have a son named Kṣemabhūmi; these ten [princes], including him, shall rule this earth for ten equal generations.
These ten lofty kings will enjoy this Vasundharā.
What indeed will come of those one hundred, ten, and two [years] for him who, out of childishness, has made a king addicted to vice into one who is not a royal Sudēva? (337)
Then another king, Devabhūmi, will rule over the Śṛṅgas;
that Kaṇṭhāyana will be king for nine years. (338)
His son will be Bhūtimitra, who shall reign for twenty-four years;
after him, King Nārāyaṇa will come to power for twelve years. (339)
His son will be Suśarman for ten years;
these four kings, the descendants of Kaṇṭha, shall be twice-born (dvija) and perform the rites of elevation.
Forty-five subordinate vassals are to be cultivated;
at the time of their succession, Tarandhā shall indeed come to be.
Then, having forcibly uprooted Suśarman along with Kaṇṭhāyana,
and having likewise destroyed whatever strength remained among the Śṛṅgas,
Sindhuka, born of the Andhra race, shall indeed obtain this earth.
Then King Sindhuka will rule for twenty-three years;
his brother Bhāta will rule for eight years, and after him, Daśa will become king.
Śrī Sātakarṇi will be his son, and he indeed shall be great; Sātakarṇi will rule for fifty-six years. (344)
Bound by his feet, he shall indeed have ten sons;
his life shall last for twenty-four years and six months. ||345||
Nemikṛṣṇa shall rule for twenty-five years;
thereafter, Hāla will be king for a full year.
There will be five kings of the Saptaka dynasty, possessed of great power;
and Bhāvya Putrikṣeṇa shall likewise rule for twenty-one years.
Sātakarṇi will be the lord of men for one year;
Śivasvāmī, however, will be [the ruler] for twenty-eight years. ||348||
King Gautamīputra reigned among men for twenty-one years, and then King Yajñaśrī Sātakarṇi reigned for nineteen years. (349)
Therefore, Vijaya shall be king for six years;
Daṇḍaśrī and Sātakarṇi shall be his sons, each for three years. Pulomā shall also rule for seven years, and others shall likewise come to power.
Thus, these thirty Andhra kings shall indeed rule the earth.
Four hundred, five hundred, and likewise six hundred years;
those five lineages of the Andhras remained established for that many years. (352)
Thereafter, there will be seven kings known as the Daśābhiras;
then seven Gardabhins, and after that, ten Śakas.
There will be eight Yavanas, fourteen Tuṣāras, thirteen Maruṇḍas, and eighteen Maunas. (354)
The Andhras shall enjoy the earth for three hundred years;
and the Śakas shall enjoy the earth for three hundred and eighty years.
The Yavanas shall enjoy the earth for eighty years;
it is recorded that the Tuṣāras shall possess the earth here for five hundred years.
There will be thirteen hundred and fifty Maruṇḍas, along with Vṛṣalas and other Mleccha tribes. (357)
The Mlecchas shall enjoy [the earth] for three hundred and eleven years;
then, by that concealed time, there will be the Koli-kila bulls.
Then, from among the Koli-kilas, Vindhyaśakti will arise;
having protected the earth for ninety-six years, he will pass away. (359)
Learn now of the past, the present, and the future Vṛṣas and Diśakas:
the son of Śeṣa, the king of serpents, is Svarapurañjaya.
The king Bhogin will be a ruler born from the lineage of the Nāgas;
likewise, there will be Sadācandra, Candrāṃśa, and the second, Nakhavat. (361)
Then Dhanadharma will follow, remembered as the twenty-fourth;
thereafter Bhūtinanda will appear in Vaideha.
At the edge of Aṅga’s Nandana grove, there will be a Madhunandin;
his younger brother, indeed, shall be named Nandiyaśas. (363)
In his lineage, there will indeed be three kings;
a grandson named Śiśuka became the king in Purikā.
And the son of Vindhyaśakti, the heroic and powerful one named Pravīra,
shall indeed enjoy the city of Kāñcanakā for sixty years.
They will perform Vājapeya sacrifices accompanied by the most excellent sacrificial fees;
he shall have four sons who will become lords of men.
When the lineage of the Vindhyakas has passed away, there will indeed be three Bāhlika kings:
Supratīka and Nabhīra; the latter shall enjoy [the kingdom] for thirty years.
The king named Śakyamāna, the lord of the earth, will have thirteen sons, Puṣpamitra and Paṭṭamitra, who will be the lords of the Māhiṣīs. (368)
In Mekalā, there will be seven excellent kings; and in Komalā, there will be kings of great strength. (369)
Those known as the Meghas, nine in number and all wise,
shall be the Nishadhan kings until the end of the Manvantara.
Those descendants born of the Nala lineage will be heroic and possessed of great strength; among them, Viśvasphāni, endowed with great valor, shall become the ruler of the Magadhas.
Having exterminated all other kings, he will turn others into the Brahmin caste—namely, fishermen, Pañcakas, and Pulindas. (372)
By their splendor, kings will establish [the teaching] in various lands;
Viśvasphāni, a being of great essence, will be as powerful as Viṣṇu in battle. (373)
The king, the sustainer of the universe, is said to be of eunuch-like disposition;
having exterminated one class of Kṣatriyas, he will establish another Kṣatriya order. (374)
Having once again gratified the gods, the ancestors, and the brahmins,
that powerful man reached the bank of the Jāhnavī and cast off his body.
Having renounced his own body, he will go to the world of Śakra;
meanwhile, nine kings will enjoy the city of Campāvatī. (376)

The Nāgas shall indeed rule over the beautiful city of Mathurā for seven generations; likewise, those born of the Gupta lineage shall rule over all these regions: Prayāga along the Gaṅgā, Sāketa, and Magadha. (377)
The Maṇidhānyajas shall enjoy all these regions: the Niṣadhas, the Yadukas, the Śaiśīs, and the Kālatopas. (378)
They shall enjoy the Kośalas, the Āndhras, and the Pauṇḍras, along with the coastal regions up to the ocean, as well as the beautiful city of Campā protected by the gods. (379)
Guha shall indeed protect all these regions: the Kāliṅgas, the Mahiṣas, and those who dwell in the Mahendra mountains.
The one named Kanaka will rule over the kingdom of women and the Bhakṣyas;
indeed, all these kings will exist at the same time.
For the Yavanas here will have little faith, be untruthful, exceedingly wrathful, and unrighteous, both in accordance with dharma, in their desires, and in their pursuit of wealth. (382)
Those lords of men will not truly be consecrated kings;
rather, those kings will be characterized by the evil conduct resulting from the defects of the age.
In the remainder of the Kali age, kings shall likewise enjoy the earth only by means of the slaughter of women and by killing one another.
In this succession of time, there will be rulers of the earth here whose lineages have risen again and again, as well as those who have risen only to set. (385)
They will be deprived of the Dharma, both in terms of its practice and its meaning; and all the regions will be intermingled with them, adopting the conduct of barbarians in every respect. (386)
They will act perversely and will surely destroy the subjects;
at that time, the kings will be greedy and devoted to falsehood.
When their turn had passed, during that age characterized by many women,
they began to fall away bit by bit from longevity, physical form, strength, and sacred knowledge.
Likewise, when the lords of the world have reached their ultimate limit among living beings,
those kings then perish, struck down by time.
Struck down by Kalki, all the Mlecchas will flee in every direction;
likewise, those exceedingly unrighteous ones and the heretics will also vanish everywhere.
When the title of "king" had vanished and the Kali age had embraced the twilight, those subjects were indeed reduced to a mere remnant; with dharma destroyed, they lived without possessions.
Lacking means of subsistence, their hopes destroyed, they were tormented by disease and grief;
they were further afflicted by drought and by mutual slaughter.
For, abandoned and terrified, casting aside their livelihoods and filled with suffering, they will leave their cities and villages to become forest-dwellers. (393)
Thus, when the kings had perished, the subjects abandoned their homes;
their affection having vanished, they became difficult to console, and their friends lost all warmth of feeling. (394)
At that time, the people will have fallen away from their castes and stages of life, will have entered into a terrible state of social confusion, and will dwell along rivers and mountains.
They frequent rivers, the coastal regions of the ocean, and mountains;
[they traverse] Aṅga, Kaliṅga, Vaṅga, Kāśmīra, Kāśi, and Kośala. (396)
Human beings will take refuge in the mountain valleys at the edge of the sages' hermitages, across the entire expanse of the Himalayas, and along the shore of the salt ocean. (397)
For the noble ones will enter the vast forests together with the barbarian folk;
and there, along with deer, fish, birds, beasts of prey, and serpents, human beings shall subsist on honey, vegetables, fruits, and roots. (398)
Having themselves fashioned garments of rags, various leaves, bark, and skins, they shall dwell just like the people among sages. (399)
Likewise, they will sow seeds in low-lying places using wooden stakes as markers;
they will diligently tend goats, sheep,
donkeys, and camels, and men will dwell by the banks of rivers for the sake of water.
Oppressing one another through their legal proceedings, the kings [were at odds]. ||401||
Respecting many [worthless things], devoid of progeny, and abandoned by purity and right conduct—
thus will men be at that time, established in unrighteousness.
In that time, people follow even the most base of base dharmas;
their lifespan is twenty-three years, and no one exceeds it. (403)
They were weak, exhausted by sensory objects, and overwhelmed by old age;
they subsisted on leaves, roots, and fruits, and were clothed in bark and black antelope skins.
Desiring to obtain a livelihood, people will roam the earth;
such is the condition of beings when this time, the end of the Kali Yuga, has arrived.
When that divine Kali Yuga of a thousand years has waned,
it shall become entirely exhausted along with the Kali Yuga itself;
and when the period including its transitional sub-periods (sandhyāṃśa) has completely ended, the Kṛta Yuga will indeed commence.
When the moon, the sun, as well as Tiṣya and Bṛhaspati, shall be together in one night, then the Kṛta Yuga shall come to be. ||407||
This entire lineage has been recounted to you in its proper sequence—those who have passed away, those who are present, and likewise those who are yet to come. 408.
From the consecration of Mahādeva until the birth of Parikṣit, this period of one thousand and fifteen years is to be known. ||409||
The duration of the Mahāpadma interval has indeed been stated as the measure;
that interval is recorded as eight hundred and thirty-six years.
Those who are proclaimed to rule until the end of the Andhra period during this interval have been enumerated there by the future seers who are learned in the Purāṇas. ||411||
Then the Seven Sages said: "O King Pratīpa, indeed, one hundred and twenty-seven Andhra kings are yet to be produced by you. (412)

Within the entire stellar sphere extending to its twenty-seventh limit, the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) remain in rotation for a hundred years each; indeed, this period of the Seven Sages is recorded as a Yuga by divine reckoning. (413)
Each of those is known as a divine unit; sixty such divine units, multiplied by seven, constitute the divine time that proceeds from them by means of those seven sages.
Those Seven Seers who are seen in the northern direction,
from there the field is seen in the center, equal to the sky.
By that [measure], the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) joined with the constellations in the sky should be known to remain for a hundred years;
this is the illustration of the conjunction between the constellations and the Ṛṣis. ||416||
In the time of the son of Parikṣit, the Seven Sages will be conjoined with the Maghā constellation for one hundred years;
in my opinion, they will likewise remain so during the twenty-fourth portion of the Andhra dynasty. (417)
At that time, however, these subjects will fall into great distress;
all of them, struck by untruth, will deviate from dharma, desire, and material prosperity.
At that time, when the dharma pertaining to the castes and stages of life— both revealed (śrauta) and traditional (smārta)— has become lax,
those of weak self-nature, being deluded, will resort to Śaṅkara.
The Śūdras will become closely associated with the twice-born;
the Brāhmaṇas will have Śūdras as their patrons, while the Śūdras will indeed be the source of the sacred mantras.
Then indeed, those brahmins, desiring a means of livelihood, will wait upon them;
for all subjects will gradually fall away bit by bit.
On that very day when Kṛṣṇa ascended to heaven, at the end of the Yuga, they will all go to their destruction, with nothing remaining.
The Kali Yuga has already begun; learn its duration:
it is said that the Kali age consists of three hundred and sixty thousand years according to human reckoning. (423)
A divine thousand years is proclaimed to be the period of its twilight (sandhyāṃśa);
when that has completely ended, the Kṛta age indeed begins.
The lineages of Aila and Ikṣvāku, along with their branches, have been proclaimed.
From Ikṣvāku, the Kṣatriya lineage is recorded as extending down to Sumitra, the son of Vivasvat. 425.
Those who know the lineage of Soma recognize the Aila Kṣatra as one whose end is security;
these sons of Vivasvat, who increase one's fame, have thus been celebrated.
Those who are remembered as belonging to the lineages of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—whether they be of the past, the present, or likewise those of the future. ||427||
In age after age, thousands of great-souled ones have passed away;
because their names are so numerous, it is impossible to enumerate them family by family.
Because they are numerous and repetitive, I have not recited them all;
for in this Vaivasvata interval, the lineage of Nimi comes to an end.
They shall thus come during the age called the Yuga, for from them the Kṣatriya power will arise;
listen as I relate this to you as I speak. 2.37.430.
King Devāpi, the descendant of Puru, who was considered an Ikṣvāku as well, endowed with the power of great yoga, resided in the village of Kalāpa. ||431||
Suvarcā, the son of Soma, will be the descendant of Ikṣvāku;
these two shall be the leaders of the Kṣatriyas in the twenty-fourth cycle of four yugas.
And in the twentieth age, there will be no beginning of the Lunar dynasty;
rather, King Devāpi Asapatna will be the first of the Aila lineage.
For these two shall become the bringers of the Kṣatriya lineage throughout the four ages;
thus should it be understood everywhere, for this is the characteristic intended for the sake of the lineage.
When that Kali Yuga has perished, in the future Kṛta Yuga,
he will again [dwell] together with those seven ṛṣis at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga.
They two shall be the initiators for the lineages and the Kṣatriyas;
during the Dvāpara age, the Kṣatriyas do not remain together with the sages.
When the Kṛta age has passed away in due course and the Tretā age begins again,
they shall indeed exist once more as the seeds for the Brahmin and Kṣatriya orders.
In this very same way, indeed, in all these intervening periods, the Seven Sages remain here together with kings from age to age for the sake of progeny.
The total destruction of the Kṣatriyas and their connection with the twice-born is recorded in tradition;
you have also heard of the lineages of the seven Manvantaras.
The succession of the ages and the origin of the Brahmins and Kshatriyas;
their manner of manifestation once they have appeared, as well as their subsequent decline.
The Seven Sages know them; may they, through their long life, grant you inexhaustibility.
By this sequential method, O twice-born ones, [the lineages] of Aila and Ikṣvāku [are established]. 441.
Arising during the Tretā age and again diminishing during the Kali age,
they follow the designation of the *yugas* until the end of the *manvantara*.
When the Kṣatriyas had been exterminated without remainder by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, all the royal dynasties were re-established by Kṣatriya lords of the earth;
listen as I proclaim those who founded the two lineages. 443.
The nature of Aila, the joy of the Ikṣvākus, undergoes a transformation;
so too do kings organized into guilds, as well as other Kṣatriya rulers. ||444||
Of those kings renowned as belonging to the lineage of Aila, as well as those of the Ikṣvāku dynasty,
there were a full one hundred royal families who underwent consecration.
The extent of the Bhojas is recorded as being twice that;
the Kṣatriyas occupy thirty [yojanas], divided fourfold according to the directions.
Learn now from me those who have passed away among them:
there were indeed one hundred Prativindhyas, along with a hundred elephants and a hundred horses.
There were one hundred and one Dhṛtarāṣṭras, eighty Janamejayas,
a hundred Brahmadattas, and a hundred Śīris and Vīris.
Then there are a hundred cities of measurement, such as Śveta, Kāśa, Kuśa, and others;
beyond those are another thousand, which are known as the Śatabindus.
They all performed horse-sacrifices with gifts of a hundred thousand;
thus have hundreds and thousands of royal sages passed away during this current interval of Vaivasvata Manu.
Learn from me how their lineages are recorded as having arisen in the world. ||451||
Now, it is not possible—even in hundreds of years—to describe in detail the succession of those continua through their prior and subsequent connections. (452)
Twenty-eight cycles known as Yugas have passed within the Vaivasvata Manvantara;
learn now of those remaining along with the royal sages (rājarṣis). 453.
And there will be forty more, along with the kings,
who are distinguished as the narrators of the Yugas until the end of the Vaivasvata Manvantara.
All this has been told to you both concisely and in detail;
because of its vastness, it could not be recounted even in the course of many ages.
These twenty-five sons of Yayāti, beneficial to the people, have been proclaimed;
they are immeasurable, and indeed they sustain the worlds.
And one obtains here in this world excellent things that are difficult to attain:
long life, fame, wealth, sons, and one enjoys an infinite heaven. ||457||
"Indeed, by means of retention and hearing, they uphold these worlds.
Thus, O twice-born ones, this third quarter has been explained to you in detail and in its proper sequence; what more shall I relate? (458) 98.464.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, named the Anuṣaṅgapāda, in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Thus ends the section on the supplementary topics.
Having heard the third quarter recited by the wise Sūta,
those best of sages then asked for the fourth quarter.
The sages said:
"This third quarter has been traversed by you as a supplement;
now proclaim the fourth quarter, the dissolution, in detail. (2.38.2)
All the previous Manvantaras, along with those that follow, as well as the current interval of the present Manu and his Seven Sages, [have been described]. 2.38.3.
Tell me everything— the details of the components and the very nature of that great-souled one— in full detail and in proper sequence.
Sūta said: O best of sages, I shall relate all of this to you exactly as it is— this fourth book, together with its conclusion.
O twice-born ones, hear in detail and in due order this account of the creation of the high-souled Manu Vaivasvata, the one of the present age. 2.38.6.
Listen as I speak in brief of the seven future Manvantaras, along with the dissolution of the worlds. 2.38.7.
These seven Manvantaras have indeed been correctly described by me in brief; now hear from me about those that are yet to come.
I shall proclaim the future descendants of Sāvarṇi, the son of Vivasvat; listen as I describe them in brief. 2.38.9.
And seven great rishis are likewise remembered here as those yet to come:
Kauśika, Gālava, and Jāmadagnya of the Bhṛgu lineage; || 2.38.10 ||
Dvaipāyana, Vasiṣṭha, and Kṛpa Śāradvata,
as well as the radiant Ātreya and Ṛṣyaśṛṅga Kāśyapa.
Bhāradvāja, as well as the son of Droṇa, the highly illustrious Aśvatthāman—
these seven high-souled ones shall become supreme ṛṣis in the future.
The Sutas, the Amitābhas, and the Sukhas are the three classes;
each of these classes of gods is recorded as consisting of twenty [deities].
I shall declare their names; listen with concentrated minds:
Rita, Tapa, Śukra, Dyus, Jyotis, and Prabhākara. (2.38.14)
Prabhāsa, Bhāsakṛt, Dharma, Tejoraśmi, Ṛtu,
Virāj, Arciṣmān, Dyotana, Bhānu, Yaśas, Kīrti, Budha, and Dhṛti—
these twenty are celebrated by name as the Sutapas. (2.38.15)

The Lord, the All-pervading, the Radiant, the Conqueror, the Destroyer, the Slayer of Enemies, the Season, the One of Excellent Intellect, the Wise, the Splendorous, he who is celebrated as the Great and the Supreme. 2.38.16.
Deha, Muni, Naya, Jyeṣṭha, Sama, Satya, and Viśruta—these indeed are proclaimed as the twenty of immeasurable splendor. (2.38.17)
Dama is the giver; Soma is the knower; Yama is the possessor of knowledge and the treasure-trove;
Homa is the oblation, the offering, and that which has been sacrificed; Dāna is the gift, the thing to be given, and the donor; Tapas is tranquility. || 2.38.18 ||
Dhruva, Sthāna, Vidāna, and Niyama— these twenty are indeed declared to be the principal ones in the first interval (antara) of Sāvarṇi.
These sons of the high-souled Kaśyapa Mārīca shall belong to the present Sāvarṇi Manu in the future.
In former times, Bali the son of Virocana was their Indra—
he who was heroic, most excellent, free from delusion, truthful in speech, and skillful.
Cariṣṇurājya, Viṣṇu, and Sumati of the Speech—
these nine shall indeed be the sons of Sāvarṇi Manu.
And I shall describe nine others during the intervening periods of the Sāvarṇi Manus;
these other future Sāvarṇi Manus are indeed the sons of Brahmā.
Those Merusāvarṇis were indeed seen by those with divine vision;
for they were the grandsons of Dakṣa, the sons of his beloved daughter.
Endowed with great ascetic power and immense energy, they were born upon the summit of Mount Meru by Brahmā and others, as well as by the wise Dakṣa himself.
Having returned from Maharloka, we shall reside on Mount Meru;
for due to our great majesty, we were born previously during the Cākṣuṣa interval.
The sages said: "How could sons born by Dakṣa from his own daughter be [the offspring] of Brahmā, the high-souled one, according to dharma? (2.38.27)
Sūta said:
Therefore, having paid homage to Pracetas, I shall describe those who will be the Sāvarṇi Manus, as well as their births and their power. 2.38.28.
For when Vaivasvata had touched [the end of his period] and Cākṣuṣa had only a little remained,
those Manus were born who belong to the future intermediate periods.
The sons of Manu who were the grandsons of Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, are five by name; four of them were born of supreme ṛṣis.
Saṃjñā’s son was Sāvarṇa, and there was also one born of Vaivasvatī;
the eldest son of Saṃjñā, named Manu Vaivasvata, was the lord.
When the Vaivasvata interval arrived, their auspicious birth took place.
These fourteen Manus have been celebrated, who increase one’s fame. (2.38.32)
In the Vedas, the Śruti, and the Purāṇas, they are all described as sovereign lords;
they are all established as the lords of progeny and the lords of all beings.
By those lords of men, this entire earth— with its seven continents and its mountains—
is indeed to be protected for a full thousand yugas.
The expansion of these through progeny and through austerity will be described in detail;
these fourteen creations, beginning with that of Svāyambhuva, are to be known. (2.38.35)
They remain in their offices during the various Manvantaras, each for his turn;
once their office has ceased, they take refuge in Maharloka.
Of those who have passed away, eight were the first, and likewise six others;
among these, this present lord Vaivasvata Śānti is the seventh.
I shall proclaim those who remain, together with the celestial rishis and the dānavas, and all the twice-born ones yet to come along with the creation of future progeny. 2.38.38.
The detailed account of them should be known through the lineage of Vivasvat;
for they are all [descended] from Vivasvat, neither deficient nor redundant.
Because they are numerous, I shall not describe them in detail; for they have already been mentioned, and the same applies to those yet to be in future Manvantaras and those that have already passed.
Therefore, let there be natural dispositions in every family; for their sake, and for the benefit of the learned, I shall explain these further in detail and in due order.
The daughter of Dakṣa, renowned by the name Suvratā, was most righteous and firm in her vows;
she was the last of all his daughters, the most excellent and devoted to dharma.
Taking that maiden with him, her father went into the presence of Brahmā.
To Dakṣa, who was seated there worshipping Vairāja with both righteousness and devotion,
and who stood close to the nature of existence, Brahmā addressed him.
This daughter of Dakṣa, faithful to her vows, shall indeed give birth to four sons who will be Manus and the auspicious founders of the four castes.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Dakṣa, Dharma,
and Bhava— those three, together with Brahmā— then mentally approached that maiden.
To those who spoke only the truth, a daughter was immediately born,
and they begot four sons who were indeed similar and well-suited to them.
They were perfected in the performance of their tasks, endowed with splendor,
and possessed bodies that were newly born and capable of enjoyment.
Seeing those self-enlightened ones speaking thus, Brahmā then became agitated and began to pull them apart, saying, "He is my son! He is mine! || 2.38.48 ||
Through intense contemplation, those sons born from his mind spoke thus to one another:
"Whichever of us is equal in form to whom, let him accept that person as his son. (2.38.49)
"Let each of you take Subhadra, who is equal to him in appearance, in prowess, and by name; let him take her whose likeness she possesses. (2.38.50)
A son always conforms to the fixed nature of his father;
therefore, a son is born who is like himself to both his father and his mother.
Having thus made this agreement, they took sons who were of the same color (savarṇa) as themselves;
for that reason, the young sons of Brahmā and the others were indeed called Savarṇas.

Because they were of the same color (savarṇa) as him, they are indeed called Savarṇas; and because of their power of reflection (manana) and their authority (mānana), they are known as Manavas. || 2.38.53 ||
When the interval of Cākṣuṣa had passed and that of Vaivasvata had arrived, there was a son of the Prajāpati Ruci named Raucya. || 2.38.54 ||
The son who was begotten by Bhūti was named Bhautya;
he was the king during the Vaivasvata interval, for there were two Manus belonging to Vivasvat.
Vaivasvata Manu, Sāvarṇa, and the renowned one—these are the sons of Saṃjñā; the wise Vaivasvata Manu is the eldest and the lord.
Another son of Savarṇā is remembered as Vaivasvata Manu;
these are the four Manus, sons of Savarṇā, born of the great Ṛṣis.
Having perfected their selves through austerity, they shall indeed be the accomplishers of all purposes and goals during their own future Manvantaras.
First, during the interval of Vaivasvata Manu, there were three high-souled sons of Merusāvarṇi, the son of Dakṣa: the Marīcigarbhas and the Suśarmans; all of these were born together. (2.38.59)
These sons of Rohita, the Prajāpati and son of Dakṣa, shall belong to the future; for each one of them, there will be a group of twelve.
Aiśvaryasaṃgrāha, Rāghava, and likewise Bāhuvaśa—these twelve are to be known as the Pārās; now learn of the Uttaras.
Vājin, Vājinija, Prabhṛti, and Kakud;
Dadhikrāvan, Apakva, Praṇīta, Vijaya, and Madhu. (2.38.62)
From Tejasmān there were two; these twelve are the Marīcis.
Now I shall speak of the Suśarmans by name; listen to them.
Likewise, Varṇa, Aṅgaviśva, Muraṇya,
Vrajana, Amita, Dravaketu, Jambū, Usthā, and Ajasraśakrakas are considered [the lords of the quarters].
The Sunemīs, Dyutapās, and Suśarmans are proclaimed;
among them, Indra shall then be known by the name Adbhuta.
Skanda, who resembles the moon; Kārttikeya, the son of Agni;
Māghātithi, the descendant of Pulastya; and Vasu, the descendant of Kaśyapa. || 2.38.66 ||
Jyotiṣmān Bhārgava, Dyutimān Aṅgiras,
Vasita Vāsiṣṭha, and Havyavāhana Ātreya.
Sutapā and Paulava—these seven were born during the interval of Rohita;
they were Dhṛtiketu, Dīptiketu, Śāpahasta, and Nirāmaya. (2.38.68)
Pṛthuśravas, Nāka, Bhūridyumna, and Bṛhadratha—
these nine sons are proclaimed as belonging to the first Sāvarṇi.
Now, in the tenth period, during the interval of the Manu Sāvarṇi, the second son of Dharma who is yet to be, ||| 2.38.70 ||
The two groups known as the Sukhāmanas and the Viruddhas are remembered as being exactly two;
they are all radiant and equal in number, numbering one hundred each.
"Those among men who restrain their vital breaths have indeed been declared by the seers to become gods;
such will they be under Manu, the son of Dharma."
Among them, Indras will be Vidvān, Bhaviṣya, and Śānti;
Haviṣmān will be the son of Pulaha, and the illustrious Sukīrti will be the son of Bhṛgu.
Āpomūrti, as well as Ātreya, and he who is remembered as Vasiṣṭha;
Paulastya, Pratīpa, and Nābhāga Kāśyapa; and Abhinyu of the Aṅgiras lineage—these seven are the supreme ṛṣis. || 2.38.74 ||
Sukṣetra, Uttamaujas, the valiant Bhūriṣeṇa,
Śatānīka, Nirāmitra, Vṛṣasena, and Jayadratha.
Bhūridyumna and Suvarcas—these ten are remembered as the sons of Manu;
they belong to the third Sāvarṇi period, the eleventh cycle.
The Nirmāṇarati gods are indeed born of desire and possess the speed of thought;
these are known as the three classes of high-souled deities.
Each of those thirty hosts of the denizens of heaven consists of thirty members,
just as the wise know that there are thirty days in a month.
The Nirmāṇarati gods, the Rātris, and the Vihaṅgamas—
these three groups shall indeed constitute the deities.
The muhūrtas are said to be as swift as thought; thus they are proclaimed by the gods.
For these are remembered as the future Manus, the sons of Brahmā.
Among them, the future king of the gods shall be Indra, named Vṛṣa;
now listen as the seven ṛṣis of that period are being proclaimed. 2.38.81.
Haviṣmān Kāśyapa, Vapuṣmān Bhārgava, Vāruṇi Ātreya, and Bhaga Vāsiṣṭha; || 2.38.82 ||
Puṣṭi, the son of Aṅgiras, Niścara, the son of Pulastya,
and Agnitejas, the son of Pulaha, are indeed the gods in the eleventh interval.
Sarvavega, Sudharmā, Devānīka, Purovaha, Kṣemadharmā, Gṛheṣu, Ādarśa, and Pauṇḍraka are considered [the sons of] Mata. 2.38.84.
These were the sons of Sāvarṇa, the son of Prajāpati Manu;
now, in the twelfth period, there was indeed the Manu who was the son of Rudra.
Now hear concerning the deities in the interval of the fourth Manu, Ṛtusāvarṇi; five groups of future deities have been proclaimed. (2.38.86)
The Haritas, the Rohitas, the Devas, the Sumanasas, and the Sukarmans and Supāras— these are remembered as the five classes of gods.
For these are the mind-born sons of Brahmā; each group consists of ten, including Aruṃtuda, Hari, and the learned one who is known by the thousands.
Parvatānucara, Apongu, Manojava, Urja, Svāhā, Svadhā, and Tārā—these ten are known as the Harits. (2.38.89)
Tapojāni, Bhṛti, and he who is remembered as Vācābandhu;
likewise Rajas, Rāja, and Svarṇapādastha. (2.38.90)
Vyuṣṭi and Vidhi—these ten are indeed remembered as the Rohita gods;
those gods beginning with Uṣitā, who are proclaimed to be thirty-three in number. ||2.38.91||
Know the gods to be well-disposed; learn from those of good deeds: Suparvan, Vṛṣabha, Pṛṣṭa, Kṛṣi, Dyumna, and Vipaścit. (2.38.92)
Valor, progress, secrecy, and charm indeed.
These gods are performers of virtuous deeds; now learn of their sons as well.
Varyodita, Tathājiṣṭa, Varcasvin, Dyutimat, Havis, Śubha, Havikṛt, Prāpti, Vyāpṛtha, and Daśama as the tenth. 2.38.94.
These gods are indeed proclaimed as having well-crossed minds;
their Indra is to be known as the highly illustrious Ṛtadhāman.
Kṛti was the son of Vasiṣṭha, while Ātreya was Sutapas; Tapomūrti was the son of Aṅgiras, and likewise Tapastrī was the son of Kaśyapa.
The descendant of Pulastya lies in asceticism, as does Pulaha, who delights in penance;
the seventh among them is known as Bhārgava, whose mind is fixed on austerity.
These are the seven perfected ṛṣis; others will be in the Sāvarṇika interval:
Devavān, Upadeva, Devaśreṣṭha, and Vidūratha.
Mitravān, Mitrabindu, Mitrāsena—who is indeed the slayer of enemies—Mitrabāhu, and Suvarcas: these twelve were the sons of Manu.
In the thirteenth period, however, during the interval of Ruci,
three classes of gods alone were proclaimed by Svayambhū;
they were all the mind-born sons of the high-souled Brahmā.
Those three were Sutrāman, Sudharman, and Sukarman.
The hosts of the thirty-three gods, who were to drink the Soma juice and were destined to be worshipped by the performers of sacrifices, have been described as the future [Tridaśas]. (2.38.102)
With clarified butter, with speckled butter, and indeed with the most excellent draught, the thirty-three gods were [worshipped] by the gods; learn now of them individually.
Let the Sutrāmaṇas be the Prayājas; let those who consume the clotted butter (pṛṣadājya) be the Ājyās now; and let the performers of good deeds be the Anuyājas. 2.38.104.
The gods are proclaimed as the Upayājyas and the Sudharmas;
Divaspati, a being of great power, shall become their Indra.
They are to be known as the sons of Pulaha’s daughter; they were the children of Ruci.
Aṅgiras was born of her, as was the steadfast Paulastya Pathyavān.
Paulaṣṭha was a seer who perceived the ultimate reality; Bhārgava was free from desire;
likewise Ātreya was unshakable, and Kaśyapa was free from delusion.
Svarūpa and Vasiṣṭha—these seven are in the thirteenth [manvantara]: Citrasena, Vicitra, Tapa, Dharmadhṛt, and Bhava. (2.38.108)
Anekakṣatrabaddha, Surasa, Nirbhaya,
and Pṛthu— these were indeed the sons of Manu Raucya during the thirteenth interval (manvantara).
In the fourteenth period, during the interval of the Manu Bhautya,
five groups of deities are said to exist who will come into being.
The Cākṣuṣas, the Kaniṣṭhas, the Pavitras, the Bhājaras,
and the Vācāvṛddhas— these are remembered as the five groups of gods.
Know that those various portions are indeed seven, designated as the Cākṣuṣas;
they know those seven to be the youngest Sāmans beginning with Bṛhat.
Seven worlds are protected by them, and there are seven rivers flowing with waves.
Know that the Ṛṣis Vācavṛddha were indeed the sons of Svāyambhuva Manu;
all the Indras of the various Manvantaras are to be understood as possessing identical characteristics.
By their splendor, austerity, intellect, strength, learning, and valor,
those Indras indeed surpass all beings— whether moving or stationary— in the three worlds with their respective qualities in every respect.

Those who speak falsely of what has occurred are delighted; those who speak of what has truly occurred remain neutral; and those who merely repeat what has occurred are attached—such are the three types of speakers among the proponents of the Vedas. 2.38.115
Agnidhra, Kāśyapa, Paulastya, Māgadha,
Bhārgava, Agnibāhu, Śuci, Āṅgirasa, Ojasvin, and Subala— these were the sons of the Manu Bhautya.
These four sons of Brahmā were indeed the Sāvarṇa Manus;
one of them, the son of Vivasvat, is called Sāvarṇa Manu.
Raucya and Bhautya, who were the sons of Manu Paulaha and Bhārgava respectively—
under the sovereignty of Bhautya alone, the Kalpa is brought to its full completion.
Sūta said: When all the Manvantaras here have passed away without remainder, and at the end of those many Yugas that period has been exhausted, it is called the dissolution (saṃhāra). || 2.38.119 ||
Then, at the end of that Manvantara, these seven Bhārgava gods, having enjoyed their station in the midst of the three worlds for seventy-one Yugas, [departed]. || 2.38.120 ||
Together with the Pitṛs, the Manus, and the Seven Sages—
those who were performers of sacrifice and others who partook of that [merit] along with them.
The lords, having abandoned the three worlds, will go to Maharloka.
Then, when they have departed for the upper realm and that Manvantara has come to an end,
these three worlds will indeed become supportless.
Then, O twice-born ones, those abodes of the inhabitants became empty;
they fell away, being abandoned by the stars, constellations, and planets.
Then, when those lords of the three worlds, together with Indra and the [other] gods, had passed away here, they went to Maharloka, where those dwellers of the kalpa reside.
In all the Manvantaras, the groups beginning with the Jitas and ending with the Cākṣuṣas—those gods of great prowess—are indeed present here. 2.38.125.
Then, after they had departed for the state of union (sāyojya) with those who dwell in the Kalpa,
all those gods assembled when the time for their dissolution arrived.
Having abandoned Maharloka, those fourteen Gaṇas,
along with their followers, are indeed heard to have reached Janaloka in their very bodies.
Thus, when the gods had passed away from Maharloka toward Janaloka, and when all beings from the Bhūtas onwards, down to the immovable things, remained behind; || 2.38.128 ||
When the vast world-regions, beginning with the earth, have become empty,
and the gods have ascended above, there is the attainment of union (sāyojya) for those who dwell for a kalpa.
Then, having withdrawn those gods, sages, ancestors, and dānavas, Brahmā indeed establishes the creation once more through his great vision at the end of the age.
In this regard, those people who know day and night understand that the day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas, and his night likewise ends after a thousand yugas. 2.38.131.
This dissolution of all beings is threefold in its true nature: that which is occasional, that which is natural, and that which is ultimate. || 2.38.132 ||
The Brahma dissolution is occasional, consisting of the conflagration at the end of a kalpa;
however, the elemental dissolution is the destruction of the instruments [of perception] during the re-absorption of beings into primordial nature.
And from knowledge, the absolute non-occurrence of causes is proclaimed;
therefore, Brahmā, having withdrawn those gods who dwell in the three worlds, [entered the state of dissolution]. 2.38.134.
At the end of the day, he brings about the dissolution of creation once again;
then, desiring to sleep, the Lord Brahmā withdraws all living beings.
Then, when the end of a thousand yugas had arrived and the dissolution of the age was at hand,
that Lord of Creatures resolved to create the subjects, establishing them within himself.
Then there shall be a drought lasting for a hundred years;
likewise, those beings upon the surface of the earth who possess little strength.
Those very [elements] dissolve here and attain the state of earth;
then, having become a chariot with seven rays, the sun rose up.
The Blessed One, his rays unbearable as he drank up the waters with his beams,
shone forth with his seven green-colored rays.
They turn back once more, slowly pervading the forest;
