the earthly wood and wealth are intensely ignited by the fire, yet it blazes all the more with water.
Therefore, it is said that water belongs to the scorching sun;
the sun does not burn because of drought, nor is he encompassed by drought. ||2.38.141||
One does not discern the sun by its absence during drought; rather, it shines because of water.
Therefore, it is indeed by drinking water that the sun shines in the sky.
Those seven rays of his drink water from the great ocean;
inflamed by that food, the sun indeed becomes sevenfold.
Then those seven rays, having become suns, burned this entire fourfold world in all four directions with their flames.
And by their splendors, they reach upwards and downwards with their rays;
the seven suns blaze, scorching like the fire at the end of a yuga.
Though drenched with water, those rays of many thousands of beams remained pervading the sky,
utterly consuming the earth.
Then, scorched by their prowess, the earth—
with its mountains, rivers, and oceans— became devoid of moisture.
It was completely enclosed on all sides— above, below, and across— by the rays of the sun, which were blazing, continuous, and variegated.
When the suns and fires have increased in intensity and merged with one another,
having attained oneness, they indeed become a single flame.
Becoming a circular mass of fire that destroys all worlds,
he quickly consumes this entire fourfold world with his splendor.
Then everything, both moving and stationary, is dissolved;
the earth becomes devoid of trees and grass, resembling the back of a tortoise.
The entire world, scorched by Mārīca, shone like a frying pan;
the whole sky then blazed forth, filled with flames.
Those beings who are in the netherworld and those who have gone to the great ocean.
Then they dissolve and return to the state of earth.
The islands, the mountains, the regions, and the great ocean—
all that he reduced to ashes, for he is the all-pervading fire.
Drinking up water from the oceans, the rivers, and everywhere from the netherworlds,
the kindled fire blazed while resting upon the earth.
Then, having transcended the great mountains,
that blazing and terrible Saṃvartaka fire, the fire of universal destruction, consumes the worlds.
Then, having split the earth, he dried up the subterranean realm;
having consumed those regions of Pātāla, he then burned the world of the Nāgas.
Having burnt the earth below, he indeed burns the heavens above,
for thousands, tens of thousands, and even millions of yojanas.
Many crests of flame rose up from that Samvartaka fire;
then, blazing intensely, it consumed the Gandharvas, Piśācas, along with the Mahoragas and Rākṣasas, as well as the entire Goloka in every direction.
The fire of time thus consumes the four worlds— Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, and Maharloka— in their terrible heat.
When those worlds, extending horizontally and upwards, were pervaded by fire,
that heat gradually reached this entire world;
then everything shone forth like glowing iron balls.
Then, terrible clouds resembling herds of elephants, adorned with flashes of lightning, arise in the sky as the clouds of universal destruction (saṃvartaka).
Some were dark like the blue lotus, some resembled the white water-lily;
some were like beryl, and others were like sapphire.
Others were like conch shells or jasmine flowers, while others resembled pure black collyrium;
some clouds were smoke-colored, and some were yellow.
Some clouds had the color of donkeys, others resembled lac-dye; some were like realgar, and others were like pigeons. 2.38.165.
Some clouds arise in the sky resembling indragopa insects;
some have the form of mountains, and others are like herds of elephants.
Some were like mountains, some were clouds resembling level ground;
some resembled circular huts, and others were like schools of fish.
Then all the clouds, assuming many forms, terrible in appearance, and thundering with fierce sounds, fill the expanse of the sky.
Then those terrible clouds, which were of the nature of the sun and had enveloped themselves in sevenfold forms, extinguished that fire.
Then those clouds released a rain with great effort;
it was most terrible and inauspicious, and they extinguished the entire fire.
And when the world is completely filled with waters poured down in great abundance,
the fire, its brilliance overwhelmed by the water, then enters into the waters.
When the fire has been extinguished after a hundred years,
clouds born of maturation flood the entire world with the outpouring of vast nets of rain.
Filled with torrents and impelled by the Self-Existent One,
some rivers even overstep their banks;
at that time, the earth, along with its mountains and islands, is indeed submerged by the waters.
O Brahmins, all that water, completely encircled by his rain, enters the ocean after having been drunk by the rays of the sun.
Water drunk by the rays of the sun remains in the clouds;
it falls again upon the earth, and by that, the oceans are filled.
Then the oceans overstep their shores on every side;
the mountains crumble away, and the earth sinks into the waters.
Then, suddenly agitated, that terrible-souled wind in the sky enveloped those clouds on all sides throughout the firmament.
When that single, terrible ocean has arisen and all things mobile and immobile have perished,
and a full thousand yugas have passed, it is called the kalpa without remainder.
Then, when the world was enveloped by water, the wise call it the single ocean;
then, while the surface of the earth, the sky, and the wind were thus in the single ocean,
all things having perished and dissolved therein, nothing at all could be discerned.
Furthermore, the waters of the earth, those of the ocean, and those of the mountains—all flowing forth from every direction—attain the single name of "water. (2.38.180)
That water is known as being ever-flowing;
it remains covering the earth, and that water is called the ocean.

Because they shine with splendors—the word *bhās* being used in the senses of pervasion and light—and because it has reached all things as ashes (*bhasman*), therefore it is called *ambhaḥ*. 2.38.182.
The element *ara* is said to signify both diversity and swiftness;
because at that time there was but a single ocean, those men were not swift by means of it.
When that day of Brahmā, consisting of a thousand yugas, has passed,
the world likewise remains as a single ocean for that same length of time;
at that moment, all the activities of the Lord of Creatures cease.
Thus, when that single ocean has arisen and all things mobile and immobile have perished,
he then becomes Brahmā, possessing a thousand eyes and a thousand feet.
Thousand-headed, benevolent, thousand-footed, thousand-eyed, thousand-faced, and thousand-voiced;
thousand-armed, he is the first Prajāpati, the Puruṣa who is proclaimed upon the path of the Triple Veda. 2.38.186
Resplendent as the sun, the protector of the world, indeed unprecedented, unique, the first, the swift victor—Hiraṇyagarbha, the Great Puruṣa, truly exists beyond darkness. 2.38.187.
At the end of a thousand cycles of the four yugas, when everything has been submerged in water,
the Lord, desiring to sleep, makes his own night devoid of light.
When all creatures adorned with their respective eggs lie dormant in the fourfold manner,
the seven great ṛṣis behold that high-souled Time.
At the time of the dissolution of Janaloka, the high-souled Bhṛgu and others, whose characteristics have been previously described, attained divine vision through ascetic penance.
Indeed, with their eyes they behold the seven worlds beginning with Satya;
and during the nights of the Great Brahmā, they behold Brahmā himself.
The seven ṛṣis perceive the time of sleep during their own nights;
because he is the supreme lord of the kalpas, he is therefore recited as the primordial one.
He is the sacrificer for all beings again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas;
having thus infused [the world] into his own self, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) remains.
Then the one of great splendor, the doer of all, having withdrawn everything into himself,
dwelt there for a night upon the waters of the single ocean of darkness.
Then, when the end of the night had arrived, Prajāpati awoke and again directed his mind, intent on creation, toward the act of bringing forth.
Thus, when the world had ceased and the Lord of Creatures was stilled,
that Brahma-period, characterized by the dissolution of all things, came to its conclusion.
In that [state], the separation of beings from their bodies is indeed recorded as occurring entirely;
then, when all beings— including the gods, sages, and eminent men— have been consumed by the rays of the sun during that dissolution.
All beings, from the Gandharvas down to the Piśācas,
who have not yet been scorched by the heat at the beginning of the Kalpa, indeed take recourse to birth alone.
Then those beings belonging to the animal realm and even those who were denizens of hell were all completely consumed by fire, their sins shaken off;
they are reborn among human beings for as long as the world endures.
When the night has dawned, all beings indeed arise once again in their entirety from Brahmā, whose source is unmanifest:
the sages, the Manus, the gods, and all four classes of progeny.
Even for those perfected ones (siddhas), death and rebirth are said to occur here.
Just as the rising and setting of the sun are known in this world,
so too are the birth and cessation of beings observed here.
Therefore, because existence lasts until the dissolution of all beings, it is called *saṃsāra*;
for just as all beings are born here during the rainy season.
Just as stationary and other beings, as well as all creatures, appear in various forms through the succession of ages, even as the characteristic signs of the seasons recur in their proper turn.
Those very same things are seen likewise during the Brahmā-night;
they possess both motion and stability during the withdrawal and the creation.
All beings enter and emerge from Prajāpati, who takes the form of progeny—
Brahmā, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), the Great Yogi.
The great god, both manifest and unmanifest, is the creator of all beings again and again at the beginning of each kalpa; this entire world belongs to him.
By the very same path by which the waters first set forth upon this earth when they were created,
even so do other waters proceed, following that very same ancient course.
Just as they revolve here and there by means of both the auspicious and the inauspicious,
mortals indeed move upward and downward by the power of the sun, due to the nature of their existence within different bodies.

And those gods, humans, lords of creatures, and others who have attained the celestial realm as perfected beings (siddhas)—by virtue of their reputation being truly cultivated, those righteous beings become [such] again by their very nature. || 2.38.210 ||
Henceforth,

O twice-born ones, I shall declare the duration of time until the dissolution of all beings, including the fourteen Manvantaras that have been described by me, along with the creation of the intellect and the gods.
Indeed, all the intermediate periods (antarā) are called a thousand yugas;
when two full thousands of these have passed, it is called a complete Kalpa.
This should be known as a day of Brahmā; learn its duration:
a moment (nimeṣa) is indeed equal in measure to the time taken to pronounce a short syllable.
Fifteen twinklings of a human eye are known as a *kāṣṭhā*;
five *kṣaṇas* constitute a *lava*, and three *kāṣṭhās* make up twenty of those [lavas].
Seven *prasthas* of water are known as one *lava*, plus a fraction;
thirty *lavas* are to be known as one *kalā*, and thirty *kalās* make one *muhūrta*.
Furthermore, thirty muhūrtas constitute an ahorātra; this is the established rule.
An ahorātra consists of six hundred and three kalās.
Their number should be known according to the movement of the moon and the sun:
fifteen nimeṣas (twinklings of an eye) make one kāṣṭhā, and thirty of those make one kalā.
Thirty kalās are known as a muhūrta; a kalā is said to be a tenth part [of a muhūrta]. A muhūrta is designated as consisting of forty kalās. (2.38.218)
The muhūrtas and lavas have also been calculated by those who know the measures;
in that place, thirteen palas of water [are used as a standard]. (2.38.219)
A prastha of water is measured according to the Magadhan standard;
four such prasthas of water constitute a nālikā, which is also called a ghaṭa.
With four gold māṣas, each having a hole and measuring four finger-breadths [in circumference],
a muhūrta indeed consists of two nālikās, both by day and by night.
Due to the specific nature of their movement, among all men it is ordained that there is always an excess of six hundred and five kalās.
That day should be known as human; however, the lunar day (nakṣatra) is ten times longer.
By means of the solar month (sāvana), this year is remembered as human.
This is the divine day and night; such is the determination of the scriptures.
By means of this day, one calculates the number of months, seasons, half-years, and years.
Then this knowledge is bound; that which is perceived as ideation (saṃjñā) is designated as "time" (kāla) due to the precise measurement of its constituent parts (kalā). || 2.38.225 ||
That which is declared to be a day of Brahmā is remembered as ten thousand times two hundred million divine years,
plus ninety thousand [years], and likewise whatever others there may be. (2.38.226)
Having heard this, the sages were struck with the most wonderful amazement; they then asked one another about that knowledge which brings about the dissolution of worldly existence.

The sages said: We wish to hear, according to human reckoning, the duration of the dissolution in its proper measure, expressed in concise words and syllables that convey the essential meaning. 2.38.228.
Having heard them, that divine lord Vāyu, who delights in the welfare of the world and possesses divine vision, spoke to them in brief, O Blessed One.
These days and nights have been previously described here according to worldly convention;
having calculated their total number, I shall now declare the full extent of the years that constitute a day at the end of Brahmā’s life.
Four hundred and thirty-two million years,
as calculated by the twice-born according to human reckoning, constitute that duration.
Likewise, there are ninety-one hundred thousand and eighty thousand; such is the duration of the Plava [Manvantara].
Indeed, the period reckoned by human calculation lasts until the dissolution of all beings;
at that time, seven suns appear before those very worlds.
When the world has been flooded by water and all moving and stationary beings have perished, all four classes of creatures dissolve into the great elements.
When the dissolution had ceased and the Lord of Creatures was at rest,
when all was devoid of light and consumed by the night-fire,
this world was then presided over by Īśvara and enveloped in a single ocean.
The period until the day of the Lord occurs should be known as the single ocean;
the night is the state of being submerged in water, and when that ceases, it is remembered as the day.
In this same manner, his day and night revolve in succession;
indeed, this period until the dissolution of all beings is recorded as a single day and night of the Lord.
Whatever beings exist in the three worlds, whether mobile or immobile, dissolve back into the primary elements;
therefore, it is called the dissolution of all beings (ābhūtasaṃplava).
Because he was foremost among all beings, he is therefore called Bhūta Prajāpati;
because he floats upon the waters until the dissolution of all beings, he is therefore called Ābhūtasaṃplava.
In the eternal and immortal Word (Śabda), there is no dissolution until the end of all beings;
for past, present,
and future creatures have been reckoned by divine calculation as being multiplied by the factor of a hundred thousand million (an aparārdha).
Twice a parārdha is also proclaimed to be the supreme lifespan;
such is the duration of the stay here of the unborn Prajāpati Brahmā, the Parameṣṭhin, at the conclusion of his period of maintenance following the re-creation.
Just as the flame of a lamp is extinguished by the force of the wind,
even so Brahmā is completely extinguished by the process of reabsorption.
For thus, when Maheśvara is unassociated with the Mahat and the rest, the Mahat dissolves into the Unmanifest; from that, the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya) arises. ||2.38.243||
Thus has this dissolution at the end of all beings been described by me;
for this is the occasional dissolution of Brahmā, a restraint that effects a complete cleansing.
Thus it has been fully declared in brief; what more shall I tell you?
He who would constantly uphold this, or hear it repeatedly, shall attain great perfection through both its recitation and its hearing.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Manvantaras," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu. ||38||
In the Ānandāśrama edition, chapter 100,
Vāyu said:
"By the twice-born, through their extraordinary conduct and by means of the remnants of the oblations and so forth..."
And indeed by those experts in the specific qualities of phenomena (dharmavaiśeṣika), who perceive with the subtlest vision.
These inhabitants of Maharloka dwell together with the gods;
these fourteen Manus have been proclaimed, who increase one's renown.
Those who are past, those who are present, and likewise those who are yet to come—
along with the sages, the deities, and the gandharvas and rākṣasas.
In their offices during the various Manvantaras, the gods, the seven ṛṣis, the Manus, and likewise the Pitṛs, are born here again and again.
For all of them, having transcended the stages of worldly existence, have taken refuge in Maharloka together with righteous Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, O gods. ||2.39.5||
By those who act truthfully, who are disciplined, endowed with faith, and free from pride,
and who remain steadfast in the duties of the castes and stages of life according to the Śruti and Smṛti,
their authority shall cease to exist until the end of the Manvantara.
The sages said:
"O Lord Mātariśvan, regarding that which was mentioned by you as Maharloka—what must be done in each of those worlds, and by whom are they presided over? (2.39.7)
O Lord, tell us with affection how many worlds it is that are not consumed by fire; for you indeed know this exactly as it is.
Thus addressed by the self-disciplined sages, Vāyu,
the knower of reality, spoke these sweet words according to the truth.
Vāyu said:
"The great seers have described exactly fourteen abodes known as worlds, in which human beings reside. (2.39.10)
Among them, they say that seven are "done" (kṛta) while seven indeed are "not done" (akṛta);
the seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ are enumerated here as being "done."
But those seven uncreated primordial abodes,
together with their inhabitants, have indeed been made into a bond.
The earth, the atmosphere, and that which is known as the divine and the great—
these four regions are remembered as being filled with oceans.
Those which are occasional and characterized by decay and excellence will likewise be described; they endure until the dissolution of all beings.
Janasthāna, Tapasthāna, and Satyaloka— these three places are exclusively inhabited by beings of pure goodness (sattva), remaining here due to their lack of worldly attachment.
I shall now declare these seven clearly defined worlds:
Bhūrloka is the first among them, and Bhuvar is recorded as the second.
The third is to be known as Svarga; the fourth is indeed remembered as Maharloka;
Janaloka is the fifth world, and Tapoloka is considered the sixth.
Satya is the seventh world, and beyond that is the lightless realm (Nirāloka).
From the first utterance "Bhūḥ," the world of Bhūr-loka then came into being.
When "bhuvaḥ" was uttered for the second time, the intermediate space (antarikṣa) came into being;
when "svar" was uttered for the third time, heaven (div) indeed manifested.
By means of these three utterances, he fashioned the world of Brahmā;
from them, the earthly realm became *bhūḥ* and the intermediate space was known as *bhuvaḥ*.
Indeed, Svarloka is the heaven; this is the certainty established in the Purāṇa.
And Agni is the lord of beings; therefore, he is remembered as Bhūtapati.
Vāyu is the lord of Bhuvaḥ; therefore Vāyu is the master of Bhuvaḥ.
Sūrya is the lord of Bhavya; therefore Sūrya is the master of Divaḥ.
By means of the sacred utterance (vyāhṛti) "Mahas," Maharloka was thus produced;
there indeed is the abode of the gods whose offices have ceased.
Janas, however, is the fifth world; from it, indeed, people (janas) are born. It is called Janas because of the birth of those progenies, beginning with the Svāyambhuva [Manu]. || 2.39.24 ||
Those [sages] beginning with Svāyambhuva who were previously celebrated,
when the world is consumed by fire at the end of the kalpa, they then establish themselves in austerity.
Or "Tapa" refers to that place where the Ṛbhus, Sanatkumāra, and others who are perpetual celibates dwell, their souls purified by austerity. (2.39.26)
"Satya" is a term for Brahman; it is remembered as pure existence.
The world of Brahman (Brahmaloka) is therefore Satya; that is the seventh [world], and it is the realm of the Sun.

The Gandharvas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, Guhyakas, along with the Rākṣasas; all the Bhūtas and Piśācas, the Nāgas together with humans; all the gods dwelling in the heavenly world and those residing upon the earth—[all these were summoned]. 2.39.28.
The Maruts, Mātariśvan, the Rudras, the gods, and likewise the two Aśvins—those dwellers of the sky who have no fixed abode, belonging to the intermediate space and the realm of Bhuvaḥ. || 2.39.29 ||
The Ādityas, the Ṛbhus, the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, and likewise the Pitṛs, as well as the Aṅgiras Ṛṣis, have taken refuge in the Bhuvarloka.
These are the Vaimānika gods who dwell among the stars and planets;
thus have these, born from the speech of Brahmā, been described in order.
The worlds beginning with Bhūrloka and ending with Mahat are recorded as being composed of the subtle elements (tanmātras); they are pure in relation to one another. 2.39.32.
Those who have passed away, beginning with Śukra and ending with Cākṣuṣa, who resided upon the earth— the fourth world is Maharloka, and there they dwell for the duration of a kalpa.
Those seven suns indeed consume with their flames all those worlds beginning with Bhūrloka and extending as far as Mahat.
Marīci, Kaśyapa, Dakṣa, as well as Svāyambhuva, Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and others such as these. || 2.39.35 ||
All the lords of creatures dwell there together with them;
indeed, they are without vital essence and without the sense of "mine," for their seed is drawn upward.
R̥bhu, Sanatkumāra, and others, who are of the Vairāja class and rich in asceticism,
are recorded as the progenitors of all the Sāvarṇa Manvantaras;
they are the causes of the recurrence of all fourteen Manvantaras.
Having established yoga, austerity, and truth within their own selves, they return at the sixth period; however, they do so in the opposite manner during the reversal of that time.
Indeed, the world of Truth (Satyaloka) is the seventh world for those who have gone upon the path from which there is no return;
it is known as the Brahma-world, characterized by the absence of obstruction. || 2.39.39 ||
The terrestrial world (bhūrloka) is known as Samiti by virtue of its extent;
that which lies between the earth and the sun is the intermediate space (antarikṣa), known as Bhuvaḥ. || 2.39.40 ||
The space between the sun and Dhruva is known as the heavenly world (svargaloka); the space between Dhruva and Janaloka is called Maharloka. (2.39.41)
The seven worlds are indeed well-known; I shall describe their perfections:
all those dwelling in Bhūrloka subsist on food and consist of the essence of taste.
All those who drink Soma and drink clarified butter on earth and in heaven,
as well as those who dwell in the fourth world, having taken refuge in Maharloka— ||2.39.43||
Their mental accomplishment should be known as having five characteristics;
by their mere thought, everything desired arises instantly. 2.39.44.
These gods indeed worship one another with all sacrifices—
those who have passed away, those who are present, and those yet to come.
Having worshipped with the first and the subsequent [mantras], and again with the intermediate and the present ones, he then returns;
thus there is no further connection once the host of gods has passed away.
For those whose mental dispositions have ceased, their accomplishment is indeed mental;
for them, that mental succession of accomplishments should be known as pure. (2.39.47)
O Brahmins, I have thus briefly described to you the four worlds and likewise the conduct of people; I shall now describe that to you further.
Vāyu said:
Marīci, Kaśyapa, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu—these and others [are the sages]. 2.39.49.
First, they are brought forth here by the mind of Brahmā;
then, having established their progeny, they take refuge in the very act of procreation itself.
At those times,
indeed, when the worlds beginning with the earth and ending with the Mahat-tattva are intensely pervaded by fire, blazing with the conflagration at the end of the kalpa.
The Śikhā and Saṃvartaka [fires] are to be known as those which people always encounter;
likewise, all the hosts beginning with the Yāmas, who dwell in Maharloka. ||2.39.52||
When the Maharlokas are ablaze, they take refuge in Janaloka alone;
remaining there, they all exist in subtle bodies.
Possessing equal power and assuming similar forms,
they dwell in Janaloka as long as the world endures until the final dissolution.
When the night has passed, at the beginning of the day of Brahmā, whose source is the unmanifest,
they are born here again in due order, just as before.
All the practitioners beginning with Svāyambhuva and ending with Marīci are indeed gods;
they are born again here at their deaths. (2.39.56)
The Yāmas and the others were born from Prajāpati in successive order, beginning with the youngest;
each preceding one was born first, and each succeeding one followed after.
In the lineage of the gods, seven divine origins are recorded;
of those born in the Kṛta age, three have passed away, and likewise, others remain.
Those gods, returning in succession and not all at once,
went ten times to the city of Javanta and returned again and again.

Then all those hosts, having perceived the impermanence of worldly states through the power of the inevitable future and by the force of the renown of their own merit, [became dispassionate]. || 2.39.60 ||
With all their mental activities ceased, established in themselves and well-disposed,
they abandon that world of men and are reborn in the Vairāja realm.
Then, at another time, those ascetics, ever devoted to their practice,
were born in their lineage through the very discourse of Dharma.
Once born here, they indeed fill those stations in every way— in the state of gods, in the state of sages, and in the state of humans.
Thus all the hosts of gods, having indeed returned ten times, were reborn among the Vairāja deities; they remain there for ten upaplavas.
Then, at the completion of each full kalpa, having remained again in the realm of the Vairājas,
they evolve in the Brahma-world according to their previous sequence.
When this Vairāja Kalpa in the world of Brahmā had passed away,
some others again fashioned the Vairāja as the place for the duration of a Kalpa.
Thus, by proceeding in due order through the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā,
when those stages have been traversed and fashioned through austerity,
they are reborn in the Vairāja world; there they remain for ten cycles before returning.
In this manner, thousands of divine ages have passed here,
as they have gone to their end in the world of Brahmā along with the ṛṣis.
Sūta said:
It is not possible to describe their detailed account in sequential order,
because time is beginningless and all things are beyond numbering in every respect.
In this very way, there is no doubt, exactly as it has been told by me.
Having heard the meaning of those words, the ṛṣis, filled with doubt,
spoke to the high-minded Sūta, the knower of the Purāṇas and disciple of Vyāsa.
The sages said: "Tell us truly what their food was, what their nature was, and what their support was; and for how long they remained as Vairājas."

Having heard those words spoken by the seers, Sūta Paurāṇika, who knew the true nature of the world, spoke these words with humility: taduktamṛṣibhirvākyaṃ śrutvā lokārthatattvavit| sūtaḥ paurāṇiko vākyaṃ vinayenedamabravīt|| 2.39.72 ||
Then all those who were pure and most purified attained [that state]; those ten persons remain there until the dissolution of all beings. 2.39.73.
All those wise ones possess subtle bodies and are of solid form; because they remain even when the worlds cease to exist, no [material] element exists for them.
When their turn had arrived, the perfected ones (siddhas) who follow the path of yoga, headed by Sanatkumāra,
spoke regarding their occasional manifestation.
Then, their minds turned simultaneously toward abandoning their positions; all those of pure intellect spoke thus to one another regarding the Vairājas.
In this very way, O highly fortunate ones, having entered the Praṇava and proceeding to the world of Brahmā, that will be our supreme good.
Having spoken thus, all those who were resolute then gathered around Brahmā;
having joined together, they all proceeded as practitioners of the yoga-dharma.
Right there they were completely dissolved, like the flames of a lamp that have been extinguished;
they entered the body of Brahmā, from which a return to this world is difficult to attain.
Having reached that world consisting entirely of meditation, and having attained the bliss of Brahman, they have all gone to immortality. ||2.39.80||
Likewise, sixfold above the Vairājas, in the intermediate space,
is declared to be the world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka), where Brahmā resides as the presiding priest.
All of them, being of the nature of the Praṇava and purified by the austerity of awakening, having attained the bliss of Brahman, indeed partake in immortality. ||2.39.82||
Devoid of the three states of being, they are not overcome by pairs of opposites;
equal to Brahmā even without sovereignty, those sages possess great splendor.
Through their power, victory, sovereignty, stability, detachment, and insight,
all those inhabitants of the world of Brahmā attained a state from which there is no return.
When the period of reabsorption has arrived along with Brahmā and the gods,
at the end of their austerity, those wise ones who perceive the moment— their nature being action and their state being intellect— all these dissolve into the unmanifest.
This is the immortal, pure, eternal, inexhaustible, and undecaying Brahmasatra; the divine sages worship this as the eternal sacrifice.
The purification resulting from the practice of ritual action is observed in the Vedāntas for those who have entered the path of non-return and for those whose vital energy flows upward. (2.39.87)
There, those practitioners, disciplined and devoted, reach the supreme goal;
having abandoned the body and all evil, they have gone to immortality.
Free from passion, having conquered anger, devoid of delusion, speakers of truth, peaceful, self-controlled, compassionate, and masters of their senses. (2.39.89)

Those heroes who are free from attachment and pure, having burnt away their sins through austerities performed without desire, are said to attain union with Brahman; for them, the worlds are recorded as being imperishable and of immeasurable bliss.
This is the divine station of Brahman, supreme and radiant in the ether;
having gone there, the immortals, together with Brahmā, do not grieve.
The sages said:
"Why is this called the 'parārdha,' and what is this 'para' that is spoken of? We wish to know this; O best of beings, explain it to us. (2.39.92)
Sūta said:
Listen to me regarding the *parārddha* and the enumeration of what follows it:
one, ten, a hundred, and a thousand according to the system of counting. (2.39.93)
One thousand is to be known as a *sahasra*, ten thousands as an *ayuta*; one hundred thousand is called a *niyuta* by the wise. (2.39.94)
Likewise, one hundred thousand times one hundred thousand is called an *arbuda*;
ten *arbudas* are a *koṭi*, and they know that one hundred *koṭis* is an *abja*.
The wise say that a thousand times ten million is a kharva;
they know that ten thousand times ten million is a nikharva.
A hundred thousand crores is called a *śaṅku*;
and a thousand times ten thousand crores, multiplied again tenfold,
those who know calculation call a *samudra*.
A thousand times ten million is called an ayuta; this is termed the middle.
A thousand times ten million niyutas is designated as the end.
A thousand times ten million koṭis is proclaimed as a parārdha;
the wise say that twice a parārdha is the supreme (parama).

They say a hundred is *paridṛḍha*, a thousand is *paripadmaka*; ten thousand is known as *vijaya*, from which come *niyuta* and then *prayuta*. 101.100 *Arbuda*, *nirbuda*, and *kharbuda* are likewise recorded after that.
Kharva, nikharva, śaṅku, and likewise padma. ||2.39.101||
The ocean, the middle [region], and then the higher and lower parārdhas—
thus, these eighteen are the places in the system of calculation.
One should know that these are designated as "hundreds" by the great seers;
the number of kalpas for the active half of Brahmā's life is recorded as a parārdha.
The remainder of his time is likewise [spent] until its end, when he is reabsorbed;
this is the supreme duration, calculated by me according to the highest number as a parārdha.
For his supreme valor, supreme longevity, supreme scorcher of foes, supreme power, supreme dharma, supreme knowledge, and supreme fortitude are all unsurpassed. ||2.39.105||
The Supreme Brahman, supreme knowledge, and even supreme sovereignty—there exists no being higher than that; nothing other than Brahman is found.
For this Supreme One stands beyond all things;
he is reckoned as the highest Brahmā, and half of that constitutes a Parārdha.
The calculable, the incalculable, and the eternal—this triad is what is called "calculable" when viewed through calculation, up to the point of the final limit (apārārdha). || 2.39.108 ||
When a heap is perceived, there is no numerical count; that is the characteristic of the incalculable.
He perceived the fivefold characteristic of infinity in what is called a mass of sand.
This has been thoroughly enumerated by the lords who possess divine vision because of their purity;
thus, being established in knowledge, one perceives everything as Brahman. ||2.39.110||
Having heard this, all those ascetics of Naimiṣa,
their eyes clouded with tears and their voices faltering with joy, spoke.
All those exponents of the Veda questioned Mātariśvan:
"O Blessed One, O Lord, how great is the distance to the world of Brahmā? (2.39.112)
The number is calculated by means of the yojana;
I wish to hear in truth the method for the yojana, as well as the measurement of the krośa.
Having heard those words of theirs, Mātariśvan, speaking with humility,
addressed them with sweet speech, exactly as he had seen it and in proper order.
Vāyu said:
I shall declare this to you; listen to what I wish to say.
From the unmanifest (avyakta), the manifest portion is indeed described as being exceedingly gross.
Ten parts of the great elements are said to constitute the gross [form] beginning with the primary elements;
and the atomic form of the primary elements is ten times greater than that.
The atom is exceedingly subtle; it is grasped by the intellect, not by the eye.
That which is most indivisible in the world is to be known as the atom.
That minute particle of dust which is seen when the sun shines through a lattice opening is declared to be the first of all measurements, the atom (paramāṇu). 2.39.118.
When there occurs a conjunction of eight atoms, it is designated as a *trasareṇu*; that is called a "lotus-dust" (*padmarajas*). (2.39.119)
Eight *trasareṇus* are known as one *rathareṇu*;
eight of those, when combined, are known by the wise as one *bālāgra*.

Eight tips of a hair of a young boy make one nit (likṣā), and eight of those make one louse (yūkā). They say eight lice make one barley-corn (yava), and eight barley-corns make one finger-breadth (aṅgula). || 2.39.121 ||
Twelve finger-joints are said to be the measure of a *vitasti*;
a *ratni* should be understood as twenty-one finger-joints.
Twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) make one cubit (hasta);
a fathom (kiṣku) should be known as two ratnis, consisting of forty-two finger-breadths.
The wise say that a bow is ninety-six finger-breadths;
this is recorded as one-quarter of a gavyūti in the calculation of distances.
A bow-staff, a yoke, and a nālī are equal in measure according to finger-breadths;
those who know calculation say that three hundred bows constitute a nalva.
Two thousand bows are taught to be one *gavyūti*,
and eight thousand bows are prescribed as one *yojana*.
By this very bow, one yojana is completed;
thus, a thousand of these should be known as the interval between two krośas of Śakra.
Listen to the distance to the end of Brahmā’s world as calculated by those expert in the knowledge of numbers, expressed in this reckoning of *yojanas*. 2.39.128.
The sun is one hundred thousand yojanas above the surface of the earth;
the moon is the same distance, one thousand yojanas, above the sun.
The entire circle of constellations shines above the moon, at a full hundred thousand yojanas from it.
A hundred thousand is the number reckoned for Meru, and again it is doubled;
each successive interval between the planets above the circle of the lunar mansions is likewise [reckoned].
Budha moves below all the lunar mansions (tārā) and planets (graha);
Śukra moves above him, and Lohita moves above him.
Above that is Bṛhaspati, and above him is Śanaiścara;
a hundred thousand yojanas above Śanaiścara [is Rāhu].
The entire constellation of the Seven Sages shines above;
it is perceived as being situated a hundred thousand *ṛṣis* high. (2.39.134)
He who, in that divine celestial chariot consisting of stars and having a small form,
is the son of Uttānapāda, is Dhruva, the central pivot in the sky.
I have thus explained to you the height of the three worlds in yojanas,
wherein the worldly worship of the gods takes place during the various Manvantaras.
Indeed, that sacrifice which is performed in this world by those belonging to the various castes and stages of life is traditionally held to be the cause of the stability of all the divine beings.
This triple world has been explained; now understand what lies above it.
Above Dhruva is Maharloka, where those who dwell for a kalpa reside;
its extent is one crore yojanas—this is the established conclusion.
In this [world], however, there are two crores of Maharloka and the others, where those who dwell for a kalpa reside;
it is there that the sons of Brahmā, Dakṣa and the rest, are remembered as the practitioners (sādhakas).
Beyond Janaloka, at a distance four times greater, is said to be Tapoloka,
where those Vairāja deities reside, who are free from the destruction of the elements.
Six times the distance from Tapoloka to Satyaloka is remembered;
that is called the world of Brahmā for those who desire not to return to death.
Because he does not fall away from there again, he worships Brahmā;
[the distance] is one hundred million and five million yojanas.
Above that, the upper portion of the cosmic egg is said to be beyond the world of Brahmā;
it measures four crores and sixty-five lakhs [of yojanas].
This is its movement at half-velocity, and another state is recorded as its ultimate motion;
this has been explained up to the point of Dhruva, according to the measurements in yojanas as they were heard.
I shall describe the arrangement of the abodes for beings destined for the lower realms—
those places where living beings of terrible deeds go on account of their actions.
The hells are Raurava, Rodha, Sūkara, and Tāla,
as well as Taptakumbha, Mahājvāla, Śabala, and Vimocana.
Kṛmi, Kṛmibhakṣa, Lālābhakṣa, Viśaṃsana, Adhaḥśiras, Pūyavaha, and likewise Rudhirāndhas. || 2.39.147 ||
Likewise Vaitaraṇī, Kṛṣṇa, and Asipatravana;
the most terrible Agnijvāla, as well as Saṃdaṃśa and Śvabhojana.
Tamas, Kṛṣṇasūtra, Loha, Asija,
Apratiṣṭha, Vīci, Aśva, Naraka, and others such as these.
All the hells situated within the domain of Yama are characterized by darkness;
therein, those who have performed evil deeds fall individually.
All those [hells] beginning with Raurava are proclaimed to be situated beneath the earth.
A man who gives false testimony, he who makes a false accusation, or he who speaks untruthfully during the fortnightly judicial session of a cruel planet, falls into Raurava. (2.39.151)
One who kills a cow, one who kills an embryo, one who sets fire to a city,
one who kills a Brahmin, one who drinks liquor, and a thief of gold— all these should immerse themselves in a pit of swine.
A killer of a Kṣatriya shall fall from his status at the very moment of the blow; having killed a Vaiśya, he likewise incurs misfortune.
This applies equally to one who commits the murder of a Brāhmaṇa and to one who violates the bed of his guru.
The one who goes to his sister, the king’s soldier, the seller of horses, and the guard of prisoners—these go to the Taptakumbha hell. (2.39.154)
He who sells a virtuous wife, he who abandons his devoted follower, and he who indeed approaches his daughter or his daughter-in-law in the Great Fire— [these go to that hell].
He by whom the Veda is sold, he who defiles the Veda, those who insult their gurus and strike them with verbal abuse; || 2.39.256 ||
A man who approaches a woman who should not be approached goes to the Śabala hell;
likewise, a thief who falls into delusion and violates the established moral boundaries.
He who travels a wicked path falls into the Kīṭaloha hell;
he who hates the gods and Brahmins, who fails to honor his gurus, and who defiles precious gems, falls into the Kṛmibhakṣya hell. (2.39.158)
He who alone eats while another—a Brahmin, a friend, or a son—is present, falls into the foul-smelling hell of Lālābhakṣa. (2.39.159)
The maker of arrows, the potter, the one who removes gold coins, the physician,
and he who sets fire to groves— he falls into the Viśasana hell.
He who accepts gifts from the unworthy, he who performs sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice,
and the man who lives by the stars— all these go headfirst downwards.
One who sells milk, liquor, meat, lac, perfumes, flavors, sesame seeds,
and other such items, shall fall into the terrible hell known as Pūyavaha.
He who binds together cocks, cats, pigs,
birds, deer, and goats— he too shall go to that hell.
An Ājīvika, a Māhiṣaka, one who lives by the discus-banner, a Brahmin who subsists on the stage, a fowler, or one who performs sacrifices for a village; ||2.39.164||
A maker of arrows, a tailor, and one who betrays his friend;
"These fall into the Rudhirāndha hell," so say the wise.
Those who feed unequally to those seated in a single row fall into a terrible hell called Viḍbhuj; of this there is no doubt.
The man who is a liar, as well as one who is foul-mouthed and impure,
that evildoer shall fall into a terrible hell filled with urine.
Men who seize honey, those who strike down others, those who are insane, those whose minds are shattered, and those who are devoid of purity and right conduct, go to the Vaitaraṇī river.

The wrathful, the givers of pain, the deceitful, and those who travel by plowing; likewise, those who cut down trees in the Asipatravana forest and those who slaughter sheep are dragged along with saws by most terrible hunters of deer.
Those who have fallen away from their hermitages fall indeed into the flames of fire;
they are devoured by crows that are black-and-white, brindled, and have iron beaks.
If there is a lapse in the vow during a sacrifice, one shall fall into the Sandaṃśa hell;
likewise, if the observances of a celibate student are spilled even in a dream.
Those who are taught by their sons, and those who are commanded by their sons—
all of them certainly go to the hell Śvabhojana.
But those who, filled with anger and joy, perform actions contrary to the duties of their caste and stage of life—all such go to hell. 2.39.174.
Above is the great Raurava, white, terrible, and hot by nature;
below it is known as Tāpa, which is extremely cruel and cold by nature.
Understand that, described in this very sequence,
there are seven hells proclaimed to exist beneath the earth.
The sons of Adharma would be those such as Andhatāmisra;
among them, Raurava was the first, and Mahāraurava as well.
Below this, moreover, is another known as Śīta-tāpa;
the third is Kālasūtra, which is recorded as having various great hells.
The fourth is Apratiṣṭha; Avīci is remembered as the fifth;
Lohapṛṣṭha is among them, and Avidheya is the seventh.
Because of its terror it is called Raurava; Sāmbhaka is known as the burner; Sudāruṇa is of a cold nature, and beneath that is Tapa-adhama.
The serpent is said to be the cutter; it is the terrible Kālasūtra.
There is no standing ground in that which is without foundation, and therein lies a most dreadful whirling.
Avīci is declared to be terrible because of the crushing by machines; Loha is even more dreadful than that, and it is so called because of the exhaustion of one's karma.
Being of such a nature due to its corporeality, it is known as being subject to non-ritualistic [actions];
characterized by the lack of remedy for affliction, bondage, and slaughter. (2.39.183)
They are said to extend upwards for the measure of a mountain and are devoid of light;
indeed, in all of them, there is an intensification of suffering caused by unrighteousness.
Both of these are equal to the worlds above, yet both are devoid of light;
and the embodied being, led by the thread, is like a heap of glowing embers.
But by those actions capable of yielding immediate experience, they are born at once;
indeed, in all of them, the intensity of suffering and ferocity is traditionally taught.
Furthermore, the torments of the denizens of hell are recorded as being innumerable;
there, suffering is experienced again and again at every moment for the duration of one's karma.
When the remainder of their karma has been exhausted, they are born among the animal species;
for both gods and denizens of hell are situated above and below respectively.
Forms are produced instantly by means of merit and demerit;
their arising occurs through the karma of rebirth for the sake of experience. (2.39.189)
The gods see the denizens of hell as facing downward and situated below;
likewise, the denizens of hell see all the gods with their faces turned downward.
Since the nature of the dhāraṇās is rooted in the anagrama, therefore, in the Lokāloka mountain, there is no state of above or below. || 2.39.191 ||
"This is the natural designation that prevails throughout the world and the non-world.
Then the Brāhmaṇas performing the sacrificial session spoke again to Vāyu: || 2.39.192 ||
The sages said:
"All beings whatsoever who dwell in the worlds and the non-worlds,
and all living creatures here who wander through the cycle of existence— " 2.39.193.
"Having enumerated them by number, speak of them then in their entirety.
Having heard those words of the sages, Māruta spoke these words:
Vāyu said:
It is not possible to enumerate all living beings in any way whatsoever;
for they are without beginning or end, intermingled, and established through manifold inference.
Their enumeration is declared to have ceased due to their infinity.
O lord of men, he cannot be known by the divine eye, nor again by ordinary knowledge; indeed, he can only be fully discerned at the very end by the eye [of wisdom].
Because it is beyond meditation and cannot be known, no question regarding it is prescribed;
however, learn that which is designated by Brahmā through numerical enumeration. 2.39.197.
If there were a thousandth part of all stationary beings here,
that would be the number of earth-born worms produced from their sprinkling.
It has been determined with certainty that all aquatic creatures are equal in number to a thousandth part of those born from moisture. 2.39.199.

Of every thousand beings that dwell in the waters, only one part in a thousand is to be known as terrestrial birds; and of those birds, that which constitutes the thousandth part— 2.39.200. —indeed, that alone exists. 101.200. If there should be a thousandth part of those birds...
The four-footed animals of the world should be known as being similar to those [beings]. || 2.39.201 ||
In this world, bipeds are everywhere to be understood as being worth one-thousandth part of all quadrupeds. (2.39.202)
Furthermore, among the portion of bipeds,
those who are righteous are to be known as equal to that which is a thousandth part [of the previous].
Those who have gone to heaven from among the righteous are [only] by a single part in a thousand;
and whatever one-thousandth part of the righteous may exist in heaven,
those who seek liberation are indeed equal to that very part.
The torments of those who dwell in the regions of hell are equal to those that lead to heaven;
for those wicked souls who die by falling from a precipice, they experience both cold and heat in the dark Raurava hell. (2.39.205)
Those who have reached the place of torment, bitter with sensations and rigid, should know that Raurava is hot, consisting of a terrible essence of fire. (2.39.206)
Then there is also the one whose nature is dense and whose nature is cool, constantly performing austerity;
thus, virtuous men who are righteous are exceedingly rare even in heaven.
This enumeration was established by the Lord, the Self-Existent One;
this calculation, both divine and human, has thus been brought to its conclusion.
The sages said:
"Mahas, Jana, Tapa, Satya, Bhūta, Bhāvya, and likewise Bhava—
these worlds have indeed been mentioned by you, as well as that which lies between the worlds."
And tell us exactly as it is what the other world is like.
Having heard those words of the sages who were perpetual celibates,
that Vāyu, who had perceived the true nature of reality, spoke this truth.
Vāyu said:
"Those whose nature is action perceive the manifest through reasoning; those who see directly perceive it through yoga, withdrawal of the senses, meditation, and austerity. (2.39.211)
The Ṛbhus, Sanatkumāra, and others—perfectly awakened ones of pure intellect, free from sorrow, stainless, virtuous, and the best among beings, like Brahmā himself. (2.39.212)
Endowed with inexhaustible joy, O Brahmā,
those yogins abide just as it was brought forth by the lords among the Vālakhilya sages.
And just as it was seen by me while remaining present there,
so too is that which is the abode of the Lord for those whose purposes have been honored and fulfilled.
The Lord, due to his atomic nature, is perceivable by the wise as a pure existence;
he is knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, austerity, truth, forgiveness, and fortitude. (2.39.215)
The state of being a seer, connection with the self, and the state of being the substratum—
these ten imperishable qualities abide in that Śaṅkara.
Indeed, by virtue of his sovereign power, the fire of Yoga, intent upon favoring Brahmā,
assumes a physical form in the world and stands ready to provide assistance.
The syllable is eternal, unwavering, and free from the eight types of calamities;
it is the supreme abode of that Lord, consisting of the nature of Māyā.
The illusory Lord Maheśvara declares that which is created by illusion;
for the withdrawal of the gods is proclaimed to have that as its authority.
Listen as I describe it to you in detail and in proper sequence:
the distance from the world of Bhūr to the world of Brahmā is proclaimed to be exactly thirteen crores and fifteen million yojanas. (2.39.220)
The Egg of Bhagavat is recorded as being one hundred and fifty million yojanas in height,
situated above the world of Brahmā.
This upward movement is indeed the limit of their course; they are eternal, innumerable, and mutually dependent upon one another's qualities. (2.39.222)
Subtle and characterized by productivity, they are therefore known as the primal natures (prakṛtis);
from them was born the presiding agent, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is designated as Brahman.
Within them is the primordial, subtle, and imperishable state of presiding;
it is the unproduced, supreme abode, the ultimate atom, and the domain of the Supreme Lord.
He is imperishable and yet subject to dissolution; he is formless and yet possesses form;
he is manifestation, disappearance, persistence, and grace.
The supreme Lord Maheśvara is the Creator, incomparable to others;
he is the radiant atom who shines beyond darkness as the illuminator.
The first staff was made of gold;
it was large, circular in every respect, and originated from the Lord as a premonitory sign of calamity.
The individual soul (kṣetrajña) is held to be non-different from the Lord as the seed;
the womb is declared to be primordial nature (prakṛti), and that is of the essence of Nārāyaṇa.
The pervasive Lord, for the sake of the creation of the world and its maintenance, manifested that emanation through his body; such is the cosmic realm of the Great-Souled One.
In front of the world of Brahmā and within the cosmic egg of Brahmā,
between those two, is his divine city, a place whose very substance is mind.
The abode of that embodied Lord of immeasurable splendor is the city named Śiva; therein lies the refuge for those who fear rebirth.
O best of the twice-born, it is fully one hundred thousand yojanas in extent within,
situated upon the circle of the earth.
With a great wall of gold, possessing the brilliance of the sun, which crushed the splendor of others with the light of the midday sun.
It was firmly and beautifully encircled by four golden doors, adorned with strings of pearls and shining like refined gold.
And that delightful, divine city in the sky resounds with the ringing of bells and other sounds;
there, death does not prevail, nor do austerity, old age, or fatigue.
Indeed, no other city can be compared to it;
it extends for a full hundred thousand yojanas in the ten directions.
That city stands pervaded by the splendor of the one whose emblem is the bull;
the ground, fashioned of gold, was laid down through the disposition of his mind.
Strewn there with precious sand, it shone exceedingly,
like the light of the autumnal moon and resembling the rising sun.
Half white and half red, they were likewise made of gold;
they were the size of chariot wheels and possessed stalks with the luster of emeralds.
With its delicate form and incomparable fragrance,
there were divine lotuses there in the groves and pleasure gardens.
Those which resemble the wings of a bumblebee, those which are to be heated,
and those that are half-black and half-red with delicate interiors.
Covered with lotuses as large as parasols, there are furthermore seven great rivers; learn their names.
Excellent, most worthy, bestower of boons, deserving of the best, possessed of excellent complexion, the giver of boons,
most auspicious, and delightful— these qualities were found in that supreme city.
The best of rivers carry water that resembles a surface of jewel-slab, mingled with the petals of lotuses and lilies, and possessing the form of whirlpools of foam. 2.39.244.
But neither the brahmin-sages, nor the gods, nor the asuras, nor the ancestors,
nor indeed any others know that city of the immeasurable Lord.

There, those high-souled ones— unperturbed, well-disciplined, and having conquered their senses— behold that city of the one whose nature is the bull among cows, while remaining absorbed in meditation.
In the center of that best of cities belonged to him of incomparable splendor,
there was a great, divine palace resembling Mount Meru, filled with auspicious beauty.
The palace has a thousand pillars, is made of refined gold, and is auspicious;
it is adorned on all sides with incomparable jewels.
With crystals resembling the moon, with lapis lazuli possessing the luster of the moon,
with [gems] having the radiance of the rising sun, and with golds possessing the brilliance of fire.
And it shone with beautiful pillars made of silver, as well as those consisting of sapphire and others made of solid diamond, all perfectly arranged.
It was consecrated with waters of various forms that were shimmering,
and it was adorned with banners as radiant as the rays of the moon.
With the sounds of golden bells, it was a place of constant joy and festivity;
it shone with the dwellings of the Kinnaras, which resembled the clouds of twilight.
Surrounded on all sides by retinues possessing the luster of golden flowers and water,
he shone like Meru, the king of mountains, with its peaks of gold.
Likewise, that city was adorned with banners made of gold;
thus did that king of palaces shine with its many stories.
In that abode of Tryambaka dwells Vasantapratimā,
as well as Lakṣmī, Śrī, Vapuḥ, Māyā, Kīrti, Śobhā, and Sarasvatī.

Indeed, these [goddesses] are always accompanied by the Goddess; they are endowed with beauty and fragrance, eternal, and beyond counting. They rely upon one another's virtues, serving as the ornament of all jewels and the source of loveliness and grace. (2.39.256)
A hundred crores of highly fortunate beings, dividing themselves by their own power,
joyfully attend upon the illustrious Great-Souled One without weariness.
Behind them were thousands of other female attendants,
all beautiful in form, endowed with splendor, and possessing lotus-like eyes.
Together with hosts who resemble mountains and are like fire, they rejoice with her through most enchanting states of being, joined with playful dalliance.
There were hunchbacks who fulfilled every desire, those with excellent limbs, and horse-faced beings;
there were also the Puṇḍras, the Vikaṭas, the Karalas, and those with flat faces.
Some had protruding bellies and short arms, some were eyeless and had short feet;
others had the faces of lions, and likewise the faces and bellies of elephants.
Likewise, there were others with the faces of elephants, as well as those with the faces of lions and tigers;
they had red eyes, large breasts, were fortunate, and possessed beautiful eyes.
There were beautiful women with short, curled hair and lovely eyes;
others were women capable of assuming any form at will, wearing various kinds of attire.
Surrounded by his inner retinue and accustomed to the dwellings of the gods,
the ten-armed Lord Maheśvara took his pleasure there.
And with Nandin, together with the hosts of great-souled ones who possess universal forms,
as well as with the hosts of Rudras who are equal in magnanimity and prowess.
Being praised and honored by those devoted to him, his celestial chariot resembled the son of Agni (Skanda), with its faces formidable with sacrificial posts for tusks.
He smelled a garland of flowers from all seasons resting upon his chest;
he was dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with large, copper-hued, and elongated eyes.
With slightly protruding, formidable lips, adorned by hosts with sharp fangs,
possessing six upward-gazing eyes, difficult to behold, and clad in beautiful bark garments.
Unwearied in battles and the destroyer of the enemies of the gods,
he stood with his arm pressed against my left side, his arm locked within mine.

As he pointed it out, there shone forth a bow of ten colors, exceedingly beautiful, held within the range of his left hand; it possessed a roar as terrifying as that of a great *bhairava* and was endowed with incomparable power and splendor. (2.39.270)
The trident, radiant as lightning, infallible, and the destroyer of enemies, blazed with its own form and was endowed with supreme splendor. ||2.39.271||
The sword, the best among weapons, and likewise the moon with its cool rays,
shone there exceedingly upon the sacrificial altar like a flame of fire— through the splendor, the form, and the radiance of the high-souled Lord of the Gods.
Standing before the god was a great, beautiful, and glorious vessel made of gold, filled with water and accompanied by a water-pot. 2.39.273.
Having placed the sword upon her limbs, she, clad in white garments,
resplendent with a great breastplate of pearls,
four-armed, highly fortunate, and honored by the world, was Vijayā. (2.39.274)
The goddess’s first female doorkeeper stood there resplendent, peerless like Śrī herself, having placed her hands in añjali before the god.
Following behind her were other women accompanied by throngs of Apsarases;
indeed, they waited upon Śaṅkara with ever-new and lovely offerings.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and augmented by their musical instruments,
the hosts born of the Gandharvas sing in accompaniment to the Lord of the Gods.
Tall and broad-chested, with a luster like an autumnal cloud,
the joyful Gopati shines resplendent in his dwelling.
And his son Skanda, possessed of immeasurable heroism, accompanied by his retinue,
was glorious, wearing red garments, with eyes like the petals of a choice lotus.
His sons were Śākha, Viśākha, and the powerful Naigameya;
they were free from malice and cruelty, and were devoted to the protection of living beings.
Accompanied by them, that great hero whose vehicle is the peacock shines resplendent;
there, the one whose face is everywhere sports with toy animals.
Those kings who were like lords of the gods and bestowers of gold, and those Brahmins who were householders living in their own dwellings and exponents of the Veda; ||| 2.39.282 ||
Those who perform secret Vedic study and ascetic penance, as well as those who subsist by gleaning grains—
these are the members of that assembly, and they are highly esteemed by the Lord of the Gods.
Many Manvantaras have revolved again and again;
now hear of the supreme wonder concerning the future of the God of gods.
And there were tigers as his followers, swift and golden-hued;
they all moved at their own will, created by the God himself.
They are indeed like death unto death, for they strip away the pride of Yama;
who, indeed, would not proclaim even their innumerable manifestations?
Henceforth, listen further to this most wonderful and supreme account of what was done for the sake of compassion toward all living beings. 2.39.287.
By the power of the lights of Mount Mandara and other peaks, which possess incomparable splendor,
they are white as pearls, jasmine, and the moon, and resound like the roar of lightning-charged clouds.
They indeed wear crest-jewels and garments resembling clouds;
they are marked with the Śrīvatsa and the vajra, and hold finger-rings and tridents in their hands. 289.
Thus, upon the pillars of that preeminent palace, which were most beautiful and possessed the forms of the gods of the quarters who excel in supreme splendor— 2.39.290.
But with separate chains made of restrained fire,
a thousand illusory lions were placed there for the comfort of the inhabitants.
Even at the pillar in the abode of Tryambaka, they did not withdraw for six [steps].
Then, having honored those words of Vāyu,
the ascetic sages of Naimiṣa, filled with great wonder, replied.
O Blessed One, O Prāṇa of all beings, O omnipresent Lord!
Who are those lions among great beings? Where were they born, and what is their nature?
By what offense against the powerful Lord of beings were these lions individually bound with nooses made of fire? (2.39.294)
Having heard those words of theirs, Vāyu spoke these words:
"Indeed, those thousands of lions,
who were formerly in the form of lions due to the wrath of the high-souled Lord, were cast out from his own body."
In former times, having granted fearlessness to all beings while bound by the bonds of fire for the sake of a sacrificial portion,
he did so then by the command of the Lord.
By that single lion, through his effortless play, their ritual was destroyed;
and knowing the wrath he had aroused in the Goddess, that sacrifice of Dakṣa was utterly ruined.
And then Mahākālī, the Great Goddess, emerged from her own self— the witness of her own actions— along with her attendant spirits.
This very Lord is Krodha, who has made his abode in the dwelling of Rudra;
he is Vīrabhadra of immeasurable soul, the effacer of the Goddess’s wrath.
I have described to you the incomparable abode of that Lord of the Gods, who is indeed the most secret of all;
hereafter, I shall declare those who dwell there.
In that delightful and most excellent of cities, upon the grounds of the celestial groves.
In places variegated with various jewels and abounding in many banners,
where every desire was fulfilled, and which were beautified by groves and pleasure gardens.
In those great palaces made of refined gold,
resembling twilight clouds and like unto Mount Kailāsa.
Those of virtuous conduct who follow the path of existence rejoice in those excellent palaces adorned with flowers, which possess desirable portions such as sounds and other sensory objects.
There were continuous sounds of Vedic chanting and various auspicious discourses,
along with the sounds of singing and musical instruments, and hymns of praise on every side.
And thus were incomparable [treasures], fashioned from various materials, gathered together;
such things as these were displayed upon the summits of their palaces.
The auspicious palace had a thousand pillars, was made of refined gold,
and was adorned on all sides with incomparable and excellent jewels.
With [palaces] made of crystal, resembling the moon; with the brilliant luster of lapis lazuli gems;
with others like the rising sun, and those made of gold, possessing the brilliance of fire.

Having heard this, the ascetic sages of Naimiṣa, overcome with doubt, spoke these words to Vāyu: 309. "The sages of Naimiṣa, those practitioners of austerity, having heard [this], became filled with doubt and addressed these words to Samīraṇa."
The sages said:
"Who are those high-souled ones there who follow Bhava,
who are most worthy of grace, and who rejoice perfectly in that supreme city?"
Having heard the words of the sages, Vāyu then spoke these words.
Vāyu said:
Listen to those by whom devotion to the God of gods has been cultivated:
they are modest, highly energetic, self-controlled, endowed with valor, and free from greed. (2.39.311)
They eat at midday and in moderation; they delight in the Self, have conquered their senses, and have mastered the pairs of opposites. Possessing great energy, they are gentle and free from envy.
Those who, remaining established in being, free from activity toward all creatures and undisturbed,
with purified action, mind, and speech, and with their inner self,
have become single-minded and have sought refuge in Maheśvara— 313.2.39.313.
By them was attained the eternal and imperishable state of sharing the same world as Rudra;
indeed, they were brought to a supreme resemblance to the form of Bhava.
All of them had Vaiśvānara as their mouth, possessed universal forms, and wore matted locks;
they were blue-throated with white necks, sharp fangs, and three eyes.
With uṣṇīṣas shaped like half-moons and wearing crowns of matted hair, all these heroes have ten arms and are fragrant within their lotuses. 2.39.316.
All of them resembled the rising sun, were clad in yellow garments,
held the Pināka bow in their hands, and all had white bulls as their vehicles.
Endowed with splendor, wearing earrings, and adorned with pearl necklaces, they surpassed even the gods in brilliance; they were all-knowing and all-seeing.
Having divided themselves into many forms and being freed from old age and death,
they sport with various dispositions, having obtained enjoyments that are very difficult to attain.
The Siddhas, who move according to their own will, were awakened by other Siddhas;
there were eleven crores of these great-souled Rudras.
For with these, the high-souled Maheśvara, the god of gods,
the Blessed One who is compassionate toward his devotees and beloved of Pārvatī, rejoices.
I do not perceive any diversity among these Rudras and the high-souled Bhava; I tell you this as the truth.
Mātariśvan spoke this meritorious account, and Īśvara as well.
Then all those sages, possessing a radiance equal to the sun,
having heard this supreme and holy narrative concerning Tryambaka, [were filled with wonder].
Having received great favor and unsurpassed joy,
and having honored that mighty Vāyu, they spoke to him.
The sages said:
"O illustrious Samīraṇa, O Lord, you have indeed told us of the eighth most excellent and meritorious austerity of the Lord, which wards off calamities. (2.39.325)
Its location and its measure have been duly proclaimed;
it is indeed the supreme abode of the Supreme Self, enriched with fragrance.
The majesty of Mahādeva is difficult to comprehend even for the gods,
owing to his own possession of majesty and his immeasurable power as the Thousand-eyed One.
For he possesses freedom from delusion toward his devotees and acts solely out of compassion for them.
She was personally graced by the splendor of Brahman, and she possessed an incomparable majesty.
Pervading the sky with moonlight and assuming a universal form,
the divine manifestation of the God of gods shines most intensely upon the celestial mountain.
All this, which flows forth like nectar from his mouth, belongs entirely to the high-souled Rudras who are equal to Mahādeva.
O you of excellent vows, although we have indeed drunk of everything with devotion,
there remains nothing unknown to us, nor anything else concerning our followers;
O best of gods, O Prāṇa, you ought to answer our question exactly as it is.
Sūta said:
That Blessed One indeed spoke: "What more shall I relate? And what must be told by me? That I shall speak, O you of excellent vows. (2.39.332)
The sages said:
"The Ādityas were on his flanks; the lions possessed the prowess of wrath;
the Vaiśvānara spirits were his hosts, and the tigers were his followers. (2.39.333)
At the time of the terrible dissolution of all beings, when every living creature has perished, what state do these [elements] come to? Tell us that according to the truth.
"These indeed are those who were mentioned by you, together with the hosts of lions and tigers; and others who have attained perfection—thus spoke Mātariśvan. (2.39.335)
And I shall declare this supreme truth for those who listen:
that the true nature of the Lord is known, as well as His unmanifest source.
Among them, those Kumāras who had arrived previously were the sons of Brahmā:
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana.
Among them were Voḍhu, Kapila, the highly illustrious Āsuri,
the sage Pañcaśikha, and others such as these.
Then, after time had passed and the succession of kalpas had come to an end,
when the destruction of the great elements was complete and the dissolution of the world had arrived.
The many crores of Rudras who are devoted to Maheśvarī [attain] the enjoyments of sense-objects, such as sound and the rest, through the eightfold path of truth.
Having entered into all beings with a splendor joined with knowledge,
he attained the unagitated state of the sky out of compassion for living creatures.
There the great-souled ones go to the supreme atom, Maheśvara;
they cross the river whose waters are birth and death and which possesses immense whirlpools.
Then they behold Śarva and the Supreme Brahman itself.
Indeed, together with the Goddess, there are seven goddesses who have been proclaimed.
That which was that thousand of lions and likewise of Ādityas—
Vaiśvānara, Bhūtabhavya, Vyāghra, and others likewise followed as attendants.
Having caused them all to enter into himself, he likewise enumerated those calamities.
All these seven worlds and the five great elements.
It unites with Viṣṇu and it also effects differentiation.
He is Rudra, who consists of the Sāman as well as the Yajus.
O twice-born ones, this very Lord, the Protector, is by certainty woven both lengthwise and crosswise, both outside and inside; he is the one, the non-existent, and the creator of weariness.
Then all those sages, possessing a radiance equal to the sun, placed the sacrificial fires within themselves and returned to their respective dwellings in the hermitages.
With purified action, mind, and speech, and with a pure inner self, they take refuge in Maheśvara, becoming single-minded in devotion. (2.39.349)
Devoted to vows and fasting, and intent upon compassion for all beings,
they have attained an incomparable and divine yoga, their doubts having been severed.
Having approached with supreme devotion and a mind endowed with knowledge,
they attained the eternal and imperishable state of the same world as Rudra.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or even a Vaiśya devoted to his own duties, who—endowed with austerity—should recite this hymn proclaimed by Vāyu; 2.39.352.
A Śūdra who does not drink liquor, who is devoted to Bhava, and who has conquered his senses, being full of devotion and free from feverish distress, attains the same world as Rudra.
Abiding until the dissolution of all beings and characterized by non-obstruction,
he attains the station of Gaṇeśa, or a place that fulfills all desires.
"The drinker of liquor rejoices together with other drinkers and with hosts of spirits;
being honored upon the surface of the earth, he becomes a granter of boons to mortals.
Thus spoke the blessed Vāyu, this excellent speech. (2.39.355) 101.355
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Excellent City of Śiva," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Chapter 101 in the Ānandāśrama edition:
Description of Pratyāhāra.
Sūta said:
I shall now declare the withdrawal (pratyāhāra) at the end of the supreme Self-existent One;
when the period of the Lord Brahmā’s maintenance has come to an end.
Just as the Lord, through his inner self, makes this universe exceedingly subtle,
so too does he swallow the manifest entirely within the unmanifest during the process of withdrawal.
But when the end of the kalpa was incomplete, at the onset of that supreme and most terrible dissolution which is imperceptible to anyone, (2.40.3)
When the end of the western Manu has arrived,
at that conclusion of the Kali Yuga, when it has been exhausted, the dissolution is said to occur.

When that thorough cleansing has occurred and withdrawal (pratyāhāra) has been established, then, during that withdrawal, there is the dissolution of the elements and the subtle elements (tanmātras). || 2.40.5 ||

When the dissolution has begun, brought about by the very nature of things, there occurs the withdrawal of all transformations, from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa).
The waters indeed first swallow the quality consisting of smell belonging to the earth;
then, with its smell taken away, the earth becomes fit for dissolution.
Once the subtle element of smell has entered [the waters], the earth comes to exist in the state of water.
Then the waters, indeed swift-flowing and loud-sounding, having filled all this, remained still and moved about. || 2.40.8 ||
The quality of water, which is its essence (rasa), merges into light;
then, at the end, the waters perish due to the dissolution of the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra). || 2.40.9 ||
With their moisture withdrawn by fire, they indeed attain the state of light;
and when the water has been swallowed, fire is seen facing in every direction.
Then, when the fire has pervaded everything, it consumes that water;
then this entire world is gradually filled with flames. (2.40.11)
When that [wind] is spread across, upwards, and downwards by its rays,
the wind then causes even the quality of light— its form—
to vanish within it, just as the flame of a lamp is extinguished by the wind.
When the subtle element of form has perished, fire is deprived of its form;
for its brilliance is extinguished, as it is utterly swept away by the wind.
Then, when the world was without light and the fire had become wind,
the wind reached its own source of origin.
Moving upward, downward, and across, it stirs the ten directions;
and that space swallows even touch, which is the quality of wind.
Then the wind subsides, while space remains uncovered—
formless, without taste, touch, or smell, and devoid of material substance.
Filling everything with its sounds, that great sphere shines forth;
it is a perfectly circular void, the sky characterized by sound.
That ether, which consists of sound alone, remains pervading everything;
then the source of the elements (bhūtādi) again swallows that ether, whose quality is sound.
When the elements and the senses have become established simultaneously in the primordial matter (bhūtādi),
this [state] consisting of self-conceit is indeed known as the tamasic bhūtādi.
Furthermore, the Great One, characterized by the intellect (buddhi), indeed devours the source of the elements (bhūtādi).
That Great Self (mahān ātmā) is to be known as volition and determination. 2.40.20
Intellect, mind, the subtle body, the Great One, and the Imperishable itself.
Those who contemplate reality call it by means of synonymous words.

When the elements have completely dissolved into the state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya) consisting of darkness (tamomaya), and when the cause of the world remains established in its own self alone; || 2.40.22 ||
When the creation has thus ceased and [the world] remains in its primordial nature (prakṛti),
it is indeed beyond perception from beginning to end, because it is unseen by anyone.

Because it cannot be described, because it is not an object of awakening, because it is beyond the reach of ignorance even for the wise, and because it is subject to coming and going, no grasping of it occurs. (2.40.24)
Having reflected upon this through inference based on the apprehension of existence, it is said:
while that eternal cause, which consists of both being and non-being, remains [as the substratum]. (2.40.25)
Indeed, the activity inherent in its own nature cannot be described as residing in the cause;
in this same way, the seven primary elements (prakṛtis) arise sequentially from that which has been cultivated.
Then, during the withdrawal and the emission, they enter into one another,
whereby this entire sphere is enveloped and dissolved.

The seven worlds, together with their mountains, extending to the oceans at the edge of the seven continents, as well as the watery covering where the luminaries dissolve—that too [dissolves]. (2.40.28)
That fiery covering which swallows space, and that windy covering which swallows space; || 2.40.29 ||

That which is the covering of space (ākāśa), the elements and so forth indeed swallow it; and the Great One (mahat), characterized by intellect (buddhi), swallows even the elements and so forth. 2.40.30.

The unmanifest, which is the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), swallows the Great One; beyond that are these two—creation and dissolution—belonging to Brahmā and the Unmanifest respectively. Thus it is again. 2.40.31.
He indeed creates and withdraws the modifications during the processes of creation and dissolution;
those who possess knowledge are perfected as the agents of the work of reabsorption.
