Having moved through these states characterized by constant flux and lacking self-restraint, the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) are once again separated from their instruments (karaṇas) during the process of withdrawal (pratyāhāra). || 2.40.33 ||

They call the unmanifest the field (kṣetra), and Brahman is called the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). Their conjunction, which is beginningless, is produced by similarity and dissimilarity. (2.40.34)
Thus, O Brahmins, it should be understood regarding the fields and the knowers of the field here;
and the knower of Brahman is to be known as distinct from each of the knowers of the field. 2.40.35.
The state of being an object and not being an object is recorded as belonging to the field and the knower of the field.
Brahman is to be known as the object; the field is said to be the non-object. (2.40.36)
The field, presided over by the Knower of the Field, is said to exist for the sake of the Knower of the Field;
and because of the multiplicity of bodies, the embodied one is traditionally remembered as being manifold. (2.40.37)
It is without configuration and is established like light by virtue of Śaṅkara;
since the perception of pleasure and pain occurs within every individual body, therefore the plurality of Puruṣas must be understood by the wise. (2.40.38)
And when the restraints of these various divisions come into operation,
they are all brought about by their own nature through the course of great time.
Then the attachment to his own abode of the Self-born One suddenly ceased, along with all those who were to be joined [with him] dwelling in the world of Brahmā.
Then, when passion had ceased, for those inhabitants of Ātmanivāsa who were dwelling there at that time and who perceived those faults, [the city vanished]. 2.40.41.
Then, detachment arises for those who perceive that [reality], which destroys the doctrine of a self and [reveals] the multiplicity of the objects of enjoyment and the enjoyer. (2.40.42)

By means of individualized knowledge, those knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) then become inhabitants of the world of Brahmā; though all were originally instruments within primordial nature (prakṛti), they have now been led to perceive various [realms]. (2.40.43)
All things—whether sentient or insentient—abide within their own self, tranquil, consisting of pure vision, pure, and stainless. (2.40.44)
Those non-returners (anāgāmins) are known to attain final nirvana right there;
because they are devoid of qualities and are without self, they are considered by nature to have transcended [the realm]. (2.40.45)
Thus has been described the primary secondary creation (pratisarga) of the Self-existent One;
at the time of dissolution, the instruments of all beings become differentiated.

Thus, this is the restraint of the principles (tattvas) together with the instruments (karaṇas); for this restraint of the principles, O twice-born ones, is remembered as that which leads to rebirth. 2.40.47.
Sūta said:

Virtue and vice, austerity and knowledge, as well as purity and impurity, truth and falsehood, the state of being above and the state of being below, pleasure and pain, and the agreeable and the disagreeable—[all these arise from the mind]. (2.40.48)
All this is known to consist of the mere qualities (guṇas) for one who has departed;
and likewise, whatever is auspicious or inauspicious belongs to those wise ones who are then devoid of the senses.
All that merit and sin is established in the primordial nature (prakṛti);
it is infused into the womb, the state of existence, and the inherent nature of embodied beings.
The merit and demerit of living beings are established in their nature;
those very merits and demerits, residing in the unmanifest, accompany the beings even when they conquer and take on another body upon the change of bodies. (2.40.51)
Both dharma and adharma, which consist of the mere qualities (guṇas), are accumulated by living beings here through their own instruments and constitute their physical bodies. (2.40.52)
The qualities, presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), dissolve away when there is consciousness;
likewise, during creation, re-absorption, and the cycle of existence, living beings are joined with and separated from their instruments, and they wander through transmigrations. 2.40.53.
The functions—rajasī, tāmasī, and sāttvikī—proceed as the measures of the qualities (guṇamātrāḥ), presided over by the Puruṣa in three ways. 2.40.54.

Sattva, whose nature is divine, is directed upwards; tamas, whose nature is of the lower part, is directed downwards; between these two, rajas is the initiator and that which causes one to revolve right here in this world. || 2.40.55 ||
Thus do these three, consisting of the qualities of the stream, revolve among all beings in the worlds; therefore, one who understands what ought to be done should not act [according to them].
Indeed, these three destinies—arising from the conditions of ignorance—are undertaken by human beings; they are recorded as being both auspicious and sinful in nature. (2.40.57)
Due to being overwhelmed by darkness (tamas), a living being does not perceive things as they truly are;
because of that false perception, he is then bound in a threefold manner.
Bound by the bond of nature (prākṛta), as well as by the bond of transformation (vaikārika), and thirdly by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he revolves incessantly. ||2.40.59||
Thus, these three bonds have indeed been declared to have ignorance as their cause:
the perception of permanence in the impermanent, and the vision of happiness in suffering. (60)

The notion that "this is mine" regarding what is not one's own, and the conviction of purity regarding the impure—these are defects of the mind and defects of knowledge, arising from perversion. (2.40.61)
The cessation of passion and hatred is declared to be that knowledge.
Ignorance is the root of darkness (tamas), and the two types of karma have passion (rajas) as their fruit;
moreover, a body born of karma leads to great suffering. || 2.40.62 ||
Arising from the ear, the eye, as well as from the skin, tongue, and nose,
that suffering which brings about rebirth is indeed produced by one's own actions.
The fool, possessed by craving, is driven by the fruits of his own actions; like one carrying a vessel of oil, the living being revolves right there. 2.40.64.
Therefore, ignorance is taught as the grosser of evils;
having determined that it alone is capable [of causing harm], one should apply effort toward knowledge. 2.40.65
Through knowledge one conquers everything; through renunciation the intellect becomes dispassionate;
through dispassion one is purified, and being pure, one is liberated by means of *sattva*.
Henceforth I shall describe passion, which carries away living beings;
for by it, even an object becomes a cause of obsession for one who lacks self-control.
For there is indeed the onset of the undesired, which causes joy, heat, and despondency;
likewise, upon the acquisition of suffering, there is the burning pain of it, as well as the recollection of happiness. (2.40.68)
Thus, this attachment to sense objects is known to be the cause of rebirth within the material world of embodied existence, from Brahmā down to the level of stationary beings;
therefore, one should abandon ignorance, for it is preceded by ignorance. 2.40.69.

And for one for whom the words of the seers are not authoritative, as well as the conduct of the learned, who opposes the duties of the castes and stages of life, and who contradicts the scriptures of the virtuous; || 2.40.70 ||
For this is the path that leads away from birth in the animal realm;
it is declared to be the very cause for escaping the state of being born as an animal. (2.40.71)
Various torments exist in that place, as well as in the sixfold animal realm;
furthermore, there is total obstruction regarding causes and sense objects.
All that lack of sovereignty is considered to be of the nature of obstruction;
such is this fourfold tamasic function of the elements and the rest. 2.40.73.
Just as the mind, when established in goodness, perceives only goodness;
so too, having seen the true nature of the principles, one perceives only that true nature through the vision of reality. ||2.40.74||
This perception of the difference between the individual soul and the Knower of the Field is the vision of the object of knowledge;
the knowledge that perceives this difference is indeed called yoga through knowledge. 2.40.75.
For one bound by that, there is indeed bondage; for one liberated from that, there is liberation.
When transmigration has ceased, the liberated one is released even from the subtle body (liṅga). || 2.40.76 ||
For being devoid of connection and lacking consciousness, he remains within his own self;
yet, even while established in his own self, he is inscribed by the one named Virūpa.
Thus has the definition of knowledge and liberation been declared in brief;
and that liberation, indeed, is said by the seers of reality to be threefold.
The first separation is through knowledge; the second is from the destruction of passion.
But through the absence of the subtle body (liṅga), there is absolute liberation (kaivalya); and through absolute liberation, one becomes stainless.
Because it is stainless, it is pure; therefore, no further leader is required.
Through the destruction of craving, the third [cause] is explained as the cause of liberation. (2.40.80)
The objective field (nimitta) consists of desired objects characterized by sound and so forth, which are non-obstructive;
these eight forms are the primary (prākṛta) ones, respectively. (2.40.81)
But those things consisting of the mere qualities (guṇas) are attached to the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas).
Hereafter, I shall explain dispassion (vairāgya) through the perception of defects. 2.40.82.
Regarding both divine and human objects of experience, which possess five characteristics, one should practice neither aversion nor attachment by perceiving their defects. (2.40.83)
The task is the complete avoidance of heat, pleasure, and dejection;
having thus established dispassion, the embodied soul shall become free from the sense of "mine."
Having reflected with the understanding that [the world] is impermanent, inauspicious, and suffering, the sattva who moves toward the end of saṃsāra attains a pure body and sense organs. (2.40.85)
For one whose impurities have been fully ripened perceives all defects;
then, at the time of departure, by means of those very defects as well as their secondary signs—2.40.86.
The heat (ūṣman), provoked within the body and impelled by a violent wind, having taken hold of the entire body, indeed obstructs all the humors (doṣas). || 2.40.87 ||
For, piercing the seats of the vital breaths, severing the vital points (marmans), and passing beyond them, the wind, provoked by cold, then ascends upwards. (2.40.88)
And this very [Self] resides in the vital locations of all beings,
while knowledge is obscured and actions are veiled in brief.
That soul, no longer presided over by its former self, causes the eightfold functions of the vital breaths to fluctuate again due to its own previously committed actions.
Having indeed abandoned the body, one then becomes breathless;
thus, being deprived of the vital breaths, one is designated as "dead. (2.40.91)
Just as a firefly being carried here and there in this world provides no illumination, so too is that leader who possesses no leadership.

The third [chapter] concerns the destruction of craving; thus has been explained the definition of liberation regarding the fivefold objects, beginning with sound, which are the locus of defects. (2.40.93)
Absence of aversion, absence of attachment, and the avoidance of pleasure and pain—these are indeed the causes of detachment and of the dissolution of the material elements. 2.40.94.
The eight primary natures (prakṛtis) previously mentioned should be known in their proper order;
they are to be understood as beginning with the Unmanifest (avyakta) and ending with the elements (bhūta), representing the dissolutions of nature. ||2.40.95||
Those who are disciplined, following the conduct of their caste and stage of life, and acting in accordance with the scriptures—
this dharma of the castes and stages of life is the cause for attaining the abodes of the gods.
The deities occupy eight stations, beginning with Brahmā and ending with the Piśācas;
for the eightfold cause consists of the sovereign powers, such as aṇimā and the rest. || 2.40.97 ||
The sign is non-obstruction with respect to desired objects characterized by sound and so forth;
these eight are the primordial forms (rūpas) in their respective order. 2.40.98.
These things, consisting merely of aggregates, are attached to the knowers of the field;
yet in this world, during the rainy season, one does not perceive them as distinct entities with the eye.
The perfected ones (siddhas), beholding with their divine eye such a living being as this, see it entering into various wombs—
such as those of dogs— and likewise entering the wombs of dog-eaters;
they see it running hither and thither, horizontally, upwards, and downwards, in due succession.
The fourfold [set] consists of the individual soul (jīva), the vital breaths (prāṇa), the subtle body (liṅga), and the cause (kāraṇa).
He is described by synonymous words that convey a single meaning;
he is the manifest and the unmanifest, the means of valid knowledge, and indeed his form is entirely complete.
That which is grasped as ending in the unmanifest and is presided over by the Knower of the Field—knowing this and becoming pure, one is indeed liberated through knowledge. ||2.40.103||
Having realized the true nature of the principles as they truly are, even when that which was lost has been recovered,
he attains perfect peace and enters final nirvana at will once the body has perished.
Furthermore, for the ignorant person, the instrument [of action] is split from the unmanifest;
thus, one is liberated entirely from the body of the qualities, as well as from the vital breaths and so forth.
Just as a sprout does not arise when the seed is burnt, so the embodied being,
whose seeds are both physical and mental, does not take up another body from the entire cycle of existence.
Purified by the fourteen kinds of knowledge, he follows his own nature (prakṛti).
They call nature "truth," while modification is said to be "untruth. || 2.40.107 ||

The existence of that [unmanifest] is to be known as unreal; its true being is called the Real. That which is without name and form is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), while name and form are said to belong to it. 2.40.108
Because it discerns the field, it is called the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña);
because it exists through the field as its condition, the knower of the field is said to be pure. ||2.40.109||
Therefore, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is remembered as such by those who know that field;
the notion of "field-ness" is observed [in the body], while the Knower of the Field is always the perceiver. 2.40.110.

Those who know the field (kṣetra) understand it as such because of its destruction (kṣaya), its cultivation (karaṇa), and likewise because of its protection from injury (kṣatatrāṇa); also because of its being that which is to be enjoyed (bhojya) and its being an object of experience (viṣaya). || 2.40.111 ||

That which begins with the Great Principle (mahat) and ends with the specific elements (viśeṣa), along with their various forms and distinct characteristics, is indeed characterized by transformation; it is both the perishable and the imperishable.
And because that very modification indeed flows forth again, for that reason it is called "the perishable" (kṣara). || 2.40.113 ||

The states of pleasure, pain, and delusion are designated as the "object of enjoyment" (bhojya); for, being insentient, it is an object, whereas that [subject] is traditionally known as the all-pervading Lord of attributes (dharmavibhu). || 2.40.114 ||
It does not perish, nor does it flow away, even though it extends through all transformations;
therefore it is called "akṣara" (the imperishable), both because it is indestructible and likewise because it does not decay.
Because he dwells within the city (puri), he is called Puruṣa;
because he is the one who perceives the city, he is designated as Puruṣa. || 2.40.116 ||
Now tell me about the Puruṣa; how is he described by those who know him?
He is pure, appearing as stainless, and devoid of both knowledge and ignorance. (2.40.117)

Whether it be "it exists" or "it does not exist," whether it be "another," or "bound," "liberated," "gone," or "stationed"—none of these apply to that which is taught as the ultimate end of causelessness and is well-spoken. (2.40.118)
Because of his purity, he is indeed not to be instructed; because of his joy, he possesses equal vision.
Acting with self-conviction, firm in essence and grounded in reason, he does not become deluded as he reflects upon that which is to be grasped through its being and inferred through logic.
When the knower perceives the Knower as the essence of vision whose nature is peace,
then that which is to be designated among the seen and the unseen is the supreme deliverance.
Having understood this, that knower then attains peace regarding both the effect and the cause, as well as the intellect and the rest, and the material elements.
Whether associated or dissociated, whether in the living or the dead, a knower is not perceived here in any way as a separate entity. (2.40.122)
The causal self restrains that very self by means of its own self;
it abides within its own self, which is both the primordial nature and the cause. (2.40.123)

Whether it be "it exists" or "it does not exist," or again "this world" or "the next," or whether it be "oneness" or "separateness," or "the knower of the field" (kṣetrajña) or "the person" (puruṣa)—[all these are mere designations]. (2.40.124)
Whether he possesses a self or is without a self, whether he is conscious or even unconscious,
whether he is an agent or a non-agent, or whether he is an enjoyer or even the object of enjoyment— (2.40.125)
Having known that which resides in the stainless Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), they do not return;
for it is inexpressible because it cannot be described, ungraspable, and without cause.
Because it is inconceivable and entirely unattainable,
that reality, once reached by means of the mind, does not stain it with conceptual thought.
When the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has become free from qualities, pure, tranquil, diminished, stainless, devoid of pleasure and pain, restrained, and has attained peace. || 2.40.128 ||
But when that [reality] is without self-nature, neither the expressible nor the inexpressible exists;
from that [reality], moreover, proceed these two: dissolution and expansion, as well as the manifest and the unmanifest. (2.40.129)
It creates and it devours; being devoured, it remains as it is.
Everything is presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), and everything proceeds once again. 2.40.130
Through that which proceeds from his presiding presence, and by his own prior intelligence, he ordains the conjunction of those two through their similarities and differences;
that conjunction is known as beginningless and born of the Great Puruṣa. ||2.40.131||
For as long as the period of creation and dissolution lasts, it remains perfectly restrained;
though previously inactive, it proceeds without prior conscious intent solely for the sake of the Puruṣa’s purpose. (2.40.132)
This process, preceded by both primary creation and secondary dissolution, belongs to both primordial matter (pradhāna) and the Lord (īśvara).
Indeed, beginningless and endless, it approaches the world accompanied by egoism, causing it to tremble with fear. (2.40.133)
Thus has been described this third creation, the primary one characterized by its cause; when this is fully understood by the wise, one is liberated from it. 2.40.134.
Thus, this threefold dissolution has been described by me in detail and in its proper sequence; what more shall I relate? Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa, the Vāyu-prokta.
In the Ānandāśrama edition, chapter 102:
Now follows the description of creation.
The sages said:
O Sūta, you have narrated this very great account concerning the subjects together with the Manus, and the gods together with the ṛṣis.
Of the Pitṛs, Gandharvas, and Bhūtas; of the Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas; and of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and even the birds.
Most wonderful deeds, the determination of dharma according to the sacred law, diverse applications of narrative, and a birth that is foremost and unsurpassed. (2.41.3)
O Sauti, as this is being told by you in gentle words, it brings delight to our minds and ears, providing pleasure from beginning to end.
Having thus gratified the Sūta and honored him, all those great ṛṣis engaged in the sacrificial session asked once more about the process of creation.
O charioteer of great wisdom, how will creation proceed again when all beings have dissolved into their bonds, when the qualities are in equilibrium, and everything is enveloped in darkness?
When the modifications have not been emitted, while the unmanifest Self remains inactive,
and when there is no activity of Brahman, how will creation then come to pass for those who have attained union with the Great? Tell this to us who ask you.
Thus addressed, the Sūta Lomaharṣaṇa then began once more to explain the progression of creation.
I shall relate to you how the creation will proceed;
it should be understood as being just like before, so listen to that in brief. 2.41.9.
I shall explain, according to reason, both that which is perceived and that which is inferable;
therefore, words turn back together with the mind, failing to reach it. 2.41.10.
Because it is imperceptible like the unmanifest, its apprehension is difficult to achieve;
yet when the equilibrium of the qualities is perceived through their transformations, [the world] ceases.
Pradhāna exists in a state of similarity with the Puruṣas; the merit and demerit of living beings always remain unmanifest within it. (2.41.12)
Dharma, whose essence consists of the quality of sattva, is established in the quality of sattva;
adharma, whose essence consists of the quality of tamas, resides in the quality of tamas. ||2.41.13||
These two remain in a state of equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) as long as there is no manifestation;
however, for every effect, the primary principle (pradhāna) will proceed with prior intelligence. || 2.41.14 ||
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) will preside over those qualities without prior conscious intent;
thus, at that time, he will enter into them through self-identification.
When both must proceed together—the field and the knower of the field—they shall enter into the relationship of the enjoyed and the enjoyer. (2.41.16)

Therefore, that unmanifest refuge, remaining in a state of equilibrium, yet presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), undergoes that very state of inequality which consists of the qualities (guṇas). || 2.41.17 ||
Then, it will clearly attain [its true nature] regarding both the field and the knower of the field;
the sattva, presided over by the knower of the field, will produce transformation. || 2.41.18 ||

The twenty-fourfold principle, beginning with the Great One (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa), shall be attained by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Primal Matter (pradhāna), and the Person (puruṣa). 2.41.19.
Then he shall become the first Lord in the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa),
and thereafter Śiva, the lord of all beings, shall be the knower of everything that is to be known.
The Lord of all liberated beings, Brahmā, the great one composed of Brahman,
the primordial deity, shall proclaim [this] for the sake of bestowing grace upon Pradhāna.
Both are beginningless and self-arisen, and they are known to be subtle;
they are joined by a beginningless union with all the knowers of the field (kṣetrajña).
Then two excellent mosquitoes, acting without prior intention,
remained within the water, unobserved and without beginning, as they drank the liquid.
When the previous creation has ceased, he will again enter into a new creation;
through ignorance, beings proceed according to the qualities consisting of passion, goodness, and darkness.

At the time of manifestation, men—overwhelmed by *rajas*—attain the state of being qualified as the Great Principle (*mahat*), the elements, and so forth; they reach the state of specific objects, the sense organs, and [the subtle body] at the conclusion of the *guṇas*, under the influence of their lords. (2.41.25)

For that meditator who speaks the truth, the qualities of passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas)—which are distinct from one another and possess different natures—become clearly manifest as the causal basis for his meditation. (2.41.26)
At the beginning and at the end, those who know that field will attain it in every respect;
having accomplished their purpose, those possessed of self-conceit are born again.
Indeed, all beings proceed from that which is unmanifest even prior [to creation];
and she who brings them forth is both the productive and the non-productive.
But as they all transmigrate, together with their respective stations and circumstances,
they shall undergo their duties and be born again and again.
And dharma and adharma, consisting of the mere qualities (guṇas),
will here engage with one another through mutual choice and favor.
At the beginning of creation, all beings, being equal, undergo transformation for the sake of discharging their purpose;
the qualities (guṇas) then rush toward them, and therefore that which is appropriate to each person pleases them.
Whatever qualities they acquired prior to their first perception, those very same qualities they assume again and again as they are created anew. (2.41.32)

Violent and non-violent, mild and cruel, righteous and unrighteous, truthful and false—impregnated by these very qualities, they resort to them; therefore, each finds pleasure in that which accords with their own nature.
The diversity among the great elements, among the objects of the senses, and among material forms, as well as the separation of beings from their qualities, proceeds from this. (2.41.34)
Thus has this secondary creation been declared to you by me in brief;
now I shall describe the origin of Brahmā in summary as well.
From that unmanifest cause, which is eternal and consists of both being and non-being,
Maheśvara is born from both Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
Furthermore, he who is designated as Brahmā becomes the progenitor;
he then creates the worlds, which consist of the qualities of egoistic conceit.

From that Great Principle (mahat) arises ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra), and from that, the elements and the senses proceed simultaneously from the Self; the various modifications of the elements arise from the elements—thus does creation proceed. (2.41.38)
The detailed account of their constituent parts has been recited to you according to my wisdom and as I have heard it; let it be understood by you exactly as it was previously told. 2.41.39.
Having heard this— concerning the origin, the maintenance, and the dissolution of the world— the sages of Naimiṣa,
having performed the final purificatory bath at that sacrificial session, became pure and attained the meritorious world.
Just as you, having worshipped the deities and others according to the rules and having performed the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), shall become pure;
so too, at the end of your lives, having cast off your bodies and attained your goals, you will reach the auspicious worlds and dwell there as you please.
These very inhabitants of Naimiṣa, having performed the sacrifice and completed the ritual creation,
all went to heaven after bathing in the final purificatory ablution (avabhṛtha) as performers of the sacrificial session (sattrin).
Likewise, you brahmins as well, having performed various kinds of sacrifices,
shall go to heaven at the end of your lives, O best of the twice-born.
In the first chapter, the process consists of the selection of the subject matter of the narrative, as well as the incidental, the introductory, and the concluding sections. (2.41.44)
Thus did the Blessed One, Vāyu himself, devoted to the welfare of the world, speak this ancient Purāṇa consisting of four quarters, which is honored by the world.
Having attended a sacrificial session at Naimiṣa for the sages, those best of sages [shall explain] the origins and dissolutions of beings without doubt, through his grace.
Having correctly understood this creation as proceeding from primordial matter (pradhāna) and likewise brought about by the Lord (Īśvara),
the wise man does not fall into delusion.
The Brahmin who, being learned, hears this ancient history, or causes it to be heard, or even teaches it; ||| 2.41.48 ||
In the abodes of Mahendra, he rejoices for eternal years;
having attained union with Brahman, he shall be liberated along with Brahman.
By proclaiming the fame of those illustrious and high-souled lords of subjects and rulers of the earth, one attains union with Brahman.
This Purāṇa, spoken by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, the knower of Brahman, is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, meritorious, and esteemed by the Vedas. 2.41.51.
He who shall spread this fame of the lords of the Manvantaras,
of the deities, and of the ṛṣis who possess abundant wealth and splendor,
is liberated from all sins and shall attain great merit. (2.41.52)
The wise man who shall cause this to be heard on every sacred occasion (parvan),
having shaken off all evil and conquered heaven, becomes fit for union with Brahman.
And whoever shall cause even a single foot of this to be heard by Brahmins at a śrāddha ceremony, that reaches the ancestors as inexhaustible and fulfilling all desires. (2.41.54)
Because this was indeed infinite in the past, it is therefore called Purāṇa;
he who knows its etymology is liberated from all sins. (2.41.55)
In the same way, those men who are preeminent among the three castes,
having heard this history, have set their minds upon righteousness.
As many as there are hair-pores on his body in their entirety,
for that many thousands of crores of years he rejoices in heaven;
having attained union with Brahman, he rejoices together with the deities.
This Purāṇa, which removes all sins, is meritorious, pure, and glorious;
Brahmā gave this scripture to Mātariśvan in ancient times.
From him it was obtained by Uśanas, and from him Bṛhaspati received it;
Bṛhaspati then taught it to Savitṛ immediately thereafter.
Savitṛ spoke it to Mṛtyu, and Mṛtyu to Indra;
Indra spoke it to Vasiṣṭha, and he too to Sārasvata. (2.41.60)
Sārasvata gave it to Tridhāman, and Tridhāman to Śaradvat; Śaradvat gave it to Triviṣṭa, and he gave it to Antarikṣa. (2.41.61)
Varṣiṇa gave it to Antarikṣa, and he in turn to Trayyāruṇa;
Trayyāruṇa gave it to Dhanañjaya, and he bestowed it upon Kṛtañjaya.
From Kṛtañjaya, Tṛṇañjaya [obtained it] and he gave it to Bharadvāja;
then Bharadvāja gave it to Gautama, and he in turn to Niryātara.
Niryantṛ spoke thus to Vājaśravas;
he gave it to Somaśuṣma, and he gave it to Tṛṇabindu.
Tṛṇabindu told it to Dakṣa, and Dakṣa proclaimed it to Śakti;
and Parāśara, while still in the womb, heard this from Śakti.
From Parāśara it was obtained by Jātūkarṇa, and from him the lord Dvaipāyana;
and from Dvaipāyana, O best of the twice-born, it was received by me once again. (2.41.66)
Śaunaka said:
"I have indeed related this again to my son of immeasurable intellect;
thus was it uttered by the voice of Brahmā, the preceptor of the gods. (2.41.67)
And the gurus should be honored with effort by the wise;
[this practice] is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, meritorious, and the accomplisher of all goals. 2.41.68.

This sin-destroying [account] should always be heard by Brahmins with self-restraint; it must not be heard by one who is impure, nor by a sinner, nor by one who has not resided [there] for a year. 2.41.69.
This supreme purifier must never be imparted to one who lacks faith, nor to an ignorant person, nor to one who has no son, nor to one who is not well-disposed. 2.41.70.
They say that the Unmanifest is his source, the Manifest is his body, and Time is contained within him;
they say that fire is his mouth, the moon and sun are his eyes, the quarters of space are his ears, and the wind is his breath.
One should know that his speech is the Vedas, his body is the intermediate space, his feet are the earth, the stars are the pores of his skin,
and all those various branches of knowledge are said to be his tail.

I, with a disciplined mind, bow down to that God of gods, the progenitor of all people, who is established in all worlds—the Great Lord, the bestower of boons, the most excellent among the excellent, the primordial Brahmā. 2.41.73.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "Description of Creation," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu. ||41||
(Ānandāśrama edition of the Vāyupurāṇa, Chapter 103) The Dispelling of Vyāsa’s Doubts:
"O Sūta, O Sūta, highly fortunate one, by you who are a venerable being..."
Through the awakening [brought about] by the grace of Vyāsa and the acquisition of the scriptures,
O sinless one, the eighteen Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas have been declared in their entirety according to the rules of introduction and conclusion.
The Mātsya Purāṇa is declared to be very clearly composed of fourteen thousand verses;
the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa is likewise declared to contain that same number, with an additional five hundred.
The most delightful Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa is said to consist of nine thousand verses;
the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa is declared to have eighteen thousand verses. 2.42.4.
The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa consists of one hundred and one thousand verses, while the divine Bhāgavata Purāṇa consists of eighteen thousand verses. ||2.42.5||
The Purāṇa named Brahma is said to consist of ten thousand verses,
while the Purāṇa called Vāmana is composed of ten thousand ślokas.
Likewise, the auspicious wind moving therein is twenty-three thousand, six hundred and ten in number.
The Nāradīya is declared to consist of twenty-three thousand [verses],
and the Vainateya is declared to consist of nineteen thousand.
The Pādma is said to be very extensive, consisting of fifty-five thousand verses;
the charming Kūrma is said to consist of seventeen thousand.
The most wonderful Saukara Purāṇa consists of twenty-four thousand verses;
the very extensive Skānda Purāṇa is said to consist of eighty-one thousand verses.
Thus, eighteen great Purāṇas have been described;
within these Purāṇas, many dharmas have been fully set forth.
For those with passion and those free from passion, for ascetics and students of sacred knowledge, for householders and forest-dwellers, and especially for women and Śūdras. || 2.42.12 ||
Those born of the mixed castes from Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas;
the great rivers beginning with the Ganges; and sacrifices, vows, and ascetic penances—[all these are purified by the sight of the Ganges]. (2.42.13)
Various kinds of gifts along with restraints and observances;
the manifold dharmas of Yoga, as well as those of the Sāṃkhya and the Bhāgavatas.

The path of devotion, the path of knowledge, and the practice of worship—which are rendered stainless by the wind of dispassion—have been taught for those whose minds are purified through ritual action. 2.42.15
The six philosophical systems—the Brāhma, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Saura, Śākta, and likewise the Ārhata—are said to be determined by their own inherent natures. (2.42.16)
This and various other matters have been described in the Purāṇas;
beyond this, there is nothing further to be understood as supreme. 2.42.17.
"It would not be known if Vyāsa were to conceal it, or perhaps if you yourself were to do so;
therefore, resolve our doubt here, for you are a master of the Purāṇas. (2.42.18)
Sūta said: Listen, O Śaunaka, I shall answer this most difficult question; it is exceedingly secret, divine, and they say it is not to be disclosed. 2.42.19.
Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, having composed the Puranic narrative which encompasses the meaning of all the Vedas, reflected upon it within his mind.
The dharma of those belonging to the castes and stages of life has been correctly proclaimed by me;
various paths to liberation have been described in accordance with the Vedas. ||2.42.21||
The distinction between the individual soul, the Lord, and Brahman has been refuted in the determination of the Sūtras;
the Supreme Brahman has been established through the investigation of scripture and reasoning. (2.42.22)
The syllable, the supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, the highest state—
for the sake of which there is the vow of celibacy, and the observances of the forest-dweller and the ascetic.

The highly wise practice various forms of concentration (dhāraṇā), as well as posture (āsana), breath restraint (prāṇarodha), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and concentration (dhāraṇā). || 2.42.24 ||
Meditation and concentration— these, together with the restraints and observances,
are the eight limbs for the sake of which the best of sages practice.

For what purpose they perform action, being solely intent on the command of the Veda—with a mind fixed on offering it to the Supreme, perfectly free from desire, and abandoned by all impurity—[that purpose is the same]. (2.42.26)
Those of pure vows resort to pilgrimages to the Ganges and other sacred sites in order to confess and cast off their own sinful conduct.
That Brahman is supreme, pure, without beginning or end, and free from affliction;
it is eternal, all-pervading, immovable, unchanging, and devoid of any artificiality.
It is the appearance of the movement of all the senses, yet devoid of the ordinary senses; unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, it is eternal, pure consciousness, and immutable. (2.42.29)
Wherein this entire universe shines forth as if superimposed like a snake [upon a rope], and which likewise pervades the universe while remaining changeless like that very rope. (2.42.30)
Just as foam, waves, and bubbles are rightly examined to be nothing other than water, so too, when Brahman is investigated, it is found not to be separate from the universe. 2.42.31
"All is Brahman alone; there is no multiplicity," so the Vedas have sung, for from it millions of cosmic eggs arise and into it they cease to be. (2.42.32)
She who exists as the foundational support by whose opening and closing of her eyes the dissolution and emergence of the worlds occur—she is the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti). 2.42.33.

That in which this [world] exists, from which this [world] arises, by which this [world] is known, that which is remembered as this [world], that through whose ignorance the world appears, and upon whose being known the world ceases to exist—[that is Brahman]. (2.42.34)
That which is unreal, inert, sorrowful, and insubstantial has been described;
that which is the opposite of this is indeed the embodiment of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss. (2.42.35)
When the individual soul is awake, it is called Viśva; in the dream state, it is known as Taijasa;
and in deep sleep, it is designated as Prājña. It is thus remembered to exist in all these states.
That which is known as the eye of eyes, the ear of ears, the skin of skins, the tongue of taste, and the breath of breaths—[that is Brahman]. (2.42.37)
The intellect and the vital breaths, along with the power of knowledge and the power of action, were unable to reach or to know him in his ultimate reality. (2.42.38)
Just as water appears in a mirage outside a city, or as blueness appears in the sky, so does this unreal universe appear, imagined by ignorance within that [Self]. (2.42.39)

Just as this great space (mahākāśa) appears divided when delimited by a jar, so too that which is called the individual soul (jīva) is [the same space] as it is delimited by the limiting adjuncts of its effects. (2.42.40)
By means of illusion, which is like a painter possessing diverse qualities and dispositions,
the incomparable and variegated universe is depicted upon it as if on a wall.
That Imperishable, which transcends all that runs and is beyond the range of speech, has been definitively established by the doctrines of the Vedas and Vedāntas. 2.42.42.
"There is nothing whatsoever beyond the Imperishable; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal"—thus it is heard in the Veda, even when investigated in many ways. (2.42.43)
It exists as the very nature of the self, even of the imperishable Self;
it is the embodiment of bliss, consisting of a mass of supreme joy. (2.42.44)
He is one who delights in the essence of playful grace, standing in the midst of the herd of cowherd girls,
adorned with a crown of peacock feathers inlaid with radiant jewels.
It was resplendent with two eyes that flashed like the expansion of shimmering lightning,
and it was as enchanting as a *khañjarīṭa* bird moving near the ears.
He who delights in the amorous play with the multitude of his beloveds in every bower, who wears yellow garments, who is divine, and who is adorned with sandalwood paste; 2.42.47.
He was enchanting the cowherd girls with the sound of his flute drenched in the nectar of the lower realms,
while he himself was the bliss of consciousness and the shatterer of the intoxication of the bodiless god of love.
It was filled with ten million digits of desire, stainless as the rays of ten million moons,
and adorned with three lines upon the neck, shimmering jewels, guñjā berries, and deer.
On the lofty bank of the Yamunā, in a forest grove of *tāla* trees,
enchanting with *kadamba*, *campaka*, *aśoka*, and *pārijāta* blossoms.
It was filled with the tumultuous clamor of peacocks, pigeons, parrots, and cuckoos,
while cows themselves were running hither and thither for the sake of confinement.
I have heard from the Vedas about the Supreme Person named Kṛṣṇa, who relishes the amorous pastimes with Rādhā, and through that [hearing], He became the object of my perception. ||2.42.52||
Thus, I have heard that Kṛṣṇa sports in that which is called Goloka—the Brahman, pure consciousness alone, devoid of qualities and free from all differentiation. (2.42.53)
There is nothing higher than this, even according to the Vedas and the Agamas;
nevertheless, the Veda declares that which is beyond the Imperishable (akṣara) is the Supreme. ||2.42.54||
The Lord who dwells in Goloka is said to be beyond the Imperishable (akṣara); who is that one who is always sung of by the Vedas as even higher than Him? || 2.42.55 ||
When a distinction has been indicated by Vedic utterances, how is it to be known?
Or else, the meaning of the Śruti must be understood otherwise, as being beyond the literal syllables. (2.42.56)
Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, having fallen into doubt regarding the meaning of the Śruti,
deliberated for a long time but did not arrive at the truth as it truly is.
Sūta said:
Even though he reflected upon it, the sage did not attain certainty regarding the meaning of the Veda;
for the Veda is Nārāyaṇa himself, wherein even the wise become bewildered. (2.42.58)
Nevertheless, he again reflected upon that great agony which torments the hearts of the virtuous: "Whom shall I go to? What shall I do? (2.42.59)
I do not see anyone in this world who is all-knowing and all-seeing, nor anyone else in the world who, having understood [the truth], can dispel my doubt. (2.42.60)
Having gone to a cave on Mount Meru, he performed supreme austerity,
where it was made continuous by nets of moonlight shimmering with gold.
It constantly obstructs from all sides the hymn of darkness that pierces the sight;
there shines that supreme wilderness, exceedingly beautiful. (2.42.62)
Resounding with the cries of birds in groves of various trees and creepers,
it was entirely free from hunger, thirst, fear, anger, heat, and exhaustion.
With various reservoirs of water adorned with clusters of lotuses, and with birds wandering upon banks lined with slabs of gold; 2.42.64.
It was fit to be served on all sides by breezes from the lotuses, presided over by auspicious states of being, and entirely abandoned by predatory creatures. (2.42.65)
It was secluded, adorned with groves of beloved celestial creepers,
filled with charming parrots and pigeons, and resounded with the cries of intoxicated cuckoos in rut.
There too was a divine cave, most beautiful, its quarters filled with the fragrance of the masses of pollen rising from lotuses. 2.42.67.
Having entered it, the sage— having conquered his hunger, mastered his mind, and subdued his posture— recalled the four Vedas with a one-pointed mind.
As he remembered for a hundred autumns, the three Vedas departed;
then the four Vedas, beautiful to behold, appeared before him.
With eyes like the petals of a shimmering lotus, wearing crowns of matted hair,
holding handfuls of kusha grass in their lotus-like hands, and their shoulders adorned with deerskins.
Their faces were fashioned from the sixteen vowels, with the *praṇava* (Om) within;
their five limbs and hands arose from the letters of the *ka*-group.
Those whose right feet consist of the *pa*-group, whose left feet consist of the *ta*-group, and whose two bellies consist of the final letters from *a* to *ra*, [are the *mātrāvṛtta*s]. (2.42.72)
With navels as their beds, beloved backs, and joyful bellies; with hair disheveled by the letters ya, ra, la, and va;
beautiful with the fire, the right side, and the rays; they were supported by the earth, their necks, and their shoulders. 2.42.73.
Established within the junctions of the internal [sounds] and manifested as articulate speech (vaikharī-vāk), they beheld Mathurā fashioned within the lotuses of their hearts. 2.42.74.
For that is indeed the place where Lord Hari himself manifested, as he cast away the illusion (māyā) situated at the foundation from between his eyebrows into Kāśī. || 2.42.75 ||
Then, Kāñcī is in the region of the *liṅga*, Avantī in the circle of the navel;
Dvārakā resides in the throat, and likewise Prayāga resides in the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
To their left and right are the Gaṅgā and the river Yamunā;
in the middle is the Sarasvatī herself, and likewise, O face, is the sacred field of Gayā.
He beheld the supreme Prabhāsa-kṣetra situated between the jaw and the neck,
and Badaryāśrama at their Brahma-randhra.
The seat of Pauṇḍravardhana and Nepāla appeared in the pair of his eyes, and the seat named Pūrṇagiri was seen upon his forehead. (2.42.79)
The seat of Mathurā was seen at her throat, the seat of Kāñcī was situated on her hips,
and likewise the seat of Jālandhara appeared upon the region of her breasts.

The Bhṛgu-pīṭha is in the region of the ears, Ayodhyā in the nostrils; the Brāhma-pīṭha is situated at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), and the Śaiva-pīṭha at the boundary of the hairline.
The Śākta [center] is situated at the tip of the tongue; the Vaiṣṇava in the lotus of the heart;
the Saura located in the region of the eyes; and the Bauddha joined with the shadows.
He performed the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice at the region of the throat, the Paśubandha upon the chest,
the Vājapeya at the waist, and likewise the Agnihotra in the mouth.
The horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) is on the region of the hips, the human sacrifice (naramedha) on the belly,
the royal consecration (rājasūya) on the head, and likewise the domestic fire-sacrifice (āvasathya) on the lower lip.

He saw the Dakṣiṇāgni fire upon his upper lip and the Gārhapatya fire within his mouth; he saw the sacrificial oblation in his ears and the various mantras situated in his body hairs—just as ancient ministers, grounded in justice, attend upon a great king. || 2.42.85 ||
Those who, through the Saṃhitās and the Tantras, have been worshipped individually by means of ritual action, knowledge, and meditation, acting for the benefit of all people.

Seeing them— divine, composed of the splendor of Brahman, blazing like suns fallen from the sky, like fires with flames rising upward, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons— the sage Kṛṣṇa became deeply amazed in his mind.
Rising suddenly, the sage prostrated himself like a staff and paid homage, exclaiming, "I am fulfilled! I am fulfilled! I am fulfilled! (2.42.88).
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my mind has become fruitful;
and today my life has become fruitful, since you have come within the range of my vision. 2.42.89.
Whatever exists, whether supramundane or mundane—whatever has been, whatever is to be, and whatever is currently occurring—that which is to be known is not unknown to you. (2.42.90)

Even though you always demonstrate those [virtues], you do not possess the fruit of active engagement here for the sake of providing a voluntary contraction of the senses to those who are still attached to passion. || 2.42.91 ||

Whether the phenomenal world (prapañca) is false or is Brahman itself, the two injunctions [regarding it] do not have as their object a delusive passion; rather, they concern its restriction and its cessation. (2.42.92)

Therefore, those who seek the welfare of the world have surely condemned, when defining the ultimate truth, the objects such as heaven mentioned by [other] teachers, on the grounds that they are perishable. (2.42.93)

By means of the instruction in action and knowledge according to the distinction of qualified aspirants, the entire world has surely been saved by those whose forms are the very embodiment of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman). 2.42.94.
Therefore, if you are compassionate, I wish to ask:
is it taught that the fruit of actions is rebirth for those whose minds are intent solely on desire? || 2.42.95 ||
For those persons whose intellect is dedicated to the Lord, even from the karma they have performed,
there arises purification of the mind, and from that, knowledge, and immediately after that, liberation.

Liberation is the oneness with Brahman; thus, that which is indeed Being-Consciousness-Bliss—in which everything is subsumed once it is known, including all that has been done and left undone. (2.42.97)

That which is non-attached, the space of consciousness, whose nature is knowledge, unrestrained, effortless, immovable, pure, devoid of qualities, and all-pervading—this is what is remembered [as the Self]. (2.42.98)
When modifications perish, that which is changeless does not perish;
just as when the world is pervaded by blinding darkness, it is dispelled by the splendor of the sun.
Just as a gem is to iron, or as fire is to the fire-drill, so too does that Being manifest its existence through a mere appearance. 2.42.100

Alas, even when that [universe] has dissolved away in the form of the individual soul, the Lord, and so forth, as well as in the form of the entire world, there remains that which is the solitary, immutable Absolute.
"What you have thus determined is indeed exactly so; there is no doubt.
Nevertheless, a mere curiosity remains within my heart. (2.42.102)
"Therefore, does something even more supreme exist, or not?
May you, illustrious ones who perceive the truth, declare this. (2.42.103)

"That very fame which is the fruit of my birth in this world is my fulfillment"—to Vyāsa, the sinless son of Satyavatī, who was speaking thus, the Vedas replied, acclaiming him: "Excellent! Excellent! (2.42.104).
The Vedas said:
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! Viṣṇu is the Self of all embodied beings;
though unborn, you seek to benefit the worlds by assuming birth. (2.42.105)
Otherwise, the bondage of the karma of saṃsāra would not be possible for you,
who have never been touched by the Goddess Māyā, whose secret is knowledge.
You assume a form by your own will and conceal it by your own will;
the very purpose desired by us has been revealed by you.
In the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and also in the Sūtras, it is stated in many ways that the Imperishable (Akṣara) is the supreme Brahman, the cause of all causes. (2.42.108)
Know that the supreme form of that Self exists as its very own nature, like fragrance in a flower or like flavor in a fruit. || 2.42.109 ||
That was experienced by us when the natural dissolution occurred.
Beyond that which is beyond the syllable, there is that which is supreme, the solitary essence; we are not capable of describing it, for we are composed of sound, yet it transcends sound. (2.42.110)
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Dispelling of Vyāsa’s Doubts," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
The Greatness of Gayā 105.
Vāyu said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme greatness of Gayā.
Having heard which, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter. ||2.43.1||
Sūta said:
That celestial sage Nārada, together with the highly fortunate Sanaka and others, having prostrated according to the prescribed rite, questioned Sanatkumāra. 2.43.2.
Nārada said: O Sanatkumāra, tell me of that holy place, the most excellent of all holy places,
which is the savior of all beings for those who read it and likewise for those who hear it.
Sanatkumāra said:
I shall describe the meritorious and excellent holy site (tīrtha) that grants liberation in all matters such as śrāddha;
listen to Gayātīrtha, which is superior even to all other holy sites in every land. 2.43.4.
The Asura Gaya performed penance when requested by Brahmā for the sake of a sacrifice;
indeed, Dharma supported a stone upon the head of him who had attained that state. ||2.43.5||

There, O best of Brahmins, Brahmā performed a sacrifice while Gadādhara remained present day and night in the form of Phalgutīrtha and other manifestations, for the sake of the immovable goal of the demon Gayāsura,
together with the deities headed by Brahmā.
Having completed the sacrifice, Brahmā gave houses and other gifts to the Brāhmaṇas;
furthermore, during the Śveta Kalpa, in the Vārāha incarnation, he caused the Gayā sacrifice to be performed.
Known by the name Gayā, this sacred field is desired by Brahmā;
fathers, terrified by the fear of hell, long for sons. ||2.43.8||
"The son who goes to Gayā shall be our savior.
Seeing a son arrived at Gayā, there is a festival for the ancestors.
Even by touching the water with his feet, what will he not give to us? (2.43.9)
He who, having gone to Gayā, gives food, thereby makes his ancestors possessed of a son;
and by residing there for three fortnights, he purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation—
or, failing that, for fifteen days, or seven nights, or even three nights.
The sin committed during a great kalpa is destroyed upon reaching Gayā;
one should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) for one's ancestors and for oneself as well, even without sesame seeds.
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru—
all such sins, as well as those arising from association with such sinners, are destroyed by the Śrāddha performed at Gayā.
Whether he be one's own son or born of another, whenever one causes a funeral cake (piṇḍa) to be offered on the ground of Gayā in the name of someone, that person shall be led to the eternal Brahman.
Knowledge of Brahman, performing śrāddha at Gayā, dying in the house of a cow, and residing at Kurukṣetra—this is the fourfold liberation for men. 2.43.14.
What is the use of the knowledge of Brahman if one dies in the house of a cowherd?
What is the use of residing at Kurukṣetra if one's son goes to Gayā? (2.43.15)
At Gayā, a wise man should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) at all times—even during an intercalary month, on one's birthday, or when Jupiter and Venus are eclipsed. ||2.43.16||
The Śrāddha at Gayā must not be abandoned even when Jupiter is situated in Leo;
likewise, when wounds have been inflicted by the stroke of fate, one who performs the Śrāddha becomes entitled to the rites once more and attains the world of Brahmā.
To visit Gayā even once, and to offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) there even once, is difficult to achieve; how much more so, then, to reside permanently in this very place! ||2.43.18||
One may die through negligence in this sacred field that grants liberation even to Brahmā and others;
there is no doubt that liberation is obtained here just as it is through the knowledge of Brahman. 2.43.19
And for the sake of the deliverance of ancestors who have died as insects and the like, therefore it should be performed with every effort by those who are wise. 2.43.20.

One should worship with offerings for the gods (havya) and ancestors (kavya) the Brahmins appointed by Brahmā; when they are satisfied, all the deities together with the ancestors are gratified. || 2.43.21 ||
Shaving the head and fasting— this is the rule at all sacred fords,
with the exception of Kurukṣetra, Viśālā, Virajā, and Gayā.
A monk who has gone to Gayā should display his staff, even if he does not offer funeral cakes;
by placing his staff at Viṣṇupada, he is liberated along with his ancestors. (2.43.23)
In the ultimate sense, the bearer of the staff incurs neither sin nor merit;
therefore, having abandoned all ritual action, the wise man meditates upon Viṣṇu.
One should renounce all ritual actions, but one must not renounce the Veda alone.
One should shave the head in the east, west, south, and north. (2.43.25)
The measurement of Gayā is declared by Brahmā to be two and a half krośas;
the sacred field of Gayā (Gayākṣetra) is five krośas, and Gayāśiras is one krośa.
Within that [place] are indeed all the sacred fords (tīrtha) that exist throughout the three worlds;
he who performs the ancestral rite (śrāddha) in the field of Gayā is truly freed from his debt to the ancestors.
He who performs a *śrāddha* at Śiras shall uplift a hundred generations of his lineage;
by merely setting out from his home toward Gayā,
he ascends the stairs to all the heavens, step by step, for the sake of his ancestors.
Whatever fruit is obtained by one who performs the horse sacrifice at every step while traveling to Gayā, that entire fruit shall surely be attained; there is no doubt in this matter.
At Gayā, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍapātana) may be performed with milk-rice,
sacrificial porridge, barley meal, flour-cakes, rice grains, fruits, roots, and so forth.
With a paste of sesame seeds, with sugar-candy, with jaggery, or with ghee;
or with plain curd, or with milk, or with honey. (2.43.31)
Oil-cake with ghee and sugar is said to provide inexhaustible satisfaction to the ancestors;
likewise, seasonal food fit for sacrifice and the sacrificial grain prescribed by the sages are recommended.
On one side are all things that possess flavor and sweetness;
on the other side is the water of the Phalgu-tīrtha, having remembered the lotus feet of Gadādhara. 2.43.33.

The offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa), the giving of the rice-balls, the subsequent rinsing of the hands, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and the formal declaration regarding the food—this is the procedure for Śrāddhas performed at sacred fords (tīrtha). ||2.43.34||
There is no invocation, no binding of the directions, and no fault arising from one's gaze;
the wise should perform the śrāddha at a sacred ford with compassion. (2.43.35)
At other times, the ancestors go toward that [other world] after being invoked;
however, they always dwell at this sacred ford (tīrtha), and therefore there is no need for invocation here.
Those men who, desiring the fruits thereof, perform the śrāddha at sacred fords (tīrtha) must constantly carry out the rite after having abandoned desire, anger, and greed.
Chaste, eating but one meal a day, sleeping on the ground, pure in speech, and devoted to the welfare of all beings—he attains the fruit of the sacred fords. || 2.43.38 ||
A wise man, visiting sacred fords, should first abandon heresy;
and he who acts according to his own whims should be known as a heretic. 2.43.39.
Those wise men who, devoted to those sacred fords, perform their rites with single-minded focus— just as those who know Brahman perceive the object to be known—
they enter the Supreme Lord, that Brahman which is the ultimate goal of all seekers of Brahman. (2.43.40)
That river of yours named Vaitaraṇī, renowned throughout the three worlds,
has descended into the field of Gayā for the sake of delivering the ancestors.
One who bathes in the Vaitaraṇī while giving a cow as a gift shall uplift twenty-one generations of his lineage.

Likewise, having gone to Akṣayavaṭa, he will satisfy the Brahmins; he shall worship with offerings for the gods and ancestors (havya-kavya) those Brahmins appointed by Brahmā. When they are pleased, all the deities together with the ancestors are gratified. || 2.43.42 ||
Indeed, there is no place in Gayā where a sacred ford (tīrtha) does not exist;
therefore, the Gayā-tīrtha is superior because of the presence of all sacred fords therein.
When the sun is situated in Pisces, Aries, Virgo, Sagittarius, or Aquarius, the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds. (2.43.44)
And when an eclipse of the moon or the sun occurs during the Makara [zodiacal sign],
a śrāddha at Gayā— rare indeed in the three worlds— is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
The fruit that a man obtains by offering the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) at Gayā cannot be described by me even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Nārada said:
How was Gayāsura born? What was his power, and what was his nature?
How did he perform penance, and how did he attain the sanctity of his body? 2.44.1
Sanatkumāra said:
Born from the lotus at the navel of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, was formerly commanded by the divine Viṣṇu to create progeny. 2.44.2.
In ancient times, he created the Asuras with an asuric disposition;
with a cheerful disposition, he created the gods, the Sumanas.
Gaya was an asura among asuras, possessed of great strength and prowess;
his height is recorded as one hundred and twenty-five yojanas.
That excellent Vaiṣṇava, Sthūla, sixty yojanas in height,
performed most rigorous penance on Kolāhala, the best of mountains.
For many thousands of years he remained motionless, without breathing;
the gods, scorched by that asceticism, fell into a state of extreme agitation.
Having gone to the world of Brahmā, the gods then spoke to the Grandfather: "O Lord, protect us from the demon Gayāsura! Thereupon, Brahmā spoke to the gods.
"O gods, we are going to Śaṅkara; Brahmā and the others have also gone to Śiva.
Having bowed down on Kailāsa, they said: 'O God, protect us from the great asura!'"
Śambhu said to Brahmā and the others, "Let us go for refuge to Hari;
in the Ocean of Milk dwells the Lord of the gods, and he will ordain our welfare.
Then Brahmā, Maheśvara, and the gods, having bowed to Viṣṇu, offered him praise.
The gods said: Om! Salutations to Viṣṇu, the sustainer of all, the sovereign lord, the radiant one, the victorious one, and the devourer of the Rākṣasas and other foes. (2.44.10)
Salutations to the sustainer of this entire universe, to the one who leads yogis to the further shore;
salutations to the infinite one who ever increases, salutations to the resplendent one. 2.44.11.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus praised, Vāsudeva granted his vision to the gods.
"For what purpose have you come, O gods? Viṣṇu asked them, and they replied to him. 2.44.12.
"O Lord, out of fear of the demon Gaja, he said to Hari, 'Let those beginning with Brahmā go to that Daitya; I shall follow after them.'"
Keśava, mounted upon Garuḍa, went toward the Asura to grant him a boon;
all the others likewise set out, each mounting his own excellent vehicle.
Vāsudeva and the others said to him: "For what reason do you grieve?
We have all arrived and are well-pleased; choose a boon, O Gayāsura! (2.44.15)
Gayaśura said:
"O gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—if you are pleased with me, [grant this] to all the gods, the twice-born, the sacrifices, the sacred fords, and the mountains. (2.44.16)
I am more protected than the gods, even than the ṛṣis, and from Śiva the Imperishable;
I am protected in every way by the mantras, the gods of gods, and the yogins as well. ||2.44.17||
O gods, may I always be more pure than those who have renounced worldly life, as well as those who perform ritual acts, those devoted to dharma, and even my own most sacred kinsmen. 2.44.18.
"O gods, may he be pure," having said this to the Daitya, they went to heaven;
and having seen and touched the Daitya, they all departed for the city of Hari. ||2.44.19||
The three worlds became empty, and the city of Yama indeed became desolate;
then Yama, together with Indra and the other gods, went to the world of Brahmā.
The gods, having been plundered by the demon Gaya, said to Brahmā:
"Indeed, authority was granted by you; O Grandfather, please accept it yourself. (2.44.21)
Then Brahmā said to the gods, "Let us go to the imperishable Viṣṇu.
Brahmā and the others spoke to Viṣṇu: "Since the boon has been granted by you to the Asura..."
Because of the sight of that [destruction], they went to heaven, and indeed the three worlds became empty.
Addressed by the gods, Vāsudeva spoke these words to Brahmā: ||2.44.23||
"Go and request the Asura, saying, 'Give your body for the sake of the sacrifice.
Thus addressed by Viṣṇu, Brahmā went and beheld the great Asura.
Having seen Brahmā together with the thirty gods, the Asura Gaya rose up,
honored him according to the prescribed rites, and bowed down with faith.
Gaya said:
"Today my birth has become fruitful; today my ascetic penance has become fruitful, since the guest Brahmā has arrived; indeed, everything has been attained by me today."
O Yoginī, O knower of the limbs of yoga, O Lord of all the worlds, O Father, O Guru!
Whatever purpose I have come for, O Brahman, that task I shall perform.
Brahmā said:
"Whatever holy places have been seen by me while wandering upon the earth,
they are not purifying for you from the body for the sake of sacrifice."
"O Asura, you have attained purity of body through the grace of Viṣṇu;
therefore, O Asura, give this pure body to me for the sake of sacrifice."
Gaya said: "O Lord of the gods, I am blessed that my body is sought after by you;
my ancestral lineage has achieved its purpose if you perform a sacrifice upon this body."
This body was produced by you alone; it has been made pure by you so that yoga may surely exist for the benefit of all. ||2.44.31||
Having spoken thus, Gayāsura fell to the earth upon Mount Kolāhala, taking refuge in the southwest direction during the Śveta Kalpa.
Having placed his head toward the north and his feet toward the south,
Brahmā, having gathered the necessary materials, created mental priests.
[He approached] Agniśarman, Amṛta, Śaunaka, Yājñavalkya, Mṛdu, Kumudhi, Kauṇḍilya, Hārīta, Kāśyapa, and Kṛpa. (2.44.34)
Garga, Kauśika, Vāsiṣṭha, the sage Bhārgava who is imperishable,
the aged Pārāśara, Kaṇva, Māṇḍavya, and Śrutikevala.
Śveta, Sutāla, Damana, Suhotra, Kaṅka,
the mighty-armed Laukākṣi, and likewise Jaigīṣavya.
Dadhipañcamukha, Vipra, Ṛṣabha, and Karka; Kātyāyana and Gobhila, and the sage of fierce and great vows.
Supālaka and Gautama, as well as Vedaśirovrata, Jaṭāmālin, Avyagra, Cāṭuhāsa, and Dāruṇa; ||2.44.38||
Ātreya, Aṅgirasa, Aupamanyu, Mahāvrata, Gokarṇa, Guhāvāsa, Śikhaṇḍin, and Umāvrata—[these were the sages]. || 2.44.39 ||
Having fashioned these and other lords of brahmins, the Creator, the Grandfather of the worlds,
performed a sacrifice upon the body of the demon Gayāsura.
Then Agniśarman, the immutable ascetic, likewise emitted from his mouth these five fires:
the Dakṣiṇāgni, the Gārhapatya, the Āhavanīya, and [the other two].
O celestial sage, he bestowed sacrificial fees upon the Brahmins for the sake of establishing both the sacred fires and the sacrifice itself, in which all sacrifices are firmly rooted. 2.44.42.
Having offered the final oblation and performed the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), Brahmā,
together with the gods, brought the sacrificial post and erected it.
In that auspicious lake, the best of waters belonging to Brahmā, he took refuge;
then Brahmā, trembling and agitated, spoke to Dharmarāja.
"Born in your house, bring a stone without hesitation;
by my command, place it quickly upon the head of the Daitya. 2.44.45.
Having heard this for the sake of immobility, Yama held the rock upon his head;
yet, once the rock was supported, the Asura, together with the rock, remained motionless.
Then he spoke to the gods, beginning with Rudra: "O gods, may you all remain motionless upon this stone. Having said, "So be it," they stood there.
Even after the gods had marked him with their feet, the Asura still moved forward;
thereupon Brahmā, becoming distressed, went to Viṣṇu, who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk,
and having bowed down and paid homage to that Lord, he praised Him while prostrate.
Brahmā said: O Lord, Master of the universe, I bow to the Protector of the worlds,
the refuge for illustrious men and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Viṣvaksena said to Viṣṇu, "O Lord, the Lotus-born praises you.
Hari said, "Bring him here. Thus addressed by Viṣṇu, he brought him.
Hari spoke to the Unborn (Aja): "Tell me, why have you come? || 2.44.50 ||
Brahmā said: O God of gods, when the sacrifice had been performed, the demon Gayāsura shook as that stone, which possessed the form of a deity, was placed upon his head. (2.44.51)
When the gods, beginning with Rudra, had taken their positions, the Asura moved;
therefore, O Mādhava, grant your grace now so that there may be stillness.
Having heard the words of Brahmā,
the Blessed Lord Hari drew forth an image from his own body and gave it to Brahmā for the sake of stability.
Brahmā also brought the image and placed it upon the stone;
yet, seeing that it still moved, he then summoned the God once more.
Having arrived from the Ocean of Milk, Viṣṇu established himself upon the stone slab under the names Janārdana and Puṇḍarīka;
for he himself, the primordial wielder of the mace, remained there to ensure the slab’s immovability.
For the sake of immobility, the Great-Grandfather (Brahmā) became fivefold upon the stone:
the Grandfather (Śiva), then Phalgvīśa, Kedāra, and Kanakeśvara.
Brahmā himself is stationed there, as is Vināyaka in the form of an elephant;
Gayāditya, Uttarārka, and Dakṣiṇārka—thus the Sun is threefold.
Lakṣmī under the name Sītā, Gaurī called Maṅgalā,
as well as Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Trisandhyā, and Sarasvatī.
Indra, Bṛhaspati, Pūṣan, and the eight Vasus of great strength;
the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvinīs, and Māruta, the leader of all;
along with the Yakṣas, Uragas, and Gandharvas—all these gods stood there with their respective powers. (2.44.59)
Because that Daitya was made firm by Hari with his first mace (gadā), he was called "Sthita" (the Firm One); therefore, Hari is known as Ādigadādhara (the Original Bearer of the Mace).
Gaya the Asura said to the gods: "For what reason have I been deceived?
My stainless body was given by me to Brahmā for the sake of a sacrifice;
why, at the mere word of Viṣṇu, am I not made firm? (2.44.61)
"O gods, if I have been excessively tormented by the gods and likewise by Hari with his mace, may you all be forever gracious toward me."
Gadādhara and the others, being gratified, spoke together with Gayāsura: "Choose a boon; we are pleased. Gayāsura then addressed the gods. (2.44.63)
"As long as the earth and its mountains endure, and as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars remain, so long may Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara,
along with all other gods, abide upon this stone; let this place indeed be a sacred field (kṣetra) by my name."
The sacred field of Gayā extends for five krośas, and Gayāśiras for one krośa;
may all the holy fords within that space bestow welfare upon men.
Having performed the libation after bathing, a man who offers the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) attains a fruit greater than that;
indeed, such a high-souled man shall uplift a thousand generations of his lineage.
May you always remain in the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest;
may Gadādhara himself be for the world the destroyer of all sins.
May those for whom this *śrāddha* with the *sapiṇḍana* rite is performed go to the world of Brahmā;
and may the sin of killing a Brahmin and other such evils perish for those who partake in it.
Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Gaṅgā, Prayāga, and Avimuktika—
may these and other sacred fords from heaven, earth, and the intermediate space always come to men, and may the gods grant them their welfare.
What is the use of much speaking? O hosts of gods, if even a single deity among you does not remain here, and if I too do not remain, then let our agreement be observed.
Having heard the words of the demon Gaja, Viṣṇu and the other gods said:
"Everything that you have requested shall undoubtedly come to pass."
Having worshipped our feet, they shall go to the supreme goal;
the Daitya, having received a boon from the gods, became joyful and steadfast.
While the gods remained present, Aja bestowed upon the Brahmins fifty-five villages, as well as Gayā extending five krośas;
having constructed divine dwellings, he gave them along with all necessary furnishings.
The wish-fulfilling cow, the kalpa-tree, and trees such as the pārijāta;
likewise, the great river flowing with milk and streams of clarified butter.
He saw streams of honey, honeyed rivulets, lakes rich with curds and other delicacies,
golden oblong ponds, and many mountains of food and other provisions.

Brahmā, while creating all things, gave the various kinds of food, fruits, and so forth; O best of Brahmins, he did not say, "Do not beg from others," but rather the Unborn One gave them [the power] to give.
Having given [the gift] and bowed to the primordial Gadādhara, he went to the world of Brahmā;
then, having caused Dharma to perform a sacrifice there in Dharmāraṇya, they made their request.
And at the sacrifice of Dharma, having accepted wealth and other offerings out of greed,
Brahmā arrived and cursed those Brāhmaṇas.
Since you have entertained greed even for all that was given by me,
therefore, O twice-born ones, you shall always remain burdened by debt.
For you there may be rivers carrying water and mountains of stone;
likewise, there may be rivers and other such water-bearers, as well as houses made of clay. (2.44.80)
"May the wish-fulfilling cow and the celestial tree attend upon our world.
Having been cursed thus by Brahmā, they addressed the Unborn One, making this request. (2.44.81)
"Everything that was given by you has all gone away because of this curse;
O Blessed One, you ought to show us favor for the sake of our livelihood."
Having heard that, Brahmā, filled with compassion, spoke this to the Brahmins:
"You shall subsist on the offerings from sacred fords (tīrtha) as long as the moon and sun endure."
Those meritorious people who perform ancestral rites at Gayā go to the world of Brahmā;
those who shall honor you, by them I am always honored.
The belly of the Daitya was traversed by the mountain Virajā;
near the well of the navel stands the goddess Virajā.
Having performed the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and other rites there, one shall deliver twenty-one generations of one's lineage.
By Mahendra-giri, his two feet were made perfectly firm;
there, a person rescues seven generations of their lineage by offering a funeral ball of rice and other offerings. || 2.44.86 ||
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu. ||44||
Nārada said: How was the stone produced by which Gayāsura was crushed? What is its form, what is its majesty, and what is its name? Tell me this. (2.45.1)
Sanatkumāra said:
There was a man of great splendor named Dharma, who had reached the further shore of all knowledge;
and his wife was Viśvarūpā, who was entirely devoted to her husband. 2.45.2.
From her, through righteousness, was born a daughter named Dharmavrata, who was endowed with all auspicious marks and, like Lakṣmī herself, was preeminent in her virtues. ||2.45.3||
Whatever virtues she possessed remained throughout the three worlds;
Dharma, searching through the three worlds for one who was devoted to the vow of righteousness, found them in her.
Then Dharma did not obtain a suitable boon for the fulfillment of his wish; saying, "Perform penance for the sake of the boon," he departed for the forest, saying, "So be it. (2.45.5)
And that maiden performed penance which is difficult for all to perform;
subsisting on air alone in the Śvetakalpa, she did so for ten thousand ages in the past. || 2.45.6 ||
The renowned Marīci, the mind-born son of Brahmā,
while wandering over the entire earth, beheld a jewel among maidens.
Then Marīci questioned her, who was endowed with beauty and youth and established in supreme austerity: "Who are you? To whom do you belong? Tell me that."
"O timid one, O lady of virtuous vows, you delude me with this form of yours!
I am the renowned Marīci, the son of Brahmā, who has mastered the Vedas. (2.45.9)
Having heard the words of Marīci, the maiden said to that sage:
"I am named Dharmavrata, the daughter of Dharma, endowed with asceticism."

"O best of Brahmins, I am performing supreme austerity for the sake of a devoted wife. To her, who was firm in her vows of dharma, Marīci spoke with affection: 2.45.11. "O best of Brahmins, I am performing supreme austerity for the sake of a devoted wife.
To her, who was firm in her vows of dharma, Marīci spoke with affection: [2.45.11]
"O lady of auspicious vows, by the sight of me you shall become a devoted wife;
for, O faithful wife, I wander the earth day and night at the will of my husband. (2.45.12)
"If you have become devoted to your husband, I shall honor you; choose me as your boon.
In this world there is no maiden like you, and there is no suitor equal to me."
"Since you are devoted to the vow of dharma, become my lawful wife now.
Dharmavratā said to the sage, "O observer of noble vows, ask for dharma."
Having heard that dharma, Dharma went to the sage;
he beheld a mass of splendor and, bowing to the excellent one, honored him with a seat, water for the feet, and other offerings.
When asked why he had come, Marīci spoke of the Dharma:
"While wandering the earth in search of a maiden, I saw that excellent girl of yours.
Give that maiden to me, and it will be for your own welfare. (2.45.16)
Having honored him with the *arghya* and other offerings, Dharma said "So be it" to him;
then, having brought forth Dharmavratā, he gave her to Marīci.
And he granted him a boon, the fulfillment of which had been so requested;
accompanied by the sacred fire, the twice-born one led her back to his own hermitage.
He sported with her as Viṣṇu with Śrī,
as Śambhu with Pārvatī, and as the Unborn One (Aja) with Sarasvatī.
A hundred sons, equal to Viṣṇu, were born to him from her;
then Marīci, having gone to the forest for the sake of fruits and flowers, returned.
Once, being weary, he said to his devoted wife:
"Having eaten, while I am lying on my bed, massage my feet."
Having said, "So be it," Dharmavratā, intent on her purpose, anointed the feet of the sage as he lay upon his bed and massaged them.
Then, while the sage was sleeping, Brahmā arrived at that place;
having seen Brahmā, he [the sage] desired to worship the Lord mentally.
