"Should I perform the massaging of his feet? Is this one worthy of worship, the Teacher of the World?"—thus she rose up in agitation, perceiving him to be the teacher of her own teacher.

Having offered the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), he worshipped Brahmā; and the Unborn One (*Aja*) took rest upon the honored couch. In the meantime, the Lord rose from his bed.
Seeing Dharmavratā, that brahmin, filled with rage, cursed her.
"Since you have gone elsewhere, abandoning the massaging of my feet and disregarding my command, therefore, O sinful woman, become a stone consumed by a curse! (2.45.27)
Cursed by her husband for violating her vow of righteousness, she spoke to Marīci with anger:
"While you were lying down, Brahmā arrived; he is your father and your preceptor."
"For you must always rise and perform the worship of your own guru;
as for me, O sage, I am a follower of dharma who has fulfilled my duty toward you."
"Since I have been cursed despite being free from fault, I therefore bestow a curse upon you:
you shall undoubtedly receive a curse from your husband, Mahādeva."
Seeing her husband so distressed, she became agitated herself and went to Prajāpati;
having bowed to Brahmā as he lay there, she kindled the fire with fuel.
Remaining at the Gārhapatya fire, she performed a most difficult penance;
and Marīci, having been thus cursed, likewise practiced a very severe austerity.
By the ascetic power of the devoted wife and likewise by the ascetic power of Marīci,
Indra and the other gods were so greatly tormented that they went for refuge to Hari.
Tormented by their ascetic penance, they spoke to Hari as he slept upon the Ocean of Milk:
"O Keśava, protect the three worlds from the chaste wife and the sage! (2.45.34)
Having heard the words of Indra and the others, Viṣṇu went to Dharmavrata.
At that very moment, the unborn Lord awoke;
then the gods, together with Keśava, spoke to Dharmavrata as she stood by the fire.
O devoted wife, who has the power to perform such penance in the midst of fire?
That supreme feat, which strikes terror into all the worlds, was accomplished by you.
"Choose a boon from us, O knower of dharma, whatever you desire.
Having heard the words of Viṣṇu and the other gods, she who was devoted to dharma spoke to the deities: [45.37]
"I am powerless to avert my husband's curse by means of my own power;
let that curse which was given to me by Marīci indeed depart. (2.45.38)
Having heard the words of Dharmavrata, the gods spoke again:
"O Dharmavrata, O daughter of Dharma, this curse was pronounced upon you by the supreme rishi."
This which has been granted to you cannot be revoked by gods or the twice-born; therefore, ask for another boon whereby the stability of dharma may be maintained.
"O you who observe auspicious vows prescribed by the Vedas, may this indeed come to pass throughout the three worlds.
Having heard the words of the gods, she spoke to the gods regarding her vow of righteousness.
When the immortals were unable to release my husband from his curse, they granted me this unsurpassed boon: "Grant me such a boon as this, most excellent. (2.45.42)
"For I shall become a stone, auspicious and purifying within the universe, more purifying than rivers, streams, lakes, sacred fords, gods, and the like. (2.45.43)

"May all the lingas in the three worlds— whether manifest or unmanifest— that belong to the sages beginning with the Ṛṣis, to the Munis, and even to the principal deities, remain forever within my body in the form of sacred pilgrimage sites."
May all the sacred fords, as well as those headed by the lunar mansions, remain present;
likewise, may all the gods, goddesses, and sages abide here.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as the five fires, Kumāra, and the others, having perceived my state, abide in manifold forms. || 2.45.46 ||
The deities, in the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest, and in the form of words, remained on the earth in embodied forms within a distance of only one krośa from the stone. 2.45.47.
Having seen her, who destroys all great sins, every person becomes purified and fit for the practice of dharma; and one who performs the śrāddha rite attains the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed in the sacred fords situated upon stone and having performed the libations,
may those for whom the *śrāddha* rite with the *sapiṇḍa* offering was performed go to the world of Brahmā.
Gadādhara is the visible tīrtha, the most excellent among all tīrthas;
men who dwell there or die there shall go to the city of Brahmā.
So too shall those at Vārāṇasī, Prayāga, and the place known as Puruṣottama.
May that place known as Gaṅgāsāgara remain eternally under the constellation Phalgunī;
may it be presided over by the Wielder of the Mace (Viṣṇu), for it is the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
May there always be liberation for the ancestors who have passed away through the performance of śrāddha rites there.
Whether born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, or as sprouts from the earth— having abandoned the body, let them become like stone and attain the very nature of Viṣṇu.
Just as all sacrifices become complete when Hari is worshipped, so too may the śrāddha, the libation, and the bath be inexhaustible here. 2.45.53.
May those who recite the Śruti and other scriptures within my body become perfected and attainers of spiritual powers without delay. || 2.45.54 ||
By means of the śrāddha and other rites, a man certainly leads a thousand ancestors, together with himself, out of [saṃsāra] and into the world of Viṣṇu. 2.45.55
O lords of the gods, may all the best of rivers such as the Gaṅgā, the auspicious lakes, the oceans and principal ponds, and the Mānasa lake and others,
dwell within me for the liberation of those men who perform the śrāddha rite.
May the deities not depart from anywhere, but remain united with this body, until Viṣṇu—the single one whose form is threefold—is glorified by the wise. 2.45.57.
"Let all the sacred fords (tīrthas), together with the deities, the sages, and the hosts of Gandharvas, remain forever upon this rock. (2.45.58)
She who is the embodiment of all the gods and possesses a divine form—
may this stone remain as long as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) endures.
And for those who chant and perform austerities upon my body in the form of this stone, [may they attain their desires].

And for those who offer oblations into the fire while standing before me, that [merit] shall indeed become inexhaustible; let the Śrāddha, as well as their recitations, burnt offerings, and austerities, become eternal. May [this merit] abide forever within me in the form of rocks and mountains. (2.45.60)
Having heard the words of the devoted wife, the gods said to her:
"Whatever you have prayed for, all that shall come to pass without a doubt. (2.45.61)

"When you become firmly established upon the head of the demon Gaya, then we shall remain steadfast within you in the form of your feet and other limbs. Having thus granted this boon to the stone, the gods vanished on that very spot.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gaya," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sanatkumāra said: O Nārada, listen as I shall describe the greatness of the Śilā, which bestows liberation, and whose majesty even the gods and the foremost of sages sing. 2.46.1.
That stone, established upon the earth, is divine in form and exceedingly purifying;
it is the stone-tirtha named Vicitra, renowned throughout the three worlds. ||2.46.2||
By her touch, all the worlds went to the city of Hari;
when the three worlds had become empty, the city of Yama indeed became empty.
Yama, having gone together with Indra and the others, spoke to the wondrous Brahmā:
"O Grandfather, take up your office now and assume the rod of Yama."
Then Brahmā said to Yama, "Keep her in your own home.
Thus addressed by Brahmā, Dharmarāja kept her in his house.
Yama assumed his own authority, such as the punishment of sinners;
thus is this exceedingly heavy stone renowned throughout the world. (2.46.6)
Just as Brahmā, just as Viṣṇu, and just as the god Maheśvara,
and just as Meru is within the cosmic egg, so too is she, who possesses a divine form.
Since she was borne upon the head of the demon Gaya due to her weight,
the union of these two sacred sites bestows liberation upon the ancestors.
Upon the union of the two purifiers, the goat performed the horse sacrifice;

seeing Viṣṇu and the others who had arrived for their shares, the Stone spoke: śilovāca | aho me paramāścaryaṃ yajñe'sminvaiśvadevike | yūyaṃ sarve samāyātā devā brahmapurogamāḥ || 1 || bhāgaṃ dātuṃ samudyuktāḥ śrutvā vākyaṃ ca me tadā | sarveṣāmeva devānāṃ madhye māṃ sthāpayiṣyatha || 2 || tato me paramaṃ harṣaṃ jātaṃ vaiśvadevike | yajñe'sminparamodāre sarvadevasamāgame || 3 || tataḥ prahasya tāndevānviṣṇvādīnabravīcchilā | māṃ na jānītha kiṃ sarve yūyaṃ devagaṇāḥ kila || 4 || ahaṃ hi pūrvamevāsminyajñe vaiśvadevike | samāgatāsmi sarveṣāṃ bhāgārthaṃ tridaśeśvarāḥ || 5 || tato me paramaṃ duḥkhaṃ jātaṃ vaiśvadevike | yajñe'sminparamodāre sarvadevasamāgame || 6 || yadi me na pradāsyadhvaṃ bhāgaṃ vaiśvadevike | yajñe'sminparamodāre sarvadevasamāgame || 7 || tato me paramaṃ roṣo bhaviṣyati suniścitam | tasmāddatta bhāgaṃ mahyaṃ yadi cecchatha jīvitam || 8 || tataḥ prahasya tāndevānviṣṇvādīnabravīcchilā | na vayaṃ jānīmahe tvaṃ kāsi brūhi ca tattvataḥ || 9 || śilovāca | ahaṃ hi pūrvamevāsminyajñe vaiśvadevike | samāgatāsmi sarveṣāṃ bhāgārthaṃ tridaśeśvarāḥ || 10 || tato me paramaṃ duḥkhaṃ jātaṃ vaiśvadevike | yajñe'sminparamodāre sarvadevasamāgame || 11 || yadi me na pradāsyadhvaṃ bhāgaṃ vaiśvadevike | yajñe'sminparamodāre sarvadevasamāgame || 12 || tato me paramaṃ roṣo bhaviṣyati suniścitam | tasmāddatta bhāgaṃ mahyaṃ yadi cecchatha jīvitam || 13 || tataḥ prahasya tāndevānviṣṇvādīnabravīcchilā | na vayaṃ jānīmahe tvaṃ kāsi brūhi ca tattvataḥ || 14 || śilovāca | ahaṃ hi pūrvamevāsminyajñe vaiśvadevike | samāgatāsmi sarveṣāṃ bhāgārthaṃ tridaśeśvarāḥ || 15 || tato me paramaṃ duḥkhaṃ jātaṃ vaiśvadevike | yajñe'sminparamodāre sarvadevasamāgame || 16 || yadi me na pradāsyadhvaṃ bhāgaṃ vaiśvadevike | yajñe'sminparamodāre sar
"Let them make a vow to remain upon this stone for the sake of the liberation of their fathers.
Having said, "So be it," the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, stood at the edge of the stone.
By virtue of their prior vow, the deities abide in the form of stone, in embodied form, and in the form of footprints, existing both as manifest and unmanifest entities.
Because that stone rested upon the shaven back (muṇḍapṛṣṭha) of the Daitya,
therefore that mountain Muṇḍapṛṣṭha bestows the world of Brahmā upon the ancestors.
Since the foot of the mountain was covered by the mountain Prabhāsa,
and it was illuminated by the sun, it was designated as Prabhāsa.
Having pierced through Prabhāsa, the big toe emerged;
the Lord who rose from the toe is celebrated as Prabhāseśa.

That portion of the big toe of the stone which is known as Pretaśilā—by offering the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) and other rites thereon, a man is released from the state of being a ghost (preta). || 2.46.15 ||
A man who bathes at the confluence of the Mahānadī and the Prabhāsādri, and Rāma, having bathed there together with the Goddess, is why that place is known as Rāmatīrtha. (2.46.16)
Requested here by the great river, "O Rāma,
may you bathe," it then became known as Rāmatīrtha, famous throughout the three worlds.
Whatever evil deeds I have committed throughout more than a hundred previous births,
may they all go to destruction through bathing at Rāmatīrtha.
The man who, having bathed with this mantra, performs a śrāddha at Rāmatīrtha— his funeral cake (piṇḍa) goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having said, "So be it," Rāma, the elder brother of Bharata, remained there together with Sītā.
O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, granter of fearlessness to the gods!
I bow to you here, the Lord of Gods; may my sin be destroyed. 2.46.20.
Whoever, having bathed with this mantra, performs the Śrāddha ceremony together with the Sapiṇḍana rite,
his ancestors are liberated from the state of being a preta and attain the status of Pitṛs.
O Lord of Gods, you are the waters and indeed the lord of the luminaries;
O God, destroy my sin born of the actions of mind, speech, and body. 2.46.22
Having paid homage to the Lord of Prabhāsa, who shines as Śiva, one should proceed;
and having bowed to that Śambhu, one should then offer the bali-oblation to Yama.
When Rāma had gone to the forest, Bharata arrived at the mountain and remained there;
having performed the ancestral offerings and other rites, he established Rāma's presence there.

The Lord established Rāma, Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, and the sages in the holy hermitage of Bharata, which is eternally frequented by those most meritorious; there, the footprint of Mataṅga is visible to all human beings. (2.46.25) 108.25
The entire essence of the Dharma has been established for the instruction of this world;
one who possesses faith, by standing upon the footprint of Mataṅga, delivers all his ancestors.
Having bathed at Rāmatīrtha and having worshipped Rāma and Sītā,
and then having bowed down to Rāmeśvara, a person is not born again in a body.
The hip of the rock was again stepped upon by the mountain;
however, being addressed by Dharmarāja with the words "Do not go," the mountain is remembered as Naga.
Yama and Dharmarāja are established for the sake of immutability;
to them I offer this oblation for the sake of the liberation of my ancestors.
There are two dogs, one dark and one brindled, born of the lineage of Vaivasvata;
I offer this oblation to them, so that they may both be harmless.
May the crows situated in the directions of Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama,
and Nirṛti accept this ball of rice offered by me once again.
"You are Yama, you are the messenger of Yama, you are the crow of great strength;
having consumed this offering, destroy the sin committed throughout seven lifetimes. (2.46.32)
Indeed, when Rāma had gone to the forest, Bharata came to this mountain;
having performed the funeral rites for his father, he established Rāmeśvara here.
Having bathed and bowed to Rāmeśa, who is accompanied by Rāma and Sītā,
and having performed there the Śrāddha ceremony along with the Sapindana rite, that righteous soul shall go to the city of Viṣṇu together with his ancestors and hundreds of his lineages.
Mount Kuṇḍa was established in the right hand of Śilā;
Timira, Āditya, Īśāna, and Bharga—these are the Maheśvaras. ||2.46.35||
There are two Vahnis, two Varunas, and four Rudras who grant liberation to the ancestors;
having reached Bharata’s hermitage, a person should bow to and worship them. 2.46.36.

O celestial sage, wherever a man bathes and performs the śrāddha and other rites in the hermitage of Bharata, he is liberated from both major and minor sins along with his ancestors; even in that degenerate age, he does not fall away from merit.
At Gayā, the Śrāddha rite is inexhaustible, as are recitations, burnt offerings, and austerities;
indeed, they say that everything given at Bharata’s hermitage becomes infinite.
The four forms of the Sun, which embody the nature of the four yugas, have been seen, touched, and worshipped; they bestow liberation upon the ancestors.
"Liberation is Vāmana"—this is the supreme rite known as the Tāraka.
For those scorched by the ocean of saṃsāra, these two lords of the gods are like a boat.
This is the Tāraka Brahman for all, both for the dead and for the living. (2.46.40)
The righteous-souled person who beholds Trivikrama and Brahmā, the Supreme Person,
goes together with his ancestors to the highest goal.
Likewise, on the left foot of the stone, the mountain Abhyudyantaka is situated;
a funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered there shall lead the ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
On the edge of the Naimiṣa forest, Brahmā performed a sacrifice together with the gods;
for that sacred site is known as Mukhya, where the deities are established.
O best of sages, O Nārada, whatever inauspicious karma exists within those very three steps— that is, the sacred fords— is utterly destroyed.
That sacred Naimiṣa forest is frequented by meritorious men;
there dwell Vyāsa, Śuka, Paila, Kaṇva, Vedhas, Śiva, and Hari.
By the mere sight of them, a man is liberated from his sins;
likewise, there is the mountain Udyantaka with a stone upon its left side.
That mountain was indeed brought there by the high-souled Agastya;
there Brahmā and Hara performed fierce austerities.
There, indeed, is the excellent pool of Agastya, difficult to find even in the three worlds,
where the eight sages attained perfection and, having performed penance, went to Śiva.
By bowing to the eight sages at that pool, one leads one's ancestors to the city of Brahmā.

Then, O celestial sage, the high-souled Agastya placed that auspicious king of mountains upon a stone slab with his left hand; thus the mountain became known as Vāditraka, enriched by divine songs and musical instruments. 2.46.49.
There, the one named Vidyādhara, accompanied by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases,
even today sings divine songs together with them.
Also [there are] Mohana, Sunītha, Śailūṣa, and Mohanottama.
Parvata, Nārada, Dhyānin, Saṅgīti, Puṣpadantaka, Hāhā, Hūhū, and others performed the gift of song. || 2.46.51 ||
Likewise, one named Citraratha, surrounded by all the Gandharvas,
sang sweet songs at a great festival on the mountain.
Therefore, that mountain is constantly frequented by the gods even today;
there resides Dharmarāja and Hara, the lord of the gods, who is smeared with ashes as his unguent.
Accompanied by Pārvatī on the mountain resounding with the sound of song, Rudra rejoices; he is the one to be worshipped and meditated upon, the supreme goal of the ancestors.
O sage, at Gayā, the Supreme Self—whether as Gopati or Gadādhara—is indeed present;
likewise, O sage, the Māyā of Viṣṇu is set aside through the worship of Rudra.
On the right hand of Śilā, Mount Bhasmakūṭa was held by Dharmarāja; there indeed dwells Agastya together with his wife.
Having bathed at the site of Agastya and offered funeral cakes (piṇḍas), one goes to the world of Brahmā;
he obtained from Brahmā a boon, a majesty difficult to attain on earth. || 2.46.57 ||
Likewise, having seen Lopāmudrā, the wife who is the supreme goal of the ancestors,
and having beheld Agastyeshvara there, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He led Agastya along with his wife and the ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
Daṇḍin, moreover, performed austerities on the mountain to the south of Mount Sītā.
The banyan tree Vaṭeśvara stands there, as does the Great-Grandfather (Brahmā). In front of that is the Rukmiṇīkuṇḍa, and to the west is the Kapilā river.
On the bank of the river is Kapileśa, at the conjunction of the new moon and Monday.
Having bathed in the Kapilā and having worshipped Kapileśa, if one performs the Śrāddha and the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa), the ancestors shall attain liberation. ||2.46.61||
There, after the Udyantaka mountain, a stream of fire issued forth from that best of mountains;
there also is the Sārasvata pool, fashioned by Sarasvatī.
O best of sages,
at each of those places where the lords of sages dwell,
a man who has bathed there and offered the Śrāddha-piṇḍas, along with his sons, including even eunuchs and the like, delivers his ancestors. || 2.46.63 ||
Even with his left hand, Śilā held up Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
there, great ṛṣis attained perfection after performing austerities in the form of vultures. || 2.46.64 ||
Therefore, on that mountain Gṛdhrakūṭa dwells Gṛdhreśvara;
having seen and bowed to Gṛdhreśvara, a person shall go to the abode of Śambhu.
There, at Gṛdhra and in Guhā, the giver of alms shares in the world of Śiva;
having bowed there to Vaṭa at Gṛdhra, one whose desires are fulfilled shall go to heaven. ||2.46.66||
Having beheld Śiva, who grants liberation from debt and liberation from sin, one shall go to Śiva.
And there lies the Śūla-kṣetra; the giver of funeral cakes shall lead his ancestors to heaven.
The interior of the rock is occupied by the primordial guardian Giri;
there dwells Vighneśa, the destroyer of obstacles, in the form of an elephant.
By seeing him, one is liberated from all impediments, and he shall lead one’s ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
On the slope of Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha lies the Devadāru forest;
by beholding both Muṇḍapṛṣṭha and Mount Aravinda, one destroys sin.
By offering funeral cakes at the navel of Gayā, at the Suṣumnā spring, one leads one's ancestors to heaven.
The mountain called Pretaśilā was established by Dharmarāja upon the left foot of Śilā; it is a mountain for the wicked intended for the departed spirits.
Cast far away from the rock by the weight of his foot,
that heap of corpses attained purity through contact with the stone.
The Pretakuṇḍa is situated there, and the gods abide at that place;
having performed rites such as the offering into the pit there, one may liberate one's ancestors from the state of being a preta.
Standing apart in great numbers, they are indeed creators of obstacles for those men performing ancestral rites such as the *śrāddha* at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) for the liberation of their ancestors;
these *preta*s take the form of archers and seize the offerings. (2.46.73)
Having seen that mountain marked with footprints, whose back is shaven and where Mahādeva dwells, all the world is liberated from sins and minor offenses. (2.46.74)
And because Gayāśiras is meritorious and free from all sins,
and because it is devoid of ghosts and the like, it is therefore most supremely purifying. Gayā is sacred among the Kīkaṭas, and the forest of Rājagṛha is sacred.
The hermitage of Cyavana is holy, and the river there is repeatedly purifying.
Vaikuṇṭha, Lohadaṇḍa, Gṛdhrakūṭa, and Śoṇaka—
by performing śrāddha and other rites here, one leads all the ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
For the sage performed austerities on Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha in the form of a curlew;
because it was marked by his footprints, it is therefore known as Krauñcapāda. (2.46.78)
Having bathed there in that reservoir of water, one leads one's own lineage to heaven;
and by offering an oblation to the crows at Kākaśilā, one grants release from debt to the crows.
Indeed, on the summit of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha dwell Lomaśa and Lomaharṣaṇa;
having performed supreme austerities, these two have attained the highest perfection.
Then those best of rivers, the great streams Śarāvatī, Vetravatī, Candrabhāgā, and Sarasvatī, were summoned by Lomaśa.
The Kāverī, Sindhu, Rīrā, and Candanā, the best of rivers;
the Vāsiṣṭhī, Sarayū, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Gaṇḍakī, and Indirā. ||2.46.82||
O dwellers of heaven, there is the river named Mahāvaitaraṇī, as well as Nikṣarā; to the south is the Alakanandā, and to the north is the one called Kanakā.
Kauśikī, Brahmadā, and Jyeṣṭhā liberate one from all sins;
Kṛṣṇavalvā and Carmavatī are two rivers that bestow liberation.

O bull among sages, when the best of rivers was summoned by Lomaharṣaṇa through his daring and the power of his asceticism, Narmadā appeared; he who bathes in all of them and offers funeral cakes shall lead his ancestors to heaven.
That man who, having entered the womb of Brahman, then emerges,
goes to the Supreme Brahman here, liberated from the peril of rebirth.
Having bathed in the Nikṣarā Puṣkariṇī, a person should perform the Śrāddha and other rites for three days at the divine Krauñcapada according to the prescribed rules;
he shall lead all his ancestors, even those guilty of the five great sins, to heaven.
If Janārdana, while on a heap of ashes, receives a funeral ball (piṇḍa) in his hand—
whether for himself or for others— even with the left hand and without sesame seeds,
yet mixed with curd, all those living beings go to the world of Viṣṇu. || 2.46.88 ||
"O Janārdana, that ball of rice which was placed by me in your hand—O Lord, that ball of rice is for him on whose account it was to be given by you once he had died. (2.46.89)
"O Janārdana, this funeral cake (piṇḍa) has been placed by me in your hand;
when my time of death has come, it must be offered by you at Gayāśiras. (2.46.90)
O Janārdana, salutations to you; salutations to you, the giver of liberation to the ancestors!
O Lord of the ancestors, let there be salutations to you; salutations to you who are the very form of the ancestors.
At Gayā, Janārdana himself exists in the form of the ancestors;
by beholding that lotus-eyed one, one is liberated from the three debts.
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, the liberator from the three debts;
salutations be to you, O beloved of Lakṣmī; be the bestower of liberation upon the ancestors.
Having prostrated himself by falling with his left knee to the ground and bowing before Janārdana, the righteous-souled Bhīma,
having performed the śrāddha rite with excellent funeral cakes, became a partaker of the world of Brahmā along with his brothers,
his ancestors, and a hundred generations of his lineage.

On that stone, the Lord of Lakṣmī remains in manifest form, existing as both the manifest and the unmanifest, together with the gods; therefore, that stone is composed of divinity. Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa spoken by Vāyu.
Nārada said:
How does the primordial wielder of the mace (Viṣṇu) exist in his manifest form?
And how does he exist in his manifest form as the soul of both the manifest and the unmanifest? 2.47.1
How did the mace originate, just as the Primordial Wielder of the Mace [did]? And how did it become "Gadolola," which brings about the destruction of all sins? 2.47.2.
Sanatkumāra said:
There was indeed an asura named Gada, firmer than a thunderbolt and more solid than adamant;
in former times, through severe austerity, he obtained a boon from Brahmā.
Being thus entreated, he gave to Brahmā the bones from his own body, which are so difficult to relinquish.
Then Viśvakarman, as commanded by Brahmā, fashioned a marvelous mace;
he held that bone in heaven, which was as hard as the strokes of a thunderbolt.
Then, after a long time, during the period of Svāyambhuva Manu,
a certain Rākṣasa named Heti, the son of Brahmā, performed most rigorous ascetic penance.
For a hundred thousand celestial years, he subsisted on air alone,
with his face turned upward and his arms raised, supported solely by the weight of his big toes.
Remaining undistracted for one [year], subsisting on withered leaves and the wind,
he chose a boon from Brahmā and the other gods, who were gratified by his asceticism, as they were givers of boons.
May I be of great strength and invincible against gods, daityas, humans, and others, by means of various weapons and missiles, and by Kṛṣṇa, Īśāna, the discus, and so forth. 2.47.8.
Having said "So be it," they vanished; Heti performed sacrifices for the gods.
Fearing him, Indra, Brahmā, Hara, and the others granted him the status of Indra.
They went to Hari for refuge and said, "Kill this weapon!
To them Hari replied, "O gods, this weapon cannot be slain by either gods or asuras."
"Give me a great weapon, for with that weapon I shall slay him.
Having been addressed thus, the gods then gave that mace to Hari.
At the outset, addressed by the gods, Gadādhara took up that mace;
having struck Heti with the mace, he went to the third heaven along with the gods.
Because he stood firm upon the stone that was the head of the demon Gaja, having first grasped his mace to ensure its immovability, he is therefore known as Ādigadādhara.
The primordial wielder of the mace (Ādigadādhara) is manifest in the form of a rocky mountain;
this rock is Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, the mountain named Prabhāsa. ||2.47.14||
Udyanta, Gītanāda, the great mountain Bhasmakūṭa,
Gṛdhrakūṭa, Pretakūṭa, Ādipāla, and Aravindaka.
Pañcaloka, Saptaloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Lohadaṇḍaka, Krauñcapāda, Akṣayavaṭa, Phalgutīrtha, and Madhuśravas. || 2.47.16 ||
The primordial Gadādhara is manifest in the form of the Dadhikulyā, the Madhukulyā, the great river Devikā, the Vaitaraṇī, and so forth. (2.47.17)
There is the station of Viṣṇu, the station of Rudra, and the supreme station of Brahmā;
there is the divine station of Kāśyapa, from which two hands emerged. (2.47.18)
Here are the sites of the five fires; beyond them are the sites of Indra and Agastya, as well as those of Ravi, Kārttikeya, Krauñca, and Mātaṅga.
Abiding in the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest, he encompasses all primary signs;
he is the primordial Gadādhara, the manifest and glorious Gadādhara.
Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Sandhyā, and Sarasvatī; Gayāditya, Uttarārka, Dakṣiṇārka, and Naimiṣa.
Śvetārka, Gaṇanātha, the eight Vasus, the lords of sages,
the eleven Rudras, and likewise the other seven Ṛṣis.
Somanātha, Siddheśa, Kapardīśa, Vināyaka, Nārāyaṇa, Mahālakṣmī, Brahmā, and Śrī Puruṣottama. || 2.47.23 ||
Mārkaṇḍeyeśa, Kauṭīśa, Aṅgireśa, Pitāmaha, Janārdana, Maṅgalā, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, and Uttama. ||2.47.24||
Thus, Ādigadādhara remained in manifest form;
when that Rākṣasa named Heti was slain, Viṣṇu returned to his city.
When the asura had been rendered motionless by Brahmā, together with Rudra and the others, the Creator,
filled with joy and tranquility, praised the primordial one who held a mace in his hand.
Brahmā said:

I bow to Gadādhara, who has cast off the impurity of time, who has come to Gayā, whose qualities are known, yet who transcends all qualities; who dwells in the cave of the heart, who resides in a home as white as the best of mountains, who is worshipped by the Gaṇas, and who is the granter of boons. 2.47.27.

I bow to that Gadādhara, the glory of the day, the supreme glory of the hosts of the thirty gods, the glory of existence, the glory that shatters the offspring of Diti, the glory that destroys the Kali age, the glory that crushes the impurities of the Kali age, and the glory who is the refuge of all. 2.47.28.

Firm yet unsteady, praised intensely by the powerful, a wondrous marvel of desire, it is both firmly rooted and devoid of growth; it reaches the heights of the wealthy, yet is offered up by those burdened with firm misfortune—a firm and radiant hymn of praise from the lineage of the self-established.

I perpetually bow to Hari, the Lord who is without beginning— the one who is bodiless, devoid of the instruments of action, unborn, adorned by the sun and the moon, the wielder of the mace, and supreme, being free from sound and all other sensory objects.

I bow to that Gadādhara who has entered my heart—He who transcends the mind, who is devoid of the reach of intellect, who is supreme and eternally non-dual, who is praised by the wise at the crest of their hymns, whose nature is pure consciousness, and who transcends all causes of the Kali age. 2.47.31
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus praised by the gods together with Brahmā, the primordial wielder of the mace (Viṣṇu) said, "Choose a boon. To him, Brahmā spoke regarding that boon. 2.47.32.
We shall not remain upon this stone, which is the form of the god, without you;
we shall stay here forever together with you, who are eternally manifest in your primordial form.

"Let it be so; may the primordial wielder of the mace remain together with Śrī for the protection of the worlds and for the sake of the liberation of all beings—clearly manifest as the lotus-eyed one known as Janārdana. (2.47.34)
That primordial and eternal form, which is inaccessible through the Vedas,
shall likewise become fully manifest once again in the Śveta Kalpa;
for in the past, during the Vārāha Kalpa, she who was unmanifest attained manifestation.
For the sake of delivering the worlds and for the protection of the gods, he will become clearly manifest upon the peak of Gayā; of this there is no doubt.
Those who shall always behold the primordial Lord Gadādhara with devotion will be liberated from leprosy and other diseases and go to the abode of Hari.
Those who shall always behold the primordial Lord Gadādhara with devotion will obtain wealth,
grain, long life, and indeed health.

Those men who, with faith, pay homage [to him] shall enjoy the virtues, fame, and happiness derived from wife, sons, grandsons, and so forth, as well as sovereignty and the city of Brahmā; having experienced these, they shall eternally attain the fruit of a multitude of merits.
Through the gift of fragrance one becomes rich in scent; through the gift of flowers, good fortune;
through the gift of incense, the attainment of sovereignty; and from the lamp, radiance shall arise. (2.47.40)
By the gift of a banner, one's sins are destroyed; the performer of the procession attains the world of Brahmā;
and he who offers the funeral cakes at a śrāddha shall indeed lead his ancestors to Viṣṇu.
Those who, with faith, pay homage to the primordial Gadādhara with hymns,
and who shall praise him after duly worshipping the ancestors, shall attain Mādhava;
Śiva too, with supreme affection, praised the primordial Gadādhara.
Śiva said: I bow to the primordial Gadādhara, the Lord whose form is unmanifest, yet who appears in forms such as Muṇḍapṛṣṭha and in the form of Phalgutīrtha. 2.47.43.
I bow to Ādigadādhara, who exists in the form of manifest and unmanifest entities, in the form of words, and in the form of faces, lingas, and so forth.
I bow to the primordial Gadādhara, the god whose form is unmanifest, who was born himself on Muṇḍapṛṣṭha in the form of Janārdana.
I bow to that Gadādhara, who is situated upon the stone slab in the form of a deity, worshipped and honored by the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
Having seen, touched, worshipped, and bowed down to him, one attains the world of Brahmā at the beginning of a śrāddha ceremony and other rites; I bow to that primordial Gadādhara.
I bow to that primordial Gadādhara, whose nature is the knowledge of the unmanifest, who is indeed the single cause of the manifest world beginning with Mahat. 2.47.48.
I bow to the primordial Gadādhara, who is devoid of body, senses, mind, intellect, vital breath, and ego, and who is liberated from both waking and dreaming states. 2.47.49
I bow to the primordial Gadādhara, the fourth light, the Self, who is free from the eternal and the non-eternal, the truth, bliss, and the imperishable.
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus praised by Maheśa, the primordial wielder of the mace was indeed pleased;
that god stood upon the stone together with Brahmā and the other deities.
Those who praise and worship here the primordial wielder of the mace, established on Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, shall go to the world of Brahmā.
One who seeks dharma shall attain dharma; one who seeks wealth shall attain wealth; one who seeks pleasure shall obtain pleasure; and one who seeks liberation shall attain liberation. (2.47.53)
A barren woman obtains a son who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
a king attains victory, and a Śūdra shall obtain happiness. 2.47.54.
One desiring sons obtains sons by worshipping Ādigadādhara;
through worship and other rites, one shall obtain everything prayed for in the mind from Hari.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the glorious Vāyu Purāṇa, as proclaimed by Vāyu. ||47||
Sanatkumāra said:
O Nārada, listen as I describe the pilgrimage to Gayā, which bestows liberation;
it was sung of old by Brahmā as the means of atonement for those who perform śrāddha rites. 2.48.1.
If one intends to go to Gayā, having performed the śrāddha according to the rules, having assumed the dress of a pilgrim (kārpaṭika), and having circumambulated the village; ||2.48.2||
Then, having gone to another village, he should eat the remnants of a śrāddha meal;
thereafter, he should travel every day, avoiding the acceptance of gifts.
He who has desisted from accepting gifts, who is contented, self-controlled, pure,
and free from egoism, attains the fruit of sacred pilgrimage sites.
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained,
and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and fame— he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
Then, upon entering Gayā, there is a great river to the east;
having drawn up water from there, one should bathe in its pure waters.

Then, having gratified the gods and others and performed the śrāddha according to the rules—omitting the offering of water (arghya) and the invocation (āvāhana) as prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (svaveda-śākhā)—[he should proceed].
On the following day, having become pure, one should go to Pretaparvata;
then, having bathed in Brahmakuṇḍa, the wise man should offer libations to the gods and others.

Being self-restrained and wise, one should perform the śrāddha for the sapindas on the Pretaparvata mountain, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin) and facing the south. ||2.48.9||
Kavyavāla, Anala, Soma, Yama, and Aryaman,
as well as the Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, and Somapa ancestors, are the deities of the manes.
"May my illustrious ancestors come here, protected by you—those who were born in my lineage and those who are my kinsmen. (2.48.11)
I have come to this Gayā for the purpose of offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to them;
may they all attain eternal satisfaction through this śrāddha rite.
Having sipped water and performed the five-limbed pranayama with diligence, for the sake of attaining the world of Brahma from which there is no return.

And having thus performed the śrāddha according to the rule and in the proper sequence, one should first invoke the ancestors, worship them with mantras, and then become the giver of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa). || 2.48.14 ||

At a sacred ford (tīrtha), at the Pretaśilā, and so forth, having first washed that place with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) individually, one should then worship the deity with those same mantras and with the five products of the cow mixed with ghee or sacrificial porridge (caru).
As long as sesame seeds are taken by men for ancestral rites,
so long do the Asuras flee like deer terrified of a lion.

On the Aṣṭakā days, on occasions of prosperity, at Gayā, and on the anniversary of her death, one should perform the Śrāddha for the mother separately; on other occasions, it should be performed together with the husband.
In the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, however, one begins with the mother and others, while at Gayā it begins with the father;

starting from the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and proceeding in order with *kuśa* grass whose tips point southward, one should spread [the grass] for the father and the other ancestors, and then perform the remainder as prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. 2.48.18.
They should offer the śrāddha for those sapindas from the southern side,
having spread kuśa grass according to the rule and having offered water with sesame seeds once.
Having taken [the flour] from them with joined palms, one should diligently offer an inexhaustible piṇḍa with a handful of barley meal using the pitṛ-tīrtha; then,
one should invoke the relatives with water containing sesame seeds upon the kuśa grass.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, may the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans,
as well as all the fathers, mothers, maternal grandfathers, and others, be satisfied.
May this offering of water with sesame seeds reach the millions of ancestors of past generations who dwelt in the seven continents, and all the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather;
the mother, the grandmother, and likewise the great-grandmother.
To my maternal grandfather, his father, the great-grandfather, and the others—
may this piṇḍa offered by me reach them as an inexhaustible offering.
One should offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) at Gayāśiras, measuring only a fist, or the size of a fresh āmalaka fruit, or even the size of a śamī leaf;
thus one shall deliver seven lineages and uplift a hundred families.
The father, the mother, one's own wife, the sister, the daughter, the father’s sister, and the mother’s sister—these seven are proclaimed as the lineages (gotras). 2.48.26.
Twenty-four, twenty, sixteen, and twelve;
indeed, the Rudras and the Vasus—these constitute one hundred and one lineages.
There is no invocation, no binding of the directions, and no fault arising from one's gaze;
the wise should not perform a *śrāddha* at a sacred ford out of mere compassion. (2.48.28)

The offering of the rice-ball, the gift of the rice-balls, the subsequent rinsing of the hands, the sacrificial fee, and the formal dedication of the food—this is the procedure for Śrāddhas performed at sacred fords (tīrtha). 2.48.29.
"Those who have died in my family and for whom no destination is known—
I shall summon them all here upon the surface of the darbha grass with water mixed with sesame seeds."
I shall invoke with water mixed with sesame seeds upon the surface of darbha grass all those who belong to my circle of kinsmen and family, and those whose destination is unknown. 2.48.31.
With these mantras, while possessing meditative concentration, one should invoke the ancestors upon darbha grass with water and sesame seeds,
worship them, and offer them the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) in due order.
For the sake of the deliverance of those who have died in my family and for whom no destination is known, I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
And for those in my maternal grandfather’s family who have no known destination, I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa) for the sake of their deliverance. || 2.48.34 ||
For those who belong to my circle of kinsmen and family, and for those whose destination is unknown—for the sake of their deliverance, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa). || 2.48.35 ||
For the sake of the deliverance of all those who have not yet cut their teeth and those who were afflicted while in the womb, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
To those who were cremated by fire, as well as others who were not cremated,
and to those killed by lightning or thieves— to them I offer this funeral cake.
To those who died in forest fires, and those killed by lions or tigers,
or by fanged beasts or horned animals— to them I offer this funeral cake.
To those who died by hanging, those killed by poison or weapons,
and those who committed suicide— to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
To those who have perished from hunger or thirst in the wilderness, on the road, or in the forest,
and to those [afflicted] by spirits, ghosts, and piśācas— to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
For the sake of the deliverance of those who have gone to Raurava, Andhatāmisra, and Kālasūtra, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
For the sake of the deliverance of those who have gone to the terrible Asipatravana and the Kumbhīpāka hells, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
For the sake of the deliverance of those who have gone to the worlds of the hungry ghosts, existing in various states of torment, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
To those who have been led by the servants of Yama to undergo manifold torments, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the sake of their deliverance. 2.48.44.
For the sake of delivering those who dwell in all the hells and amidst the various torments, I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
To those who have entered the womb of animals, and to the birds, insects, and reptiles,
or those existing in the form of trees— to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
To those who, wandering through thousands of different births by their own karma,
have found this human state so difficult to attain— to them I offer this funeral cake.
To the ancestors and kinsmen dwelling in heaven, the intermediate space, and on earth,
and to those who have died without having received the funeral rites— to them I offer this rice-ball.
Whatever ancestors of mine exist in the form of pretas, may they all forever attain satisfaction through this funeral cake (piṇḍa). 2.48.49.
"Whether they were non-relatives or relatives, or those who were my relatives in another birth—may this pinda offered by me reach them and remain inexhaustible. (2.48.50)
Those who have died in the paternal lineage, those who have died in the maternal lineage,
and those other kinsmen of the teacher, the father-in-law, and relatives who have passed away.

Those in my family for whom the funeral offerings have been interrupted, those deprived of fathers and wives, those whose rites have been neglected, as well as those born blind and the lame; ||| 2.48.52 |||
May this funeral cake offered by me reach those in my family who were deformed, those who died in the womb, and those known or unknown; may it remain inexhaustible for them.
Those who are born in my paternal lineage up to Brahmā, as well as those born in my maternal lineage;
those who have been servants in both families, as well as employees and dependents. (2.48.54)

Friends, disciples, animals, and trees—both those seen and those unseen who have rendered me assistance, and those with whom I was associated in other births—to them I offer this *svadhā* and the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*). (2.48.55)
Having combined all these mantras ending in the feminine gender,
one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) as before, for women, in the order beginning with the mother.

Whether within one's own lineage or another's, if the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) by husband and wife is not performed separately, the Śrāddha rite, the cake-offering, and the water-libation are all fruitless. (2.48.57)
Having placed sesame seeds in the alms-bowl and filled it with pure water,
having sprinkled it three times over all [the offerings], one should conclude by prostrating.
Having dismissed the ancestors and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should cause the gods to hear as witnesses:
"May the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Īśāna, be my witnesses;
having reached Gayā, I have performed the rite of expiation for my ancestors. (2.48.59)
"I have come to Gayā, O Lord Gadādhara, for the sake of the ancestral rites;
you alone are my witness, O Blessed One, that I am now free from the three debts."
O Nārada, in all such places, one should offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa);
beginning from the Pretaparvata, one should perform this in due order at the sacred fords (tīrthas).
Then, O divine sage, one should cast barley-meal mixed with sesame seeds upon the mountain of the departed (Pretaparvata),
wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder and facing the south.
Whatever ancestors of mine exist in the form of pretas, may they all attain satisfaction through these barley-meals mixed with sesame seeds. 2.48.63.
"May everything that exists, moving and unmoving, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, attain satisfaction in every way through this water given by me. (2.48.64)
O Nārada, his ancestors shall be liberated from the state of being a preta;
by his greatness, the state of being a preta shall not arise again in his lineage.
On the peak of Gayā, there is a place known by the name Pretaśilā for the sake of liberation;
and there resides Ādigadādhara in the form of sacred sites, mantras, and so forth.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the glorious Vāyu Purāṇa, as proclaimed by Vāyu. ||48||
Sanatkumāra said:
First, regarding the procedure at the five sacred fords (pañcatīrtha) and at Uttaramānasa:
having sipped water (ācamya) with kusha grass in hand, one should sprinkle water upon the head. || 2.49.1 ||
One should go to Uttaramānasa and perform the ritual bath with this mantra:
"I perform the bath at Uttaramānasa for the purification of the self. (2.49.2)
For the sake of attaining the perfected state in the world of the Sun and other realms, and for the liberation of one's ancestors,
one should first satiate the gods and others, and then perform the Śrāddha rite accompanied by the offering of rice-balls (sapiṇḍaka).
For there is indeed the Mānasa lake here; therefore it is called Uttaramānasa.
Having bowed to and worshipped the Sun, one shall lead one’s ancestors to the world of the Sun. ||2.49.4||
Homage to the Blessed Lord, the Sustainer, who takes the forms of the Moon, Mars, and Mercury; who manifests as Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu. 2.49.5
From the Northern Mānasa, the silent sage should go to the Southern Mānasa;
it is called the Northern Tīrtha, where the northern [practice] bestows liberation.
Having bathed here, a human being goes to heaven in his own physical body.
In the midst [of it] is the sacred ford Kanakhala, renowned throughout the three worlds;
having bathed there, a man shines like gold and attains purity.
And on its southern side is the sacred ford Dakṣiṇamānasa;
from this, the unsurpassed sacred ford known as Kanakhala became famous in the world. ||2.49.8||
In the Dakṣiṇa-mānasa, three sacred fords (tīrtha) are proclaimed;
having bathed in them according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the śrāddha ceremony separately for each.
I perform my bath in the southern Mānasa lake for the purification of the self,
for the attainment of perfection in the worlds of the Sun and others, and for the liberation of my ancestors.
O Sun, for the sake of liberation from the torments of the flood of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin,
I perform my bath here at Dakṣiṇamānasa.
I bow to Sūrya for the satisfaction of the ancestors and for their deliverance, and for the increase of sons, grandsons, wealth, sovereignty, longevity, and health. 2.49.12.

Having performed the ritual bathing, worship, and other rites, and having performed the *śrāddha* ceremony with the *sapiṇḍana* rite, one should bow down to Maunī Arka and recite this mantra: || 2.49.13 ||
From there, one should go to Phalgutīrtha, the most excellent among all holy places;
through the performance of śrāddha there, liberation is always attained by both the performers and their ancestors.
Requested by Brahmā, Viṣṇu indeed became Phalguka in ancient times;
the dust offered there into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire became the Phalgutīrtha.
In that place, even a weak cow bears fruit, as does water and the earth;
for because it has entered the range of sight, the Phalgutīrtha is never fruitless.
All the sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist throughout all the worlds come together with the gods to bathe at Phalgutīrtha.
The Gaṅgā is the water for washing Viṣṇu’s feet, while the Phalgu is where the wielder of the mace (Viṣṇu) himself resides;
therefore, they know the Gaṅgā to be superior.
One who might perform a thousand times a thousand horse-sacrifices does not obtain that fruit which one obtains at Phalgutīrtha.
At Phalgutīrtha, in the waters of Viṣṇu, I perform this bath with reverence,
for the sake of the ancestors' attainment of Viṣṇu’s world and for the accomplishment of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having bathed at Phalgutīrtha, a person should perform libations and the Śrāddha rite along with the offering of the piṇḍas, as prescribed by his own Sūtra; he should then bow down to Pitāmaha.
Salutation to the auspicious God, to Īśa, to Puruṣa,
to Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta, and to Śambhu.
Having bathed at Phalgutīrtha and beheld the god Gadādhara,
a man shall immediately deliver himself, as well as ten ancestors and ten descendants.
Having bowed to the god Gadādhara, one should worship him with this mantra:
"Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva, and salutations to Saṅkarṣaṇa. (2.49.24)

Having bathed at Pañcatīrtha for Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Śrīdhara, and Viṣṇu, a man leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā. This bath with the five nectars (amṛtas), adorned with flowers, garments, and other offerings, [is prescribed].
He who does not perform it for the wielder of the mace, his Śrāddha is fruitless.
From Nāgakūṭa, Gṛdhrakūṭa, and the northern Mānasa, this is declared to be Gayāśiras; that is called Phalgutīrtha. 2.49.27.
Below Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is the unsurpassed Phalgutīrtha;
here, by means of śrāddha and other rites, all the ancestors attain liberation.
The procedure for the first day has been declared; on the second day, one should go to Dharmāraṇya, where Dharma performed a sacrifice.
O Nārada, by going there, the attainment of the world of Brahmā certainly occurs for one who,
having bathed in the Mataṅga-vāpī, performs libations and the śrāddha rite.
Having gone and bowed to Mataṅgeśa, one should recite this mantra:
"May the deities be my authority, and may the guardians of the world be my witnesses. (2.49.31)
Having come here to this Mataṅga, I have performed the expiation for my ancestors;
for previously, one should perform the Śrāddha and other rites at the Brahma-tīrtha in the well. ||2.49.32||
Between that well and the sacrificial post, he delivers all his ancestors;
having bowed to Dharma and the Lord of Dharma, he should pay homage to the Great Bodhi Tree. 2.49.33.
Salutations to you, O King of the Aśvattha tree, whose self is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
to the Bodhi tree, which delivers both doers and ancestors.
May those kinsmen of ours in our maternal lineage who have fallen into a miserable state attain the eternal heavenly realm through seeing you and by your touch.
"O King of Trees, having come to Gayā, I have discharged my three debts;
by your grace, I am liberated from the ocean of worldly existence and from great sin. (2.49.36)

Having bathed in the third Brahma-lake and having performed the Śrāddha rite with the Piṇḍas according to all requirements, by means of the mantra, and in accordance with the prescribed rule, O son, || 2.49.37 ||
I perform my ablutions at this sacred ford for the sake of liberation from the three debts;
it leads one’s ancestors to the world of Brahmā between that well and the sacrificial post.
Having performed a sacrifice, the sacrificial post (yūpa) arose; it was designated as "the sacrificial post" by Brahmā.
Having performed the Śrāddha at the Brahma-lake, one delivers all one's ancestors.
By circumambulating the sacrificial post (yūpa) clockwise, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
and by bowing down to Brahmā, one leads one's ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Salutations be to Brahman, the unborn, whose nature is the birth and other states of the universe;
salutations again and again to the savior of devotees and of the ancestors. 2.49.41.
The mango trees situated near the cow-pasture were established by Brahmā;
by merely watering them, the ancestors attain liberation. ||2.49.42||
I sprinkle this mango tree, which has arisen from the Brahma-lake, which consists of the deity Brahmā,
and which is the very form of Viṣṇu, for the sake of the liberation of the ancestors.
A lone sage, with a water-pot and the tips of kuśa grass in his hand, pours water at the root of a mango tree;
the mango tree is watered and the ancestors are satisfied—this single act is renowned for accomplishing two purposes. (2.49.44)
Then, with self-restraint, one should offer the bali-offering to Yama with this mantra:
"O King Yama and Dharmarāja, you who are established for the sake of the immutable! (2.49.45)
I offer an oblation to those two for the sake of the liberation of the ancestors;
thereafter, O Nārada, one should give the dog-oblation with this mantra.
To the two dogs, Śyāma and Śabala, born of the lineage of Vaivasvata, I offer this oblation; may they protect me always upon the path.
Then, O Nārada, one should offer the *kākabali* with this mantra:
"To those belonging to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama, and likewise to those of Nirṛti. (2.49.48)
"May the crows accept the rice-ball offered upon the ground;
then, on the fourth day at Phalgu-tīrtha, one should perform the ritual bath and other rites. (2.49.49)
Then, one should perform the *śrāddha* rite with the *sapiṇḍa* offerings at Gayāśiras;
there, Gayāśiras itself is present in person, established within the Phalgu-tīrtha.
[It is situated] north of Nāga, Janārdana, Brahma-yūpa, and Uttara-mānasa.
This is declared to be Gayāśiras; it is called Phalgutīrtha.
Having reached Pitāmaha as far as Uttaramānasa,
one should know that Phalgutīrtha is difficult to attain even for the gods.
From Krauñcapāda as far as Phalgutīrtha is the actual Gayāśiras;
this is the mouth of the demon Gaya, and therefore a śrāddha performed here is inexhaustible.
Directly below Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is that Phalgutīrtha,
where the primordial Lord Gadādhara resides, manifesting himself in both manifest and unmanifest forms.
In the form of the station of Viṣṇu and the other gods, it serves as the cause of liberation for the ancestors;
this divine station of Viṣṇu destroys sin through its mere sight.
Whether by touching it or even by worshipping it, that which is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible;
having performed the Śrāddha with the offering of rice-balls (sapiṇḍaka), one delivers a thousand members of one's own lineage.
Having performed a śrāddha, a man shall lead his hundred generations of kin to the divine station of Viṣṇu— endless, auspicious, and imperishable— and to the station of Rudra.
Likewise, by himself, that man leads his ancestors to the city of Śiva and to the station of Brahman; having uplifted a hundred generations of his lineage, he leads them to the world of Brahmā.
One who performs a śrāddha at the footprint of Kaśyapa leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā;
one who performs a śrāddha at the footprint of Dakṣiṇāgni leads his ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
By performing a śrāddha at the site of the Gārhapatya fire, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
by performing a śrāddha at the Āhavanīya fire, one obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having performed a śrāddha at the site of the Sabhya fire, one obtains the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice;
one who performs a śrāddha at the site of the Āvasathya fire leads the ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
Having performed a śrāddha at Śakrapada, one leads the ancestors to the world of Indra;
having performed a śrāddha at Agastyapada, the performer of the śrāddha leads the ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
One who performs the śrāddha at Krauñca and Mātaṅga leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā;
one who performs the śrāddha at Sūryapada leads five sinners to the city of the Sun.
One who performs a śrāddha at the station of Kārttikeya leads his ancestors to the world of Śiva;
one who performs a śrāddha at the station of Gaṇeśa leads his ancestors to the world of Rudra.
One who performs the libation with Gajakarṇa water leads his ancestors to heaven;
furthermore, by performing a Śrāddha at the site of others, the performer of the rite leads his ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
O Viṣṇu, the station of Rudra is indeed the best of all;
and the station of Brahmā is also proclaimed there as the most excellent. (2.49.66)
O Nārada, at both the commencement and the conclusion of those [rites], the recollection of any one of them is remembered as being conducive to the welfare of the performer of the śrāddha.
Long ago, at the divine site of Kaśyapa, the sage Bhāradvāja,
having performed the śrāddha ceremony, was prepared to offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to his ancestors and others.
Then two hands, one white and one black, emerged after breaking through the ground;
seeing those two hands there, the sage fell into doubt.
Then that great sage questioned his mother Śāntā:
"In which of Kaśyapa’s divine feet—on the white or the black part of the hand? (2.49.70)
"O mother, the funeral cake (piṇḍa) must be offered by me; tell me who the father is. Śāntā said:
"O highly wise Bhāradvāja, offer the funeral cake to Kṛṣṇa."
Then Bhāradvāja prepared to offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to Kṛṣṇa;
thereupon the invisible Śveta said, "For you are my own legitimate son."
Kṛṣṇa said, "My field is mine; therefore, give me the funeral cake.
Then the wanton woman spoke of giving it to both the owner of the field and the sower of the seed. 2.49.73.
Then Bhāradvāja offered the funeral cake at the station of Kaśyapa;
both of them went to the world of Brahmā by means of a celestial chariot yoked with swans.

As Rāma was intent on offering the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) at the *śrāddha* for the station of Rudra, his father Daśaratha emerged from heaven, extending his hand. Rāma did not give the cake into that hand; instead, he gave it at the station of Rudra.
Fearing that Rāma might transgress the meaning of the scriptures, Daśaratha spoke to him.
"O son, I have been delivered by you; may I attain the world of Rudra.
By the offering of this funeral cake (piṇḍa) into your hand, there shall indeed be no further rebirth for me in heaven. || 2.49.77 ||
And you, having ruled and protected the kingdom for a long time, and having performed sacrifices with liberal gifts for the twice-born and the subjects, shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having spoken thus, Daśaratha went to the supreme realm of Rudra, together with the people of Ayodhyā and even with the worms and insects.
Bhīṣma, having summoned his own father to the preeminent Viṣṇupada,
performed a śrāddha ceremony and prepared to offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to his ancestors and others.
When his father Śantanu’s hands had emerged at Gayāśiras, Bhīṣma offered the funeral cake (piṇḍa) into his hand; thereafter, he gave it at Viṣṇupada.

Śāntanu, being well-pleased, said: "Since you are unwavering in the meaning of the scriptures, may you possess the vision of the three periods of time; and at the end, Viṣṇu shall be your refuge. (2.49.82)
Having said, "Let death come by my own will," he attained liberation;
[he visited] Kanakeśa, Kedāra, Nārasiṃha, and Vāmana.
Having performed worship on the northern path, one shall deliver all the ancestors;
he who offers funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at Gayāśiras in their names [achieves this]. || 2.49.84 ||
Those dwelling in hell go to heaven, and those dwelling in heaven attain liberation,
he who offers a funeral cake at Gayāśiras even the size of a Śamī leaf.
Or one may offer roots, tubers, fruits, and the like; thus one leads the ancestors to heaven.
Wherever footprints of Viṣṇu and others are seen, [one should offer there] in front of them. (2.49.86)
Having performed the Śrāddha rite and the Sapiṇḍana ceremony, one leads the ancestors to their worlds;
everywhere, Mount Mūkapṛṣṭha is well-marked by these footprints.
All the ancestors went to the healthy world of Brahmā;
for the head of the asura Heti had been split in two by the mace.
Because it was washed there, that sacred ford (tīrtha) is known as Gadālola, the most excellent of all, leading to liberation. || 2.49.89 ||
At the great tirtha Gadālole, by virtue of Hari’s washing of his mace, I perform this bath for the sake of spiritual perfection; may I attain the imperishable state. (2.49.90)
On the fifth day, at Gadālola, having bathed, one should perform the sapindikarana rite;
such a śrāddha leads the ancestors to the world of Brahmā, as well as oneself.

One should worship the Brahmins ordained by Brahmā with offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya) and so forth; when they are satisfied, all the deities together with the ancestors are gratified. 2.49.92.
When a śrāddha has been performed with effort at the Akṣaya-vaṭa tree, one leads the ancestors to the eternal and imperishable world of Brahmā by means of that very food. 2.49.93.
But near a banyan tree, even by feeding a single Brahmin with vegetables or water, ten million have been fed. (2.49.94)
The sixteen-fold gift should be given by the sons with great effort, having properly worshipped the priest of the Gayā-tīrtha with garments, perfumes, and other offerings. 2.49.95.
Whatever is given to the ancestors at Gayātīrtha and Vaṭa becomes inexhaustible;
having seen, bowed to, and worshipped Vaṭeśa with a well-concentrated mind. || 2.49.96 ||
One leads the ancestors to the eternal and imperishable world of Brahmā by [offering] at Gayā,
at Dharmapṛṣṭha, and likewise at the lake of Brahmā.
What is given to the ancestors at Gayāśīrṣa and at the banyan tree (Vaṭa) becomes inexhaustible;
for he who lies at the foot of the banyan tree during the single ocean of dissolution, absorbed in yogic sleep—‖ 2.49.98‖
Salutations to you who assume the form of a child, who lie in the state of Yoga, who are the weapon against the tree of worldly existence, and who remove all sins without exception. 2.49.99.
Salutations to the giver of imperishable Brahman and to the eternal Banyan tree;
because in the Kali age the worlds belong to Maheśvara, Gadādhara assumed the form of a Liṅga—I bow to that, my venerable great-grandfather. (2.49.100) 111.83
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the glorious Vāyu Purāṇa, as proclaimed by Vāyu. 49.
Sanatkumāra said: King Gaya performed a sacrifice with abundant food and many sacrificial fees, wherein it was impossible to calculate the number of the collections of materials. || 2.50.1 ||
Twenty-five mountains, beginning with Annādi, are situated at Gayā;
there, the twice-born ones, being highly honored, offer their praise in every region. 2.50.2.
Neither have any performed it before, nor will others do so in the future—just as the sands in the world or the stars in the sky [are beyond counting]. (2.50.3)
Likewise, there have been countless sacrificial fees consisting of much gold and other riches;
neither those of the past nor others yet to come shall ever equal this here.
Satisfied and highly honored in every land, the twice-born praised him;
and Viṣṇu and the other gods, being pleased, said to Gaya, "Choose a boon. || 2.50.5 ||
Gaya then made this prayer for those who had been cursed by Brahmā in the past: "May these twice-born ones become purified and honored at the sacrifice. (2.50.6)
For the performance of the śrāddha at Gayā, there are fourteen twice-born ones who are like personified forms;
even if Brahmā himself were present, he would carry out their word. (2.50.7)
Gautama, Kāśyapa, Kautsa, Kauśika, and Kaṇva;
Bhāradvāja, Auśanasa, Vātsya, and likewise Pārāśara. ||2.50.8||
Haritkumāra, Māṇḍavya, Lokākṣi, Lokasaṃgraha, Vāsiṣṭha, and likewise Ātreya—these are their fourteen lineages (gotras). 2.50.9.
"May this city be known by my name as Gayāpurī, just as Brahmapurī is renowned.
Having granted this boon, "So be it," the gods then vanished.
Having enjoyed his pleasures, Gaya went to the supreme realm of Viṣṇu.
In Viśālā, there was a king named Viśāla who, being childless, spoke to the twice-born.
"How may I have sons and other blessings? the twice-born asked him;
"By offering the funeral cakes at Gayā, all this shall be yours," he replied. (2.50.12)
Although Viśāla had offered the funeral cakes at Gayāśīrṣa, he remained childless;
seeing three men in the sky—white, red, and black—he spoke to them.
"Who are you? he asked them, and to Viśālaka, one of them who was white, he said:
"I am your father, Śveta; I have come here from the world of Indra. (2.50.14)
"My son's father was a killer of Brahmins, a great evildoer who was red with passion;
this grandfather of mine, O Kṛṣṇa, is the one by whom the sages were slaughtered. (2.50.15)
They reached the Avīci hell, but were liberated through the offering of your funeral cakes—
to your father, grandfather, and likewise your great-grandfather.
"O subduer of enemies, O best of beings, because of those words 'I shall gratify you' which were spoken by you when this water was given, our union has occurred simultaneously. (2.50.17)
"Liberation has been achieved by you, my son; we shall go to the highest heaven.
In this manner, the supreme liberation for the ancestors must be performed by their sons.
And you, having ruled the kingdom for a long time and enjoyed pleasures difficult to obtain,
and having performed sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees, shall thereafter go to the city of Viṣṇu.
Thus, having obtained the boon, the king ruled his kingdom and ascended to heaven;
the king of the pretas, along with the pretas, ascended to heaven by virtue of the śrāddha performed at Gayā.
A certain preta, for the sake of liberation, spoke to a merchant:
"Perform the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) at Gayāśīrṣa in my name. (2.50.21)
"For the sake of liberation from the state of a preta, please accept my wealth;
taking all that wealth, perform the śrāddha rites at Gayā."
I have indeed given you sixteen-fifths [of the kingdom],
and I have duly and correctly declared my names to you according to the rule.
Having gone to Gayā and Gayāśīrṣa, he offered a funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the King of the Dead, and then,
together with his kinsmen, he gave offerings to his own ancestors.
A deceased person, liberated from the state of being a ghost, returns to his own home like a merchant;
so too at the sacred field of Gaya, and likewise of Śambhu, Viṣṇu, and Ravi.
Then, having fasted at the Gāyatrī-tīrtha situated on the Mahānadī river, [one attains this].
Having bathed before the Gāyatrī, one should perform the morning twilight devotion (prātaḥsandhyā).

Having performed the Śrāddha ceremony with the offering of rice-balls (sapiṇḍaka), a man should lead his family to devotion toward Brahman after bathing at the confluence of sacred waters in front of Sāvitrī.
Having performed the midday twilight worship, one should lead a hundred generations of one's lineage to heaven;
thereafter, one should perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) for the ancestors with the desire for their liberation.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rites at the Prācīsarasvatī tīrtha and performed the evening twilight devotions (sandhyā), one leads one's ancestors to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having been liberated from the omission of the twilight prayers committed over many lifetimes, he performed the three daily rites at the Lelihāna Tīrtha in Viśālā and at Bharata’s hermitage.
At Muṇḍapṛṣṭha marked by his footprints, near Gadādhara,
at the Ākāśagaṅgā tīrtha, and at the mouths of the Gari rivers.
Having bathed and then offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), one leads a hundred generations of one's lineage to the world of Brahmā;
having bathed in the celestial river Vaitaraṇī, one leads one's ancestors to heaven.
One who bathes in the Vaitaraṇī becomes a giver of cows and shall uplift twenty-one generations of his kin;
this is the truth, the truth, and again the truth regarding the Vaitaraṇī, O Nārada.
They say that twenty-one generations are saved; of this there is no doubt. That river which is named Vaitaraṇī is renowned throughout the three worlds.
She descended indeed into the field of Gaya for the sake of the liberation of her ancestors,
as well as into the Godāvarī, the Vaitaraṇī, and likewise the Yamunā.
One who offers the śrāddha at Devanadī, Gopracāra,
Puṣkariṇī, Ghṛtakulyā, or likewise Madhukulyā shall lead his ancestors to heaven.
At Koṭitīrtha, one who offers the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to Rukmiṇī leads his ancestors to heaven,
solely by fasting for three nights and by visiting that sacred site.
By not giving gold and cattle, a man is born poor;
[but by giving them, he obtains] a stream of ghee, a stream of honey, and the great river Devikā.
Where the confluence of the Śilā is celebrated as Madhusravā,
a man who performs an ablution there obtains the merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices.
Having performed the Śrāddha ceremony with the offering of the Piṇḍas,
a man shall uplift a hundred generations of his lineage and lead them to the world of Viṣṇu.
One who offers funeral cakes at Daśāśvamedhika, Haṃsatīrtha, Cāmarakaṅkaṭa,
Koṭitīrtha, and Rukmakuṇḍa leads his ancestors to heaven.
Having bathed in the Vaitaraṇī, in the stream of clarified butter, and likewise in the stream of honey, and having seen Koṭīśvara after bathing at Koṭitīrtha; || 2.50.42 ||
One may become a Brahmin for ten million births, wealthy and a master of the Vedas;
by bowing to Mārkaṇḍeyeśa and Koṭīśa, one becomes a savior of one's ancestors.
In ancient times, Śaṅkara sported in secret with Pārvatī in the Pārijāta grove for ten thousand yugas.
Marīci went to the Pārijāta grove for the sake of its fruits and flowers;
having seen [the Lord there], he was cursed by Maheśa because he had obstructed his pleasure.
Fearing that he might become miserable, Marīci praised Śiva;
being pleased, Śambhu said to him, "Choose an excellent boon."
"May my liberation come from the curse," Marīci said to Śaṅkara;
"Your liberation shall be at Gayā," Śiva declared, and he went to Gayā. (2.50.47)
Standing upon a stone, he performed penance that was difficult for all to accomplish;
in ancient times, Marīci, having been cursed by Īśvara, attained a state of blackness. 2.50.48.
Through fierce austerity in this world, that brahmin attained whiteness;
Hari said to Marīci, "O son, choose a boon."
"What is unattainable when you are pleased? Marīci said to Mādhava:
"May I be released from the curse of Hara, and may this stone become purifying;
may it also bring about the liberation of my ancestors. Having said, "So be it," he departed for heaven.
Having reached the lotus pond of the celestial dwellers, the pure man—
Wherever an offering given to the ancestors becomes indeed inexhaustible, there a man who has bathed goes to heaven in his own body. (2.50.52)
He casts off his evil, just as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin;
that holy lotus grove is frequented by those who perform meritorious deeds.
"There indeed lies the Pāṇḍuśilā rock, where a śrāddha becomes inexhaustible;
O sage, Yudhiṣṭhira went there to perform a śrāddha. (2.50.54)
At that time, Pāṇḍu said, "Give the funeral cake (piṇḍa) into my hand.
Having released his hand, he placed the offering of the cake upon a stone. || 2.50.55 ||
Delighted by the offering of the funeral cake upon the stone, the son of Vyāsa granted a boon to his own son: "Rule the kingdom upon the surface of the earth."
"O son, you have indeed protected me completely and without thorn;
go now to heaven quickly, surrounded by your brothers. (2.50.57)
"By the mere sight of you, lead those dwelling in hell who are completely purified to heaven.
Having spoken thus, Pāṇḍu departed for the eternal, imperishable state.
Whether born from sprouts, born from sweat, born from eggs, or born from a womb—
having reached Madhusravā, even those who had died went to the city of heaven.
By performing a śrāddha at Daśāśvamedhika and Haṃsatīrtha, one shall go to heaven;
and by bowing to both Daśāśvamedha and Haṃsa, one shall go to the city of Śiva.
One who performs a śrāddha at Bharata’s hermitage leads the ancestors to the abode of Brahmā;
one who performs a śrāddha at Mataṅga’s footprint leads the ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Having churned the fire from within the womb of the *śamī* tree, Brahmā, together with Viṣṇu and the others,
obtained a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) renowned throughout the three worlds for the purpose of sacrifice.
That sacred ford is known as Makha, which bestows liberation upon the ancestors;
having bathed there and performed the libations, one who offers the funeral cakes shall attain liberation.
By bowing to Aṅgārakeśvara at the confluence, one leads one's ancestors to heaven;
by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at Gayākūṭa, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having bowed to the Lord at Bhasmakūṭa with ashes, one shall deliver one's ancestors;
freed from sin and liberated, one should perform a bath at the confluence.
Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, performed a sacrifice known as the Aśvamedha. Upon the completion of the sacrifice, Śambhu emerged and said to Vasiṣṭha, "Choose a boon."
Vasiṣṭha also said to him, "O Śiva, if you are pleased with me, you must dwell here, O Lord of Gods. Having said, "So be it," Śiva remained there.
By offering funeral cakes at Dhenukāraṇya and at the sites of the Kāmadhenu,
and having bathed, bowed, and performed worship there, one leads one's ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed at Kardamāla, Gayānābhi, and near Muṇḍapṛṣṭha,
and having performed the śrāddha and other rites, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
One should worship Phalgucaṇḍī, Śmaśānākṣī, Maṅgalā, and the others;
and by the ritual release of a bull at Gayā, one shall deliver twenty-one generations of one's lineage.
Wherever they may be situated, even the gods and sages who have conquered their senses meditate upon the primordial Gadādhara by means of offerings such as funeral cakes and ancestral oblations.
Having uplifted a hundred generations of his lineage, he shall lead his ancestors to the world of Brahmā;
for Gayā, Gaya, Gayāditya, Gāyatrī, and Gadādhara [are all present there].
Gayā, Gayāsura, and the six Gayās are the bestowers of liberation.
That man who constantly recites this meritorious narrative of Gayā [attains the highest goal]. (2.50.73)
He who listens with faith attains the supreme goal;
or that meritorious man who causes the narrative called Gaya to be recited for the Brahmins.

By him the Gayā-śrāddha has been performed; by him it has certainly been performed, O Nārada—whoever, being composed, studies the greatness of Gayā. By him the Rājasūya and the Aśvamedha have been sacrificed.
One should write it oneself, or cause it to be written, or even worship the book.
In his home, prosperity shall remain firm and well-pleased.
This meritorious narrative shall abide in the house as long as this book remains there.
No fear arising from snakes, fire, or thieves exists there for one who recites this supreme majesty of Gayā at the time of a śrāddha ceremony. (2.50.78)
Even if performed deficient in ritual rules, all that is equal for the ancestors to Gayā itself.
Whatever sacred fords exist in the three worlds, they are indeed seen there;
O Sage, by whomsoever the narrative of Gayā has been known, heard, or recited.
Sūta said:

Having then related this meritorious story with devotion to that bull among sages, Sanatkumāra took leave of the master of music and departed for his own hermitage, which was endowed with sacred groves. 2.50.80; 112.68.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Gayā," in the glorious Mahāpurāṇa proclaimed by Vāyu. ||50||
This Vāyupurāṇa is completed.
